If you noticed the picture of the packaging, there are two asterisks aka a catch. On the back of the packaging it reads: **Reads speeds from drive to computer up to 150MB/s. Write speeds lower and varies by capacity. USB 3.0 port required. Based on internal testing; performance may be lower depending upon host device. This isn't an issue for me as one cannot expect every device to perform as advertised. There will always be a limiting variable preventing you from ever reaching max advertised speeds. People need to understand this. Your old Galaxy S3 micro USB port (for example) will not push this drive to its limit. Onto the write/read speed test using H2testw. Using this drive on a USB 3.0 port and H2testw I was able to reach a peak of ~55MB/s write speeds at the start of the test. However that didn't last long and the drive steadily slowed down to 27.9MB/s 10min into the write test. At 1 hour, 25.7MB/s. When verifying the written data the drive peaked at 141MB/s. By the end of the test the drive stabilised at 103MB/s. I believe the drops are caused by thermal throttling of the drive, as it did it hot to the touch during testing. Please note, this isn't real world performance. H2testw is writing very large files, one at a time. Transferring photos will not reach these speeds as they are small files, the transfer speed will peak then drop back to zero before peaking at the next file. Transferring videos is similar to the test, as they are large files where the drive can ramp up to it's max possible speed. Again, depending on the host device and many other variables. H2testw is a free Windows utility that verifies the true capacity of the drive by writing "dummy files"; writing until the drive is full or "full". Then the utility reads them to verify the files, ideally the verify will complete without error. If it ends with an error it will show at what amount it ended. For example, if it ended at around 16GB but you purchased a 128GB; this simply means you received a counterfeit drive and should return the drive. If the test ended on an obscure number, the drive is faulty and needs replacing. The drive I received passed with a final capacity of ~117GB for the 128GB model. This is normal as some space is taken up by the MBR, the "library" of the drive where all your files locations are kept. This is how the host device knows what goes where, what is empty and what is not. There are two files already on the drive, a PDF manual and a APK file of SanDisks app for Android. I don't know why they bother including the APK as Android users would have to enable "Install from unknown sources" in their device settings. Just search for the app in the Play Store if enabling this makes your weary, although you can simply disable it right after you install the APK. But again, there's no point in the first place as the included app is probably outdated and will be updated by the Play Store soon after.

First the bad: This radio is not especially sensitive (to pick up weak stations) or selective (to separate close adjacent signals). The whip antenna is short, too short IMO, but it is certainly adequate. Now the good: It's relatively small and lightweight, well-built, no fancy electronics to fail but instead "old-fashioned" analog dials for volume and tuning and a mechanical switch for the three bands. The only "fancy" things are the solar cell and windup power - which work spectacularly. When I got the radio it already had some charge to the battery and would play, but I gave the wind-up lever 100 turns - three days later using it about 6 hours a day in only gloomy gray daylight for the solar cell, I finally noticed enough volume loss to give it another 100 turns. For the price this little radio is a really good value. I'm even liking the green color. Update: With little sun here, I've had to use only the wind-up handle. After a few days of use I find I need to give it 100 turns or so, for at least several hours of playing time. Not as good as when it first arrived but I'm still pleased. If you're only used to modern digital radios, yes, you may find it hard to tune at first, but it's fine for what it is - an inexpensive radio that never needs batteries, good for casual or emergency listening - not a DX machine, not hi-fi, not loud enough to blow the doors down, etc. etc.

I have a Brother HL-3140CW color laser printer. Our household was able to print via its WIFI interface for a couple of years. After which, the WIFI interface became intermittent and then failed completely. Since the printer still worked well via its USB interface, I researched print servers. I tried the IO Gear GPSU21 since there were many reviews. I'm happy to say that this unit allows all computers in our the house to share the Brother printer. I didn't give this unit a 5 star rating due to the installation process. The provided instructions (and the instructions downloaded from the IO Gear site) only provide guides for Windows XP/Vista and MAC. My PCs use Windows 7 and 10. Therefore, I had to guess my way through the process. After many failed attempts, I was about to return this product. After one final attempt, however, I finally got it to work. Once I got one PC to print, I got the remaining PCs (and MAC) to print quickly. My recommendation to others is to do the following: 1. Connect your printer to your PC via USB. 2. Install the latest printer driver software for you printer and ensure you can print. 3. In Control Panel, remove the printer (Note: the drivers will remain on the PC). 4. Connect your printer to the IO Gear GPSU21 and connect it to your network via Ethernet. 5. Download the latest IO Gear GPSU21 software and run the setup application. 6. Run the print server wizard application. 7. When asked to select a printer, you may see the printer you deleted (step 3). If so don't select it. Instead select add a printer. You will then be guided through multiple pages. 7a. Select local rather than network printer. 7b. Select LPT1 for port. 7c. Select your printer manufacturer, model and driver 7d. Select the printer in the list with LPT1 port. 7e. Do not share printer. 7f. Do not print a test page since the port setup won't be completed until after the summary page. 8. After this process you can now print from you PC. Setup will be painful the first time, but the print server does work and works well. Now when I print, the document shows up in the print queue only briefly before it prints. This is so much faster then the printer's original WIFI interface.

I tested this lens on a Sony a6000, the attached photos are unedited. I had been looking for a medium range lens to round out my standard array of prime lenses. Having used the Sigma 30mm I'd have to say I'm very happy with the purchase. The focal length and wide aperture provide a lot of flexibility for all types of shoots, ranging from portraits to landscapes. Seems to work well in bright light as well as low light situations, although I haven't tested the latter extensively. The lens is sharp on-center with limited falloff toward the edges. I haven't noticed any vignetting or color casting. There is a bit of chromatic aberration on bright reflections, but much less than on my Sony 50mm f1.8. The auto focus also works quickly and I'm satisfied with the construction of the lens. This kit with the added accessories is also nice, especially the inclusion of a couple filters of surprising quality. I've been using the polarizing filter quite a bit. There are a few negatives, but certainly nothing that would prevent me from buying this lens again. This lens can get very, very sharp with manual focus but AF leaves a bit of sharpness on the table, which I find a little annoying. Also, the colors aren't the most vibrant and I end up doing quite a bit of retouching.

This is a big improvement over my previous Nuvi 1450, and the best of the many Garmins I've owned. I only gave it 4 stars due to a few issues and difficulties which I've listed below. But overall I am quite pleased with the performance and features of this gps. Pros: The 7" screen is a perfect size with excellent resolution, contrast, and brightness. The touch screen has ideal sensitivity.......huge improvement over my old Nuvi. Most of the features are displayed logically and clearly. Navigating around the menus is quick and reasonably intuitive....most of the time. While navigating a route, the next turn is displayed at the top of the screen and the current road is at the bottom......perfect. The live traffic works well thru a bluetooth connection to a smartphone once set up. However set-up was not easy (see below) Voice Command works OK if there is little ambient noise. Out on a highway we had difficulty getting the GPS to understand. Cons: The display is glass which results in quite a bit of reflection if not looking at the screen head on. The traditional suction cup mount is as useless as ever. We opted for a mount inserted in our CD player, which works perfectly, especially since the touch screen requires such a light tap. The connection between the gps and the mount is a bit difficult to release with 1 hand. Would have preferred a magnetic mount. The set up of live traffic thru the smartphone was not intuitive at all. It was especially confusing that connection to the Smart Link app showed up as another paired device on the gps. Took me a lot of trial & error to make the Smart Link connection, but then disable the phone (I didn't want phone calls, texts etc coming thru the gps). And if you don't have the Smart Link app running on your phone at the time the gps turns on, you won't get traffic and won't know that you're not connected. (After a while I realized that I can quickly check the Smart Link connection on the gps by looking for the Smart Link symbol at the top of the main gps screen. Since my wife and I both use the same vehicle with the gps and each have our own phones, I tried to figure out an easy way to switch between phone pairings depending on who was using the car. The gps will automatically pair with the phone it was most recently paired with. That worked great as long as you only have 1 phone. When I paired the gps with both our phones, I expected the gps to connect with the secondary phone if the primary (last used) was out of range. Not happening. I couldn't figure out an easy way to switch phones without going thru several steps to unpair and re-pair the secondary phone; then close the Smart Link app and re-open it. So we'll just use the 1 phone unless we're desperate. And lastly, driver alerts might be helpful to some, but I found them just plain annoying (notifying me every time there's a curve in the road, school crossing, change in speed limit, etc. At least you can disable the audio alerts, but you can't stop the visual alerts popping up at the top of the screen. It sounds like a lot of negatives, but as I said initially, this is the best Garmin yet and we're very pleased with it.

I should say that I am a long term audio nut with a strong penchant for separates. Nonetheless, technology has evolved and this product has gotten glowing reviews (no surprise) from the youtube know it alls. I was looking for convenience and good to excellent sound quality. I did not get the latter and the former is not all it's cracked up to be. Getting them online went quickly, and the new KEF app is world's better than the two apps they put out for the LS50 wireless first gen model. However, the download of current firmware caused a system freeze, and multiple reboots of my phone and power cycling of the speakers were required to get it going. I used Spotify connect and the Spotify app found the speakers immediately and music was had! So, first thing is that any volume control of these speakers is software based. There are buttons on top of the primary speaker and you can use your phone but there is no way to program an "initial volume" so if your phone is at max volume when you connect to the speakers you will get a full blast of sound that cannot be good for your ears or the speakers. Also, the speakers are on your local network, and other devices like my Sony TV will find them and can "synch" with them, so when you turn on the TV you once again get a full blast of sound from the speakers. I was able to find a menu in the Sony to de activate the synch factor but be prepared for this with any products you have connected to your LAN. Lastly the sound quality. I hate this part because it's just my opinion and you know how that goes. However, I did compare to others, a pair of Revel 106be (much more expensive) and a pair of ELAC debut ref (much less expensive) and there was no comparison at all, the KEFs were completely out of their league compared to either of the other passive speakers. So take this for what it's worth but with no bias whatsoever I listened to these speakers and there was little detail, they sounded dull as if the noise/distortion was quite high. Perhaps the best "tell" was that I did not want to turn up the volume and did not want to continue listening, exactly the opposite of the response you should get with a good speaker. By all means try these if you value the convenience but for the price you can put together an excellent 2 channel setup with the only inconvenience being a few cables. A nice Yamaha integrated and a pair of ELAC debut ref speakers would be just one example. Check out audiosciencereview.com for product reviews and measurements that are actually unbiased and truly useful.

After having played around with this thing for a month, I must say I am very happy with my decision to buy this. Quite a few different selections out there in this price range and I ultimately decided to get this particular device based on the reviews. I picked up this bodycam as I work in a private security patrol unit in a major metropolitan area. The job has me going to some pretty sketchy places and dealing with some sketchy people so I wanted something to cover my rear in case I have to take action at a property. Very first thing I noticed when I took it out of the box was how solid the unit felt. There was no creaking, no rattling, no shaking, nothing. I've messed around with some coworkers' body cameras (from other manufacturers) before and most felt very cheap and fragile. Not the case here. It came with everything you needed to get it up and running: two types of clips, a data/charging cable, wall charger, and the paperwork needed to set it up. Admittedly I found the instructions somewhat confusing as they looked like they were written in another language and then tossed into a translator. Nevertheless, I was able to figure out the basic controls and then work through the remainder of the settings on my own. Some of my favorite features are the auto switching between daytime and night modes (off by default) and the pre-record function that attaches the previous 15 seconds of footage before you push the button to the video file. Very important feature to help provide some context to an incident prior to you starting to record. I would have loved to have had 30 seconds of pre-recording instead of 15 but that's just a me thing. The cool thing that I was not expecting is the pre-recorded footage also has sound for the duration of those 15 seconds, unlike some police-grade cameras you'll see out there that will only pre-record video without sound. The auto-switch between day and night modes has been working very well so far. Only thing is that the camera emits a noticeable click when it switches. Not really a deal breaker but working nights like I do and going back and forth between lit areas and dark areas, it can get a little annoying after a while. There are several video quality settings to choose from as well. I find myself running it on the 1080p30fps setting most often. I feel like this provides the best balance between video quality and file size. It's not a professional grade recording device by any stretch of the imagination but will do just fine in the majority of situations I could possibly think of encountering. One thing I was particularly worried about was the battery life of this unit. I am happy to say that by running it on standby for an 8-hour shift (on and pre-recording, not actively recording footage), I still have a good two-thirds of my battery left at the end. I still charge it up after every use but could easily see this lasting two or three shifts before needing to be recharged. Speaking of which, it charges easily and relatively quickly using the included cable and wall adapter. That being said, I usually set it to charge before going to bed after a shift and have yet to run the battery down to empty so I can't really comment on how long it takes to juice it back up. All I know is that it's ready to go when I wake up again and that's all I really care about. The clips were another point of concern for me when looking at all the different options out there. The connection point turned out to be pretty solid, with no movement between the camera and the clip when properly secured. The only issue I have with this mounting system is that the clips slide into a plastic bracket that is molded into the casing of the camera. If something happens and it snaps off, there is no way that the user would be able to replace or repair that bracket. I would have loved to see a mounting system that screws into the back or something else that could easily be replaced if broken off but no joy. I haven't had any issues with it so far though so hopefully it stays that way. The last thing I wanted to touch on was the display and controls. Although it is advertised as a one-touch system for the buttons, I found that double-pressing them tends to work a lot more reliably that a single press. Another issue I ran into was then when going through the menus to play back footage on the camera itself, it can sometimes start recording during that process. Somewhat annoying and I have had to basically power the unit down and then back up after playing recorded video just to make sure no weird stuff happens. It's a rare occurrence that I'm playing video back on the camera (I usually download the footage to my computer before viewing it) but something worth noting. After the restart, everything seems to work just fine. All in all, it's a solid choice if you're in the market for an affordable body camera. If you're looking to use this to record action sports or something, I would look elsewhere. For more professional applications, this is a great unit. I'm hoping I'll get a lot more use out of this but will definitely update this review if anything changes.

One of the worst experiences I have ever had. I purchased this PCI express card in hopes to take advantage of the USB 3.0 speeds offered by my newish external hard drive: [[ASIN:B004W7DR02 Hitachi Touro Desk Pro 3 TB USB 3.0 External Hard Drive (HTOLDNB30001BBB)]]. I've had the hard drive for about a month and it's been working very nicely but it saturates USB 2.0 (hits about 38Mbps and stays there, which is about the limits of USB 2.0 after signaling overhead is accounted for). I followed the Sonnet instructions exactly. First, install the PCI card in either slots 3 or 4. I put it in slot 3 because slot 4 has a raid card in it. It took two power cycles for the computer to boot upon installing it (hung fist time, not a good sign). Then, I downloaded the drivers from the sonnet website, loaded them without incident. Computer rebooted no problem. Powered off, plugged in the Hitachi drive into one of the USB 3.0 slots, computer would not boot, just powered up to a white screen and sat there after several attempts. Unplugged the USB connection and the computer once again rebooted. Here's where it gets interesting. With the computer now running, I then plugged in the USB into the Sonnet port and the drive actually shows up. But guess what, now the Bluetooth stops working and my mouse disconnects. I discovered that the mouse would sort of work if I kept it right beside the computer. All the signs of electronic noise interfering with the blue-tooth radio waves, or perhaps it's something in the PCI express communication, but probably interference due to a major degradation in function as the mouse is moved away from the blue-tooth receiver. I moved the USB back to the MAC's 2.0 USB port and the problems vanished. Moved back, lost the blue-tooth connection. I tried re-seating the card, I tried both USB 3.0 slots, I tried power cycling the hard drive. If the computer had not hung so many times during this process, I would be inclined to fault the hard drive somehow. At this price point it makes me question this company. A complete waste of time for me.

Immediately after installing 2x8GB 3200MHz sticks, I started having random crashes and occasional blue screens of death. After a few days I made the connection and ran Memtest86 which would start showing errors almost immediately -- and sure enough, after trial-and-error with removing individual memory sticks, I narrowed the errors down to one of the sticks. Based on the memory addresses it seems that there was probably one faulty chip, but of course there is no way to replace one chip on the stick. Amazon's return process seems to have dropped me in a void somewhere (UPS marks the return as delivered, but Amazon's status is still "return started"). While I'm sure Amazon will eventually refund me, this has been a huge waste of time to discover a faulty DIMM (running memtest86 takes hours each time) and then have to replace it with something else.

The good: - Very easy to put together. I’d say the entire process took about 30 minutes. - Looks great. The stand looks sharp, does not LOOK to be too cheap. The especially concerning pieces are the bottom supports for each arm. I don’t have an exact measurement, but I’d say there is close to to 3/4 inch of lateral play. I’m assuming over time this will just get worse. - Varying spring strengths out of the box. The upper part of the arm which houses the springs seem to be set differently out of the box, or one of the arms is faulty. One of my monitors is heavier that the other. The arm with the lighter monitor droops vertically, and the pitch of the heavier monitor droops. -_- tried adjusting the spring to fix the vertical issue, but no luck. The ugly: - instructions for adjusting the spring arms are for a different model... For example, the pitch tension adjustment if on the side, but the instructions say they are on the top - Quality control. My last point is the single most unacceptable failing of this product. The package comes with set screws to lock the rotation of each joint in each arm. In the instructions it shows to use the provided Allen wrench to install the set screws. One slight problem, the set screws that were provided used a FLAT HEAD!! I do have several flat head screwdrivers, but a miss as glaring as that in the quality control process is laughable. Final Thoughts: - If the machining were done with less tolerance so there was less play in the arms, the springs were set similarly right out of the box, and the instructions and tools that came in the box were actually entirely relevant; this would get 4-5 stars from me.

I'm pretty discriminating as a music listener but don't consider myself an "audiophile". I've owned a LOT of different speakers in my days and played in bands, so I know a good bit about sound. If you're into sharp highs, clear midrange and thumping bass, save your money and buy something better. You're not going to get those attributes with any Sony speakers.

I bought this with much trepidation after reading about all the troubles people have had with DVD recorders. Maybe it helped that we're using this with a Samsung 4669 46" LCD TV, but I found it a snap to set up and start recording with it. I've only gotten one coaster, and while I can't recreate the circumstances that produced it, I have a hunch it was my fault--that I tried to make it do two things at once that I shouldn't have. Other than that one time it's just worked. I have an older, low end DVD player that couldn't read the disks, but all the newer DVD players I've tried do fine. Even my cheapo $500 Toshiba laptop recognizes the DVDs and plays them as well as it plays any DVDs (it lacks dedicated Video RAM so it can't play movies smoothly). I've read complaints about the manual, but it worked well enough for me. However, I'm a computer journalist who's been using/building/troublshooting computer systems since 1981, so what seems easy and obvious to me might be more opaque to a civilian. It also makes it easier if you have a DVR. We have one from Comcast that came with the digital TV service. So 99% of the time we're recording from that and not from the TV directly. Normally I blip ads by just fast-forwarding through them while the Samsung continues to record, but you can stop/restart the recording at each juncture to eliminate the ads. This creates a lot of files but they play in sequence automatically. Here's how you record a program off a DVR like Comcast's box: 1. stick a disk in the Samsung. If it's new a dialog box will pop up asking if you want to initialize the disk. Hit Enter on your remote. Initializing takes a few seconds. 1. pick your recording speed (it's the button on the remote labeled "rec speed"). As you toggle through the speeds, an onscreen display tells you how many minutes you have available at each speed. I generally use SP for standard programs, XP for HD ones (though I'm still not sure XP is necesssary), LP for longer shows I want to fit on one disk, and EP for talking heads programs (CSPAN, PBS etc.) where the lower resolution isn't a problem). 2. push the red "rec" button to start recording. If you push it again, it times the recording for 30 minutes, then stops. Hit this button again and it records for 60 minutes, and so forth. 3. If you aren't doing a timed recording, hit the "Stop" button to stop the recording. If you want to stop a timed recording, hit the "stop" button twice. 4. Label the track you just recorded by hitting the "title list disc menu" button. You can label tracks by highlighting the track you want to label, using the up/down arrow buttons, hit "Enter," then choose "Rename." You'll get an onscreen keyboard on which you can move the cursor around to select letters/symbols. If you move past the edge of the keyboard the cursor reappears on the opposite side. This makes typing labels a lot faster. Hit the onscreen button "Save" to save your entry. You can erase any/all of what you wrote, now or even after you've saved it. 5. When you've recorded everything you want on this disk, hit the "Menu" button, then choose "finalize." After a minute or so the disk is done and ready to be played on other DVD players. That doesn't sound hard, does it? Then for playback, you have various menu options to experiment with to get the best image on the screen you have. With the right options a DVD movie looks amazingly good on a good monitor like our Samsung 46" 120Hz TV--you can wait to get a Blu-Ray player until the prices come down (assuming they do). We've watched the BBC "Planet Earth" series this way--and that's used as a demo disk in its Blu Ray version--and it looks fantastic. So. All in all this DVD recorder is easy to use, easy to set up, relatively cheap, and integrates well with Samsung TVs especially. And even when you do get an HD player it won't be able to record DVDs, so you'll still need this. And if you do get one, please don't write a review griping that it doesn't have a tuner. It's clearly labeled as such, and anyway you don't need one if your have a TV with a tuner--and nearly everyone does--and/or cable/satellite. Thus far I really have no complaints. It works, the remote works--and it's clear to me--and I don't get coasters. I haven't tried the VCR part yet but expect the same there. And Amazon had about a $40 lower price than local stores (figuring in tax)--and I live in Silicon Valley, where stores are forced to compete a bit more than out in the boonies. And the Amazon shipment arrived in a timely manner. I also ordered a 100-disk stack of Verbatim DVD+R disks with the recorder. They arrived in good shape and worked perfectly, as have a stack of Fuji DVD+R disks I've also burned. As I recall this machine requires +R disks, which if fine with me because they're superior anyway. --------------- UPDATE August 5 2008 I've now successfully burned 250 DVDs with this recorder--including the new recorder they shipped me after I sent in the first recorder because I thought it was broken (it wasn't--I'd just pushed the wrong button on the remote without realizing it). Today, as I was recording a program, the screen suddenly froze and I got a loud buzzing noise through the speakers and a "system error" error message on the screen that told me to turn off the recorder. I did, and when I turned it back on again the disc wouldn't load--it had turned the recording into a coaster. This is the first time this has happened. I've had the replacement recorder for several months. Other than this glitch, the recorder has also turned half a dozen disks into coasters when I had too many chapters on the disk. Sometimes it just wouldn't finalize the disks. Then, at least, I can play them on this recorder, if not on other makes. Other times the recorder coasterized the disk. The number of chapters that trigger this varies, but on my machine at least, you're safe with 6 chapters or less. The user's manual hints at this--it says every time you put a disk in this recorder (before it's finalized), the recorder optimizes the disk for recording--and if it does this too many times it won't finalize the disk. But it doesn't specify just how many times "too many" represents. I'm guessing six, as I've said. At this point I think I'd give it three stars. When it works, it works fine, and it works most of the time. But you'd better not delete something from your DVR until you finalize the disk. And the firmware is buggy. It often freezes when you fast forward to the end of the disk. The system freezes and you have to eject the disk, then reload it, to make it work. Sometimes you even have to physically unplug it to get it going again. And as others have said, tech support is iffy. For example, they claimed it won't record DVD+R disks--and that's all I've ever used, and the manual allows you to use both + & - R disks. Problems notwithstanding, I'd say this is probably a decent buy at what I paid for it in March: $169. It has never shown the problem that ruled out Sony and others for me: refusing to record content from a TV set for copyright protection reasons--even when it was a regular show on TV. No problem there. But for its current $500 price--I'd look long and hard for alternatives.

I have had the Y500 for just over a week and overall I am very happy with my purchase. I opted for this i5 version since the i7 doesn't really add any value for gaming and I’d rather spend the money on other upgrades own the road when I need it. This model has the SLI dual graphics, and at the current price, this is a steal! The laptop arrived safely no thanks to Amazon. I order a ton of stuff through Prime and even cheap kids toys have at least some bubble wrapping and are placed in a standard shipping box. This was shipped in the original (and small) laptop box from Lenovo and with no additional packaging materials. Why??? Now onto the hardware…. All of the built-in hardware seems great with the exception of the slow but ample 5400 RPM 1TB hard drive. It’s by far the biggest bottleneck of the system, but it’s not a deal breaker. Most people will appreciate the huge capacity for storing large game libraries. Apparently you can toss in a compatible mSATA SSD and boot from this or set it up as a cache. I would set it as boot drive and keep the 1TB drive for data if given the option. The screen is VERY nice and clear. Colors look great and overall I can’t find any flaws with the screen. This is true HD running at 1080p. Most other gaming notebooks in this price range only provide 720p (do not want). I updated the Nvidia drivers from Lenovo’s site and they do seem to perform better than what was included. SLI is awesome to have in a notebook and I’m super impressed with how all of my games are performing so far. Steam Big Picture mode works well on this when connected via HDMI to my Panasonic plasma TV. The case is very basic and to be honest, does have a somewhat cheap feel to it. However, I have no concerns of it breaking or coming loose. It’s also a grease magnet, but I knew that before from other reviews. I’m surprised that the laptop feels so light for the size. The PSU is huge, but I've seen bigger. There is a minimal amount of external ports on this laptop, which is a bit of a surprise for a laptop of this size and intended use. There is nothing truly lacking for gaming, although, I would have loved to have an eSATA port included as well. Opening the case for the first time was a bit scary. Some of the hinges come off easily and others do not. It took me around 10 minutes before I finally had carefully opened this up. Once opened up, it’s easy to replace the internal components (RAM, HDD, mSATA, etc.,). The keyboard is good. I’d give it a solid B. I would prefer a slightly stiffer response as I find the keys a bit spongy for my liking. Not a deal breaker by any means though. The backlit keys look cool and be turned down to a lower setting or turned off completely using the function keys. I was very concerned about the track pad due to all of the noise online about this. Take a deep breath - it is fine, but far from perfect. I’m not crazy about the texture and I would have preferred physical mouse buttons, but these are unfortunately getting harder to come by and only seem to be found on much more expensive gaming laptops and/or models geared for business use. The detection of the right and left mouse buttons is good and basic tracking is also fine. The gestures, however, don’t always work but I hear that you can disable this. The battery seems OK and matches the 3 hour advertised average when used for non-gaming use. I will keep it plugged in to AC power when gaming. Apparently the GPU’s throttle down when not on AC power, but I can’t imagine ever gaming without it since you would maybe get 1 hour tops of playing time before having to plug it in back to charge. Onto the included OS and build from Lenovo… Like all OEM consumer PC’s, there is a fair amount of crapware/trailware included, which I immediately uninstalled before attempting to do anything else. McAfee was the first to go. Just use the included Microsoft Security Essentials and be done with it. All you need to keep on this system is the drivers and some of the Lenovo utilities. The rest can be removed. For those who don’t like the new Metro interface (and I assume this is the root cause for the hatred of Windows 8) should download and install Classic Shell for free. Windows 8 performs great and is a bit faster than Windows 7. This will give you the best of both worlds (a great interface and great performance). You can get this from ninite.com (an awesome site for downloading a bunch of apps at once). Final Verdict: This system provides a lot of value for the money and you will not find a better gaming laptop for the price at the moment. If money is not a factor and/or if you don’t want to upgrade any parts yourself down the road, you may instead want to check out an Asus ROG model. Of course, if you are not going to use this for gaming, there are better laptops to be found in the same price range.

Explained more below If you have FreeSync enabled, and attempt to switch from a low refresh rate to a high refresh rate setting in a full screen game or program's settings, it results in what you see in the video, a chopped up mix of squares of your image, or this horrifying overexposed blue LCD effect across the whole monitor which definitely cannot be good for it. I did a lot of research on amazon looking for a shielded cable like this one that wasn't as expensive as monster cables, but was actually shielded-- this one suited my needs perfectly. You can find similar length cables at half the price, but they don't look like they're really shielded-- no more so than any wired cable, like a phone cord, cheap extension cord, etc. And of course you can find top-end stuff from monster, etc for 3x the price. I already had a 15 ft, unshielded 3.5mm to RCA cable that I've been using to connect my MP3 player and my laptop to my stereo's aux input, but unless I had everything just right, I was liable to experience a hum-- feedback interference. In addition, the old cable would occasionally cause my MP3 player to freeze up, which never happens when I'm using headphones. I've had this cable for a few weeks now, and with daily use, on both the laptop and the MP3 player, I haven't had any issues at all, so I'm pleased. It seems to be heavy duty cable, well made, and durable. It's very flexible for it's thickness though, so I think anyone needing to route the cable around corners, etc will have no problem at all. 4 stars instead of 5 just because the 3.5 plug housing is rather long and heavy, (which makes it pretty durable-- I doubt I'll be suffering from a bad joint connection, but--) I sense that it's going to cause some problems with my laptop jack eventually, because it weighs so much I can see how the jack will get loose over time, especially with daily use. It would have been better designed with an elbow plug, if possible. Otherwise, I think it's great. Great deal for the money. update 1-5-13: happy to report my cable still works great; everything is the same. Just want to clarify that I bought mine from cablemart for approx $10 + $5 shipping. Glancing at a few more recent reviews, I can't guarantee that the cable advertised is the same one I bought. I don't think the picture is the same either. the one I bought looks like this one: http://www.amazon.com/Quality-Shielded-Connecting-Receivers-Accepting/dp/B002XWRVIC/ref=sr_1_6?s=electronics&ie=UTF8&qid=1357381992&sr=1-6

Be very careful. The wording in the terms is tricky and confusing. I bought this for coverage on an expensive scientific calculator, thinking it would cover accidents and battery failure. "C. ALL OTHER PRODUCTS: i. This Protection Plan provides coverage for parts and labor costs to repair or replace Your Product where the problem is the result of a failure caused by: [...] 2. Accidental damage from handling (ADH), such as damage from drops, spills and liquid damage associated with the handling and use of Your Product, if the coverage has been offered and purchased at the time of sale with your Protection Plan; 3. One (1) battery repair or replacement, when the original rechargeable battery is defective as determined by Us and at Our sole discretion, if the coverage has been offered and purchased at the time of sale with your Protection Plan.; 4. One (1) bulb replacement, replacement of a faulty bulb during the first three (3) years of the Term, if the coverage has been offered and purchased at the time of sale with your Protection Plan; [...]" If you read carefully, it says "if the coverage has been offered and purchased at the time of sale with your Protection Plan" -- now, the first couple of times reading this you may think "Great! Yes, this coverage was offered and purchased at the time of sale"... but what it means by "the coverage" is if EXTRA coverage (Accidental Damage from Handling coverage, Battery coverage, Bulb coverage) is offered and purchased. No thanks. These terms should be updated to remove "if the coverage has been offered and purchased" and replaced with "if Accidental Damage from Handling coverage has been offered and purchased" and "if Battery coverage has been offered and purchased" and "if Bulb coverage has been offered and purchased". Really items #2, #3, and #4 should just be removed in their entirety from this section because all they do is cause confusion. But I think we know they won't do either of these things. In reality, all this coverage covers is: "1. Normal wear and tear; 5. Dust, internal overheating, internal humidity/condensation; 6. Defects in materials or workmanship; 7. Power surge/fluctuation. Please see section 11 “POWER SURGE PROTECTION” for details." Try getting a refund for any of these reasons on a scientific calculator 3 years after the purchase date.

Best price around at the time and it arrived in 3 business days (direct from Amazon, $439). Included was a wired mouse and a wired keyboard, both very basic with no extra features. If you need help learning Win8, go to the Microsoft website, they have some 'getting started' videos. I had read that you don't HAVE to create a Microsoft account, but figuring out how to use a "local" account wasn't obvious. Must have done it right since I never did create a MS acct. Very minimal junk to uninstall, which was nice! Came pre-loaded with 6mo of McAfee and a trial version of MS Word -- dumped both. Subsequent installations including an internet security program, OpenOffice, Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox and Thunderbird all went smoothly. Likewise, no problem installing my wireless printer (it initially recognized the printer and actually printed, but then printing failed and the software had to be manually installed). Took some time figuring out how to customize and configure the general settings. Not a fan of this OS, but I appreciate that the Metro screen and the standard desktop are both easily accessible. Toggle between them using the MS icon at the bottom left where the Start button used to be, or the Windows key on the keyboard. When you can't figure out how to close something, hover your cursor at the top right corner of the screen, the red X will appear. Hovering at the bottom right brings up a menu that includes search and settings. (Wish you could return to Win7? See UPDATE #2 below) This machine runs VERY quietly, though the optical drive is a bit noisy when installing from disc. A pleasant surprise -- 8 USB ports: 4 [2.0] + 2 [3.0] in the rear and 2 [2.0] in the front. The processor is definitely more snappy than my previous dual-core (and if you're considering the less expensive i3 instead... don't). But do note, Amazon's lists this as 3.2GHz, it's not -- it's actually 2.9GHz (with turbo boost to 3.4?). Apparently the RAM is expandable to 16GB, but as-is, this is a very good processor/RAM combo for the price. I didn't have any luck with the MS Easy Transfer program present on both pc's, couldn't get them to communicate (probably user error, maybe a firewall issue). Therefore, I manually transferred important files (photos, documents, music, etc) via my home network and then used a thumb drive to move stored email items. Overall, I'm extremely pleased with this purchase. Unlike another reviewer, I've experienced absolutely no issues with the WiFi while running several devices on the home network. UPDATE #1: Using the Dell Backup and Recovery app, I successfully created a bootable backup on a 16GB USB thumb drive, actual space needed was just over 10GB. Then created a utilities and drivers backup on a separate 8GB USB, actual space needed was <1GB (so a 2GB thumb drive would be sufficient). Each process formats/erases current content so you can't use the same thumb drive for both, or at least I wasn't able to figure out how to do so. Regardless, very easy and quick to do, took about 20mins + <1min to complete both. UPDATE #2: Following the suggestion of fellow reviewer K. O'Meara, I did some reading and decided to download "Start8" from Stardock(.com). Completed the 30-day trial, then purchased for $4.99. It causes your OS to look/run just like the Win7 design (doesn't actually change the OS) with a traditional desktop, Start button and Start Menu. It can be configured to boot up to this desktop instead of the Metro screen (which is still accessible via a button within the start menu or the 'Windows' key on the keyboard). All the familiar items are there within the start menu -- plus you can pin quick launch items to it, or to the task bar, just like Win7. Very cool. No more struggling trying to find stuff, makes Win8 bearable! I have since heard of another program called Classic Shell (classicshell.net) which is said to be similar, but I have not personally tried that one.

I've had a few weeks with the PL-660 and I've not had any problems so this review is really just a subjective report of my impressions with the radio. Ergonomically, it's small and feels small and sounds small. The rotary tuning knob feels loose and cheap. The pushbuttons won't always respond to a push by finger and have to be pressed with my fingernail. The display is adequately sized but I have to tip the unit forward to see if I'm on SSB or check the bandwidth. The little flap of plastic that supports the unit at a tilt is just asking to be broken. The speaker is not fooling anybody of its size. That's the bad news. But it's a character that it shares with most of the receivers in this class. Having bought it sight-unseen, I expected it be a little larger would have opted for a larger unit model had I known how small it really is. This is my one and only receiver and it will rarely leave the house so a larger box would have been a better choice for me. My bad. The good news is that this little unit performs very well. My primary use is shortwave and it leaves little to be desired in its ability to pull in and select broadcasts. The sideband operation and BFO are stable and responsive. The bandwidth selector is just a 2-position switch but it's a feature that is rare to find in a little unit and works well. Likewise, the "bass and treble" control is just a high-end roll-off switch but it's adequate. There are timer functions that I will never use and air and longwave bands that are as dead as disco, but it's nice to have them there anyhow. I'm a little puzzled about the automatic "slow" and "fast" tuning speeds that never seem to be where I'd like them to be. The display light is also designed to be "intuitive" but but just seems to be contentious. I'd like to be able turn it off sometimes, but it doesn't have a switch. So, in short, if you are looking for a portable, almost-pocket-sized receiver that performs like the big boys, you won't be disappointed. If, however, you're wanting a Cadillac and not a Mini Cooper, pay a little more for the ETON Satellite 750.

I wanted a NAS to use as shared storage in my home office. I wanted large capacity with full redundancy to protect against drive failure. I bought this device over other competing brands for a few specific reasons, and I'm still glad that I did: 1) it takes off-the-shelf drives, rather than having to buy branded drives for 2x-3x the price. 2) It uses standard RAID formats rather than some Brand-specific variant. 3) The drives can be recovered in another computer should the unit itself fail. 4) It can run Squeezebox Server to host my music collection to my audio system. On paper, it does all of these things. In practice, it still does, but slowly. I installed my device with a pair of [[ASIN:B002ZCXJZE Western Digital 1.5 TB Caviar Green SATA Intellipower 64 MB Cache Bulk/OEM Desktop Hard Drive WD15EARS]] drives running RAID1. I run the unit on my 100Mbit network, as my older computers and home router do not have gigabit. Both of these will impact the speed of the unit through no fault of its own, but both of these are also likely to be common for other users. In practice, I am seeing write speeds averaging around 5 MByte/second. The network limit should be twice that. I believe this is at least partly due to the drives, as I saw the same write speed from a large disk-to-disk copy using the USB connector as well. This is not an exhaustive test or benchmark, just one user's experience. This device, and others of its kind, is basically a Linux-based mini-computer. All of its special functions are just software running on the Linux OS, and subject to the same limits of other computers: processor speed and available memory. I experimented very briefly with the built-in photo manager software. I fed it a few hundred full 12Mpixel images off my camera, and watched as it set to grinding its way through them to make thumbnails. The slow processor really showed itself here. I gave up and removed the images from the photo album after a few hours of constant processing did not finish the folder. I cannot imagine feeding my entire 30+GB photo collection to the album software. Just storing the photos as unprocessed files still works fine, of course. The Squeezebox software was a pleasant surprise in that it is available as a package download from the Synology site, and doesn't have to be hacked in as I first expected. It runs, and feeds my squeezebox quite well when running on it's own. It does eat a lot of the small CPU and memory while running. If I do some heavy file movement from another computer, I can get the squeezebox to stall out. The software takes about an hour to reindex my collection of 3800 music files. Just playing music is also an exercise in patience. Click a button, wait 5-30 seconds, get a response. Click a playlist, wait a few seconds, music starts, few more seconds, current song appears, even more seconds, playlist starts to fill in on the screen. It works, but it's slow. Something I saw on the website that might have swayed my decision: yes, it runs standard RAID1. The drives can be recovered in another computer, but... you will have to adjust the format of the drive to get it to work on a x86 processor because the integer byte-order is reversed for the CPU they use on these units. Too technical? If you plug one of these drives into your windows box, it won't read it. If you have a x86 linux box, it can be made to read it with some adjustments. Google the Synology website to find the details. Bottom line: I'm happy with it. It does what I need. I'm willing to put up with waiting on the tiny CPU/memory to get the job done. If you want faster, pony up the bigger bucks for a faster, office-quality unit and server-quality drives.

I've have the original bestview since Feb of 09. The toggle switch has been worn out with use, but overall a great device. Still works. We really got our money's worth and will continue to, it seems. Along came another baby and decided to upgrade to the new one, so I could have an additional camera and cover 2 babies rooms, and scan between the two. It fails miserably compared to the original model. 1. Picture is nowhere near as good, specifically in night vision. I can actually get past this. It's a 2.5 inch monitor and your eyes learn to adapt. But it's very choppy, very dark, makes a ticking sound, break ups and pauses in the audio, etc. The original one had a much better picture if you had to mount the camera a distance of 5 feet or more away. I have compared the two extensively the past few days. The range is not as good either. My bed is 100 feet from my daughters room, and that is when the audio really gets choppy and cutting out, on this new one. 2. The rechargable battery doesn't have much of a cycle. Couple hours if you are lucky. It will only get worse with future use. The previous version used AA which left some control in the user's hands. I would buy the highest rated mah rechargeable AA batteries I could get (2450 or 2600) and a single charge would last longer than the entire day, with picture ON the entire time. Then it would recharge itself when plugged in at night, next to my bed, but still on. I replaced batteries once a year as their cycle shortened. 3. Here's where they lost me as a customer. Summer infant has tried to remedy their new inferior battery design by having the unit turn the monitor out ITSELF! Every 3 minutes, the screen goes black and you are left with an overpriced audio monitor. After a day or two of having to repeatedly press the monitor button ON every few minutes, I'm packing it up and returning. Worthless battery or not, the consumer, not the maker, should dictate when the monitor goes to sleep. The original version gave you the option to turn out screen if you wished....which we never did. Summer Infant overlook the consumer on this. You see, people spending this kind of money for a baby monitor want to SEE their kids, without having to hit a button every 90 seconds. I can't tell you the COUNTLESS times I've glanced at my monitor (although everything sounded fine) only to see something that needed by attention. Babies with things covering their face Dont CRY OUT morons! If they can't breathe, they wont cry. You have negated the sole purpose of the portable video monitor. Perhaps I'm a little paranoid and over protective....probably true, after all I paid $300 for a monitor didn't I? Here's another problem, I can't find the damn thing! I move the monitor from one table to another, take to the kitchen on my way to the fridge and leave on the counter, or leave in the hallway while I jump in and out of the bathroom real quickly, and the screen times itself out and goes black. I'm so accustomed to that illumination, specifically in the evenings, I keep losing this thing when it times itself out. You can't glance at it anymore. You have to find it, press the button and remember where you left it. However, the design and concept are great. Had summer infant just used the original battery design, minus the toggle switch that wears out with usage, but with the 2 camera and scan ability....they would have knocked it out of the park. I guess it's true, you can't please everyone. People with no basis of the original BestView may love this monitor. I don't believe those upgrading due to more coverage or more babies will like it one bit, and that would have been the target market! The repeat customer. I've own several Summer Infant products and believe they are of the highest quality. Bummed with this.

Just completed the install of this over the last weekend, here's why I gave it 3 stars... First I have a 46" Sony flat screen tv and it weighs right at 66 lbs. so I am at the upper limit of allowed weight. The manufacturer allows up to 55" and 66 lbs. (although they claim to have tested it at 3 times that weight). So anyway I am within the specs. The setup and install went pretty well and lot of hardware was included. My first impression of the build quality was pretty good also, that was until I got it mounted to the ceiling and the TV on it. My first concern was that the Vesa mount is only attached to the motorized head unit by 3 small screws! That's 66 lbs. of flat screen TV hanging and moving around on 3 small screws. Most of these kinds of mounts have a sliding lock and then screws or bolts to keep the TV in place on the lock. I was and am very uncomfortable with this arrangement. Also the set is kind of wobbly on the mount. By that I mean it is secured but the entire mount would move in a strong breeze (if I had it mounted outside in a patio). Again not confidence inspiring. Additionally my TV does not sit level to the ceiling when in the up position. TV's have lots of components inside the the builders do not place them according to perfect balance from one side to the other. Therefore my TV is a little heaver on one side than the other and because this mount is so loose and flexible, one side of mine hangs lower . Finally the remote and motorized unit are prone to unusual behavior, I.E. stopping in weird places and responding to buttons on the remote that are unexpected. It's possible that this is due to programming on the remote but I have no real way to be sure because the setup instructions are so limited. Bought this 4TB SSD for my DJ performance laptop to store media files. My idea was to not have to use an external USB drive for my files. After installing the drive, I started transferring media files to it. For unknown reasons the drive would simply disappear from the system. This seemed to occur most frequently when I'd attempt to move a large folder of several hundred gigabytes (using TeraCopy). Part of the way through the move, the drive would vanish. Restarting the system didn't find the drive. But, if I got into my BIOS, usually it was at least recognized there, but sometimes not. Without making changes in the BIOS, if I saved and restarted, the drive would sometimes magically appear. Thinking it was a driver issue, I updated all drivers for my system. (LEVEN does not seem to offer any firmware updates to its drives.) This seemed to have resolved the disappearing drive issue. Until the drive vanished in the middle of a wedding reception. That was it. It is now relegated to an external USB enclosure. I swapped it out for a high capacity spinner which will no doubt be 100% more reliable. So, I highly recommend this drive if you want to install it in an external usb drive case to have on hand just in case. But, if it's your bread and butter, there are better options. Look for a drive that has a DRAM controller built-in.

I got this camera because I spent a full half of my day in virtual meetings some days. But this webcam won’t remember your settings like every other webcam I have ever used will. Meaning you zoom it in and get it setup right, and as soon as you stop using it for a few minutes, then go to do your next meeting the camera turns on and all your settings are wiped out… no zoom, no tracking, nothing. I spoke to customer service and no, this isn’t a bug, that’s how the software is intended to be… I put in a request for a basic feature like that to be added. I tried their auto zoom feature to see if that would help, and it does zoom in perfectly, but has some serious bugs that make it zoom in and out and in and out all the time. I spoke to customer service about this and provided a video clip to show them the issue upon request. I’m hoping this gets fixed soon as it seems to be a common bug. It seems that the only real workaround is to keep their software open 24/7 and setup a preset for how I want the camera to be, and I literally have to go to the software and click the preset every single time I want to use the camera. This can be dozens of times per day… So overall it’s an amazing webcam with the best quality picture on the market. I just hope they can get the software sorted out soon, currently it’s half baked at best.

Update 2 (4 stars, January 17, 2022): ===================================== The seller sent me the following instructions on what to do in my situation: "This is because Apple computers have a memory effect on battery capacitors, which can be caused by installing a battery when the built-in capacitor of the previous battery still exists. The 5% battery level is a critical point we set to protect the battery and the computer. Solution: Disconnect the battery and leave it alone for 24 hours and then reinstall it. If your battery still behaves abnormally, we would like to provide you with a refund or a new replacement since the battery have a warranty." Yesterday, I tried to do just that. I have removed the battery from the laptop, put it aside, and tried to boot the laptop without any battery (it should work - I used my laptop without any battery for about 4 years before I bought the battery discussed here). Result: the laptop would not boot (was doing repeatedly the following: "beep, beep, beep, pause, ..."). What do I do? Have I just killed my laptop? So, I put the battery back into the laptop (the battery was out of the laptop for about 5 minutes). Miracle: the laptop booted successfully and the battery came back to life! The battery charges fine again and works well! But, it seems my laptop might be "addicted" to the battery now (refused to boot without it) ;) Update 1 (2 stars, Mid December, 2021): ============================= 2.5 months later (56 charge cycles), the battery is dead... I discharged the battery by accident to 5% and that killed it. It did solve my problem (I was able to change system preferences related to mouse gestures and to set to ignore built in touch-pad when an external mouse is connected), but beyond that it seems to be a poor quality product. Original Review, submitted shortly after the battery delivery (5 stars) - Oct 5, 2021: ====================================================================================== I got the following in Catalina right after installing the battery: Apple Logo > About This Mac > Overview > System Report > Power: * Manufacturer: SMP * Full Charge Capacity (mAh): 6084 * Cycle Count: 2 * Condition: Normal * Amperage (mA): 1273 * Voltage (mV): 11945 In addition, installation of the battery solved my problem with the built-in trackpad, since if a battery is not installed in a MacBook Pro unibody, then MacOS would not detect presence of a trackpad in system preferences (if you go to "System Preferences > Trackpad", you would see "No trackpad found", e.g. in Catalina). Once I installed the battery, trackpad reappeared in system preferences and I got back the option to disable the built in trackpad when a mouse is present (in "System Preferences > Accessibility > Pointer Control > Mouse & Trackpad"). So, it appears, the battery was recognized as a proper one by the MacOS. The included with the battery screws are for the bottom of the laptop cover. The screws are not for the battery! However, the small screws work as a left battery screw, and the big ones work (with a little bit of force) as a right battery screw.

It is not going to be the choice for any CW contest, but I am finding it nicely does the job with my TX-500 setup. On the price, I do think it could have been priced lower, considering how cheaply this is made and everything, but also considering the small market and the competitive pricing, I also understand why the price is higher than that. Overall, I would say the price is not bad compared to how overpriced other ham gear has been. So, I do recommend this item, but just make sure your expectations are low even considering the price. This is about the cheapest way to go, and yet it is still not awful. I would have no regrets buying another one and having it sit alongside my VibroPlex collection in the shack. Another thing I am considering, like most hams, is how to improve it. I think with some material improvements and just a minimum of design changes, which will add a small amount of weight and cost, I can make a set of much better paddles. So, one final benefit of this item is the inspiration for innovation, which is part of why we have this hobby.

I was using this with a 5 drive set-up on both Windows and Mac OS. Windows 10, and Mac OS Big Sur 11.4. The positives: The enclosure is quiet and kept all of my drives cool enough (~80-90 degrees Fahrenheit). USB-C was nice (and rare for this size enclosure at this price), and R/W speeds were ~240 mb/s. The box is fairly small, and the drives were secured without issue. I consistently transferred the connection with this enclosure between two devices, sometimes on the same OS and sometimes on different OSes. Never had an issue with hot-plugging, or OS recognition. That is about the end of the good. The negatives: Cheap materials, even if it is machined aluminum. No soundproofing inside. I didn't need it, but if your drives are loud, then good luck. The most annoying part of this enclosure, though, is the fact that it goes to "sleep", forcing the drives to sleep as well. Sometimes all of them, and sometimes only the ones that aren't in constant use. And there's no way to turn that off. AT ALL. In my Mac system settings, I've selected to "never put the hard drives to sleep" -- so this shouldn't happen. Yet it still happens, and it isn't the OS's fault. This wasn't a problem with my old QNAP DAS, and it isn't a problem with my newer (replacement for this) 8-bay OWC enclosure. For some reason, as many other reviewers have mentioned, this enclosure just puts the drives to sleep. If that doesn't seem like a big deal, read on. Because if you are someone that plans to use this to access media on an HTPC or streaming device (i.e. Plex, Jellyfin, etc.), the drive sleeping is ANNOYING. Videos take minutes to load, sometimes throwing failures that they cannot be played. On other DAS and NAS enclosures, they take seconds (or less) to load. Folders (on both Mac and Windows) take minutes to load with this enclosure, sometimes freezing the OS (or Finder / File explorer) in the meantime as the enclosure slowly wakes up and brings the drives back online. I thought it was going to be a non-issue for me; or at worst, a small issue. But the drives go to sleep every 15-20 minutes (unless you are constantly using/browsing the specific drive that you are needing to access). And even if you use just one drive and that specific drive isn't asleep, the others likely WILL be. It got to a point where trying to load media information on my streaming device would take minutes. I couldn't even scroll through my media because folders were just grey, default icons. I could click on a video and instead of seeing a description, play button, etc, I would be met with a buffering sign because the media hadn't been accessed yet (because it couldn't). It got to the point where I began to expect to see a 'buffering' icon anytime I wanted to access anything on my HTPC. For those of you using Plex, you'll be seeing a lot of blank posters, artwork, descriptions, etc. For those of you doing video work in After Effects or Premiere, good luck. Would not recommend buying unless you plan to use this as housing for your backed-up files, which you plan to access maybe once every few weeks.

However, my Apple Watch 7 shows frequent tracking updates. So, why can't the Watch share that with the iPhone, where I have a larger screen and can see more detail on the map, zoom in etc. I could live with that but the real deal killer, is that even after a year of this feature being requested, Apple still have not added family sharing. I bought this because it was fulfilled by Amazon, so I thought it can't possible be fake. However, my doubt was confirmed after receiving the product. Firstly, the headphone did not have the usual pearly shine it should have, the pink color is just some cheap plastic looking tacky pink. Secondly, the headphone line looked very poorly made and also it had "Monster" logo on the headphone line. The authentic one should have "Beats" written on it instead of "Monster". Thirdly, the part where you can adjust volume on the headphone line looked broken, even though it was working. The real one should not look broken, it should look very intact. Fourth, the product came in a similar looking pouch as the real one, but with some poorly printed paper pamphlets. They looked like an effort to imitate the warranty that came with the real one. However, an authentic one should have a very thick warranty and instruction book. They would look almost like a CD album and weigh heavier than a normal CD album. Lastly, the sound quality was quite poor. Beats by Dre headphones or earphones should generally have a strong bass output, and the noise cancelling effect should be very good. This fake one does not do all those. It just sounds like a very common no-brand earphone, not even like a headphone. So here ends the comparisons. However, on a related note, my package came in damaged. The product was intact, but the box was opened up. The tape with "Amazon Prime" printed on looked cut open intentionally. When I picked up my package, I was really surprised at how broken the box looked like. I lived in a school dorm so all packages will go to school's housing front desk. They told me the package came in to them broke. I would trust the school staff that they would not open up any body's packages, so the only conclusions I have left were the package was opened up by someone shipping the product or the delivering company (UPS).

I've purchased two of these items and I love them. I got the first directly from Datel and the second here on Amazon. They are great. The seem more more durable, OVERALL, and reliable than the standard Go-tcha model. My only complaint is that both of them have failed within a week or two of purchase as a result of shoddy soldering on the board that connects everything together. The first one failed by the black wire which connects the Go-tcha portion of the Ranger to the control board broke free of the soldered connection. The second failed when the black wire from the battery broke free of the soldered connection to the control board. Fortunately the Ranger is much less of a closed system than the basic Go-tcha model. By simply removing the both USB ends from the storage positions you can take a box knife or any thin device to separate the two sides or the case. Once this is done there are two screws holding down the control board. Remove them and you're set. Both of my Rangers were easily fixed with a rudimentary knowledge of electronics and possession of a soldering iron. If you don't have both of these things then I might suggest holding off on buying one of these until they get the manufacturing process a little more nailed down. If the connections on the battery itself or inside the actual Go-tcha side of the connector it would have been a considerably more difficult fix. I love the device and, after the fixes, they are VERY reliable. I give the product 5 Stars but the construction flaws bring it down to a 3.

USB-C is confusing because of how many different standards can exist within it. I went through the trouble of testing this cable out for you in different scenarios and let's go over what works and what doesn't. First, here's what I WANTED to use it for: I have my gaming PC in my home office. Sometimes I like to game from the couch in the living room. GameStream via an nVidia Shield TV works alright, but I can't get higher than 60hz and there's always a liiiittle too much latency. So, I also have a HyperDrive Gen2 USB-C dock, perfect I thought -- put this dock under the TV and run a 50-foot fiber optic USB-C cable from the office to the TV! While this should work, this cable unfortunately is not the correct one to make this happen. This is because, as far as I can tell, this cable is *literally* only a displayport USB-C cable and nothing more. I'm talking *only* displayport lanes pass through this cable. If any application you need with this cable requires USB data throughput, it won't work simple as that -- look for a cable that supports USB data PLUS DisplayPort. What worked: Connecting this cable from my MacBook Pro to my Wacom Cintiq Pro 24's USB-C input, the video came up just fine, 4K/60, no latency, no drop-outs. This part works. However, the USB-data throughput would not come through, this means no pen tracking on the display, nor other connected USB devices to the Cintiq worked. This is what ultimately let me know this cable *does not* transfer USB data. What didn't work: Connecting to both a CalDigit USB-C Pro Dock and HyperDrive Gen2 USB-C Dock, (both of which are powered with their own power supplies for outboard charging of connected devices,) didn't work at all with this cable. Their power light would blink briefly when detecting the cable, but they would ultimately not be able to handshake with the connected computer because there's no USB data to complete it. No handshake means the docks don't power on, which means no display, and ultimately no docking. Also, connecting to a powered Hard Drive enclosure didn't work either, (a CalDigit AV Pro 2.) The hard drive would spin up when plugging in the cable, but would ultimately never connect to the computer, again because there is no USB data to complete a handshake. Remember of course this cable can ONLY be used with powered devices such as a USB-C equipped monitor. You cannot charge devices with this cable, you cannot transfer data with this cable. You can, however, do 4K/60, 1440/120, and 1080/120 video with this cable just fine. If that's all you need, this cable is a great value compared to the more expensive ones that (as far as I can tell) also transfer USB data or in Corning's case, full Thunderbolt 3. I'll ultimately be returning the cable because my particular use case didn't pan out, but I still recommend it because it DOES work for exactly what it's intended for. In the Q&A someone asked if this cable can send data, to which MonoPrice responded saying it does, as well the title of the product is "USB 3.1 Cable" and not "USB-C DisplayPort cable." As far as my testing goes, it doesn't do USB (thus misleading, so 4 stars,) so that seems to be an inaccurate answer. However, maybe MonoPrice can let me know if I simply have a defective cable where the USB data is broken.

Received my T7 unit today. Unboxing and installation was pretty straightforward. The unit seems well-constructed, and the fit and finish are quite nice. Fans run quietly as advertised, and move enough air to drop the temperature 15 degrees F in about 5 minutes in my rack. I have only one complaint: Air flow is BACK TO FRONT. That's not even the issue... the issue is that this is not stated in these terms anywhere. The closest allusion to this configuration is as statement that the fans exhaust hot air. One must then consider what that must mean, considering the location of the fans. A reverse mode would be nice, but high-flow low-noise fans like this are almost universally designed with directional blades... so it isn't surprising that no such feature is included. I'll have to disassemble the entire unit and re-mount the fans in order to have the airflow required for my application. In my case, all other components in the system have front-to-back airflow, and the rack enclosure has an exhaust fan on the back side. Having this unit move air in the other direction would be counter-productive. Again, the T7 is great in all respects... just make sure BACK TO FRONT is what you want, or be prepared to make some modifications.

I’ve bought and returned/sold many pairs of Bluetooth headphones for running and general use the last few years, and a few have been pretty good, but these are the first truly satisfying (even exciting!) ones I’ve found. The best ones before these were the Powerbeats Pros, but those I could only get the very best sound from when I pressed them into my ear canals. I didn’t especially want to press my earbuds into my ear canals at all times, so I continued my search, and finally I found an article online listing the best running headphones that mentioned these Jabras. It had never really occurred to me to get on-ear Bluetooth headphones for running or general portability, but I’m so glad I did. These are comfortable, easy to use, stable, and, best of all, great-sounding no matter what I’m doing. They’re on-ear, not over-ear, so they still allow some outside sound (which I want), but they certainly can be turned up loud enough to block out outside sound when you want. Sound is rich across all frequencies. Bass is nice and deep without overwhelming the clarity of the mids and highs. I like the buttons on the earpiece. Pretty easy to use, though I have occasionally accidentally activated Siri, which is the button directly opposite from the volume and play/pause buttons, so it just takes a little getting used to how you grab the ear cup to not do that. And even though the 3-button vol +/play-pause/vol - combo is easy to find by touch, you have to feel around them a little bit to sense the difference between them. But I like that they are solid buttons that click, so you really know you’re pressing them. And they make a nice little clicking sound in the earphones. I also like that when you do use Siri or voice dictation or whatever, it plays the actual sound of your voice as you’re doing it in your phones. Little weird at first, but neat and helpful. Bonus: battery life is incredible. I’ve used them several times, not sure how many hours, and every time I turn turn them on, the lovely lady voice of the headphones says “battery high.” I couldn’t be happier that I’m leaving the world of earbud headphones. Two last little things, one negative, one positive: Negative: The “thunking” sound in your ears when you walk or run is probably worse than with typical earbud headphones. I got used to it quickly, and it’s made up for for me by the fact that the sound is so good and doesn’t fluctuate because there’s no earbud subtly moving in and out of the air canal as I walk/run. It’s just constant deep, clean sound. Positive: It comes with a neat extra feature of various sounds you can play through the app, such as white noise, running water, thunderstorm sounds, etc. It’s an unexpected bonus feature, and it’s really easy to use. It came in handy when I recently took an airline flight a week after getting the headphones, because it was something that I could still listen to without Internet when I wanted to block out some of the noise around me. Immersive and relaxing.

People not familiar with the odd way that Nooks have to charge would think that this cable doesn't work. Needless to say, if you force it in the wrong way, it ain't gonna work! If the Nook ***has no charge***, or is too low, follow these steps if the Nook doesn't turn on or charge; 1) Plug it in to a proper wall charger. Not all USB wall chargers will work. Nook & Blackberry do work. 2) The green light will turn on for less than 2 seconds and then turn to amber. LEAVE IT PLUGGED IN FOR 2 TO 4 HOURS. 3) The Nook should turn on now, assuming that you have a good charger. REMEMBER: not all chargers will work with a nook. 4) When the Nook turns on, LEAVE IT ON. The screen will turn off, but MOST Nooks need to be in the ON state to charge.
