Overall, this is a great next generation gaming system, as well as an entertainment center. Pros: - Graphics look great for games that are built for the next gen systems (Forza looks absolutely gorgeous) - The ease of recording and uploading game clips to Twitch is awesome (although not having the Kinect you miss out on being able to say "Xbox Record That") - Growing number of Apps that make this system a complete entertainment center (Hulu, Netflix, Amazon, ESPN, etc) - Snap apps are handy like snapping ESPN or your fantasy football scores, while also being able to still watch tv - Xbox's party system that allows you to talk to your friends who are playing different games is really cool - Big fan that should hopefully avoid Xbox 360 meltdown issues - Controller: although I don't like it as much as the 360's because of the bumpers and batteries, it is still amazing and one of the reasons I prefer Xbox to PlayStation - Titanfall: it's just plain awesome and only on Xbox (and PC) Cons - Looks: its a big black box with no style at all that looks remarkable similar to the original Nintendo system (search for xbox one Nintendo skins and you will see) - UI: the new interface makes some things like joining friends much less intuitive - Controller batteries: for those that like the Xbox 360 easily replaceable batteries, you will probably be disappointed by the new controller. They start you off with standard 2 AA batteries (lame), but changing batteries isn't nearly as convenient when your controller runs out in the middle of battle. You could also get their rechargeable battery, but you have to use wires to recharge it (I hate wires) - Headset: This is probably my biggest peeve with the Xbox. If you have a wireless headset, you can only use it if it has a digital microphone out and then only if you buy Microsoft's buggy headset adapter. I HATE WIRES!!! - Can't play Xbox 360 games and there aren't a whole lot of Xbox One games out yet (but same issue with PS4) As a note the Xbox User Experience is focused on having a Kinect, so not having it makes some things more difficult and a couple things you just can't do at all. Voice Commands with the Kinect sometimes result in you having a shouting match with your xbox, so if you are looking for a cheaper way to get a really good gaming and entertainment center, this is a good option

This is my third week of using the CPR V10000. I suggest you read the many comments about the product before purchasing. Once you receive the call blocker carefully read the 14 page manual. I suggest you simply do the simple setup procedure and see how many fewer annoyance calls you receive. After a couple of days of use, go to page 11 of the manual and start adding some call blocking features. The Each time you add a call blocking feature such as "Blocking all Unknown Callers" you reduce the number of unwanted calls -- but, you also may eliminate some wanted calls! Try to limit the call blocking features so you get a proper balance of unwanted calls stopped while not seriously interfering with receiving calls you do want. Note the process for turning off the various call blocking features -- You can easily activate or deactivate the various blocking features. The most powerful and most satisfying tool is specifically banning certain numbers. First, you receive and unwanted call, next you push the red "block button" or you press the "#" key and then the "2" key on your phone. That will "ban" the number from calling again. Then you hang up the phone. One really persistent spammer kept switching numbers but after about ten phone numbers were banned he stopped trying to sell me a medic alert bracelet. -- Finally the small manual is well-written and is packed with useful information. Now we are down to about one unwanted call per day and block them with the #2 treatment.

I'm just an amateur when it comes to photography. After unpacking the DC3400, I spent about 10 minutes getting it set up, and proceeded to take a few pictures. Another 10 minutes or so, and I had the photo software loaded on my laptop. Connect the USB cable, and I was able to load the photos onto the laptop immediately. The camera shows up as an icon, like a disk drive, which you can double-click to open and transfer the pictures to a folder on your hard drive -- piece of cake! The quality of the pictures is amazing. I use the Ofoto service, and had some prints of some of my digital photos sent to my mother. According to her, you could not tell the difference between the digital images and those taken with a 35mm film camera. The colors were vivid, the images sharp -- just what you'd expect from the Kodak name. I'll agree with most everyone else and say that batteries might be the only downside to this camera. It's definitely worth the investment to get the Kodak NiMh rechargables and the charger. The ONLY time I use NiCads is when I'm my NiMh set is in the recharger, and I need to snap a few pictures. For the money, I don't think you can top this camera in terms of features, quality, and ease of use.

Let me begin by saying there is a truly fantastic and extensive review of this keyboard on the overclockerz website. I am in full agreement with every statement in that review and recommend it to anyone trying to decide whether to buy one of these keyboards. On to my personal experiences now... I'm old enough to have begun on Alps mechanical keyboards, and hadn't realized how much I missed the tactile feedback they provide! I am a fan of this keyboard. Pros: - Build quality is outstanding, far superior to many Razer products. This is a heavy, solid product. The phrase "built like a tank" comes to mind. - Tactile (and audible) feedback is also outstanding. They may initially take some getting used to if this is your first mechanical keyboard, but it felt like "coming home" to me. As another reviewer has commented, the (modified) Cherry Blue keys are ideal for normal typing. I also find them perfectly well suited to gaming, although I can only speak to World of Warcraft. I would like to see how Blues compare with (more expensive) Browns, but that is only based on theory. These keys work fine, and I really like them. - The key contours and angles fit my hands perfectly and are very comfortable. Each key has been deliberately positioned, and I found the fit excellent. I prefer an ergonomic keyboard, but have no complaints about this straight board. - Backlighting: As far as I know the Black Widow Ultimate is the only mechanical keyboard offering this feature. It's certainly the only one at this price point. The adjustable brightness levels should let anyone find a setting they like. The ability to use an individual light under each mechanical key (instead of the more diffuse lighting method used with a membrane keyboard) really improves the appearance over every lighted board I've owned in the past. - Five additional "macro" keys on the left add useful functionality. Because the keyboard can be programmed with profiles that trigger depending what application is active, I can use these for gaming when playing games, and for the common "office favorite" functions found on many keyboards when I'm not playing. I have them set to open a Web browser, my e-mail client, a text editor, etc. - The typical media control functions seen on many gaming keyboards are available using some "F" keys with an alternate function key (similar to a laptop keyboard). This helps keep an uncluttered appearance. Cons: - Ports are on the right side of the keyboard, which interferes with my cabled mouse. I don't know why Razer didn't locate them along the side facing away from the operator, as they have done with other keyboards? I have given up using the USB extension for now, (and see next item). - The headphone extension cables are braided together so closely that they only reach back panel ports on the tower. Since these ports are filled by speaker plugs on my system, I still have to plug my headphones directly into the front panel ports on the tower. I have therefore given up using the headphone extensions as well. Depending on your configuration, this may not be a problem, of course. - No N-key rollover. If you're not hard-core enough to know about or want this function, you won't miss it, although I feel a keyboard billed as "Ultimate" and "gaming" should have included it. - No wrist rest. This is a thick board, and I did not find it comfortable to type on until I purchased a third-party solution at the local office supply store. Subjective aspects, aka "your mileage may vary." - Appearance is visually interesting, and as a touch typist I have found no issue with the non-standard font on the typefaces. - Yes, the shiny surfaces attract dust and fingerprints. However: The same microfiber cloth I use to clean the monitor wipes off the keyboard just as well. Problem solved for me. Incidentally, hang on to the transparent plastic cover it was packed with and use it for a dust/impact shield when not typing. - Software is not provided in the package and must be downloaded from the Razer website. Personally I think getting the latest drivers this way is better than loading potentially obsolete drivers from a pre-packaged CD. In my case it turned out that at least one download (drivers or firmware, don't recall) had been updated just one day before my board was delivered! - Another reviewer pointed out that the "F" keys are offset a bit to the right of their normal locations. Even though I am a touch typist, I found I adjusted quickly. In summary: Although perhaps not the "Ultimate" gaming keyboard possible, and even though there is room for improvement in some of the feature it provides (at least in my opinion), this is an terrific keyboard that I highly recommend. It perfectly does everything I need it to, plus adds a number of very nice to have features, and looks good while doing so. It is a great addition to the rest of my blue-lit gaming rig, and I could find no equivalent at this price point. Perhaps the ultimate endorsement is that my spouse informed me within two days of its arrival that I had to buy another for her. She had never used a mechanical keyboard before, but became an instant convert!

My car is a 2010 Toyota Prius and it doesn't have built in bluetooth. I've been in enough cars with bluetooth to realize that I now want it. My desired uses for bluetooth are listening to podcasts and music from my phone, hands free phone calls and GPS navigation voice directions. My alternatives were buying a new, bluetooth enabled radio for hundreds of dollars or trying an inexpensive bluetooth add on like the SoundBot. I've very glad I decided to try the SoundBot. It works very well and it satisfy's all my major requirements. Delivery with Amazon prime was fast and on schedule. I mounted the SoundBot on the left center of my dashboard in the area recommended in the instructions. It's easy to reach the buttons and the microphone is straight ahead of me. I ran the cable under and into the center console where the AUX and power outlets are located. In test phone calls I placed to an answering machine my voice was clear and understandable, even when I was driving on the highway with the fan on. My Prius isn't the quietest car around so this means that the SoundBots built in noise cancellation works well. Music and podcasts sound great. I can't discern any sound degradation from beaming the music through bluetooth. I'm very happy with this purchase and I'd definitely buy it again. Pros • It's small and light. Easy to attach to the dashboard in an inconspicuous area. The SoundBot is black and it matches my dashboard well. • It attaches to the dashboard with a well designed magnetic mount. The magnet is attached to the car with mounting tape. • It pairs quickly with my windows phone (don't laugh, windows phone isn't bad). • The cords are long enough to reach from the dashboard to the center console AUX and power outlets with no extension needed. • It works well with Cortina, the windows phone version of Siri. • The included cigarette lighter USB power unit works well. Cons • The controls don't allow you to fast forward or reverse in a song or podcast. The controls only allow for next and prior song. • No cable hangers are included. You need to route and attach the cable to the dashboard yourself. • A blue LED on the SoundBot shines when a phone is paired. It's bright enough to be annoying at night. I dimmed the light by covering it with tape and then coloring over the light with a black magic marker. Comments • The power and head phone/AUX cables are joined coming out of the SoundBot. This means there's only one cable to route. They split near the end of the cable. After the split the USB power cable is about six inches long and the head phone/AUX cable is about 18 inches long. In total the cable is about three feet long. Update: After 10 months use I'm still enjoying the soundbot. It was a great purchase.

Here's why I bought it: * It was advertised as being "rugged". * It had Android 4.0 (Ice Cream Sandwich). At the time there were very few capacitive touch screen tablets of this size under $200 that had that version (or newer). In fact, it may have been the only one. * After some research I was able to determine that it could be rooted. This was absolutely essential: I will never buy an Android device that I do not have absolute power over. * The processor seemed to be fast enough to play all the latest Android games (3D). Here's my take on those things: * It is no more or less rugged than any other Android tablet. * Lenovo has released updates to the firmware since Christmas but they are just bug fixes. Still no Jelly Bean (4.1 and 4.2) and that is what really turns me off about the device more than anything. It already feels like it has been abandoned by Lenovo. * Rooting the device was easy enough. Once it was rooted I was able to install adblock and "freeze" the bloatware that comes with the device (among other less important things that require root). * The processor isn't the fastest but it is fine. It plays Temple Run 2 (which is a fairly new game) nice and smooth. There's some other annoyances: * For whatever reason you cannot apply firmware updates unless you set the default storage location to the internal SD Card. It also refers to the external SD Card as "USB Storage" which is confusing. * The screen resolution is not great. It's fine for a child's toy but I would find it to be unacceptable if it were my personal tablet. Text is not smooth and crisp. * There's not very many accessories available for this tablet. It took a long time for me to find a decent case. * Whenever the device shuts down or boots up it plays a annoying sound at FULL VOLUME which is quite disturbing. There's no way to mute it! What were they thinking?!? Other important notes: * Battery life is acceptable. He can play for hours and the lowest I've seen the battery go is about 30% and that was after a rainy day involving many playing sessions (3D games and whatnot). It's charge time is pretty much the same as any other tablet. * No stability problems whatsoever and the wifi works well. * The device takes an oddly long time to boot up. Probably 1.5-2 minutes. It isn't the longest boot time I've seen but it is still stupidly long. Would I buy this tablet today? No way. There's better/cheaper devices (~$100) running the latest Android version. Always try to get a device that runs Stock Android or "AOSP" because those are the ones that actually keep up-to-date (because all the manufacturer has to do is download the latest source code from Google and compile it--no extra customization necessary).

I bought this printer as a backup/experiment printer to my Creator Pro, plus I figured I could use those 1KG PLA spools piling up against the wall. So I unpacked the printer, loaded the spool that came with it, noting it seemed smaller than usual, but passed it off as just not paying attention or something.. Followed the instructions, found a test print (the 2cm box) after going through the level process, which is the easiest in the business I've experienced so far. The test went perfectly, my next print went off without a hitch, and it's so quiet too! After using the Creator Pro for so long (it's not a subtle printer), I can't even tell if the Finder is printing, all I can hear is the cooling fans, it's great. No problems with prints not sticking, they even include a gluestick (a well known easy way to get that first layer to stick if you are having sticking problems with a non heated build plate), and the easily removable build plate is a fantastic idea I wish more printers had built in. So it is almost the perfect beginner printer. The touch panel works great, as a relative beginner myself in some aspects of 3D printing, it's easy to navigate and know what state your printer is in, and the graphics of the print themselves next to the file name is really cool. The operation of this printer has been virtually flawless. My issue. I know there are workarounds. The requirement of 6KG spools is really tough. I would have no problem purchasing them.. but they are not available.. anywhere. I think I've found a spool or 2 around the internet but this being a new model, you'd think there would be a supply.. or better yet, knowing the standard spool is 1KG, built the new model to accommodate the standard spool? It was frustrating when I found out, having a large supply of good quality PLA filament, I was not able to use that supply out of the box. There was nothing in the description, or sales blurb about needing 6KG spools to fit the filament chamber, or that 1KG spools will not work with this printer out of the box. Some may say this is a mountain out of a mole hill, you can even print the parts you need to work with 1KG spools.. but that should have been advertised with the printer, or some clip on parts included to make it a non issue. It said it came with a small spool, but nothing about "you will need special spools of filament to run this printer". So what would have been an easy 5 star review from me, has been knocked to 3. I don't think I should have to add/make parts not available in the box, to enable my printer to work with standard supplies. Otherwise, this is an amazing printer so far. I haven't tried anything really detailed with it yet, but it has been easier and quicker to get up and working consistently than the Creator Pro, but the CP is made for the more advanced enthusiasts that love to tinker and work with all the settings, it takes some finesse to get prints to work, but the ones that do look amazing, and it's an incredibly versatile machine. Having it as my first printer was probably a leap, but I've learned and am still learning as I go between the community and CS (which is good). Both have been more than helpful working through problems with me. Now that I have bought an entry level machine, it's so cool to compare. Apart from the versatility of the Pro, the Finder prints just as well (in my experience so far, to be clear) as machines much more expensive than it is, especially after the price drop, and also catching it on sale :-) It was money well spent, for the decibel change alone.. ;-) lol. I'm just amazed with the look of the design, the quality of the prints, and several small details other printers just don't have that make the process just that much easier. The required filament spools that are unable to be found, even on the manufacturer's website, is a huge issue to me design-wise. Amazon even pairs the printer with a 1KG spool in their little "buy this together" deal lol, that's just wrong.. I'm in the process of printing parts from the internet that are supposed to enable me to use the larger spools, I will update after I've completed the aftermarket modification to let you know how it goes. EDIT: I have since written to FlashForge about the spool issue, and after discussing with the rep, and so many clean prints since opening and beginning use of the printer, the frustration I initially experienced has passed for the most part. I still see it as a poor design decision, but the ease at which it can be bypassed or fixed sort of makes it a non issue. You can just set the 1kg spool on the ground next to the printer and it'll unwind around the rim, you can use the bottom of a kitchen paper roll holder to sit the spool on and it will spin as needed, or there are more elegant solutions that the community have come up with.. some have designed their own solutions that connect to the printer that you can print yourself. So you can print the part(s) that will fix the problem with the printer.. both a testament to the community, and to the idea of home 3D printing in general. It really is a fantastic printer that spits out perfect print after perfect print. Worthy of the seasoned pro but aimed at the plug and play beginner. The availability of the 0.6kg spools is not as bad as I first thought, they do have a selection of 8 colors on their website, even if the shipping is a bit hefty ;-) The alternative of finding a way to use the standard 1kg spool is much easier and practical, after all, we bought these printers to make useful things. tl;dr - this is the single extruder, small form 3D printer you've been looking for

This does exactly what it was built to, dropped the temperatures of my 960 Pro 1TB considerably. Using onboard M.2 slot : Idle Sensor 1 = 38c Idle Sensor 2 = 58c Load Sensor 1 = 51c (max) Load Sensor 2 = 80c (max) Using Angelbird Wings : Idle Sensor 1 = 33c Idle Sensor 2 = 43c Load Sensor 1 = 39c (max) Load Sensor 2 = 59c (max) I knocked 1 star off for a couple reasons: 1) This is an incredibly cheap unit, probably cost them 15$ to manufacture, with extremely minimal R&D required. It's basically just an adapter to convert the pins of your M.2 SSD to that of a PCIe slot, no controller or anything required. Then slap a piece of aluminum on top. It's a shame there isn't more competition so they couldn't price gouge. 2) The white LEDs. They probably don't fit with most peoples case design. They should be RGB or at least have an off switch. It bugged me enough that before I installed, I had to replace all the white on-board LEDs with blue ones. Was about 3$ in SMD LEDs and an hour with a soldering iron. If anyone is interested in doing the same the LED size/package you need to look for is 0603, the resistor size/package you need is 0402.

I decided to use the TL2 satellites for front left and right channel to better blend bass response with the TL1 center. I also purchased a pair of TL1's for the surround speakers to save a few bucks (like $40 each), since the surround channels are less critical of bass response, IMHO. I am VERY pleased with this setup. I just did an automated setup using my Yamaha 5.1 amp and Onkyo 10" ported sub, and the whole system is seamless, with great separation and clarity. I felt compelled to add about 3 db of bass response to the automatic settings, but otherwise haven't touched it. With the (supposedly) matched Onkyo HTIB speakers that I previously used, I had to tweak with the automatic settings a bit to try to balance the sound across all channels...but never could quite make it sound right while doing a pink noise check. All in all, I highly recommend this setup!

This is my fourth or fifth Kindle. I took advantage of the Prime Day 2019 sale plus buy back to get the Oasis at an affordable price. The Kindle I sold back to Amazon was a first or second generation Kindle Voyage. I was tremendously excited about the grip on the Oasis because it was something that I felt the Voyage needed. I was also excited about it being waterproof; this feature would allow me to take it to the public pool without worry. I had expected that there would be a suitable Amazon cover for it but I can't seem to find one that would allow me to read the way that I generally read. Here were my problems: 1. The screen and item are much smaller than I expected. No, I did not read and measure out the dimensions but every Kindle I have had has had about the same size area for reading. Not the Oasis. To get the same feel, I have to turn it sideways but your options are to either have it sideways or up and down which leads me to ... 2. The screen orientation does not change automatically like a phone. You either have to set portrait or landscape. It will then automatically flip 180 degrees in that orientation. I understand why they would choose to do it this way but a better option would be to have a quick to reach toggle that makes it stick. Right now I have to do five presses to switch between portrait and landscape. If I read in bed and need the grip, I have to change it to portrait mode. At the gym, I have to change it to landscape (it's much more stable on the cardio machine holds with the grip toward the ground; otherwise the grip slants it). 3. I don't know if I got a bad one but battery life sucks even without use. I have it in airplane mode 99% of the time (which means Bluetooth is turned off) and the light setting is at 11. I used to get approximately 3 weeks of life out of the Voyage. I am not getting a week out of the Oasis and I have been using it significantly less than previous months (it's been a slow reading month). 4. The thing is so small and thin that the grip doesn't do much to make it easy to hold. The first problem I had was that holding it on such a way that I could somewhat use the grip made the buttons on the thing awkward to reach. Thankfully they do have the option of reversing the buttons. 5. The power button is way too sensitive. I tried using this at the gym initially in portrait made. I naturally hold this thing in my left hand so I placed it on the machine shelf with the buttons and grip toward the left. This means the power button is on the bottom. Just placing it on the shelf turned it off. I had to flip it around. Okay, I thought, stupid me. Nope, I constantly turn this thing off and on just handling it 6. Which brings me to, why is this thing so slow to turn on? The NuForce NE-6 earphones are very good sounding earphones and an exceptional value. I am a long time audiophile (some would say audiophool) and my main audio system is definitely reference quality helping me appreciate what recorded music can and should sound like. I generally share my biases at the start of my reviews so there is no ambiguity about where I am coming form. And I have many points of view regarding headphones/earphones. Although head and earphones can match and often surpass the accuracy and resolution of high end speakers they do not get the sound stage right. The music always appears to be coming from the middle of your head versus from a natural space in front of you. So spending a lot of coin to achieve the last degree of accuracy and tonal quality but never achieving even a remotely lifelike soundstage seems like a fool's errand to me (unless you are using the earphones as performing musician - a whole different kettle of fish). There are headphone amps that add circuitry to correct this but then you are mucking up the sound quality with another layer of processing. I prefer the sound and comfort of over the earphones to in-ear phones but for anything active or on-the-go, forget that. Even just walking around who wants to use big ol' "cans". So unless your are listening at home I opt for in-ear. Finally, my point of view is that nearly all earphone use today is with iPods/MP3 players. While iPods are capable of excellent sound quality, practically that is rarely achieved. The music files need to be lossless and many of the devices lack the output juice to drive phones to their dynamic potential. Because of all this my feeling is that phones for an iPod should not cost a lot. Well these baby's cost less than ANY Apple iPod. An excellent starting place. They come with four different earpieces. Finding the right one is critical because if you don't get a solid seal inside your ear you will not hear the bass these phones are capable of producing. The sound of the NE-6 phones is very musical. Very good detail and great tonal balance. The strength of the phones is in the mid-range where most of the music lives. The errors of the phones are ones of omission. The treble lacks that last bit of sparkle but for long term listening that is a thousand times preferable to pumped up, exaggerated, hurt your ears high notes. The slightly rolled off top end is in balanced with a lack of the lowest notes - to my ears the bass rolls of around 30 or 40 Hz - but make no mistake, there are plenty of deep and realistic low notes. Perhaps most meaningful, these phones sound many time better than the standard white earbuds. Better in every respect. To get better sound than these you will need to spend three times their cost. The quality of the phones seems solid for the price. NuForce is the real deal too. They are coming on strong as a company offering an expanding line of superb sounding products at industry altering, reasonable prices. If you listen to highly compressed digital files (e.g. 128 kbps) using an inexpensive iPod/MP3 player have your fingers run to Amazon.com, don't walk, and pick up a pair of the NE-6 earphones. It's a most complementary match. And a waste to spend more and a crime to keep listening to the stock white phones. If the ratings allowed a half star I'd give the NE-6's 4 & 1/2 stars. For value they'd get 5 stars plus. For absolute sound, 4 stars, which for the price is a home run. I'd also like to see all earphones come with flat wires to minimize tangling. Bottom Line: You can spend more or less for phones but why when these sound so good and are less than $40.

Purchased this router to replace an older Lynksis 2.4 ghz single band router. Many parts of my home received poor quality reception due to the plaster and lathe construction - particularly the kids rooms in the back of the house. In addition, when multiple people were streaming video or otherwise using the wifi, it was impossible to stream Netflix on the television in the master bedroom. I thought a mesh system was overkill for a 2100 square foot ranch - even with plaster walls - and the reviews and price point of this router were good. Installation was simple out of the box, and setting up the multiple channels was also easy. I assigned each television to a separate channel to avoid streaming conflicts - which has worked out well. Excellent choice for wifi - YMMV as to parenting. The one thing you need to know is whether your device will support the 5ghz band, though. The older TV does not - so it was assigned the 2.4mghz band priority. All of the iPhones, Android devices, Smart TVs, AppleWatches etc... support 5ghz though. For around $80 this is an excellent upgrade for an older router. The real plus is the ability to block a device (hypothetically, for example, an Android telephone belonging to a teenager who has decided that math homework is optional - not that I would do that! - or his Playstation or Xbox - or all of them). Works nicely with the "No Data for You" functionality of the AT&T app, for example. Not a panacea of coverage, but exactly as advertised.

First off, this review is for the 240GB S55 3D VNAND TLC flash listing and therefore may not apply consistently with the other offerings SP has for sale. For the price, it is really hard to complain about the drive, but the speed ratings that have been presented for this drive are misleading. The drive is quick, it does what it is supposed to, and it certainly beats out a hard drive for nearly everything especially application loading, but my complaint is mainly with the sustained sequential writes. The ad touts up to 450MB/s writes for this particular drive which I cannot even get close to with actual file transfers, but in reality that might the speed you are getting with the SLC cache. At the start of a transfer to the drive, the speeds are around 150-200MiB/s, but quickly start coming down. As soon as the cache fills up with the first few GiBs of data in the first 10-15s of a transfer, the speed for writes falls to a measly ~55MiB/s for the remaining duration of the transfer, about half of what I can achieve by writing to a 7200RPM 3.5" hard drive. Reads aren't much of a compliant as I can get ~350MiB/s sequential reads on large files, more than adequate. So, the bottom line is that if you are looking for something that is truly faster than a hard drive in every way, don't get this drive. Spend an extra $10-$20 for one of the better known brands where you will most certainly get speeds that don't fall to ~55MiB/s after the cache fills up. If you are looking to save a few bucks and don't plan on doing a whole lot of 5GiB+ sequential, incompressible writes, then this drive will be a solid choice, especially in a laptop. UPDATE: 5 Months later and this drive is still working with about 3,200 hours on it, and 16.5TiB of data written to it. I have noticed that performance is definitely degraded since it was initially installed. Many of my writes fluctuate heavily from the ~55MiB I typically get with a large transfers often dipping down into the single digits for many seconds before coming back up again. I haven't used any of the software that SP has for their drives, but my tools to review S.M.A.R.T. data no longer show the life or total reads/writes of the drive which started happening once the drive got to about 95% life remaining. 95% life with only 16.5TiB written is very poor when compared to my much older 120GB MLC drive from another manufacturer that has had the same amount of data written to it and it still shows 100% life with significantly more S.M.A.R.T. stats to show. Lastly, it seems that the temperature sensor is stuck at 33C at all times. At this point, I think i'll end up putting this into something else and getting myself something a bit more reputable. For the price it is great for internet, email, and most applications, but it is not a good fit for larger data sets and somewhat heavy use.

Overall Thoughts Lovely receiver, well designed, perfect power for medium sized rooms, and extremely easy to set up. It is also future proofed for sometime to come with the latest HDMI spec on all HDMI inputs (UHD bluray players, Xbox one s, 4K content). Just completed setting up a new HT system in my game room. This recevier has the right amount of power for my Definitive BP8060ST speakers (Fronts), Definitive pro center 1000 (Center), SM55 bookshelfs (surround), and A60 (Atmos speakers). Running a complete Atmos package of 5.2.2 and the sound is incredible given the size of my room which is around 3000cu ft. I am an electrical engineer and assuming all the efficiencies of the power supply and the transformer this receiver is mostly putting around 70watts RMS to all channels when are all driven together. Any area of over 3000cuft, and you are better off buying a more powerful receiver or running this receiver with an external amplifier that is capable of at least 100 watts per channel. The other option would be to get higher efficiency speakers (Klipsch, Tekton Design etc). Audessey Set up This is my first time using Audessey calibration and the whole process was painless. this model comes with the mid level Audessey solution MultEQ-XT. The higher versions have a seperate Sub EQ which will help users with multiple large subwoofers. I skipped this since my room is medium sized and this does come with the basic bass eq through calibration. Set up the provided microphone on a tripod and move it between 8 spots in your listening area. Once the readings are done, the receiver does its calculations for the speaker size, speaker distance, reflections, overall sound level and equalizes all the peaks and nulls to get you pretty flat response. I highly recommend turning on the Dynamic EQ setting as this is what is tailored for your particular room. The dynamic volume is also a great feature that does apply compression to the audio signal to make the signal flat. This really helps with the impact of the movie when watching at night at lower volumes. There is also a seperate Dialogue enhancement setting which helps with the level of the dialogue through the center channel. Overall the entire system rocks especially when it comes to movies in a HT setting. You can easily reach theater level sound in a medium sized room - 0db with headroom to spare. Remote The remote is well laid out and easy to use. I use a universal remote so this is a moot point. If i need to access a hard to find setting once a while, I could always reach for this remote. Connectivity This particular model works well with the 2.4GHZ bandwidth signals. Anyone running only 5GHZ in thier home might need to think about this. The setup process was like any other device, ask it to scan for networks and then enter the password for your network. Once it is connected you have the following options open up 1. Internet Radio - This is exteremely good for quickly finding a radio station and playing your favorite music. 2. Online Music - You have option of pandora and few others. I have not used this since i normally stream music through pandora on my Blu ray player anyways. Power, Music and Movies Power - As mentioned in my initial section. This recevier is great for a medium sized HT room where you plan to entertain 6-8 people without any additional power needed. If you are targetting a much bigger space, highly recommend augmenting this with a 3x100 or 3x150 amplifier for the fronts and let the receiver power the rest. Movies/Music For movies this receiver is perfect. You can achieve theater like sound without stressing the system with some headroom to spare in medium sized rooms. I watched Transformers- Age of Extinction, Tron Legacy which are both great for torture testing a HT system and the experience was amazing. It almost necessitated getting a larger 4K TV compared to my 46inch Samsung HDTV which i currently own. Cannot wait to upgrade to a 4K TV to check out movies in UHD Blu Ray. Music is probably the only place where I was left wanting. I am a professional musician and am used to live music as well as listening through large powered systems, and several thousand dollars worth of monitors. So my expectation for music might be biased. I had to Turn off most of the Audessey enhancements to dial the sound I wanted manually. But once you start tweaking settings it defeats the whole Audessey measurements on the movie front. I am used to a Sony Elite receiver and that one is still amazing when it comes to music dynamics. This receiver is ok for Stereo music, much better using one of the enhanced sound modes like Dolby surround or multichannel stereo for getting a better overall sound. But since this recevier is in my dedicated HT room which will mainly be used for movies, I am not docking a star of my rating or the receiver. Thumbs up to Denon for making such a great product. I lucked out purchasing from Accessories4less on a refurbished unit which is in perfect condition, and does everything a new units do. Unless you need 5 GHZ support and the Sub EQ i suggest you skip the 3300W model and pick this one instead when supplies last. A steal considering the newer model is selling for $1k. Update: My initial impression of this receiver not being good for music was pretty short lived. After reading a lot of other people having similar issues like mine, I ended up checking out audessey forums and found my answers. In the Dynamic eq section there is a space for reference level offset. I had it at 0db for movies and never changed it when listening to music. I had to move it to 15db for all music and then all music seemed to have a better balanced tonal quality. The receiver guides you on screen for the settings 5db, 10db and 15db offset and what they are used for based on sound you are listening to classical, jazz and modern compressed music. In the end I choose modern compressed music which seemed to work the best for all the types of music that I listen to. Your preference might vary, but I wanted to provide this information to other users who are struggling with the right setting for music. Overall amazing product that ticks all the boxes.

Pros: Works fine with an 8TB drive, USB3=>SATA interface seems to perform well (>200 MB/s on OS X w/ Seagate ST8000VN0022 8TB drive), interface seems solid (no errors over 8 hours of solid file copying - not always the case for USB3 drive interfaces). Drive spins down when idle long enough (this can be a pro or a con, depending on your use case). Cons: No SMART support, so you can't query the drive temperature or configure auto-spin-down. The cooling is really not sufficient. The fan is very quiet, but it also doesn't move much air. After my drive was operating overnight in a 70°F house, it was almost too hot to touch. Measuring its temperature with an IR heat gun, the bottom of the drive was 57°C, which is almost beyond the manufacturer's maximum temperature (beyond which they may not honor warranty claims) of 60°C. Note that modern drives internally record the maximum temperature observed, so if your drive overheats in this enclosure and you return it for warranty, it may not be honored. Note that the drive I'm using is relatively power-hungry at 9.0 W. Lower-powered drives may do better, but given the marginal cooling I'd recommend avoiding this dock for continuous use. And I'd really recommend staying away from the fanless dock.

I originally bought another brand that offered higher resolution, but found that the interface was clunky and the fan noise was way too loud. I hesitated buying the Nebula because the resolution was only 480p and the brightness was rated at 200 lumen. After doing a bit more research was convinced the the resolution would be adequate for my needs; I wanted a small, very portable projector that I can plug my laptop into and run presentations, videos, and maybe stream a movie or two. This device does it all. First the resolution. Yes, you can tell that it is a lower resolution picture, but when the movie is playing you really don't see it. DVDs are rated at 720p and streamed movies come in at 480p or 720p, so you're really not missing anything unless you want to watch BluRay or other hi-rez content. So, for my needs, 480p is fine. Brightness is next and at 200 lumen you can watch a movie in a shadowed room with the projector about 4 feet from your wall. That gives you a 50" diagonal picture that's bright and very easy to see. The darker the room the further back you can move it, but don't go pass 6 feet. I have mine on a coffee table that's about 4 feet from the wall. I can move it forward to 4 feet and back to about 5 feet on the table. Works out great. Nebula runs a version of Android and it appears to be regularly updated. It comes with several streaming service apps like Amazon Prime and Hulu. I use Prime and have been satisfied with the service though I wish they'd offer more. Because it is Android you can also get other apps and games. I have VLC for playing movies from a DVD player. I haven't tried that yet, but I have a movie I made on a USB hard drive and it plays perfectly using VLC or the built in player, so I don't think using a USB DVD player will be a problem. Sound quality is surprisingly adequate. The built in speaker is loud enough for small rooms, but you might want something bigger if your environment isn't..., um... cozy. A few other things. I like the auto-tilt correction. I wish the fan was a bit quieter, but it's not obnoxious like the crappy thing I had before. Get a small tripod to mount it on. Makes life a bit easier. Also download the apps and use your phone to control it, better than the touchy touch interface on the top of the projector or the useful, but spartan remote. All in all, it a solid product and I'd recommend it.

Pictures are typically bright, clear, and finely detailed, as appropriate for the 7MP digital chip inside. On the road I was getting roughly 250 images for each set of 4 AA batteries (We forgot to pack our charger for the rechargable batteries we bought). The flash was bright and well illuminated group photos at a twilight family reunion that was turning to full darkness by the time we broke up. Switching to the landscape mode provided excellent landscape shots. We had a lot time under bright hazy clouds and full overcast, switching to the aperture mode let you focus on the building or feature you wanted to photograph so it wouldn't be too dark when the photo was snapped. However, sometimes this led to an over-exposed appearance for the images. The 10x Zoom was really useful for wildlife shots (Grizzly, elk, buffalo, antelope, deer, coyote, prairie dogs, etc.) The software packages allows you to enter some brief comments on the picture subsject as well as recording the date and time that the pictures are taken. Where could the improvements come: This is a complex camera with the various settings. A few days isn't enough time to really learn how to use it, especially under a variety of weather conditions and types of composition. I don't know that you can really blame Fuji for this, but users should understand there is a learning curve here. If you use the viewfinder (which I use a lot for outdoor shots in bright sun) your nose smudges the LCD. After taking a shot, you have to hit the "OK" button to advance the camera, but the "OK" button is in the center of a variety of other controls so unless you hit the buttom exactly dead on, then you may trigger other functions like flash, brightness, etc. I was spending a lot of time resetting controls as a consequence. The software was a little balky at creating a duplicate image for cropping. I ended up doing that work in the MS Picture Manager package that is on my Windows. Overall, this is a fine camera with a lot of versatility, but you'll need awhile to learn how to use all the capabilities and a fine touch on the controls since things are bunched close to one another on the button next to the LCD

For less than $25, I got a decent tripod that's reasonably stable, with several nice features. Each leg has two extensions that will lock at any point along their lengths. Having used it only twice at the range, I can't say if the leg locks will continue to hold firm, but for now, the friction is good and the platform is quite stable at any height I can conceive of needing. As Range Safety Officer, while watching things pretty close, I can also spot for several shooters at a time, sometimes for five hours at a stretch, and I need to stay comfortable. My spotting scope has an angled eyepiece, so I look down into it -- the tripod can be shorter than I'd need for a straight eyepiece. I'm 5'10", and with the legs fully extended I only need to crank up the height adjustment two or three inches to be able to use the scope without bending over at all. This tripod would be equally comfortable for a person who was 6'5" or more. In addition to the usual crank-up height adjustment, There are three "attitude" adjustments: a protruding handle lets you swing the scope (or camera) vertically; a knob lets you pan the scope/camera horizontally; and a small "wing-nut" lets you tilt the scope/camera 90°, but ONLY TO THE RIGHT. That seemed like a problem at first -- when shooting at a bench, I like the scope to be to the right of the bench, with the angled eyepiece tilted LEFT toward me. If you'll check my photos, you'll see that I just reversed the scope (it'll mount either way), and tilted it left. There are two levels built into the tripod, one to let you ensure that the platform is level, the other to ensure that the vertical adjustment is level. For a spotting scope, this isn't much of an advantage, but for a camera, it would be nice to have fewer photos with a drunken horizon listing 15° to starboard [...and I KNOW I ain't the only one who takes FUBAR photos like tipsy Uncle Gargle.] The rubber-clad feet are plastic ball-sockets that fit onto balls at the ends of the legs...they swivel around easily, giving the tripod secure footing, even when the ground is uneven. I thought the handle was an unnecessary add-on (never had one on a tripod before, so didn't figure I needed one). Plus, it seemed to be in the wrong place. But it ain't. With the scope (or a heavy camera) mounted, you can give the center-lock a quick twist, raise it to pull in the legs, and securely carry the tripod and scope from one end of a busy firing-line to the other, then set it back up in just a second. Sweet. Those are all the good things. What about bad and/or ugly? Well, the ball at the end of one of the feet on my tripod had snapped off during transit, and was loose in the bag with its rubber-coated socket-foot. I needed the tripod that weekend, so no time to exchange. Fortunately, the plastic spindle at the end of the foot (which ends in the ball) is NOT solid plastic, but a tube. I took a bamboo chopstick, whittled/scraped the end until it fit tightly into the tube, cut off a 1/2-inch piece to form a plug, doused one end with super glue, rammed it into the leg, doused the other end with super-glue and rammed it into the ball. Waited five minutes. Now I can't tell which leg I fixed. Damn I'm good. So is there anything really wrong with this tripod? Nope. It is not a beefy piece of over-engineered Mercedes-Benz hardware. It is more like something off a Yugo. It's light-weight, it's Chinese, and you aren't going to be passing it down through the generations. But what the heck, it works, and I can afford to replace it, if it gets damaged.

The NEC LCD2490WUXi2-BK 24" WIDESREEN LCD MONITOR is a beautiful little monitor. It has "Professional Quality" written all over it. Viewing DVD movies is enjoyable as is surfing the internet, but the key is to couple this unit with a NEC Display Spectraview II Calibration custom Sensor Colorimeter with its included software (software and device are MAC and PC compatible as is the monitor itself). This mouse-like object sets over the middle of the screen and performs a calibration of the screen to insure consistent color reproduction be it by print, video, web, or any of several other calibration methods. Once the screen is calibrated for your particular media selection, the software automatically creates an ICC Calibration Profile for that particular media so you can reproduce the look you see on the monitor to the selected output media (at this point I have not performed an accurate check of how well this does work, but some of the items I have posted on the web appear to look like I expect them with accurate color balances). The Colorimeter works its magic by directly modifying the NEC monitor internally with no operation manually required by you. This is possible because the Colorimiter is hooked to your computer through a USB port as is the monitor itself so they can easily communicate. The size of the 24" monitor is enough to show spreads comfortably. If I had the extra bucks, a larger version of this unit would be nice, but I am quite happy with the 24" version. You won't be disappointed at all.

Oh, Tibetan chants, Gregorian Chant, in Cathedran music, and voice are fabulous. I can hear the individual hairs in my ears responding to individual waves! I purchased the 130" 16:9 screen and I couldn't be happier. I recently upgraded to a 1080P projector and the painted wall I used for my prior projector didn't cut it. I also bought screen samples from another source and evaluated several surfaces and colors to use in my controlled light basement. Saw the Vevor in the hard to find 130" size at a reasonable price and decided to buy expecting due to size, pricing, no need to construct a frame Etc this should be an economical quick easy way out. Turns out the stretch white PVC fabric is a dead on match for my second choice from the sample pack. Instructions were better than adequate although I would suggest wearing vinyl gloves throughout and, after assembling the frame, mount it to wall then dismount, stretch fabric, remount to wall and enjoy. For me that was under 2 hours of easy work using extra hands only for final mounting. The very sturdy frame is an aluminum extrusion with channels for all the hardware. Mine came with extra stretch anchors so I installed the "spares" near the corners so if in the unlikely event one of the stretched to anchors should break replacements are right there for the sliding and re stretching. The combination of stretched fabric sheet, robust anchors and stress distribution rods results in a flat tensioned surface. The wall mount clips slide in a groove so final positioning on wall is a snap. The velveteen frame covering does a fine job absorbing overthrow and looks fine with the lights on or off. It is claimed to be water washable but I'm hoping just an occasional feather dusting is all I'll be doing for quite some time. The picture is excellent in all areas with the room darkened to theater lighting. Room lighting is supplied by ceiling mounted cans with adjustable eyeballs which I keep pointed away from the screen. Using moderate lighting the picture holds up remarkable well for a projection onto the neutral white screen but dropping the lights turns the picture from good-very good to awesome. Excellent color brightness and contrast. I have not tried this with short throw, 4k or 3d but would expect at least very good results. The theater room is 11 feet wide, 28 feet long and (white) acoustical ceiling height of 7 foot 8 inches. Wall to wall broadloom is gray in color as are the walls, which are painted with neutral gray eggshell paint. The 4 feet of ceiling closest to the screen has been painted with flat black to remove the distraction of abstract motion on the ceiling as well as reduce light backsplash. The (medium throw) projector is mounted 15 feet back from screen and seating is at 12 feet. To wrap up I couldn't be more pleased. I would not suggest this for use in a brightly lit area but there is an acceptable reduced quality picture seen under moderate indirect lighting so pitch black is not mandatory although desirable. Fit and finish seem top notch, as does choice of materials. I look forward to enjoying this excellent product for a very long time. Considering a highest performance top shelf name brand screen costs about 15 times what this cost I believe the value this excellent performing screen provides is remarkably huge provided it stands the test of time. In the unlikely event that replacement is needed in a few years I still would feel I got my monies worth. More likely this could outlast a few projectors if properly (not) handled and not smoked on. Big thumbs up for performance and value if you have a dark room, thumbs up for value under moderate lighting and meh under more lighting. I'd get in line to buy this again.

I just received this and am writing to share my first impression after setup and some test use. The exec summary is that I'm very pleased with this for my intended use. Details below. Background: I shoot shows and events professionally. I usually carry two camera bodies (Nikon D700 and D800) with two different f2.8 lenses mounted (24-70 and 70-200 or larger prime depending on the venue size). Up to now I have usually carried both bodies on BlackRapid straps. So I've also tried having one camera on a Gitzo monopod while the other is on a BlackRapid strap. Again, this has worked well, but the mix of strap and monopod always feels awkward, especially when I'm using the camera on the strap, as I have to somehow support the monopod without my hands, which can be distracting/awkward or worse. So I got this horizontal mounting bar to try mounting both cameras on the monopod, with the hope that it would allow me to easily carry around and use both cameras with the support and control I'm looking to add. Out of the box impression was very positive. The bar and clamps look and feel pro level. One small issue is that the setscrew on the Gitzo's mounting plate does not line up with the receiving hole on the base of the Vanguard's mounting clamp. However it was possible to tighten the setscrew up against another indentation in the base of the mounting clamp, and the result seems to be holding well so far. I may end up drilling another hole in the bottom of the mounting clamp base to eliminate this as a concern. And my cameras attached easily/solidly to the bar. I saw some other reviews that complained about the Vanguard having just 3/8" mounting screws on the camera brackets. But mine had 3/8" adapters OVER 1/4" screws. It was easy to remove the adapters so my 1/4" camera sockets fit perfectly on the mounting clamps. So everything went together out of the box as hoped. Use. Everything feels very solid, and the balance is good. There's plenty of room to operate both cameras. Based on 15/20 minutes of trial shooting outside the house, it seems like this rig will work very well. I'll report back if there are problems.

Decided to order this wire as the specs suggested it was of a very decent quality, and they were right. I needed to temporarily put my outdoor TV antenna up on the hill above my house, which is a fairly long run of about 375 feet, and this coax was indeed sunlight resistant and very well-insulated, so for the price I couldn't find anything comparable for my temporary use. It came as a 500 ft. coil on a plastic spool, inside of the cardboard pullbox. Distribution of the wire couldn't be easier, just take the spool out of the box, remove the plastic wrapper, and remove the knockout on the end of the box and insert the wire to unwind from the bottom to your selected knock-out, and fold up the top of the box into the handy carrying handle. I had the wire unwound in less than 15 minutes from my antenna sight - - piece of cake - - and the rest of the spool stayed kink-free and had no problems unwinding on the way down the hill. I purchased some decent-quality connectors and they attached easily. The wire is nicely-insulated, with good-quality copper clad steel wire core and several layers of foil insulation and high-quality braided insulation under the tough black exterior. It's fairly flexible, and seems like it will last for years. In the end, I picked up lots of good stations and have a high signal strength now on all my TV's, so I'm very pleased with this wire. While this brand is not near the costliest coax available, I'd say it's tough and heavy-duty enough for most any application. I would highly recommend this wire to most anyone. I've done a good bit of installation of TV and audio over the years and I've seen some crummy coax, and some excellent - - this product seems to be of the excellent variety. NOTE: A little trick I learned on unrolling wire from a pullbox - - take the spool out of the box before you start, and notice where the edges of the spool lay on the bottom of the box (you'll see a couple of long indentations in the pasteboard box bottom) - - take a candle and rub wax onto these two lines (liberally) and also around the edges of the spool where they touch the bottom) and replace the spool. You'll be amazed how easily the spool unrolls!! But, be careful and not let it outrun you now, especially downhill!

For the price, these are excellent speakers. They sound super-clear with accurate full-range reproduction and even a bit of bass. i got them at a sale price which made them somewhat of a no-brainer, although i considered Yamaha and Sony 3-way bookshelf speakers and the Polk tsi100 which is almost functionally the same except it has an active crossover, which these lack. However for my purposes, that didn't matter -- i am using them as surrounds in a 5.1 system, all Polk, with a Sony receiver. You could pay more for surrounds, but why? Sound quality is excellent, and they handle transitions between complex passages to more isolated ones faithfully. They also do well with both acoustic and electronic musical elements. If i had to describe the soundstage, it's present, with clear separation between frequencies. They are maybe a little on the crisp side but not shrill, in terms of tonality, though that will also depend on what music you play through them. (EDIT: It's been a few years now, and I've listened to lotta of music and movies through these speakers. As long as you know their limitations and strengths, you'll be fine with these.) I havent done extensive testing yet, nor put them through their paces with a home theater audio source, but their performance with music raises no expectation that they wouldn't handle typical movie audio as well. They are only rated to 50w continuous/100w peak, so that is something to consider if you are thinking of using them as mains. (EDIT: in engineering these, Polk chose to emphasize sound fidelity. These aren't going to have bass like a 3-way speaker. They have a max. volume rating which may preclude use as mains in larger rooms. But they are under $100 for a pair and sound fantastic for what they are.) I would say they are perfect as surrounds in a 5.1 system, which places lower power demands on rear speakers so the wattage rating doesn't matter. But i could see going with 4 of these in a home theater set-up, or 4 plus a subwoofer, for a small room. The freq. response only goes down to 60khz, so you are not going to get deep bass from these. But you will hear some bass, which sounds surprisingly clean on sound selections where low-end is isolated and "ripples" through all channels. I personally chose the Monitor 60s as my mains because I listen to a lot of music. I bought my EdgeRouter 6P as an upgrade from an EdgeRouter POE, and so that I can have two working routers and do not have to be offline while upgrading the firmware. I previously tried an EdgeRouter X for this purpose and found it to be useless because the ER-X has so little storage. Just enable logging, and the ER-X hit disk-full and stop working in two weeks. The ER-6P is another story. It has 4GB of flash storage to the ER-POE's 2GB, 1GB of RAM to the ER-POE's 512MB, and four 1GHz MIPS64 cores to the POE's two 600MHz cores. It is a MUCH more powerful router for not very much more money. It arrived back-rev'd on the firmware, but it is a matter of a couple of commands to reflash it to the latest version. Also unlike the ER-POE, the EdgeRouter 6P has an optional rack-mount kit available (that will fit anything from an ER-4 to an ER-12). Some users complain about the administration GUI. I find it OK, but I don't use it for most configuration tasks, just for traffic monitoring, preferring to ssh login to the router and use the command-line. I also don't use the supplied firewall functionality, preferring to use Shorewall instead, which I find both much more powerful and much easier to configure. (The rule-chains interface used by netfilter is cryptic and pointlessly arcane.) My ER-POE is now a spare; I will use it to test out new firmware releases and while updating the 6P. If you have an older EdgeRouter and want to get more performance, this latest generation of routers is a good upgrade. If you're just getting started, they provide much better performance than anything Netgear or D-Link will sell you — but you DO need to at least somewhat know what you're doing. You will still need a cable or DSL modem; these routers will not do that for you. If you want to have WiFi, the EdgeRouter won't do that either; consider trying one of Ubiquiti's Unifi wireless access points instead. A Unifi WAP will give you much better wireless coverage than almost any wireless router appliance on the market, for less money, and you can add additional WAPs if you need more coverage much more easily than you can add additional consumer wireless routers.

I only wore them once, when I first got them - they were purchased for traveling on airplanes. I used to promote Monster Products at some events that I used to coordinate back in 2013 and 2014. I became so enamored with the way everybody would gush over these headphones, that I bought a pair of these Monster DNA Pro Over-Ear Headphones for myself and the smaller DNA On-Ear versions for my kids (at an affiliate discount - direct from the manufacturer). My kids wear theirs all the time and have had no problems in the 2 years they've had theirs. I also bought the Bluetooth iSport Freedom On-Ear headphones and a pair of iSport Earbuds for working out and outdoor activities. Like I said, I only wore my DNA Pro Over-Ear headphones once, then I put them back in the original manufacturer's box and on to a shelf for safe keeping, because I had left the company I was working for at the time and I stopped traveling for a living. Since I prefer my Bluetooth headphones and earbuds for everyday use, I didn't really have much of a need for the bulky over-ear DNAs. Anyway, I've managed to get into another job that requires travel and my first business trip was to the Philippines in August of 2016. I was so excited that I was finally going to be able to use my DNA headphones for what I bought them for...travel on noisy airplanes and 15+ hour travel days. I reached for the box, pulled out the headphones and low and behold... I found they had ripped ear cushions. WHAT?!?! Why? How? Those kids! I went down the line and grilled each and every one of them, "Who broke my headphones!?" They all declared their innocence; and admittedly, the box looked untouched. I called a friend to see if they had any airplane appropriate headphones, and knowing about the Monster box on the shelf, he asked me why I didn't just use my Monster Pro DNAs. I explained what had happened to the ear cushions, and he confessed... the same thing had happened to his. Really?! I couldn't believe it. You see, I convinced him to buy a pair at one of my events. In fact, I convinced several mutual friends and acquaintances who attended the events to buy a pair. It was part of my job. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ He told me that several of our friends had the same problems...but they all thought it was from constant wear & tear. In their line of work, they use headphones...a lot. (It's an industry thing.) But, mine were in their original box, on a shelf...untouched. Even my friend was befuddled. I live in a home with climate controlled central air and my thermostat is set at a constant temperature, so there are no random fluctuations of hot or cold. (My home is never empty with three kids, so the thermostat is never turned off.) So, it couldn't be due to poor storage conditions. If it's not wear & tear, and it's not fluctuations in temperature...then what? The only answer is a manufacturer's defect. Mine were first generation, brand new off the assembly line, so it must have been a flaw in the way the DNA product line was designed. Has it been fixed? I don't know...perhaps; but when I look a the official website at monsterproducts-dot-com, Monster is no longer selling the DNA product line. I'm guessing that what's being sold on Amazon is that first batch of leftover defective and abandoned overstock. I don't know if Amazon is an authorized dealer of Monster Products, because I never actually worked for Monster. I was just an event coordinator for an affiliate company. Monster does have some great products. I love my Bluetooth iSport Freedom headphones and my iSport earbuds. But neither are really comfortable for extended wear of more than 6 hours because they are meant to stay clamped to your head or lodged in your ears during heavy activity. I have to admit, that it's very disappointing for me to have to post this poor review of the DNA Pros because they are super comfortable and the sound is pretty darn good; but I pride myself on honesty and this is an honest review. I give them two stars for sound & comfort and the fact that I CAN still use them (they still function and feel exactly the same as they did before the pads ripped); but a flaw is a flaw and a rip is a rip... even with my discount, I didn't get value for my money. P.S., If you have a pair of these headphones, keep the professional aux cable, it's great!

UPDATE 10/5/12: In Mexico for work and everything is working great! So happy to have my Directv channels in my hotel room. Using my laptop wired to internet and hdmi to the tv. I just received this to set up with my directv receiver, hoping to get to watch all my fall shows and football games while working out of country. SET UP: Set up was a breeze (I am typically good with electronics) and I have never used any equipment similar to this or slingbox etc. Just connect the cables from the @TV to your receiver as shown in the diagram, then the IR blasters sit in front of the receiver where the remote sensor is. This @TV is capable of working on wifi, but my router is near my receiver so I went with the wire connection with supplied Ethernet cable. I then downloaded the software program to my laptop. Install and open the program, to initially set up the equipment you must run through some prompts. FIRMWARE UPDATE: When running the initial set up it told me a firmware update was found. But you have to have your laptop/PC connected to the same home network and WIRED. My laptop was on wireless and it kept failing, until I switched to wired to the router. Then all went smooth and completed initial set up. USE ON LAPTOP: I got on my wifi network at home to try it out. Streaming was super easy, there is a full size image of the directv remote on screen that I can interact with. There is a small lag delay when pressing buttons, but I can get over that. Make sure to set your receiver settings to auto detect the channel's resolution. If the channel is SD you will see a 480i output, and when a channel is HD your receiver should always adjust to 720p or 1080i. The @TV program easily reflected this also. It was a notceable difference in an SD and HD source, and the window size adjusts wider for HD channels. Now, on your PC you will NOT see true HD as clean as you would on your actual TV. You are at the mercy of the component cables and your connection. But it does look very clean! I am impressed! USE ON IPAD: Using wifi at home. The app is free as stated, then you just log in. Works the same as the PC program, but you won't see a full size remote. However the interactive remote it shows is easy to use and navigate to do all the functions you would on PC. I think quality looked even better on the ipad because of the smaller screen size. HD shows looked awesome. Notes: Your TV at home does not need to be on when using streaming remotely. But the receiver will power on whenever you are watching remotely. That makes sense, but I didn't realize it had to be on at first and couldn't get a picture. So I brought up the interactive remote on my laptop screen and hit the power button and there was the picture. I even had a friend across state dl the program and log in and he said it worked great. WHAT I LIKE: -Ease of use -Interactive controls are just like being home using the remote. -Clean set up. -Nice picture -I can access my DVR list of shows. -I can record shows to my PC or iPad. WHAT I DON'T LIKE: -short lag when pressing remote buttons on the software, but it isn't horrible. -not much else yet. Will see how it looks and operates with a worse connection when I am out of country. Right now I am just on wifi at home and it is a pretty fast connection. Will report back later once I test our of country. But so far I am very pleased! I did lots of research and this exceeded my expectations. I highly recommend.

I can't say enough good things about the Sony DSCW80, but I'll mention 10 features that I've been particularly pleased with: 1. Battery life is excellent and charging time is reasonable. 7. The mode selector provides brief on-screen explanations as each mode is selected. 8. The camera has a view finder (which is invaluable when the sun is shining on the LCD screen). 9. The camera includes shutter-click and other useful sound effects. 10. The flash is well-synchronized and it can be manually calibrated to provide higher or lower flash intensity - a great feature! I could be describing a camera that costs $1,000 and weighs 2 pounds, but the DSCW80 offers so much in such a tiny, low-cost package - it's just amazing!

This is my first fitness band. I've worn it for 4 months. People seem to enjoy the pro and con review style so here you go ... PROS - the band and watch are comfortable and not at all cumbersome. - the band size is great if you prefer a small form factor. And a great trial option if, like me, you haven't worn a watch in 30 years. - the display is good and maximizes the information available for a small screen. - watch faces are limited but a decent number of options for a low-end band - the swipe control is good, not great. - phone notifications work well, but not so great for long text messages. - water proof -- necessary feature to be able to wear in the shower and the pool - step tracking seems to be very accurate - blood pressure readings are accurate as verified by our Omron BP monitor - sleep tracking is pretty accurate when the band fits properly (see associated con below); may record as sleep when lying still, but I believe that to be true with most bands. - fitness activity tracking is good, but information is limited. I play soccer twice a week and while the band is good at recording heart rate, it does not track distance which would seem to be an obvious metric for that activity. CONS - I am generally very gentle with electronic devices, but the Galaxy Fit screen has 3 noticeable scratches on it. Can't recall what version of gorilla glass was supposedly used, but it needs to be drastically improved. - I am in between sizes, so when I first started wearing the band it was loose, and tracking data was not accurate. After a couple of weeks, the band stretched enough to move down a notch without cutting off circulation. With a snug fit, the tracking information improved greatly. - maybe the most important con to me so far is the battery life. For the first 30 to 60 days, I was easily getting the advertised battery life of 6 days which was great. Since then, battery life has continued to decline at the same activity levels and using the same settings. I am currently lucky to get 3 full days before having to recharge. I am concerned this downward trend will continue. - sleep data is touchy after waking up. I generally have to scroll to the sleep data screen immediately in order for it to save to the app properly. If interrupted by other processes -- alarms, etc. -- it sometimes will not record the sleep data. It will then say "no data available" and there is no way to retrieve it. - the associated fitness app is okay, but information is limited. My wife's Garmin has significantly better fitness information, trends, etc. - alarms sometimes freeze. The workaround is to hold down the power button for a couple of seconds and the band seems to do a soft reset and then performs normally. - there were a couple of updates within the first 30 days of release to add watch faces and software updates. But no new updates in the last 90 days. Overall this is a good starter band at a decent price. And knowing that I'm okay wearing a watch again, I will certainly upgrade to a more advanced band.

I bought this card to replace my RX 570 graphics card hoping I would get a major boost in performance. That hasn't been the case so far. I have Windows 10 up to date, the right graphics card drivers, the right power supply, everything. Everything is right in MSI Afterburner and power limit is set to +20. But still this card performs worse than my RX 570 at times, I'll be playing and my Core Clock frequencies will be all over the place, dropping to as low as 300mhz for no reason then spiking back up to 1750mhz, then up and down over and over again. No matter what I lock the frequency to, it still will go all over the place. This makes the frames rates range from 10-165 FPS and it creates massive stutters. I've done everything I can to get this card working properly it still, nothing. Definitely wouldn't recommend as of now. (Edit) I bought a replacement card and got the same result. I think I found the problem and I'm pretty sure it has to do with the VRM's (Voltage Regulator Modules) and a bad cooling configuration. Every time I start up a game, it seems to do fine, only for a minute or so. It starts off by running at it's intended frequency and proper power supply voltage, then GPU frequencies and power supply usage will drop drastically, then go back up and down again. These issues can be caused by overheating of the VRM's, which explains why my GPU's back plate gets unreasonably hot after only a few minutes of gaming. I guess I shouldn't be surprised though since the RX 5700's older brother (RX 5700 XT) from XFX got bad reviews from critiques because of bad cooling, and both cards look similar when it comes to the heating configuration.

Bought the 10 pack of adjustable buck regulators for a LED lighting application. You get what you pay for in this case. These are so terrible! A quick test on my work bench proved just how bad... I tuned it for 5V(no load), 12V intput. At only 0.5A load these exhibit > 1.0Vpp ripple at 340 KHz! BAD! The regulation dropped to 4.4V average... So I turned it up to 5V. (was then 7V at no load) Things only get worse from there. At 2A, it started to cut out periodically. The thermal camera showed the chip as the hottest part, about 70C on the surface. The ripple was now at 2.5Vpp (now at 160 KHz). Unacceptable junk. I will try to see how much cap is needed to make these work. The efficiency is only marginally better than a linear regulator. Nowhere near 90%, much less than advertised. Cap will not help this. So, they got my money. I'm only out 6 USD.
