I upgraded from a 2017 HD 8 that was always incredibly slow when doing almost anything other than watching videos or reading eBooks... once you finally got the apps opened. The 1.5GB RAM was an anchor in the 2017 HD 8 causing significant usability issues. I went with the 2021 HD 10 Plus to maximize the amount of RAM, and after all is said and done with my use case (web browsing, streaming apps, social media, eBooks... not gaming, which might push it over the edge), I haven't seen the free RAM dip below 2GB, so the processor upgrade is helping, too. 4X A53 in the 2017 HD 8, but 4X A53 + 4X A73 in the 2021 HD 10. FYI - this is even with Google Play Services and Store sideloaded and running, and free RAM is still plentiful. For $180, this isn't a great deal, but it's been on sale for $130 (even less for the non-Plus) which definitely works. $180 is too much for this device; the screen, while 1080p, has the issue of early smartphones where the display layer is physically farther from the touch layer and looks "dead" compared to an iPhone or Samsung flagship, where it feels like you're touching a layer of glass on top of the display elements instead of interacting directly with the items rendered on the screen. This sounds like an unquantifiable touchy-feely (no pun intended) complaint, but try this tablet, then an iPhone or Galaxy S6 or higher, and you can immediately tell. Beyond that, the touch isn't quite as responsive as an iPhone or Samsung flagship. BUT, it's $130 (on sale... less if you get the non-Plus). That's a killer deal. Whether you need the Plus is up to you. I haven't found that the extra RAM has been needed (which is 1) based on my use case, and 2) a statement that NEVER remains true as time goes on). The soft-touch finish is nicer than the standard finish; pessimistically, I'm concerned it'll wear off, where the normal plastic on my HD 8 never did, but in about a month, there are no signs of wear yet. The wireless charging is nice to have if you need it. If you repurpose an existing wireless charger, just a heads up that the tablet doesn't have any visual indication of where the inductive coil is, so the first few times you charge it, you need to be careful that it's lined up correctly so that it actually charges. This is solved by buying the official wireless charger where it sits in such a way as to force the correct placement. It would've been nice if the Plus came with 64GB storage by default instead of by upgrade. So... 2021 HD 10? — absolutely. Especially when it's on sale for around $100. HD 10 Plus... it'll be up to you if you expect to need the RAM and/or really need wireless charging.

I have several hundred movies I have taped over the years on VHS tapes and decided I wanted to transfer some of them to DVD before they started to deteriorate so I purchased the Turtle Beach Video Advantage USB. The first consideration you should make in purchasing this device is whether your computer will be able to support the heavy demands of the Video Advantage USB (and transferring VHS to DVD in general). I had recently purchased an HP Pavilion Laptop with Intel Duo Core T7200 2.0 GHz processor, 2 GB RAM and an 80 GB 5400 RPM hard drive. The laptop has done admirably in the capture process even though my hard drive is below the recommended 7200 RPM. You may want to consider the advice in the users manual to purchase a separate hard drive dedicated to video capturing. The size of the captured files is quite large (up to 10 GB for a 2 hour movie) so make sure you have adequate hard drive space and the hard drive is not highly fragmented. I would not even consider running the Video Advantage USB on my older Dell Dimension with a P4 1.8 GHz processor and 1 GB RAM. Also beware -- Video Advantage USB does not "officially" work on Vista (although the Turtle Beach site has some sort of work around listed). The actual Video Advantage USB has worked quite well -- I have experienced no dropped frames or sound. The mysterious "copyright error" others have mentioned has popped up but it has not caused problems (I notice it when I use the time limit function when capturing). I did have to buy an RCA adaptor ($2 to $3) as my VCR has only one audio output and the Video Advantage USB has two audio cables (they neglect to tell you this in the set-up instructions although it is on the Web site). You also need to consider whether the provided editing software is adequate. AD Full Cap is not what I needed and doubt I will ever use -- it is more for professional grade movies as the files it creates are huge (64 GB for 1 hour). Of course I did not learn this until after I started my first movie. If you are transferring movies like I am then you will use Power Producer and Power Producer Express (both by Cyberlink). Let's just say I have had my share of headaches with them. One of my movies had sound almost inaudible after I burned it to DVD -- little did I know that the input for the sound was too low and was adjustable in the process of creating an MPEG file. Also I found cutting out commercials to be less than intuitive although I finally was able to do so with much effort. Also this process can be quite time consuming (which is why I am glad I have the laptop to do it and can use my Dell for other things). The total time to transfer a two hour movie to standard quality file (MPEG) and burn to DVD is about 3.5 to 4 hours. Not that you need to be at your computer the entire time but your machine will be seriously tied up. Fortunately most of what I want to transfer is commercial free otherwise it would be even longer. Overall I give the Video Advantage USB good marks but the software provided lower grades. I figure once I am further along the process of transferring from VHS to DVD everything should be smoother. You may want to consider simply purchasing a video capture device and editing software separately -- software that one person loves is another person's nightmare so you can see what you like before you buy. Most importantly make sure you have a computer with not only enough processing speed, power, and hard drive capacity/speed but also the ability to dedicate almost completely to this process.

I purchased my DS1812+ last week Friday. I had 3 2-tb drives ready for install. They plug and play pretty easy. Install of clean drives took about 30 minutes and was simple with the browser interface. Install, add folders and shares, and then ready. One issue, with 2 network cables hooked up, the software shows 2 connections with 2 I.P. addresses for the Dockstation. It then is ready to install the software to the Dockstation. Install to one and reboot. Then it will show both are installed and ready for use. If you wait and don't reboot, it will show the second one needing to be installed to. I created the folders and started the network copy, got speeds of 75-80 megs. Once complete I added 2 more 2tb drives. Add them and tell it to extend the volume. With the additional drives I am looking at around 50-hours for it to complete. Once done, will add 3 more 2-tb drives for a total of 8. With 16-tb of storage I should have around 10.5-tb of drive space. The drive tools that come with the browser do a nice analysis of the S.M.A.R.T., on the drives. One drive was found bad and waiting for my replacement from Seagate. The good part is it still used the drive as it had not failed. Very impressed with the speed and complete software. At this point I would buy one of these again. My HTPC is hooked up via a 2 path 1 gigabit switches. Hard wired cat5 cable. When pulling video and audio, the response is pretty instantaneous. I was unable to detect any lag. The largest file I tried was 10 gigs, no stuttering.

I got the case because I had some PC parts I wanted to re-purpose into an HTPC upgrade and was tired of the chunky/desktop sized HTPC cases out there. I also didn't want anything tiny. Since I wanted to re-purpose my parts, I had very specific requirements. I needed a case that was Slim form factor, able to fit micro atx boards and able to fit larger PSUs. I also wanted something that looked really nice. I don't like them looking too plain and I don't like them looking gaudy. This case was perfect for my needs in every way. It's just an all-around great case. It's one of the nicest ones to look at that I've dealt with in a while. It's solid and nothing feels overly flimsy or wobbly. Since you get so much frame space, there's a bar to hold the frame so it doesn't become warped or bent when you load it up with your parts. The case is 105mm from top to bottom and 140mm of comfortable PSU room so you really must plan accordingly. Things get cramped fast. Here are a few tidbits of advice for your build experience. - You want to remove the frame bar and the nylon/rubber drive cage before you do any work in the case. This is in the instructions, which I recommend reading. - You have 140mm of PSU room before you cut off some of the 2.5" drive bay on the floor beside the PSU bay. Any longer and you'll also likely hinder your ability to install anything but 2.5" drives in the 5.25" bay (maybe you won't be able to install anything at all). - At 105mm top to bottom, make sure you get the right CPU fan. Depending on your build you may not need anything too big or powerful. I did, as my build is a re-purposing of my recently redundant system (Q6600, 8GB RAM, 750w Modular PSU, 3 1TB HD). I got a Cooler Master M4 GeminII Slim which worked perfectly for me. This fan is both powerful and very quiet. It keeps my Q6600 at 45c idle and 50c load while running at its minimum speed. - If you're placing a 3.5" under the 5.25" bay, install the cables to the drive before you place it. It will be very difficult to do it afterwards. Keep in mind that installation of this drive will involve turning the case upside down to secure the drive to the case. - If you're placing a 3.5" onto the Nylon drive case, be wary of whatever on your microatx board is close to it. If there's a mobo power connector or ram slots there, connect / install whatever needs to be before you put the drive in, as it will block whatever is under it. Not sure if these issues would be present with itx boards. - I highly recommend sourcing a PSU with the right dimensions. The case is pretty tight on space. Failing that, do yourself a favor and buy a modular PSU. For reference, my Ultra X4 750 is ~160mm and at that size, took up 1/2 of the 2.5" drive installation space on the base of the case as well as rendered the 5.25 useless for me, unless I install a 2.5" there (which I likely will when I decide to add an SSD to the system. The good news is that you're flexible IF you don't need anything installed to the 5.25" bay. My plan was to buy an external BR drive anyway so I didn't need the space. - My system is somewhat of a legacy system, so I don't expect others to have this issue but just in case, heads up - if you buy a USB 3/SATA add in card and it has a power connector of any kind, make sure the connector doesn't face the roof. I made the mistake and now the card is useless for me. There's almost no space between the edge of any cards installed to a board and the roof of the case. - There's no going around it, the case is cramped. It'll be really hard to route cables after the fact so if it's your thing to make it nice and need, pre-route as many cables as you can. - Ultimately, my recommendation would be to pre-build your system (put the mobo, cpu, fan, ram together) outside of the case and just drop that in when ready. - If this were a new build for me, I'd have skipped on using 3.5" drives and stuck to 2.5"s for ease of installation. I am using 3.5"s because I had them readily available and this is more of a revamp/retrofit than a brand new build. That's about all I can come up with. In terms of some nice features you may have missed: - Light has a dimmer, REALLY great feature - Front panel can be locked - Power button can be locked / Reset button is behind door so no accidental resets if you lock the power button and the door - Comes with a filter for the roof. The filter has magnets so you can just leave it on the top above the fan vent It's an amazing case. I have no regrets. Building wasn't too challenging but it definitely does take some work and planning if you want to get it right. It looks really nice among my entertainment center equipment. I will likely use this for many years. My next HTPC upgrade will probably be housed in this same chassis, that's how much I love it. I recommend it with flying colors for anyone who is looking for a SFF case that isn't tiny or an HTPC case that isn't big and chunky.

The lag on this thing is crazy bad. I've had this motherboard for 4 months now and it's been running fantastic, except for a driver issue, which I'll get to. I was making a new computer for my 3Ds Max modeling work station and really wanted a motherboard that was up to date with all of today's latest technology and this mobo was the oasis in the desert of high priced motherboards for the budget PC enthusiast. The first 2 months of use was good; my computer ran alright and I could do heavy multitasking without any performance issues or errors/glitches. It's been very stable up until I would get random system freezes (running Windows 7 by the way) and I would have to do a hard reset, only to get another complete system freeze a half hour later. Usually I wouldn't care about problems like these unless they're persistent, in which case I'd rabidly troubleshoot the problem for hours, accumulated into as long as a full blown day to fix the problem. I had made a temporary fix (somehow) until 3.5 months of use, when the problem came back with a vengeance and my system would freeze 2 minutes after logging into Windows. After using a friends computer (since mine was OOA), I had found that this motherboard uses 2 different drivers on its rear 6 USB slots. The above 4 are driven by the VIA PCI driver, rather than Intel USB3 driver. Having pin-pointed the problem, I was able to find that many others with this motherboard have had the same problem and the cause is that the VIA PCI USB3 driver is disabled in the BIOS or not updated to the latest version. I have since had the problem fixed, and if the problem hadn't existed, I would have given this product a 5 star review. Yet, it was frustrating that it was so hard to know what the problem was. The VIA PCI USB3 driver provided in the drivers disc for the motherboard isn't even compatible with 64 bit operating systems, and they're becoming a standard in today's age. All in all though, if you're looking for a not-so-pricey motherboard that will not bottleneck any of your new hardware, I'd definitely recommend this one, but not without strictly pushing the motion of updating your VIA driver immediately. Just as an afterthought, the problem I've had could be specific to my hardware, and the likeliness of anyone reproducing the problem might be less if the build is different from mine. - Intel i7 3770k - Nvidia GTX 670 - OCZ Fatal1ty 750W Modular Gaming 80PLUS Bronze - Corsair Vengeance Blue 16 GB DDR3 SDRAM Dual Channel Memory Kit CMZ16GX3M4A1600C9B - Creative Sound Blaster X-Fi XtremeGamer Sound Card - (2 HDDs\RAID 0) Seagate Momentus XT 750 GB 7200RPM SATA 6Gb/s 32 MB Cache 2.5 Inch Solid State Hybrid Drive ST750LX003

After living with three of these with three children, I simply cannot recommend this device. We have three of these, and we use Kindle Free Time with a subscription. Despite buying a 64GB SD card and telling everything to install to the SD card, the 8GB internal storage basically cripples this device. About once every other week one of the children comes to me with their Kindle not functioning because it has run out of space. Usually this manifests as the WiFi not working. I am not sure who thought it was a good idea to disable the WiFi when it runs out of it's tiny internal 8GB memory, but that's what it does - I guess to keep you from downloading more stuff? When the device runs out of space, which is frequent, your only option is to use the 'Manage Storage' feature. A slow, buggy, crash ridden application that most decidedly doesn't allow you to manage the space on the device. It will frequently report large amounts of space as "Other" with no way to manage or delete it - once I had to do a factory reset to get rid of a large block of space. Currently, again despite telling the device to install everything to the SD card, my son's tablet is out of space. When you open the "Manage Storage" list, be prepared to wait. It can take several minutes until it is usable, in the meantime items will be disabled and say "Refreshing", and while they are refreshing quite possibly report the incorrect size. Currently it says my son's got 2GB of Apps and Games. If you click on the list of apps to try to delete something, you are presented a massive list of everything installed, including system items like "Proxy Handler" and "HTML Viewer". None of this is sorted by where it is installed, or even by size - at least at first. Get this - it starts out sorted randomly, as the sizes are loading, and then, once ALL of the sizes are loaded, it sorts by size. Hope you are patient, it took me awhile to figure this out. So finally you can see the largest apps at top, and click on them. You are presented a technical looking screen, with everything grayed out 'Uninstall', 'Force Stop', 'Move to SD card', 'Clear Data' - all disabled. There is a little three dot button in the upper right, and when you click that you get "Uninstall for all users", and oddly it's not disabled, it works. How does this differ from the disabled 'Uninstall' button, not a clue. Frequently you will find apps that have the "Move to Tablet" button enabled, indicating that they were installed to the SD card, but they still report 50-100MB of space taken in the "App on Device" column. How does this happen? Not a clue. So you spend a nice half an hour being confused by this very technical, clunky "Manage Storage" application, and hopefully you can get the device enough free space that it starts functioning again. But rest assured, your kid will just go off and start installing applications that will eventually fill up the internal space yet again. It's inevitable. There are no 'don't show my kids apps that won't install to the SD card', or no 'don't use internal storage for application storage' settings. If your kid uses the device and downloads apps, even with everything set to use the SD card, you will eventually run out of internal storage space. Oh, and there's a nice "Archive" option, which offers to archive less frequently used items. Every time I've clicked it I get "No content available for archiving". Helpful. Next up, offline play. So you take the Kindle on the road, you are tooling down Route 66, and suddenly your kid starts complaining their apps don't work. You check, and sure enough, apps that are downloaded and installed on the Kindle are saying they need WiFi to continue. It turns out apps have to phone home periodically over the Internet, and if they go long enough without checking in, they won't work without WiFi. Isn't that wonderful? There's no way to tell all the apps to checkin before you go on the road, it appears to just happen randomly via usage. So, if there's a favorite app your kid hasn't used in awhile, make sure to open it and use it before you go on the road. Then there's the times when they just lock up and become mostly unresponsive. I just had to restart my daughter's because some app or background process made it mostly unresponsive. We've actually taught our kids how to hard reset the Kindle, because this happens so frequently. Sad. Overall I'd say that this is frustrating, clunky, underpowered device with too little internal space and no good ways to manage that space. The app DRM is frustrating and frequently locks your kids out of applications when offline. If your kids can get into their apps because there's WiFi, and if the WiFi is working because there's enough free internal space, well then it's just an OK device. You will see tons of poor reviews for this product. Most of them unfairly point to the drive as an issue, but instead I believe they reflect on a lack of foresight from the user ("lost my data!"), inability to navigate a website ("visited 3 websites, impossible to find how to file a warranty claim"), or just the bad luck of being part of the small percentage of people who receive a DOA drive (that happened to me too, but read on). I've purchased over two dozen of these Canvio drives (sizes anywhere between 500GB and 1TB), mainly because they work just fine, and the warranty covers you when they don't. All drives will fail, that's the nature of the beast (really, they do; just google Google's case study, or BackBlaze's "How long do disk drives last?" article). Portable drives tend to fail a bit sooner, mainly due to them being subject to more "movement" than the 3.5" drives sitting inside your computer case: moving them while in operation (which is why the original iPods had a huge rate of failure amongst people who strap them to their arm and went about their normal exercise routine), carrying them in bags or pockets, whatever the case might be... they are, after all, portable. That said, some drives will last you over 5 years, some will be DOA out the box, and most will fall somewhere in between. While I have had ONE of these drives not work straight out of the box (to be expected, considering how many we've purchased), the rest have been about average, and I can't say we noticed any difference with any other brands as far as performance or reliability. We used to buy Seagates, but stopped when they axed the 2- and 3-year warranties. The 3-yr warranty on these is just great for the purposes of peace of mind, and I've had nothing but great experiences with the claim process for the few of these that have failed throughout the course of their natural lifespan. For reference, if you are having troubles locating the warranty claim website, it's [...] Just hit the "START" button and follow the prompts. Very simple, relatively-painless. Speed is more than decent for a 2.5" drive, mainly thanks to the high-density platters: even though they're 5400rpm, the bottleneck will always be the USB interface with these. Never had a need for the built-in software, so I can't speak for that (most of mine are being used as Time Machine targets without any issues). Access time is meh, about what can be expected from a 5400rpm drive; no surprises there. As a parting note, please keep in mind always that your data is not backed up if it only lives in one place! No hard drive or any other storage media is fail-safe, so unless your data is in *at least* two places, it is subject to the danger of vanishing into imaginary 1s-and-0s following the failure of said media. If your computer is running out of space, don't just move data to an external drive to make room in the computer! (unless you backup that external drive, that is). Don't rely on a single drive to hold your pictures/documents/tax information/etc.... always backup!

I just bought one of these. I wanted a lightweight device for displaying thumbnail photos from my web page when I'm on a buying trip, so I can quickly determine whether I have an item or not when considering a purchase. My web site has over 2,000 different varieties of the items I expect to see on my next trip, so this will be a convenient reference in places where I know there will be no Internet access. This tool allows me to create a nice index of thumbnails that is exactly what I had in mind, so I'm pleased with it for that reason. There are other things I'm not that pleased about. Right out of the box I'm hit with something I don't like because if I want to use my iPod Touch for any purpose whatsoever I have to use an iTunes interface on my desktop computer to load media onto it. To do that, just to install the iTunes application I have to give Apple a "payment method" IN ADVANCE before I can do anything else. Apple has already sold me a pricey piece of hardware, but now before I can even use it I have to set myself up for more payments by putting my pocketbook on the line with this "payment method." This portends some other nasty things. There is nothing really objectionable about the way iTunes provides a channel for moving pictures from my web site to the iTouch. Still, I can't just use the iTouch as free hard drive space where I can name all the folders myself and move or remove image files with basic Windows commands. I have to use a new set of Apple applications, folders and commands with far fewer choices. I compare this iTunes tool for capturing shoppers to other portable devices such as the ones Creative makes that just give you storage space with some simple media player functions. No iTunes! Apple should give users options for loading their media with or without iTunes, with or without providing Apple with a "payment method" and with or without using Apple's plan for organizing their media instead of their own. I know Apple is not open to suggestions like that (if it were the iPhone would be sold with an unlocked option) but it needs to be said anyway. It amazes me people are willing to pay such high prices for Apple devices without getting for their money versatile and flexible tools they truly own themselves. This is what "style" mania does to people: put me in handcuffs, but make me look good! (I didn't have any of my own ideas anyway) There is no reason why an iPod Touch can't access the internet using its USB connection, but for some reason Apple chose to make it wifi only. That makes it more difficult for me to prepare mine for a road trip with my home configuration, because I don't use wifi here for security reasons. For the price it should not have this limitation. The audio department is where Apple gets most most egregiously meddlesome. In the big computer world one can take any mp3 file and put it in any directory with one's own chosen directory name. Not with an "iTouch." Your mp3 files have a "media type" definition (which you don't even see--or need to see--in Windows or Unix) which can be audiobook, music, or nothing. If your file's media type is audiobook, it has to go into Apple's audiobook folder, like it or not. If your file's media type is "music," it has to go into Apple's music folder, too bad if you'd rather put it someplace else. If the "media type" is not defined (nothing), the file goes into the music folder whether you like it or not because that's the default. There is no way to put such files where they belong if where they belong happens to be the audiobooks folder. If the media type is "music" or "audiobook" you can change it. For anyone with lots of of media files this is a needless inconvenience, but at least it is an option. If the media type is undefined, you're stuck with that and it can't be changed without reloading or recreating the file from scratch. If the mp3 files you are working with are audiobook files with an undefined media type definition and you don't want them mixed with other music files, the only option on this iPod Touch device is to create a playlist named after the title of the book. They'll still be mixed with the music files, but as a playlist you'll be able to access them separately. This scheme is unnecessarily rigid. The designers probably have reasons why the mp3 media type definition is useful but if it is useful it should be used to facilitate use and access. It should not be used to prevent users from deciding what folders to use for their media. The inability to name folders is bad enough. For now this is the only tool I know about that lets me make the kind of pocket photo index I want, but when I find something else that does the same thing but works more like a computer that belongs to me instead of someone else's selling platform and style widget I'll convert to that and drop this.

I purchased the Emotiva UPA-200 solely based on internet research. In the old days, I would never have purchased an audio component without hearing it first in some audio system, ideally, in my own audio system. My circa 1995 NAD 214 power amplifier was on the fritz and I decided to replace it rather than try to get it repaired. A large part of the reason I settled on the Emotiva was that I could try it in my system and return it if I didn't like it. Also, Emotiva's 5 year transferable warranty gave me confidence that, at the very least, I could expect to use the stereo power amp for 5 years. I used to be part owner of a high end audio company, Expressive Technologies; we made some of the best moving coil step-up transformers, preamplifiers and interconnects, so I've heard a lot of gear, albeit many years ago. Anyway, I wasn't looking for a state of the art or ultimate solution, just a way to play Pandora and CDs for background music. When I received the Emotiva UPA-200, I was immediately impressed by the build quality and modularity of the small, simple circuit boards inside. From my design experience, it struck me as very well thought out and executed. One nice touch is the cloth bag that the amp is shipped in to keep it clean and scratch free. The only faults I noticed were that the metal case's top bowed slightly in a convex manner, something that would not affect the performance one iota but was visually less than ideal. The other fault was that there was no instruction manual or warranty card in the box. I notified the company via email and they cheerfully send out a printed manual and warranty right away via US Priority Mail. I use the Emotiva UPA-200 with a Grace Internet radio, an Audio Research SP-9 preamp and Celestian SL6 loudspeakers. Interconnects have shields grounded to the preamp's ground post and speaker wires are relatively short. To date, and I've used it every day for a month, the amplifier has functioned without a single glitch. So how does it sound? Very darn good for a $350 power amp. The first thing that impressed me was a relatively solid, articulate bass. Most amps in this price range don't have nearly the control of the Emotiva in the lower registers. Now, the Celestians don't really produce any deep bass, so I don't know what is going on at subwoofer frequencies, but the mid bass is pleasingly and solidly reproduced. Bass is one of the key distinctions between mediocre and better audio components and the UPA-200 passes in this regard. It is also a part of the frequency spectrum that, in theory, won't suffer too much from less than ideal, digitally compressed, sources. The rest of the spectrum is also well reproduced to a point. At low to mid listening levels the amp is pleasant and clear. Voices, guitars and so forth are well reproduced though lacking the ultimate detail of the best class A power amps. Where the UPA-200 shows its sonic flaws is when the volume begins to rise, even well before what I believe is distortion due to clipping. When pushed, the amp loses its composure. At even moderately high levels, the thing starts to sound noisy and strained. That said, as far as I can remember, the Emotiva UPA-200 sounds much better than my old NAD 214 ever did with the little, reserved Celestians. It drives them better, so they sound more dynamic and lively. For background music, I'm enjoying the system immensely, and a number of people, who know nothing about high-end audio, and have not been made aware of the audio system per say, have commented on how good the music sounds. This small, inexpensive power amp really does provide a little taste of high end audio for very short money. Update on September 20, 2013: I've been using this amp for about three months, it has worked perfectly, and I still really like it. Update on August 11, 2016: This power amp has still has functioned flawlessly and I'm still very happy with this purchase.

In terms of sound quality, I rate the E500PTH's [as in, $500: Priced-Too-High] four stars, because I think there's significant room for improvement. In the realm of current earphones, I think they do rate five stars, although I don't have competing models from Ultimate Ears, Etymotic, or other reputed earphone makers to compare them with. What I did do is compare them with two highly regarded headphone models I happen to own, not to imply that the headphones are practical substitutes for earphones in ultra-portable music players, but to see what qualities the E500's have by comparison, and where they may fall short. I compared the devices using a well-recorded SACD of orchestral music (Mussorgsky Pictures on Naxos) played though a mid range Denon multi-disc player and pre-amp. The Sony MDR7506 is a closed-air headphone while the Sennheiser HD600 is an open-air design. Actually, they are not dramatically different with respect to timbre and the balance of sound distributed over the audible spectrum. The Sennheiser's have an edge over the Sony's with respect to spatial definition of instruments within a complex orchestral fabric, but the Sony's are well worth their $99 price tag. The E500's are nearly as dynamic as the two headphones, and they are similarly well-balanced in intensity across the spectrum of frequencies. Where they do fall short is in timbral definition and sound resolution. In other words, an oboe sounds more like an oboe on the headphones, and it is more effectively differentiated in the orchestral texture from, say, the violins. This isn't to say that you'd mistake an oboe for a violin with the E500's, but they're definitely less well defined and more homogenized over a given bandwidth. Using the same stereo equipment, I also compared the E500 to the single-driver E4c. As you might expect, the E4c sounds more boxed in, and it suffers more from the limitations described in the previous paragraph. Although quite good, I never felt I was doing justice to a new recording when listening through the E4c's. With the E500's, I don't always regret that I'm not listening on my stereo. My conclusion is that if you do a lot of stationary audiophile listening using earphones in relatively quiet environments, you might consider getting a set of high quality headphones that are sensitive enough to be driven by a good MP3 player. The Sony MDR7506's fit that criterion--too bad they're designed with such a heavy coiled cord. In circumstances where you need the extreme portability and sound isolation that earbuds can provide, the E500's likely are your best option, if you can accept the price tag.

I admit it, I abuse these things, to a certain extent. But this cable is by far the flimsiest one I've encountered. Anyone who's had an audio cable give out on them will probably notice that it's at the base of the cable, the connector, where the wire begins to fail and the user notices audio that is barely audible. It starts with just a little sound giving out, but if you wiggle the connector then you can hear it fine again...for a while. But inevitably it fails and you're left with a useless cable. As I said, I've owned this for maybe 3 weeks, and already I'm needing to wiggle the cable to hear audio. I expect it to fail anyday now. On the positive side, they were inexpensive. I don't regret trying them, but I simply cannot recommend these, particularly for anyone who plans to use it with a phone/MP3 player. If it's going to sit on a shelf and never be touched, it would probably be fine. Otherwise, I recommend you avoid this product.

The worst might be in VR. It's actually physically nauseating. I'm not using the cable for VR, but it's connected to the PC that renders, so the world gets stuck in place. The cable is being kept on laminate wood flooring. The temperature in the house is usually stable around 68 degrees Fahrenheit. My TV is a TCL from 2018 capable of 4k and 60hz. To clarify, the image is good except for when the flickering is occurring. The flickering also occurs whether the cable is set to "disconnected" in windows or not. I have tried adapters on both ends of the cable which are compatible with 18 Gbps to ensure the cables are secure. Occasionally after a flicker the screen will not come back on. Reconnecting the cables to an adapter on either end will not fix the issue, but reconnecting the cable AND the adapter will fix the issue. Also, when NOT using an adapter and the screen does not come on, I can fix the problem by re-plugging the HDMI cable directly into the HDMI port as expected. *Edit* This cable now no longer works under any circumstance. I even removed the cable and inspected it for damage, but I couldn't find any.

I purchased this lens to act as a standard lens for my Nikon D300s. I find it to be incredibly sharp, but the more that I used it I started noticing a few issues. Some have mentioned that this lens can make a loud high pitched wine when focusing as if metal were rubbing against itself. I also found the auto-focus to be somewhat slow. As such, I sent it back to Nikon to be repaired. Got it back, same problems. I shoot a lot of long exposure night scenes and this lens displayed such extreme rainbow flare that the shots aren't really usable. In fact, if there is any bright spot in a scene day or night, the lens flares badly. It is not a lens hood issue and I don't use filters. I started asking around to others that had the lens and showed examples of the flare and for the most part others lenses did not exhibit this problem. So, I returned it to Nikon again. The said it was fine, sent it back and as an added bonus scratched the front metal. But, the problem still exists and I just can't use this lens. If you get a good copy of this lens and shoot primes on a DX system then it can't be beat, but if you are like me and get a lemon that Nikon refuses to call a lemon, then it's time to look elsewhere. Unfortunately there aren't a lot of options, especially considering Nikon's new prices of their lenses. I tried a Sigma 30mm, but found it to be mis-calibrated so it would overexpose like crazy especially at f/5.6 and it was nowhere near as sharp as the Nikon. Having said it, it didn't flare and focused much faster and quieter.

Although the description of the Clip Zip states that it will play audiobooks that's not totally honest. Audible.com is the largest provider of online audiobooks. The Audible books are in files with an .AA extension. The Clip Zip will not accept this file type (even though the Clip and Clip + do). As a result Audible's Audible Manager rejects the connection of the Clip Zip. It makes no sense that Sandisk would decide to exclude the AA file type but they do. So if you're getting the Clip Zip to listen to Audible Audiobooks forget it -- at least until Sandisk comes to their senses. Otherwise the Clip Zip is a flashy little device with color screen but for one who uses it strictly for Audible audiobooks it makes a nice gizmo to hold up my running shorts.

The bad: Typing is not highly responsive. The processor is a dual-core where as other devices built to be primary devices can be had with quad-cores. If this comes out with a quad-core, I think it could have quite a slice of the market. That's my only complaint. The device is born of its roots as a e-reader, and that functionality is simply mind-boggling in its simplicity and beauty. So... the good: Unimagineably beautiful display. So glad I went with the 8.9 vice 7 inch model. I bought the Kindle Fire HD specifically for the hdmi output port. I tried in on a 24" Viewsonic 1080p HD computer monitor, and content rendered quite nicely. Especially nice when reading magazines or books. HD Movies played great on the larger screen (also tried on an Insignia 32" 720p HDTV) and this makes it quite fun and convenient. However, the display on the Kindle Fire HD really blew away the images on my larger monitor and TV. Great Navigation. It was pretty easy to get up and running with the device. But where my ownership gratitude meter really got pegged was when I downloaded the CNET user guide book in the lending library. Special Offers: I find this tolerable enough to where I don't see the need to spend $15.00 for the no-ad device. There's an ad on the unlock screen, and then that is it. I say live with 'em and spend the 15 bucks on books, magazines and other content. Reading: Unqualified. Magazines display so nicely, they're almost preferable to me than hard copy (certainly the aspect of all those trees that gave their lives so I can have something interesting to read is a guilt-trip I no longer have suffer with :) ) I also like how you can zoom on the magazine pages and enlarge them to your own reading comfort level. Power: The device is VERY SLOW to charge if you use any other device than the PowerFast charger. I didn't order one when I got my Kindle, as I assumed any of my existing mini-usb chargers would work. They do. But it takes many hourse (overnite, actually) to charge. I've since ordered the PowerFast adapter and eagerly await its arrival. Particular Scenario of note: I was unable to get an appointment for an eye exam I needed to do this past weekend. The rep told me told me the walk-in wait would be 2-3 hours. So, I rented an HD movie I wanted to see (you can only download videos if you rent them, a reasonable requirement to me) for $3.99. Most enjoyable wait time I've ever had. I did go for the 32G of storage. I did so for several reasons not the least of which is storage of my digital photos, etc. I think it is the smart move. I don't regret it at all. (Update) - Forgot to mention about the device's weight. The 8.9-inch device is a bit on the heavy side. With the Otterbox I purchased to protect it, the combo weighs in at 2 lbs 5 ozs. It doesn't sound like much but it is a bit too heavy to comfortably hold and read with 1 hand. However, the otterbox serves a dual purpose: as a solid protective case as well as the fact it converts into a tray to stand or lean the device in. This works well, as doing so makes a VERY comfortable to hold in your lap and read/watch your content. Matter of fact so comfortable, I would hesitate to own it without the Otterbox (some reviews of the otterbox complain it changes the screen dynamics because of their protective screen - I have not found any problem along that lines. However you can if you wish remove the screen and put a screen protector straight on the device. I didn't see the need as I didn't experience any viewing degradation). Overall, I am completely enthralled with the unit. Just to revisit what I was saying about the CNET lender book "Mastering the Kindle Fire": The Device is set up to primarily direct you to Amazon's content store. You can override that, but it's not easy to find the how-to's. This book takes you through that so you can load and run non-Amazon approved apps and content safely and without risking damage to your Kindle's OS. I highly recommend grabbing that book. Also, I have Google Play and found a website with instructions on how to set that up on the Kindle, as you will have to side-load the Google Play App. I've not done that yet, but once I do I will update my review. I will also update on how it goes installing and using Calibre as I do have a library of e-books I want to side load on the device. Happy reading y'all!

I love this camera bag!!!! I mostly just take my camera to family gatherings and to cemeteries for photographing headstones (I am a F-A-G volunteer), but occasionally I go on nature walks and just out-and-about taking photos. This well-designed bag fits my every need. And it is small, very compact, extremely well made, and great looking. It feels extra secure because in addition to the shoulder strap I can strap the bag around my waist with the extra strap that when not in use can be hidden securely within a flat flap attached to the bag of the camera bag and fastened with snaps. Check out my photos to see how this waist strap works/looks. There are also ridged rubber runners on the bottom of the bag from prevent wear and to protect the bottom of the bag. This unassuming looking bag will actually hold all I need for any of my outings. The following list of equipment fits fine in the bag. In main body (very well separated with, and safely stored between, velco attachable, movable well-padded dividers): Cannon Rebel EOS 500d 10.1 MP camera; with strap + Cannon 18-55mm lens (including lens cap and ultraviolet filter) + PUFFER flash diffuser, all attached to body. Cannon 55-250 telephoto zoom lens with lens cap, ultraviolet filter, and lens end cap attached. Cannon fixed 50 mm lens with lens cap, ultraviolet filter, and lens end cap attached. Wall-Plug Cannon Battery Charger. Wall-Plug Sony Battery Charger. A small change-purse can also be tucked in for ladies who don't carry wallets in their pants pockets and don't want to tote a purese. In Top pocket: Camera instruction book (the inside zip mesh pocket will not zip, but book fits well within top of bag and is quite secure and accessible). In Front pocket: Sony CyberShot 7.2 pixel Digital Camera. Extra battery for Cannon Camaera. Extra battery for Sony Camera. Extra Data Cards. 58mm Heavy Duty Rubber Lens Hood. 52mm Heavy Duty Rubber Lens Hood. Pen. Small note pad. While strong and well made with metal clasps for the shoulder strap and to safely fasten the top of the bag closed (top also closes with a zipper closure designed to allow extra room in the top of the camera bag), the bag itself is extremely lightweight. In fact, the bag with strap attached and all the above listed equipment weights only 5 pounds and 13 ounces. That is only a little more than the every-day purse I carry most all the time. Of course, I don't need to carry all this camera equipment for every excursion. Granted it isn't easy to get everything out of the bag quickly when it has all the above listed items packed inside. However, once I am where I am headed I usually put my camera around my neck; that opens up a lot of space to be able to get to other items, get them out for switching lens and put them back in place in the bag much quicker with the camera body not in the bag. If there are any cons worth mentioning about the Cannon Deluxe Gadget Bag 100EG, there are only two minor ones that come to mind: 1) The clasp on the strap that hold camera bag around your waist works like most clasps on fanny packs but with a stronger, heavier clasp than the fanny packs. In fact, this can make the clasp a little bit difficult to open. This of course makes it safer for your equipment. However, I have just a touch of arthritis in my fingers and for me it is a bit difficult to open. I have to concentrate and grasp it exactly in the correct spot on the clasp. But - it just takes a second longer. 2) I am too dense to understand the point of the 'curved' shoulder strap. The strap itself is well padded for comfort. But the reasoning for the curvature escapes me. I have to assume that it has something to do with comfort. However, you really couldn't get enough weight in this bag, due to its compact size, for it to be too uncomfortable on your shoulder even if it had just a straight style strap. To me this curved designed lessens how secure the strap feels on my shoulder. I don't think I have seen this mentioned in any other review, so I am guessing it must just be me on this one. I checked this bag out at some local stores, at nearly twice the price I may add ($44.97 and $49.95 at discount stores).I wanted to get a visual feel for whether I could fit at least my camera body with attached lens, puffer, and strap and my telephoto lens both in the bag. Actually, I didn't feel after looking at the bag in person that I could get even those minimum pieces of equipment to fit. I am, obviously, not a very good judge of logistics. So I drew a diagram to scale and measured my pieces of equipment. The measurements didn't lie. When I received that bag and got everything inside, I found the bag had originally fooled me with its compact size. But I wasn't ever fooled about the price, which is why I bought it at Amazon's great and economical price and added a toy for my kitties in order to get free shipping to boot. Shipping was surprisingly fast. What an extraordinary deal!!! Now I can quit toting my camera in a hot pink six-pack cooler. Believe the reviews when they tell you - you'll be pleasantly surprised if you have 2-3 lens and a body plus extras gadgets.

I have a Marantz amp/receiver with a 7.2 speaker sound system and decided I wanted to upgrade my turntable because my vinyl records sounded compressed compared to my CDs. I had read reviews of acrylic perspex mats in various audio forums, blogs and websites and thought the product might make a small improvement to my turntable. When the item arrived, I removed the rubber mat that came with my TT and replaced it with the white acrylic perspex TT record mat directly onto the metal turntable. I decided to use my "Chicago V" vinyl LP to test the acrylic mat, thinking this album had a nice variety of instruments, particularly brass instruments I could sample. When I dropped the needle on the record, the sound coming through my speakers was immediately and significantly improved!! The clarity of the high and mid range sounds, and the clean detail to the bass and vocals made the vinyl record sound thrilling! The white mat, unlike the black rubber mat I had, also makes translucent colored vinyl records look fantastic because now you can really see the color. Highly recommended!

I recently purchased the Panasonic RF-P50 because I was in need of a portable radio that has a built in speaker. I have discovered that this is hard to come by in a brick and mortar store. So I did a little search on Amazon.com and came across this product. I also own its direct competitor - the Sony ICF-S10MK2. The Panasonic radio is great because I can carry it around anywhere and always have music with me where ever I go. I especially like to use it in hotel rooms when I go on trips, but it's also nice to have in order to listen to music in all of the rooms of my apartment. The Panasonic RF-P50 has a telescoping antenna which can be swiveled back and forth, and on/off/volume switch, band selector, and tuning dial. The speaker measures at 2 and a half inches. I live in a basement apartment, so it is not always easy to get a fantastic signal. I have discovered that this radio pulls in all the major FM stations quite easily - although sometimes I have to fiddle with the tuning and antenna to get a good reception. The few local AM stations can be pulled in as well. The appearance of this radio is quite nice. It appears that Panasonic has taken some time into building a radio that is pleasing to the eye. It's a pocket radio with a nice contemporary look. The radio frequencies are listed on the unit quite clearly - much bigger than what I've seen on similar units from other companies. Also the tuning light, which lets you know when you've locked on to a strong station just right, is bright and easy to see. This Panasonic pocket radio comes with a wrist strap. This is one of my only gripes. I wish it came with both a wrist strap and a belt clip. Another nice feature that would make this radio better is if one could remove both the wrist strap and belt clip. How does it sound? Keep in mind, it's a pocket radio, you're not going to get huge sound as you would with a stereo system. However, for its tiny size, the speaker sounds surprisingly good. The sound quality sounds clear, but not too tinny. I've ehard models with much harsher sound. Also don't expect glass shattering bass, you won't find it here. But as I said, for its size, it has a pleasant sound. In comparing this model to the Sony competitor, I notice a few things. 1. I like the appearance of the Panasonic model over the Sony model. I just feel that the Panasonic model looks nicer. 2. In terms of when I'm holding both radios in my hands, the Sony model seems to have a better build quality (harder plastic, less flimsy feel to the radio). However, I've had the Panasonic model for a while and have had no issues with its build quality. Of course, I'm very careful with my electronics, I don't abuse them. 3. Both models seem about equal in terms of receiving FM signal. Both models pull in the local stations quite easily. The Sony model seems to have a slight advantage in pulling in the slightly weaker stations but this could be due in part to the fact that its antenna is longer. 4. AM reception on the Sony is much better than the Panasonic. It seems to be able to pull in the stations with more clarity. But again, the Panasonic radio can pull in the strong local AM stations just fine. 5. To my ears, both of these models sound exactly the same. Sound quality of music/talk shows sound the same with both units. NOTE: People should note that the headphone jack on both of these models are in mono only. This means that when you plug stereo headphones in either model, you'll only get sound in one side of the headphones. Please bear in mind that this does not mean the radio is broken. These units were designed this way. The Bottom Line: I definitely consider the Panasonic RF-P50 a steal at ten bucks. It's a small sized radio that you can carry with you anywhere to listen to music, or get the latest news. Both the Sony and Panasonic models are what I consider to be excellent deals. I prefer the Panasonic over the Sony model though. For most cases I'd recommend the Panasonic model. But if you're looking for slightly better build quality and better AM reception, then I'd recommend the Sony model. Of course get the Sony model if you prefer its appearance over the Panasonic model.

This is because these headphones do not recognize audio input / output in "headset" mode, and go to sleep every 10 minutes. You must use headset mode in order to use the build-in mic. Thus, these headphones cannot be used as a headset for a Windows laptop - you will constantly be disconnected from audio during your zoom, skype, and other teleconferencing activities! I contacted customer service about this issue. They gave me a generic response, and after A MONTH are still trying to claim that their "engineers will look into this problem." The other major flaw is that the headphones can only be charged when powered down, plugged into a USB C port, and then a button must be held down for two seconds to activate charging. This is ridiculous. If I plug in the headphones, I expect them to start charging. HiFiMan claims that this was done in order to prevent accidentally draining the battery of the device you're plugging into, but any device with a USB C port will have a much larger battery (if it has one at all) than the one in the Ananda. Even after owning these for a couple of months, I still sometimes forget to "turn on" the charging, and start the next day with a totally drained headset. I'll be returning these.

We just bought a TV (40" LCD) for the first time since our daughter was born 3 years ago, and we really wanted to be able to enjoy it in the evening after she's in bed. The problem? There was only one place to put it -- on the other side of a wall from our daughter's crib. Enter the Senn 120 headphones! We're by no means audiophiles, but for ordinary folks like us, they're a great deal for the money. When compared to my in-laws' home theater, the sound is definitely inferior, but it's quite adequate for our needs. Even without surround sound, sounds locate very appropriately and there's a rich response throughout the frequency range. Even better, I can turn my unit volume way down for my supersensitive hearing, while my husband can bombard his eardrums to his heart's content. We bought one base unit and one additional headset. The only drawback to this setup is that only one unit can charge at a time. That's not really a problem, though, since the battery life exceeds 20 hours! The charging mechanism is easy to use, and we were able to mount the base directly to the wall next to our television. One minor quibble -- the top part of the headband is a little uncomfortable for both of us, so we have to loosen it and rely on the earcups to stabilize the headset. A major positive is that the earcups are not nearly as snug and clamped-down as most of the more expensive units we tested. I'm very sensitive to pressure on my head, but I can wear these headphones for hours without a twinge of migraine. All in all -- it's not perfect or theater-quality, but for the price, the value is amazing! NB: This is the additional headphone listing, which comes with only the headphones and batteries. You'll need a transmitter/charging unit to use the product.

Ok. Let me start off by saying, my daughter loves this laptop. It is able to do everything she needs it to do, she is working on entry-level 3D animation as an artistic outlet. Despite some of the negatives, this machine is well worth what we paid for it. I would like to say the product description is somewhat misleading, or easy to misinterpret. We ordered the AMD A6, which is supposed to come with Windows 8.1. I assumed it was 8.1 installed. I will say this is not the case. On the upside, it does come with Windows 7 PRO and the upgrade discs for Windows 8.1 PRO. The down side, there is no optical drive. The lack of optical drive was known, since that is in the product description. The upgrading process was more laborious and tedious than I anticipated. They were nice enough to include step by step instructions on how to easily perform the upgrade. Unfortunately, the step by step instructions were wrong about the first step, at least regarding my laptop. It called for pressing the F12 key during the boot sequence, in order to enter and make changes to the BIOS. After several failed attempts to access the BIOS, I read the Quick Start guide and found the NOVO button. The NOVO button is essentially a 1 button recovery, startup, BIOS or reset option. So, I tried using this and was able to finally access the boot menu. After getting through this road-block, it was just the waiting game for everything to get reformatted, transferred, etc... The upside of all this, we ended up with a Windows 10 laptop, since it almost automatically wanted to switch to Windows 10 after Windows 8.1 finished installing and it has been running great.

This board has seemed decent enough for what I have needed to use it for. I have been happy with the m.2 performance and things work pretty well, other than a few things I will list here. I have not done any benchmarking, but that would be heavily dependent on the other components anyway. The most egregious problem is the lack of wifi and bluetooth despite the product listing saying it has these features. There are two versions of this board which do, B550M DS3H AC and B550M DS3H AC-Y1. But this is not either of those models. If I had known this, I would have bought a different board. I've actually been having a lot of trouble ever since with bluetooth because I have been struggling to find a bluetooth adapter that actually works. Onboard bluetooth has worked great with my devices on other boards, so I know this is the problem. Still the only fault there was incorrect product information. I would return the motherboard, but that would mean having to tear apart my whole computer, go without for awhile, and reactivate Windows. I might still have to do that just because of this problem. It's been quite a struggle. The other issue I have had was with the Q-flash. This is another feature I bought the motherboard for. Knowing that only the more recent bios would support my cpu, and not having any guarantee of having a recent enough BIOS, I went ahead with this one thinking I could just flash it to the most recent using this feature. Unfortunately this feature did not work at all. The power supply was the problem here, most likely, because the board did not receive any power when pressing the required button. I foudn out later you need to have a power supply that supports the Q-flash feature. I don't know whether there is a list anywhere for that, but be aware of this. If the BIOS has been updated to f14 or later (the January 2022 version), you'll have full CPU support. If not, it won't power on and you won't have any way of knowing whether the BIOS is teh wrong version or you have some other problem. Lucky for me it came with F14 so this may not be an issue for you. This is the main purpose for Q-flash - to be able to flash without having support for your CPU, and indeed with no CPU or RAM installed.

These are great value priced SD cards. I've bought from this vendor/brand a few times now, and the capacity of the cards always tests true, and I haven't had one fail on me yet. I typically test the capacity of these value cards with FakeFlashTest, which requires the card to be reformatted afterwards. I always just reformat to exFAT. Well, since these cards have always been trustworthy, I stopped testing them (and thus reformatting them to exFAT), then found myself unable to transfer a too-big (>4GB) file one day. It turns out these SD cards ship as FAT32, and I had not ever noticed before, since I always tested and reformatted. So, just to keep everyone informed, you may want to reformat them to your favorite file system upon arrival, since it's a pain to do it later once you've started using them. FAT32 will work for most people just fine, and if you don't know the difference between FAT32 and exFAT, then this subtlety likely doesn't even matter for you. These are definitely 5-star cards for the price, and just a great overall value.

After much research for a small radio that can receive shortwave for an extended overseas trip, I settled on the Sangean 606. I already have a Sony SW7600GR (standard in the industry IMO) but wanted something smaller and less valuable (the Sangean is about 1/2 the size as the Sony). Initial thoughts were that 1) it was chunkier than I was expecting and 2) the plastic casing seemed cheap. I've now lived with it for ~2 months and I'm thrilled. Reception for FM and AM is on par with the larger and more expensive Sony and it is marginally easier to use. I also prefer the sound of the Sangean over the Sony (NPR talk radio mostly). With automatic station setting, fine tuning, alarm, light, etc., it is an ideal travel radio. Other nice features at this price point is the protective case, SW reel antenna, and AC adapter (not included with the Sony!). I've used it daily for ~2 months on the same set of batteries. If I were doing a lot of shortwave listening the Sony would still be preferred, and the quality feel of the Sony is 2nd to none. Biggest complaints? the flimsy up/down tuning buttons and that Amazon suggests buying an additional antenna that already comes with the radio. Full disclosure- this is my 4th Sangean but that just speaks to how good they are in receiving tricky AM & FM radio stations. UPDATE: I paid ~$115 for this Sangean and when I bought my Sony SW7600GR it was ~$200. If you can get the Sony for ~$25 more than this Sangean, I'd probably go for it. Just make sure it is the same made in Japan radio it used to be!

I almost didn't buy this lens because of another review. The GF1 is my only high-quality camera and I got it with the pancake lens for better portability. As any owner of the GF1 can attest, the GF1 performance is so good with the pancake lens that it turns anyone into an artist. However, it does not have a zoom. So, my quest for a zoom lens began and I eventually decided on the Panasonic 14-140mm. I dreaded that it might be too uncomfortably big, but it's not really an issue as you learn to balance the camera by its body and lens. I did follow someone else suggestion on getting a 2 Million Dollar Home Crumpler bag for it and I'm glad I did. Trying to carry the lens around the neck would probably not make much sense. Anyway, I had removed the neck strap a while back already and replaced it with a sturdy wrist strap. I've been using it for a few weeks and I couldn't be happier with my purchase. I only use it during the day where the slower shutter speed is a non-issue. I'm very glad I got the 10x zoom instead of the 3x zoom from Olympus. The latter might have been better as a replacement for the pancake, but that wasn't my objective. The optical image stabilization (OIS) feels almost like a must have, especially at the longer zoom range. With the Crumpler bag, the camera is easy to carry, protected, and generally not obstructive when the 14-140mm lens is attached. I haven't relied much on the silent focus and progressive exposure change which is built into this lens. It's mostly useful for video, which I don't use often. But I did weigh the presence of these features in my decision to buy this lens. In short, if you have a GF1 as your primary high-quality camera and you're looking for a quality zoom lens, I don't think you can go wrong with this lens. Most wireless extenders on the market require you to plug directly into your wireless router and broadcast an additional SSID. The Linksys RE1000 is a little different however as this one does not require you to plug directly into the router to extend the signal. It does indeed broadcast another signal but the easy setup uses a startup CD that you just put into your laptop and answer a few questions and it will match your existing settings. You can get a little more granular with settings afterwards although there is not much else to change other than the admin password (recommended) and the ability to view connected devices. The beauty of this extender is the ability to just plug into any wall outlet in the building and it is somewhat inconspicuous. You also can't really beat the price compared to others on the market. The only downside to this device is that it won't extend on the 5Ghz band if you have a wireless router with that capability and are looking to extend that band for less interference. Luckily, the signal strength, ease of use, and flexibility more than make up for it. This extender worked flawlessly with a DLink router already in use.

This cable was a complete and total let down. Absolutely atrocious performance. I simply cannot understate how poorly this cable performed. First, when it was working: I got this cable after breaking the cable that came with my phone...after having used it for almost two years. The Titan M performed as advertised for about 5 hours. Then it started making these awful creaking noises whenever I tried to reposition the micro-USB end. A minor annoyance, but nothing terrible. Probably enough for a four-star review, with the fifth star being deducted purely because of the annoying creaking and the immense pain in the ass of opening the packaging. But fast-forward four weeks, and then the real problems start (seriously, this indestructible cable lasted FOUR WEEKS)... The first problem I encountered was a bit of wiggling -- my phone would slip around and wobble a bit when I used the cord as a stand. I didn't think much of it at first. Then the cord would start coming unplugged randomly while my phone was just lying on my bed or desk. A little weird, but nothing bizarre. It's a heavy cable, so maybe the weight was pulling the plug out. Understandable. And then the plug broke. I noticed that the micro-USB plug looked a little crooked one day when I pulled it out of my phone (this was maybe 4 days after I noticed the wiggling and random unplugging), and when I took a closer look I noticed that the metal shroud which covers the 4 pins of the USB plug was coming off. I pushed it back into place and plugged the cord into my phone again. The next time I unplugged, the shroud actually stayed inside my phone's charging port. Now we have a problem. With the cable in this condition, my phone will literally only charge if I'm holding the cord in one hand and my phone in the other, making sure they stay at just the right angle and just the right distance from each other to not come unplugged. It's absolutely ridiculous and I plan on returning this cable as soon as I get home. Hopefully the replacement will perform as advertised. For the time being, though, my advice to you is DO NOT BUY THIS CABLE. You can afford to buy 50 knockoff chinese cables on Alibaba for this price, and each one of those cords will last longer than this piece of garbage. Note: I have not been using this cable in any sort of abnormal or abusive way. Most of the day and all of the night, it is literally just lying on my bed plugged into a power strip on the floor. When it's not in my room, it's either plugged into a car socket on my dashboard or a wall socket next to my couch while I'm playing video games. At no time did it ever experience abnormal stress; in the EXACT same conditions, normal rubber USB cables have lasted over 20 times as long. So I say again: DO NOT WASTE YOUR TIME AND MONEY. Additional note: this problem that I've had with the metal shroud is NOT a new issue. If you read the reviews on the Lightning variant of this product, you'll see that many other users have had the exact same problem. Stay. Away.

I receive many, many calls claiming to be from my "credit card company," or political spiels. I have asked them to stop calling, they ignore my request and just hang up, because they are looking for the next person to scam. They ignore any "Do-Not-Call" list. These people are crooks. They don't follow the law. They are just out there to collect all the information naive people will give them, so they can steal. Reporting these callers is a total waste of time. I have reported them to the FCC. All I get back is a letter claiming there's nothing they can do. So yesterday I installed the TeleBouncer TB-1000 on our line. Unfortunately the company, Dasym, I'm told, is no longer in business, so you might have trouble finding one. I ordered mine from Amazon, and it was shipped very quickly by I-Net Sales. Ignore that Amazon says there is only 1 left. It said that when I ordered mine last week, and it still says that. I think it's I-Net Sales way to make you think you're grabbing the last one. It came new in a box. What the TeleBouncer does, is answer the phone for you, silently, with a recorded announcement that the caller should press a certain number to be connected. If the caller presses this number, it connects to your regular phone. The scam crooks are using auto robo calling computers, and there is a delay in the connection, so they don't hear the start of the message with the number. Plus they don't want to bother with waiting, they want to make more calls to find some poor sucker to fall for their criminal schemes. In the few hours since installing, it's answered our phone for us twice (you can see from caller ID), and both were scams, which the TeleBouncer intercepted. There are several ways to hook this up, so it's important to read the instructions. I hooked mine to the main phone line, then the phone base station to the TeleBouncer. A Caller ID (separate box) is also hooked to the main line, so I can see who calls. When calls come through, the phone base station rings the other phones in the house. There are four modes on the TeleBouncer: - Standby - allows all phones to operate normally - Telemarketing - answers the phone call immediately, no ringing. A recorded message (which you can record, or use the default one) instructs callers to press 1 to be connected to your phone, or to leave a message. - Do not disturb - answers phone immediately, no ringing. A recorded message instructs callers to press # if it's urgent, otherwise leave a message. - Caller ID - waits for caller ID to be sent, which is after the first ring, so phones will ring one time. Once caller ID is received, the TeleBouncer answers silently, and gives the same instructions as in Telemarketing mode. Basically what this unit does is answer your phone for you. If the caller presses 1, 2, 3 or # during the recorded message, they are connected to your regular phone. If not, they are switched to your answering machine. What this means for most users who already have an answering machine as part of the phone system, when the caller presses 1, the unit switches to your regular phone system, and your phone will ring. If you don't pickup, your regular message system will answer. But if the caller does not press a number or #, the TeleBouncer will, after the recorded announcement, switch to answering machine mode, which means it's good if you connect a separate answering machine to it. (The TeleBouncer does not have its own answering machine). I picked up a cheap answering machine for this purpose from WalMart. So far, the TeleBouncer works very well, and I'm very happy with it, and the peace and quiet it gives by not having all the bothersome telemarketers calling. It's like having your own calling service intercept all your calls, and only put through the ones you want.

I am so annoyed. This item has multiple issues and is a poor design. I brought 3 Ring stick up cams and solar panels. So got 3 gutter camera mounts (this product) and 3 gutter solar panel mounts (Aobelieve brand). First the 2 gutter mounts (solar and camera) are similar except the solar bracket is on top and the camera bracket is facing downward which makes sense. BUT the design is 10X different. The solar panel gutter mount has a long screw for the camera and based on a ball swivel joint for a full 360 degree adjustment. Not this camera mount. All 3 of my camera gutter (this product!!!) mounts had long screws that were too short and would not tighten the unit to the gutter. I had read some reviews of this but thought it would not happen to me. Some guys said they went to Home Depot and brought longer screws. My solution was to cut up an old door mat that was rubber and thick to act as a placer or wedge to fill the gap so the long screw would tighten and hold in place. . The above issue was with the mounting screws to the gutter. The real issue was with the main screw that attaches to the camera. it was too short. When screwed in the camera was at an angle. To align the camera straight up and down, you would have to unscrew and back off the camera (unsafe). So when screwing the camera onto the screw all the way, the camera would be at an angle. Un-screwing the camera 1/2 or 3/4 a turn would only leave a partial connection and risk it falling out. Next like on a tri-pod, you have another screw nut that you are supposed to use to tighten against the camera to lock the screw in place. Well this screw nut was too small to tighten with your fingers. the screw nut was very small and my fingers could not reach the screw nut. it was too small (I do not have big / fat fingers!!). My solution here was to remove the screw nut completely so I could screw the camera in all the way. Then when I had to back off (un-screw the camera) to make it up and down and not at an angle, I would see how much space is needed and place washers to fill the gap. Lastly, the screw that I discussed above is connected to 2 things. One will move up / down and the other left to right. This is ONLY 2D, not 3D. Note I mentioned the solar panel gutter bracket was based on a 360 degree ball socket. This camera gutter mount is NOT. Poor design. So you are limited on the angles you can adjust your camera. The good news, the Aobelieve gutter mount for the solar panel will actually work for the Ring camera too. All you have to do is un-screw 4 small screws that hold the bracket on top of the unit and re-attach it on the bottom so the bracket is pointing downward. this took me less than 2 minutes. First the Aobelive solar panel gutter mount has full length screws to attach to the gutter. The main screw into the camera is long enough to go in fully and the screw nut to tighten to the cameras is large enough anyone can manually tighten. Did I say, it also is based on a ball and socket design to give you full 360 degree adjustment. This product does not have that. i am going to return these and do not believe all the short one line reviews that say this product is great.

We have been happy Filemaker users since around 1990. Our current version is Filemaker 4 which we licensed about 11 years ago. Our primary customer database became corrupted recently and, to our disappointment it wasn't recoverable. So we went to our backup and discovered that the backup software had stopped working in 2008. The database files saved there were fine except they didn't include about 30 months worth of entries. Our Filemaker 4 had run without any issues in a networked setup which allowed us to access the files from any of our three workstations. We decided to upgrade to the current version 11 and found that no upgrade was offered. We still decided to license and install the current version 11 even though it meant purchasing a totally new license. We reviewed the information at the Filemaker website and saw, among other things, that the sales information stated that it would work on up to 9 workstations simultaneously ... the same as version 4. So we purchased a new copy and installed it only to find that the rules had changed and now a full license is required for each workstation, bumping our investment cost from $299 up to $897 to equal what we had. It may work on up to 9 workstations simultaneously but only if you are willing to accept an outrageous difference in price. Next we tried updating our database files to version 11 which worked successfully on all the flat, non-relational ones but was a total bomb on the three which were relational. After 8 hours of tracking down incorrect field conversions with many more remaining, we finally threw in the towel and just went back to using version 4. For our purposes, Filemaker 11 was a complete waste of money and the company policies as well as their customer service was nothing short of unacceptable. We once recommended Filemaker to anyone who asked. We will now steer anyone who asks away from a great product ruined by a greedy company and a non-backward looking development path that leaves their oldest customers abandoned and twisting in the wind.
