**NOTE: My pictures were taken a few hours after I had the drive running for a bit. When I first tested the drive, it has 0 power on hours! So, first thing I want to say is this drive is advertised as a retail drive but is in-fact an OEM drive. Normally this isn't an issue except that when you have an OEM drive from Western Digital (WD) the warranty is now on the OEM to uphold instead of WD. The OEM in this case being the seller (Hard Drive Geeks for me). The only physical difference on the drive is the Western Digital label on top is replaced with a white label. I set my rating at 3 stars because it clearly shows a retail drive but is instead a OEM drive. The main issue is that Western Digital WILL NOT warranty this drive because it is an OEM drive. If your drive has an issue you MUST go to the seller. A lot of the times, this is fine but it all depends on if your seller actually backs their warranty. That being said, the seller MUST maintain the same warranty period or longer. Since WD warranties this for 2 years, so must the seller of the OEM drive. The decision should be up to you really on buying this. The warranty of most hard drives don't cover data recovery in the first place (unless you have higher end NAS drives) so I don't expect most people to use the warranty even when there is an issue. I expect most people to contact a data recovery service. So... long story short is that if you are concerned about getting a retail drive with the retail warranty, I would look to the manufactures website for purchasing options, otherwise the OEM version of the drive (for me) was brand new and performed at expected levels for a 5400 RPM spinning disk and will work fine for me needs as a secondary storage drive with an SSD cache on top to speed things up a little. TL;DR: The drive is a genuine new Western Digital drive sold to a third-party seller with a "white label" on top instead of Western Digital branding. The drive should be new (install Crystal Disk Info to check) with 0 hours of power on time. Western Digital does not warranty white label/OEM drives, the warranty is up to the seller to take care of. That being said, the seller is required to maintain the same warranty period or longer, which in my case was the minimum of 2 years. This drive performs as expected and is for all intensive purposes the same physical drive as the retail version, just no WD branding on top.

I'll start off by saying this is my second IBuyPower PC in the last few weeks! So I'm a pretty happy customer. I bought this one because my teenage daughter's GeForce 780 video card (on a custom built 4 year old PC) decided to blow a VRM. There is never a good time for that to happen, but right now is really bad (January of 2018) because the cryptocurrency mining craziness means it is extremely difficult to find a good video card. I looked for several days and couldn't find a good 1060 video card for a reasonable price, so I decided to buy this one. I really liked the first IBuyPower PC that I bought a few weeks ago though it was a higher end model. This machine is just about perfect for what I need it to do and right in the price range I wanted to pay. I estimate it saved me around $200-$300 over what it would cost me to build myself, especially when you consider that it includes a copy of Windows 10 Home. Overall this is a nice mid-range gaming PC for the money. The components are solid. The HDD was a Western Digital Blue which is a decent drive with low failure rates. The motherboard that was in mine was an ASRock- a good name brand manufacturer. They also put a single 8GB memory stick in, which is good, because I can easily add another 8GB if I want to upgrade to 16GB. My board has 4 total memory slots, so I could go up to 64GB. The RGB lighting is also a nice touch. It's basically a single strip of LED's at the top of the case, and they include a remote to change the colors. Wire management isn't bad, and unused cables are all zip-tied together to keep them nice and neat and out of the way. I did end up moving a few of the cables around so they wouldn't be as visible. While not really an issue, the motherboard is a bit smaller than what I normally use. There are only two PCIE slots on the board, and one is in use that holds the 1060 video card. If you are planning on upgrading to SLI (two video cards) and still need a PCIE slot for an add on card, look for a different model. Despite the smaller motherboard, there are still plenty of USB 3 ports, and even a USB C port. There are two USB 3 ports and a headphone jack on the top of the case which is nice for USB sticks and headphones, etc. I did encounter a couple of minor issues. I heard a rattling noise in the case when I went to take out the foam that comes in it for shipping. After digging around and taking off both sides of the case, I eventually found a small piece of plastic on the bottom of the case. I don't know what it goes to, but it doesn't seem to be necessary and it runs just fine. It looks like it might be a cover for something. Anyway.. while taking off the glass sides of the case, I also noticed that the screws holding the 1TB hdd had come loose. I read through a lot of reviews on this item and the skipdoctor products, and finally decided on this unit because it runs on a/c power, is fully contained and automatic, and was about $10 less expensive than the most equivalent skipdoctor unit. Both items had mixed reviews - mostly positive, but I found that most people who tried to make the units work and put in some time and effort were satisfied with both products. I'm very satisfied with my purchase it has repaired two discs that could not be played at all, and one that skipped. This product repairs a disc to "useable" condition, it does not repair it so that scratches are not visible. I can still see, but not necessarily feel the scratches. It's also important to remember that some scratches do not affect performance. If a disc plays well, but shows scratches - I just clean off the finger prints with a cloth or use the unit to clean the disc and see if the performance is satisfactory before attempting a full repair. I agree that the instructions with the unit could be better. I saved the instructions provided by another reviewer to use with the provided instructions for clarity. I noticed that I could cut down some of the repair time and solution usage by repeating the buffing/sanding (pink disc) process several times in a row for deeper scratches before using the repair. I ran one disc through 3 times in a row, then used the repair cream solution with yellow pads and it played fine. My lesser damaged disc only required one pass with the buffer and one with the repair until it worked great. I usually clean the disc (manually with the cloth or with the machine depending on severity of grime), then buff, then repair. It can be time consuming to repair a disc to functioning, but it does save the disc and my discs play like new despite the scratches that are still visable. I think this was good purchase and not overly complicated to use.

Note that the technology is WORTHLESS for accelerating: -SSDs of any type (M.2 PCIe SSDs, or even SATA/RAID SSDs.) -Secondary mechanical 'data' drives. -Non Windows, or older windows Operating Systems. If you are building a new system and want to accelerate your boot drive, go directly for a M.2 PCIe SSD and skip Intel Optane altogether.

I've decided to give these headphones a try because my previous ones ( also from a $100 price range) didn't transmit the bass well, and Sony MDR-XB90EX In-Ear Extra Bass (specifically the ones imported from Japan) were #1 in the 2016 list of the greatest bass headphones. They arrived on time, packaged well, and at first I was quite happy with them. However after 3 months of using them I noted a few annoying issues: 1. After a short while (at the end of 3 months) the right earpiece started to malfunction - one of the sound channels (that reflects the higher sound range) started to spontaneously fall off and back on. It would even have been more tolerable (albeit quieter in one ear) if it fell completely off, but constant flipping on or off is very aggravating and ruins the experience. It doesn't seem to happen in the wires, but in the round box near the ear plug (or very close to it), so it doesn't look like anything could be done to help with the issue. This is especially frustrating because the headphones were used very lightly - they are plugged into the speakers on the desk most of the time, and were only used several times for a few hours. 2. The earpieces don't fit very well (and I have quite a typical ear, for which the default medium-size plugs usually worked well in a number of my previous in-ear headphones). Maybe because they are a bit heavy (the round box on them about the size of a cherry, and slightly heavier by weight), after a short time of plugging them in, they tend to slide out, so they required frequent re-adjustment (pushing them back in), which irritates the ears after a few hours of doing that. This effect is especially noticeable when the ear is wet (e.g. after showering). I've tried to change the plug size to smaller or larger, but it didn't improve the situation and only made it worse. Perhaps it will fit better with a memory foam plugs sold separately, I haven't checked those out yet. This is quite annoying - especially because I've only used them while sitting at desk in front of the laptop, so it wasn't due to vigorous movement. 3. The earplugs are very sensitive to the position they are inserted due to their asymmetrical shape: push them a little too deep, and the sound is blocked, like using the common earplug; shift the position a bit - and they won't hold in the ears, or insulate well. The only right position for them is the one shown on the photo, and as stated above, it doesn't fit very well and tends to slide out. I would have returned them, if I could, but I'm out of luck now - the return window is already closed. Very frustrating - my previous headphones were holding for about 2-3 years on average (which included traveling with them and a lot of movement), but these didn't even last 3 months of light use.

I got two Gladiator Joe VESA bracket adapters (model #GJ0A0055) for use with two Acer G227HQL Abi 21.5" monitors. The overall quality is good and the fit is excellent. I would buy them again even knowing what I do now (see below). I was happy to find out that there are adapters made to convert my Acer monitors to a VESA mount - I thought I was going to have to fabricate something myself. Now, for most people this mount will be just fine and I could easily give 5 stars. For the rest, I'll show the things I felt were shortcomings or disappointments even though some may consider it nit-picking. That's why I removed one star. 1. The top image for this model adapter on Amazon shows the monitor mount welded to the BOTTOM of the back plate. The adapters I received had the monitor mount welded to the MIDDLE of the back plate. Although the forth image down shows a monitor attached to the mount welded to the middle of the plate. I do not see any reason to have this mount welded to the middle since the mount is just as strong in the bottom position, and both HDMI and VGA connectors on the back of the monitor will not be affected. Some of their other adapters have it mounted to the bottom where it should be. Looks like someone did not update the image when a change was made at the factory. With the monitor mount welded to the middle of the VESA plate, 1.5" of the back plate will be visible below the monitor. The left monitor will be mounted to the wall above my desk, so this negative is only cosmetic. But the right monitor not only has 1.5" of the back plate visible below the monitor, it also takes up space on my desk since this monitor is situated 5" above my desk. I corrected this by cutting 1.5" off the bottom of the back plate so the monitor mount is now flush with the back plate. Grinding the welds off and welding the monitor mount to the bottom would also have been an option. I drilled two holes at the bottom of the back plate, next to the monitor mount since I removed the bottom portion. This modification removes the full VESA mount, but it doesn't matter for me since I have them installed on custom mounts. 2. The monitor mount is 2" deep to the back plate. That does not leave much room for a straight HDMI connector. It will fit, but a sharp 90° bend has to be made right at the connector. My thin (0.215") cables are easy to connect, but my thick (0.375") cables are a little more difficult, but will certainly fit. A much cleaner installation is to use a left (90°) or right (270°) connector. When an HDMI socket is orientated so the shorter length is on the bottom then looking at a socket this way, a "left" cable will go to the left (90°). A "right" will be 270°. Search Amazon "left HDMI cable" or "right HDMI cable" for their selections. This is not to be confused with an HDMI right-angle adapter for "bottom" being referred to as 90°, and "top" is referred to as 270°. A "top" would exit to the top of a monitor in this case, a "bottom" would not fit since the monitor mount is in the way. 3. One adapter had cold welds. This means that during welding, not enough amperage was used to create enough heat to melt the metal, which results in poor penetration. A weaker joint is the result although it is still strong enough in this application. My other adapter had good welds. 4. The paint was not dry (hard) on both adapters. Upon receipt (both packed VERY well), there was a strong petroleum smell and slightly tacky - not to the point where fingerprints would be left, but it was VERY easy to scrape the paint off with somewhat light fingernail pressure, leaving bare metal. If an adapter was left on paper, it would stick to it. No primer was used. After two weeks there was not much change so I stripped the paint so I could repaint them (this time with primer).

NOTE: This review is for a new (not refurbished) "CT" version of the Arris tm822g which WILL work with Comcast. Be sure you are buying the modem designed to work with your ISP. have been using this with Comcast Xfinity with voice for 33 months without a single problem. BUT, as others have said, Comcast will not make the process easy. When I decided to switch to Comcast, I balked at paying a monthly fee for a modem. Comcast sales phone rep really tried to convince me that I needed to rent their equipment. After researching and reading reviews at Amazon, I went online to check modem compatibility at mydeviceinfo and confirmed that this modem was compatible. After decades of never using cable services, the lines to our house needed upgrading so self-install was pointless. I set up an installation date. Expecting to get an argument from the installers about the modem, I then went online to Comcast chat to get something in writing from someone at Comcast stating that the modem is indeed approved to work with Comcast Xfinity Blast. I saved the chat for the expected argument from the installers. And I got the argument. BUT, these installers were two really nice, very helpful guys who were not trying to pressure me to rent their modem; they just really could not get the thing to work. The installers called someone at Comcast who told them that the modem was not approved to work with Xfinity. The installers were apologetic. I whipped out my Comcast chat which clearly stated that the modem is approved to work with Xfinity and the installers made another phone call. They eventually got to someone who was able to walk them through the setup (which did not take long) and voilá, there was internet and it was good. The installers also connected my own wifi router and provided me with new power line adaptors to move the router to a more central location for better coverage. Speed and reliability has been extraordinary. Wifi coverage was spotty in some far-flung areas of the house, as it was with every other wifi setup we ever had. About a year ago I replaced the wifi router with an Airport Time Capsule, primarily for backup, but the router swap also vastly improved coverage in the house. It was very helpful not only to me as the customer but to the installers to have the saved chat and the mydeviceinfo on hand so that they had more to go on than just me telling them people at Amazon said it's supposed to work, lol.

Don't get me wrong, I own several Logitech products and enjoy them, but this URC A6 is great for 5 reasons: it programs quickly, is device based, works with my Tivo, independently controls TV/Receiver volume and actually gets used by my family. Reason 1: it programs faster than my Harmony 520. With the URC A6 it took me 20 minutes to track down the codes and teach the URC how to perform a few custom commands. The Harmony took multiple hours to program on my laptop, download to the remote, test, reprogram, redownload, retest, repeat. Reason 2: it is Device based, not Activity based. Because of this, the A6 stays in sync with the power state of my home theatre components more easily than my Harmony 520. Ask someone who owns a Harmony remote if their remote ever gets out of sync w/ the devices mapped into their Watch DVD or Watch TV Activities and you'll know what I mean. Reason 3: it works well with my Tivo HD. I love the "peanut remote" that came with my Tivo HD, it is so well executed, and the A6 is the closest I've come to that experience on a universal remote. Sure, the A6 has no thumbs up/thumbs down button, but I never use those. Reason 4: it allows you to independently, easily, control volume for both the TV and a receiver. This is GOLD! I use "punch through" to let my receiver handle audio most of the time, but I can very easily switch volume control back and forth to the TV for, ahem, other members of my family. Harmony does this, but the URC A6 does it better. Reason 5: it is the only universal remote I've ever owned that the rest of my family is willing to use. They reach for it before they reach for the component remotes. That never happened with the Harmony 520.

I had a number of issues initially trying to get my Macbook pro to run in full resolution (5120 x 1440 120 Hz). Things that didn't work, ever: 1. cheap cables (this is a good time to go through that bin-o-cables and toss out old HDMI cables from years past, they probably won't work with contemporary TV/monitor resolutions. 2. trying to run my USB-C output to a port hub, and then to the monitor using same cable for power/data. What did work: 1. A quality usb-c to Displayport cable, direct from Macbook to monitor. Look for cables that support full 8K with DP 1.4. 2. I use an app called SwitchResX to save off all of my display settings (one for full ultrawide display, another for PIP half screen). What I love about this monitor: 1. Multiple inputs with PIP. I switch back and forth between full ultra wide and PIP with side by side displays. If you had one of those Mac thunderbolt displays way back when, they were QHD resolution and this is exactly like having two QHD displays side by side when you use PIP mode. 2. My Macbook can drive the screen in full resolution and I can still use the laptop screen at the same time. 3. Doesn't have built in speakers, but it does have audio out. I will accept that as a valid answer. I run the audio out into an Echo Dot (full size) and use the Dot as the speaker. 4. Curved display looks cool, and it's cleaner than having two displays side by side. Back looks really nice and clean as well. I had no problems with using the cable cover in the back. This monitor pairs really well with a 120deg desk, I'm using an UPLIFT 120 desk and it fits perfectly. Things that initially annoyed me, but I got over it: 1. The first desk I used really didn't have much access behind it to change inputs and cables. Since the ports all face downward, I ended up having to use my iphone to take pictures upside down to figure out which port was which, and then it was awkward trying to insert the cables the right way. This got a lot easier when I switched to a lifting 120deg desk: I had a much easier time accessing the back of the monitor, and I could elevate the desk so it was higher and that also made it easier for port access. 2. The back cable cover can be a pain to work with. Every time I would take it off I had that question ringing in my head, "Am I going to break it? Am I going to break it?!" I've done it enough times to be okay with it as I haven't broken it yet. And for me it's more important to have tidy/hidden cables where possible. 3. There's one joystick like button on the bottom right of the screen and that's used to power monitor on/off, change sources, and configure other things like PIP. Initially it was kind of a pain to work with but I got used to it. Once the settings are dialed in I mostly now just use it to change sources, enable/disable PIP, and when running two screens, sometimes I use it to change which screen will have the sound output. After all that I still wish it had: 1. built in speakers 2. build in camera 3. built in usb hub ... but for lack of having those things I found it was easy to address outside of the monitor. So yeah, initially it can be a pain to work with but now that I have it all sorted out, I wouldn't change it for any other monitor.

tl;dr: If you can get over the viewing angles like I have, and if you're even slightly tech-savvy or know someone who is, then this is by far the cheapest way to properly experience the joys of tablet computing for the first time. My use case: -Technophile college student (on a budget) with a desktop computer, looking for a more portable computing experience -This was bought to essentially replace a recently sold laptop for watching videos, reading, note-taking, music-listening, and studying on the go. THE GOOD -Rock-solid hardware. -Half the price of the competition. I paid $319 here on Amazon about two months ago, and even then, this was the cheapest dual-core tablet, bar-none. This tablet is an absolute steal at the price it is today ($260) -10.1" screen is an ideal and pleasant size. It won't fit in your pocket, but it's still half the size of my smallest textbook. -Small enough that I take it with me to work and to class every day without a second thought, but large and powerful enough that I actually want to. -Impressive battery life. I'm used to only getting 2-3 hours of active use out of a laptop, but the gtab can literally go all day with moderate usage. -Full USB port!! This is a serious asset. Most ROMs have keyboard and mouse support, if that's your scene. Most other tablets don't have this, including the iPad 2. -Multitouch, capacitive touchscreen. If we're comparing this to other cheap Android tablets, this is a very big deal. If we're comparing it to the iPad, note that the screen only recognizes up to two fingers touching it (this is normal for most devices these days, but the iPad supports three, four, and five-fingered gestures). -Most, if not all, other tablets in this price range are smaller, single-core devices that don't have this tablet's kind of community behind them. Again, this tablet is a steal. -There are MANY ROMs available; you mostly can't go wrong with any of them. My personal recommendation, after trying out Honeycomb, stock, VeganTab 7, etc etc, is CyanogenMod 7 *nightly*. Make sure that if you're using CyanogenMod or a CM7-based ROM (VeganTab 7, etc) that it's no older than *NIGHTLY BUILD 54*. Build 54 added partial hardware acceleration, which completely changes the quality of this tablet's computing experience. The Gtablet is called "harmony" on the CM7 site, named after its chipset. THE BAD -You absolutely must flash this tablet to a different ROM. This will stop some people from even considering this tablet, either for reasons of technical competency or the belief that these things should "just work out of the box." -Poor screen viewing angle. **There's no getting around it. **The up/down viewing angle is the problem. It's especially bad if you're trying to use the tablet in portrait mode (i.e. as an overlarge e-reader). **You will get jealous of the iPad's screen, and when you do, remember that you can buy three G-tablets for the price of one iPad 2 32GB. **Do not expect to comfortably use this tablet on a flat surface. You won't be able to see the screen properly unless you're hunched over it. -Lower screen resolution than most comparatively-sized tablets (Xoom, iPad 2, Galaxy Tab 10.1) THE UGLY -IMPORTANT NOTE ON HARDWARE ACCELERATION: You gotta read the fine print - or search for it - when you're looking at ROMs. Froyo ROMs (any of the stock ROMs, Vegan 5.1, a few of Roebeet's 1.2 ROMs, etc) have full hardware acceleration, and (to reiterate) CyanogenMod 7 *NIGHTLY BUILD 54 AND ONWARD*, based on Gingerbread, has partial hardware acceleration. Any of these latter ROMs will play tablet-quality content (HD youtube videos, etc.) without stuttering, skipping, or freezing. Most of the Gingerbread and Honeycomb ROMs available have this problem. -The bezels are asymmetrical! The top bezel is much thinner than the bottom one. This bothers me a lot in portrait mode. -Can't charge on USB, so if your gtab dies while you're out (unlikely), you can't just borrow your friend's USB cable and keep going. You'll also need a different car charger from your phone, if you decide you need one. -Poor support for video chatting on Android at the moment, so the front-facing camera goes unused for me. Once Google Talk for Android gets video calling, we'll be in business. Check out VTok in the meantime. This isn't an Android review, but you should know this before you get too excited about video chatting with your family on your shiny new tablet. -Poor support for document editing and collaboration on Android at the moment. If anyone knows a good way to do this, let me know and I'll correct this review. This is one of the primary reasons why I invested in a tablet and a portable keyboard. -Makes a great reading device, but don't expect to be able to use it outside during the day. THE BOTTOM LINE -For the current price, there's no question that you should buy this tablet if you're on a budget but still looking for something portable and powerful enough to be useful every day - especially if you managed to read through this giant review. -On tablets in general: Most people don't understand what they're getting when they buy a tablet. The device will just be a toy that'll be left unused if you already have a good method of portable computing. However, if you're looking for more portability, a tablet just might fit that niche.

First, some transparency; I was given this unit to test and provide my review. The review and opinions are my own and not influenced by the seller of this projector. Second, my review and ratings are based on this class of projector. This is an $80 projector, and although I may compare some of the specifications and features to more expensive projectors, my rating will be based on this class of projector and it’s intended use. This projector is intended for viewing in a dark room or outside at night. It is very small and lightweight which makes it ideal for packing up and to take with you for a movie night with family or friends. It is not intended for daytime, bright rooms or for use with a computer to display applications such as Word, Excel, Powerpoint etc. However, watching a movie from a computer works just fine. The projector is only 8” wide by 7” deep and 3” high. I did not weigh it, but the specs indicate it is .9kg (2lbs). I can easily hold it with one hand, it is very light. The unit they sent me came with a nice soft carrying case, a portable 100” movie screen, a remote control, AV, HDMI and VGA Cables. The projector has three inputs. A composite AV, VGA, and an HDMI can be found on the side along with an audio out (mini headphone) and a TF Memory Card Slot. The speaker and IR receiver are located on the back. The top of the unit has a focus ring and a keystone slider that can correct to +/- 15 degrees, a very nice feature for a projector at this price point. The native resolution is 800 x 480 but it will support 1080HD. It will project a size of 37 - 170 inches at distances of 3.8 - 18 feet. I found the sweet spot to be 100-110 inches at about 10 feet from the screen. There are no lumin ratings and projectors in this price range usually measure their brightness in lux, I won’t bother with either, I will just give you my opinion of the brightness, clarity and overall picture quality. This projector is plenty good enough for a fun movie night with the kids. It is sufficiently bright and the picture quality is great for a projector at this price point. The speaker works well, but let’s face it, you will need to attach a set of computer speakers to the projector to get any type of sound quality. If you need a great projector to entertain the kids this projector will get the job done and you can’t beat the $80 price tag!

On the plus side, this is a pretty good improvement over the previous generation. You get a bump in the Android OS. Bluetooth audio works much better and battery life is greatly improved. So there's a bunch of stuff to like. Some of the problems, however, make it almost useless if you plan to use the tablet with Audible. If you don't care about Audible, it's a good upgrade. The problem with Audible is that it takes FOREVER to download a book. At about 10MB/min a book can take 30 minutes in the low fidelity mode. The problem is you have to keep messing with the screen, otherwise it goes to sleep, kills the download, and you have to start all over again. Some of that can be mitigated by changing the screen sleep to 30 minutes, but there are plenty of books that won't download in 30 minutes. This problem exits on two different HD 8's on two different accounts. This problem doesn't exist on any other device connected to the same Wi-Fi access point. The only way I have found to fix the problem is to reset to factory defaults, sign in again to your Amazon/Audible account then immediately download everything you want to listen to. They will download nice and fast. When you quit using the tablet, it will automatically "upgrade" Audible to the new, fancy version of the app (which you cannot downgrade or uninstall independently) and you're back to the slow downloads. For reasons I don't understand, the Audible app works the worse on the Fire devices. It has been problematic for years through various updates and on different versions of the Fire tablet. By contrast, Audible works just fine on my iOS devices through Echo, or via the web browser. So if you're planning on using this table with Audible, look somewhere else. I would normally rate this tablet at 4-5 stars. It's not an iPad but then again it doesn't have the iPad price. But a key built-in feature is just plain broken and broken so badly that it hints at poor testing and software development. For that reason, I give it a one. I'll check back should the situation improve. I've had messages going back and forth about this problem over the last month, so I am actively trying to find a resolution. But so far the responses have been formularic and have not helped. Maybe this review will get some attention applied to the Audible problem once and for all. (One can always hope.)

Most people who do photo editing buy the 15" models with maxed out specs (like me). I don't want to bring that to campus. That's too much money to be slinging in my bag to just browse the web. So, let me be clear. This laptop is excellent. The build quality is amazing for the price. Build quality is great of which I was surprised. The keyboard reminds me of the Macbook and the track-pad keeps up with my fast paced motions quite well. It's light and I can have four to five tabs open running different processes at ease. It does like to stutter when I do multiple things with a video running though. Expected for a tablet processor though. It keeps cool and charged for a days use. The front camera is great for chatting. I will admit, this little computer will replace your daily use computer you lug around currently. I used the Chrome Remote Desktop today on campus and was amazed at the speed and ease. UPDATE 11/24: I've been using this for a good while now and I haven't had any regrets. The computer does what I need, when I want and I only miss running Netflix at school. To clicks on your computer and you're done. They have been updating the OS and the Chromebook is acting a little better now. Overall, I'm still loving it. Just remember, it's NOT for everyone. UPDATE 02/06/13: I love this computer. It is all I use around campus and for class lectures. I barely use Microsoft Office for my notes or spreadsheets in class. Keep your documents available to you at all times and collaboration is simple. It has made my life much easier. Just thought I'd let you all know. UPDATE 04/11/13: Netflix now works! UPDATE 07/10/13: Now that the school season is upon us, I thought I would go ahead and write an update of my handy-dandy little Chromebook. Let's just say, it's still alive and working. Drops, falls, and tosses across the couch and slides across the table this little tabcom is doing well. Software wise, Google has been working at it and getting all the bugs out of the system to provide an even more fluid experience. I love having the ability to use Google Print from ANYWHERE I am and have it waiting for me when I need it. Everything syncs up across platforms and this has really come in hand during projects. Just try the Google Docs as a team compared to Word with Review and you won't go back when doing initial collaboration. Battery is still holding up to 8-10 hours (I know, right)- that's with smart use of the brightness. I honestly don't know what else to say. It works and is the perfect complement for my Macbook that is collecting dust at home. The Macbook is used via my Google Remote Connection and it's just wonderful. The question to ask yourself though is if you are really secure online? You can get a better laptop as some commentators have stated and that is very true. Second update: Mid 2018 and my Fintie iPad case is still going strong! Amazing durability. The color and design elements have never worn off, still looks terrific. Perfect protection, not a single scratch on my iPad despite dropping it several times onto concrete floors over the years (while encased in its Fintie, of course.) I certainly got my money's worth with this one. Now my husband has bought a new and bigger iPad and is considering buying a Fintie case for it. Naturally, I'm encouraging him. Update: This Fintie case has held up surprisingly well for nearly two years now. A few bits of vinyl trim and a couple of threads have worn off at the inside corners, but they are not noticeable to anyone but me and overall the case still looks like new. The fit is still quite secure and though I have dropped my iPad a few times in the past two years the case has protected it completely, with not even a scratch to the screen, to which I have never added a separate screen protector. When closed, this case still appears to be quite elegant but not ostentatious. A casual observer might mistake it for a leather bound book. The swivel still works smoothly to quickly change screen orientation. I have used that function several times daily. The vinyl has never cracked at any point and looks like new after many air, road and ship travels despite being repeatedly crammed into tight bags, tiny room safes and backpacks. It's held up perfectly and protected my iPad in all kinds of watery weather. And it's repeatedly proven itself to be a useful tool for displaying recipes during cooking, entertaining sticky-fingered children, and reading in bed. The magnetic closure still turns off the screen automatically when I close the case cover and all the openings for the camera, various control buttons, connection ports and speaker have remained perfectly aligned. The only reason I cannot give this iPad case 5 stars is that the grooves for holding up the screen at two different angles are a bit too shallow to keep the iPad from falling flat on occasion, usually during use on my less than perfectly flat lap. Deeper grooves or a nonslip surface might prevent these infrequent but still irritating slippages. Otherwise, I have no regrets in purchasing this case and if I had to choose a case again I would definitely buy this one again. I like this case so much I may have to select my next iPad based on whether it will fit into it! Thanks for listening. FYI, I always pay full price and am never bribed for any of my reviews. Original review: This iPad case fits very tightly but securely on my iPad 4 and looks great from a distance. It is made from a vinyl type material that is attractive and has no odor that I can detect. I expect the padding and reinforced corners will protect my iPad should it ever be dropped. The decorative design pressed into the cover of this particular color is also very nice. The case swivels easily from portrait to landscape position and automatically turns the iPad off when closed, wasting no power whatsoever. It is also configured properly for all the openings needed for the camera lens, power outlet, speaker, etc. My iPad also stands more securely in the deep grooves of this case than it did on my previous case's shallower grooves, though it would be nice if there was a third groove that would allow the iPad to lay at a flatter angle for easier use on my lap. The reason for only three stars is because after only a few days of very light use by a careful adult the stitching on various parts of the case is already beginning to fray. Everywhere a thread stops it frays. This makes me wonder how long the case will last if I don't somehow find a way to stop the fraying with some sort of glue or sealant that would not detract from the appearance of the case.

I'm only giving it three stars because the lubuntu 18.04 software pre-installed in the eEMC is not properly configured. You basically can't configure anything until you create a password for the root account because gksu (or an alternative) is not setup correctly. This is just plain bad practice. You launch config programs from the menu that require root privilege and they fail to work because they require a root password that has not been set. Root passwords are considered bad practice these days, normal distributions properly configure gksu (or whatever) so control-panel code that need root will work properly when launched from the menus. Overall Lubuntu is just plain lame, and despite its alleged "lighweight" design, it is very sluggish with poor UI feedback -- you click something and nothing happens, no acknowledgement of the click, then about the time you think its crashed something pops up. I tried their latest lubuntu-20.04 from the digital-loggers website and it mis-configured the same way. If you don't need the GPIO and other "extra" hardware on the board, its an Atom CPU so you can install any distribution that you like. If you do this and need the extras, be prepared for a long slog as saying the documentation sucks would be complimenting it. Installing a good distribution like Ubuntu-Mate gives you a nice system for the money, I used mine with a Coral TPU to run AI person detection for my security cameras. Supports significantly more cameras than a Pi4 for roughly the same cost. I endorse the hardware, but only if you are skilled in Linux or whatever OS you put on the thing, and aren't afraid of patching to use the "extras" that need non-standard drivers. Edit: I think the GPIO support may be part of the "standard" Atom board support package when you do a "normal" Linux install, but the other extra hardware may need drivers. I haven't looked as I've no use for these, but I have looked for documentation which seems minimal. I know the WiFi works and the Bluetooth seems to (the disable/enable icon appears and toggles when selected) with a standard Ubuntu 20.04 installation. Mine is sitting 10 feet away from my router so in norm weaker signal situations you may need to buy and antenna, I just used it minimally as I was curious if it worked with the standard installation. First off, I'm reviewing the Ninja Majestouch-2, Tenkeyless "Click Action", which entirely use Cherry MX Blues. This means they have an audible click and a tactile feel when they actuate at 60cN (about 61 grams or 2.1 ounces) of direct pressure. If you need to know more about the switches and how they work, do a quick search on whatever engine you prefer or buy some samples from WASD Keyboards and feel them out for yourself. Think a kit is somewhere like $15. Not bad to figure out which switches are for you, instead of dropping $80-160 on a quality mechanical keyboard only to find out you don't like the switches. Most gamers will like the "speed" and relatively quieter reds or blacks. I hate them, but the consensus is that they are "gaming switches". Brows are a middle ground of tactile--feel the bump as it actuates, but little sound unless you are bottoming out hard while typing. Blues tend to be the loudest of the easily found switch types, and have the tactile bump of browns. Greens are beefier actuation resistance switches with the bump and click of blues. Not going to go into clears, whites and the rest as I have little experience with them. I like the blues the most because the feedback seems to make me more aware of my typing and key actuation, so I tend to type faster and more accurately. When gaming, I know the key registered before I see the visual feedback due to the sound and feel. It's just my preference, though and everyone's varies. Reminds me more of the buckling spring switches from back in the day. One of the good points of mechanical keyboards--options for just about everyone. I digress...to the review! I borrowed my friend's Filco "Tactile" (MX Browns) Tenkeyless to see why he spent $150+ on a keyboard that had no features and not even a numpad. I was currently using a Logitech G19, which are pretty pricey but have an extremely long list of features. And an LCD screen. And millions of color options for backlighting. Filcos do not come standard with any of this. Not even dedicated media buttons or volume controls. They are just keyboards, and this model doesn't even have a numpad. So why did I buy it? After a week I found that I was typing faster and more accurately, I had all but stopped using the numpad and had become faster using 8 fingers for numbers instead of 3 on the numpad, realized that without the numpad my mouse was more ergonomically aligned and my desk space was more efficient. I didn't miss a single one of the bells and whistles of my G19. Even the volume controls. I had quickly learned all the hotkeys and shortcuts for most of my programs/games that I would have to use without the extra buttons and features, and was faster it without them. The biggest difference was when I went back to the old rubber-dome topped light-show that was formerly my favorite gaming toy. It felt cheap. It was $30 more than the filco, but it felt cheaper by far. It wasn't nearly as sturdy (Filco's feel like they could be used to break down a door, exceptionally solid and a little heavy). The Filco never budged while typing or resetting my hand position after grabbing paperwork. The G19 is made of plastic and it felt very flimsy after using the steel back-plated Filco. The G19's keys felt squishy and likely to fail. It felt huge, bulky, gimmicky and why did I need back-lights? I know where the keys are. When using the filco, I pretty much didn't look down at all. I just knew that everything is where it was supposed to be, and there was never a need to check my work. I only had 87 keys to keep track of--only regularly use 70 or so. I think the G19 has 136. I soon realized that I preferred the essentials. Though my typing did retain it's accuracy, I did lose some speed without the mechanical switches. This was a few years ago. I finally ponied up and dropped some dough on the last keyboard I may actually need. Mechanical keyboard switches are rated up to 50 million keystrokes each. Rubber dome are 1-5 million keystrokes. All in all, I'd say Filco's are expensive, but justifiably so. They are made to last, and sacrifice bells and whistles for reliability and ergonomics. I've had mine for 2 months. I gave my wife my flashy other keyboard. She prefers the soft-feel of the rubber domes and how quiet they are, but thinks the LCD screen and extra keys are silly. Now I'd say I agree with the latter. If you know someone who has one, see if you can borrow it for a week. Try before you buy. But for me, this is the greatest keyboard made since the IBM Model M Keyboard. Which--if you're too young to have used or never had the pleasure--was a true pleasure to type on.

Outlined Review: Good, for the price. Who are these for: Anyone who wants a convenient speaker but needs the RGB lights as a priority. The Plan: I wanted Bluetooth speakers I could pair together for left and right stereo sound and carry anywhere. First Look Impressions: These look and feel hearty. You can tell Anker put some time into this and built it with quality materials in mind. This has a good weight to it and I expect these to last a long time. I had already done my research on these and had the SoundCore app installed on my phone before they even arrived so I knew the RGB lights were on the bottom and controlled through the app which works well. I also like how compact the speaker is and the rubber flap on the back hiding ports when not needed. The buttons on top have a short travel so barely touching them can toggle the top functions of the speaker. Listening: Here’s where things become mediocre... After pairing with the app and messing around with settings, I settled on what I liked and started playing music. Immediately I heard a lot of mids. So I opened the app back up to see what I need to change. After a brief confusion about where the bass button is, I found it on the top of the speaker and pressed it. The bass boost came on, I saw it light up where the button is, but I can’t hear any change in bass or the music at all. I keep trying off and on to no avail. At this point, I figured maybe it wasn’t picking up the low frequency bass, so I plugged them into my tv using the auxiliary input from the tv to the speakers and have the speakers plugged in for power. No change there either when trying bass. Now I know I am a huge bass fan, it I can’t figure out why I don’t hear any change in bass at all. I bring in other people to see if they can tell I difference and if I was going insane. But they couldn’t tell either. Bittersweet moment, I’m glad I’m not insane, maybe, but I was hoping they could hear it change. I went back and paired them with an iPad to use as I intended to use them with originally. I can’t get past how drowned out how the highs and lows are. The mid sound levels are great but I can get that kind of sound from my iPad already. Feature, RGB Lights on bottom: These are amazing and comes with genius options from the app are more than enough to find what you’re looking for and very unique. I get asked all the time about the lights as they are very eye-catching. Anker has done very well with these... So well, that I usually turn the volume all the way down and just keep them on to watch the lights while listening to things from other speakers I have. In conclusion: Anker is one of my favorite companies on Amazon and anywhere really. Their power banks are second to none as is their customer service, truly outstanding. I have an IT business and use many Anker products daily with multiple customers seeing me use them and recommending them daily... Overall, the speakers are OK for the price. Audiophiles may not find that these meet your needs. I don’t consider myself an audiophile, as I mentioned previously, I love bass. I just wish it was a stronger bass boost than what it is I guess... Pros: - Compact and convenient design. - One of the best app RGB options ever made. - Waterproof. - Quality materials used. Cons: - Missing sound highs and lows. - Sometimes can take a moment to sync with each other. - Slightly loud connection sound once paired (Not sure if this is adjustable.) I would recommend these to anyone wanting a speaker that you won’t request a lot out of but still gets the job done and with an RGB light bonus. With that said, I would not recommend these to audiophiles and bass fans. Thank you

This Newtonian reflector telescope is very well made and very easy to use. If you have realistic expectations (it is not going to produce a stunning large image of Saturn, even at 200x magnification, which is its maximum useful magnification), they will be fulfilled by this model. You would likely need a few additional Barlow lenses (I would recommend the affordable and well made lenses by Meade, such as their 3x and 2x Barlow lenses--around 30$ per lens), but other than that, you will be able to view the night sky comfortably with this scope. It is great for observing the planets and their moons (mostly Jupiter's), the Moon, and even some deep sky objects like the Great Orion nebula. The provided eyepieces offer a 20x and a 40x magnification. With a 3x Barlow lens, you can make that a 60x and a 120x magnification, which would allow you to see the planets (their image will be still reasonably small, though, but if the Barlow lens is of good quality, it will be quite clear). The only part that requires a bit of assembly is the EZ Finder II Reflex Sight. Make sure that you align it with the object that you see in your eyepiece when daylight is lower (maybe 30-40 minutes before twilight, so that you can see clearly the LED red dot). Aligning is reasonably easy (I had no prior experience doing so) and it works well. Once you attach the EZ Finder II to the scope, you are good to go. You can put the scope on a small 3- or 4-legged stool, or on a table. You can also use a tripod that has a 1/4 screw (or a quick-release plate). The scope will weigh about 7 to 7.5 pounds with the Barlow lenses, so the tripod should be able to support that weight. At this price, there is a lot that you can do with this Newtonian beginner's model, and it is very well made. This is my second telescope (until now I've been mostly using Celestron astronomical binoculars), and I am enjoying watching the starry skies with it!

The Pillowsonic and Sangean have a lot of dead zones where the pressure of your head or the pillow mutes the speaker. My only gripe is that the cord is ridiculously short and cheap. It barely reaches my iPhone on the nightstand. Twice now I've snagged the cord as I was rolling over causing the phone to leap into the air and smash into my head. (It's in the drawer, now, but this means another snag will probably pull the cord apart.) The cord itself is extremely thin. and bends 90 degrees at the jack. Higher quality cords have strain relief to make the cord bend in an arc instead of sharp angles. (Sharp angle bends break the wire) If you are handy with wire cutters, I strongly recommend an extension cord: [[ASIN:B003SGFVKC Aurum Cables 3.5mm Car Stereo Auxiliary Male to Female]]. It will improve usability and may extend the life of the speakers. [UPDATE] I DON'T recommend that you cut into the pillow to completely replace the wire. Inside the pillow is an unexpectedly complicated layering of foam and cloth. You'll never get it back together properly. I completely destroyed one pillow trying this.

These are NOT the drives you're looking for if you're buiding a RAID array. WD purposely cripples consumer-level drives so they don't play nice with RAID arrays. Aside from error correction issues (where drives can be dropped from the array because they don't respond fast enough), these drives also have power saving features that park the drive heads after only a few seconds of inactivity. This causes the drives to go to sleep and wake up every 12 seconds or so, which will contribute to a premature drive failure. There is a workaround that I chose to utilize, but that is in no way supported by WD. Google around for an utility called WDIDLE3 which allows you to disable the power saving feature, as well as tweak the error-correction setting. It's a DOS utility, so you will have to create a bootable DOS CD or USB stick.

Yes, it is a great price but there are some problems with Fire that should have been fixed before release, and would not have added to the device cost. The first problem: the lack of a physical "home" button (or at least a virtual home icon that is *always* displayed). This issue, combined with a touch screen that is unresponsive about half the time - or way too responsive when scrolling through the library - is the single most annoying feature of the device. Second: multiple-step process for buying and installing apps and games. Third: the virtual keyboard, which is ridiculously unreliable (this is probably the touch screen issue again). Fourth: the entire "bookshelf" metaphor - for everything. I'm not sure who finds this an intuitive way to organize things - but I certainly do not find it intuitive, even for books. (How about lists, under appropriate headings like "books," "apps," etc.? The designers could use appropriate graphics for the headings if they assume people are too stupid to read the words.) The final issue could not have been solved without significant hardware changes and added cost, but it is disappointing: no ability for videoconferencing via Skype or any other, similar app. Please note that I am an Amazon fan, have long been a Prime member, and own multiple Kindles (including the Fire). I won't be buying a second Fire. A P.S. after owning the device for more than a month. Finding help for problems (e.g., wifi connection issues) is riduculously difficult.

It is a very cute/discrete small package that feels solid and doesn't require another power input making it ideal to place on a desk. It comes with a ~4 foot USB cable and is clearly designed for desktop usage. The volume knob is pretty small but it easy to turn - the output volume is nice and linear to "ear damaging" volumes. It is really nice to be able to adjust the audio volume by hand. There is a HI and LOW gain selector on the back which definitely does increase the output volume. Since it is digital output to the FiiO 10k I set the windows audio to 30% and leave it which allows better fine-tuning of the volume on the FiiO. With the windows audio output at max I cannot turn the volume past 2/8 without it getting uncomfortably loud! [If it is too quite, make sure the audio driver virtual volume is turned up .. or clean your years.] It powers my Sennheiser HD 650's (high impedance) much better than my PC built-in sound card and really enhances the entire sound profile and clarity. The little bass boost helps the 650's during movies, which are pretty neutral. However, for sound quality compared to a better dedicated amplifier (eg. the Schiit Valhalla), it simply can't compare: it's an entry level product at an entry level price. Comparatively the FiiO's amplifier itself, especially in the bass, feels compressed and even a bit dull. The DAC and line-out feed the Valhalla pretty well which really opens up the dynamic sound stage and liveliness with more openness. The Sony MDR-X11's (32 ohm) that I have, which are mediocre headphones at best, did not have any noticeable improvement from just directly connected to the PC. The MDR's sound like wanna-be-bass-blah pretty much always. This amplifier/DAC is probably best for decent low-impedance headsets that are known to benefit from a 'little' amp. Some headphone drivers need a little bit of help to reach their potential; others simply won't sound any better no matter how much you try and help them. Also, if you already have a good/discrete sound card this probably won't be an upgrade. For a a laptop something like the Dragonfly, for a little bit more money, may be a better choice. 4/5 stars because it still makes a better DAC then my built-in sound card and is "good for the price". I am currently using it only as a DAC and am fairly satisfied with it .. at least until I can afford another :)

First off, let me say I was really excited when I purchased this product. I had been using my Garmin Nuvi 350 for about 3 years, and I loved it, but I thought it was time for an upgrade (keyword "upgrade"). The newer ones have much bigger screens, and I was really looking forward to the lane assist that this model offers. The bottom line is I really wanted to like this product since I loved the features it offers on paper. Anyway, I had it overnighted from Amazon because I needed it for a trip home from college, and I took it out for a test run the night before I was leaving. So, the first place I wanted to go I found in the "points of interest". To make a long story short, I followed the directions, got to the location, and the place wasn't there. I talked to some friends after and they said that the place was never in that location. I'm really not sure what the issue was here, but I was more than willing to let it slide since I'm well aware that points of interest are fairly inaccurate on all GPS systems and I could always just use my phone or a computer to get a recent address for where I was looking to go. Then comes my drive home. I don't really have much to say for this part except the fact that my old Garmin 350 has gotten me home from this precise location many times before with no problems. I thoroughly expected the new one to do the same. It didn't. It was fine most of the way, but when it got near my house on the highway, it simply told me to get off about 4 exits too soon. For me, this was the last straw. I couldn't be using a GPS that has inferior routing capabilities to the 3 year old one I was seeking to replace. That's not how it should be. I have no idea why this is the case, but many reviewers have said the routing in this unit is terrible, and they are 100% correct. And just to be clear, during my experience, traffic was turned off, so it definitely was not taking me off the highway for traffic purposes. The last thing I have to say about this unit has to do with the screen. The screen is great looking, but it isn't great "functioning". The actual touch capability on the old Garmin is far superior to this touch screen in accuracy. This screen seemed very inaccurate, and the interface seems almost too bloated for the actual on-board processor. To sum it up, I can't really think of a valid use for this unit. The routing is just brutal, the touch screen is pretty crummy, and these two major components are sure to overshadow anything good it does. Yeah, the traffic and lane assist are pretty cool, but are useless when the core routing system fails to actually work like it should.

I have owned many TomTom GPS units over the last 10 years and have liked them all - each with their own advantages and disadvantages, but this is probably be the last TomTom I will buy. 1. I feel that the user interface is just awful compared to every other TomTom I have owned. It seems little thought has gone into functionality and how users interact with GPS devices. Here are a few examples: to navigate to your home (or any other saved place) requires at least 5 presses/swipes of the screen - why should it be that hard? It used to be much simpler in the older (and much better) TomTom units. Another annoyance is that only 4 menu items are displayed on the screen when there is plenty of space to put 8... so you end up having to repeatedly swipe to find the menu item you want. Also, the menu ordering makes no sense - saved places are at the back, whereas the function to report a traffic camera is at the front - my guess is that you want to go places more often than report a traffic camera, so why not prioritize the menu accordingly? Another annoyance is that the screen is nice and large but to open the menu you have to deftly target a little area at the bottom left of the screen... why make it so unnecessarily hard to open the menu? 2. Voice control simply does not work. It is completely useless, even after doing everything suggested by TomTom support. My guess is that the marketing guys absolutely needed this as a selling point and don't really care if it worked or not. 3. Android app. The app is always and and always in your notification bar. To disable this, you have to disable notifications for the app. Another annoyance. 4. Searching for points of interest along your route simply does not work - points of interest completely off your route are displayed (like half way across the state!), including those you passed an hour ago on a long trip. Why? This feature used to work quite nicely in older TomTom units, I'm disappointed that it's useless now. I could go on and on. Let's just say I am disappointed simply by comparison to previous TomTom units. It's a shame because the display is huge and the moving map is very nice. UPDATE: 12/19/2015 1. I still can't believe how big of a backwards step this GPS is. First, I cannot remember my old TomTom GPS' taking me to the wrong place but this one has done it 3 times already. See attached photo. Instead of taking me TO THE ADDRESS, it tried to take me to a point on a HIGHWAY close to the destination I chose from points of interest. Ridiculous. USE THE ADDRESS, NOT A GPS COORDINATE. YOU MAY NOT STOP ON AN INTERSTATE HIGHWAY, TOMTOM. This is simply not acceptable, especially as cheaper and older units would not have done that. (See photo. The star is my intended destination, but the GPS tried to route me onto the interstate) 2. Find a point along the route: Older TomTom's you could enter the NAME of a place along the route (e.g. Burger King), and it would find those names along the route. This version you have to search by category - for example, "Restaurants". Well, that's of no use to anyone as there are tens of thousands of restaurants along many routes. 3. The update software is clunky: Even when your phone is connected to the GPS it won't tell you that updates are available. To find that out you have to log in to your TomTom account on your PC. And then it only says you have updates available, it doesn't tell you WHAT the updates are so you can prioritize. I don't care about speeding camera updates so please don't waste my time with making me connect my GPS and downloading the updated to see what they are. What a sad mess of a GPS. Poorly thought through.

I really like the design of this telephone stand. It arrived with a few scratches and scuffs, as well as a crack in the upper-right hand corner. However, I'm going to apply the benefit of the doubt by assuming this will be replaced without incident and am NOT reflecting the defects in my review. USE | I purchased this to use at my work (I'm a RN in a healthcare clinic). After researching the available options available on Amazon, I selected this one due to the built-in storage located on the item's left side, as well as the overall design and the material. APPEARANCE | Clear acrylic takes up less visible space and since there's enough junk floating around at the clinic I felt this would be the best cosmetic approach. STORAGE | There are 5 individual compartments on the lateral storage space. The longer/taller space the perfect size to keep the laminated contact list for our physicians on-call numbers within reach while the smaller ones accommodates several writing utensils. They're ideal for pens and pencils but probably a little too short for large scissors. The narrow groove on the top houses a writing utensil well. DESIGN | The small lip on the front of the stand secures the telephone in place. The unit is stable and sits securely on a table due to the folds on each side. It also contains 4 small circle shaped indentations, presumably to enable easier mobility and to prevent it from making a horrible scraping noise when moved. QUALITY/DURABILITY | The telephone stand appears to be decent quality. It can probably withstand a few accidents. However, I would prefer the acrylic to be a little thicker as I want it to endure heavy use for many years; but, for the price, it's acceptable. MATERIAL | I do not consider this to be 100% transparent. The acrylic has an ever so faint blue-ish hue. This is a sign of lower quality material. Again, I feel it's acceptable for the price. I know I'm being particular, but allow me to share my idea of a perfect telephone stand (and one that I would gladly pay more for): Higher quality and thicker acrylic, storage on both sides to accommodate multiple size office accessories, and a shelf on the bottom to place items such as a calculator.

I have a very mixed review. I bought this as a player to listen to audiobooks, I have more than 650, and my iPod does not have enough space to store all of them. Yes I know this exceeds the "music" function's ability to access files, but my homework indicated that I would still be able to us it. The Good - feel of the player in my hand, is nice. The buttons are all solid and easy to use, function of each is very simple. Sound is good, I have not compared the sound of the same files over different devices, so take it for what it's worth. I did use a high quality set of head phones. A 256 mini SD card is supported and all the files can be read by the player. From the perspective of listening to MP3 files there is nothing wrong with this player, it works and works pretty well. The Bad - these are all software (firmware) issues. I did my homework before I purchased this, so I knew before I bought it that the "music" function would not show all my "songs" (book chapters) or "artists" (authors), but there were plenty of reviews that said you would be able to access all your files in the "file management" function (true). So I figured it might call for a little "extra" work to access everything but i accepted that. There are a number of problems that make this player unusable, at least for me. 1st the directory in the file function only recognizes 25(ish) characters, the file structure I use for my books include the series name, book number, and the title, there is a good chance that all the books in a series will show up as individual files with the exact same name. This makes it impossible to figure out which file is for the 1st book in a series vs. the last book. 2nd within the file directory function, when you navigate to a specific book so that you can play it the chapters are not sorted in order. My files are all numbered correctly and they have the correct order number, but they don't sort so you can't start play on file #1 and expect is to then go to #2 when it is done (No I do not have it on shuffle). I had to go through a lot of effort to rename my files so that they were labeled such that they should sort correctly, a complete waste of time. 3rd You are supposed to be able to use a 256 GB Mini SD Card, which does actually work I can see all the different files that are on the card, but I can't navigate to a book and hit play. I was counting on being able to do this to get around all my files not showing up in the "music" function. I have to open the book and hit play in the chapter view which is a problem due to my second issue above. 4th In the "Music" function when you sort by "artist" (author), the complete name is cut off after 10 characters, not a big deal because I can recognize who the author is, but because I included the series name in the file name all the books in the series are lumped together. 5th In the "music" function sorting by "album", again because it only recognizes 20 something characters it lumps all the different files together. What this means, from a practical point, is that I have a book series where the series name and book number is to long for the software to recognize so I have one entry for a series of books (all the books in the series) and all the chapters for all the different books are lumped together into one entry, for example a series with 5 books will show up as 1 book but it will have 5 introductions, 5 chapter 1s, etc. Which means if I hit "play" all 5 introductions will play then all 5 chapter 1s will play, etc. Which again defeats the whole reason for my buying this player. At this point I don't know what, if anything I can do in order to use this player. My bottom line, I can't use this for the reason I purchased it. VERY DISAPPOINTING. I DO NOT recommend buying this is you are planning on using it for audiobooks, unless you only have a few books (less than 10) or only use a memory card that is less that 64 GB (the smallest card I have). I think all my "issues" could be fixed, but in all reality I don't expect that will ever happen and I will never be able to use this. If playing your files in order is important to you, choose something else.

The nominal 64GB drive has a true capacity of 61524148224 bytes, or 61.52GB, or 57.31GiB, or 120164352 sectors of 512 bytes each. This is before any partition table or filesystem is created. I created a FAT32 filesystem on the drive, and sequentially wrote 60 files of 1.00GB each, containing encrypted zeros (effectively, random data). The total time was 4744.81 seconds (including the sync command), for an average rate of 12.6MB/s. Non-sequential writes would be slower, but 12.6MB/s should be considered the maximum possible write speed of the drive. On reading back the files, the first 52 files were error free. After that, the drive failed, and seemed to reboot its controller repeatedly. I noted that the drive was too hot to touch, even through its plastic case. I disconnected and reconnected the drive, and the rest of the files verified correctly. The overall read speed was 142MB/s when there weren't any errors. All these tests were done with the drive sitting in open air, at 72 degrees F ambient temperature. Reading a huge amount of data off the drive should be done carefully, in shifts, to avoid overheating it. Idling and write accesses don't seem to make the drive overheat, but the metal connector always feels uncomfortably warm after unplugging it, even if you hardly do any operations. Note that I did all these tests on a USB 3.x superspeed port. If you use a USB 2.0 or USB high speed port, your speed will likely be limited to 30MB/s. I removed 1 star for lying about the capacity (3.9% is missing from the advertised size), and another star for lying about the write speed (it claims to be 10 times faster than a 4MB/s USB drive, which is 40MB/s, but it actually can't write faster than 12.6MB/s). I still gave 3 stars, because it is faster than other USB flash drives I've tested of similar capacity.

Initial review - Opening / Setup: Just received the Parrot Zik 2.0's in black. Parrot put some thought into even the packaging. This is something that a lot of companies dismiss, but considering that this is your consumer's first interaction with the product that they have purchased, there is some value in that first impression - and Parrot certainly recognizes that. Having said that, it did take a little work to get the box open; and again a little work to get the battery out of its little spot in the box. But otherwise, a wonderful opening experience. Instructions were easy - to the point where they are almost not needed. That is the simplicity with which you want to design your product. When you open the Zik's, you connect them via the provided USB cable to your computer to charge the battery. The red charging indicator turns white once the battery is charged. Once the battery is charged, you press the button (which is where the charging indicator is), go into the Bluetooth preferences on your iPhone (or whatever you're using), and the Zik's show up for you to pair them. There are audible indicators to indicate power on, power off, and pairing. Fit: Some have mentioned with regard to the original Zik's and the Zik 2.0's that if they don't have a petite head, the Zik's aren't the best fit. My head isn't huge, but it also isn't small. The Zik's fit comfortably on my head. What may be of concern is the fit of the earpads around my ears, since I don't have the smallest ears. I really like in ear monitor's that have a good fit (I use a pair from Etymotic), or a circumaural (around the ear) design for headphones. I have tried supra-aural headphones (have a pair of Sennheiser HD 25-1 II's that sound just great), but they cause my ears fatigue after a period of use - so my son uses them now. Some also have mentioned the weight of the original Zik's. As you may know, the Zik 2.0's are lighter than the original - but not the lightest headphones around. They feel comfortable enough on my head - we will see how they feel after a while. App / Sound / Bluetooth performance: The app requires you to register. I'm not sure why that's necessary, but fine. As soon as you register, you're told of a software update. It downloads and then transfers to the Zik's via Bluetooth without issue. After the update, the Zik's reconnect to the iPhone, and this is confirmed by an audible signal. However, the App isn't aware of the presence of the Zik's. Killing and restarting app makes the app of their presence. The app gives you a great deal of control over the sound - you can literally shape it in Producer mode, or use a simplified equalizer. You can turn noise reduction on and off. You can enable or disable the feel / size of the room. All of this control results in the ability to really get the Zik's suit how you like to hear. The app also shows you the battery level of the Zik's. I'm getting what I believe are some dropouts - I thought at first it was due to Bluetooth, but it may be that the Bluetooth connection is fine and it's the app that drops out. I can reproduce it, setting my iPhone down on my desk. My head is no more than 18" from my head. And unlike what I experience with another pair of Bluetooth earphones, the dropout isn't short - when it drops out, it easily takes 5 to 15 seconds for it to resume. I don't think it's the iPhone, because I can stream via Bluetooth to the UE BOOM speaker I have from a different level on the home. This will be a deal breaker if I can't figure out a way to resolve it. It seems that you cannot use the Zik's over the wired connection when they are turned on - it isn't possible to be wired + noise canceling + equalized + concert hall sound. If they are turned on, and on your iPhone you select wired headsets, it switches back to Bluetooth headsets. I connected the Zik's to the headphone jack on my Mackie 802VLZ4 mixer, and they sound just awful when they aren't turned on. Turning them on provides a better sound, but it doesn't seem natural - not like what I get from the Etymotic's or from the Sennheiser's. Not only that, but there is a noticeable delay in the sound being delivered through the Zik's - something which is completely unacceptable. I then connected the Zik's to the headphone jack on my MacBook Pro, and listened to the same track that I heard on my iPhone. They sound just awful turned off (passive). And again, turned on, they don't at all sound the same as they do on the iPhone. So it seems that their app is doing something - like the sound is processed through the app. The changes you make in the app don't affect the Zik's directly - they affect how the sound is processed and sent to the Zik's from their app? Further, I noticed that when I turned the Zik's on, and received a text message on my iPhone, the Zik's stopped providing audio from the MacBook for probably 5 seconds. So they at the same time are doing Bluetooth to the phone, and are wired to my MacBook. This isn't really what I want. With all this technology in the headphones, you would think that wiring them would disable Bluetooth. You would also think that you wouldn't leave the Zik's crippled in the absence of the app. So because this app isn't on my Mac, and certain not on a mixer, the only way I can hear the potential of these headphones is with their app on a mobile phone. It seems that there are a lot of elements of the Zik's that haven't been well thought out. They have a place and a purpose, but it seems that they focused a great deal on bells and whistles and missed the boat on the basics. For me, it has turned what I initially considered a one star product to a one star product.
