Where to begin? I loved the idea behind this drive, and despite a lot of bad reviews, I ordered it. Why? Reading through the Seagate forums, it's quite hackable and I thought I could solve some of the problems people were complaining about. After weeks of using it and trying to hack it into some reasonable shape, I must say this is one of the worst designed product I've ever used. Seagate's engineers and programmers should all be shot. First, this thing must act as your AP, it can't really join an existing wireless network. The recent firmware upgrade just let you bridge onto your home LAN, which is a bit different than simple joining. Stupid. Second, when you connect it via USB, it kills the wireless. So after you copy a bunch of stuff onto it from your computer, you have to reboot, bridge connect to your wireless AP before you can start using it. Again, stupid. Third, the battery life is atrocious. I don't know what they were smoking when they advertised their battery life. I get about 2 hours of streaming, and maybe about 4-5 hours of standby. It wastes tons of energy doing stupid things like constantly cataloging your stuff in the background. There's no sense of organization on this thing. You can throw media files into any folder you want, and if it's a movie file, it will show up under video; if it's a music file, it will show up under music etc. Sounds convenient, but at the cost of heavy battery usage, since it must scan through your whole hard drive and figure out what's what - ALL THE TIME! It would have much more sensible to have a movie folder, music folder, picutre folder, etc. Why is Seagate's method stupid? Well, if you have album art in your music folder, it shows up in the pictures section. I can't imagine what kind of stupidity made them seem like this was a good idea. Fourth, the wireless dies constantly, often in the middle of streaming, forcing you to reboot it. Also, the DHCP server often takes a long time handing out an IP #, and sometimes outright fails. Such problems are indicative of substandard parts, very much like the kind you find in a clearance bin at your local electronics hole in the wall. It's pathetic to a large company like Seagate using such low quality parts. So, I was able to telnet into it and shut off the DLNA server, otherwise it would have barely lasted long enough to see one movie. I noticed that it used Django as the web server platform. I went through the code, and it's just littered with comments from the various programmers who's worked on it. That would not be that much of a problem were it not for the fact that the firmware sits on a SD space that's about 50MB in size, and it's pretty much 99% full. Removing DLNA saved me about 10MB, and in its stead I put in SAMBA, so I don't have to deal with the stupid web interface, or use their GoFlex app. I also wrote a simple script to constantly monitor the web server, the wireless and other services and restart them if they're down. And you know what? It's having to restart services ALL THE TIME. I also have it automatically connect to all my known wireless networks I may use, and that seems to work sometimes, not all the time. I'm also trying to figure out how to have it join a wireless network rather than just bridging to one. Then I thought, I'm having to have to redo everything the knuckleheads at Seagate should have done in the first place. Why did I buy this to go through all this trouble? I think it's easier to just build one of these things myself from scratch. I'm past the time to return this product, because I had spent more than 30 days trying to debug and re-engineer this product. Learn from my mistake. Don't buy this drive. It's just amazingly bad.

My work environment is in manufacturing (semiconductors) and there is a lot of equipment that could cause signal interference. The BT signal range is a lot better than I expected in this environment. I tested it and it easily exceeds the 30 foot range in my work environment. Pairing was easy and painless. There is a nice audible beep when the connection is established. I've not had any problems pairing it to my phone or tablet (Android). It reconnects seamlessly after the initial pairing. Sound quality is good (see cons below). A nice feature is to pause the audio you just have to press the button. To un-pause just press it again. The supplied charger is your typical USB style charger. It's a separate changing bring that plugs into your AC socket and a separate USB to micro USB (typical Android phone style charging port). One thing about the supplied cable is that it is a charging cable only. It would be nice if it had data transfer capabilities. At least mine only charges. I tried it with my phone and a few Windows laptops/desktops and I've never gotten the computers to recognize my phone with this cable. I guess they do this to save money for some reason. This is not a big deal since I have many data cables. Just thought I'd mention this. Cons: I've notice when listening to music it's skips every once in a while. I have not determined if it's this unit, my phone/tablet or the app (I'll update this if I figure it out). This unit was bigger than expected. I guess it has a large battery which makes it big. The button mentioned above is sensitive if you have this in your pocket and are kneeling etc. a lot and pauses the audio when you don't want to sometimes. I'd like it if it had some sort of guard around it or was not as sensitive as it is. There is no clip which would be nice. The pairing/connection audio beep is a little loud so be careful when you pair/connect with earbuds. I think the manufacturer could reduce this volume a little. Overall this is a good product other than the few con's listed.

And I don't think I cracked any solder joints or points. Seems to work fine. I ripped out the USB and replaced with a vertical dual USB 3.0, swapped the stock fan for a Nictua 120MM to keep my 12TB drives nice and cool. I dropped a 350 Watt Mini ITX piwer supply in, loaded Win Servwr 2018 DCE and its been running ever since. Well worth the money but would reccomend the vertical dual USB 3.0 and fan swap right off the bat. NAS, Server, VMs and more, all in a Mini ITX form factor. I'm I terested to see how long the drive trays and backplain last though as they are a little bit flimsy. Will report back with any issues. Update as of 1/14/22: Well,,, unfortunately my NAS started throwing some power errors. After some research and digging into the hardware, I found that when installing and because of the tight fit, I cut some solder traces and tore off a resistor from the motherboard when installing it. It was so tight, I had to drill out the motherboard bracket grommets, both top and bottom, to get the MoBo out to inspect and ended up tearing off another resistor. $350.00 down the drain. If you do decide to ourchase, take so e precautions and predrill the motherboard bracket grommets out, install the motherboard and then use a small 4/32 x 1/4" machine screws to fasten them back. I should have done this before hand. It is just too tight of a fit to get a real motherboard installed in it without doing this, or damaging any of your components. The layout just doesn't quite make sense. Something the manufacturer should have done instead of using grommets to fasten the pot metal pieces. Good luck!

When an ordered this drive as intended to put it into a LaCie enclosure I had lying about, though when I did the drive would just turn itself off (though when I placed another hard drive into the enclosure it worked fine) implying the problem wasn't with the enclosure. So, I contacted Amazon tech support to help me figure out what was going on and was told that the drive was designed to fit in a computer, and I had to open up my machine to use it. Which is absolute bullocks. A hard drive, as long as it's able to connect to the enclosure, can't tell whether or not it's in a computer or an external drive. It's literally a meaningless difference. So I deduced that there was something about the LaCie that was preventing it from playing with the new drive–as in 3TB was beyond it's abilities to address–the drive in the space was less than that.. I don't know if that's actually the issue, but it sure as heck made more sense than the nonsense he Amazon rep told me. So I purchased a new enclosure–$20 on eBay–assembled it, plugged in the new HD, connected it to my computer and everything worked fine. As I said, the moral of the story is be VERY, VERY wary of tech support people who know less about computers than you do because they can cause all sorts of problems.

This is an impressive and capable camera for the money. I wanted a unit that could mount behind the rear-view mirror but remain accessible, and that had GPS capabilities. This is NOT a high-end device, though...it's just on the high-quality end of the "dashcam-on-a-budget" line. Notes from about a month of use: 1. Occasional random and unexplained cutouts, possibly related to heat. 2. Use care in routing the cabling for power and the GPS antenna, and don't rely just on the little adhesive tabs supplied...get some good double-sided tape to hold the hooks. 3. The supplied MicroSD card is good enough for routine commutes, but if you want full records of long commutes, get a larger card or two, and be ready to swap them. 4. Some states restrict how devices such as this can be mounted in your vehicle. Pay attention to the law and install accordingly. I've gotten double-takes from law enforcement when they see the camera, but so far, nothing beyond that. 5. I haven't reviewed any of the nighttime recordings yet, so I can't speak to the camera's low-light capabilities. 6. The G-force sensitivity settings seem to be "feast or famine"...high sensitivity locks recordings after hitting small potholes, but medium sensitivity doesn't seem to recognize emergency braking, which to me should be a trigger for locking a recording. 7. It takes TWO button pushes to manually lock a recording, not one. Granted, you're pushing the same button twice, but it's still two separate actions. 8. READ THE MANUAL. TWICE. It will answer almost any question you might have about installation and operation, right down to making sure the time zone is correctly set and the clock automagically updates from the GPS.

The first photo depicts an open between the tip of one end of the cable and the tip of the other end of the cable. I am pretty sure there should be continuity here. This should be the Left channel. The second photo depicts an open between the 3rd ring of one end of the cable and the 3rd ring of the other end of the cable. I am pretty sure there should be a connection here. This should be the ground channel. The third photo depicts a wonderful connection between the tip of one end of the cable and the base of the other end of the cable. I am pretty sure the Left channel on one end of the cable is connected to the ground of the other end of the cable. All of the individual rings on one cable end have continuity with individual rings on the other end of the cable. The individual 2nd rings actually match !! But, the ground is crossed :>( . This is a flat keyboard with the keys angled so that the wrists are not bent at odd angles to the body. (I wanted the split keyboard with the arch to allow the hands to fall naturally, but that model is not 'keyed' for Mac.) This is a compromise and the improvement in comfort is slight compared to the Mac's keyboard. Most of the 'Mac specific' buttons actually do what they are supposed to. Exceptions: Zoom only magnifies text and only in some programs, where the Mac's zoom magnifies the entire screen, I miss that feature. (Mac's zoom is availed by pressing a combo of three keys, that combo does not achieve the zoom on this keyboard) I was not able to get the 'expose' button to work on this mouse, and even if it did, it is in an uncomfortable position. Other than that, the mouse is comfortably arranged. The issues with signal strength that others are having are present in this keyboard and mouse. The most annoying part is the frequent window telling me the signal strength is low....etc, etc. From day one, I have never had more than two bars out of five worth of signal strength, regardless of how close the keyboard/mouse is. Even though the signal strength indicates 'low', the keyboard and mouse function fairly well. The convenience of wireless is outweighed by the signal issues and lack of USB ports. Next time I spill the coffee on the keyboard, I will get a wired one and probably stick with Apple's. Which reminds me, the software has to be installed before the keyboard is connected, and you need a keyboard to do that.... usually. Apple Care helped me around that. Pros: Keys arranged in a curve. Padded palm rest Extra keys to program in favorites No wires Cons: Signal strength issues Pop-up warning about signal strength Inadequate zoom tool One mouse button 99% useless for me Silver colored plastic No wires (it is a pro and a con)

This is sold as a display good for gaming but when I hooked this up to my computer it has been nothing but problems. First off, they don't include a HDMI 2.1 Cable. Cables come with every computer monitor standard and if LG wants to compete with that market they need to include a cable. Going to buy one presents you with many cheap cable options, many of which include reviews that say the cables are not what they are supposed to be, so why LG doesn't include a $30 cable with a $1700 TV is beyond me. I can't enable HDR in windows while at 4k so I don't know whether its the TV, Cable, or Computer but LG should have eliminated this variable by including a properly rated 48Gbps cable. Monster cable doesn't sell anything over 27Gbps so I'm very confused as to whether a true HDMI 2.1 cable even exists. Calling LG tech support was very disappointing, after connecting remotely to the TV and being explained the Instant Game Response keeps launching even though it's turned off, they simply passed the buck to Computer Tech Support (Video card manufacturer?) which is not cool. The computer has nothing to do with why the display keeps flashing and whether or not the cable is no good. Include the proper cable with the TV and fix the problem with the Instant Game Response turning on even though it's turned off in the menu. I'm going to give this TV one more try with another cable and than I'm returning it and getting a proper monitor. Lesson learned, if you want something for gaming, get a monitor and avoid the headache. Maybe this is good as a TV but who would want to pay the extra money for game settings that don't even work or might work if you get lucky buying the correct cable online somewhere. (Update: I'm learning that my 5700XT videocard only uses HDMI 2.0. Club3d offers a Displayport to HDMI 2.1 adapter that will fix the 10bit problem but at the lost of VRR. When the BIGNAVI and 3000 Series videocards come out this should address that problem but now I'm learning that the CX model is limited to 40Gbps HDMI 2.1 Input so I'm going to return this for the C9 model unless LG is going to publicly plan on updated the firmware to allow for 48Gbps.)

Upgraded from a 10 year old SOHO commercial firewall which was faithful and reliable to end. Trying this product out and going from an expensive high end firewall to a relatively inexpensive no-name brand was a bit nerve wracking. However this product (non-WiFi edition) was something which I got stood up and working within minutes. Kudos for TPLink for the simplicity of this product. As with any hardware appliance I would highly suggest that no sooner that you get your Internet connection that you immediately download the most current firmware and apply it to the latest release, in order to address any possible instability issues. The firmware update process was seamless and took only about 5 minutes to get completed. The features of this device are very comparable to the features of a high end commercial SOHO product. I've leveraged so far the Dynamic DNS capabilities supported with this product (it just works) as well as the native DHCP capabilities. In addition the ability to setup rules whereby at certain times which Internet or services can be available is very nice in order to ensure that the teenagers go to sleep in the wee hours of the night. This detailed rule set capabilities within the firewall product was one of the drivers for getting this product and it works like a champ. As with any firewall product, wire speeds will vary. Line speeds which I've tested with it this range between average around 443Mbps Up & 514Mbps Down. This average is with about 33 IP enabled devices standing behind it which is quite impressive for sustained throughput. The native capabilities for VPN and authentication services is quite impressive although I've yet to test it fully at this time. The only noticeable drawback I've found with this product is the performance hit that you take when you enable HTTPS management. While enabling the capability doesn't impact it too much, what is noticeable however is the impact if you enable HTTP to HTTPS redirects. My recommendation until this is addressed in a future firmware release is not to enable that redirect feature. Outside of that noticeable performance hit everything else works impressively well. No real complaints with this product, highly recommend.

Original Review: April 2017 Like any reasonable person in the 21st century, I am extremely paranoid about the amorphous menace that lives in the internet and is probably watching me via my devices when I don't know it. I used to hand-wave this away, and then one day I noticed the little light on my webcam lit up even though I hadn't opened FaceTime in months. Probably no one was spying on me, but ever since then I've kept a little something covering the webcam. Previously it was washi tape, but I finally decided to upgrade to these when I was buying them anyway as a birthday gift. The set of 3 was much more economical than buying them individually, so I went with it. I was worried that it would be too bulky or interfere with the laptop closing, but it doesn't. It's really a very tiny little thing--it fits on a fingertip. The adhesive seems to be the right strength to stay on easily but not take half the finish with it if you want to remove it or if you need to reposition it during application. It hasn't budged since I put it on about a week ago. The little disk slides easily back and forth and completely covers the camera lens. When you open the camera you see nothing but black; slide it over and there you are! Make sure to be at a flattering angle, lest you startle yourself. I put one on mine, one on my son's, and gave the third to a friend as a birthday gift. Each one went on smoothly, operates perfectly, and makes Foucaultian paranoia just a little bit more convenient.

I've been a big fan of Buffalo, who produces a huge selection of products in Japan, and starting to have a larger presence in the US. I actually bought my first WZR-600DHP in Japan when I just started getting into DD-WRT. Previously all my routers had been Netgear, but with my expanding needs for a more powerful router, the built-in convenience of the DD-WRT in the Buffalo makes this an easy choice. DD-WRT If you are unfamiliar with this software, it is an open router interface that can be installed on compatible routers by "flashing" the router's original firmware. DD-WRT opens up powerful functionality of your router to do some pretty amazing things. My personal objective with DD-WRT was to setup a VPN for private web browsing and obtaining access to location specific online media. (Some of you may be aware of the limitations of Netflix and Hulu in certain regions...well, this is your solution to that problem!) Thru a tremendous wealth of information on forums and wiki pages, I was able to build 2 types of VPN server on this router (PPTP and OpenVPN). I am extremely happy with the results! In a way this is a plug for DD-WRT, mostly because Buffalo has embraced this open standard as it's core router engine. Here are several of the features that I found particularly useful: 1. Dynamic DNS: Perodically checks your external (public) IP address and updates various services to keep alive any free dns acounts you may have. I personally use no-ip.org which is free, easy to update and has a nice looking domain name. The one glaring exception is dyndns.com, previously one of the most popular services, which has stopped allowing automatic updates, now making it difficult to use. 2. USB/Network Attached Storage(NAS): You can plug in a USB flash drive or hard drive and make it accessible anywhere on your network. Thru built-in SAMBA support, you can access the device thru windows like a network drive. Very nice feature indeed. 3. USB/Printer Server: Have an old USB printer without ethernet support? You can attach it to the router and make it accessible to all network devices. 4. VPN (PPTP or OpenVPN): THIS is why I got interested in DD-WRT in the first place! You can setup your own personal VPN server with great ease. Since it running on your router, it is ON 24/7 without need for an additional computer. Used in conjunction with Dynamic DNS, you never have to worry about what your external IP address is! I recommend PPTP if you are new to VPNs, it is fast and sufficiently secure (but not 100% impenetrable). If you're an advanced user with some networking understanding you can setup OpenVPN which allows the strongest encryption available, virtually 100% secure. However, OpenVPN takes some work to setup properly. What can you do with VPNs: a) Make your internet traffic appear to originate from another location. This is particularly useful for getting around media streaming sites (Netflix, Hulu and one other that rhymes with Bamazon) which do not allow streaming beyond country borders. You can try signing up for Public VPNs to do this, but the streaming sites track down Public sites and block access from them, rendering them useless. You need a Private VPN to get around that. Mine is setup in Japan where I have accounts, and I can stream to anywhere in the world I have internet access. Clearly a handy feature for international travelers who pay for online content! b) Establish secure connections around company firewalls and public networks. Does your company block certain websites, forbid certain words in searches? Are you afraid to use public networks at Starbuck for mail and transactions because you don't know who else is sniffing on the network? Once you signin to your VPN, all traffic between your device and your home VPN server is encrypted. That is, network administrators and other rouge users on the network cannot peak into your web browsing. So browse that network with confidence! c) Use it with any device that supports VPNs. That includes PCs/Laptops, iPhones/iPads. PPTP is natively supported on Windows 7/8, iOS, MacOS, so setup is a breeze! d) VoIP? One area that I would eventually like to explore is the use of VoIP phones which would allow you to connect an iPhone to your home phone so that you can receive home phone calls on your iphone. With VPNs this is possible, but I still have yet to explore. (There are blogs on the internet about setting this up.) Wireless Supports 2 bands of Wireless-N traffic. This is extremely useful for load balancing your wireless devices and ensuring the best antenna signal given device placement. Remember that the wireless bandwidth is not limit-less, so this router essentially doubles that bandwidth. Gigabit Not much to say about this feature other than it's fast! CONS Really don't have much bad to say about this. I've been using 2 of them (one for testing and one for production) for about 4 months now in various configurations with very few issues. However, I will say that the base plate is not particularly sturdy. I ended up mounting it flat on my wall, as the screw holes conveniently lineup to outlet base plate holes! I can't imagine that's co-incidental. I posted a picture of it under customer photos. It seems much sturdier in that configuration, slides up and off the bracket for accessing behind the unit. Overall, this is a great router that allows users to really make the most of their router by shipping with DD-WRT pre-installed. I highly recommend it! UPDATE 12/29/2013: I'm still so pleased with the performance and functionality, I've now bought 4 of these routers to handle multiple sites. The most helpful critical review seems to have had issues with starting and stopping his wireless connection. He also restarts his router on a daily basis. I wonder if he has a defective router as my router in Japan has been on 24-7 for 6 months without a hitch. His last comment was more than 1 year ago too, so maybe there was an manufacturing improvement (although I use the same firmware version he does.) I use the VPN on it daily, and the only times I go into the administration pages are to copy the settings to my new routers. Honestly, these routers are stable as a rock. UPDATE 2/21/2014: Just in case it's not clear from my review, the router is PRE-INSTALLED with DD-WRT. You just have to turn on the option to boot into that configuration. Very simple to use, no messing around with flashing like other routers. Feel free to leave a comment/question, as I'm happy to respond. Thank you.

The Eufy products are okay, but the motion detection is worthless. I have the latest wireless doorbell, 2 wireless camera pros, and 1 of the cameras on this review. First, if you move really fast the camera will not detect anything. Second, if you move really slow the cameras won't detect you. Third, if you're farther than 7ft from the camera and not in direct sight of the camera any motion will not be detected hence no even recordings. All stars have to align for these cameras to records events. All of my cameras have the latest firmware, all are set for optimal recording, all are set for the highest motion detection for any motion not just human. One of my cameras is looking at my driveway, another camera is looking at my front yard. I've moved my vehicles and the camera doesn't capture anything, it I drive slowly into my driveway the camera doesn't trigger. If I walk in a rush into my doorbell the camera only captures my door closing. Only reason I have them is to look around my property without having to get up and walk. If you're looking to protect anything of value look elsewhere, go with anything wired over any wireless product.

I've written this review before, spewed platitudes and espoused my affection for these very budget cans. I owned and have owned a large handful other headphones. Been seduced by YouTube reviews and other online teasers, some of which I bought; some I have not. The cans that have stayed are the Sony siblings ( these and the MDR-7506) and the Sennheiser sisters (HD's 600 and 650). The Senns are almost exclusively tubed because they're so good at it. The Sony's do solid state duty. They've stayed for a reason. They all sound great and despite their apparent similarities they have their differences from their twin. I won't get into the senns here because I've written those reviews except to say you get more bang for your buck here. Sorry; it's true. No they aren't as detailed, no they aren't as smooth nor as polished nor as comfortable and the Sennheiser house sound is vastly different. The sound quality is at a different level...but not by as much as you'd think. Neither the MDR V6 nor 7506 are a giant killer but man they're really good. They aren't Hi-Res certified, They aren't well suited for portable use. They don't have the urban cool of the beats or the M50x for that matter. (stop wearing enormous over ear headphones out of the house, you look ridiculous. Just stop it. There's many many great IEM's out there, the Mee M6 Pro being a great option under $100) Get the little Micca OriGen G2 dac/amp, whether you're a noob or not, on a budget or not. Listen to them stock, For awhile, then swap out the pads for the Dekoni platinum replacement for MDR-7506, listen some more. Rip some cd's or better yet Get a power adapter for that little OriGen, A used CD player with an optical output and ignore the internets and their notifications for a while. Listen to Hi-res sources with your laptop with either MDR and be surprised. Despite posted specs, the resolution is stunning but "standard" redbook resolution is surprising with a half decent playback device. I could be completely content with either MDR and a great CD collection. Have been actually. The MDR's get used so much more often than the senns, the senns are great, amazing really but the Sony's get listened to more. I prefer the sound of theV6 just slightly over the 7506. They're durable, I have a four year old...parents will all get why that matters. They isolate really pretty well, particularly with the upgraded pads. Both MDR's are a tremendous listen and a tremendous value.

I was looking forward to this pair of echo buds 2 given the good reviews, however, I am quite disappointed. First, the pairing is not as easy as it sounds. I already have the alexa app installed on my android phone due to other echo dot products. The pairing did not happen as written in the instructions until I repeated the process multiple times. Second, the sound seems to lack base, but I assume this can be fixed by using the equalizer in the app, so this is not a major issue for now. Third, I heard no difference in the low rumble of the dish washer with the noise cancelling on or off. I understand this type of noise cancellation is only good for lower frequency sounds. Lastly which is the worse design decision possible, is not to include a way to turn off the buds without placing them into the charging case. Every other pair of buds I have can be turned off by some gesture control. Sometimes one just wants to turn off the buds without continuously charging them. The construction appears to be solid but slightly too bulky. Since it sticks out of the ear a bit, the weight distribution out side of the ear makes the buds to fall out easier unless the tips are securely fitted inside the ear canals. The wing tips might help, but I generally do not like to use them as they are not comfortable. With alexa voice commands, it does offer some convenience as to control the buds without touching them, but some command had to be repeated multiple times. Hopefully I can find a good use for these pair of buds somewhere. Updated 4/13/2022 After getting accustomed to these buds, I am updating it from 1 star to 3 stars. I really want the future gen 3 of these buds to succeed. 1) The sound might not be the best, but it does not tire out your ears with an hour of listening as with some other brands of buds. For the current reduced price, the price to sound quality ratio is very good. 2) Need to start the Alexa app everytime to guarantee voice commands get recognized. 3) With the proper fitting, passive noise cancellation with active noise cancelling does an ok job, but since I go for walks on the streets with these buds, some background rumbles to warn me of nearby cars are preferred. 4) No off feature still sucks, but I have learned to use the case. Make sure to push on the buds after placing them back into the case which ensures a proper contact is made. When this pushing is not done, many times the case get drained of battery very quickly without using the buds. Overall these buds did grow on me. The construction is solid and appears to be reliable. The connection to bluetooth has been consistent and reliable. The way it stick out of the ears is still inconvenient where wave of the arm might knock it out of one's ear, so it does take some getting used to. Updated 7/7/2022 Took these buds on vacation. What a disappointment. Could not use these buds most of the time due depleted charges. Would charge it up for an hour or so at the hotel, but when the time comes to use these buds, the battery is empty. This is an electronic device, and it is of no use when there it does not have juice regardless of the wonderful features it has. Should have brought my other pair of ear buds, which clearly tells me 'the device is turning off' when I manually turns it off. My suspicion is the Echo Buds turns on in the casing during travel, however I cannot be sure. The only sure thing is it was useless during my vacation. Reduing the rating to one star again.

In all that follows, the Kaidaer should be powered ON to function, except when only charging the built-in battery, in which case it should be OFF with the Data/Charging Cable connected to a USB charging source. Mode Button ---------------- Three audio sources can be connected simultaneously but the active source is selected by cycling through the three alternatives using the MODE button. Each click cycles the Kaidaer through the following THREE states, in sequence: Use the internal FM Radio Use the Line-In source Use a USB source, as explained next USB Sources ---------------- There are three receiving slots clustered together: miniUSB slot (marked as `USB 5V') microSD slot full size USB slot the microSD slot is just above the full size USB slot and either can receive a memory stick/card that contains mp3 files (in their ROOT directories, NOT in a custom folder.) If a memory stick is inserted into the full size USB slot AND a card is inserted into the microSD slot, only the memory stick will be recognized. Therefore, conceptually, these two slots are regarded as a unit and either a memory stick/card is present, or not. In the same way, either the Data/Charging Cable is inserted and used to connect the Kaidear to a USB slot on the PC, or it is absent. A special condition arises when BOTH the Data/Charging Cable AND a memory stick/card is present. The PC will recognize the memory stick/card and offer to open a window in Windows Explorer where you can read or write the content of the memory stick/card. If the Data/Charging Cable is NOT connected, sound will be played from the memory stick/card if they are inserted and the Kaidaer will flash blue: Repeat Button: Will repeat the currently playing track/file Play/Pause Button: As it says... Back/Vol- Button: Single Click: go to the previous track/file Click and Hold: decrease volume until released Forward/Vol+ Button: Single Click : go to next track/file Click and Hold: increase volume until released Lastly, if the Data/Charging Cable IS connected, and a memory stick/card is NOT inserted, the Kaidaer will now act as an alternative sound card with a speaker for the PC. On the PC, select `Control panel', then `Sound' and then select the `Playback' tab (or, right-click the speaker icon on the task bar and select `Playback devices'.) You'll see an entry for the Kaidaer described as an `USB Audio Device'. Rename it if you like and set it as the default sound device. To play audio from the PC, turn up the volume on the Kaidaer, and make sure the MODE Button is cycled to the USB source position. Line-in Source ------------------ Use the supplied double-ended 3.5mm plug to connect the line-in jack to any audio source with a corresponding 3.5mm headphone or line-out jack (Smartphone, PC, TV...) Make sure the source is playing some audio, turn up the volume on the Kaidaer, and click the MODE button until you hear it playing. Repeat Button: Unused Play/Pause Button: Mute/Unmute Back/Vol- Button: Single Click: Unused Click and Hold: decrease volume until released Forward/Vol+ Button: Single Click: Unused Click and Hold: increase volume until released FM Radio Source ---------------------- Setting up the radio: Connect an audio source that you can recognize via the Line-in cable. Connect and play a different audio source on the PC using the supplied Data/Charging Cable (no memory stick/card). Now cycle through the MODE button: one of the three alternatives will be silent or will hiss. This is the MODE Button's Radio position. Plug one end of anything with a 3.5mm plug into the ANTenna jack (the supplied cable with a 3.5mm plug at each end will do; so will any headphone cable; you van also buy a $2 antenna with a 3.5mm plug). Press Play/Pause. The Radio will begin to scan for available FM stations and store them for future tuning. You can stop the scan and select any station you hear during the scan by pressing Play/Pause while station is being heard. After scanning, the radio will begin to play first station found. To tune to other stations, press Forward button to select higher band stations found; press Back to select lower band stations. My Setup ------------ I have a TV and a Laptop on my desk. Line-in is connected to the TV's headphone jack. The Data/Charging Cable is connected to the Laptop. I use headphones. The Mode Button cycles me effortlessly through TV, Laptop, FM Radio. To hear the quality of the Kaedaer as soundcard, I plugged the Laptop's headphone jack into Line-in instead of the TV. Wow. BTW, I have a tin ear and the EQ button does nothing for me. It may be broken. It's supposed to cycle through normal, pop, rock, jazz, classic, country. But the rest works so well it doesn't seem worth the bother to return it.

The pros for this machine would be: - It has a i7 4710HQ processor, which is way better than the i7 4500U processors that a lot of cheaper laptops currently have. - It has 8GB of RAM which is quite a lot to run most everyday applications. - 1TB of hard disk space couple with my own 1TB external HDD means I won't be running out of space any time soon. - Decent size and weight means I can carry this on my back all day when I move from class to class without feeling too sore. - Bluetooth 4.0 which is energy efficient and offers fast connectivity. Average points would be: - Battery life is decent.Just about makes it through a 2 hour movie or video leaving some juice to spare. - It has 2 USB 3.0 ports and one USB 2.0 port. A lot of HP laptops for similar prices will give you 4 USB 3.0 ports. - No touchscreen. While there are more expensive computers without them, there are cheaper computers which do offer touchscreens. This is more noticeable because I would move my finger on it and the mouse would stay still on the screen. - The graphics card is the inbuilt Mobile Intel HD graphics. For this price I expected better especially when there are laptops with lower prices that offer better graphics. Overall, this is a good laptop and it ticks most of the boxes. Decent processor, more than decent hardware and a reasonable price keeping in mind the specs on offer. As for the problems I encountered, I don't know if anyone else has encountered them but for me, they are an occasional occurrence; not too frequent to really bother me. I expect this laptop to stay with me for a few years without falling too far behind new tech that is being released every year.

Now that I've been using it for a bit over a week I feel that I have thoughts worth sharing. (I started with a Kindle Keyboard and then switched to the Kindle Touch.) I'm very pleased with the Paperwhite. The upgrades from the Touch are all relatively minor but, when combined, they make for a really fantastic reading experience. The letters are crisp and clear, the light (which is not a backlight) improves the contrast even more. You can't turn the light completely off, but you can set it to be very dim. I've kept mine on 17 (out of 20) for the entire time I've had it. I haven't had any problems reading in the dark, which is pretty awesome. The light also means that I'm able to ditch the case and can read the PW "naked." I keep it in a sleeve so I can toss it around without worrying about scratches, but since I don't need a lighted case anymore, I don't need to read with it in the case. Of course this makes it quite a bit lighter than my previous Kindles, but the PW itself isn't that much lighter than the previous ones. The PW made the switch to capacitive screen from IR screen. I wasn't sure how I've feel about this change, but I'm finding that I quite like it. One of the problems I had with the Touch was that I'd have to turn it off to get something off the screen because any touch would engage the screen. Now, if I have to wipe a hair or something off the screen, I can just use a fingernail and the page doesn't turn. This is a small thing, but it makes me happy. The PW learns your reading speed and can predict how much time you have left in the chapter and in the entire book. This seems like a software update, so I'm not sure if it will be implemented for previous Kindle models or not. Again, it's a small thing, but it's nice to know how much longer "let me just finish this chapter" will actually be. Or whether you really should stay up to finish the book. With the PW, you also have the option to view your books using "cover display" instead of the list display. This isn't an option I've chosen, but other people might like it. The link to "archived items" has also been removed and, instead, there's a tab for "Cloud" and one for "Device." When looking through collections you can now choose "recent" for a sort instead of just author and title - I'm very happy with this since I tend to get a lot of freebies each day and it can be hard to find a recently downloaded book. The lack of home button took me a few days to get used to, but it's not posing me any difficulties now. The interface is fairly straightforward. I believe that you can't turn Wifi off as easily with the PW as you could with the Touch and the Keyboard. You've got to go to the home screen > Settings > and then turn on Airplane Mode. Other than that, I assume the new fonts are nice, but I haven't used them since I'm happy with the default font. I assume the "experimental browser" is still a clunky pain in the butt to use - this is NOT a tablet. I found out that you can increase/decrease the font size with the pinch gestures like zooming on an iPhone - but you could do this with the Touch as well. And there you go. It's a lot of little changes but, when taken together, they make for a lovely reading experience and I'm very happy I decided to upgrade even though I had my Touch for such a short time. I was worried I'd feel silly for upgrading so soon, but I don't - not even a little bit. :)

I run half marathons and needed a new pair of headphones. My previous headphones (pictured) were the JBL Reflect Contour which lasted about 3-4 years before 1 side quit working and the battery life was declining. I opted for these Powerbeats Pro after reading about them in an online article for running headphones. I specifically need a style that wraps around the ear as any ear bud does NOT stay in my ear - even if I sit perfectly still, they still fall out. PROs - there's essentially no set-up. These automatically connected to my iPhone straight out of the box. This smart, auto-on feature is very convenient (when it works properly). - snug fit, the "arm" that wraps around your ear has some flexibility to it so I squeezed it down for a tighter fit. These headphones stay put for my 90+ minute runs. They do not cause any discomfort. They do not interfere with my Oakley Half Jacket sunglasses. - fast charging, 40% charged in about 10 minutes after they died overnight from not returning them to the case. CONs - there's no auto-off feature and I learned that the hard way. When you take them out, you HAVE to return them to the charging case to power off. After my first wear, I took them off and set them on the counter thinking they would automatically turn off in the same manner they automatically turn on. I came back to the headphones the next day and they were completely dead. - the sound quality is lacking, particularly on a windy day. These aren't noise cancelling in the slightest which is probably a good safety feature while running. But my previous headphones (JBL Reflect Contour) were noise tight. - sometimes only 1 side connects. When this happens, you have to return both ear pieces to the charging case, "forget" the Bluetooth device on your phone, turn off your Bluetooth, and hard reset the headphones by long pressing the button on the charging case for 10-15 seconds. This entire process is highly inconvenient, annoying, and frustrating. I have only had these headphones for about 2 weeks now and have already encountered this process twice. I am not looking forward to constantly having to reset them. I will keep these headphones and continue to use them throughout the duration of their lifetime. However, based on my experience so far, I would NOT repurchase these in the future nor would I recommend them.

[[VIDEOID:5288b4749c024f057b23b63d54e7f001]] ///The video attached to this review is in regard to the problem with this product, shown much farther below in the final 2 paragraphs./// So, I use this product for a couple of things, mostly digital animation and digital painting. If you are using it for those two purposes, this is rather serviceable and you can get a lot of mileage out of it. Ignoring that you can only bind one layout at a time, usually one setup for a program you use frequently like photoshop is all you need. It has definitely streamlined my work process since most of the common bindings I use like B and E, [ and ], and stuff like Ctrl+Z/ Ctrl+Shift+Z are all pretty straightforward and much easier to hit if I'm drawing on my tablet with this thing. If you do something like streaming this product is actually just a top tier godsend of a product because you can actually bind the keys to non buttons and instead opt for opening programs or executing short scripts. Example: You can press a button to open a program like OBS or a video game you play frequently as long as you bind the button to that programs executable file. If you're particularly savvy and determined and can write scripts with AutoHotkey you can essentially just have your entire computer bound on this tiny keypad. Essentially, if you draw a lot like I do, it allows you to disconnect your left hand from the keyboard and have a lot more freedom without having to constantly look over at your keyboard, which is awesome. And if you are a content creator or constantly open and close important programs this thing is absolutely nuts. However, this product does have a bit of a "quirk" that you either need to get used to or it will just piss you off constantly. And, I really do mean CONSTANTLY. I haven't found a fix for it anywhere and I use Huion's most updated driver for both my tablet and this Key dial so its definitely a design flaw/oversight with the actual keypad's design and not the software and drivers themselves. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ //////So, here's the quirk and what you need to know about this product before spending $50+ on the key dial; it's 2 problems that play off each other in a really annoying way.\\\\\\ ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ 1. [The smaller problem] You can't press 2 keys together to combo them like a normal keyboard. Example: If you want to Ctrl+Z to undo a mistake, you have to set a specific button as Ctrl+Z, you can't have one button be CTRL and another be Z and press them together. So, this limits the keydial a bit but this isn't as big a deal on it's own. Personally, I have CTRL+Z and CTRL+SHIFT+Z on two separate buttons next to each other, so it works out fine. 2. [The extremely annoying problem you NEED to know about] Pressing a key while holding another key will get the key first key "stuck" and constantly input itself as if you were holding the key down on your keyboard. This is just honestly a nightmare and took a lot of muscle memory to get used to. I've come to terms that this might have been intentional for... god only knows why... but I'll try to explain why this is such an annoying problem. Like I said, they are a problem together since using a normal keyboard your entire life you kind of just expect to be able to press two keys at the same time which is an absolutely no-no for this product. So, scenario. Lets say I have a key like CTRL or ALT bound to they keydial. CTRL or ALT do a lot of modifying in programs like photoshop, especially when you are trying to use a tool. Pretty much an essential as hell key along with Shift. If I'm working quickly and just happen to be holding down the CTRL bind the same time I hit a different button without thinking about it, you completely just ruin your workflow for a moment. It's really disorientating to be working on a drawing, just for the tablet to stop drawing because CTRL is permanently being held down and pressed. Even worse is when you go to hit a tool shortcut on your actual keyboard and god only knows what happens because key number whatever the F you just pressed is constantly inputting itself and photoshop keeps trying to press both of them together. I've seriously had entire projects get formatted improperly or had to spend a few minutes changing photoshops layout back to normal because having a modifying key held down is such a disaster. This is already annoying on it's own BUT YOU CAN ONLY "FIX" THE PROBLEM BY HITTING THE ORIGINAL KEY YOU MESSED UP WITH IN THE FIRST PLACE ON THE KEYDIAL. So, if you're getting used to the binds you made now you have to figure out which button you accidentally pressed until you finally re-press it. You can't hit whatever it's pressing on your actual keyboard, you have to actually go back and re-find the keydial bind you made and re-press it. If you use this product as much as I do, you start to be able to immediately recognize when it's doing this and I can quickly fix the problem now, but the fact that it's still happening to me several dozens/hundreds of hours in is a testament to how terrible of a design flaw it is. In the video I've attached to this review I tried to give an easy to understand example of how this problem works and how annoying it is. I don't use this keydial for gaming, as you can tell by the rest of the review, but for a visual sake I thought it was appropriate. I bound the keydial to W, A, S, and D for movement in this game. You'll notice that if I press the keys individually, they work as intended, but as soon as I hold down my binding for moving left (A in this case) and press another key, the keybind permanently holds down the left movement bind (A). The only way to fix the problem as seen in the video is having to re-press the original binding that is causing the problem. It's annoying, and it can be a total disaster when using creative software and having ALT or CTRL being permanently pressed down and causes a bunch of problems before you realize what's going on and daddy photoshop has his way with your project and layout. Still, it's a great product even with the quirk. I DO recommend using it, it's just you really do need to know how annoying it is to get used to the design oversight before committing to this keydial.

The USB hub is great if you have multiple devices you switch between like work and personal laptops and want them to instantly connect to other USB devices (like a docking station). I keep my USB wireless adapters for the mouse and keyboard plugged in the monitor and just switch the laptops when needed. I use it with my HP Elite X2 and by connecting it with the USB-C cable, I get the following: 1) Charges the laptop and keeps it at 100% while using it. 2) Delivers HD video and audio to the monitor without the need for HDMI or DP cables. 3) Activates the USB hub in the monitor (3 additional USB Type A ports for the computer) without the need to connect the USB Type B cable. I just bought a 75 foot coil of speaker wire from Walmart for $15 which I then cut and spliced onto the existing wire so I could run them down through floor, across the floor joists, and then up through the floor to place them where I wanted them. The only other minor issue I had is that for the first couple of days it would not start up and shut down properly. I don't know that there's such a thing as a "Bluetooth expert" but I'm about as veteran as they come - I've used Bluetooth headsets regularly since before Bluetooth even existed on phones (yeah, when you had to have an adapter to plug into your old 3.5mm jack). We're talking nearly 20 years of experience using Bluetooth. But those are stories for another day. I'll cut straight to it - there is no better Bluetooth headset I've found below $50 that work as well as these. I'd even argue that they're better than most headsets over $100 I've used. Could the mic be better? Perhaps. But I admittedly use these 95% of the time to listen to music/podcasts/videos on my phone. If I really want to talk to someone on a BT headset, I use my plantronics set with superior noise cancellation (I can have running water in front of me while conversing and the other person just hears my voice loud and clear). These bad boys last a LONG time - we're talking 8+ hours - and they work one bud at a time so I can literally charge one while using the other and hours later when it's running low I simply swap one bud for the other, charging the dying bud with the fresh one and never skip a beat on whatever I'm listening to. One expensive BT bud brand, for example, only works in the left ear or both ears but the right ear doesn't work on its own. Why the hell would they design it this way?! Once your left bud runs out of juice, you cannot just swap to the right bud you have to wait for lefty to recharge. Horrible design... These also connect quickly and easily (some BT buds or headsets are a PAIN) and stay connected! They're also water proof - I wear them in the shower almost daily (have I mentioned how I listen to podcasts almost all day long?) I've tried a handful of "cheap" BT buds with very similar design/price range and this one outperforms them all with all things considered. And the case even charges wirelessly! Can't say that with half of the ones I've tried in this range. I've even tried the T6 and while I like it, I still prefer the T10 - the T6 charges in the T10 case but T10 doesn't charge in the T6. Really the only con I can think of - besides call quality perhaps - would be the sensitivity of the touch button on the unit. But I rarely have an issue accidentally activating it and the ease of using the touch button to turn on/off, connect, pause/play etc is far better than any other BT bud I've used. Some are so poorly designed you can only imagine the designer hates humanity and is getting his revenge on it...

1byone 30 antenna (without amp) works pretty good. No antenna gives good reception no matter what, but this one is superior for an inexpensive price. Move it around, compare channels, tape it up and walk away, seek the Sweet Spot. I also like the Mohu Leaf, which has become the industry standard for indoor antennas, this does just as well for half the cost, so I give 1byOne five stars. I tested both antennas downstairs 25 miles from transmitter with Signal Strength indicator on 24" Samsung TV. Other brands I have tried such as Wsky physically look the same but much less signal, especially on certain channels. I really like the long thin cable on the 1byOne, very helpful for finding the best location such as in a window. Warning, if you get the amplified 50 version try it with and without the amp, sometimes an antenna works better barefoot. I am a TV Broadcast Engineer and answer peoples calls for poor reception, it is nice to find an indoor antenna that seems to work pretty well. Of course outside antennas pointed the proper direction do better, but that is expensive and requires maintenance. In many cities all the stations are NOT the same direction. Even the indoor antenna may need to move when you change channels, contrary to advertisement they ARE directional. Often if you experiment enough (with patience) there is a placement which will work on most channels most the time. Like I said to start, rarely is an indoor antenna going to work perfect 100% of the time on all the channels. Your mileage may vary.

Just recently purchased through Amazon. Shipment came fast and with no problems. Packed really well. Setup took around 30 minutes and was very easy. There are many reviews here on Amazon, which I used in making my decision on which sound bar to buy. I’m happy to say that the Sound bar delivers. Many reviews here will talk of the mid range being non-existent. It is there, but can easily be over-powered by the subwoofer which is awesome. It’s probably best to keep the subwoofer below 20 to hear everything clearly. Upon setting it up, it’s important to remember that the wireless speakers do need to be charged. They take 3 hours to charge. What I do is after using the speakers, just plug them in at night before bed, and if you unplug them in the afternoon, you will have more then enough time with them as they last 10 hours on a charge. If you are coming from a 2.1 or below speaker setup, it’s important to change all your media (if they can be changed), to utilize 5.1 audio. This is a true 5.1 setup. It may not be super high end, but it functions like true 5.1. After setup, I tested with several games and movies. One notable movie was Jurassic Park. It’s known to be a staple for good surround and boy did it deliver. The bass rumbled even with the setting below 20, and the surround worked wonderfully. The audio was accurately reflected through the speakers. I heard rain from the movie all around, and in the chase sequence in the jeep with Jeff Goldblum, the T-Rex roared through all channels and you could hear his footsteps with the bass. It was amazing. This was true with other movies as well. Thor: Ragnarok rocked with the music sequences and examples of force on-screen. Again, I have to stress how accurate the sound reproduction was. Every effect was done through the proper channel. I guess proper calibration is key and should be done immediately. I positioned the calibration antenna behind where I would be sitting and seems to work as best it can. Also, you can adjust the surround volume, which I have at +6 which seems to work well enough. Another movie example is: X-men: First Class. The bass kicked in with every example of power on display by Magneto. I had to turn the speakers on “night mode” due to watching it during the day because the bass was so intense. It was appropriate for the scene, but boy did it rumble. I also tested with Pandora and Youtube on various music tracks from rock to classical, and it did not disappoint whatsoever. Instruments sounded great and did not sound muted, and voices sounded very clear through the center channel. Overall, I’m very sastisfied with the JBL Bar 5.1 system. For those of you on the fence: no worries.. you can purchase with confidence. Just be sure to configure it properly and don’t let the bass get too heavy and you’ll be fine. I’ve read online too that this system allows for firmware updates and if so, maybe down the road, JBL can fix the small mid-range issue. I say small because it is. With proper configuration, it’s not really noticeable. Again, can you find a system with better performance of course? But for below $1000? I really don’t think so. Great value, and features for the price. 3 HDMI in.. one HDMI ARC out. Dolby surround as well as DTS. Competition doesn’t offer all this, and it represents a great value. Must buy.

Does the item work? Yes it does. It is study, but nothing extreme. There is alot of play in it if you push on it. I used this with a 3080 TI with the 1.5 slot cooler. It is large and the amount of sag I had from normal installation seemed ridiculous. So I bought this. Buyer beware, there is no mention of this in the description, but it does not have enough depth from the rear of the case to where you would normally plug into your video card, so if you have a case that has the slats that dont completely open up, you will be cutting a hole open in the rear of your case. Some of these adapters actually have about a 1 inch depth to it so you dont have to do that, but this one does not. For people confused about what im saying - when the card is vertical, the video card outputs (HDMI/DP) are also vertical, so your cable will not fit into the slots on the back of the case where normally the output ports would line up horizontally. So you have to cut out the slats or the cable will never plug in. If you have a really expensive case, you may not want to do this. Other then that, it does work. It is a little on the cheap side, but if you are careful it will work fine. I have had no issues with mine. It works and is detected as PCIE 4.0.

Outdoors, the variable filter was softer shooting away from the sun and softer with more flare shooting toward the sun. In other words, for maximum sharpness you would need other filters. Inside, shooting compact fluorescent bulbs, the variable filter gave double images of the bulbs because of the two lenses in the filter; it could also have something to do that the inside element of mine rattles (is a little loose) but it won't fall out. The unedited colors were slightly different from the standard filters but that is not as important since most shooters do a little editing of IR images. Bottom line, it works but the quality of the image is not as good as standard filters. If you want to do some inexpensive testing and don't need or want to pay for higher-end filters, it will do the job.

First off, I have done a few home based set ups of modems, routers and wireless devices. I'm not a professional but can follow directions, if given. This review is based off my needs, the most important one was a device that had an ethernet port where I could use a sim card from a jetpack. The same need that may have brought you to this device. I currently have 2 jetpacks, both with unlimited packages (plan is only $10 each). The ethernet port option is the only thing this unit is good for, here is what I experienced-- *The wifi signal is extremely weak. If this unit is in the same room, fine. Move it to the next room over. Not so great. My wireless devices would pick up my router across the yard in my garage or the one on the lower level of my house before this one. This causes hiccups for my wireless devices and everyone knows how annoying that is. I thought I could have 1 internet device upstairs and 1 downstairs. Nope. *Because of the 1st issue above I decided to try a wifi mesh system, this unit being the base. Thinking I could use this to feed all my wireless devices such as my Amazon Fire Sticks, Kindle and echo devices, etc. Noting that typically I only have 1 device running at a time. I just have devices in every room. That did not work either. The unit showed internet signal and connection but would intermittently keep cutting off connection to the base wifi mesh unit. I hooked up my wifi mesh unit to another router to test it and it worked seamlessly. Tells me again that this issue is with this product. Note that I did turn off wifi signal on this modem as recommended by the manufacturer when using a mesh system. Long story short, if you keep this unit in 1 room for wifi and can run an ethernet cable directly to your device then it's fine. Anything beyond that it is useless. Am I missing something in a set up? Possibly, but that would require advanced skills that most users wouldn't have. This unit has its perks but also has it's downside. Hopefully this helped explain them. You can take away with what your needs would be.

Amp works and sounds fine at all volume settings as long as you use the AUX plug. I tried the bluetooth connection, and as others have noted, the sound cuts in and out above around 1/2 way volume setting. BT pairs easily enough and works great at low volumes. But as soon as the volume level gets on the loud side, the sound cuts in and out in 0.5sec pauses. Rather annoying. AUX input works fine though, so I just removed the BT antenna and use AUX only. Nice and small, sounds good, and plenty loud enough for general listening. I may take it apart sometime to see if I can fix the cutting in and out issue. Being a class D amp, I suspect a shielding issue between the class D amp and BT sections. [EDIT] I was able to fix the issue where the bluetooth cuts in and out at high volume. After taking the amp apart I found the negative speaker output jumper wire (from the PCB to the binding post) was routed directly over the bluetooth section. The very close proximity of the speaker output was apparently interfering with the low-level bluetooth circuits. I just bent the wire away a little and voila! Problem solved! The only tools needed is a 2.5mm allen wrench for the rear screws and a pair of needle-nose pliers for the 3 volume controls (pull knobs off first).

Jawbone has a Web-based utility that makes it easy to ensure the firmware in your headpiece is up-to-date. Additionally, you can add up to 20 phone numbers to its caller-ID library, so it will tell you who's calling in the earpiece by name before you answer. You can also change the voice that the headset uses in telling you connection status, talk time remaining, etc., as well as re-program what the headpiece does when you press and hold its single button. The headset supports A2DP, so you can stream music or other programming to the earpiece from your iPhone or other source. You have to use their Web utility to enable A2DP on the headset first, though. You only have to do this once if you want to use A2DP. A cool feature is that this unit can connect to two devices simultaneously. For me, that means I can connect it to my GPS and get turn-by-turn directions in the headpiece, and also answer calls from my phone when they come in. My GPS uses A2DP for this, so you need to make sure that the Era pairs with the GPS before pairing with the phone, so the right device gets control of the A2DP channel (i.e., leave Bluetooth off on you phone until you have connected to the GPS). With the iPhone, I did run into a quirk, but it's really an iPhone issue and not a problem with the Era. If you have A2DP enabled, the iPhone will pair with the headset using that protocol, so you can stream music to the earpiece. The problem is, when you get an e-mail or text message, the email/text sounds are so short that the iPhone fails to "wake up" the Era in time for the sounds to play. When A2DP is on, the sounds don't play on the phone itself either, so you can miss text/email alerts. This doesn't happen with other phones (I tried it with a Samsung Galaxy II), so it must be an iPhone thing. Another, less desirable workaround is to turn off A2DP in the Web utility. This causes text and email alerts to still sound from the phone speaker itself, but you can no longer stream music or connect to a device that needs A2DP, like my GPS. But the way I worked around this was to use Garage Band on my Mac to import a couple of short tones I found on-line as MP3 files into Garage Band, add a 2-second delay to the start of them, then export them to iTunes, then to my phone, as ringtones. With the brief silence at the start of the tone, they play through the earpiece just fine (although the phone vibrates a couple seconds before the sound is heard). But this is fine with me, and I'm a happy camper now. Overall, this is a great value in one of the best bluetooth headsets out there. Highly recommended. UPDATE: iOS 7 for the iPhone fixed the problem with missed email/text sounds when using A2DP as described above. If you have iOS 7, there is no need to create special "delayed" ringtones for use with this headset.

Let’s face it. It is not easy to design any standard “phone protection accessory” for the Surface Duo. Other than Microsoft’s “Duo bumper” there’s no cases available for the Duo that provide the same kind of protection as for other phones. The Duo’s foldable design also seems to have limited our options for third-party screen protection. Too thick and the two screen protectors laying atop each other when the Duo is closed means the device won’t close fully — that thickness challenge also means no good quality tempered glass protectors. In the case of Supershieldz’s Screen Protector for the Surface Duo, you’re getting 3 very thin standard screen protectors per pack. Trust me, you’ll need all three as your first attempt will likely mess up. Why? Since these are so thin, most folks applying these will face the normal challenges of applying a screen protector (air bubbles and dust particles). In the case of this protector, since each panel is so very thin, there tend to be many more air bubbles than you’d have if this were a piece of tempered glass. In most cases, when you have bubbles, all you need is a soft plastic-edged squeegee or credit card to push the bubbles out to the end of the protector. This is where you’ll run into problems with the Supershieldz protector. First, because the protector is so thin, using too much force to push those bubbles out (especially the tiny ones) can leave faint scratches on the film (not at all ideal). Also, if you push too many bubbles out at the same point of the edge of the protector, it will weaken that area and, I think, over time (as a couple other reviews mentioned) will mean the protector film will “lift up” at those edges. The other challenge you’ll have is if dust particles are trapped under the film. In the case of a tempered glass protector, this is relatively easy - just take two pieces of clear tape, use one to lift up the protector, then dab at the screen or the rear of the protector where you think the dust particle is sitting, then re-apply the protector and make sure that particle is gone. That’s a little harder with a film protector, you have to peel up the edge in a way that doesn’t ruin it (but 60%+ of the time will ruin it). With this Supershieldz protector? Don’t even bother. Either choose to live with that particle under the protector or be ready to remove the film and try again (and again, if need be, since you have three protectors for each side of the Duo). SHOULD you successfully apply the film, no air bubbles and no dust particles, you’ll face one last challenge: finger smudges. The glass of the Surface Duo can collect finger smudges, but you’ll hardly see them when the screens are powered on. Not so with the Supershieldz’s protectors installed. After just an hour or two of using the Duo with the protective film, I could see smudges clearly on the black background of whatever was on screen. I am VERY pleased with these binoculars. Good quality at this price point. Pros: 1) Clear (Bak-4 Prism and Multi-coated lenses) 2) Sharp image focus 3) Realistic colors. Even the edges don't appear to have a significant amount of chromatic aberration 4) Great for the price. (These aren't $1,000 binoculars... but they don't cost $1,000 either). Cons: 1) Although these focus well, you may find you need to make some small adjustment when viewing objects at different distances to get both eyes focused. Note: This is an issue with binoculars at any price point, but I find these might need to be adjusted more often. To do this you will need to cover the right objective lens (without touching the lens) and use the focus wheel to focus on an object. Then, cover the left objective lens and rotate the diopter ring (which is on the right eyepiece) until the the object is in sharp focus with the right eye. Now both lenses should be in focus. Not hard to do. 2) Hardly worth mentioning, and I'm not sure I am explaining it well, but, for those who care, there is a slight bit of field curvature which means straight lines may appear slightly curved at the edges of the image. This isn't really noticeable if you are looking at stationary objects. The only reason I mention it is because if you are looking through the binoculars and sweep them from side to side, it makes the image appear to waiver a bit. Again, I almost hesitate to deduct one star because the pros far outweigh the cons. Get a pair of these and have fun!

I'm glad this was driver-free and/or the plug-n-play type of capture device. Works well, fair quality compared to VHS to TV. The main Cons are that the quality isn't as good, but more importantly it causes audio sync issues which must be corrected by low-level video capture software such as AmaRecTV. If you use that software, make sure to use a 3rd-party video codec such as lagarith, huffyuv, x264, and such. It's proprietary AMV codec is unsupported by many programs. The firmware for this capture device does not allow permanent setting changes to contrast. Contrast seems to dynamically change on its own from 96 to 144. The other video settings can be changed but are set to defaults after video capture software is closed. I would recommend brightness to be between 40 and 65. Saturation up to 200 is good (mine is usually 150 to 180). To avoid choppy video/audio recordings, you must set high buffer (cache/memory) sizes for the encoder as well as high to realtime CPU priority. Compression should be as minimal as possible, otherwise your HDD and CPU may get overwhelmed. I noticed that disabling playback audio in the capture software fixes a few recording issues as well, especially in CyberLink Power Director and VirtualDub.

Traditionally, KVMs can be tricky pieces of hardware. When they work, they work great. But if you have problems, they can be difficult to track down the cause and resolve. This Dual DisplayPort KVM is no different. My main PC has a video card with dual DisplayPort outputs. That was the main reason for me getting this particular KVM (over something more traditional like a dual DVI). Both of my monitors only have HDMI inputs, but when planning I figured I could just use an active displayport - HDMI converter. This is what I did, and at least this conversion worked perfectly. The rest of the conversions I had planned sadly didn't. Things got more complicated as I started planning it out. I wanted the KVM so I could use my monitors, keyboard, and mouse between my home PC and my work laptop. My work laptop only had HDMI and VGA out ports. Originally I figured I could simply use converters for these (there appeared to be tons on the market), but that's when my ignorance on cable converters bit me. Most of the converters are one way, namely DP -> HDMI or DP -> DVI/VGA. When I plugged the converters in, nothing worked because I was trying to convert opposite direction. Having figured out the error of my ways, I replaced a number of different converters with a different set of converters. Unfortunately the converters working the opposite way (converting to DP) were more limited, more expensive, and sadly very unreliable working through the KVM. The HDMI - DP converter I purchased had a bad habit of stop sending the video signal just as I started working, but Windows still detected that it was connected and required a disconnect and reboot to get going again. The VGA to DP converter locked the resolution to 800x600 (even though it advertised it could go up to full HD). However, I only experienced these problems when using them with the KVM; if I bypassed the KVM and connected them directly they worked perfectly, so clearly the problem was how the KVM was handling the converted signal. Eventually I shifted gears to using USB video adapters. I purchased two Pluggable USB3 - DisplayPort adapters. These worked well through the KVM and I was actually able to use them for an 8 hour work session successfully. Sadly, they weren't completely flawless; one of my monitors would freeze on one solid color, and I had to disconnect/reconnect the USB cable to get it to reset. Also, having all of my laptop's limited USB ports taken up by the keyboard/mouse cable and the two USB video adapters made it unwieldy and limited my ability to connect other peripherals. I returned the Pluggable adapters, and instead purchased a [[ASIN:B012VKW900 StarTech.com Triple Display Docking Station - 2 x DP - 1 x HDMI - 5 x USB 3.0 - 4K - Universal Laptop Docking Station - USB 3.0 Dock]]. This allowed me to connect both video cables and the keyboard/mouse connection from the KVM into the laptop dock, then all I needed to do was connect the dock, with one USB cable, to my laptop. The end result works perfectly and provides a much cleaner setup. So far the video performance has been perfect, and switching between the KVM inputs works flawlessly. So the takeaway from my experience? 1) Read the instructions on how to connect the KVM to your devices. Other reviewers touched upon this, but doing things in the right order ensures the KVM learns your devices properly and you will avoid problems. Check StarTech's website for the proper way to do this. 2) Try to work as "natively" as possible. Just because DisplayPort is an open standard, and there are seemingly endless numbers of converters to other kinds of cables and connectors, you can't rely on those converters (even active converters) working well in tandem with this KVM's chipset. All of the converters I purchased worked fine when connected directly between the device and the monitor, but exhibited strange behavior when going through the KVM. It was a learning process for me, but I'm very happy with the end result. This KVM can support up to 2k video, so I now have an excuse to upgrade my monitors from HD. :P
