Here's a fine example of taking a first-rate product and making subtle improvements to make it truly excellent. This [[ASIN:B008MOHLVC amPen New hybrid stylus]] is an example of product evolution at its best, and the key to this new stylus is in its tip, as can be seen in the photos on this page. The engineers have taken an already very good soft rubber tip and replaced it with a conductive fiber/rubber hybrid tip, and the result is a stylus that offers a smoother action as you access the screen on a tablet, along with an increased level of sensitivity. But please note: now there is a newer version, the [[ASIN:B00F2ORM3W amPen (TM) New Hybrid Stylus (Black)]], and this one is available in more colors, yet this newest version is marked as having a 'Replaceable Hybrid Tip' in the product description. So what makes this amPen New Hybrid Stylus a good choice for tablet users? + Conductive fiber/rubber hybrid tip offers smoother responsiveness on the screen + Lightweight compact design; has a metal (not plastic) pen clip + Newest version has user-replaceable hybrid tips (more on this later) + Corded attachment piece plugs into the headphone jack; no lost stylus + Packaged in a simple box; there's no clamshell to have to cut open + Excellent pricing for a superb product ◆ In Use: Skeptic that I am, had to put it through its paces, and thoroughly, trying it with many different scenarios on my Kindle Fire, trying it with many installed apps, using it to highlight passages in books, and during access to the Internet. The increased sensitivity was apparent, as was the smoothness during actions like highlighting text. Putting it simply I ended up being pleasantly surprised. It's really hard to compare this with other stylus products, as it's slightly different in feel due to the conductive fiber/rubber hybrid tip vs. the soft rubber tips on the others that have become my standards. When I first bought my Kindle Fire, I tried to use it without a stylus, and after going through screen smudges and clumsy moves on my part, did some local looking at various stores and here on Amazon to see what was available, in a wide range of prices. After going through a number of different products, I had ended up with two that I found to be better than most: the highly rated [[ASIN:B0059KTEBC amCase (TM) amPen Ultra-sensitive Capacitive Stylus]] and the [[ASIN:B004GCJEZU AmazonBasics Stylus]], both of which I found to be a 5-star products that have not had tip failures over time like some of the others... and it happens. But the bottom line is that this amPen New hybrid stylus sets a new standard in smoothness and overall functionality, and this stylus also has a metal pen clip. While many of us won't be putting it in a shirt pocket, it was easy to clip to the elastic band on my [[ASIN:B0079R8KO0 Marware Vibe Case Cover]]. This makes for a very convenient combination when mobile... and this combined with the attachment piece plug on the cord keeps the stylus from being misplaced. It might be suggested that the hybrid tip of this or just about any other rubber tipped stylus will pick up skin oils or perspiration if you run your fingers on it. This might come from accidental touching it after rubbing your skin, but it can have an effect on performance, and will also streak your tablet screen. Should this happen, just lightly wipe the tip with a microfiber cloth like you might use for cleaning eyeglasses or the screen of your tablet device. I use the [[ASIN:B004Z8W7DG Nikon MicroKlear Microfiber Cleaning Cloth]] on the tip of this stylus to remove skin oils, but do it gently. This stylus is excellent choice for users of the Kindle Fire, Kindle Touch or the iPad series based on personal use. The way that it slide it across the screen when highlighting text makes it the smoothest that I've experienced, so there must be something good to this conductive fiber/rubber hybrid tip technology. Looking at performance, feel, and real functionality and performance, this new stylus highly recommended, and thinking of the friends that I have who have had issues with various types of stylus products, I already know what they're getting as birthday gifts and such. Considering the excellent price in comparison with the better grade stylus products that I've used makes it an outstanding buy. [UPDATE: 1/20/2013] Since I posted this review, I've ordered a few of these as gift for friends, and last fall ordered another for use with my new Kindle Fire HD 8.9" device. My search for the "perfect stylus" has been put on hold, as this product has met all of my needs. Keep in mind, as in many things, my findings are subjective and based on the performance that I've had with these. [UPDATE: 9/24/2013] This review has been updated to note the newest version of this stylus, the [[ASIN:B008MOHLVC amPen New Hybrid Stylus (Black) for iPad Air, iPad 2, iPad Mini, iPhone 4s, iPhone 5/5s/5c, Nexus 5, Nexus 7, Galaxy S4, HTC One (Interchangeable Hybrid Tip Feature)]]. This updated version is the one that I would recommend over the older models, as the tips are user replaceable as noted in the product specs. And note that the [[ASIN:B00DY6KZ2A amPen New Hybrid Stylus Replacement Tip (5-Pack)]] is available as well, filling a need for which many have asked. [UPDATE: 1/22/2014] For those who prefer an longer stylus with a gel pen included, TechMatte recently released the new [[ASIN:B00HQ2GWKC amPen Hybrid 3-in-1 Stylus]] in either black or silver. This new stylus is longer, at 5½-inches overall length, and also uses the interchangeable hybrid tip. But the best part of this new one is that it uses the the readily-available Pilot G2 gel ink refills, so that you can customize it to your own style. My new favorite, it's well worth a look. ◆ Summary: Whether you pick the updated [[ASIN:B008MOHLVC amPen New Hybrid Stylus]] in black or another color, or the newest model noted above, it will not disappoint. Just be sure that it's marked as having the 'Replaceable Hybrid Tip' before you click on the order button. These are excellent choices for users of tablets and smartphones alike, and the way that they slide across the screen makes them the smoothest that I've experienced, so there must be something good to this conductive fiber/rubber hybrid tip technology. Looking at performance, feel, and real functionality, these stylus products are highly recommended. Considering the excellent price in comparison with the better grade stylus products that I've used, these are an outstanding buy. 7/29/2012, updated 1/20/2013, 9/24/2013, 1/22/2014

This pickup is not cheap, but it's well worth the price. Permanent installation requires only a hole drilled in the tail block; it can be removed without damage. The best part is the sound, though -- even with the mic dialed out, the "electric" tone is much more "acoustic" than the cheap undersaddle pickup I replaced. Adding the mic into the mix makes the system more prone to feedback, but the fact that you can control this tendency gives you the flexibility you need on stage. When played through my Fender Acoustasonic 90 amp with the feedback-control feature switched on, I can dial the mic completely into the mix with no feedback, and the sound from the speaker is good and loud, and very "acoustic". The pole pieces are adjustable for each string. If you don't mind the appearance of a pickup in the sound hole, the Mag Mic is a great way to make your acoustic guitar as loud as the rest of the band.

As a professional photographer looking for a gift video tripod for a local high school's class, this looked like a good candidate for an entry level tripod. I opened the box, pulled the tripod from the bag and one of the lower legs fell out on the floor. No biggie. Ive had to put screws back in tripods before. This one doesnt have screws. It looks like a one shot assembly that snaps together and once done, is not meant to be repaired... at least not on site. I realized what keeps the leg from coming all the way out in normal use, is a very small plastic nib. When the leg is extended it hits that tiny plastic nib and stops. This probably OK for the careful user but anyone that puts this thing through any typical use that Ive experienced over the years, will surely break that nib and have legs falling out. And once its out, I dont see any way to repair it. The leg will not lock once this thing comes apart and you try to put it back together. Naturally I was disappointed at first but then thought Im glad it broke. I got to see the quality of construction and knew the high school kids would destroy this thing in a hurry. Im returning it for credit and ordering a far more expensive unit with hopefully better results. For a casual user that takes care, this is likely a decent tripod for the money. Mine just happened to be the lemon.

Picture quality and camera features and low cost are a big priority for me. I did a lot of research before committing to a security system, this is my first setup, but have seen and worked with many. So as you can tell I decided to go with Reolink after all the research, I ordered their 16CH POE 4MP NVR & RLC-423 PTZ Camera from them directly in Beijing. Then I ordered a few RLC-422 Camera's from Amazon! Along with a RLC-420 Camera. -------------------------Camera Only Review------------------------------------- Pro's of RLC-422 Great picture quality! Up to 4K resolution 30fps Motorized Zoom plus Digital Zoom Built very nice, does not feel cheap Uses star head screws instead of phillips heads to secure dome top (The RLC-420 uses a phillips) Motion detection and email with photo works great You do not need a NVR or DVR, you can use a PC to record, or do it manually form your phone Comes with a mounting template for easy install Con's of RLC-422 No microphone if you want that, I did not care personally (Advertised with microphone is some places) No PTZ feature, which would be awesome with this camera setup! Reolink seems to have the camera only features down and they are nice! Cameras with their NVR is slightly different, see that review below. --------------------------------Camera with Reolink NVR Review---------------------- Pro's of RLC-422 with Reolink NVR Easy to use and work POE is a nice and easy install straight from NVR with single Cat5e cable Camera is connected directly to NVR, so the high data traffic does not effect your office or home network traffic NVR has all the same software features as the camera itself and more. Con's of RLC-422 with NVR Saving settings from remote locations using their Web Client or phone apps do not seem to work well in some areas, like motion detection, they need to be set on NVR itself sometimes. Notification emails with photos are not working with all cameras on the NVR, I only get the text email, with no photo. Cannot update camera firmware from NVR, you have to disconnect the camera, reset it and update the firmware then set it back up on NVR. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Final Thoughts: I am working with Reolink to try to resolve some of these issues I am having, and customer service is great so far. Only down side is the time difference between Beijing and Houston and a very slight language issue with them understanding English, they are trying to help though. Since this is a review for the camera itself, I give it 5 stars!!!!! My review for the NVR would be slightly less just because some of the features are not working properly yet.

First of all, this is my first smart watch. I have been using Timex IronMan watches for decades. In summary, I like the watch and I'm keeping it. I have hopes that some bugs will be fixed soon, but overall the watch is a good purchase for the price and is a good first smart watch. Likes: 1. The number of features offered are great. Personally my favorites were notifications from my phone since I'm always missing them on my phone, heart rate monitoring, step counting, and the many clock face options. 2. Battery life seams good, I can make it about 2.5 days before I have to recharge or risk the watch turning off. Charging seems fast enough, maybe not 3 hrs for a full charge. 3. The screen is bright and colorful. I keep my watch on the lowest brightness setting and that is perfect day and night. I can even use my watch face to light my way around the house at night when the lights are off. 4. The calendar feature shows a month at a time and is very nice. 5. The music feature lets me control my music with Play/pause/next/previous track. 6. Value for the cost is good. 7. The watch band is very comfortable, probably the most comfortable I've ever worn. 8. The watch sends the health data to my iPhone where I can analyze it in the Apple health app. 9. I love the find my watch feature from the app, the Anti-loss feature that alerts me if my watch and phone get to far apart, and the find my phone feature from the watch. 10. I like the altimeter, calculator, barometer, and blood pressure features as well. 11. The seller was very responsive to my questions +++! Dislikes: 1. The notifications will work for a day or so then I have to turn the watch off and back on to get them to work again. This is inconvenient, but I expect the software will be updated and fix this in the future. 2. The watch has no sound, just a vibrate alert feature. I don't need the sound but it would be useful in many situations like hourly chimes, and audio alerts if my watch isn't on my wrist and I therefore can't feel the vibrate. The software has audio/volume settings, but the watch has no speaker. 3. The weather feature seam buggy at times and doesn't update. 4. The instructions are very limited! Even confusing in places. I think the instructions should include much more about the watch features and what each feature does, also include more troubleshooting tips. Many features and watch apps have no description or instructions on how they work. 5. Its great that this watch supports many languages, but the English instructions and some of the words in English are not correct. The grammar in the instructions need a little cleaning up to help eliminate confusion. 6. The compass is ok, the accuracy isn't great but neither is my iPhone 7. I haven't gotten the remote camera to work yet, but I haven't spent much time on it either. 8. Notifications don't word wrap, instead they letter wrap to the next line which would be ok due to the small screen, but the text of the message doesn't use the full line and so I get messages where each line only uses half the screen before wrapping to the next line. I'm sure this can be fixed with a simple software update (I am a software engineer of 18yrs and have worked on mobile devices before so I'm speaking from experience). 9. The touch screen is a bit sensitive, however, since this is my first smart watch I'm not sure if its me. 10. I'm not getting very much data from the sleep monitoring feature, perhaps I just move to much at night and it doesn't think I ever sleep.

This is a very very good case at its price point and in red, she's quite pretty, with a huge see-thru window. A few things could really be improved upon though. First off, no removable 2.5 in. drive trays on the back side? So I have to remove the motherboard to install a 2.5 in. drive? Give me a break. I'll pay another 10 bucks for that feature. Its 2018 for Pete's sake. Plan ahead. Cooling is 1st class in this case with vents and mesh everywhere, but the bottom of the case is the best with a magnetic removable mesh dust filter, by far the best feature of the case. The front is great, but cleaning any dust is harder with no removable filter. Great space in front for a radiator but the top could've also been a great spot for water cooling if they made the 5.25 in bracket better. It sticks out a bit far and this must be considered when mounting anything larger than a 120 mm rad on the top. If you mount a drive on the lower position of the 5.25 bracket, you should be fine, unless it is a long optical drive, in which case the mounting will be very tight, but could still work. Also, invest in the good fans for this case, its wide open, with plenty of mesh dust filters, but that doesn't help noise. I have a 240 and a 120 water cooler in this case (with Noctua static pressure fans) as well as a 120 rear exhaust and 150 mm top exhaust (barely fits, mounting holes don't really align), and the case is VERY quiet with fantastic cooling; both CPU and GPU are overclocked. If the top of the case was better designed, dual 240 mm radiators would be very possible for a great cooling, cheap, smallish ATX case. And the rear 2.5 in mount is a small sin that is a real pain, but with M.2 drives growing in popularity, its less of a sin as time goes by....

I had a very positive experience with the Canary device up until this point -- I have owned it for over a year and it has worked reliably. The company has also offered quick and helpful support via Twitter. Unfortunately, that positive experience is now over. I purchased this device specifically because it did not require a paid membership to watch full clips recorded while in away mode (i.e. when all residents are outside of the home). The only caveat was that after 24 hours, the recordings would expire. Today, the company announced that all of their customers would now be limited to 10-second "previews" of these clips, and only paying members would be able to see more than 10 seconds of potential break-ins or burglaries, making the product entirely useless for its primary purpose. Furthermore, since I made the purchase based on the description of the product from the company that is no longer accurate, Canary is guilty of false advertising (in addition to shockingly poor regard for their own customers). Their public explanation for this change is essentially that they needed to increase revenues; it seems they chose to price the device too cheaply to meet their revenue goals, requiring all new and existing customers to continually pay for a membership plan to maintain the advertised features of the product. Shame on Canary for this choice. I will no longer be purchasing any present or future products from this company, and I encourage you to make the same decision.

Out of the box, this equipment was ready to use. There was nothing to put together except for attaching the camera bracket to the armature. The camera bracket comes with a 1/4" thread (for the camera attachment) but I was so glad that a 3/8" bushing was included to allow me to attach a quick release plate (Manfrotto 323RC2 adapter w/ a 200-PL-14 plate). This 3/8" bushing could easily be overlooked because it was screwed in to the camera bracket- just know it's included. As noted by another reviewer, the weakest point of this equipment is the actual connection point to the tripod- not a stable/rigid connection. There were two solutions for me, but one worked better. The first solution was removing the tripod head (I'm using a Gitzo G1270M) and connecting the armature directly to the tripod (Gitzo G1212). This provided a secure connection but I lost the ability to rotate/pan the device (this articulated arm does not have the ability to rotate around the stem). The second solution was attaching the device to the tripod head (so I wouldn't lose the ability to pan) but installing a 1 1/4" diameter washer to stabilize the connection (I put the washer between the armature's stem and the tripod head). This worked really well- the connection is rigid and stable plus I have all the adjustments available from the tripod head. Overall, I'm very happy with this product because it allows me to precisely, quickly and easily position my camera where I want. As with all Manfrotto products, it's well-built, well-designed and extremely functional. Highly recommended.

My first Kindle was the Kindle Keyboard when that model was new. I loved it and was converted instantly. When Amazon released the Kindle Touch, I decided not to upgrade because my Kindle Keyboard was only a year old, give or take, and I was still very happy with it. I decided to purchase the Paperwhite because of the increased pixel density and faster page turns. The light wasn't a big selling point for me, but I appreciated the fact that the light was designed to point at the surface of the Kindle, not at you/your eyes, thus reducing or eliminating eye strain. PROS: -Crisp text with incredible contrast. I noticed this difference immediately when switching from reading on my Kindle Keyboard to the Paperwhite. Text is rendered beautifully, and whether the light is turned to its highest or lowest setting contrast is very good to excellent. -Faster page turns. This may be a non-issue to some people, and it's not necessarily something that I anguished over with Kindle Keyboard, but I recognized that being able to turn the pages more quickly would just make the reading experience smoother. And it does. The page turns very quickly on the Paperwhite. -Improved home screen. The layout is more like the Kindle Fire's home screen. Whereas on the Kindle Keyboard you are simply presented with a text list of titles, on the Paperwhite you see book covers (which look good thanks to higher pixel density), and you have improved sorting options. It's more inline with how we've come to expect libraries (whether music, book, etc.) to be organized on a tablet or smartphone. -Responsive touchscreen. Those who already owned a Kindle Touch may not think this a big improvement, but for someone coming from the Kindle Keyboard, it's a huge step up and makes so many operations on the device much simpler. No more slow navigating, etc. CONS: -The light does not shine 100% evenly/uniformly across the screen. Amazon has not advertised this device honestly, and that's a big disappointment. Turn the light to a higher setting, and you will see significant hot spots and dark spots at the bottom of the screen where the LED light source is. It's distracting to say the least. As I mentioned above, the light was not really a big selling point for me. Keeping the light at a very low setting minimizes or completely eliminates the hot spots/dark spots problem, and this works for me in the majority of situations (I rarely/never have a need to read in a low light environment) so I don't see this as a big issue. If the light is a major selling point for you, you may want to reconsider or at least buy with the knowledge that what Amazon shows you in its commercials (ie a screen that is lit brilliantly with no hint of dark/hot spots) is not entirely accurate. -The bezel is just too small. There is barely anything to hold onto here. Maybe this is not a problem for someone with small hands, but I have big hands, and almost a week into using this device, I'm still struggling to find a way to comfortably hold this thing for longer than a couple minutes. I have to constantly readjust how I'm holding the Kindle or I start to get carpal tunnel-like pain in my wrists. Awful. I plan to look for a case/cover that gives the device more bulk at the edges. If anyone has a recommendation on this, please leave a comment for me. I'm not saying the Paperwhite needs to have the same amount of space at the bottom as the Kindle Keyboard, but Amazon needs to find a middle ground. In light of the non-reporting of SMR drives from hard drive makers, its becoming more and more apparent as to why they were not more transparent about the technology. It's because SMR or Shingled Magnetic Recording sucks. It is buggy, slow, and causes a lot of read/write errors where Windows was constantly running check/repair disk. I only expect this kind of hard drive behavior from an old and tired hard drive, not a new one out of the box. Do yourself a favor and don't buy this hard drive, or any of the latest SMR hard drives that Seagate, Western Digital, or Toshiba are currently releasing. Do some research, and buy certified non SMR or buy from older tech inventory. No matter what they say or what you hear, no matter what your intended plan of use is, save yourself the frustration and don't buy this or any other SMR hard drive. As for this particular hard drive, I've nothing but buyer's remorse for it. I cannot return it, because I've had it too long, and I really can't trust it. I was using it as a clone drive to support multiple computers, and it sucked at doing that job. So I put in a laptop to be a system drive, it sucked at doing that too. Windows installation takes a long time to complete, sometimes driver installs would take a time to install, and then writing anything at all just takes a long time. Reading isn't bad, but then some document files get corrupt or Checkdisk goes ape and wants to repair the drive. I had a very large spreadsheet that Excel reported was corrupt and needed repairs. When Excel finally opened the dang file, several "sheets" were missing from the spreadsheet altogether. So now this drive is unreliable, easily corruptible, and untrustworthy. Researching about SMR technology led me to the conclusion that SMR tech just isn't a good idea.

I self-host my email and travel internationally. I've had situations where Comcast Business (my old ISP) and Google Fiber (current ISP) were down for hours (so much for business-class), and I want to get a n inexpensive backup when my primary ISP is down My idea was to get one of these Netgears with an inexpensive prepaid data plan (unfortunately the Cellco cartel in the US has enough market power that they won't let data-only prepaid plans that don't expire, so you have to keep paying every month even if you haven't used up your data, but that's another matter). I plugged the Netgear LB1121 into my Ubiquiti network. PoE works, that's great. I turned off DHCP on the Netgear so it wouldn't conflict with my network's DHCP. I set up an iPad to have a manual IP in the 192.168.5.0/24 subnet with 192.168.5.1 as the default router, and verified I was able to connect using my #GB/mo $20/mo US Mobile prepaid plan. So far so good. Unfortunately, I also noticed my iPads were now unable to connect to the WiFi any more, but if I turned the Netgear off, everything would go back to normal. On further examination with port mirroring and Wireshark, I discovered the Netgear doesn't just behave like a router, but it also sends gratuitous proxy-ARP packets whenever it sees an IP, even if it's not on its own subnet. Presumably that's Netgear attempting to be "helpful" for misconfigured devices or network, but the side-effect is that it breaks properly configured networks by stealing via proxy-ARP the IP of a device trying to connect to WiFi. Furthermore, there doesn't seem a way to disable this behavior from the web UI. My solution was to put the Netgear in a VLAN along with a dedicated Ethernet interface on the system that I will use as the emergency remote access backdoor. I suppose i could have connected them directly using a crossover Ethernet cable (not sure if the Netgear does MDI-X), but then I'd have to use the DC power supply instead of PeE, and I hate wall-warts. This workaround works for me, even if it's not ideal, but make sure you understand the constraints in the context of your use case before plonking down your hard-earned cash.

Excellent quality of the incoming voice on the other end when using the BT microphone in a quiet environment. - In 3 weeks of heavy daily use never cut out when ip6s+ in proximity up to 6 feet (when walking streets , at home, jogging, talking over the BT mic) - Relatively long BT range (and around walls) when connected to my ip6s+. A switch to a standard wired Apple headset made a conversation possible while in the same environment. - Too much heat around ears after longer use (but all over-the-ear headphones have this problem) - Statement “BT range 4 times longer than industry” is not precise. I purchased this along with the StarTech.com DP2MDPMF6IN 6in DisplayPort to Mini DisplayPort Video Cable Adapter to connect a 30" 2560x1600 HP monitor to a Dell M4700 Precision Laptop. The Dell laptop has many known issues with display resume on non-DisplayPort devices. After trying several cheap passive DVI to DisplayPort adapters, the Kanex was my last try before ditching the monitor for a new DisplayPort native model. Fortunately, it works! Using the adapter to connect to a full-size DisplayPort, the display works perfectly. Now for the one quirk which took me several weeks of trial and error to isolate. I originally had the USB port (which is used for power only) plugged into the Dell laptop dock. This resulted in the monitor randomly blinking, ranging from once every few days to every few minutes. It also resulted in the monitor being very spotty in turning back on after the laptop had gone into sleep mode and then being woken back up. This was all resolved with a cheap USB wall plug. By plugging the USB port into a permanent power source, every issue went away. No more flickering, no more sleep/resume issues at all. It appears that the USB port on this device can draw quite a bit of current (more than the standard .5A that most USB laptop ports support) and that causes the strange flickering behavior. I've used this continuously for almost 9 months now as my primary work display. It goes through 20+ on/off cycles a day as I dock and undock my laptop between meetings, and resume from sleep. Hasn't missed a beat and still works perfectly.

Just got my Coby CSMP88 yesterday, so I can't speak to long-term reliability but modern electronics tend to keep working if they are OK in the beginning, in my experience. That aside, I'm happy with the sound quality, look, size / proportions, functionality, and ease of setup. At the price, it's an impressive piece. As others have mentioned, you should just leave it in "3D" mode, because that's what it does best; fill the room with dynamic sound. I have it situated just ahead of and below my TV screen. Overall sound quality is very good. Bass is very strong from the rear-firing port, the speakers are clear and clean, and center-channel reproduction is very good. It produces plenty of volume, both from the sub-woofer and through the normal speakers. Setup could hardly be any easier. The remote, and the buttons and LEDs on the front, are simple and effective, with all the functions you need in a straightforward arrangement. RCA cables and remote batteries are included. I did use a set of high-quality RCA cables already in my wire & cable stash, though honestly I've never noticed any difference between variations on these cables, so the supplied cables are probably just fine. But I had the fancy ones, so I used them. That brings us to the one caveat concerning this unit. While it has multiple inputs so you can have, say, your TV and your MP3 player connected at the same time, the Coby ONLY accepts RCA inputs from your TV. I'm sure this is one reason for the relatively attractive price. And it's fine for the right application. I have an affordable 32" Sylvania LCD flat-screen that only has RCA audio outputs, anyway. The Coby is the perfect companion for a budget setup like mine, but you have to make sure your TV has RCA ouputs or you can't use it. It's possible a nicer TV would only offer HDMI, optical, or both, but no RCAs. You have been warned. One thing about the 3D sound is that, because it is so dynamic, it may actually be TOO dynamic for some types of programming. I find that I am mixing the TV's internal stereo speakers with the Coby to strike a balance, by adjusting the relative volume of each. Still experimenting, but there doesn't seem to be any noticeable issue with 'echo' doing it this way. Unfortunately, the Coby does not repond to my TV's internal equalizer function, which I suppose means that the TV's RCA outputs don't pass through the equalizer. Bummer, but the sound is good enough that it's not a problem, and I still have some control because I can still tune the TV's speakers with the EQ and use the relative volume of the two to get the net result I want. Finally, a factor in my purchase was the ability to get it directly from Amazon. That means I got Amazon customer service, return policy, and the option to use Super Saver shipping (which I did). I was told to expect delivery in 5-8 business, but it showed up in 3 business days. Gotta love that. It came well-packaged. Happy customer!

It is a PDF named for the usg60w, but the actual doc is universal to the usg 20, 40, and 60 it seams) The biggest issue was probably bandwidth for the WAN. While plugged into a fiber connection with 50 mbps up and 50 down, any device hooked into it was only managing to pull 4-5 mbps. That's right, a 10th of the available bandwidth. I tested multiple computers directly into the OLN (with different patch cables), and they all achieved the 50 Mbps up and down. So I looked through the manual, searched through it for something helpful. Found several things, including looking at bandwidth management, which I toyed with none of which helped. Looked through ZyXel's support resources and found nothing. Found a couple suggestions on other online resources which were minimal at best (which suggested checking bandwidth management). Still nothing. After disabling nearly every extra added feature, security management, extra VLANs, I was able to get about 14 mbps down, and about 7 up. (I tested directly to the link AGAIN to make sure computers were pulling down the full 50 with out the zyxel). Port forwarding setup is messy at best, and never successfully got it to work (this was before disabling the features). I set the security settings to accept all incoming connections to try to get it to work. Set the IP for the destination server, and the ports, set protocol to all, but when trying to hit the port on the IP address remotely wouldn't work. I thought perhaps I should try to flash the firmware. So I double, triple and quadruple checked I was downloading the firmware for the right model. After considering time "uploading" the new firmware to the usg40w, it would error out with a "file invalid" error. Alright, so I pulled the firmware version and went and downloaded the exact same firmware for Zyxel's site just to see if it flash the same version of the firmware. It too failed with the same error. I never even got to the point of setting up VPN as I had already invested considerable amounts of time trying to get basic functions to work right. It's possible this is just a hardware failure. But the interface is so bad, and documentation is so limited - I spent copious amounts of time trying to figure out if I had missed something or done something wrong. I've read every review and all of them are honest reports. The product is only a metal base plate that sits around your 12700 or 12900 CPU, replacing the lever armed cpu bracket. This gives a bit of heat sink capability and greater surface area to dissipate heat. This may/may not decrease your CPU operational temperatures, but it certainly won't increase them. All you receive is a tiny, but larger than itsy bitsy, box that contains the base place, a hex allen wrench and a tube of cpu paste. I suggest to wear thin latex gloves so your skin oils are not left on the CPU or area around it. Use 91% Isopropyl alcohol and a paper towel to clean the old CPU paste. You can use washed hands in replace of gloves and 71% alcohol instead, but realize the 71% alcohol has a higher water content and dries slower. Ensure every area is free of alcohol and paste, ensure the CPU is exactly placed into it's socket, add the base plate and tighten in phases in a criss-cross pattern. The reason for phases in criss-cross is that unform pressure is applied to the cpu during/after installation. After about 2 rounds of tightening, the screws should meet hard resistance. You are done. As for the cpu paste, you can place a large dab in the center of the CPU, ensuring there are no air pockets in the dab, or you can smear a veneer of paste over the cpu surface trying to get it relatively even. Thin is better than thick when it comes to paste, too thin is too little and too thick reduces heat transference. Old tips from an old pro installer. For this install, I waited until I received an AIO water cooling kit and installed everything over a few hours (cause I kept losing misthreaded screws into tiny case holes over and over and over.....) Give me a break here. Have fun.

I suppose I could have let the Windows-provided utility handle the card but, in the end, I unchecked the box that allowed it to manage the card. This let me use the Linksys utility to handle the setup and things were smooth from then on. Signal strength is excellent - much better than from the SMC PCI card I'd been using earlier. Whether this was a function of having the antenna, rather than SMC's back plastic PC-card type protrusion, I don't know. One more thing, Linksys makes easy work of updating drivers, utilities and firmware from its very well-organized web site. It's worth availing yourself of these updates.

Recently moved from suburban forest to small-town desert and had to upgrade my optics. The prisms move diagonally, crossing X-wise, when the screws are turned, so there is only one possible combo of screw settings that collimate. Hence those reviews here claiming this method is flawed should probably be dismissed. Under clear dark skies these optics gave me the visual high I wanted but couldn't get with Celestron's 10x56 or Bushnell's 10x50. Clusters and galaxies appear with startling brightness, clarity, and negligible aberration. The crescent of Venus is well defined. And as I hoped, holding these by hand is not a problem. Now I am eager to view the Milky Way this summer with these. -1 star: While not too heavy to hold, the eye relief is inferior to that of other binoculars I own, and the eyecups only interfere with alignment with my narrow IPD. I mitigate this by folding back the cups and resting the nocs on the bridge of my nose. It works, but it could be better. At this price range ($110) it's not a cause for buyer's remorse.

I was looking for the smallest footprint home server case that could accommodate four 3.5" drives plus at least one 2.5" drive. This sits on a desk in my office so both size and appearace are important to me. Appearance/Fit & Finish ======================== I am happy with the overall appearance. When the mesh door is closed it is a black cube with an attractive semi-industrial look to it. Though it looks good on the outside, once you open it you can see is definitely cheaply made. The case is constructed from thin metal and plastic, the drive bays are a bit tricky to get all the way seated. Even with the mesh door closed the power and HDD activity LEDs are too bright, I put a small drop of paint on them to dim the brightness. Installation ============ - Power Supply: You need a Mini-ITX power supply, I ordered a 250w (MFX9250). The PSU is easily installed and the case is designed to fit multiple style backs. - Motherboard: Installation takes a little patience because you need to slide it in while also plugging in the connectors and finally screwing it down. All with virtually no clearance. To make this easier I partially disassembled the case and temporarily bent back the rear and tilted up the drive trays. This made it much easier and everything went right back together. - CPU Cooler: There is little clearance between the motherboard and the bottom of the drive tray so you need a low profile CPU cooler I used a [[ASIN:B004PLWJCC Rosewill 80mm Sleeve Low Profile CPU Cooler RCX-Z775-LP Black]]. - Only one side of the drive bay has an access hole to plug the power and SATA connectors into the back-plane. Since my SATA connectors were on the opposite side I just ran them up the side and over the top. - The HDDs screw into the hot swap drive bays, then the bays slide into the case. The components do not fit well so it takes a little wiggling to get everything to seat properly. Other notables (good and bad) ============== - The provided case fan 3 wire 80mm. My motherboard uses a 4 wire fan connector and cannot control the fan speed so I replaced it with a 4 wire PWM fan. - The back-plane / drive bays have individual power and activity lights so you can see that each drive is plugged in and operating. - I added a second 2.5" HDD next to the existing 2.5" drive mount by mounting with velcro. This gives me a total 6 drives, 4x 3.5" + 2x 2.5". - When figuring the cost you need to account for the price of a new PSU as well as a low profile CPU cooler and maybe a new case fan. - If you plan to swap drives in and out a lot I would get a different case with better drive bays that include quick connectors. Recommendation ============== I am very happy with my purchase and would buy this product again. Though not perfect, it fit my needs.

This is my first day with the little machine, and so far I am very happy with it. I've bought dozens of computers over the years, for both business and personal use, so I am rather picky, and at the same time, rather patient with little differences between products. Love the screen, its matte finish makes it comfortable to use in all light levels, and the quality of the image is excellent. The keyboard feels good, a quality tactile experience, although I am used to typing on a full sized keyboard and I have to slow down a bit to adapt to this slightly scrunched layout. Setup was painless, and thanks to Google and Chrome, all my browser preferences and bookmarks were there instantly. The first thing I did was download Chrome, as i will not use Internet Explorer if I can avoid it. As small format Windows PCs go, the machine is better than you'd expect at this price. Not loaded with memory or a really fast processor, the performance is suitable mainly for straightforward websurfing, email, watching some videos, shopping, banking, googling. CPU intensive or memory intensive apps and games will probably not fare all that well on this little guy. But for everyday student-homemaker use, it's great, and I like it much better than a Chromebook for various reasons, one of which is, there are windows apps that won't run on a Chromebook and I am not willing to give those up. Now, the biggest single thing about this laptop: It's a Windows 8 machine, and this is my first exposure to that operating system. My daily driver laptop, which I have been using heavily for 5 years, is a Windows 7 device, and before that I was a devoted Windows XP fan. Windows 8 has gotten a lot of bad press, many people seem to hate it because of its quirky "Start" interface with its flashy tiles and confusing layout. So let's talk about that aspect of this little Lenovo. First thing: Win 8 is not nearly as awful as its haters say it is. I figured it out in about 20 minutes, and that's after 25 years of using just about every Windows version that has been out there in that time. Win 8 is windows, and the hated Start interface can be brushed aside in favor of the familiar Desktop very easily. I figured it out in minutes, and then, I went back and visited Start again just for the fun of it ... it's odd, but really rather charming in its own odd way, and useful at times. So, if you take the few minutes to familiarize yourself with the methods of flipping from one interface to the other ... from Start to Desktop and back again .... it's really a pretty easy workspace to handle for anyone familiar with Windows. So, if Win 8 is a worry for you, and you haven't used it, don't be afraid of it. It's just another way to see the machine, and its quirky interface goes away with a click and the familiar Desktop is right there. My initial batter life looks to be in the 4.5 hour range but I will report in a week or two after more time with it. Last but not least, my hunch is that one reason for the low price on this machine is in fact Windows 8, now that it has been "replaced" in the product lineup by Windows 10. Maybe they want to get rid of Win 8 inventory, or maybe they are getting Win 8 licenses for cheap, I don't know, but that explains for me why the machine is so cheap. It's not cheaply made, it looks and feels very nice. But it has a lightweight processor, a smallish amount of memory and onboard storage, and last year's Windows version that people have not loved, but really, is just another Windows system and doesn't deserve the hate. All in all, this machine is a bargain at the well-under-200 dollar price, and I recommend it.

Here's the dilemma: You're in a some kind of job that frequently subjects you to "death by Power Point". Yeah, I feel for you. Now for some reason, the office projector is (more often than not) out on the road or in the repair shop. Good news, right? So instead of getting a little extra nap time in the "bored" room, the boss decides he wants you to go through all the backlogged crap from 1970 to 2008 and make a detailed report that he will likely glance at for 15 seconds and then ask you why your other work is getting behind. You'd have been better off listening to Captain Sominex deliver his presentation, but noooo... John from sales needed the projector for a conference 3 states over. Wouldn't it have been great if you could whip a projector out of your pocket so you could kick back and eat a donut while pretending to care what some windbag is mowing over? What about a POCKET PROJECTOR?! Sounds great, but then the thing arrives and you realize you're about to unleash a new level of pain on top of something that everybody already hates. The Aaxa P2 is currently the Cadillac of the picos. Seriously... You're not going to find a better one. Even the pocket laser projector is going to be hard pressed trying to match this puppy. The P2 has a 33 lumen output. On the surface that really sucks, but other Picos are sadly maxed out at around 11 or 12 lumens. Still, a typical projector is going to have 1000 lumens on the low end. 33 lumens looks like a faint stain on the screen by comparison. The P2 has a native resolution of 800x600. Still not great, but other picos are still using 640x480. On the bright side (bright?), it "simulates" higher resolutions, but the picture gets fuzzier the higher you go. The P2 comes with a mini tripod for positioning. Sadly it's about as stable as David Hasselhoff at an open bar. Battery life? About 45 minutes. You can plug it in, but it won't recharge the battery while the projector is in use. Noise? Yes. The cooling fan makes more noise than you'd expect. Built in speaker? A sad joke. The fan is louder than the speaker, so make other sound arrangements. Image quality in a dark room? Fairly decent. Great for an impromptu movie night or gaming. Ease of use? Getting it to turn on is a little janky. First turn on the power switch, then hold the button to turn on the lamp. Say a prayer, be sure the computer is sending output through the provided VGA cord, and check your connection if the blue screen persists. Focus? Rather touchy. It's not easy getting it right on that sweet spot, and don't ever expect perfect focus using a resolution higher than 800x600. The bottom line is this: The person in charge desperately wants to show their latest Power Point. Your new Aaxa P2 is going to be the only available device for the task. It's dreadfully underpowered for the job, a little clumsy to get set up, but it will save the day and afford you a nice little coffee break while the big guy draws circles on the wall with his daughter's cat exerciser in a vain effort to highlight the most relevant aspects of his washed out presentation. It's a trolls gold. EDIT: About two years after I got it, it stopped working. The light came on, and it projected a blue screen, but that's as far as it would go. This device wasn't cheap back then, and when I contacted AAXA, they basically blew me off by pointing me to their newer models. I'm actually kind of shocked this projector (and my cheeky review) is still around. Today there are better pico's out there, so I'd strongly recommend against buying this even though the price has been considerably discounted since 2009.

Purchased 4 units from the same vendor at the same time, however received two packages of two units each from two different Amazon centers. Buyer-Beware... even though the products are advertised as the same, and the product numbers are all the same, the packaging and instruction sheets were slightly different. Come to discover during installation and reviewing SmartThings IDE, the difference was firmware versions as one set of two was an earlier and reports less detail than the other set received. Not a “real” problem, however I don’t have the Aeotec stick required to load the newer firmware (that’ll cost another $50 or so). Update: 11/07/19, using SmartThings hub, a week later... units were having problems not responding or extremely late in notifying open/close action. One unit "sticking" in to open position while another one was "stuck" in the closed position. I performed the following in an attempt to solve: - changed from small to large magnets (even though the contact distance is suitable for the smaller magnet) - unpaired and repaired the door sensors to the hub - perform Z-Wave Utilities "Repair Z-Wave Network" with all devices in permanent location All door sensors are very close to other Z-Wave devices (door locks and light switches within a few feet), so there should be no hub communication issues. All units were responding correctly after network repair... will advise if continued failure occurs, wherein these sensors would be totally useless for intrusion detection. Update Nov 20th 2019... I’m still having issues with the two sensors that have older version firmware (v1.02). One door sensor indicates “unavailable” every morning, even though it does respond to an open/close event, while the other sensor seems to stick “open” when the door is closed. The second set of two sensors with newer firmware (v1.03) appear to be working just fine. I really like the footprint of these sensors and want to make them work correctly, therefore I will be forced to purchased the AeoTec z-stick so I can update the firmware (at $45 from Amazon, that effectively increased my per unit cost another $11+ each)! Therefore lowering my rating from 3 stars to 1 star until I can get all four sensors working as advertised.

Although I can't verify the speed potential or power delivery potential for this, it did the trick to hook up the front panel USB-C in my new build since the motherboard didn't have it. Coulda/shoulda picked a different motherboard although the price difference to get an on-board connection for USB-C was more than this. That said, this feels pricey for only one port. If you've installed any add-on cards or video cards before, this is relatively straightforward to deal with. Plug in to the appropriate PCI slot (it will not work on a basic PCI-E X1 slot) and connect the SATA power connector. In Windows 10 you won't need to do any more than that, no drivers needed. Since I can't verify performance I'll assume it does the job it needs to do. That's not to say I don't have criticisms and there aren't opportunities to improve the product. Given the price and the location within your case, it would be rather nice of Silverstone to include a SATA power extension cable. The location puts the power connection fairly far towards the back of your case . Unless you have neighboring hard drive or SSD mounting points that you are using, it's not really a place I would want to route a SATA power cable from the PSU given how bulky they are and the fact that you only need the one connector. In addition to that, a header cable extension would also be really nice because it's right near the limit of how far the cable in my case can reach. That, or moving the header connection to the edge of the card next to the SATA power connection would also vastly improve the ease of connecting front panel headers. Edit: Perhaps I should be taking points off for this because an additional rear USB-C port would be nice and improve the value proposition for this part. It looks like the ASM3142 controller this is using could support a second port based on the specs from Asmedia.

I've owned my previous HK receiver for over 15 years, and it still works wonderfully. I wanted to upgrade to more power and features, so my old receiver will be relocating to my basement. First off, the HK 3490 is absolutely stunning. I've always been a fan of HK's commitment to minimalism but this receiver takes it to a new and beautiful level. The one horizontal row of slim buttons is not visible at all when standing a few feet away, creating the appearance of a completely buttonless perfect space, but when you're standing at the receiver, each button is clearly visible for easy operation. When turned on, the white glow of the power light and volume knob is very cool; the reading is clear, but along with the volume knob light, it can be dimmed or shut off. When turned off, the power light glows red. The sound is amazing. I'm noticing strong bass but more impressively strong mids and highs, so much so that, maybe it's just my imagination, but I think I'm hearing things in my music I never heard or noticed before. Stereo separation is good, and the receiver creates a very wide soundstage with a lot of presence. I do have two issues with the receiver, though they're very minor. The Volume takes some getting used to--I can be listening through the speakers at a perfectly comfortable volume, but when I switch to headphones, it's deafening. I have to remember to lower the volume by at least 15db before putting the headphones on. The other issue has to do with the power button on the remote control. Some have reported that the remote is rather big, and, well, it is, but that's not a problem for me because I use a Sony Universal Remote instead. What bothers me is that there are two separate buttons on the remote control for On and Off, which is somewhat awkward when switching both of those commands to the universal remote. Again, these are minor MINOR issues. Overall, this is a great receiver and a great price! UPDATE: 28 Months Later (and 4 months out of warranty)! My HK3490 is dead. I moved last week, and despite packing it carefully back into its original box and taking it in my car rather than trusting it with the movers, my HK3490 is no more. It worked for a day after I moved. Then mysteriously, the next time I turned it on, it automatically shut itself off and displayed the error code "Voltage Protect Check Inputs." Even after unplugging all of the inputs, the error code still displayed, which the HK tech explained meant that there was an internal problem--a short or something come loose. It's not worth the trouble to ship it somewhere to get it repaired, and be without music for weeks or longer, so, already committed to the HK aesthetic with my other components, I just ordered a new one. I guess they don't make 'em in China like they used to in Japan or the US. By the way, my older HK receiver, now 17, is still going strong. It survived the move without a hitch.

These headphones are the closest thing I have found to a pair of Bluetooth headphones that I can use while swimming laps in a pool. They are completely watertight and the straps behind the head design means that they do not fall off when you are cutting through the water. For those of you that have DYI skills, and would like to make these lap-swimming able, here's what I did. I had to modify the ear-buds because the ones that come with the headphones do not keep the water out of your ears while submerged. I used [[ASIN:B00BMDJUAU Swimbuds Replacement Waterproof Earbud Pack]] ear-buds and modified the headset to make them stay on better. 1) Remove the 'stock' ear-buds from the headset mount tubes. 2) Use a soldering iron to (carefully) melt a ridge at the end of the end of the mount tubes. (see pic) 3) If the melting blocks the hole, you might need to take a drill bit and reopen it. 4) Place the new ear-buds on the mount tubes. (see pic) I just keep my phone with music in a backpack on a chair within 20ft of the pool and can do laps with good tunes playing. If water gets by the ear-buds, pull them out, empty out the water, and reseal. Note: radio signals do not go through water, so signal will cut out if your head is submerged. Antennae seems to be in the right ear unit. Cuts out if I breath to the left and submerge it. Hey BlueAnt: If you redesign the antennae to wrap around inside the headband, I am sure you could eliminate that problem. Then all you have to do is upgrade your ear-buds and you will be the cat's meow in lap swimming music delivery. K

I bought this mouse because I was starting to get hand/wrist pain, and I wanted to try out different ergonomic mice to see if they would help with the problem. In short, this does not. It's true that your wrist is not twisted, but there is another problem with it. It's too small in the wrong places, requiring you to grip the mouse too much to press the buttons. With a regular mouse, when pressing buttons, you're pushing the mouse into the mousing surface. With this mouse, when you press buttons, you're pressing them into your thumb, so your thumb has to press back in order to squeeze the button. This made my hand hurt just as bad if not worse. It's not *too* bad if I rest my thumb on top of the mouse, but then I have to kind of grip the mouse by cupping my palm and that's not ergonomic either. And my thumb hits the DPI button. In short, this was designed by someone who thought vertical mice are cool but have no idea how they work.

I have had three generations of iPad and with them many, many different cases. Some cheap, some mid range. I've lost count of how many. I use my iPad every day, many times a day. Many a case has not survived even a year. The plastic starts to crack, the materials start to peel. Mostly to watch videos or read, in my room. And the occasional travel by plane. People, I'm by no means putting these things through a war zone or something. Needless to say, I know a good case when I see it, simply because many just don't make the cut. This is by far, the best case I've had, so far. It ticks all the boxes. It's good looking, it's easy to put on and remove, it protects the corners of the device in case of drops, and the strength of the magnet is the stuff of legends. My favorite thing is that the iPad is encased when it closes, as opposed to the screen flap coming all the way to the edges. It means your iPad won't get dirty or accidentally awaken when you put it on your bag. I have had this for several months and the thing I find that really sets this baby apart from others is all the reclining angles. The most comfortable and best I've seen of any case I've previously had. If you put your iPad on your lap frequently to type or read. Or to watch videos while laying horizontally in bed or the couch, get this case. Not only does it give you a great angle for viewing the screen while laying down, but the magnet is strong enough that the weight of the screen won't let the iPad topple forward and fall on your face. We've all been there, don't lie. As for the negatives.. I'm actually not super confident in the durability of the inner fabric. It's a sort of fine suede with a stamped logo (the branding is kinda ugly, but you can't really see it since it's at the bottom all the time when open, or inside when closed). In my experience, this sort of material eventually will start to peel off or bubble. Which would really be a shame since this case was so expensive. I also wish there was one more recline slot to make the screen near upright and hope the designer considers this for the next version of the case. Overall, I give this case five stars because it's beautiful, easy to put on and off, it protects the ipad, it's well designed and it's extremely practical. I think it is worth the investment. However of course, I will come back at a later time and amend the review if I find any issues with the material. Update on Dec 2022: I still own this case and use it every day. However in the past six months the exterior fabric has begun to peel and flake off around the hinge area. The fabric on top of the cover has also begun to separate from the backing around the edges. The plastic components have not been compromised and remain sturdy, no cracking. The inner suede-ish fabric I predicted might come off eventually is surprisingly still standing strong. It catches every speck of dust and pet hair though which is annoying. The magnet has remained strong. And the case has saved my iPad a few times I’ve accidentally dropped it. Unfortunately I think the choice of material for the hinge of this makes it so it’s inevitable it will start to flake eventually.

The Cougar 700M has some good features, but I am writing this review because of the problems that I encountered with the first mouse product that I have purchased from this company. I am not a big fan of the "Transformer' appearance of the mouse, and that is not why I bought it in the first place. I wanted a mouse with high precision that had good placement on the buttons. In general I like the button layout on the 770M, and the feel of the mouse in your hand is good. I don't like the deep grooved surfaces on the left and right sides, they do not need to be that textured, and they tend to pick up dust and other debris over time. They are also hard to clean because the grooves are relatively deep and very narrow. The braided cord also tends to pick up dust and lint over time. The software is good, and gives you lots of control over the mouse setup. You get 4 settings for different dpi/sensitivities. Now for the problems. After about 5 weeks of normal use (no dropping or other issues that might have affected reliability) the left mouse button started performing "double clicks" when only a single click had been made. At first I did not pay too much attention, but it began to happen more frequently, often while working on a spreadsheet or when selecting files from a folder. So rather than selecting a file or folder, the file or folder would open. I would go to select a cell in the spreadsheet, and instead it would go into text editing mode while I was trying to do a "Ctrl-C" to copy the contents of the cell. As this happened more and more, the mouse became less and less usable, and very frustrating. I began testing the left mouse button extensively to see how often the double click problem happened. I would go across a row of folders on the desktop and single click on each one to see if the folder was selected, or opened. Sometimes I could go for dozens and dozens of clicks before a folder opened, sometimes it would happen in the first 10 clicks. The company claims that the "Omron microswitches" are rated for 5 million clicks, so it is curious that my 700M started having switch problems after barely more than a month. When it became obvious that the problem was not going away, I contacted the company (The HEC Group) to request an RMA to have the mouse replaced under warranty. The first reply was swift and decisive: "Hello As Amazon is not one of our authorized resellers, please process returns with Amazon. Thank you HEC GROUP USA rma@hecgroupusa.com" I wrote back to explain that the 30 day return period was over and that I needed to process the RMA through them. Again, I got a swift reply: "When purchasing on Amazon, if that particular ad for the item states " Sold by MALABS, fulfilled by Amazon" then warranty service can be processed by HEC as MALABS is one of our authorized reseller. Unfortunately, that is how the rules work as there are many individuals and small stores out there that sell through Amazon, and we cannot authenticate the nature of the products unless they are our registered resellers. HEC GROUP USA rma@hecgroupusa.com" The mouse was sold from and fulfilled by Amazon. I found it extremely strange that a small outfit like MALABS was considered to be an authorized reseller, but that Amazon was not. Nonetheless, I contacted Amazon and explained the situation to them, and despite the fact that they did not have an obligation to fulfill Cougar's warranty, they immediately cross-shipped a replacement and sent me a return label to return the defective mouse. I have the new mouse installed, and so far no double click problems. We will see what happens over the next few weeks and months. If I have any problems I will update this review. I thought it was important to let other potential customers know that The HEC Group is prone to looking for excuses to not offer warranty support for their products, and that the switches might not be quite as reliable as the company claims. *Update: 700M Cougar Mouse Number 2 I received a new 700M and at first all was well. However, within 2 days the new 700M mouse began to show the double click problem much worse than the first one. Sometimes almost every click was a double click (folder or file would open rather than just get selected). So I began to think that it must be some other problem with my computer (Intel i7 3.3GHz, 12GB RAM, Windows 7 Ultimate). I went into full diagnostics mode. 1) I first moved the USB plug for the mouse from a USB 3.0 socket to a USB 2.0 socket. Same problem. 2) I put an older (~ 1 year old G400s) Logitech mouse on the original USB 3.0 socket. No problem with double clicks at all using the Logitech mouse. 3) I disabled the Cougar mouse control software (UIX) at Windows startup. Same double click problem. 4) I adjusted the double-click speed in the Windows 7 mouse control panel. No luck. 5) Plugged the 700M into a different Windows 7 computer (I noticed a very long driver install time) and guess what? The first click opened a folder rather than selecting it! The problem was just as bad on a different computer, without the Cougar mouse control software having ever been installed. 6) Just for the heck of it, I plugged the 700M into a 14 year old Windows XP computer that was still functioning well. The first click on a folder opened it! Bottom line, there is something very wrong with some Cougar 700M mice. Maybe a bad batch of switches, maybe a design flaw in how the switches are mounted in the frame. Who knows? I have never experienced this problem with mice in the past, and I have owned many different mice from different manufacturers. Right now the Logitech G400s is working perfectly. I have uninstalled the UIX software, am returning the mouse for a refund, and I won't be buying mice from Cougar again. Cougar mice are made by a Chinese company known as the HEC Group who specializes in aluminum, pharmaceuticals and resorts. Clearly, they are not focusing on their computer hardware quality. *additional update: After looking into the issue more I see that Logitech mice have gotten many complaints about this issue (although I have not seen this particular problem with any Logitech mice I have owned, which numbers in the dozens). However, one person on the Logitech forum mentioned that in low humidity environments an electrostatic charge can build up on the plastic, and cause the microswitch to misread the clicks. We just had a polar vortex come through with temps around 0, and the humidity in the house is down to around 38%. Using your breath to humidify the switches supposedly fixes the problem. I have the 700M boxed up and ready to ship back, so I did not test this to see if it worked. Either way, it is a design problem that could be easily fixed with metal switch covers that are grounded. I am tempted to take it out of the box to test it. If I do, I will update. *Final update -SOLVED; I couldn't resist. I had to test out the low humidity hypothesis. I took the 700M out of the box again, and plugged it in. The problem was severe. I breathed some humidity onto the mouse, and immediately the problem was lessened, but not gone. I slipped a small piece of aluminum foil under the left switch and touched it to a metal object. I removed the aluminum foil and breathed on the mouse again. Problem gone. Unfortunately, we are having a very cold period now and our whole-house humidifier struggles to keep the house at 38 to 40% relative humidity. So until this mouse is redesigned with grounded metal switch covers, or with special non-static plastic switch covers, I just don't want to keep breathing on my mouse to prevent the double click problem. Additional update: I have been using the Logitech Proteus mouse since I returned the 700M, and I just don't like the Proteus for a number of reasons, including the fact that the bottom cover on the laser emitter falls off while playing games at times (held on by a small magnet). I waited several months before trying to purchase the 700M again, but I really preferred it over the Proteus, so the other day I ordered another 700M. It was nice to have it back again, until I noticed that mouse button 4 (back button while web surfing) did not work. I then installed the UIX software to see if I could get it going, but no luck. Mouse button 4 was dead. I am returning the 700M for a replacement, let's hope the 4th time is the charm. Fourth Cougar 700M mouse: I received my 4th 700M mouse, and everything worked just fine, with one problem that cropped up quickly. The aluminum frame on this one was slightly bent so that the front lip was lower than the pads keeping the mouse off the table surface. This led to the aluminum frame wearing away on the desktop, which then scratched and stained the nice cherry wood. I have so far been unable to get the aluminum stains out of the wood surface, forcing me to use a mouse pad to protect the table top from further damage. See image showing the worn aluminum frame and permanent damage to the desk top.

I bought this camera because Amazon was selling it for $20 less than it's usual price. I said hey that's a deal I'll get it. Shortly after, I found out that Sharper Image had an instant camera that was a lot cheaper than what this camera was ($20 brand new on eBay, $11 at Walmart). So I bought them both and decided to do a side by side comparison. If I liked one more than the other, I could return one. If I liked them both, I'd keep both. Both cameras used the same Fujifilm mini film so you don't have to go out of your way buying different film for both which is nice. They also both have the same types of functions on them - indoor, outdoor/cloudy, sunny, hi-key. very easy to use and uses AA batteries. The Fujifilm camera has a little mirror on it for selfies and an attachment for upclose shots, but the sharper image camera did not. They also both look very different but for turning them on was the same concept. You pushed a button and the camera lens popped out. When taking the pictures I decided to just take a photo of the same thing, on the same setting just to see how each photo came out. The Fujifilm photos printed out vertically whereas the sharper image photo came out horizontally. Each took about the same time to spit out the film and develop (30secs-45secs). The first 2 photos I took with the Fujifilm came out black which is unfortunate because it's a waste of film. I took an additional 2 and they came out normal. The first picture was of my fish tank. It came out clear and showed the entire tank in the photo. It had a black dots in the middle which I will attribute to either the flash or my own error because the same thing appeared on the same image with the sharper image pic I took. With the sharper image photo, it didn't show the entire tank. It was more wide. It makes more sense I suppose because of the orientation of how the film comes out of the cameras. I also took photos of my fish in a jar on both cameras. Fujifilm came out clear and vertical, sharper image came out blurry and horizontal. Upon closer inspection of the photos, the Fujifilm pics came out much clearer. You can see the details more clearly and it is more focused. The sharper image photos came out blurry, more fuzzy. Upclose shots were particularly bad, far away- not as noticable. However, the Fujifilm camera did have some black photos come out which is a no no considering how expensive the film is. If it spits out 4 or 5 black pics every packet of 10 that's a waste of money. I'd much rather take the chance of a slightly blurry pic than waste film. Ultimately it's up to you though. I'm going to keep both and use them more to see how they continue to compare with one another. Worse comes to worse, I resell lol. Update: I ordered a replacement for my Fujifilm camera because some of the film kept coming out black. It wasn't defective film, more like a defective camera.

I wanted a bookshelf system for my kitchen with CD player, decent radio, and iPod and auxiliary inputs. The DM-38 delivers all this with a striking elegance of design that makes my engineer heart happy just to look at it. I like it so much that I'm ordering a second unit for my office. There's no need to buy an iPod dock. I connect my iPod Touch 32G (third generation) to the USB port. I can operate the iPod in either of two modes. Normally I control it by tapping on its screen as usual, calling up apps and playing music. I can, for example, run the NPR News app, sending the audio over the USB cable. That's a win because the digital signal is converted to analog inside the DM-38, which does a much better job than the iPod. Or I can press the "browser" button on the DM-38 remote. Now the iPod goes into "accessory connected" mode and I can control the music player with the remote -- start/stop/pause and forward/reverse work. The two-line display on the DM-38 shows the song info. Here's why I didn't go all the way to five stars: *) No HD radio. None of the competition has HD either, but still ... the British version of this product handles digital radio, why doesn't the American? *) No support for RDS, the metadata in the radio signal. My car radio can tell me what station I'm listening to and the name of the current track, but the DM-38 cannot. There's a "DAB/RDS" button on the remote that does nothing. *) When playing MP3 files from a USB storage device (like a flash drive), the DM-38 doesn't sort by the track number meta-information in the files. Instead, it uses the order in which the files appear in the directory. This means that the only way to get the correct playlist order is to format the USB device and then carefully copy in the files in track order. Portable MP3 players don't have this silly limitation. *) No option to leave the USB port hot when the stereo is turned off. This means I have to unplug the iPod from the stereo and connect it to a separate charger to keep the battery full. And no, you can't put a self-powered USB hub in the circuit; the DM-38 doesn't work with hubs.

I was excited when I found this product and received it within 2 days. I have about 800mbps coming into my home in my office, but using an EERO mesh wifi system across my house, I get down to 50 to 100mbps when you get to the end of my house. I wanted to try this because I have cable running throughout my entire house and hoped this would help me achieve better speed in other rooms. In the end, I am able to get up to 700mbps at the far end of my house using this product, which is awesome, but I had to figure out a few things that were keeping me from hitting that speed, so I want to share it: 1. As others have posted, make sure that you are using the supplied ethernet cables or at least recent cables. When I originally hooked up both adapters to the cable outlets in my office and son's room, we were only achieving the lower speed setting of 100 mbps (green light) instead of 1,000 mbps and the cause was because I was running an old ethernet cable to the first adapter from my Xfinity modem/router. Updating to a new cable fixed this and lifted the speed up to 1,000 (blue light). 2. When we got to the end point / my son's room, even with high speed showing across the adapters, I was only getting around 100 mbps download speed at my son's computer. We were going from A. Cable coming into room to B. Moca Adapter to C. Ethernet cable supplied with adapter to D. Ethernet to USB adapter to E. In on his USB port. What I figured out, and this is really important, is that you need to be using a USB 3.0 port and not any port. Once we switched to his USB 3.0 port on his laptop, we achieved about 750 mpbs, nearly the full 800 mbps that I am receiving in my office. This is really a great product. I hope this info can help others during their installations.

I am pleased with this lens for its low weight and compactness that rides easily in my spiderholster. For a reasonably, but not super-, sharp lens that is a good package. It gives you a 300mm reach at a reasonable cost. I use it on bird watching trips. A 300mm lens isn't really up to the task, but anything longer would strain my back on long hikes, so it's a compromise I am willing to accept. My subject is usually at the center of the image, so although I wish it were a tad sharper, sharpness is adequate. If I were buying this lens today, I would take a close look at the new Nikkor 300mm f/4 PF as a substitute. It is equally light and might be a superior lens. The auto focus is super fast. However, when photographing birds, focusing is usually a two step process and the second step is difficult with this lens. Step 1 is Autofocus to get an approximate focus. Step 2 is Manual focus to fine tune. If you are photographing polar bears, there is no need for step 2, but with birds, step 2 is often necessary because the autofocus gets tricked by leaves and branches. The fine tuning is very difficult and very often impossible before the bird flies away. Such difficulty is to be expected when attempting to photograph birds, which are notoriously uncooperative subjects. However, at f/5.6 there is not a lot of light to work with and it is very difficult to tell when the subject is in focus even if it is perfectly still. The tiniest of nudges seems to turn the focus ring from under-focused to over-focused and the focus ring has a tiny free play whereby it moves a bit before it engages. This manual focusing difficulty might be an issue with digital photography in general rather than with this particular lens. The old manual lenses were by comparison a pleasure to focus. The 28-300 works very well as a macro lens as well. For nature travel, this lens allows you to capture landscapes as well as distant animals. For the price and weight, it is well worth having.

I had been considering buying a second Roku for a secondary TV, but when I saw this new device, I bought it right away! Here are my thoughts: SET UP So simple to set up. Including opening the package, it took me 5 minutes (I timed it). All I had to do was connect the device to the HDMI and plug it in. Then I put in my WIFI password. Because the device is so slim and small, I have it sitting under my HDTV on the console. I feel like the cords are neater there. It took an additional 38 minutes to update the software, so it did take a while to actually be able to use it. I loved that as soon as it finished loading, a short, fun and helpful startup instructional video ran. Since I bought it for myself on amazon, it was automatically uploaded with my account info. NAVIGATING AMAZON VIDEO CONTENT It gave me the option to add parental controls in the form of a pin to my account, which I did, because I didn't want my kids to accidentally (or on purpose) buy an episode.
