Update 3.17.17: We rented a 2017 Nissan Rogue for a trip last weekend. The Rocker would connect to the Rogue (with, again, multiple failed pairing efforts upfront), but it would not initiate playback; it would show the file metadata but never actually begin playing. If you tried to simply turn the Rocker off at this point, it would essentially crash and lock up, with the only solution being to hold the power button for 10+ seconds to fully restart the Rocker. Our phones had no problem just pairing and just playing on the Rogue stereo over Bluetooth. I have also had continued issues with both pairing and reconnection on two of three BT receivers including my own factory car stereo. I have had some continued correspondence with the US distributor, but between the multiple Bluetooth issues and the nasty pops between files over the headphone jack (both of which are allegedly being worked on, but who knows how long fixes will take and/or if they are ever forthcoming; the distributor insists the Bluetooth implementation works flawlessly on their end), I don't think the Rocker is worth keeping. If it were a device sold for a couple dozen buxx and not an "entry-level audiophile" device with a entry-level audiophile price to match, I might feel differently. But persistent file-start-and-end pops over the lone analog output and the BT flakiness are certainly not very audiophile. And in general, I think the practice of rushing a product to market and expecting your paying users to do the job of the bug testing and translation issues you should have hired folks to do BEFORE release is pretty questionable, and at the current asking price I'm also uninterested in supporting that business model. So it's going back. Also, it took me a while to figure out based on the correspondence with the confused distributor, so I'll share this clue with other folks: In the English translation, the current "Auto Shut-off" in Settings is actually a sleep timer. On v1.1 firmware, the Rocker will shut down after 2 minutes of idle no matter what you do or change. Update 3.9.17: The US distributor, Linking Port, contacted me to point me to a firmware upgrade, v1.1. When installed, this seems to make two main changes (when running in English at least): 1) The system font is changed to a much cleaner-looking bitmapped font which allows three add'l vertical characters in each displayed row, changing from 16 max to 19 max. This actually does help a bit, in some situations, with navigating larger collections / longer titles. I have a new comparison photo that I've just added to the review - with 1.01B, the album titles for New Brutalism cannot be seen, while with the system font changes in 1.1 you can at least now see the *start* of each New Brutalism album title in the same screen. 2) The unit now has auto shut off applied *mandatorily*. In the settings screen, there is still a line for "Automatic Shut-off," it is *still* disabled ("No") by default, and it still re-disables itself (back to "No") on every restart... but the unit will shut itself down automatically after the time limit set on "Automatic Shut-off Timer" in settings, *whether or not Automatic Shut-off is enabled or disabled*. Linking Port advises me that they are working on other aspects of the firmware and looking into some of the things that reviewers and early adopters have pointed out. So there's that, and it's certainly to their credit that they are working and listening to customers to iron the bugs out of the Rocker. ** Here's my final review on the Rocker; I have archived my original impressions to the comments, and some of them were wrong anyway. For this last go, I will try to keep this succinct, but I usually fail. This review is based on the 1.01 beta firmware, which is the most current firmware I have been able to find as of this writing and after a lot of searching. Never mind whatever I said before (I think I was having a bad day?): the basic playback audio quality of the Rocker is actually pretty faithful, flat, and clean at a basic level over both Bluetooth and the 1/8" output. This statement is based on a bunch of tests I did capturing the output of the Rocker and analyzing that output closely against the source file *and* a reference reproduction device in several purpose-made applications. The Rocker has no obvious scoop, inaccuracy or deficiency in frequency response with the software EQ turned off, and the Bluetooth output level is evenly matched with my reference device. However, here's something that is likely to annoy much of the presumed target audience: Over the 1/8" phone jack, the current firmware is VERY aggressive about switching off the headphone amp as soon as file playback stops. This produces nasty, unmissable high-level DC pops at the start of playback and at the end of playback. In a gapless-full-album situation, you'll hear it at the start and end of the record. But if you're in shuffle mode or playing songs manually, you will be hearing these pops *between every single song*. Be careful about connecting this via analog to external gear / speakers and playing it loud until (let's hope!) the poppin' thing gets resolved. (This is not a problem found on the Bluetooth output, thankfully!) I also doubt the Rocker is going to have the internal oomph to drive higher-end / -impedance phones or to make love-it-louders happy. It pushes my 30-60 ohm headphone collection to volumes that make me happy enough, but I am a moderate-volumes listener. The Rocker's 1/8" jack, at least under current firmware, is only capable of about 2dB more output than the headphone jack on my Samsung Galaxy Note 4 (!) when fully maxed out. It might have more than 1.7x the available power of my Note on tap, but it's not tapping it right now. Battery life is... not even as good as claimed (10 hours continuous phone-jack playback, 7 hours continuous BT playback). 30, 40 minutes of playback from a full charge with the screen off, and the unit is consistently already at 2 of 3 battery bars. This is compounded by a seeming bug / annoyance in the current firmware: Auto shutoff, which for SOME reason is disabled by default, will *always re-disable itself after the unit is turned back on*. If you don't manually power down every time, you'll quickly find that the Rocker drains its battery faster when unused / @ 100% idle with the screen off than the secondhand Android smartphone you had in 2010. (No joke - if you plug it in overnight, disconnect, and then forget to shut the thing off by hand, it'll be completely dead by the next morning.) The current Bluetooth implementation is-- how can I put this nicely?-- not very robust either. In fact, it's flaky to the point where it currently *entirely* negates the major selling point of the unit. Under 1.01B, the Rocker is sensible about auto-connecting with one of my three tested Bluetooth receiving devices, but simply refuses to consistently auto-connect with the two others. And I should add that none of my three test receivers have any problems connecting to any of my other BT playback devices (...otherwise I would have replaced them long ago!). Manually connecting the Rocker to a receiver means a series of multiple button presses to get the Rocker back to the home screen / into the Bluetooth dialog, then a *repeated* series of manual attempts to get it to re-connect with the device from its stored list. You might get it to reconnect on the first try. You might have to sit through two or three failed attempts. Who knows? At one especially tragic point in my weekend testing, the only thing that would get the Rocker to re-connect with a given stored receiver was a full factory reset of the Rocker and a re-pairing with that receiver from scratch. Initial pairing itself often requires at least three, four, maybe five or six tries. That's a lot of fun if you have a receiver that has a conventional 1- or 2-minute timeout for discoverability. Several times in just four days of ownership, I've also had the Rocker drop established Bluetooth connections mid-playback for no obvious reason and within 2 feet line-of-sight. And this one cracks me up: with all the pickiness about connecting, the Rocker also stops playing *over the analog headphone out* if a BT device it just happens to know in the vicinity is switched off or removed from the communication range. But enough about Bluetooth... other than to say it really does sound good on this device, *when* it works. If you want to browse your Rocker by any means other than folder mode (and I do not, but to each their own), be aware you'll be waiting around a lot for database rebuilds. Add *one file* to the Rocker and it rescans THE ENTIRE CARD. That takes one second per 35 songs. On my currently-loaded 22GB, ~2600 song library, that means a nearly 2-minute wait for a full DB rescan every time I drop a new album on. You can cancel this, but then you'll be restricted to only folder-view mode for finding music. Speaking of that, I normally like a device that stops on a folder boundary by default, but it would be nice if there was some way to play through ALL folders automatically other than generating a scorched-earth playlist of everything on the device. On the current firmware, there is not. You can play a whole folder... or you can shuffle within a folder... or you can repeat that folder. If you start in that folder, well, pal, your playback is ending in that folder. (...and Pop! goes the headphone jack.) Playlists also cannot be created on the device. For that matter, premade playlists don't magically appear under "Playlists" in the home screen either, no matter where you place them (the manual says nothing; I tried a /playlist and /playlists folder at the root level, no dice). And then there's the display. Five lines tall, 18 char across, only 16 char available for text display in file selection modes. Try navigating through even, say, just 250 albums five lines at a time, with only an up-down rocker to do so. Then, once you finally get to the "L"s, Heaven help you telling which Led Zeppelin album of their complete discog you're about to select for playback. Before now, I never thought I'd feel like the ~22-character width of my old Clip+'s display had been spoiling me rotten with visible metadata. (In my photos, you'll see this problem as depicted by the three New Brutalism albums with the titles all pushed off to the right - the only way to tell is to select each, one at a time, and then waaaaait for the scroll.) If all this sounds like fun to you, you may be ready for the incredible convenience of the on-release Rocker Bluetooth experience! But otherwise, and/or unless AGPtEK works out some of these bugs and releases a fix... honestly? You'd probably just be better off with a lower-priced DAP and a cable. After all, per the Rockbox developers, a working port is "a looooong way off."

I had high hopes when I bought this router to upgrade from my ISPs provided WiFi. I looked around and read all of the reviews and decided the TP-Link Archer C7 was the one. I chose it because it was dual band supporting both 2.4 Ghz and 5GHz, seemed to have good reviews, and a reasonable price. I was excited when I took it out of the package because it just looks more substantial than the junk my ISP supplies. I set it up adding it to my network and disabled the WiFi on my ISPs equipment. I connected all the various devices in my house to the 5GHz network. A lot of my devices are newer and already supported 5Ghz. I had a few devices still on 2.4 Ghz and I connected them the the 2.4 Ghz network. Everything seemed to be good for a few days. Then the lost connectivity started happening on various devices. Sometimes devices would work fine, then start to lose connectivity. The entire 5Ghz network would seem to drop out of existence and no device could see it. At other times the 2.4 Ghz network would drop out and could not be seen. Each time the only cure was a reboot of the TP-Link to restore connectivity. I am an IT guy with 20 years experience in the business. I am the guy everyone calls to troubleshoot and fix their tech. I have done everything short of sending the device back for a refund to try and make this router more stable. When it works, it is super fast and life is good. Then seemingly at random, things go south and a reboot is the only cure. I know that this is a piece of consumer grade equipment and I shouldn't expect it to perform like a business grade piece of equipment that costs 20x more money. However this thing frustrates the crap out of me anyway. I am very close to writing a script to reboot the router nightly when no one uses it. In that respect it works exceptionally well. In terms of absolute sharpness, it's probably not significantly sharper than the standard 18-55 kit zooms Canon ships with the Rebel models. In terms of the build quality and the look of photographs, it is light years ahead of the kit zooms. Color and tonality are both superb and I find I need to do little in the way of tweaking the Raw files when converting them. The edges and corners of the photographs do give up a little sharpness compared to the center image but the loss in these areas is not as important to me as the gains in the overall image quality. Objectively, it's easy to come up with optical limitations in all lenses. But the important thing to me is the way the picture looks and the 17-40 produces a damn fine looking picture.

I purchased three similar products from Amazon simultaneously and received them today: [[ASIN:B00009KH63 Kensington Expert Mouse Optical USB Trackball for PC or Mac 64325]] [[ASIN:B001F42MKG Logitech Trackman Marble Mouse]] [[ASIN:B002OOWB3O Kensington K72337US Orbit Trackball with Scroll Ring for PC or Mac]] This is for a Mac. My large hands and my wife's small hands explored using all three devices. Our feedback on these products is in relationship to the other ones. -The Kensington "Expert" Mouse was too big and clumsy. I've owned this router for a little over one year, 16 months as of this review to be exact. It has proven to be the most reliable router I've own since my Linksys WRT54G of 16years ago. Since then I've own Netgear, Buffalo, and TP-Link. This router just works and the throughputs I get are nothing short of amazing. It has tons of advanced features including both client and server VPNs, intrusion detection, very customizable firewall, basic NAS software, media server, download station, cloud station and including some other features that I don't use such as RADIUS and DNS Servers. Best of all, its' administration portal is like none other found on other routers, no matter what the router brand. It has a very attractive graphical Windows-like UI but Linux based operating system. Setting up the router is super easy because how user-friendly the DSM operating system works. Other router makers should really strive to emulate the UI of Synology admin portals. They are light years ahead of the game. The router will also produce monthly professionally looking report about the operation of the router, and detail data usage of every device on the LAN, and the type of data that streams through the router to your email or smartphone. It can also provide real-time intrusion alerts to your cell phone. Wow. very impressive for a consumer router. While other routers are lucky to get two or three firmware upgrades in the product's lifespan. Synology pushes out new updates on a monthly interval. 16 months later I still get regular updates! When the life cycle of this router comes to an end, I will look to Synology again for an upgrade. I am very impressed with the rt2600AC. Wifi signal strength is strong and consistent, the VPN client has a kill switch that stops a data connection if the VPN gets dropped which helps protect your data. The intrusion protection gives me a status on internet bots and port scans. It will automatically take action on its own to prevent intrusion and I can tell it to block an IP address after several unauthorized attempts. I can block IP address blocks by IP number, by group of IP numbers, by geography. It's one hell of a router. I'm quite happy with it and I hope Synology continues to add to their router product line. I'm actually considering buying a NAS to hold movies and based on my experience with Synology's router, I will get a Synology brand NAS since they both share a very similar operating system and UI. Its a phenomenal router with many enterprise-level features inside a consumer router box. UPDATE: NOVEMBER 9th 2018 Since the last firmware update, my Synology RT2600AC now supports the latest Wifi encryption WPA3 and a wider 5GHz Channel width of 160Mhz. AMPDU, extended NSS and 802.11r has been added at no additional cost. This router gets better with each update. The Intrusion Detection is now out of Beta and supports many new advanced features with intrusion definitions downloaded weekly via updates just like an Antivirus. I am very happy with this router.

I bought the 2-pack of white 1.3" OLED displays. Based on the reviews, it looked like everyone had success with the Adafruit_SSD1306 library. However, none of them seemed to work at all with this particular driver chip. Upon digging a little deeper, I found that the 1.3" displays I got actually have the SH1106 driver IC on-board, not the SD1106. Whether or not this was caused by the supplier simply mixing and matching sets based on what was lying around at the time I ordered these, I'm not sure. The U8g2 library, which is very fast and lightweight compared, worked perfectly the first time with it. The specific instantiation you want to use for this particular display is: U8G2_SH1106_128X64_NONAME_F_HW_I2C u8g2(U8G2_R0, /* reset=*/ U8X8_PIN_NONE); Use that, and you're up and running in no time flat, without any problems. Just call u8g2.begin() in your initialization and everything else is easy.

I really don't like sound signatures like Bose's or Sony's ones, Bose's sound is not natural and Sony's is too bass-heavy. These 85h are a bit treble emphasized and the base may not be powerful for most of the people. It might make your ear fatigue after a long time listening because it's not something like Sennheiser's warm sound signature. But I'll take it, I like the sound. [Build quality and design] The build quality is first-class. The material they used is very good. And the design looks cool and handsome. It's around 300 grams, so heavier than most of BT headphones. Overall, it's a good looking, quality headphones. --- Cons --- [ANC] I really don't think their ANC is working well. It only decreases a small amount of low frequency, and that's it. The ANC performance is much worse than Sony or Bose. It's even worse than a $60 ANC headphones I bought on Amazon. Just disappointed. [Volumn] The volume is not enough. Trust me I'm not someone loves to play the music to shake the car door. I need to set the volume to 70 - 85 % for the music, and 90% for movies. Yes, 85% is enough for me and I won't go higher for the most of the time, but it makes you feel less confident about the volume and the battery may drain faster than other headphones. [App] The App is really buggy. That's it. --- (Personal) Deal breaker --- [Comfort] I'm 5'9" 155 lbs. I don't think I have a big head. But the headband is not long enough for me, even I extended it all. If I try to place my ear at the center of the earcup, I need to push the headphone downward hard which makes a lot of pressure on the top of my head. After 20 mins wearing, the top of my headphone is in pain. BTW, The earcups are comfortable, not as well as Bose's but they are fine. [No power off button] These headphones use a mechanism that enables to auto turn on and off when you rotate the hinge. So if the right earcup is facing forward, it will be turned off. And if the earcups are facing to each other which is like when you are wearing them, they will be turned on. This is smart. However, for me, I don't want to leave these in the case when not using them. I have a headphone hanger and I used to hang my headphones to make them handy. When I hang these, earcups need to face to each other. For these headphones, I can't turn it off in that way bc there's no power button and it will be always on like that. Why can't there be a power button... --- verdict --- I can't keep these because of the above two deal-breakers. Those are very personal though. I can endure those three Cons because I love the sound and the design of these. What a pity, I think I have to keep looking for my next BT headphones.

I was originally happy with the camera in general. The picture quality is actually pretty good. I was able to connect it to my wifi after figuring out the somewhat convoluted system. Once I knew how, it wasn't too hard. Here is the bad though: The camera seems to only work if you use their web service. You need an account to access the camera, and the camera REQUIRES internet access to them. I did not WANT a camera that used a 3rd party service, I wanted an ONVIF compatible cam that worked only using my internal storage server. But, I can say that the internet accessibility does work real well with my iphone. I do not like using 3rd party servers from a security and privacy perspective, so this will have to sit outside my main home network now. These days I trust nobody. Next: The wifi config doesn't allow you to connect to NON broadcast SSID at all. Not even once you have it configured can you turn off broadcast. And, when I reboot my AP, the camera loses connection and I have to do the setup process again. Because of all this, the security is lessened a little and it forced me to not be able to put it on a separate network as well. So if you want home network security and don't trust companies to do that for you, find a different product. The product function itself is great...too bad this minor issue turns so major for me. Now for the deal breaker. Originally I gave this a 4 star, but after fighting this multiple times, I think I will return my 3 cameras. EVERY time you have a power outage for more than a minute or so, the camera loses its wifi configuration for your SSID. This means that every time you have a power outage, or move the cameras from room to room, you will have to go thru the whole wifi setup process again and add the device back to your device list. If someone wants to break in to your place, they just have to wait until there has been a storm, and you won't get any alerts or video anymore. If there were a fix for this, I'd consider keeping them, but 3 strikes and it's out.

We use this as a baby monitor (video and audio) and for that it generally works very well. I liked the prospect of the zoom feature, but to be honest I keep it zoomed all the way in 99% of the time. It required a little tweaking, but overall I'm happy with it. PROs: - The resolution is way better than my last cam. - H.264 encoding means the impact on my WiFi network is minimized - It supports HTTPS connections, so you're not sending your password over the network in clear text. - The pan/tilt is quiet and smooth, a huge improvement over my previous foscam camera. - It's compatible with lots of good software like Blue Iris on the PC and TinyCam on Android. CONs: - The white model gets significant IR glare off of the white housing when pointed downward at night. This was a huge problem, as we kept the camera on a high shelf to look into the crib. Once you get close to the bottom of the viewing range, the picture loses all contrast. You can tip the camera forward but a better, more stable solution is to cover up some of the white housing. I taped some black tape that doesn't glow in the infrared over the bottom parts of the housing in front of the lens and that fixed the problem. But I shouldn't have had to do that. - The picture could be a bit clearer for an HD camera. I'm wondering if the zoom lens was set just a tiny bit out of focus. It's not terrible, but I feel like it could be just a little better if I could just focus it a bit. - There is a network LED that blinks on the back... constantly. I put some electrical tape over it because there's no way to disable it with the software interface. - Pan/tilt control over HTTPS can be a bit laggy depending on the software you use. - Foscam's free PC software leaves a lot to be desired. Configuration is tricky and there is no indicator for if you've got the audio on or off. Fortunately you don't need to use their software as the cam is compatible with other software. I'd buy another Foscam camera but this particular model could use some revisions.

I bought this back in late May of this year. Right from the start, the battery would never charge to 100%. I could leave it on the charger all day and it would only go to 99%. On top of that, I was recharging it every 5-6 days. Then as recently as yesterday (June 20th) in a matter of hours, with the kindle merely sitting on my nightstand, the battery percentage went from 99% to 70%. That’s maybe within 5 hours and probably 2 hours of that was reading time with brightness adjusted to a lower setting. Called Amazon and they quickly sent me a replacement. I received it today (June 21st). I put it onto charger and removed it at 9:20pm when it was 100% charged. I’ve read for maybe 15 minutes. It’s now 10:03pm and the battery percentage is down to 94%. I shut down the unit and restarted it and I’ll put it back to charge shortly but I suspect I’ll have the same results and this Oasis doesn’t hold a charge for 2-3 weeks as I was told by the Amazon rep. It could be because it’s refurbished and not new…who knows? I’ll update after I’ve tried fully charging the battery a few times. Beyond the battery problem, I do love this Oasis better than my Paperwhite. I love that I can set it so books in a series are all grouped together and I love that I can listen to my audible books as well if I choose to. The storage capacity and design are what drew me in, and the claims of a longer battery life. We’ll see how that last one goes. Overall, it’s a great ereader, if you don’t mind having to charge the battery once every 5 or 6 days. ******UPDATE AS OF JUNE 29, 2021******* I put the replacement kindle on to charge Sunday night and removed it Monday morning. It was 100% charge, but today as of 5:30p.m. (Tuesday) the battery is at 83%. That’s with maybe a total of 8 hours reading time since removing it from the charger. Bottom line: BATTERY LIFE SUCKS on the kindle oasis. It certainly doesn’t last 2 weeks as indicated in the description and as was told to me by an Amazon Customer Service rep. *~*~UPDATE 7/21/21*~*~ I am now on my 2nd replacement. The last replacement mentioned above still had the same issues. Third time’s a charm? Let’s hope so or I’m done with the oasis. *~*~UPDATE 7/29/21*~*~ Received the 2nd replacement on 7/21. Opened it and battery was at 12%. Charged it while setting it up and downloading a few books. Charged quickly to 100%. Logged all read times and battery percentages. In 9 days, and 16.5 hours of read time, plus no more than 10 book downloads, the battery was at 30%. Well 9 days isn’t quite the 2 weeks Amazon promises but it’s better than the 5-6 days with the previous 2 devices. I put the device back on the charger at 30% and it took only an hour to charge fully to 100%. I will note that this time around, I kept it away from other electronics as much as possible and it did seem to help extend the battery life. Better, not great, but I think I’ll keep this one. And bump my rating to 3 stars. Actually 3 1/2 but since we can’t do half stars…

UPGRADING THE RATING OF THIS PRODUCT To 4 Stars (August 12, 2014) Ok, quick update; the image quality and camera field of view of this system is very good, overall system performance is very good also. Per Zmodo product manual recommendation I installed a high performance 2TB Seagate ST2000VX000 harddrive with this system. At highest image quality settings and 25 frame/second each camera uses about 25 Gigabytes per day disk space. So, that's about 100 Gigabytes/day for 4 cameras or about 18 days of constant recording using BEST CBR quality at 25 frames/second. If image quality is reduced from BEST to Very Good, and change CBR to VBR, and reduce frame rate from 25 to 15, the recording time can be increased about 50% while sacrificing very little on image quality. As far as I know, among all ZMODO products 720p cameras offer the best image quality, even better images than the 960h analog cameras. All things being equal a digital camera seems to have better color detail than an analog camera such as 960h. Unfortunately, if you reboot the cameras in the dark, they will not focus properly and images look blurry until sunrise or a bright flash of light (such as car headlights) shines on the camera and allows the camera to refocus. So I avoid restarting the system at night and fortunately after a few days of tweaking/configuring the system once you adjust the configuration settings to your liking, you won't have to reboot frequently. I hope this problem will be addressed in the future firmware updates... The other downside with this system is that there are 3 different user interfaces that you need to use in order to access all the functions/configuration settings of the system (direct Console offers some functions, but not all, ZVIEWER software has some functions but not others, and finally using Internet Explorer ACTIVE X plugin gives you some other functions (firmware upgrade and browsing video files is easier using AcvtiveX mode). But unfortunately there's not a single user interface that provides all the functions and configuration settings in one place, so you have to switch back and forth using 3 different user interfaces to adjust all system configuration settings and functions. Hopefully in the coming weeks/months ZVIEWER software interface will be upgraded/refined so all system settings can be configured with it. Browsing and downloading previously recorded files through internet explorer interface is much easier than ZVIEWER software. You can see details such as file size, duration information using internet explorer. But, you must use ZVIEWER software to change default recording length or image quality or change frame rate of each channel. ================================================== Original Review Below: Do not reboot or power cycle the cameras at night or when it's dark or the image will become blurry/out of focus. I just got this system couple days ago with 2TB Seagate hard disk, and just like another reviewer I found that my cameras become blurry if I reboot them at night! If a bright flash of light shines on the camera (like car headlights) the image restores to normal (or you have to wait till morning for the sun rise). Rebooting the camera or resetting image settings does not help at all once camera becomes blurry. ZMODO please test this problem in your lab/factory and hopefully issue a software fix. I believe during the reboot that takes about 30 seconds, the camera is initializing image settings (white balance, focus, etc...) and during this time the IR lights may not be turned on or it maybe too dim for camera to properly initialize the camera. Whatever the problem, this is very disappointing. Otherwise (as long as you don't reboot the cameras in dark) the images during the day and night are very detailed and clear. The wide viewing angle (2.8mm lens) allows me to see the entire street 180 degrees with just 2 cameras. There's some learning curve with the software, the IP cameras individually have too many configuration settings that are redundant (NTP, etc) Zviewer software can not remotely make all configuration as from the console and the console does not have some of the features as the ZVIEWER software, so you end up going back and forth using both of them. I'm thinking about returning this system and getting the analog 960h version.

Despite a few bad reviews, I decided to take a chance and purchase this product to use in my Canon Rebel camera. I wanted to be able to use the same SD/SDHC cards that my wife uses in her compact canon so that we could exchange cards should we ever need to (sometimes one or the other of us forgets to bring an extra). Also, It's a lot easier to store SD-size cards than the much larger CFs. The adapter has worked perfectly with the three different (types and memory size) SD and SDHC cards I have tried. I had to format the cards in camera first in all cases but after that there were no problems. I think, like others have suggested, that the adapter might have caused the camera to operate slower but I have not had a chance to compare similar cards so there is no way to be certain. Also, I was using a flash when I did my only serious picture taking so far and the flash recharge determined the camera speed, not the memory card. Otherwise, just shooting test shots around the house without the flash, the adapter seems to perform very well. A nice side benefit is that the card reader I have in my computer is older and can't read SDHC cards but it can when they are in the adapter in the CF slot. If I planned on taking series of rapid shots I think I would get the fastest CF card I could and bypass the adapter, but for normal picture taking the adapter works perfectly. For me, I’m above intermediate at both. The initial set up is fairly straightforward but it reminded me of messing around with The Windows 95 comand prompts and the English translation on some parts had me laughing. I still don’t have all the cams set up after the first three days, and the four I do have I’m still fine tuning and then need to officially route cables. This is where you will struggle if you don’t know about wire management. First off I recommend that you take your time and set one camera up at a time, and perhaps not even screw it into the location, use tape or something and see how it looks and check all the angles. If you don’t like it you can move it. That’s why I’m only on 4. Then you will have to figure out how to get the wires there and how to hide them properly. For me so far, this has involved running the wires straight up to my ceiling and then through it untill it come to the exterior wall where I then drilled a 1/2 inch hole to run the wiring for a couple of cams out of. I’m going to probably use pvc to run the cable into, but that will be after I get the final locations figured out. It’s a process to get this system set up for your individual needs, but worth it and you get a lot for the price. My complaints are that I was supposed to get a sticker set that says you have cams, that’s not the biggest deal in the world because I have similar things, but I was supposed to get some. The big one though is that I’m still having problems setting up the app on my phone to view the cams from there. It keeps telling me that my email is not valid although it is, and yes I double triple and quadruple checked my spelling. So that’s annoying, but great but either way. Lastly I will say if you read this and you are confused by the set up process I described, then consider finding someone to help you before you buy, or spend a little more for a wireless system or drop cams. Like I said there was a reason I wanted wires.

I was going to replace my 18-55mm IS lens and my 75-300mm lens with this one lens. After using it for about a month, I find that it is excellent for outdoor use, but only OK indoors. I used the lens to take pictures of fireworks on the 4th of July, and the results were amazing. I was able to get some wide shots of the entire display, and then zoom in and take some incredible closeups. I then took it to the Chicago Botanical Garden, and tried all sorts of shots from wide angle shots of entire displays, zoom shots of far away displays, and even some cool macro shots of flowers. I even got a good one of a bee landing on a flower. It was nice to have so much versatility in a single lens. Indoors, however, the results were different. Because of the high amount of range this lens has, it slows down very fast. Therefore, indoor shots will not let in as much light as outdoor shots. I had to either slow down the shutter speed, or use the flash to get the same shots as the lenses I was going to replace. I made the judgement call that I would keep my original lenses, and keep this lens. When you're outdoors, you don't want to be changing your lenses frequently. There can be a lot of dust and other material that can land on the glass, or worse the sensor when doing so. This is a great outdoor walk around lens that you can use all day without having to swap lenses. However, once you get inside, you will either need to use a flash, or swap out to a faster lens.

After setting up two MagicJacks for my parents, I broke down and bought one for our house. They have one for the home business (the old model that requires to be plugged into a turned-on computer to work), and a home phone line (this one, which plugs straight into the router and does not require a computer to function). They work great for them, so my wife and I bought one. It's pretty easy to set up. It requires a computer to do so, but that's the only time you'll need a computer with this version of MagicJack. It guides you through the setup process, prompting you to pick your phone number and optional renewal options (on top of the free year that is included). Beware, the pricing is sketchy. The price is $19.95 per year if you buy in five year increments. Buy in 1 year increments, and it's $29.95 per year. That's still a steal. Also, it tries to upsell you on a lot of things. Want a vanity number? That's an extra charge. Want to port your old phone number over? That's an extra charge. For us, we skipped all the extras and picked a free phone number. After the PC setup is complete, it plugs straight into your router, which is nice, because it ensures a steady, reliable, always-on connection. Then, plug your phone line into the back of the MagicJack and you're good to go. It's easiest if you avoid the house wiring and go with one of the wireless bases with the satellite phones. That way, the base plugs into the MagicJack, and you can put the satellite phones wherever you want. How does it work? Exactly like you'd expect it to. It just works. Caller ID works. 411 works. Call waiting works. It has voicemail options as well, which we skipped, because we'd rather use our physical answering machine than have our messages stored online somewhere. With the Verizon FiOS 50/35 internet package, I don't notice any delay at all. It's not quite as clear as a regular land line would be, but it's clearer and more reliable than a cell phone, for sure. There's a little bit of static, but my MagicJack is buried in a pile of wires behind my entertainment center, and I suspect that there's some interference from that. It's so minor that I don't care enough to try moving it around. I really don't understand the negative reviews. Anybody could set this thing up. It's pretty self-explanatory. My boss bought one and returned it because he couldn't port over his existing number. They fixed that. The call quality is fine. I've never had issues with delays or dropped calls. Customer service may or may not be sketchy, I've never had to use it. And seriously, how picky can you be at this price? At $19.95 per year, it's cheaper to pay for a year of MagicJack than one month of Vonage. And Vonage, like MagicJack, is also VOIP (Voice Over IP). Any connection issues you run into with MagicJack, you'll likely run into with Vonage. I just don't know how people can complain. It works, it's easy, and it's CHEAP. That's a perfect mix for me.

UPDATE APRIL 13, 2019 - Please read my update if you are looking for a simple point and shoot camera. DO NOT purchase this one anymore as it is very outdated and the price is outrageous. I've provided a comparable camera for 2019 in my update attached to this one. ----- I originally had my doubts about this particular model, mainly due to the price. I can firmly say that upon receiving it, the camera is comparable to other entry-level cameras at a fraction of the price. Overall, here are the pros/cons: +++ PROS +++ 1) LOW COST You will NOT find another digital camera that is even halfway decent for $50. 2) SIMPLE CONTROLS The camera seems to cater to people who want minimal controls. Instead of having tons of different "modes" the camera reminds me more of a "point-and-shoot" from back in the day. 3) EASY TO LEARN Due to the lack of options available, this camera is very easy to learn quickly. 4) DECENT RESOLUTION For the money, the camera takes very good shots at a higher resolution than older models you can obtain for the same price. The auto-balancing works well and white balance/exposure are set for you. --------------------- --- CONS --- 1) LACKS ADVANCED FUNCTIONALITY If you're looking for a camera with different shooting modes (sports, night time, etc), this camera is not for you. It has very few options, and even fewer buttons. Think of it as a "no frills" quick point-and-shoot camera. 2) SMALL BATTERY The battery is quite small, and using the mechanical zoom often will drain it somewhat quickly. 3) BATTERY MUST BE CHARGED INTERNALLY My biggest complaint was that the battery needed to be charged inside the camera as opposed to more expensive models that come with a separate charger. I'm afraid that using the USB port so much (for power and exporting photos) will eventually cause it to break over time. -------------- Overall, this camera is so low in cost that you could purchase multiple quantities and have them around for moments when you need them (accidents, UFO sightings, bigfoot, etc). If you're looking for a simple digital camera, or would like to get one for your kid with minimal investment, Look no further.

Overall I like the computer and am happy with my purchase ($899, no sales tax for the base i5 8GB model with 128GB storage) Things I like: Keyboard feel is very nice Small power brick is appreciated Screen is bright and high quality Plenty of power (for my needs, more on that later) Tablet mode is nice to have, but I dont know if I will be using that much personally Fanless cooling is the way forward USB c all the things (but there are some limitations) Things I dont like: The power supply is on the plug instead of the middle of the cord which can block other outlets Some of the new shortcuts are really strange for me having some from windows and cant be changed The backlighting on the keyboard is not very even, this is most obvious on the dimmest backlight setting but fixes itself if increased Not being able to expand the icons on the task bar like windows (this is a big deal for me) Quirks: To get 4k 60Hz you have to use a dedicated dongle due to the bandwidth requirements The keyboard has lower case letters which seems more childish or less mature in a way (personal opinion) I would rather have a delete key instead of a settings hot button over backspace The minimum volume though the speakers I think is to loud (have to turn down the volume slider on youtube to compensate) Finding quality chargers is a pain, might just have to fork over the $50 or $60 to google to get a "real one" The smart unlock with a pixel phone I dont find useful at all (I have a Pixel 2) I wish there was a show screen button in the lower right corner of the screen I wish there was a hotkey to full screen an application Things I am looking forward to: The main reason I got this computer was to use as a laptop as opposed to a heating blanket. This FM transmitter/charger (hereto referred to as "the unit") is excellent. Prior to using this, I was using the [[ASIN:B00067LYFW iRiver AFT 100 Mobile FM Transmitter]] which is going for about $40 right now. This less expensive unit puts out a clearer signal than the iRiver transmitter did (when using the 87.9 FM frequency, at least), *and* it charges my iPhone at the same time. Some reviewers on Amazon have stated that they've had issues with audio from the iPhone not carrying through. I am glad to report that I have had no such issue with my 16GB iPhone. I only hook up one cable - the standard iPhone connection port - and that takes care of charging my phone as well as transmitting my audio. Every time I connect the unit to my iPhone, I get a message asking if I'd like to put the iPhone into Airplane mode; so that I don't lose the phone functionality, I hit "No" and it works fine from there with only the occasional cell phone/speaker noise. I really like the adjustable nature of the holster. If a friend wanted to use their music player, the holster will easily conform horizontally to fit; and, with the included male-to-male headphone adapter, it should work with anything that has a 3.5" jack. Another advantage of the built-in holster is that it's great being able to clearly see my iPhone at all times while it charges in the holster. That way, I can use the Maps application without either holding my iPhone or keeping it in the seat next to me. My only reservation in giving this unit 5 stars is that the cigarette lighter adapter's neck sticks out several inches, and it's only adjustable at one point - right behind the holster. In the next version of the unit, they should also make the neck adjustable and twistable right at the point where the unit sticks out of the lighter adapter - that way, it could be angled upward more and be less out of the way for certain vehicular configurations (read the next paragraph for more about that). Lastly, I'd like to mention my vehicle's configuration with this unit. I own a Pontiac Vibe and the automatic gear shifter (which is in the center console, rather than attached to the steering wheel) rubs against the unit when the vehicle is in Park. If your cars gear shifter is close to your lighter adapter then make sure you have enough room before you purchase this. I doubt that this unit would work very well in a Vibe with a manual transmission - it would probably get in the way quite often. Overall, this unit is a great buy - highly recommended. I bought mine from Wild About Digital here on Amazon and got a great price (and shipping was very fast as well).

I really wanted to like this speaker. But I don't. Here's why. Upon first impressions, I was quite happy. It comes with an adapter for the guitar amp port, it comes with an aux cord, a charger, and everything is pretty much perfect. The build quality is fantastic and it's heavy and feels super solid. I assume most of the weight is battery, considering the sound quality, but I'll touch on that later. It packs quite a few great features, namely the obvious Bluetooth, AUX, and doubling as a power bank. But it also boasts an FM tuner which is quite nice, a USB play mode, and a guitar/mic mode which will play over music. This is a fantastic set of features that I really like. Unfortunately, the sound itself sounds terrible considering the size, weight, and wattage of this speaker. I have a smaller, lighter 30w speaker which sounds miles better than this one. It simply has no energy. Although the back looks like a grille, it's actually solid, and the only speakers are two ~3" drivers on the front. These two "full-range" drivers are also augmented with a pipe for each one. However the bass response simply isn't there. There is SOME bass, for sure, but those drivers just don't put out anything below like, 125Hz. I literally pulled those bars down to -10 on my equalizer and nothing sounded any different. Don't get me wrong, it gets loud, but there is simply no energy, not even at low volume, because of this lack of low bass. Kicks don't come through (not even on old acoustic rock and country) and any low-ish bass is completely lost. If you are someone who plans to use this as a mic amp or even a small amp for a guitar or violin, this may work perfectly fine. But as a speaker, it sounds terrible. At this price point, a Sony SRS X55 or Turcom Acoustoshock will do you much, much better, though with slightly less features. The energy and sound quality is just not there. Don't buy this thing. Save your money and buy a JBL Xtreme or Boombox or something. Monster simply didn't put any effort into actually engineering this, it seems like they just slapped some shit together and hoped for the best. Sometimes that works - not this time.

Do yourself a favor and go to Fotodiox - fotodiox.freshdesk.com/support/solutions/articles/17000002162-pro-softbox-assembly-use - or to their YouTube channel and watch the softbox assembly video instead of following the manual. It saves time and frustration and you’ll put this thing together with minimal effort. I didn’t do that and wound up wrestling the softbox! Assembly challenges aside, this softbox is a great value for the money. The material is sturdy and the unit is well-constructed. The silver interior reflects light well and the baffle diffuses it nicely. There are vents on the sides to dissipate heat and the included mounting ring is strong, well-made and fits my Elinchrom strobes perfectly. The ring also allows the softbox to rotate, a feature that comes in very handy. One issue is excess fabric extending past the mounting ring which interferes with the softbox coupling to the strobe - just open the hook and loop slits, attach the softbox to the light and then close the slits again. Also, the outer diffuser cover doesn’t quite meet the corners leaving small gaps through which light may leak. Gaffers tape will help, if necessary. Neither of these issues is a deal-breaker for me. Overall, this is an excellent value for the money, especially for a hobbyist, and an Elinchrom-branded 24” by 36” softbox would have cost three or four times what I paid for the Fotodiox. Satisfied customer!

I really wanted this keyboard to work the way it was advertised to do. But one crucial aspect of this keyboard wasn't up to par. Physically and mechanically speaking, it is a winner. It is light, has all the necessary keys and best of all, the right firmness and responsive tactile sensation that floating keys provide. The sound of rhythmic clicks are produced when typing away and I really enjoyed using it. The price is great as well, and would have been of greater value had one aspect been existent. It isn't waterproof. The title of this product listing is "waterproof and washable". Unfortunately, one wash with cold water under a running faucet resulted in 2 keys not working, basically rendering it useless. I had allowed it to dry and even removed the "T" and "I" key covers for quicker drying but alas, they were dead. I've had a number of waterproof keyboards and one common feature that is missing on the keyboard are drainage holes on the bottom side of the keyboard. They are included in other brands to allow water that has seeped into the keys to drain out so that the board isn't damaged. I found that for the money, the IRocks line of waterproof keyboards stand up to washings. They run for about $20-24. The best yet priciest is one made by Logitech at $70. It lasted through many many washings, had floating keys, the right firmness, ideal key sizes and spacing. So if anyone is looking for a waterproof keyboard, this one may not stand up to even 1 washing.

I've been using Microsoft's 4000 Ergonomic keyboard for years, so I had high expectations for this keyboard, which is probably the best successor to the 4000. The wireless part is more of a drawback than a plus for me, since I don't mind wires but prefer to avoid the hassle of batteries. Apart from that, pretty much everything is perfect with this keyboard. The 4000's layout is maintained (two separated halves), but the problem of keys being a bit too high/deep is solved, thus combining the joys of an ergonomic keyboard with the usual feel of laptop keyboards. Everything is well thought out: the piece of plastic to elevate the bottom of the keyboard is magnetized, so is the lid of the battery compartment, which also has a small slot to keep the bluetooth receiver. The separate number keypad is also great, allowing people who don't use it much to leave it out (smaller keyboard then) while pretty much not impacting people who do use it (can be placed similarly). The layout can take a little while to get used to (arrow keys, page down and up, delete, home, end) but works really well once you get used to it. My go-to keyboard from now on! Update: After using this keyboard for a few months, two small problems I'm seeing. 1) The toggle between "Fn" keys and media-type keys is more annoying than useful. I find that I often have to toggle so that I can access, say, F11 as part of a keyboard shortcut, then toggle back to be able to access play/pause functions for my media player. 2) While I usually take out the two AAA batteries for the main keyboard when I'm travelling with it, the numeric keypad's battery is much less convenient to remove (needs a screwdriver), so I just leave it in, but have found at least twice that the battery had been depleted, probably because the keys were being continuously pressed while in my luggage. Not an issue if you're not travelling with this keyboard, but some sort of smart logic that would prevent the numpad from being powered on when the main keyboard is still off would have been nice. Overall, I stand by my comment of "combined benefits of an ergonomic keyboard, and a laptop-type keyboard". Still very much my keyboard of choice.

This review is for the UN55J6300. I bought this after having to send back the 2015 Vizio M55 C2 due to horrible upscaling of lower resolution content as well as the 2015 UNJU6500 for severe inconsistent judder. Compared to those 2 TV's in the same price range, this TV hit the sweet spot. The TV was well packaged, shipped fast, and connected easily. Set up was a breeze. Although there was some worrisome TV and remote lag for the first day or two, (15-20 seconds at start up), this has since been very responsive. As for Apps, they have been as smooth as the JU6500, loading and playing just as quickly as on either the Vizio M or Samsung JU6500. Out of the box, the picture was bright and colors looked good. After the suggested settings from Rtings, (Thanks Rtings!) the 6300 is brighter than either of the others and colors are stunningly accurate in comparison to the 6500. Both the Vizio and the 6500 came out of the box dull and washed out taking alot of adjustments. The 6300 has really good blacks, very similar to the 6500 but not to the levels of the M. Colors are very accurate especially skin tones. The 6500 was a bit oversaturated taking fine details out of colors and had a mild but consistent red tint on skin tones that I could not clear up. Both are fantastic on the 6300. The 6300 also has the same fantastic upscaling as the 6500. Upscaling was the deal breaker on the M as lower content especially SD, was virtually unwatchable: huge pixel issues and noise shadows with one good example being Lester Holt turning his head but his forehead would be pixelized and lag behind. The only downside I have found is some greying or cloudiness in the top corners. On a full white screen or in a shot of a bright clear blue sky, the TV can show some smugginess especially in the top corners. This is almost entirely on commercials where these conditions are present. Neither the M or the 6500 showed this at all. But for the vast majority of content even when specifically looking for it, you cannot see it. The other issue is that it isn't 4K, and I fell for this hype as well. The M in 4k is just the most stunning picture I have seen. But most people don't watch just 4k and Bluray in a dark room where the online review sites appear to be done. The M in SD or 720p was nothing short of unwatchable. And 4k "downscaled" on the 6300 would be hard to see any difference from the 6500 outside of a 2-3 foot viewing distance. This is a fantastic TV with as good or better color, better bright room display, and as good or better overall picture than either of the other 2 TV's. I would have put 5 stars without the clouding in the corners.

Overall I am very happy with the DV7-4070us laptop. I purchased a Dell for my wife last year, a Toshiba for myself just a couple weeks ago, and now this HP for my mom, so I think I have a fairly good point of reference. I chose the HP based on a Consumer Reports review and its specs, as well as some faith in the HP name. Pros - With the i5 450 processor, performance on Win 7 64 bit with MS Office Pro 2010 (added after purchase) is very good. Resumption from standby is nearly instant, and all programs are very responsive. Sound quality for a laptop is very good also, much better than my Toshiba (tho the HP is a bigger unit which helps). I also like that the HP has single finger buttons for volume and other commonly used features - they are clearly labeled and you do not need to hold a function key (but you do trade off needing to hold a function key to get F1, F2, etc.). Battery life has also been very good, and the display is the best of the laptops I have. I would also say the overall feel of the unit, with its metallic feeling shell is excellent - no plastic creaks when you pick it up and the hinge seems substantial. Keyboard also is very good, a nice layout without annoying function key presses for home, end, pg up, etc. lie on our year old Dell. Keyboard feel is ok, good throw but I would like a little more positive tactile feedback. Installed software on the HP (webcam and other features) is very good, and the way it walks you through setup is very used friendly. Cons - The touchpad is less responsive than my Toshiba. Single finger pointing is fine but gestures like two finger scrolling took some getting used to before they worked reliably for me. I'm also not a fan of the buttons being part of the pad - they are stiff, and clicking sometimes moves the pointer unintentionally. Click and drag takes some practice. The Toshiba with a smaller pad but dedicated buttons and a lighter touch is much better to use. Another oddity is that the power and disk access lights are on the right edge of the unit, and you can not see them in normal operation. Perhaps it is because I'm a tech geek, but I really like to see the disk light to understand what is going on when a PC gets busy. Last oddity to note - after loading MS Office 2010 Access did not work - it would most always hang when opening a table for view. Turns out this is caused by the DigitalPersona software loaded for the fingerprint reader. After stopping and disabling the "Biometric fingerprint.." service Access is fine. This quirk is apparently shared with other HP and Dell laptops that have fingerprint readers, and impacts Access 2007 as well. See the thread at [...] . When I receive word from HP on a permanent fix I will update this review. Overall I think this is a great unit. Everything has worked smoothly, wireless has been reliable, and performance is great. Be wary tho of any laptop with a fingerprint reader if you really intend to use it along with MS Office pro and MS Access.

I purchased this computer after seeing great reviews on the CNET and PC Magazine websites. I would agree with both reviews that you get a lot for your money with this package: Windows 7 64-bit 4 GB RAM the energy miser i3-350m processor Great display Sturdy aluminum accents DVD optical drive - for those of us still clinging to an increasingly obsolete format 320 GB hard drive 802.11n wireless capability All of this adds up to a quick, highly capable machine that should satisfy all but hardcore gamers and high-throughput multimedia types. Other features deserving mention: - The chiclet keyboard is a real treat to type on, with a great tactile response. Despite the smaller computer (I used a 15.4 inch HP before), I don't find my hands significantly cramped. - The multitouch pad has won me over. I find it difficult to use my older computer's touchpad because I have already gotten used to these time-saving fingerstrokes. - DVD drive is much quieter than others I have used before. - Battery life, battery life, battery life. Having used a Core Duo HP before (getting a meager sub 2 hours of battery life), I was relieved to see that I might actually be able to watch two movies on a single charge or perform basic work duties for somewhere between 6 to 8 hours. - Weight - at between 4 and 5 pounds, it's no featherweight, but certainly is easily totable without causing scoliosis. - Ships in an appropriately sized cardboard container - Only a little bloatware as opposed to what I've had to tediously delete of my HPs in the past Negatives worth mention: - Despite the nice touches offered by the aluminum, let's face it - Apple still does a better job with overall appearance; that being said, this is one of the more visually pleasant PCs I've used - Integrated speakers are acceptable in terms of range and volume (given what they are), but being located under the front of the computer, it's easy for your wrists to muffle the sound while you work - The thumb button on the touch pad requires far more pressure to activate the "left click" than the "right click". As a result, I've left the touch-click feature active on the touchpad, just because my thumb gets too sore. I've already noticed that the resistance is decreasing with use, but I shouldn't really have to deal with that - it should be good to go from first use. - Would have been nice to have a blu-ray drive instead of DVD, which may actually become obsolete before the rest of the computer In summary, I'm very happy. I've only dropped a star because of the aesthetic issues I've mentioned above, but if those are not a concern for you, feel confident you are buying a great machine at a very nice price.

I absolutely *LOVE* how it will go from 80 C (under extreme load) to 40 C in less than 20 seconds. I love how cool it is and how I don't need a cooling pad not to get burned. I *LOVE* how rocking fast it is, especially with the RAID SSDs. I also totally frickin dig how they have Windows 7 x64 drivers for (almost) every device! But the downsides, while few compared to practically all laptops, are very severe (ranked by severity ascending): 1. It comes with the shortest power cord I've ever seen in a device, much less a laptop. I measured it, I was in such disbelief: 2 feet for the wall cord, 1 1/2 feet for the computer cord. I couldn't even sit on the sofa with the thing (the power cord wouldn't reach to the middle seat!). It was very, maddening, restraining, esp. since I bought this because it is so light (~6.7 lbs). 2. There are two fundamentally missing drivers for Windows 7 x64, which were incredibly hard to find, relatively: Intel 7260AC wifi driver (conspicuously missing from their downloads page) and the Monitor driver. 3. The LCD monitor never seemed to work properly, however, particularly while watching movies, that the screen banded in high contrasts (like flood lights, stars, etc.). Not as bad as 16-bit banding, but not nearly 32-bit. I tested my setup and it was stuck in 24-bit mode. I tried everything under the Sun, invested over 30 hours into finding a solution. Nothing. The monitor's issues also continued in Linux. On a lark, and to see if it fixed other issues listed below, I begrudgingly reinstalled Windows 8, but no. I contacted tech support and this is what they said, in total: "Kindly note that the screen does not support 32-bit color." Man. I've never owned a laptop that didn't! Here's a picture where you can see the banding. Taken from the HD Star Trek: Into Darkness: https://www.dropbox.com/s/8owd5kdbz2806wp/Aorus_X7v2_24bit_Color_Depth_issue.png?dl=0 4. The Intel 7260AC wifi adapter. Seriously, google it, combined with the terms "latency" or "packet loss." This thing is HORRIBLE! I spent at least 20 hours trying to get it to work. I even reinstalled Windows 8 where it's quality was better but still bad. Linux *hated* the thing. As far as I can tell, the WIFI adapter could only handle one connection at a time well, and maybe 2 or 3 connections at a time max. I was never, ever, able to use bittorrent with it. More than 5 connections via a downloader and the internet ground to the halt. It was so ridiculous! I would open up the cmd.exe and ping -n 1000 8.8.8.8 and would get 20% packet loss if I was doing NOTHING. If I started browsing news sites, it'd jump to 60% packet loss. I then realized that if I played a game or anything involving the GPU, I got nothing but 100% packet failure. Yeah, the card stopped working during gameplay. On a gaming laptop. I tried every Intel 7260AC driver from 13.x to their latest 18.0.1. I've tried every single frickin setting, to such a degree that I have a complex spreadsheet of all the options I tried (so I could keep track). I reinstalled Windows 8 and it went down to 20-30% during active browsing and "only" 50% loss during gameplay, but that is still intolerable. Also, the max speed I ever got was around 700 kb/sec, with periodic jumps to 1-1.5 MB/sec on a connection that routinely does 5 MB/sec (FiOS). I bought a $20 USB Wifi adapter, and that worked fine. But still, ti's a $2,400 laptop. 5. Bluetooth (part of the Intel 7260AC card) never worked. I never successfully got it to team with any device, at least in Windows 7. Maybe a driver issue. 6. Even other radio devices, such as my logitech mouse and keyboard had latency issues!! My keyboard would lose about 1/2 of the keystrokes during gameplay and 1/8 during routine usage. It was *intolerable*. I still have no idea why. 7. There is ZERO, absolutely ZERO customer support! If customer support contacts me via this review, it will only tell me they are more in damage control than not. I submitted separate tickets to customer support for the issues #2, 3, 5, 6, and 7. Over 5 issues over the course of a month. And ... NOTHING, except for #4, a one sentence reply (see above). So, sadly, I'd have to say, avoid this laptop ;-( It gets *so* much right, awesomely right, but forsakes a lot of basics in the process.

This 1660 is an excellent 2nd card if you just want to add more monitors, but don't want to pay as much as you did for your first card. To be clear, I don't game, I don't render video, I just trade stocks on this PC. I already had 4 monitors, but between utilizing multiple timeframes on the same ticker to make decisions, multiple order entry boxes(Level II), time and sale (tape) and then the desire to have more windows from my scanners up and more tickers to just be able to watch outside of the ones I'm already in, I felt I'd need to add a couple more monitors. Right now I'm only running 1 more hdmi out to a TV and I have a scanner running on it full screen, which works great, as opposed to what I was doing before, which was minimizing a browser which would block one of my trading screens when I pulled it back up. I thought when I first started trading that 2-3 monitors would be all I'd need. I could not have been more naive. Every bit of information you could possibly have, I'm willing to take. I'm a bit annoyed that I asked on here whether I could add another card. I actually got responses saying they didn't think so, meanwhile I KNOW I've seen other traders with 6-8 monitors, and having already a 3060ti in my build, I know in Zotac's Firestorm I've seen where the software allows you to click between up to 4 graphics cards in order to overclock them differently. So despite the responses received and using some logic to determine this was ok, I decided to go ahead and buy the 1660 and figured I'd return it if it didn't work out. I'm glad I did. My bequiet PSU actually had another set of 8pin outs that I wasn't using. My 3060ti was only using one, so I was able to use the other for the 1660. Worked like a charm! When I booted up my computer after install, it did take a little longer to boot up, but once I got home screen, I opened up Nvidia settings, I went straight to 'setup multiple monitors' and just fiddled around with things and I must say, nice and smooth. The 1660 is not as bad as I thought it would be. Actually almost just as clear, but the 3060ti is clearly a few notches above. It's just smoother and snappier. You can tell this with just the mouse movement alone and how it feels in your hand. This is partly bc my first pci slot is getting pci 4.0 and the 1660's pci slot is only able to offer 3.0 come to find out. All in all the 1660 was not intended to be some high definition card in the first place. At least not for my build. Overall, I'm happy. So now I'm running: AsRock x570 Taichi Razer Edition Ryzen 9 5900x overclocked to 4.4ghz at 1.25v Noctua Nh-U12a CPU Cooler Corsair Vengeance LPX 32x2 3800mhz cl18 (I could not get even 3600mhz using 4x16, which is what I really wanted bc it looks better imo) Zotac RTX 3060ti (you do not need more than this for trading) Zotac GTX 1660 BeQuiet Straight Power 850w Platinum PSU (I'm pulling about 265w total with both cards in, but that's with only 1 hdmi out being used on this new graphics card. I could end up pulling more one I use some of the display ports) Arctic F14 (2 in front, 1 in rear) Arctic P14 (2 in top) - The system is nice and quiet :) I have a monitor sitting in storage that I think I'm going to try in order to arrange my screens. Will report back if anything changes...

My drive came in Firmware 320XXXX and the most recent one is 322XXXX, which Kingston labels as an Urgent update. This meant that I had to upgrade the firmware out of the box. It didn't give me problems with the firmware it came with though, and actually my Windows 7 x64 installed easily without a hitch on the previous firmware. Remember guys, to fully access its potential you must enable AHCI (not IDE mode) in BIOS and your motherboard must support 6gb/s SATA 3, although it can still run on IDE and SATA 2 albeit slower than its potential. In fact, this drive is plug and play when installing Windows 7 32 or 64 bit. PROS: Incredibly fast read speeds. CrystalDiskMark shows 500MB/s average for me. I get WEI rating of 7.9 for Disk Transfer Rate. CONS: Write speeds is not as advetised for me. I'm getting 160MB/s average. I've tried upgrading my BIOS, newest Intel Rapid Storage, enabling cache writing, etc. and still no luck. My board (Asrock extreme4) also has a Marvell controller, and that too gives 160MB/s write speeds. This is what Kinston specifies as their advertised speed for this drive: Sequential reads 6Gb/s 3 -- 555MB/s for all capacities Sequential writes 6Gb/s -- 510MB/s for all capacities For the typical user, this is crazy fast. But it is just hard to accept much lower write speeds than advertised when spending top dollar for the best computer parts. UPDATE 12/20/2011********** Ok, I've done some research and it turns out that my results are normal. First of all, Kingston's claims are based on ATTO Disk Benchmark 2.41 results, which uses compressible data. CrystalDiskMark uses incompressible data by default, which are more closer to real-life applications. When transferring videos, pictures, songs, zip fils and the such, its closer to incompressible data. After retesting using ATTO, I get 550MB/s max read and 510MB/s max write, which is pretty much the top claim. Lots of manufacturers, especially those who use SandForce controllers, like to use ATTO because it favors its performance. Comparing other review sites I see similar 170Mb/s write speeds using CrystalDiskMark. One more thing to note, the 240gb hyperx version does almost twice as better for write speeds at 300Mb/s versus 170Mb/s for the 120gb version. My rating technically is now 5 stars, but I'm leaving 4 stars because I still feel a little decieved. Dont get me wrong, this drive IS one of the fastest out there right now equal or better to the likes of Crucial M4's, Intel 510 series, or OCZ Vertex 3. UPDATE 1/26/2012 ******* I do not know what happened, but somehow this drive has reduced its incompressible write speed from 160MS/s to roughtly 130MB/s and the WIndows WEI hard drive score is down to 7.8 rating. Weirdly enough, the compressible write speed is still a blazing 510 MB/s. I spent several days of my time and numerous reformats trying to figure it out but its still a mystery to me. I retested using AS SSD benchmark and I also discovered the Access Read Time is a paltry .200ms on avg which is like mechanical disk speeds. To be honest, I am being a little nitpicky here but again, the purpose of paying top dollar for a Sata 3 SSD was to get Sata 3 speeds. And I'm not feeling completely satisfied with this one. I'm tempted to reduce the rating to 3 stars to "It's OK" status, but if you can find a deal where its about 1 dollar per GB then its still a good buy in my opinion.

I did. Because it was either this or the Apple keyboard folio at nearly twice the price of this one. And after swallowing the cost of a new iPad, I was in the mood to save a few dollars. I’ll start with the good. The engineering is solid and sturdy, and the cutouts are accurate to my 4th gen (2020) iPad Air. The magnetic flap closes satisfyingly, and the tilt angles are sensible and useful. The typing is experienced is mixed (I’ll get to that later), but the keys have surprisingly generous travel and my typing speed quickly approached my standard laptop typing speed. There is even a row of function keys at the top that are, somewhat to my surprise, actually useful. It’s nice to have a physical home key, which I lost moving from the 2nd gen iPad Pro. The task switcher, lock, and keyboard toggle are also nice features; like the media keys, they essentially prevent the constant switch back and forth between touchscreen and keyboard, which I appreciate. And the case does an admirable job of getting out of the way of the speakers, which sound just as clear with the case as without it. And… boy did I hate this case. Its first crime, which I tried to overlook, was that it is big, bulky, and ugly. The iPad Air itself is a marvel of sleek slimness, but with this case it feels like one of those early 2000s laptops, thick as an expensive dictionary and just as heavy. The case adds considerably to the bezels, and does so with copious amounts of plastic that reminds me of nothing more of a children’s toy. A dull, gray, children’s toy. And these bezels, thick as they are, greatly impede the ability to quickly access Touch ID (with the case on, you can only use Touch ID with your finger perpendicular to the screen, not parallel to the screen as would be natural when you are using the iPad as a tablet). The typing experience, as I mentioned, isn’t bad. The feel is actually pretty decent, despite the same flat, gray, cheap-looking plastic and retro-without-being-cool chiclet key. I am unable to give it a win in this category due to a couple unfortunate design choices. The worst of these is the choice to put the function (fn) key in the lower left corner. Thus, the prime pinky finger location is occupied by a key that has very few routine uses (except toggling delete/backspace, which is nice to have but only confuses the positioning further). As a person who makes constant use of keyboard shortcuts to navigate, copy, and delete more quickly, this is an unforgivable sin, because no amount of time will make it natural for me to curl my little finger in toward my palm to reach the modifier keys. I don’t believe the designers were avid keyboard shortcut users, because the arrow keys are also squished tightly into the corner. I get that real estate is limited, but it’s unclear what the designers were maximizing for. Not me, that’s for sure. If you’re like me and saw the photos but thought, “surely it must look better in person”, heed my warning: It doesn’t. It looks and feels like a monochromatic hasbro toy. Its design aesthetic is very precisely the oppose of the device it is designed to house. It is bulky to the point of absurdity. It is that thing which is worse than a horrible product: a pretty good product swaddled in a thousand suffocating swaths of poor design choices and ham-fisted aesthetics. And because the iPad is an Apple product, I have one more thing: The darn thing is a pain to open. Perhaps it would get easier in time to pick the perfect angle of attack to separate the seem between the screen and the keyboard, but I will never know. Time is up. Take my money, Apple—what little I have left—if it will save me ffrom this hell.

The overall quality of these is solid. The issue that I've had is one I've googled and found has been going on for awhile and it's that they have an issue connecting to iPhones, which... that's a pretty big issue to have. What this results in is a super frustrating case of typically needing to put in and take out my earbuds sometimes 3-4 separate times before they automatically connect to my phone. It might not sound like a big deal but when you're on the go and they have a magnetic case having to take them both out of the case and insert them, and then put them back, and then insert again etc. is very tedious. It's particularly frustrating because I've found that the issue is wildly inconsistent. Sometimes they connect perfectly, other times I have to repeatedly insert them and put them back in the case, and on a few occasions I've had issues where only one will connect at a time and I need to reset the earbuds. I've done research into the connectivity issues too and some of the contributing factors seem pretty ridiculous. One reported cause is if your phone has bluetooth enabled for awhile but isn't connected to anything it will have issues connecting. Another suggests that low battery for either the phone or earbuds impacts connectivity. I've had much cheaper buds in the past and never experienced these issues with other brands. Another issue I have with them is the battery display. The battery life is really good, but the on-screen indicator that pops up when the case is open seems to pop up at random for me. I've had like $30 wireless buds before that show the battery in the top right corner of your iphone next to the phone battery so long as they're turned on, and I'd honestly prefer that to this fancier feature that doesn't work all the time. The bottom line is if you don't experience the connectivity issues then these are high quality earbuds. If you do, the issue is so frustrating and frequent that you're better off looking elsewhere. I often find myself walking my dog, or to the bus for work and thinking that I'd rather just have wired earbuds that I know will never have any issues connecting than go through the steps of trying to get these to connect.
