These are generally a nice pair of binoculars with acceptable quality. However, I will have to return them due to incorrect claims regarding their magnification. I already own a pair of 13-39x70mm by ESSLNB. I bought the Beta Optics 10-100x68 to double the magnification I have to get closer to objects during stargazing and moon matching. I was excited when ordering them but disappointed when trying them out. The magnification is not larger at all than my 13-39x70. I have tested them side by side with all kind of celestial and terrestrial objects, from looking at the moons of Jupiter, to the craters on the moon, to street signs in the distance, to measuring the field of view at various magnifications. I cannot get any closer with the Beta pair than with my ESSLNB pair. They go both right along until 39x with field of view and magnification and there they both stop, maybe 40x or so for the Beta Optics but no more. So, I now have two pairs of binoculars with mainly the same range of magnification. Additionally, the images of the Beta Optics 10-100x68 is somewhat hazy and blurred at full zoom and hard to focus, so that they actually offer me less usable zoom than my 13-39x which is clear, sharp, crisp and easy to focus at full zoom. At first I had considered keeping the Beta Optics as they are much smaller and lighter than my 13-39x. They also have a nice feel to them and allow a sharp focus at closer up images, as well. However, in the very low zoom they have a rather small field of view so that I am much better off with my regular 10x50 to cover that area. And in the higher zoom they don't get me any closer than my 13-39x but with less quality. So, they don't cover any range I don't already have. If you want an good pair of zoom binoculars for bird watching they would work just well. They are not bad quality at a real 10-25x. If high magnification is your goal you might want to look at something that actually offers a true 100x. I dont know how they measured their numbers but they don't even get me half way there. Otherwise I don't have many complains about this pair except that I bought them under the wrong impression to double my magnification range. I am returning them simply because I cannot afford to buy something for the same range twice and will have to buy another pair to get me to a real 100x. Otherwise, nice pair.

I ordered these renewed PA7017 (AV1000) units to replace a pair of AV600 units I'm using to connect a POE router to my main gigabit data switch in my house. The POE serves four hardwired IP cameras, so the powerline connection needs to handle streaming video 24/7. As measured by the TP-Link Utility, my AV600s were giving me about 120 to 130 Mbps. I went with the renewed AV1000 units to save a few bucks, figuring that they would be open-box or returned units that didn't meet the customer's needs. What I received were the OLDER PA7010 (AV1000) units, which are not the ones pictured and are much larger than the PA7017 Nano units. They are so large that they block other outlets when I install them where my AV600s were. They were also in pretty rough condition, looking like they had been in use for a long period of time. Finally, I only got one ethernet cable with the pair, not the expected two cables. On the other hand, these PA7010 units did work and did pair with each other quickly. According to the TP-Link utility, my power line connection has jumped up to a steady 210 to 220 Mbps, an increase in speed of over 65%. In fairness, the older PA7010 units sell for more than the newer PA7017 units, but I really wanted the newer Nano form factor and the most recent hardware/firmware. I'm on the point of returning them and spending the extra $12 to get a brand new set of PA7017s.

What an incredible disappointment. I bought this camera for one reason: To capture memories from a scuba diving trip my brother & I had planned for Monterey Bay in California. It was totally unreliable--wouldn't power on when needed. This camera has nearly a thousand reviews on Amazon. I read through a great deal of them (mostly the 1 & 2-star reviews) looking for anything negative that might cause me concern when using the camera under water. Most of the relevant comments talked about how the case flooded with water and ruined the camera. I found that hard to believe, considering the case was specifically designed for underwater use. I just assumed those comments came from morons and I proceeded with my purchase. (For what it's worth, the manual states very clearly that you have to be careful with the seal. It specifically mentions that a single hair or grain of sand trapped in the seal may cause it to leak. I had no such trouble--the waterproof case worked flawlessly on two dives at depths more than 50ft.) The camera arrived one week before the dive. I charged the battery fully, then sat down with the camera & manual and went through every page. As I read through the manual, I tried every feature on the camera to be sure I fully understood what the book was describing. Confident that I knew exactly how to use this thing, I headed to the dive site. We put on our gear, performed a quick buddy check, and I took a 2sec video to make sure the camera was working properly. Then we headed out into the kelp fields. We descended about 30ft. Visibility was good. I pushed the power button. Nothing. No response whatsoever. I fussed with it for several minutes, staring at it in disbelief, slowly coming to the depressing realization that I wasn't going to capture any memories of this fantastic place. We finished our first dive and headed back to the beach. I tried turning the camera on again but it was completely unresponsive. I opened the case, removed the totally dry camera, and swapped batteries (I purchased two extra batteries as a precaution). The camera sprang to life. Huh? Was I a moron? Did I forget to charge the first battery? No--I replaced the original battery and the camera powered on just fine with the display showing a full charge. Not wanting to take any chances, I swapped batteries again. I turned the camera on & off several times and took another 2sec video to make sure it was working properly, then we geared up & headed back into the water for our second dive. We swam out to the kelp beds again and this time I decided to turn on the camera at the surface before descending. Fail. Again. No power. The damn thing just wouldn't turn on. Were my gloves too thick? Was I not pushing the button hard enough? No, that wasn't the problem. I pushed that button many times. The camera was totally unresponsive. Again. Back on the beach after the second dive, I tried turning the camera on again. Nothing. Completely dead. I removed & reinserted the battery, and just like before, the camera sprang to life. WTF? That made me even more upset. Back home, I googled for "gopro wont turn on" and found lots of youtube videos & other links from people having similar problems. In fact, GoPro's own website admits they know about this problem! (Google for "HERO3 Camera Will Not Power ON"). But not to worry! The fix is simple--just remove & reinsert the battery and everything will be ok. Really? How am I supposed to do that OUT IN THE F*CKING OCEAN?!? Come on, GoPro. Seriously. How do you screw up a product this badly? I'm sending it back. Update: In case anyone is wondering if the problem is related to my choice of SD card, I used this one: http://www.amazon.com/Sony-microSDXC-Class-UHS-1-Memory/dp/B00E1XI94Q (purchased locally from a very reputable electronics store rather than from Amazon). It's not on GoPro's "recommended" list, but it certainly fulfills their "We recommend only purchasing name brand SD cards through reputable resellers" statement.

First off, let me say, I love Bushnell Binoculars. I've owned a set of 7 x 35 Bushnell Porro's for 25 years and the optics are fine and I really liked them, but they were beat up and I just wanted to upgrade to a brighter pair (42mm lens) and Roof Prism's. I chose Roof Prism Binoculars as they are more compact than the Porro Binoculars which make them easier to tote and travel with. 1. The optics, the focusing knob, and the eye relief in these Bushnell's were just fine. HOWEVER! 2. The ERGONOMICS and FEEL of the binoculars is AWFUL. a. RUBBER COATING. The rubber coating on the outside looks great and feels strong, but the ridges incorporated into the rubber skin got very uncomfortable after just a few seconds of holding. b. STRAP MOUNTS. The strap mounts on the barrels are placed in too low. These Roof Prism Binoculars aren't very long barreled (5" vs most Roofs which are at 6") and the strap holders hit the joints of my pointer fingers every time I held them. AND since the barrels are short, it is hard to reposition your hands to overcome the bulging neck strap mounts. Now I'm 5'5" with small hands so having large hands wasn't the issue, in fact, if you have BIGGER HANDS than mine the "strap mount issue" would be EVEN WORSE! c. Weight. These Bushnell 8 x 42 H2O Waterproof Roofs weigh in at 25 oz. I thought that when I got them that the weight wouldn't be an issue. I was wrong. These suckers are HEAVY which led to ARM FATIGUE in a hurry. I compared the H2O's with a pair of 8 x 42 's Vortex Crossfire Roofs I bought at Dick's Sporting Goods. The Vortex weighed in at 21.5 oz and, although 3.5 oz seems like a small weight difference, it made a huge difference in arm fatigue. BOTTOM LINE - Buy a lighter pair of binoculars or with better weight distribution, ie. longer barrels. I felt bad returning these Bushnell's, I really did, because the optics of the Bushnell's were fine, but the ergonomics were just too uncomfortable to overcome. UPDATE: I bought a pair of the 8 x 25 Bushnell H2O's Compact Binoculars (the mini-me's of these) and I LOVE them (see my review). They are light, comfortable to hold, have two hinges for compact carrying, have really nice optics and look great. For the 8 x 42's I wound up with the Vortex Crossfire II Roofs (see my review) from Dick's Sporting Goods which were a bit more pricy than 8 x 42 Bushnell H2O's ($75 vs $120) but the optics and especially the ergonomics were so much better.

The T11 is both highly functional and terribly amusing. If you're looking for a backlit TRUE mechanical keyboard (this is NOT a "faux mechanical", but uses true mechanical switches) at a reasonable price with a certain element of fun/whimsy, this is a good choice. No, it doesn't change colors (colors are fixed per row), but there are numerous amusing light show options for when you're bored or pondering and feel like zoning out while staring vacantly at your keyboard, and some of them are even interactive/reactive (i.e., respond to your typing). For gamers (I assume), there's an interesting feature that lets you edit and store multiple "lighting maps" that just illuminate selected keys. The details of how to access all these features are spelled out in a slick looking and surprisingly readable user information card that's about as much manual as a keyboard should need. It's important to note that all these features are controlled with Fn-key sequences on the keyboard itself, requiring no special drivers or other software on the PC, so it all works on any platform - I'm using it with a Chromebook right now as I type. The lights can be controlled for brightness (including all the way off) and speed of light show effects (where applicable), except for the bright blue LEDs on the underside of the keyboard, which are illuminated whenever there's power coming in from the USB port. The only other comment I'd make about backlighting is that the purple lighting used for the home row keys (ASDFGHJKL) isn't as bright as the other rows - it might be helpful if Velocifire could equalize this by running them one step brighter than the other rows - at full brightness (which I doubt I'll ever use) it wouldn't matter anyway. In terms of packaging, I find the thing gorgeous. The switch-mounted keys stick up directly from an aluminum plate with no "surround" plastic, etc. Combined with the transparent case and visible circuit board on the bottom, the overall effect is a bunch of keys mounted on a board and floating on your desk. Despite the product description's claim, the front "lip" isn't really big enough to act as a wrist rest, so is purely decorative - the keyboard rests on rubber feet under the key area. I think the one significant misfire in the physical package design is the usb cable sticking out of the right hand side of the keyboard instead of coming out the back and being routable straight back or to either side. For the great majority of users, this means the cable extends the effective width of the keyboard by impinging a bit on the area where you might want to move your mouse. Combined with the decorative front lip, this may make the keyboard unsuitable for some setups with limited keyboard/mouse space. Contrary to the assessment of some reviewers, I do not consider this to be a lightweight keyboard - it has more than enough heft to stay in place on its non-skid rubber feet, and is actually heavier than any other keyboard I'm currently using. [PLEASE NOTE: At the time of my purchase, Velocifire offered the T11 with choice of Zorro Blue or Brown switches, and this review is for the version with Brown switches. It appears that the T11 is now offered only with Zorro Blue switches, so issues like feel, noise, etc. will not be exactly as described below. All other observations should apply.] Considering the T11 as a keyboard, I'm not the sort of Cherry switch connoisseur who can ramble on in detail about actuation forces and tactile feedback, but I will say after years of working on mushy membrane keyboards that it's great to experience the retro feel and sound of real mechanical switches. The Zorro switches used in the T11 are intended to mimic the behavior of Cherry browns, apparently not as loud and clicky as Cherry blues, but loud enough that I'm more comfortable using it in my home office (where it is) than in the agency cubicle farm where I spend most of my week (the keyboards we use there are near-silent) - i.e., the Zorro browns are plenty clicky. On the other hand, effort/resistance is not high. I've had to learn to moderate my touch a bit to reduce bottoming out, but at least for me that learning curve is fairly automatic as your fingertips learn to protect themselves. My typing accuracy improved significantly after the first day as I adjusted to this new/old mechanical key experience, and at this point I think I'm typing at least as well - I'll give it another week before I try some typing games/tests for my own comparison (not worth sharing, as I'm sure results would be highly personal/subjective). Speaking of subjectivity, I've heard some comments that these switches aren't as nice and substantial as true Cherry switches, but I've no idea how that would be quantified. I personally find the T11's feel quite satisfactory, and when I had the chance to compare the T11 side by side with a friend's high end keyboard using genuine Cherry Browns, I could not tell the difference. A side note on the keycaps - these are double shot with clear and white plastic, not printed stencils on a translucent key that could wear off over time. When the backlighting is on the effect of this is quite impressive. An apparent consequence of the manufacturing process is that there are no "closed loops" in the graphics, so there are gaps in any letters/symbols with such "closed" areas. Look closely at enlarged product photos to see what I mean, particularly with letters like A, B, Q, O, etc. This mostly just makes those letters appear somewhat stylized, but a few characters, notably the 0 (zero) and # (hash/pound sign) are barely recognizable. Overall, the T11 is a fun alternative to more conventionally back-lit keyboards, and a great value considering that it's a true mechanical and offers such colorful behavior. While the rainbow backlight and larger than expected effective footprint might not be right for everyone, I think it's a solid 4-star experience. At this price for the quality, however, the value kicks it up to 5-star. I'm very glad I bought it; if this looks like what you're looking for, I think it's a purchase you won't regret.

This review will be short and sweet. There are a lot of great detailed reviews here about every feature . . . I'm going to just talk about what I think matters with this camera. #1 - Picture Quality. I have a HP 2.1 MP camera that I just used to take a picture of my sons under the Christmas tree, then printed it out on photo paper. When I got my Canon A75 camera, I took the same picture of them, then printed it out. The difference was stunning! The color and quality of the Canon printed picture was 10x better than the HP. It looked like a photo center picture. #2 - Software. It's okay, but not the best. For organizing and viewing after downloading, it's fine. I wanted to print a picture, and all I could find was Album printing and "contact sheet". It didn't give me size option (4x6, 5x7, etc.) I ended up using my HP Printer software. #3 - Fun Stuff. There are some fun things - like sounds. When you are in the Canon software, you can go to "My camera options" and change the sounds and opening screen picture (while your camera is connected). I have a nice Christmas scene for the opening picture and some cute Christmas sound effects. They have other themes like baseball, cats/dogs, wedding, etc. #4 - My biggest problem with this camera is shutter speed. It takes a few seconds to actually take a picture. By the time my kids are done saying "CHEESE" the picture snaps. So I've learned to tell them to say cheese a second after I push the button. I have a feeling I'm going to miss some good shots because of this issue. #5 - Batteries. Sure, it eats batteries, but all digital cameras do. But comparing it to my HP, the Canon A75 lasts twice as long. And does even better with a good set of rechargable batteries. I would surely recommend this camera. It has amazing quality and a ton of features for the price.

I plan on keeping this review up to date, so as things change I will keep adding to it. I will also try to answer any questions in comments. April 2, 2010 I received this player from Amazon today. Within the first hour I had it hooked up to my home theater system, connected to my wi-fi network, updated the firmware over the web, connected to Netflix, and connected to Pandora. At that point I was ready to log in to Amazon and post a 5 star review. I am glad that I held off because there have been a few problems, but not enough to make me want to return the player. Even though I have the latest firmware, 1009.1, Vudu does not work for me. I get an error message when I try to start it (I will post the error here tomorrow; right now I am watching a movie!). I was able to set my location in Accuweather and change it from Celsius to Fahrenheit. However, when I went back into Accuweather the location was correct but it reverted back to Celsius. I went in and out of it several times and set it back to Fahrenheit but each time it would go back to Celsius. I went to the Vudu site and did some searches on Samsung, but could not find anything helpful. I also did some Google searches without much luck. The most useful information always pointed back to the Amazon reviews for this product. I played a regular DVD and it did an OK job although it seemed a little over-exposed. I will update my comments as I play more DVDs. I haven't played a blu-ray DVD yet because I don't own one but will pick one up tomorrow. Pandora radio sounds excellent! I have a Pioneer VSX-9040TXH receiver (which I love -- highly recommended) with some quality 5.1 speakers and the sound is amazing. At this point I am irritated that Vudu shows up as an app on my player, but it doesn't work and I can't find any useful information about why. I am also irritated that Accuweather, in spite of reports from previous reviewers here, doesn't work. It seems like someone is dropping the ball. It would be nice if the blu-ray player would provide some kind of status about whether an app is functional or not so that I as a user do not have to waste my time trying to fix something if it's unfixable by me. Right now I am keeping things in perspective. As a DVD player, blu-ray player, Netflix player, and Pandora player it is still worth the money. I am certainly glad that I didn't get just a standalone blu-ray player because Netflix and Pandora both add a lot of value. April 3rd 2010 I was showing my friend the Internet features of this player today (Day 2) and was surprised that when I went into Vudu, the error message that I had been getting went away, and I was able to start my Vudu service! Setup was very easy. Accuweather, however, still would not keep the temperature in Fahrenheit. More later ... April 4th 2010 I watched two Vudu movies yesterday. Things worked very well. The HDX quality is very good, as is the 5.1 audio. I don't like the Vudu interface as much as Apple TV's, but the quality is as good or better. There is also a very good selection of movies on Vudu. So, if you want HD-quality streaming videos with great audio, this blu-ray player can do that through the Vudu service. Very nice feature. I tried a few more things: Rovi TV listings. You set it up on the blu-ray player. It shows what is on TV over a 2 hour period. It doesn't appear to let someone browse through shows more than 2 hours out unless I haven't figured that out yet. I added another location in Accuweather. I set both locations to Fahrenheit, exited, went back in and again it reverted to Celsius. Why do they even bother to put out software if they can't do it right? They have had time to fix it and haven't. It gives Accuweather a bad name. The Blockbuster app appears to be working, but I didn't watch anything because I am a Netflix subsriber rather than Blockbuster. USA Today news is something I may use. What I like is that I can get titles of news stories by category, and quickly bring up the article. It's a very fast way to get the news compared to a web browser for example. YouTube appears to be working. There is a log in options so it should be able to access your account if you set one up. I don't have a YouTube account so didn't try that. At this point I have tested all the apps and the only one not working correctly is Accuweather. I will try some of the other features this week, including playing a blu-ray. Any suggestions for my first blu-ray movie? April 13, 2010 I was able to set up Blockbuster on Demand. Even though my main computer is a Mac and Blockbuster on Demand doesn't run on a Mac, I was able to register a new Blockbuster on Demand account on my Mac and confirm it just by entering a 5 digit code on the Samsung player. At this point I have rented movies using the Samsung's Netflix streaming, Blockbuster on Demand, and Vudu apps, and have been able to listen to music on Pandora. In addition, I have watched many blu-ray movies (about 20 to date) without any problems. April 18, 2010 I have played more blu-ray and regular DVDs and have not had any problems. Everything played fine. Tonight I checked for a software update and one was available. I like that I could check right from the player, and not have to download separately. There is an option to use a USB drive, but it's not necessary if the player is hooked up to the network. A MAJOR ANNOYANCE: AccuWeather is STILL not working. When I go in and change it to Fahrenheit, go out, and come back in, the temperatures are all in Celsius. Who is dropping the ball -- Samsung, it's your player, and obviously you should know about this problem, so WHY aren't you fixing the problem or getting AccuWeather to fix it? Do you care about your product -- well if so, then FIX THE PROBLEM. Fortunately, the major services work fine: Netflix insta-queue streaming, Vudu, Blockbuster on Demand, and Pandora. June 4, 2010 AccuWeather now works. The Fahrenheit setting sticks. This will be the last entry of this review. I would buy this player again. The Internet features are very nice. Netflix streaming, Blockbuster on Demand, Pandora, and Vudu being the main ones. I have not had any problems playing normal DVD's or blue-ray DVDs. They don't rewind or fast forward as smoothly as I would like, but it does what it needs to do. It's not an expensive player, and it does a lot. So, I recommend this player.

This is the very first time I've ever used a pen display tablet for which I could draw directly onto the screen, so in my case, I may be a bit biased toward praise. For me, the tablet is awesome. Drawing on the screen feels satisfying, and the parallax is minimal (i.e., the tip of the pen is very close to the mouse cursor when moving the pen along the screen) so the accuracy is excellent. I've enjoyed using this tablet so far and am very pleased with it. The tablet does, however, have a few flaws. I've been able to work around them, but they are worth mentioning. The tablet does have fits where it disconnects and reconnects repeatedly. But I have come to find that it only does this if I've left the tablet sitting for a while without working on the piece I have open on it. While I'm drawing on it, it doesn't slip into a disconnect/reconnect fit. That said, this hasn't really been a huge issue for me. My laptop's screen display settings are set to "expand" so that I can use my laptop for other activities (like watching YouTube videos) while having Photoshop open on my tablet screen. So whenever the tablet disconnects and reconnects, once it's done, I'll just open HuionTablet driver (I have a shortcut to it pinned to my Taskbar), go to the "Workspace" link in the tablet buttons tab, and select the tablet screen side as the workspace again. Then things are fine and I continue working. The factory-set calibration of the tablet screen is pretty off. The screen is very dark and a little bit blurry, but I believe these settings are intentional so that the user doesn't end up straining their eyes too much while using the tablet. It's actually felt a bit easier on my eyes and I've kind of appreciated it, but there are ways in which you can adjust the screen settings on it. You can even sharpen the screen as well in its settings. For those who need the colors and gradations in their art to be super accurate, they may not appreciate the factory-set screen settings. There was an instance when I was perhaps moving too fast and the tablet began to glitch out. During that instance, the shortcuts mapped to the tablet and pen buttons were all shuffled around. It took a few seconds for the tablet to get itself back in order again. Turning it off and back on or closing the program and reopening are simple fixes for this kind of mishap, and so far it's only happened once or twice. Sometimes the tablet does seem to freeze up a little, although this is very rare and only lasts a couple of seconds at most. All in all, I'd consider these to be short footfalls, as, in the grand scheme of things, I've otherwise been able to draw with more accuracy and speed than I was with a regular drawing tablet. So to me, it's worth it. For someone who is used to digital drawing but has never had a pen display tablet before, I'd say this one is a fine pick and works well. But for someone who's looking into more serious firepower for their artwork, this one might not quite be up to par.

If your employer is jumping onto the 'open concept' or 'high density' office layout with no walls or sound dampening, these headphones are for you. Put them on and turn them on, and your coworkers' voices will disappear. These headphones have far and away the best noise cancellation I've ever tried (AudioTechnica and Bose). You'll be able to get plenty of work done without being distracted by the loud guy an aisle over, and you won't need to deafen yourself with a set of earbuds to do it. Meanwhile, the sound quality is Sennheiser superb. The "Talk Through" button may seem like a gimmick, but I use it regularly to prairie-dog on conversations without needing to remove the headphones. It is a very convenient feature. The integrated volume control is useful as well. Overall, the featureset, cost, and bulk of these headphones makes them far better suited to an office environment than an aircraft. IMO they're quite a bit too large and heavy to be lugging onto a flight, unless you are headed to an antipodal location, e.g. New Zealand. And luggage gets dropped, items forgotten. Best to leave your $3-400 'phones out of your travel plans. Oh, and the build quality? If Mercedes-Benz was to ever build a headphone they would look a lot like this. You pay for it, of course, but: pick them up - heavy, huge. Run your hands along the outside: aluminum, high-quality plastic, stainless steel. And that just might be real leather lining the band and earcups. The headband extends with a smoothly detented 'snick' that is reminiscent of high-grade machine tools or firearms. The earcups articulate smoothly and silently. You put them on and turn them on and the outside world disappears. It's a lot like wearing an E-Class on your head. Pricey. But you get what you pay for. And if you want to have a choice about hearing your coworker's biology noises or noisy conference calls, you want these headphones.

With the woods around my neighborhood it is important to be able to move easily into a clear position, or else the telescope would not get used much, plus I did not want to worry about temperature stabilization and collimation such as a reflecting telescope can need -I just want to get up and go, it should be easy to use, and get good quality images. A 4 inch refractor with an alt-azimuth mount such as this one does the trick well. Frankly there were few choices in the four inch or more range that fit my criteria, so I was very l pleased to get a good quality 'scope at a good price from Amazon. The manual tracking on the mount is reasonably smooth and the easy to us as well. It did not get five stars because the spotting scope, while fairly accurate, is only useful with bright objects due to the lack of a lens. This 'scope is big enough to look for dim objects, which can be hard to find without navigating help through dim star fields. Celestron should offer a lensed spotting scope instead on this unit. I purchased an Orion 6x30 right angle finder from Amazon which was a direct fit to the mount on the body of this 'scope, problem solved! Also be aware that this scope only came with one low power eyepiece (in my case) as was clearly advertised, and while this is also a very useful lens which I very much like, if you are new to astronomy be aware that more need to be purchased for the higher magnifications that this is capable of. But overall I am very pleased with this purchase.

I tried this with a Samsung Galaxy TAB 2 tablet mounted to my dash. Downloaded the V-Car app and wired it into the car as described. The expectation is that the app runs in the background and detects the Wifi signal when it activates from the backup lights, switches to the app and displays the backup image, then restores you back to whatever you were doing when you switch out of reverse. This is what it leads you to believe it does in the Engrish instructions, but in fact, it doesn't do that at all. What it does is disconnect your existing Wifi, connects to its own Wifi signal, and then does absolutely nothing else. You get to manually start the app, look at the pointless image of a car with a green wifi signal coming out its rear end, then tap a TINY, INSCRUTABLE LITTLE ICON in the upper right corner to enable the rearview image. Then when you're done, you get to back out of the app, go into your settings and reconnect your existing Wifi network manually, because of course it disables it, then switch back to whatever you were doing before this whole process began. It's more hassle than it's worth. If it did what it said, it would be great, but it's just because of poorly-written software that it doesn't. Which of course, will never be fixed nor open-sourced, because this was basically alpha software written hastily and turned loose without proper testing. Outside my return policy now and can't send it back.

Update 3/24/12 I have basically been using the eyetv HD as a tuner for my iMac. The quirky streaming (which may not all be Elgato's fault due to all the factors for getting video out of my house to my iPhone/iPad) got occasional use, but mainly I would have a TV window running while doing other things on the computer. When I installed Lion last year (and this is probably nothing more than coincidence), the eyeTV began acting erratically. Mostly, it would keep switching back from HD to non HD mode, continue to buffer and stall video and basically became unusable. I spent quite a bit of time going back and forth with Elgato tech service by email and we tried all sorts of things that never seemed to work. Finally, they determined this was not a Lion issue, but that the hardware was defective. Even though I've had this box for almost 2 years, they had me send it back and they replaced it (not sure if this is a new or refurb, but I don't care). So I'm pretty pleased with the way Elgato backed up their product. I still think that the best way to think of this device is that of a HD tuner with some occasionally useful "beta features" that kind of work. Since I like having a tuner in my computer, and like the cable box interface, I'd recommend this to anyone as long as they understand what they are getting. Elgato backing up their product is also a definite plus. I've had eyeTV tuners on my macs for a long time. Most recently an eyeTV hybrid. It was ok with mediocre video quality (in small screen. Horrible in full screen on my 23" iMac), but I just wanted to be able to see a small TV window to glance over at when I was doing other things on the computer. When Elgato released the eyeTV app for the iPhone and iPad I bought it ($5) and tried to configure the SW to stream on my wireless network and over 3G. I could not get it to work reliably on WiFi and was completely unsuccessful getting it to work on 3G. I kept getting a message saying my router was incompatible (which was nonsense because I had other remote access SW that works fine). I read about the EyeTV HD and thought this would be interesting to try out. If it stunk on ice, I'd send it back to Amazon and return the HD tuner to my cable company. The hook up (between the cable box, EyeTV HD box and mac is pretty easy. I was having problems with the video stuttering until I realized I was using one of my external HDs as the EyeTV DVR disk. Once I switched to the macs internal drive the video cleared right up. I was able to record and stream HD programs to my iPhone and iPad on my home network with pretty good results. Its still a bit buggy in that sometimes have to go and re initialize EyeTV on the mac before I can stream. Otherwise I get a "channel not available" message for no apparent reason. I could not get the 3G streaming to work at all and the tech support for Elgato didn't help very much. Its difficult to describe a wireless routing problem when you are not well versed in all the set ups configuration lingo and what the effect would be on your system. I finally googled around enough and found an article on Wikianswers that lead me to the solution. You have to port forward port 2710 (I think that's the one), reserve an address for your computer on your wireless system (assuming you're using DHCP), and next thing you know you're streaming over 3 G. So, now that you have it working you can see where you need to have your expectations set right so you don't get disappointed. Most of the time I can stream in my house to my iPad with very good results. I can carry my iPad around and view any of my regular or premium pay channels anywhere in the house. That by itself was worth the money to me (even though occasionally I need to reset the EyeTV Sw on the mac to get it going). Streaming over 3G is another story. Sometimes the quality is very good. It stalls once in a while, but not too bad. Sometimes the quality is so poor its unwatchable. You can dork with the quality settings to try to improve the image, but if the network won't sustain the data stream there's not much you can do about it. I would assume this is the same problem any Slingbox type streaming video would have. Its interesting to note that the quality of recorded video on the EyeTV is much better and consistent than the streaming video. So you could remotely tell your mac to record a show and then watch it later (much later because you have to wait for the rendering during export to complete which can take hours if you recorded a long show). The other complaint I have is that the file size is huge compared to movie files you can rip from DVDs using Handbrake and the like. A full movie in iPad resolution done with Handbrake is on the order of 1.3 Gig. (for a two hour movie). With the EyeTV you are getting file sizes around 5 Gig per hour. That gets pretty hefty if you are recording a Nascar race or a football game. Hope this helps people decide if this is a product that's worth their time and money.

This is an excellent tripod. The head is metal, the panning handle is about 11inches long, the dovetail attachment is very secure. The dovetail is secured by two screws. One that screws into the dovetail at 90degrees, and the other safety screw that screws in at 45degrees so nothing will slip. If your scope does not have a dovetail, you can use the optional dovetail attachment with screw (the attachment comes with the tripod) to screw on a camera or binoculars. One thing I did do when I set up the tripod (and before attaching a telescope) I released the horizontal movement screw and moved the tripod head a couple of times in both directions to loosen up the movement. I also did the same for the vertical movement by loosening the panning handle and moving the head up and down. When lining up an object in the night sky, remember to aim lower (object appears on the upper portion of the eyepiece) on the object being seen. Then when the panning handle is tightened, the tripod head will move slightly higher and the object will come down lower in the eyepiece of the scope. Just the same thing that happens with any tripod with the same type of mechanism. I am fairly certain that the legs of this tripod are made of steel, and not aluminum. This is a big, sturdy tripod. I only use it for astronomy so I am always seated. I do not know if this tripod would be a proper height for binoculars, using a binocular attachment. Although I think that it would be an acceptable height. Very nice tripod.

Yes I put a brand new battery in it. It worked on the first day 50% of the time and today it just stopped. I think the remote control is really unnecessary and only served to pull down ratings. 2. The indicator LEDs are hot garbage. Regardless of whether my device is turned on or not, LEDs sometimes remain indicating "online". My second "online" LED now no longer works on my second day of usage, but the screen and peripheral USB switch still works. I have to unplug the device 2 USB B connector from the KVM switch and replug it in to make the LED light work properly. Which brings us to... 3. The peripheral USB port stopped switching properly. When I switched to device 2, my keyboard and mouse remained connected to my first device, even though the screen had switched to device 2. Similarly, I had to unplug the USB B connector of device 2 and plug it in again. If I wanted to do USB juggling, I wouldn't have bought a KVM switch. Recommendations: a. Have a single button remote for 2 device KVM switches. Since it's apparent 6 button remotes are hard to engineer. b. Upgrade the ports to USB 3 or even USB C, this is 2020. I highly, highly suspect the crappy online detection and USB problems are due to the usage of USB 2.0 with newer USB C devices. Also since I'm connecting a USB 3.0 USB hub to the KVM switch, having a USB 2.0 port means that all my USB 3/C devices have their speeds dropped to crappy 2.0 speeds. Then again maybe I'm asking for too much from a $100 device. It is undeniably cheap, and does what it's meant to majority of the time. So 4 stars.

I bought it because it's cheap, and I'd had enough of some of the other brands I've tried that continually failed, so I refused to further support those camera manufacturers. Perhaps I should just buy a cheap smartphone with no calling or data plan simply for the camera use?

Just installed and working well. Replaced an older stock Intel cooler. There was one problem that everyone should pay attention to, the locking pins. These are the black pins that run through the mounting feet and force the white plastic tabs out to lock the cooler to the motherboard. The instructions show the direction that the pins should face while attaching but two of the four black pins were extended and the fan would not attach on the first try. If you try forcing the locking mechanism, you will bend the tabs. I had to remove and pull the black pins all the way back and then the cooler mounted easily. I think a notation in the instructions should note to check that black pins should be fully retracted.

OK, this mount is just that, a mount. I had imagined it was more like a case that protected or enclosed the whole camera but it’s not. So let’s describe what it is. It is a 3-sided holder with an awning in the front. There is nothing to enclose the bottom of the camera, and the side-cover is fastened to the camera with edges that clip under the camera between the camera body and the built-in grey base. Installing the holder/mount is a two-step process. First you slide the camera in from below and then you clip the “roof” or lid over the camera. This assembly can then be screwed on to the wall bracket that comes included. I think this is fine if you’re going to place the camera outdoors but not directly under rain or snow. I don’t think this mount gives it enough protection from direct elements… Under the eaves of a house, on in a porch should be perfectly fine. Lastly, the 360 degree swivel mount is not that good. Yes it rotates 360 degrees, but the tilt is limited to one direction. I mean, it’s not like the mounts you see for cell phones these days where you can rotate and angle the phone in any direction you want. Because the ball-mount is not directly attached to the camera, you are limited to tilting it only in the direction of the slot which gives you the tilt. That makes for a funny looking angle on your camera that I think could be easily remedied with a little design tweak.

First things first: if you’re trying to use wired headphones with this, don’t plug them in completely! The connection will be HORRIBLE if you do, I assume because the MP3 player thinks you’re trying to use the headphones as an antenna even if you’re not using the radio function. Plug them in until they’re snug but not fully flush against the player, and they’ll work fine. Also throw the provided headphones in the garbage, they’re as awful as you’d expect. Alright, on to the actual review. I bought this to keep myself from going insane during my long shifts in a noisy lab/factory, because we’re not allowed to use our phones on the floor and the radios we have barely work. I didn’t expect a whole lot from this, but it’s actually a pretty nice little MP3 player. The UI isn’t anything fancy, but it’s easy to read and navigate. The most annoying thing is having to use the buttons to scroll, but that’s not too bad. Also the player will turn off super quick if you’re not using it; the default setting for that is like 2 minutes, but you can change it in the settings menu. The speaker quality is better than I’d expected but still not great, but honestly, I don’t know why anyone would use the built in speaker when you can connect Bluetooth to this instead. The Bluetooth works a lot better than I expected, though I frequently have problems with my headphones but I think a big part of that is because my headphones are cheap and shitty. Usually when they’re acting up, I just have to go manually select them and hit connect, or restart the player if that’s not working. A little inconvenient but not horrible. The battery life is great. It charges super fast, and it lasts quite a while! I though they were exaggerating about how long it lasts, but I work 8 hour shifts and use it the whole time and I’ve yet to have it die on me. I usually charge every other day, but that’s more because I want to add more podcast episodes rather than because the player is fixing to die. It’s yet to die on me or even come close. I listen to more podcasts than anything, so for those of you also interested in listened to podcasts or audio books: the player WILL remember where you left off, but only if it was the last thing you listened too! Also if you do like I did the first day I had this player and accidentally skip to the next ep instead of fast forwarding, it’s a pain to scrub back to where you are. You have to have the episode playing and then hold the next/fast forward button down. It’s a slow process, but once you get used to it, it’s not too bad. I’d say the only real con about this MP3 is that it scratches super easily. The first day I used it, the screen was covered in scratches just from being in my pocket with nothing else in there. They don’t obscure the screen when it’s on, but it is annoying to see them whenever the screen is off.

I had encountered so many issues with this chassis, that I'm almost considering giving up. What should have only taken 15 minuets to install, has taken me 4 hours and counting. To start, the ITX power supply that I purchased "Apevia ITX-AP300W Mini-ITX / Flex ATX 300W (PN: B01M6V8O8T)" does not line up with the holes in this case. Each hole is about 2mm shifted to the right. This required cutting away at the lip on the case that the door rests on so that I could get the PSU to line up with the holes. Secondly, the screws that were included with my power supply have heads which are too large for the opening on this case, so I had to use the screws included with the case; problem with this is, all of the screws are cheaply made, and strip far too easily (literally one time is all it takes, hope you have steady hands). On top of this, the screws come thrown all in one bag with no labeling or organization whatsoever, so you'll enjoy separating them and figuring out where they go. I'm not docking any stars for this one, but be careful that your motherboard's rear cover isn't regular height, as this case uses a slim rear cover (not sure if that's a given, but it's not mentioned anywhere in the description). Although it's mentioned in the description, I am shocked that this product does not come with case fans, as those are typically a given on cases, especially ones in this price range. Again, not docking stars for this one. Also, if you aren't very good at cable management, I recommend looking elsewhere, as this case leaves virtually no room for cable management. Again, not docking stars for this, as it was known prior to purchase. As well, as can be seen from another reviewer's photos (Since the sellers refuse to upload pictures for whatever reason), a traditional 5.25" HDD can fit in here, but a SSD can not fit with it. Summary: • PSU Bolt Holes Not Aligned on Case: -1 • Disorganized Bolts Included: -1 • Cheap Bolts Included: -1

I mean, not a clear picture of anything. - After literally downloading only Angry Birds and a few other drawing apps for him, it wouldn't download ANYTHING else due to low space. (How on earth will this tablet be of any use to him if he can never download another single app ever again? My experience with nice turntables started in the 1980s when I bought the new Bang & Olufsen Beogram TX2 Linear Tracking Turntable with an exceptional Audio Technica cartridge (VS245LP). It was a beautiful piece of audio equipment with superlative sound reproduction. The linear tracking tonearm was one-of-kind, and it was a fun conversation piece whenever my friends would come over. The fact that it was "fully automatic" made it even more special. Reason: Audio component manufacturers no longer make high-end "fully automatic" turntables. You will soon understand why that is relevant to this story. In late 2018, my Beogram TX2 Linear Tracking Turntable started to show its age. It was no longer able to "spin" my newly purchased 180 gram (remastered) vinyl LPs at the proper speed. The additional weight (thickness) of the new 180 gram LPs was just a bit too "heavy" for the motor such that the albums played a bit "too slow". So the time had come to buy a new turntable-cartridge. I did quite a bit of online research, which is half the fun if you're like me and enjoy reading what the experts have to say about your exciting new investment. I'm so glad that I decided on the new Music Hall MMF Black 9.3 turntable. I won't go into its state-of-the art specifications---you can read about that in the product description here or the Music Hall website. Suffice it to say this is a perfectly engineered audio component. That was readily apparent from the first time I lowered the cartridge/stylus onto the virgin vinyl with the perfectly synchronized tonearm lever. The "remote" (detached) motor design is brilliant. Reason: there is no "constant low level hum" in this turntable which is audible in most other turntable designs where the motor sits just below the platter. I added a new deerskin turntable platter mat to give my "mint condition" LPs a clean, soft "static free" playing surface. A sweet bonus on this turntable is that it comes with a well-made (and very attractive) acrylic dust cover---a wonderful feature for a collector like myself, who likes to keep the dust off my LPs while they are playing. If I have learned anything about audiophile-quality turntables, I now understand the importance of "isolating" the platter from any unwanted vibrations that may be generated by nearby speakers and the constant "foot traffic" on the "pier-and-beam" hardwood floor surface near the turntable's location. For that reason, I bought the Black Mapleshade Platform with XL sized-Isoblocks (feet). This gorgeous four (4) inch thick solid block of maple wood (cut and air-dried by the Amish) was well worth the cost ($378). Treat yourself to a tour of their amazing products at www.mapleshadestore.com. Finding the perfect cartridge for my new turntable was a side project in and of itself. After reading dozens of rave reviews about Ortofon's 2M Black Cartridge with the nude shibata (diamond) stylus, it was a no-brainer. If you can scrape together $750 for this cartridge, you will never look back. I wanted to make sure there were no "weak links", so I purchased the Audioquest "Water" Analog Audio Interconnect RCA 1.5M Cables ($625). These gorgeous state-of-the-art cables are the best sounding interconnect cables on the market, as verified by the dozens of internet expert articles and audiophile guru reviews by people who work in the industry. These cables are connected from my turntable to my Onkyo P-3000R Reference Hi-Fi Preamplifier ($1,700)--a perfectly engineered audio component which purifies the sonics for all of my home audio and video components. I enjoyed reading the glowing customer reviews on Amazon about my Onkyo preamplifier. They confirmed what I already knew. I have listened to many uber-expensive "esoteric" turntable-cartridge demonstrations at the most exclusive home audio showrooms in Dallas and New York City. I can honestly say that none of them holds a candle to my current set up. As it turns out, the "icing on the cake" was a completely unexpected item that I stumbled upon as I was researching turntables (without cartridges) in the $2,000 range. I am referring to the stainless steel version of the "Tru Lift Tonearm Lifter" from Integrity HiFi Canada. It is sold on Amazon, and you can view how it works on YouTube or go to their website for a "demonstration video". This amazing little device is a $259 "must-have" for LP enthusiasts who don't want to be a slave to their turntable while they are busy in the kitchen, working at their computer, taking a shower, etc. Without the tonearm lifter, we all know what happens. The stylus on the cartridge plays the final song on the album. It then glides through the run out groove until it hits the edge of the record label. It continues to make that dreaded "thumping" sound until you lift the tonearm away from the spinning LP. Since the "fully automatic" option no longer exists in high-end turntables, the Tru Lift Tonearm Lifter is a lifesaver. It gently lifts the tonearm off the spinning LP after the final song is played. Priceless. I have acquired some very cool new 180 gram vinyl remastered LPs which sound amazing on my new turntable. "Snow Patrol---Final Straw". "The Cure--Mixed Up". "Alice in Chains--Jar of Flies/Sap". "Frank Sinatra--In the Wee Small Hours". "Jethro Tull--Songs from the Wood", just to name a few. I realize we all spend our hard-earned money in different ways. This project was a significant financial investment that may not appeal to most people, who are perfectly content streaming their compressed MP3 digital music through a mediocre "wireless" Bluetooth speaker system. But for those of us who appreciate the subtle nuances that can only be reproduced on pristine vinyl playing on analog components of this caliber, there is no substitute for this turntable-cartridge combination.

After about one year it would do nothing when turned on - dead as a door nail. The fuse was fine. I opened it up and tested the power transformer input and outputs - dead. There are no replacement parts available for this unit and I really didn’t want to put an OEM transformer back in anyway. Fortunately, there is an output schematic label on the transformer so I knew what I needed. I ordered 4 transformers from Mouser to provide the different voltages required. I was (barely) able to fit them into to cavity thanks to the fake transformer box on top behind the tubes. I spliced in the connectors, tested the output voltages, and put it all back together. Works perfectly fine and a bonus is that the little meter on the front panel now works. It was a lot of trouble to go to but it has turned out good for me. Unfortunately, it added about $60 to the cost but I hated to just throw it out. Hope this helps someone with a similar problem.

I needed a KVM to share keyboard, monitor, and mouse between two PCs. I settled on this. It seems like even in 2021, KVMs are overall bad. By the time I filter out the ones with obsolete connectors such as VGA, and ones that have HDMI but fail to support high resolutions and refresh rates, there is not much left. The ones that remain often have concerning reviews. I opted for a KM switch instead - I hook both PCs up to the monitor directly and use the monitor input to switch between them. That way I get 1440p/144Hz, guaranteed. This switch handles the keyboard and mouse flawlessly so far. It even has two extra ports if I need to plug anything else in. In that regard, it is more like a USB hub that connects to two PCs. I have not plugged anything in that requires more speed than a keyboard or mouse, such as a flash drive or USB hard drive. I am only reviewing its use as a KM switch. My only two gripes are its size and power. First, it is small and light. Very small, very light. It does not stay put on my desk. I have to wedge it in between other stuff to keep it from falling off the back of my desk. Second, it allegedly works without using the included power cable. When I do not use the power cable, the mouse does not work. Plug in the power, the mouse works. Just plug in the power cable. It seems like other products have similar issues, so I will plug it in to power and call this one a draw. Anyway, this works very well for my use case and I can easily recommend it if your needs are the same.

The keyboard feel is great.. keys are responsive, and the large 12.2" size allows for a really natural-feeling keyboard with a full compliment of control keys. It connects quickly to the tablet, and the internal battery goes on and on. The tablet stand works fine in either orientation, but be careful about using it on your needs or a soft surface -- if it tilts forward, the tablet falls down. The snap-together assembly of keyboard+tablet is also lame. I would have preferred a more solid hinge over the two-handed snap-apart-and-assemble drill you have to go through each time. The pen works quite well, and it's a luxury to be able to use it on the Note4 and Tablet with fluid ease. I'm not here to review Android. If you're buying an Android tablet, you know basically what you're getting. It's your Android phone, made large. The UI is almost identical to the Note4, with some added multi-app split-screen magic. The major weakness of this system is that the keyboard is not well-integrated into the system. There is *NO* system spell checker. Remember that it's your on-screen keyboard that does most of your spelling correction, so when you move to a Bluetooth keyboard, it all goes away without replacement. All email, web forms, apps -- nothing highlights incorrectly spelled words. I had no idea how much I would miss this, especially for business mail where simple typos can be a distracting embarrassment. Samsung needs to add a BT Keyboard spell-check mechanism for this to be a usable laptop alternative. Second, the on-screen keyboard keeps popping up! The BT keyboard is connected and working, but any pen-clicking on the screen slides up the on-screen keyboard as well. I had to install the Null Keyboard from Play to keep this from happening, but it has its own downsides if you switch to tablet mode. I have no idea why the key next to the space board would be "on screen keyboard". Who thought this up? You have a full keyboard, and one of the actual physical keys is devoted to bringing up the on-screen keyboard. Think about that for a moment. Battery life is okay, not great. Modern laptops can equal it, if you use the tablet all day. The screen is most of the power drain, so standby times are great. Bluetooth mouse support is also nice, and makes a great remote-desktop terminal with the keyboard. The split-screen functions are a bit limited (not all apps work) and buggy. The whole machine is a little buggy, in fact. It reboots itself randomly about once a day. Apps do not transition well from full screen to partial screen, and most are nearly useless in quarter-screen, so don't put too much faith in that multi-app functionality. Surprisingly, the apps work much better when used in the "windowed" mode where they float over the standard Android screen. This is pretty nice, if you are willing to work with very small text. All told, it delivers on the promise, but at this upper price point (competing with a top-of-the-line iPad or bottom-end Surface Pro 3!) it falls short of providing an all-day laptop replacement. The software really needs a real-time spell check and better multi-app support before it can be used for essential functions. I end up carrying both my laptop and this tablet, which rather defeats the point, right?

Great camera. I upgraded from using multiple DVX-900B units. Some small features garnered big points from me about this model: Lens: Incredibly wide and has excellent zoom properties. Though I wish it was a servo zoom - or at least had one more faster zoom speed, it is smooth and precise. I don't see a need to buy an additional wide angle with this superior lens. I love (finally) having ALC for audio (but still has the limiter function if you prefer) when I need it. Low light: Excellent. Maintains colors well, has more choices for gain (with very little noise compared to others) and maintains colors well in crappy lighting conditions. Battery life is good. Menus are complete. All the things I didn't like about the DVX900 series have been remedied here. Startup-to-record time is fast (and the PreRecord is great). Overall I am very happy with this purchase. A few things to note: Mine came from Electronics Basket. DO NOT BUY FROM THEM: Mine is a Canadian unit which has NO US WARRANTY. You can send it to Canada to have it fixed and also register there for your 3-year warranty, but NOT in the US. The seller denied knowing about this. They had to know - that's how the price was so low. To be fair, they offered a refund but wouldn't send another unit because they "wouldn't know if the same thing would happen on another unit." I asked if they would open the box of another to confirm US warranty but they would not. You'll know it's NOT US-bound if the warranty card says "Mississauga, Ontario, Canada" on the warranty card address, or you can call Panasonic to confirm country of destination (the units are cosmetically identical, however). Nonetheless, if it fails, off to Canada it goes. NOTE: Panasonic US tells me that if your model number is anything less than AG-AC130AP - specifically the AP - you do not have a US unit. AP designates North America (Including Canada and Latin America)...FYI. You can buy extended warranties from several places to solve this problem, if you think you might need service. I haven't ever serviced any of my three DVX-900B's in five years of ownership, and those units have a tape mechanism. More: This unit is significantly larger than the DVX-900 series. No biggie for me - the bigger the more impressive looking, though weightier (and it fits in none of my existing camera cases, save for flimsy ones). You pretty much need to stick to the original Panasonic batteries if you care about battery life. I bought BestDeal USA & MaximalPower additional batteries for a fraction of the cost and am paying the price. They are light: you can feel the lack of battery within. They are larger (lengthwise) and while secure, stick out farther from the rear of the camera. But the real problem is time. They claim to be 5800mAh (MaximalPower) & 6600mAh (BestDeal USA) but they top out at 2h55m for recording time after a full charge. I could live with that but in my tests they lasted nowhere near that. In fact, if you pause recording, power the camera off and then turn it back on, you'll see the remaining time drop before your eyes: It dropped from 2:40 to 1:55 in one second. Then I let it record 10 minutes, pause for two minutes and viola!, the remaining record time dropped from 1:50 to 50 minutes. In a matter of minutes of powering the unit off and on, I saw the power drop to 20 minutes. This is real-world use for me; I typically power off over long stretches to save battery power. To be sure, I was at an event with 30 minutes of remaining power, so I powered off. 10 minutes later I turned the unit on to discover only 10 minutes of power remaining. I hit record and maybe got 7 minutes of run time before the battery died. In other words, those remaining minutes (after a bit of use) seem to accelerate. Since I've tried three different batteries (two were MaximalPower), I suspect that all these cheapie batteries have an abbreviated life. It's no telling how long (many cycles) I will get out of them, either. When your file sizes reach 4GB, a new clip is created. My NLE (Newtek's SpeedEdit2.5) sees each individually, thus a multiple frame gap is evident in the clips. Other programs, like Premiere Pro CS6, use other data on the SD card folders to reconstruct the files to appear as one continuous clip (so I've read). I have CS6 but I don't like its obtuse nature, so I don't use Premiere at all. I always shoot multi-cam so luckily I can pull audio or another shot if needed to cover this issue. I love the quality but have noticed a slight moire pattern on some surfaces. My Sony A65 DSLR still has a big edge on color fidelity (colors outside are richer and the depth of field is as well), but we can't compare since the AC130 blows away the low-light capability of the A65. I was happy to learn that my Varizoom (Panasonic DV/HD) controllers work perfectly with the AG-AC130AP. Others have written that it is not compatible, but Panasonic is smart enough to see that the jacks and functionality are the same. At least I saved money there. Finally, the layout of the controls, including selecting mic/line input, engaging the power zoom and all pertinent controls are logically arranged on the user side (left) of the camera. No more flipping over, going around to the other side and otherwise searching for controls, compared to the DVX-900B. All of the jacks/connectors have snug-fitting snap-on covers (some attached to the unit) to allow easy access but protection when not in use. Well done, Panasonic. The menus offer a lot of customization and the only omission from Panasonic is the inclusion of a printed full manual. You'll get an abridged User Guide in the box, but you'll need to consult the included disc for the full manual. One utility I have put to the test is Panasonic's file recovery. I accidentally deleted all of the files from a recent job (which I never thought I'd do, but I didn't mark the SD cards and didn't run simultaneous recording on both cards). Panasonic's included software located and restored EVERY clip to my hard drive in one simple step. Now I know.

This product is good for the price point. It went up pretty easy, and is holding my 10lb tv with no problem. However, I'm deducting a star because of the lacking instructions regarding the 15-degree tilt capability. After reading many reviews, it's obvious that many are confused by this, so let me confirm that this unit does in fact tilt down 15-degrees, but it's not obvious how to do it from the instructions, so I'll offer up some advice. First, don't try to change the tilt after the TV is placed on the mount, it will be next to impossible. What you should do is attach the "X" like bracket to the back of the tv with the 4 bolts, then adjust the tilt BEFORE placing it on the mount by loosening the center nut (with the small wrench provided) then pivot/slide this square piece down until it stops (this will be the 15 degree point). At this point, you can tighten the nut again with the same wrench provided. After this, you can go ahead and place it on the mount, making sure to secure the center piece to the mount with the two tiny screws provided (which are also not mentioned in the instructions). These tiny screws attach to the threaded holes on either side (and below) of the center nut that you adjusted in the prior step. Good Luck.

**CAUTION** Certain microphones+phone combinations will work. I own Samsung S9+ and so far only one mic has worked (AT2100) due to it's capacitance isolation circuit used in the dual USB + XLR outputs. Several typical balanced 600 Ohm microphones will not work as it simply appears to be a short on the outer ring to sleeve of the TRRS plug. A test "fix" could be to make a barrel (XLR male+female) inline adapter with a small capacitor on PIN 2. The XLR adapter in this kit simple runs PINS 1+3+barrel together (ground) and PIN 2 (hot) to the matching TRRS pins with a 10K ohms resistor across it -- rather simple and irritating and basic circuit. Might work better on other Android or IOS devices. Should have gotten Line input instead and just used external pre-amp.

I love these for a couple reasons. I had a set of Rowkin Bits for almost 2 years until they fell out of an unseen hole in a coat pocket and I got to watch them roll down a sewer in downtown Indianapolis. These tend to do it more when I have both headphones paired and my phone in a front pocket. So I keep my phone closer and it lowers the amount of drop outs or I sit my phone somewhere and stay in range (the range is pretty good most of the time; I have a 2 story house and have left my phone upstairs with no issues while cleaning or doing laundry). With a single headphone (I use these more one at a time so I can hear around me) there’s never any drop outs. I’m not sure I buy their videos about “aligning the antennas” to prevent drop outs, but I guess they need to put out something. There’s no boom mic on this so the sound quality isn’t great during calls. I’m ok with that, as long as they can hear me. As I’ve pointed out in my review of the Bit stereo, these headphones go from good to great with Comply Foam tips (600 series fits; very snug installation). The noise isolation, bass, and overall clarity improves dramatically with a good seal and fit. Comfort isn’t an issue at all with the foam tips and I’ve gone for 14 hours switching one single ear piece to the other in the same ear with no fatigue. The charging case made that possible. There’s no issue with the headphones fitting in the case with medium foam tips in my experience. It’s tight, but they fit. Some others have complained that they don’t get a firm click when they close the case. Not sure if mine is different somehow but I’ve not experienced that. It clicks shut and won’t just open on it’s own. Charge is good, I’ve gotten several charges out of the case itself before I’ve needed to recharge it. I really wish I could advance tracks with a double click, but for the size and audio quality (with the foam tips) I’m ok with how these work. I use my Apple Watch to advance tracks and adjust volume so it’s not a big issue for me. The charging case feels nice and sturdy, and at it seems to be a nice median between the lipstick tube size Bit case that I used to have and watched roll away and the larger Bit Charge case (I’ve not owned a Charge but the size of that case is a turn off). The lipstick tube didn’t close once the headphones were in it either so there would be lint inside the tube. That case was magnetic too so anything metal would stick to it. The Micro case doesn’t seem to have any magnets and the size is just right for me. I can feel it in my pocket but it’s not annoyingly large. If anything I wish it wasn’t so shiny. It gets fingerprints pretty easily. Overall I’m pleased with the Micro after losing my Bit. Everyone asks what I’m using because of how small it is so a few coworkers have purchased sets and been pleased as well.

After a (probably far too) long time of scouring Amazon's laptop selection, I eventually settled on this model. I've had it for about 1 week, and in that time, I can say I am fairly happy with the purchase. Pros: Price. Considering what you are getting, this computer seems like a quality product for the amount it costs. Display: It's slightly larger than I expected and quite crisp. Battery: While this doesn't boast the 8+hours I've seen on smaller models, it has been hovering around 4-5 hours on batter. Keyboard: I enjoy the well-spaced out chiclet keys. It feels less cramped than other laptops I've used in the past, although, having the full numerical keys on the right will take some getting used to. Speed: This thing is a powerhouse compared to my last laptop (Acer Aspire 5100 with 1 GB RAM). The i3 seems quite quick and the 4 GB of RAM appear to have ample processor speed to handle most of what I do (Web browsing, streaming and light gaming). I think I will, however be upgrading to 8 GB RAM shortly, mostly because I can, when I figure out which sticks will work best. Windows 7 Home Premium: Having used the starter kit on some netbooks, this seems like a much better user experience. Protection plan: Since I haven't needed it (yet), I can't speak to how Asus is about fulfilling the drops and spills protection, but, being a clumsy person, I appreciate the piece of mind. Frame: The aluminum around the keyboard makes it seem like a much nicer computer than the price tag suggests, and so far it has stayed quite cool despite sitting in my lap. Undecided: Track pad: It has a nice feel to it and I enjoy the multi-touch functions, however, I have inadvertently clicked while trying to type emails on several occasions. This is a bit annoying, but I may just need to fiddle with the options. Cons: Setup/bloatware: For the most part this was easy; the initial setup took maybe 10 minutes or so. The downloading of the necessary updates from Windows, while not Asus' fault, took quite some time. Another gripe I have is the amount of bloatware. That probably took 2 hours to figure out what was necessary and what was useless crap (the facial recognition, while kind of a cool idea, is pointless to me [especially when I wear so many disguises]). One wish I have is that computer manufactures will start selling PCs with minimal software to allow customization without having to undo what they have already planted. Pipe dream, but I can bitch nonetheless. Cord: I wish it was just a bit longer. It's pretty easy to pick up a replacement, and I may do that. Speakers: They are laptop speakers, what did I expect? They are generally adequate for me (my apartment is pretty quiet), but if you live in a noisy environment, I would invest in some external speakers, or choose a different model. Conclusion: For the price, I think this laptop is a nice buy. I think this would be a great computer for people who do not frequently need to do labor-intensive computing (i.e. Photoshop, heavier-type games [WoW, etc.]). I imagine this will be fine for the occasional Photoshop session, but I think it would be slightly frustrating over time. It's a little larger than a netbook, but IMHO, it is far more functional and comfortable, while not adding significantly to the cost or heft. I would also suggest this to people heading to college as a computer that is portable, yet large enough to be comfortable. I'll post edits after I (find the correct and) install the RAM upgrade.

UPDATE: I finally reformatted this thumb drive and put it back into use. Having used less than 1/2 of it's available memory, I've already discovered missing files, entire folders of files in fact. I transferred about 10gb of data to it just last night, to free up some room on several other thumb drives. Between removing it and inserting it less than five minutes later, I noticed the remaining data had changed by nearly 10GB. Upon investigation I discovered that not only had several entire folders completely disappeared (fortunately I have them backed up elsewhere too), but a number of the files I'd just transferred couldn't be opened at all, as if they were already corrupted, though they aren't weren't corrupted on the thumb drive they were copied from. I use an assortment of nearly a dozen thumb drives from other brands and have never had a problem with any losing files (knock on wood) before this one by Silicon Power. Again, I can handle slow speeds, but reliable file storage integrity is an absolute must. This product is simply not trustworthy. So, we will avoid this brand in the future. At first this feels better made than the similar PNY version I've always used. But, it's very possibly an illusion created by the added heft of the rather robust steel guard. The device itself has already caused me some concern, as I've seen several files on it seemingly disappear. All of the sample image and/or video files that it came with disappeared the first time I saved anything to the drive. Only the warranty registration file remained. Take note: if you actually want to look at their sample files, do so before doing anything with this drive, as they may be coded to disappear upon first use. I also had one of my files disappear. I was moving a file into a folder, there was a sort of loading freeze before I could drag it to the folder, and next thing I knew the file was gone. I couldn't find it anywhere. I presume it was some sort of lag from moving another file just moments before and have been careful not to move them too fast since then, with no repeat of the incidence, that I can tell (I don't always check the folder I'm moving a file into to make sure it actually made it). Another oddity is how this drive shows a maximum capacity of 115gb, where my 128gb PNYs show 125gb of usable space. So, it seems you lose a lot of space from the factory formatting, which it comes formatted via FAT32, so that was convenient. I'm guessing those factory sample files are still on there, just hidden - though 10gb is a LOT of sample files - wonder what was on it. The connector does feel warmer to the touch than my PNY's. It's especially odd to feel how warm it is upon ejecting the drive, after a long period of not being used. That, combined with write speeds that are slower than even my older USB 2.0 drives, makes me ponder if I should scan the device for spyware from the factory. While this is still being advertised as USB 3.0, the drive amazon sent me (same Blaze B30 product name) says on the device and packaging that it's USB 3.1 instead. So, they're apparently doing a running upgrade to 3.1, rather than creating a separate product. It still works with both my USB 3.0 and 2.0 devices, but, again, even my older USB 2.0 thumb drives from PNY and Sony seem to work faster, at least when using USB 3.0 and 2.0 devices. Maybe if I actually had a USB 3.1 device I'd see some improvement in speeds. But so far this thing has even been slow to move files around on the drive itself, compared to others. And actually writing files to the drive itself, it seems to write in spurts and then pause for a bit, before resuming - rinse and repeat, rinse and repeat, depending on the file size being saved. Personally, I don't care about the slower speeds, but there's no excuse for vanishing files. Reliability is prerequisite. So I'm disinclined to gamble on this company again.
