First, although these LG 24" monitors retail for $299, I was able to pick one up on a price drop for $239 with free shipping and no tax here on Amazon. Most know monitors are one item where the prices fluctuate frequently, and if you are patient, you can score some pretty good deals. With that pricing, it makes this in the same price category of an ASUS VG248QE, which is pretty much the direct "competition" for this LG monitor. Plus, due to the everyday better price, and better marketing and availability of the ASUS, it is the top seller among the 144HZ, 1080p monitors. WIth the price drop here on the LG 24GM77, plus the more features and slightly better contrast / adjustments of the LG, it made picking this up a no-brainer. Then, as you will see, I also think this LG monitor is a better choice than either Benq offering - both the XL2411Z and the XL 2430T. One important fact about these 24" 144Hz monitors that most don't realize ---- all these "competing" 24" 144hz monitors use the same panel as the underlying build. T he ASUS VG248QE, the LG 24GM77, the BenQ XL2411Z, the BenQ XL2430T, the AOC G2460PG, the AOC G2460PQU, to name a few, ALL have the same panel. That's right - they all use the "AU Optronics M240HW01 V8 panel" - which means essentially they are the same monitor, and what really sets them apart is only hardware features (like a USB port) or software / firmware (like MotionBlur vs LIghtboost vs Blur Reduction). Then, how they handle the color via dithering might be different, and why some say the LG has "better color" than the Benq for instance. But they are ALL built on the same 6 bit + 2bit FRC panel. Next, there are some very real differences that you should consider when picking out these monitors: - The BenQ XL2411Z does not have a Display Port. That is an important fact considering DP is the future and DVI is being phased out. This monitor is priced fairly close to the ASUS, and a little less than the LG (retail pricing). Feature-wise, the LG has the edge on both the BenQ and ASUS. - The BenQ XLX2430T is bug ridden, and is not even able to save its configurations correctly from the OSD menu. This monitor has a lot of great potential and features, but the fact you cannot use the features because of bugs make it way over-priced. Don't believe me? Go read Blur Busters forum, there is a long 20 page thread entitled "Benq XL2430T Settings" which, toward the end, will give you a taste of the issues with this monitor. If you don't mind spending hours and hours installing Tweaks, configuring, taking risks, then this monitor is for you. It's really too bad, this monitor has great potential with its Blur Reduction - but using it is a whole 'nother thing. Also realize the BenQ is the most expensive of the bunch at $349 retail, and is hard to find on sale. - The LG 24GM77 - this IMHO is the best choice, and it also has 2 USB ports and a headphone jack that is on the side and more accessible than the other monitors. Some say the colors / contrast are better due to the dithering method used (remember, it is the same panel as the ASUS and BenQ), and I found this to be the case in my testing / experience with the Asus, Benq and LG side by side. So I agree with conventional wisdom here - I find the LG has better colors, and better blacks - running the "Lagom" suite of tests also verified the LG is better at contrast and black levels than this ASUS (and the Benq for that matter). Calibrated and configured, they both look good and are comparable, with an edge to the LG. Realize the LG will cost as much as $50 more than the ASUS RETAIL... but of course shopping and being patient can smash any pricing models - I was able to get the ASUS for $235 and an LG for $239. The BenQ XL2430T and the LG24GM77 were a virtual tie in picture quality, but the BenQ retails for $349 and is harder to find on sale. - The AOC monitors are usually your budget choices and the cheapest price wise. I have never owned one, but realize there is a reason for the low price leader - it is the same panel, but fit, finish, QC and support might not be as good in some instances. Many happy customers with the AOC of course, but have read some instances of the opposite being true. I will reserve any judgment on the AOC models since I have never owned or used one, but will parrot some of the luke warm responses for some of the users on the forums (although that always needs to be taken with a grain of salt). To add more color, I recently upgraded two home computers to EVGA 1070, and wanted to match those systems with new monitors. I bought three monitors home to try out at 1080p 144Hz - the monitors I tested with these systems were: this ASUS Vf248qe, an LG 24GM77, and the BenQ XL2430T. Before they arrived, I expected the BenQ to lead the pack, and I was wondering how the other two would stack up to the vaunted BenQ XL2430T.... but after setting them up and testing them, I am returning the BenQ XL2430T, and keeping the other two. Why did the highly touted BenQ XL2430T not make the cut? As already mentioned above, although it has a myriad of configurations and features, firmware bugs and other issues result in the monitor not being able to take advantage of these features, and the monitor is basically gimped / reduced to similar operating features of the the $240 price range monitors. It's a shame also, the 2430T had so much potential, but it is not worth the hassle IMHO. On the other hand, this ASUS, and the LG setup quickly, easily with no issue and just WORK!! Note: I don't use the Lightboost feature on the ASUS, nor the MotionBlur 240 on the LG - this is personal preference. Anyway, if you are shopping for a 1080p 144Hz monitor, and wondering if the ASUS will do the job, and balking due to all the forums out there calling the ASUS "old tech", etc.... hopefully this helped clear a few things up. The ASUS is a no frills, well priced option that plays at 144Hz well, and in the end just as good as any other choice. It may not have all the bells and whistles, nor have the latest Blur Reduction features, but ask yourself what you really need and don't need, and realize many just turn some of those features off anyways because in real life they cause more issues than they solve sometimes. What DON'T I like about the ASUS? First, operating the menus - the old "push button" menu operation on the ASUS is counter intuitive, and a pain in the nuggets to use and frustrating at times. Conversely, the best choice for operating OSD menus would be the BenQ XL2430T with the S-Switch - that makes menu operation a breeze. Next, the LG with its joystick is light years better than the ASUS, and another reason I like the LG more. Recall I am returning the Benq due to many other issues, mainly the number of bugs it has in the firmware. (many). Personally, I rated the ASUS a 4 out of 5, mainly because I think the LG edges it out, and the LG is more a 4.5 out of 5 rating. The LG just had better blacks and contrast. Summary of the LG vs ASUS vs Benq from the two units I received, and set up, testing, gaming, surfing: - The LG had better blacks - better than both the Benq and ASUS. - The LG had better contrast - as verified from Lagom and calibration tests - The LG had a much better menu operation joystick - only the Benq was better, the ASUS is the worst. - The LG comes out of the box with the best configuration and least tweaking required. BenQ is the worst, and even if you want to use it to its full potential, you are hampered by a myriad of bugs. The ASUS needs adjustment also, however, it is the most lacking in configurability. - The ASUS does not allow for Gamma mods in Standard Mode, and other options like Sharpness are grayed out The ASUS is a little "gimped" in Standard Mode. - THe LG has two USB ports, just like the BenQ XL2430T, and ASUS has none. - The LG USB ports and headphone jack are accessible on the side - the ASUS headphone jack is hard to access. The BenQ has the best accessibility, and includes a Mic port too. (I wish the BenQ didn't have so many issues, and didn't require the user to do the engineers job to make it work - e.g. Tweaks, accounting for bugs, etc). OK - so what is NOT to like about the LG 24GM77? Well, if you read the reviews on line, some touch on this also - but the biggest issue is the implementation of the DAS Mode and Motion Blur 240 feature on the LG. Simply put, if you want to use MotionBLur on the LG, here is what you have to deal with: - Motion Blur can only be used in 100Hz and 120Hz mode. This might or might not be an issue for some, but the bottom line it is a limitation. - Motion Blur cannot be used with DAS enabled - and vice versa. What does this mean, and what is the impact? Well, basically, when MotionBlur is enabled, DAS is disabled and your input lag / response time worsens. How much worse? I have seen some say it goes from like having a 1ms GTG monitor to having a 6ms GTG monitor, and the difference is vast. Others say the impact is real, but not that noticeable. Either way it is real, MotionBlur increases your input lag. - MotionBlur will impact the brightness and contrast. This is true of most monitors in this class - for instance the BenQ XL2430T also looses considerable contrast / brightness when BlurReduction is enabled. WIth the LG, the Brightness is automatically bumped to 100 when you enable MotionBLur to account for the darkening, and even though it helps I still see some contrast loss. The automatic bump to 100 brightness to me is a little "cloogy" - but then again, most of the implementations of Blur Reduction, Lightboost and Motion Blur all come with trade offs, compromises and negative impact in some ways that make them marginal in their value. As a result, I (or my sons' who are the gamers) just leave these features off and appreciate the inherent gain already realized by the 144Hz monitor. Overall, I think the LG is the best choice for the reasons mentioned above. Then, if you can get it for $239 with no tax / ship, then it becomes a no-brainer choice. What is interesting, the LG is probably the least known and least purchased of the three monitors which is mainly due to marketing and availability. But for those that chose the LG, you will see mostly high praise for the monitor. Thanks for reading, happy monitor shopping. Oh, and keep an eye on pricing for this ASUS - about a week ago, Best Buy and Amazon had this for $219 for a couple of days - I jumped on it, and don't regret it. This and the LG I bought seem to fit the bill well for the two gaming boxes that are now equipped for 144Hz and GTX 1070!! As of writing this review, the price of the LG monitor has climbed back up to the $299 range -- when I bought it for $239 from Beach, Amazon, Newegg and BH had it for $249. Who knows when it will see that level again, the monitor prices seem to change frequently.. EDIT::: I wanted to briefly address if this monitor is something you can use on a daily basis, and not just for gaming. Let's just say if you are doing video editing, and need 100% color accuracy, and only have space for ONE MONITOR for both gaming and every day use you would be best served looking elsewhere. All TN panels were not made for this, they are made for the low input lag and are better for gaming. Then, even if you don't do video editing, and you have always worked with an IPS monitor, are a stickler for the finest details of resolution, sharpness and may even like a glossy screen, then again, a TN display may not be the best for you as an EVERY DAY monitor. Again, the assumption is you have to use the same monitor for gaming AND everyday use. But it doesn't have to be an "all or nothing" proposal in the first place - for instance, my sons' who use these LG's for gaming have a SECOND monitor that is a 60hz IPS monitor. That way, they can decide which monitor they want to use for any particular endeavor. Playing a game and want high refresh? They use the LG. Surfing the web, or doing homework? They have a choice of using the IPS monitor, or even having the luxury of using BOTH!! In other words, if you have the space for two monitors, and you like to game at high refresh rates - get two monitors with dual purpose in mind. All this being said - if you can only have ONE monitor in your setup, and you want to game at 1080p in high refresh rates - then obviously your choices will be limited. But, realize this LG and even the BenQ XL 2430, are great monitors for TN panels, and although not as crisp as top level IPS in contrast / sharpness quality, they can very well be used as an every day monitor. Depends what your needs are, and MANY people use these TN panels for every day use. END EDIT

Generally, it is a well made, good camera when it works. It gives me a certain peace of mind that I will have a better chance fighting insurance companies which in most of cases refuse to pay unless you had a witness in your car who would testify in your favor. The camera came without any real manual but with something like a "quick start" instruction written in broken English. There was no manufacturer name-address or any information related to a warranty. So, it is a gamble. And then like many other people I experienced the camera stopping working after recording for several seconds or a minute. Since it was already too late to return it, and the address for warranty claims was "to Mainland China", I had to get to the bottom of this or to toss the camera into a trash. I finally discovered that the camera did not like my 16 GB SanDisk Ultra Class 10 UHS-1 micro SD card. Replacing it with a 8 GB SanDisk Class 4 micro SD card from Walmart solved the recording problem and I have been using the camera successfully for the last two months. Obviously, the problem is related to a firmware which is my case was LDJ72B-20120712-v.4.0. The picture resolution is good to read a plate if you are close enough. Video quality is subject to the lighting conditions, of course, as it is with any small digital cameras, and to how clean your windshield is. Dirt on a windshield does not interfere with focusing but may significantly reduce resolution. Camera is practically a Plug and Play devise. There are very few settings that can or need to be changed. You hook it up and then it starts recording when you turn your ignition on, and shuts down after you turn the engine off. Important questions are: what size of a SD card one needs, and what to do if you recorded an accident and do not want the camera to erase the recording while looping (longest loop available is 10 min)? 8 GB card is sufficient, as the size of the 10 min recording video file at highest resolution is about 1.5 GB. This means that even with 8 GB card you can record for almost an hour. I recommend a 5 min loop as it will make it easier to play your videos on a computer. The camera creates a separate file for each loop and places all the files into a folder labeled according to a date of a recording. It keeps all the videos on a card until it runs out of space. The camera was easy to attach to a windshield. Clean the spot where you want to attach it. Attach the mount during the hottest part of the day and do not remove it unless it absolutely necessary. Do not keep the camera mounted in the car if it gets hot in your area as no electronic equipment can sustain high temperatures. The camera is very easy to remove and to reattach to the mount. I take it off and place it into a small heat insulated "lunch bag".

My other digital is the Finepix s9100. My previous photographic equipment experience spans 35mm through 120; 4x5, and 8x10 view camera formats; and darkroom work. I currently do not print larger than 8"x10", at a minimum of 300 dpi. I am enjoying the camera. Has a good balance of features, good optics, etc. A notable point about this model is its performance (for a non-DSLR)at ISO 400, and in a pinch ISO 800. That combined with its RAW mode and 28mm wide end. I would recommend it to: Someone that does not want to go to DSLR, but is used to film and manual lens work, and wants an all-in-one camera. I am finding mine exspecially nice for general use by hand, and "street-shooting". While a beginner can use it, (the program mode is very nice, I would think this model would be most satisfying for a person who has been doing photography for awhile. Pluses for me (so far): 28mm wide end. The most recent update of Adobe Photo Raw 4.1 recognizes this camera. That Adobe plug-in is compatable also with Elements 5.0. I do not use the Fuji software at all. RAW mode. A manual zoom ring. The superior performance at mid-ISO (for a "superzoom), such as 400. I can obtain nice 8x10 in color or B&W, at that speed. 800 ISO gives you night/street/carnival etc. options that are useful in an informal way. The "chrome" mode looks like Fujichrome 50 at about -1/3 stop. Figures I guess. But nice if you are shooting color and used to slide film. Downside: While it has been functioning well, I would pay more if this model/design had more metal in the body, and the tripod socket (it is plastic) were metal. XD cards. 2gb limit. More expensive than SD/CF, etc. While it is not an issue for me, the time lag to write a RAW file is long. If you want to shoot action in RAW, this is not your camera. JPEG is fine, and with this model, I use it mainly in JPEG (handheld)anyway. As others have pointed out, the RAW mode choice should be "under" the F button, not in the setup menu. Recommended.

Overall a *fairly decent TV, especially for the black Friday price of $350. However,the cheap price comes with a cost. *Picture quality during HD playback seems quite good. Like most other LED televisions, picture and settings will need to be adjusted to get the most out of the experience. I found the "movie" picture preset to be a good starting point. *Bright scenes tend to be colorful and vibrant. No complaints. *TV does not do well with SD cable, although this is normal for many LED/LCD HDTVs. *Sound is sub-par at best, but can be remedied via external sound systems. **The biggest issue with this set in my opinion is back light bleed (especially in corners). I returned the first set as I deemed the extent of the bleed to be unacceptable. During normal viewing the experience is often ruined by the pervasiveness of light bleeding through into the picture, destroying the atmosphere and mood of dimly lit and dark scenes. Once you see it, it cannot be unseen. You will find your eyes being pulled away from the picture to focus on what appears to be the soft glow of little street lamps extending out in a fan pattern from the corners of the television set. The replacement I received had similar issues, though just slightly less extensive than the first. Other reviewers have pointed this out as well, and unfortunately this seems to be the norm with this set. The response from Seiki Tech Support regarding this issue: you can not compare lcd with led. led is the backlight. you will have bleed through. lcd does not have led lights. just has one long light bulb. example. lcd: one long blun at top and shoots light all the way down. led: 10000 led lights that fill the screen so there is no compares-en . this is why you can tell. there is nothing that can be done. -- Jerry Tech Support In closing,this TV gets the job done at a cheap price. It's thin, light, has and has the potential for good quality HD playback with a little tweaking. It shines during bright, colorful scenes, but disappoints during dark moody scenes due to back light bleed issues. Be aware of the pros and cons prior to purchase.

Pros: - Great Picture Quality: especially if you hardline your device instead of connecting it to wifi. - Roku built in: allows us to search multiple subscription services and channels at once for the content we're looking for, then select from a list based on cost. Incredibly convenient. - Voice search: My favorite feature. Just hold the button on the remote, say the name of the content, or a keyword, or an actor, or a genre, etc, and get a list of matching or related content to choose from. Awesome. - Longevity: Little to no risk of burn-in (unlike OLED TVs). - Remote: clean layout, easy to use by "feel" in the dark. - Sound: This TV's sound is actually pretty impressive out of the box. We use a Samsung soundbar and sub, but if you don't plan on using externals, the TV can handle audio well. Cons: - Misleading search results in Roku: content often says "free" but then when you select it, they want you to subscribe to the channel and pay (often after a free trial period). - Minor navigation annoyances: Roku makes you leave a channel before you can use search. This can get annoying if you search for something, enter the channel, then find out they want your to pay (due to the misleading "free" indicator mentioned above), then you have to leave the channel and search for the content again. - Subtitles are not customizable: The subtitles are too large on this already-large monitor, and you cannot make them smaller or more transparent. - Standby light: the light on the front of the TV when the TV is off is large and bright grey. If this TV is set up in your bedroom, it is like a giant night light. - The feet/stands: these are placed very wide on the TV. If you were hoping to put your TV on a table, you're table needs to be wider than the tv; other TVs have "central" feet/stands that allow you to place the TV on more surfaces. (We bought an extra VESA mountable stand to address this problem.) - Remote: the block of four "branded" buttons at the bottom of the remote are an issue. You cannot customize these, so if you don't have Hulu, Netflix, Disney+, or Sling, you have 4 useless buttons on your remote. Summary: I know there are a lot of cons there, but this TV is *such* a good deal -- excellent quality for under $1000 -- that these minor annoyances do not affect the recommendation. I highly recommend any of TCL's new microLED televisions.

Overall, I'd give this product a 4.5 out of 5.0. My personal satisfaction is a 5.0, but I think for most users, the technical savviness required would dock a partial star. I've owned the 5010, 5020 and both hardware versions of the 5222L, all shipped from Amazon. The 5222L is much better than the older non-HD versions, and the Rev B of 5222L is even better than the 5222L Rev A hardware. I ordered the exact same 5222L model from Amazon on two separate occasions. My first order from May 29, 2014 shipped with the Rev A hardware. My second order from June 15 shipped with the new Rev B hardware. I'm very happy with the 5222L, and am a little bit happier with the Rev B. I will actually be exchanging my Rev A with the Rev B. I just ordered my 3rd 5222L from this page, and hope to receive the Rev B hardware again. Here are some major differences between the 2 hardware version: Rev A - Slightly larger and heavier body. - Smaller field of view -- it's a more zoomed in picture so you see less. - Need to plug in external speaker for sound output. - Wifi is great. I stream exclusively this way on this cam. Rev B - Smaller body, closer to the 5020L in size. - Wider field of view. I found the HD picture clearer, perhaps because it wasn't as zoomed in. - I prefered the picture quality of Rev B over Rev A. The colors were great. The light sensitivity performed very well in day mode. Night mode is awesome and gives you extremely clear images. - Built-in speaker. I love this! I can talk to the baby and sitters when watching from work. - The UI has more features. It's a bit more responsive, and you can scroll the liveview with a mouse, which is actually extremely useful since the picture on this is enormous when looking from a browser and you'll usually want to center the image when you first login. - Night-time IR mode controls are more automated and no longer on the main live-view screen. I found this to be an improvement. The day/night detection is a little better and general picture quality in poor light conditions are overall improved, so I don't miss having to manually flip between night/day modes from the main live-view controls. - Wifi seems just as good as Rev A. Remote viewing on mydlink.com was relatively easy to set up, but I actually found better performance when connecting directly with the camera using the dynamic DNS service (dlinkddns) that comes free with this camera. I have all my cameras mapped to different DDNS ports. I find this way gives you much better controls over the camera remotely. It definitely requires a lot of patience and fidding to set up, but you'd get better results. I also have all the cameras set up this way and accessed on our mobile devices using the "IP Cam Viewer App" on Android. I've found that all D-link cameras are supported well by several of the top-rated generic android and iOS webcam viewers. The D-link drivers, including the 5222L drivers were in most of the apps I've tried. I would still recommend going the mydlink.com route for most users. It works and is easy to set up. (Tip: if you decide to use mydlink.com, you will be required to update to the latest firmware versions. Don't do it the automatic route when mydlink prompts you. It's much faster to download the firmware yourself and to manually install it by logging into your camera and going to the Maintenance tab. Updating over-the-wire from the mydlink website had me stuck at the progress timer for a long time and ended up not completing properly.) I think this cam received a lot of poor reviews here mostly because of user friendliness. It's a bit hard to setup, but to be honest, I think all PTZ netcams are pretty complex if you compare them to a Dropcam. The D-Link-suggested mydlink.com setup route is actually very very simple compared to other netcams I've owned. D-link webcams are great. I find them more reliable that other brands I've owned (Panasonic) and that they rarely need to be restarted or reconfigured once you get it up and running.

As other reviewers have noted, the sound on these headphones is remarkable especially considering how small they are. I also really like the noise-cancelling pads, which actually do work quite well to block out noise. On those two counts, these are exceptional headphones. However, again as noted by others, the life of these phones is exceptionally short as well. Sure, it's certainly possible that if you treated them with kids gloves 24/7, hardly moving them etc., they would last a long time. It's possible, though I will never know. I use them as I would a normal set of headphones, and after 3 months they began failing. I know the problem isn't with my iPhone since I tried other headphones and they work without a problem. These, however, after a mere 3 months, are almost unusable. Sometimes both ears work fine, sometimes one ear is off, either totally or at a lower volume. This makes for a jarring experience. I can't even listen to a talk podcast without the sound shifting from ear to ear or going in and out in one ear. To get both ears working properly, I need to fiddle around with the wire until that happens. As a result, these days I use it mostly when my iPhone is stationed on a table, and I jiggle the wire so the sound is good in both ears, and then don't touch it. If I touch it, it might revert back to playing through one ear. In short, 3-4 months is an awfully short life for headphones. For this reason, and this reason alone, I DO NOT recommend purchasing this. I say this with sadness, since I would have loved to give it a 5 star review since the sound is fantastic especially for the size and price.

I had some concerns seeing reviews of these phones not lasting long. After only two weeks, those fears are not completely alleviated. But I can give some initial impressions and observations. First off, I have to say the build quality seems pretty solid, and it makes me wonder what people are doing to their phones that they're breaking in half or falling apart. We'll see as time goes on how they hold up. This is my first pair of planar magnetic driver headphones (I'm comparing with Sennheiser HD599 and Grado SR80i). I think there is definitely a break-in period, and the longer I listen to them the more they warm up and sound more natural, less sterile and digital. The first thing I noticed was a huge stereo field, wider than any headphones I've had before. But along with that comes the symptom that anyone nearby can clearly hear what you're listening to. That's open back headphones for you, but these HiFiMan HE4XX seem even more open back than others. I can clearly hear separate instruments in a mix, panned across the stereo field. To some extent it depends on the mix, and mixes with very little panning do sound smaller and more intimate. The second thing I noticed was the balance. Most headphones have at least some noticeable emphasis on certain frequencies. My Sennheiser HD599 certainly have more bass emphasis. The Grado are more neutral. But all the frequencies seem to get the same attention here, and I like that because it gives me the choice to boost the frequencies I want using an EQ, and I feel more confident tracking into my DAW with them. In other words I'm less worried about emphasized frequencies throwing off my perception. The third obvious thing was how the different frequency ranges were presented. The bass, while not emphasized or boosted, is very smooth and clear. It does not sound distorted or mushy at all. The highs, while crisp and clear, are never harsh or hissy. They are sort of rounded in a way, but without going soft. To me that is pretty awesome. Fourth, I found that with other headphones, I find myself turning them up probably a little too loud to hear more details or hear the music better. With the HE4XX, I can just turn up to a comfortable level and hear everything clearly. Less fatigue after an hour or two. If there's a downside to the HE4XX, it's that they take a fair amount of power to drive them. More than my iPad Pro has to give. So when connecting to mobile devices, I have to have an headphone amp in between. I'm currently using a FIO E17K, which offers a good amount of distortion free volume boost along with EQ when needed. With my HX Stomp (used for connecting studio monitors and recording guitar) I don't need a separate amp, but I do need to turn the volume up significantly compared to my other phones. Overall, I love these headphones and they're definitely an upgrade from my previous headphones.

Summary: This is a robust mount for certain applications, particularly for televisions that do not require the included VESA brackets. However, the use of screws with small pan heads and narrow washers are an imperfect match for larger, heavier TV's. The two-screw with press-nuts mounting plate is also no more than a light-to-medium duty design. Incorrect M8 screws originally included. The TV being mounted was a 65", weighing approximately 63 pounds with VESA 400x400 mounts. The mounting bracket that affixes to the wall is robust, unquestionably. Also, the 3 1/2" lag screws are very strong (appear to be 5/16" size) -- in fact, we used our own 2 1/2" 1/4" lag screws (qty 6) as the included screws were too long, but the bracket will be very strong when mounted with any similar screws into studs. The hinges on the bracket also come tight, and seem like they will last. The key reason for returning this -- and this is a very big concern to me -- is the included screws and washer (parts C & D within the instructions) are too small to hold the VESA brackets. I'm not sure how the attached photos will be ordered, but there are 3 in sequence which shows me placing a pan screw (C) into the bracket slot opening, and the screw just drops right through. The next picture shows the washers (D) that are intended to be used with this screw, but they are narrow profile. Despite the robust mounting plate, lag screws and terrific hinges, all the weight of a VESA mounted TV is going to be carried through these 4 screws which don't correctly fit the bracket sizes, and the 4 undersized washers they go through. I could almost accept this with the right washers, but the washers are thin, and I don't know the grade of the screws. If you have a smaller TV that doesn't require the VESA brackets, this isn't an issue. I’ve installed many types of custom fixtures and equipment, using standards called NEBS, Telcordia, etc. The included hardware here, for a VESA mount, would not pass these. My experience tells me we are getting into the danger zone with this design. There are also two pictures showing the construction of the center mounting bracket, which attaches to a smaller bracket which is permanently mounted to the hinges. There are two issues with this: i. There are only three screws, approximately #10 size, pressed into this bracket. Almost all TV mounting systems use 4 screws at this point, and they are usually larger than this, around #12 or 1/4". Some even use 5 screws. ii. The screws are pressed into the TV-side bracket, which makes them flush, but all the force of the TV rests through these three points. I would much prefer removable screws/bolts. Also, the top screw slides in a notch, rather than through a drilled hole. A relatively minor point, but the included docs indicate that "M8 45mm 1.25" screws are included...unfortunately, what was actually included was the 35mm lengths. Somebody at QC isn't watching. (pic included showing 35mm screw) As an aside, no reviews are showing this so I included a photo on a center-stud wall. The wall plate must be offset to one side. Our old non-articulating plate could pull apart sideways to mount across 32", allowing symmetry across the walls with a center stud, giving inherent centering. This new mount (like almost all mounts today) isn’t that wide, requiring you to choose which side of the center stud to mount. The TV can easily be centered once mounted, but you lose about 8" of your extension range just to center it. No one talks about that. Think about this when wondering how much extension you'd like the mount to have. I'd like to give the OEM credit for the things done right, and including the 35mm screws is obviously an oversight. However, the use of lashing together VESA brackets and using small screws to do it, should be re-thought. Most modern day mounts don't use screws here, relying instead with TV-side brackets with notches than hang on the wall-mount side. If you have a larger VESA mounting requirement, I'd suggest looking at that option.

I've only had my Fab Quality HD 720p spy pen camera for a few days but so far it is definitely worth the price. In addition to the spy pen I received an instruction manual, five replacement ink cartridges, and a 16GB micro SD card already inserted into the pen. After ordering this product I received an email from the company thanking me for the purchase and providing a link to a short Youtube video tutorial for this spy pen camera. There was also an attachment to the email containing what was stated to be an updated instruction manual but it looks the same to me as the small one in the box. Taking photos with this pen camera requires a decent amount of light, and most indoor shots will turn out below what most of us would accept for our pictures. Outdoor and well-lit photos look good. Video does look better than should be expected for the price of this camera. I was happy with this as it was of course the main reason for buying this device. The quality of videos goes up with the amount of light and this doesn't work great in low light conditions, but still isn't that bad. The motion detection mode works fine so far. When I first set the camera pen to this option, if no movement is detected in three minutes the camera pen shuts off. However, if I set the pen to motion detection and trigger it once, it will record until three minutes of no movement and then will stop recording but stay in MD mode and continue cycling between recording and waiting for movement until the battery runs out. Connecting the spy pen to my computer running Windows 7 was easy but each time asks if I want to scan and fix removable disk. I choose continue without scanning and have had no problems. Windows Media Player opened the video files automatically but they look better using VLC media player. After a full charge I can get a little over an hour of continuous recording before the battery runs out, but then it can take over one hour forty-five minutes to fully charge again. I accidentally dropped this spy pen camera into the sink and it hit pretty hard, it later fell about five feet to the ground without the pen half connected, but the operations all seem to be fine after each. So far I am pleased with this purchase and may order another.

I purchased four DCS-930L cameras to set up a DIY home surveillance system. Overall I am happy with what they can do with such a low price tag. The installation was easy. After opening the box, I connected cameras to my router with network cables. And after I inserted the CD into my computer, the auto-run program led me through the entire process step by step. The program had no problem finding the cameras, and registered them to mydlink.com. That was the only time I needed that CD-ROM. Any additional setup, such as wireless, video, audio, motion detection, email, or ftp, etc, could be performed via mydlink.com. I could change the settings from anywhere with internet connection. And unlike other products, mydlink.com is free. This is indeed terrific! Setting up the wireless for DCS-930L was not difficult either. If you have the experience of adding a few window-based PCs into your home wireless network, you will find the process to add DCS-930L is exactly the same. I entered the SID and the WEP password, disconnected the network cable from the cameras, and unplug/plug the power cord. In about 1 minute the cameras (now wireless) showed up on mydlink.com! The wireless range on this camera is very good. I think D-link really listened to their users, since there were lots of complaints on the poor wireless range of its previous version DCS-920. I have a big house with many rooms. In a few remote rooms with many walls in between even my itouch cannot find wireless signal. But DCS-930L can! And the connection is always stable. So far I have never lost any video feed yet. Without wireless connection concerns, I can put the cameras anywhere there is a power outlet. (Yes, DCS-930 does need a power line. So it is not completely wireless. But I could always find outlets close enough to plug my cameras in.) A new feature you cannot find in DCS-920 is the motion detection. Again, via mydlink, I turned on motion detection, adjusted the detection sensitivity, and then selected the areas in the view point to be on/off motion detection. The sensitivity and the areas depend on what the cameras point to and the lighting condition of the time. So it took me a few days to experiment different settings in morning/evening sun-light, etc. After that, I went to the email setup page and select "motion detection" so that emails will be triggered by the motion detection. I intend to use it when I am away from my house. Again, DCS-930L has an enhancement over DCS-920: I can set up SSL emails so that my email password is always protected. The video quality is 640x480, which I believe is the same as the DCS-920. However, DCS-930 has an enhancement: Audio. I could hear the sound from the camera even when I clap my hand in a different room! Of course the quality of both video and audio is no where near HD. But given the low price tag, I have no complaints. The only major issue I can think of is the lack of the night vision. Without it the camera can hardly see anything during the night, and the entire surveillance system is therefore useless. (However, no camera in this price range has night vision, at least I could not find one.) Overall I am very happy with the camera. And I will not hesitate to recommend it to anyone.

I love the fact that this is a cheap device with great performance. I am so looking forward to playing with this on a regular basis. I am thankful that this was out there. It was either buy this $15 device, or drop about $1500 to $2000 on a more high-end 4K Television that would give me the option to use more than one HDMI port for HDMI Color UHD (which is the name of the setting that you have to have turned to "on" in the picture settings for Samsung 4K TV's to get the HDR feature). Because I have heard some reviews, such as..."this splitter would make red lines/dots on the screen", or "no sound from second port", or "Ordered at the beginning of May (2017). I use the HDMI Splitter for both my XBox One S and my PS4 Pro. Both work amazing on my console. This is the second *high performance* SSD I have purchased - the first was an MTRON 32GB - for $900. This drive is about 50-100% faster than my MTRON, with ~150 MBps writes and 156 (random) and 201 (seq) MBps reads (256k blocks). Its also about 70% cheaper and has 4x the storage. I am using it in my unibody Macbook. OCZ publishes firmware updates for this drive, but I didn't install them to get these speeds. The firmware update process pretty much requires a desktop Windows XP computer with a spare sata port that isnt running an NVidia chipset. Oh and you will need a spare motherboard jumper laying around. I attempted it with my Vista 32 desktop (with NVIdia chipset), and I just couldnt get it to flash after an hour of trying the workarounds, and didnt have the patience to try any further. Don't let that dissuade you from getting this drive - its still an incredible drive and great value out of the box! I ordered this on 4/1/09 and it had the 1199 firmware. One last note: not to downplay what a great drive this is, but it really underscored for me how great the MacBook is with its default 320GB 5400RPM drive. I have not really noticed the difference as much as when I updated my 7200RPM drive to the MTron under Vista, and I really think that is due to the fact that the MacOS performs so much better under lesser hardware. So, if you're a MacBook user, you might want to reconsider this drive unless you are running some apps which are definitely going to make use of it. Upgrading just for better boot speeds and app start speeds might leave you a little underwhelmed.

I have put this monitor through some extensive testing with various movie formats and PC games, and it generally passes with flying colors. It does take some time to adjust the desktop and video playback settings, in order to get it the way you want it, but that was the only real complaint I'd have. When my Acer 24" 241W monitor went dead (it had been going downhill for some time), I wanted a brighter, clearer monitor that offered more vibrant colors and better movie playback in particular. After doing research and reading reviews, I settled on this Samsung 23" slim LED backlit monitor. As others state, blacks are "black" and rarely looked washed out, but that is also dependent on the quality of the media you are viewing. Streaming HD video from Netflix or Hulu looks fantastic, as do regular DVD's, in particular if they fill up the entire screen in 16:9 format instead of letter boxing on the sides (which I cannot stand). It's important to note that I have a Nvidia 285 GTX 1024MB video card, which is still rather high end at the time of this review, and Directx 11c. I also installed the trial version of PureVideo from Nvidia, and it "seems" to have somewhat dramatically improved video playback, but it's hard to tell if that is from my tweaking or the program's enhancements. In any case, I had the best luck tinkering with the video color and playback settings in the Nvidia control panel, pushing up the sharpness and noise reduction to about 20% and tweaking the brightness and contrast to my liking. Games simply look great out of the box, colors are bright and vivid, accurate and the 2ms response time serves games well. The monitor's built-in menu is easy enough to navigate and only takes a little practice, but I have let my video card's settings take over for the most part, as noted above. It was very hard to find an LCD/LED monitor that had across-the-board high reviews, most of them are still lacking with multimedia. This Samsung model is probably the best, and paying an extra $50 for the quality seems to be worthwhile thus far. The monitor is sleek and attractive looking, lightweight and slim. It was a bit more of a size reduction than I anticipated from my Acer 24", but you get used to it fairly quickly, and is due more to the slim profile of the entire monitor, than the screen size. As HD video becomes more available and popular online, along with the great enhancements in Windows 7, this monitor stands above most of the others, and is again very much worth the extra $, you get what you pay for, and I've learned that lesson time and time again! Two thumbs on this model.

First the minuses. (-) Multicolor cable is pointless and serves zero purpose other than to increase cost. (-) Breadboard is segmented and has two groups of power rails. The ad shows this but I missed it. This means if you want the power rails to be contiguous, you have to jumper them. More of an inconvenience than anything else but it does cost you 8 pin positions. (see my attached photo where I added red and black jumper wires ) Pluses (+) Breakout board is narrower than most GPIO Breakouts and therefore gives access to three rows of pins on each side.(Blue board in my pics) Competitors products such as the Kuman board(Red board in my pics) are too wide and sacrifice a row of pin access by blocking two rows. (+) Board has separate power pins which plug directly into the power rails. This is a HUGE benefit because it eliminates the need to run power jumpers directly off the already crowded GPIO power and ground and makes wiring much simpler. (+) The board has an LED power light "H U G E!!!!" advantage because it gives you that extra confidence that you have the ribbon cable plugged in correctly and that you have power going to the breadboard rails. This alone is worth buying this product. I can't tell you how many times when I am swapping out breadboards I inadvertently plug in the ribbon cable backwards. This fixes that. Note: Most breakout board use the Kuman(Red board in my photo) method and make the board too wide and require you to sacrifice a row of pins. There are other's that have the power pins like this board but I don't think they have the LED power indicator light. There's only one thing I wish they had which only one manufacture I've seen ever produced. That would be the ability to jumper select whether or not the power pins are 3Vdc vs 5Vdc. Unfortunately the maker of that product was in England and went out of business.

[[VIDEOID:9038c5d60a1fd3a70f20a335ff82c5ed]] I am a professional photographer for over 18 years and have a full time working studio. I bought this to use for on-location headshots in which taking a full background stand and seamless paper are too hard to set up by myself. PROS - It is very robust, the frame is solid, it's well built, and I love the value of the added reflectors (I didn't buy it for that purpose but it was a nice bonus). Great value for the money, and the size is great for headshots and one-person portraits, though you could probably snuggle two or three family members together in tight and have just enough room, with maybe a little Photoshop to fill in the corners. The finish is very matte and did not reflect the light at all. Big plus. The fabric had a few small wiggles in it (I would not even call them proper "wrinkles" as they were so small) but if you're shooting with the subject a proper distance from the background (4 to 6 feet), and you're using a long lens with a lot of background compression (recommend 70-200), you're never going to see them. Now, if you're using this to shoot video with an iPhone, or you don't have enough space to account for that background-to-subject distance, then yes they may be more noticeable depending on your aperture. CONS - The white is not a super crisp bright white. You can see from the photos and video that it is a much "duller" white than the other white items I have positioned around it. I believe this is because the black reverse side and the slightly thinner fabric means it absorbs a bit more light than I'd like. To combat this, you will need to use a background light to give it that nice crisp clean white look. I do also wish it was just a teeny bit more "square-ish", as my standing shots I could just catch the roundness of the edges....nothing a little cropping won't fix and not necessarily a reason not to buy it, but ideally would be great if it were less oval and more "rounded off square", if that makes sense. OVERVIEW - Would I buy it again? For shooting on white, I would probably choose another product personally. For the other colors, and the value for the money, or if you need a giant reflector, definitely a good buy.

I really wanted a QLED TV, namely by Samsung, after seeing them in stores. They were always the best looking and always showed individual things on their screen with better contrast and color. I looked into higher models and was happy to learn I could also get one that was 120 hertz for the best motion fidelity. When I saw this particular offer for this model I was excited because it was quite a bit less than anything comparable, and it was the newest 'NEO' QLED which I'd read was even more impressive than regular QLED and basically the closest yet to OLED but with notably better brightness and no burn-in risk. This is indeed an impressive TV...it has very robust brightness, a nice compact remote and smart system that I learned to use in a few minutes, and comes with all kinds of extras like hundreds of free channels ready to watch, ALEXA capability, basic internet browser, loads of apps, 'ambient' screen mode (very pretty), etc. etc. Everything also is super-crisp from the aggressive 4k upscaling and yes, motion on my games does look very strong and clear, with plenty of options to customize/enhance that aspect as well. The only thing I'm sort of bothered by or just getting used to is that, well, it's all a bit TOO MUCH. Things I watch really want to jump into being super-bright and high-contrast, pretty much all the time. Context is key - this is a very inexpensive smart watch (~$40). Comparing it to Apple/Google/Samsung/Fitbit is unfair. So let's just talk about what you do get and why it's a good value. --Useful fitness/health tracker: This watch has great heart rate, Sp02 sensor, exercise detection, GPS integration and more. It's also well water-proofed for open water swimming. Honestly, for fitness tracking alone, it's an exceptional value and should be considered for anyone thinking about getting a Fitbit since most of those don't have lots of bells and whistles either. This watch is less expensive and more capable than those competitors. --Helpful extras: Weather, music control, text/call notifications, and Alexa integration - these make the device a "smart watch" and give you some added convenience around the house. Experiment, and you'll find yourself using it - especially if you're in a room without another smart speaker and want to control household devices easily. --Comfortable and attractive: The first thing I noticed out of the box was how comfortable the included silicone band is. It comes in two sizes, so it can definitely fit pretty much any wrist. I think it uses standard wristwatch band connection points as well if you'd like to change it out. You can choose from a variety of watch faces - I showed the one I prefer in pictures because it has most of the relevant status indicators I like. From the outside, it looks and feels like a high-end smart watch. Great build quality. Cons: No review would be complete without discussing cons. This watch has a few - but try and keep in mind the price point. That's why I didn't take any stars away. --Cannot reply to texts - you can read them, but no ability to reply --Cannot see what music is playing - you just get basic controls (volume, play/pause, next/prev track) --No wireless charging - don't lose the included cable --Touch interface is slightly laggy. Not unusable, just not buttery smooth. Probably a trade-off for improved battery life. Bottom line? This is a capable smart watch. I'm amazed it can be sold for such a low price. If you're looking for a fitness/health tracker, I'd say this is for you. If you'd like to dabble in smart watches to see if you like having the extra features on top, this makes for a great entry point. If you find you don't care for using a smart watch, would you rather be out $40 or $300? Easy question in my book.

This is a great telescope for those who are getting into amateur astronomy. First of all, the Schmidt-Cassegrain telescope design offers great focal length at a compact size and are generally cheaper than refractors. Portability was one of my biggest purchasing points. Celestron's reputation was another buying point for me, in addition to other reviews about this particular telescope. I have used it a couple times since receiving it this week and I'm very happy with my purchase. For those who are considering buying the Celestron NexStar 5SE and are just getting into this hobby, I strongly recommend that you read the manual prior to using it, for you are investing a decent chunk of money on this telescope, and it deserves to be taken care of and used as intended. On to the good stuff, the pros and the cons. PRO's: The optics are very impressive, and the telescope is collimated at the factory, so there's no need to worry about that when you take it out of the box. Images are razor sharp and the light-gathering amount (aperture) is more than good enough to view your typical solar system objects like the moon and the planets. I was especially impressed with the fact that I was able to see the following objects under considerably light polluted conditions (including the moon in a late Waxing Gibbous phase): M57 (Ring Nebula), M11 (Wild Duck Cluster), M16 (Eagle Nebula), NGC 869 and NCG 884 (Double Cluster), M6 (Butterfly Cluster), and of course--Saturn. The tracking on the NexStar 5SE is acceptable to say the least. Additionally, I'm very happy with the portability of this telescope, especially considering the high focal length compared to its size. Also, I was able to put it together in less than 10 minutes. CON's: Battery life. The NexStar 5SE can run on 8 AA batteries, but that won't be enough if planning on extended observing. I'm running my 5SE on 8 rechargeable Energizer 1400 mAh NiMH batteries, and I was able to squeeze a little less than 2 hours out of it before the declining tracking accuracy and motor stalling made it obvious that the batteries were drained. I strongly recommend purchasing a Celestron power tank and an AC adapter for extensive observing, which in itself has it limitations because the adapter is subject to cord wrap. Also, if the batteries are taken out of the telescope, one has to reconfigure the time, date, and coordinates when batteries are re-inserted. The finder scope was a little tedious to align as well, but with time and patience, aligning it right will give you the most accurate tracking possible. The tracking is also not perfect--when I found the ring nebula, it went just outside my eye piece's field of view, but with a slight manual tweak, I got it back into view and was very amazed at what I had seen! SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS: I'm giving it four stars because of the battery life, the cord wrap when using an AC adapter, and the considerable effort put into aligning the finder scope, which I strongly recommend doing during the day on a distant object like a street light or a communication tower. Aside its limitations, I was very impressed with the quality of the images, the portability, and the ease of assembly. My recommendations are as follows: READ THE MANUAL BEFORE USING THE TELESCOPE! Buy an AC adapter and a Celestron power tank if viewing is planned for several hours. Also, buy a Barlow lens, which will increase the magnification of your eye pieces. I purchased a Celestron Omni 2x Barlow. Eye pieces can make all the difference in the world, but why settle for a set that can cost you hundreds of dollars? I recommend the Celestron 8-24mm zoom eyepiece (93230); it will save you money and space. In conclusion, I highly recommend this telescope for the beginning stargazer. Learn the ropes of this excellent product before graduating to the bigger, more sophisticated telescopes. One last word of advice--the images seen through the telescope are NOT going to be like the Hubble or Kepler telescope photos seen on the Internet. Those photos are the result of long exposure astrophotography and the complete absence of atmospheric turbulence. Our eyes are very poor at processing colors in the dark, so deep sky objects like nebulae and galaxies will be seen in shades of grey, or black-and-white. Nevertheless, seeing those things through a NexStar 5SE was a truly amazing experience for me, and this was under considerably light polluted skies that also included the light from the moon in a very late Waxing Gibbous phase (where it's nearly full). I can only imagine how much more star clusters and nebulae are going to stand out with the absence of moonlight. I can hardly wait!

TLDR; If you want to use a 5ghz network, understand that you may need to tinker with your router to get it working. I would AVOID this card if you don't know how to do that. -------------------------------- This card has been frustrating to figure out. I have Gigabit Google Fiber, so maximizing my wireless connection was important to me. This card connected flawlessly to our 2.4ghz network, and was able to get about 90mbps/90mbps up/down. That's pretty good, and honestly with my previous internet provider would have been more than fast enough. But not good enough here. I bought this card to connect to a 5ghz network. And here's where the problem came in. After installing the latest Windows 10 drivers from TP-Link's website, I couldn't get the card to see my 5ghz network. Further, it actually saw some 5ghz networks from the neighbors. Just not mine. I spent hours researching and trying things, including third party drivers, with no success. Nothing I did could get it to see my 5ghz network. Googling this issue is frustrating because there are apparently many causes, including Windows 10 when it originally came out, so there is an overload of solutions. What I finally found a reference to is that some wireless network adapters have trouble reading a 5ghz network on higher channels. Your 2.4ghz network operates on channels 1-11 generally, and seem to cause no problems. 5ghz networks can operate on channels 36-160 or so, with wide bands of those not used. So apparently this card can't see any channels that are 100+. Which of course my Google fiber router had automatically selected. I manually set the router to broadcast 5ghz on channel 36 (the only sub-100 option I had), and luckily, the card will connect now. It works great now, download at 390-ish mbps and upload at 200-ish mbps, which is basically what the Google fiber router is speced to handle on wifi.

I own two JVC KW-NT3HDT navi receivers and purchased this on the demonstrated strengths of the NT3HDT's. While the 500 has a lot more pixels in its screen and much better negotiation of directory structure in the thumb drives or SD media cards, it is truly disappointing in their revised GPS software. All these recent units use NAVTEQ data for the GPS. That data is more than complete, and it allows naming virtually every street, lane, etc. in the US. The problem is that there is a bug or overt omission in the 500's GPS software that makes it refuse to name any local street unless you are traveling on it. For individuals who make their own route plans and use the GPS just to stay oriented, the absence of street names makes the unit virtually useless. To add insult to injury, I called JVC Customer Service about this problem. The first call resulted in an admonition that the unit wouldn't work unless the Vehicle Speed Sensor line was hooked up. In my car that is a very demanding job, and shouldn't be needed when using a 12 channel GPS with WAAS capability. I called three more times, and was informed that the mandate for the speed sensor line was obviated by the latest firmware update (which I had already done). I was finally connected with a "supervisor" named Joe who allowed that my unit was functioning the same as a new unit (KW-NT810HDT) that was on his desk, and that it was unlikely that JVC would see it necessary to change their software to meet my expectations, even though the previous instruments did perform flawlessly. Since the GPS portion of the unit is defective, I am attempting to return this unit. If you want a unit that has good audio and good management of directories, you can buy a lot cheaper panel unit than the 500 or the 800 or the 810.

This review is for: Sony DVP-FX780 Portable DVD Player (Introduced March '12) OVERVIEW: ----------- We have been using Sony portable DVD players for many years and have always been very happy with them. However, although this has the usual GREAT PICTURE AND SOUND we expect from Sony portable DVD players, CONSIDER A HIGHER END SONY MODEL. This is an excellent entry point into Sony's portable DVD players. However, for only $20-$30ish more one can leap to a 9" screen (9" diagonal) with higher resolution to boot, a much better choice. The 9" models available at the time of this review: [[ASIN:B007F9XHCM Sony DVPFX980 9-Inch Screen DVD Portable]] [[ASIN:B006U1YUJ0 Sony BDPSX910 Portable Blu-ray Player]] One negative that stands out is its RIDICULOUSLY SHORT CORD compared to past models. The new cord plug-in port is incompatible with past cords so if you are replacing an old model, you can't use the old much longer cord. Sony said they don't sell a long version of the new cord, if you find one from a third party company, please add that information in a comment :). The Sony line-up has changed considerably. Gone are the mid-range models with 6 hour battery, 2 headphone ports, etc. They are now just offering very competent models at the low end and getting to high-end features is now a $200ish affair (at the time of this review). I hope to see models with 6+ hour batteries in the low to mid-range models again. IF MONEY IS NO ISSUE: ----------------------- If an additional $100-$150 to get the best works for you, skip this review and get a Sony BDP-SX910 (there might be something better by the time you read this, of course) whether or not you play Blu-Ray discs, due to superior overall features that apply to DVDs, too. It was introduced April 2012 so hopefully they have ironed out any new model easy-fixes by now. [[ASIN:B006U1YUJ0 Sony BDPSX910 Portable Blu-ray Player]] PROS: ------ - The usual GREAT PICTURE and SOUND of a Sony portable DVD player. - Excellent BATTERY TIME: --> 3 hours 30 mins at default backlight setting of 10 (out of 1-20). --> 3 hours 45 mins at backlight setting of 5. - Includes car lighter charging adapter. - An A/V (Audio/Video) input/output port. - As always for the Sony's appears well built, a simple good-looking design with a hard shell. CONS: ------ - RIDICULOUSLY SHORT CORD (3'2") compared to past Sony DVD portable players. - I hesitate to mention this since I never noticed it until I looked it up, however the resolution is 480x234, whereas even the lower-end 9" version that costs $20ish more has 800x480. - 7" Diagonal screen, which although works fine, again for only $20ish you can get a 9" screen which is a much better option. - In previous models you could Fast Forward and Fast Reverse with right/left arrows. This new model refresh instead only recognizes dual use of the skip buttons to cover FF/FR AND Skip, depending on the timing of the push. It is thus now easy to ACCIDENTALLY SKIP INSTEAD OF FF and vice verse. That said, you should be able to get used to it once you figure it out. - If the design needs to be so stingy as to have a super shorter cord, it makes one wonder where else money was saved that one can't see. FEATURES ON SOME HIGHER END SONY MODELS: ----------------------------------------------- Before committing to this model, you might consider looking at some of Sony's higher end models. Here are some of their features to consider: - A 9" DISPLAY size is easily worth the extra cost in my opinion. - 3.5-4 hours BATTERY TIME is excellent for inexpensive players, however, look for 4.5+ hours at the high end. - This model has 1 headset port, the top end Sony Blu-Ray/DVD portable player has 2 HEADSET PORTS. - The top end Sony model's SCREEN CAN SWIVEL to face any direction. - Higher end models come with a REMOTE CONTROL. LESSER CONS: -------------- - The CORD IS INCOMPATIBLE WITH MOST PREVIOUS MODELS' CORDS, so you probably can't use an old cord to overcome the very short cord with this model. - I hesitate to mention this since it is not an issue for us, however the spoke that holds the DVD is a tight fit for dvds (compared to our other Sony DVD portable players), so to avoid breakage you might not want little ones changing DVDs on it. - Doesn't charge while used (see below under "Tested"). TESTED: -------- - Actual BATTERY TIME IS 3 hours 30 mins (at default backlight level of 10 out of 1-20), 3 hours 45 mins at backlight level of 5. The first blinking yellow charge light warning came on roughly half an hour before running out. - From same tests as above, confirmed there is NO VALUE TO CHARGE AFTER YELLOW CHARGE LIGHT TURNS OFF. - I semi-confirmed the claim that it mostly DOESN'T CHARGE WHILE PLAYING (but it keeps it from draining). More precisely, limited tests suggest it charges at a rate of roughly 1 min per 8 minutes of play time, so there might be a very slight bit of charging up going on. CORRECTIONS FOR REVIEWS: ---------------------------- - It RETURNS TO SAME SPOT YOU WERE WATCHING AFTER YOU TURN IT OFF AND ON. One review said you can't, this is incorrect. - You CAN ADJUST COLOR, CONTRAST, Hue, and Backlight. One review may suggest you can't adjust the first two, this is incorrect. - The screen is 7" diagonal, one review could be construed to suggest it may be smaller than this, which would be incorrect. ACCESSORIES: -------------- - The Sony parts phone # is 1-800-282-2848. - Sony Part#988516759 is a $36 adapter that plugs into the unit's A/V outlet and gives you standard/composite out (red, white, yellow), allowing you to DRIVE A LARGER DISPLAY. It comes standard with the 9" model. USAGE NOTE: ------------- - To SKIP FORWARD tap the 3rd button up on the skip forward icon once with a quick tap. - To SKIP BACK tap the 3rd button up skip back icon twice with two quick taps. - To FAST FORWARD hold your finger on the same skip forward button for a second or so. Do that again for more speed. Do that yet again for even more speed. - To FAST BACK, it is the same as Fast Forward but with the skip back button. Hope this helps someone :)

I would start with a reasonably priced zoom lens (the celestron works fine), but I also got some additional sets. Additionally, unless you live in a very dark sky area, consider a broadband light pollution reduction filter. Even in relatively dark areas, it makes things like nebulas pop. You will probably also need some type of power bank. I have a lithium ion battery designed primarily as a car jumpstarter. Works great. You might also need some dew heaters, or at least a dew shield, depending on where you live. Finally, some type of adjustable chair is helpful (I got one from amazon designed for this purpose). I say all this to inform that things can get a bit pricey. How far you go down the rabbit hole is up to you. After a few weeks, I have to say I've gone pretty far, with everything from vibration reducers to the heat control module, and I see that there is much more I can do still (and I haven't even gone in the direction of photography thankfully). For me, though, it has been worth it. All that said, I am sure many are wondering if this is outdated compared to some of the other models, as I did. The wifi module seems to solve issues on that front. It interacts with the latest apps great, whether that be what comes with the telescope or the upgraded SkySafari Pro app. I have done some limited testing with a PC, and it works fine. It tracks well, and the mount is sturdy. All in all, I have enjoyed it immensely and I am happy with the purchase.

I purchased this USB headset to replace a Plantronics Bluetooth headset that seemed to be giving me a Dragon Naturally Speaking error rate of 5-10%. Other sites claimed that these headsets were of high quality and had excellent noise cancellation. Even though they were wired and expensive, I was desperate enough to try them. I spent many hours installing and training Dragon for them but my error rate did not seem to improve. The types of errors got much worse though. Instead of misinterpreting a single word, Dragon was misinterpreting entire phrases of 3 or 4 words and often missed words entirely. When I finally noticed that Dragon was occasionally displaying an error message indicating poor microphone quality I realized that this headset was not providing a loud enough signal to Dragon. I tried starting over with a new Dragon profile and calibrating the mic with a quieter voice but Dragon indicated that the microphone quality was too low and refused to accept it. I do not know whether I got a defective headset or not because it does pick up my voice and eliminates room noises but to get it to work at an error rate of 5% on Dragon I have to project my voice directly into the microphone as if I were giving a lecture at the front of a class.I have quit using this headset and have gone back to my Plantronics wireless Bluetooth earpiece and have set it up again with Dragon but using a faint voice when calibrating it so that Dragon will use a higher amplification. Now when I talk normally into the Plantronics it seems to miss interpret fewer than 2% of my words. I also found the cable on this headset to be very heavy and annoying. The cable weighs 90 g. If you are thinking about using this product with Dragon, I would suggest you wait for other reviews to be posted. Update 3/15/2014 work-around found I examined some of the reviews of the cheaper models of this headset and several raved about its performance with DNS. I therefore went back and created a new profile for this headset. When I went to adjust the microphone position and angle, I discovered that the microphone appeared to have rotated about 30° from where I had set it the first time I tried it with DNS. I removed the foam microphone covering and found that the noise pickup microphone was mounted directly to the back of the voice microphone but facing 180° outward. This 30° misalignment would've caused the noise microphone to pick up more of my voice and subtract more of it thus reducing the amplitude of my voice. I twisted the microphone back to point at my mouth and whispered into it while performing the DNS microphone set up. This greatly increased the recognition accuracy and DNS no longer fails to detect words and it stopped replacing entire phrases with completely erroneous phrases. It still misinterprets some of my individual words, but is at least as good as my old wireless Plantronics. The angle of the microphone slowly rotates over time and I find that I need to readjust the angle every other day which is a pain. This is why I have upgraded my rating by only an additional 2 stars.

I checked it using a polling rate checker, and it clocks in at 140hz, which is the same as the Razer Blade 14 Laptop I have. It would've been nice to have it be a bit higher since this is a dedicated peripheral, but it's working beautifully. It doesn't have any deadzones or issues that cause erroneous presses, so you're free to set this to High Sensitivity and use it reliably. I tried the Apple Magic Pad 1, and that thing is a bit of a turd turd. From the erroneous presses, to the shallow and too easy-to-press click that you have to train yourself to avoid, to the polling rate being less than this. The 90Hz polling on Apple's Magic Pad lineup makes it a poor fit for use with a high refresh rate monitor. I can't tell if it was the polling rate or the latency, but it felt inadequate. I immediately found this one to be much more suitable. I'm using a 144hz monitor, so for now, this is pretty fine and serviceable in place of my 1000hz wireless mouse. Some more Pros: Feet are grippy Size is appropriate - not as colossal as Apple's Accurate with no deadzones Minimal latency Cons: Price is a bit high Zero clue about this brand (or lackthereof) The Micro-usb cable that comes with this is a bit short, like 3.3ft. Only at the third attempt did the pre-installed serial number work with its pre-installed software, but not for long because then I got the next error message: "Application has generated an exception that could not be handled. OK Cancel" After several tries with both these options while attempting to copy the about 90 GB on my C drive to the Verbatim Disk I got a message from NeroBackitUP Agent that "Nero BackitUp (name) is running. Prosess status (blank). Remaining time: Calculating, Elapsed time: Calculating. Hide, Abort". I left this on for nine hours but even then the status bar was still entirely empty with no progress shown and still "calculating". Checking the Verbatim drive then with Windows Explorer in my Windows XP I found 22 entries on that drive, all named "20130725 06351 130725CdriveBackup NDA file 4,153,346 KB", all identical except that some had 4,153,347 KB instead. None of these entries let me open them or find out their content. I deleted those useless files and tried to back up my C drive with a copy of Acronis backup software that I had bought in 2005, but it gave me the message: "Error E00640068. Failed to create the scheduled task. Error #1722 -- "The RPC server is unavailable (0xFFF0)" OK". By the way, registering the Verbatim Drive did also not work. Their error message tells you instead to check your internet or firewall settings and try again. Asking Verbatim Tech Support about the backing up did not help either. They only replied, as pasted from their email: "Nero is one time complimentary software provided and it's preloaded on our external drives. However, the Verbatim external hard drive are plug-N-play devices and doesn't require any software to be installed to make it work. In other words, although Amazon's product description says "This external hard drive features Nero BackItUp & Burn Essentials software that allows full system backup and restore functions", the Nero BackitUp&Burn software is not even meant for backups on that Verbatim drive, according to Verbatim's tech support. I've bought at least a dozen of these motherboards over the past year to couple with the A6-3500 or A8-3800 APU in the Realan E-i5 and E-i7 mini-ITX cases to sell as barebones HTPCs. This has allowed me to get to know the ins-and-outs of this motherboard pretty well. In general, it's a pretty good motherboard with alot of features at a decent price point. These days it's really the only FM1 mini-ITX motherboard available so there is not other choice. Of the dozen or so I've had three go bad that I've had to replace. Usually the complaint is that it will no longer POST. I've been through one RMA with ASRock which wasn't too bad and took a couple of weeks to turn around. The rest I was able to replace through the retailer, either Amazon or the 'Egg. That means 1 out of 4 have been bad. The biggest complaint I have with this board is the behavior of the BIOS. When in the BIOS, the A6-3500/A75M-ITX combination draws close to 90W as measure with a Kill-a-Watt. That tells me the BIOS is running the APU at maximum. It only takes 10 minutes or so of sitting in the BIOS doing nothing to get the CPU temperature reported as over 70C and the CPU fan running full blast. And, yes ASRock, the heatsink is seated correctly and the BIOS is the latest version. I have consistently reproduced this issue on every single A75M-ITX. As a matter of fact, I have one sitting right next to me as I write this and in open air the BIOS is reporting 76.5C and the fan is running at 2954RPM. Once you have Windows installed, idle at the desktop does not have this issue. Unfortunately, I have to explain to each and every customer this will happen so they don't freak out. The Gigabyte GA-A75N-USB3 board I have does not exhibit this behavior but I only have one and it's not available any longer. One small complaint is a strange one but it's the I/O shield. Facing the back of the PC, there is a lot of blank space on the left of the I/O shield. If you accidentally press against this area, there is no support behind it so it will pop into the case. You then have to get inside the case to pop it back out. Since this is the only FM1 mini-ITX available and the FM2 mini-ITX motherboard is an absolute nightmare, it'll have to do. Most of the time it works and most of the time it's not running at now 79C and consuming 90W. ASRock really needs to get their act together with their quality control and their BIOS behavior.
