The Sandisk 128GB dual drive comes formatted as FAT32 with an Android APK file and PDF manual in the root drive, explaining how to install app on phone. 118GB available space. I used the Microsoft Windows Media Creation tool to download and format this drive for Windows 11 setup. It created a 32GB partition and after 4GB install has 28GB free for swap files and driver additions.. however the rest of the drive was unallocated space. Run Disk Management and create a Simple Volume in NTFS to create an 84GB partition. Then backup your data so that it can be transferred to a formatted drive/system. My beef with this device is speed. I have a brand new system: Z690/i7-12700KF/32gb/3070Ti/usb 3+3.2 headers. I get a hard motherboard fail if I try to stick the USB-C end of this device in. BIOS hard stopped on reboot to tell me there was a USB OVERVOLTAGE error and would not reboot until I removed the drive. With the other 'blue' end plugged into a blue 3.0 port I am getting 30MB/sec at the start of a transfer and 10-15MB/sec for most of the long haul. It took me over an hour to copy 44GB of files to the fresh NTFS partition. I really expected much more performance, considering it's rated at 150MB/sec. By contrast my NVMe PCIe x4 SSD is 750MB/sec to copy videos from one folder to another. This USB device is the bottleneck.

I listen to a variety of R&B, funk, old school rap, contemporary jazz, classic and alternative rock, and metal. I was looking for a ruggedized speaker with enough power to use in a garage or backyard. I'm not an audiophile, but I like my music to sound clean enough to distinguish vocals and the main instruments. I've never heard of W-King, but bought the D8 speaker based on the numerous positive reviews and a promo coupon. There are lots of YouTube videos comparing sub-$100 speakers and this speaker always comes out on top for its raw power, strong base, and good mids and highs, even at high volume. At its price point (I paid about $60), I can see why it appeals to a lot of people. It's well-made, portable, rugged, pairs easily, has a strong feature set and is simple to use. Sound-wise, it just wasn't what I was looking for. I think the W-King D8 is more typical of its price class than a stand-out - punchy/booming bass at low volumes and compression/distortion at high volumes. The bass was good with the EQ off, but the mids and highs were weak and muddy. With the EQ on, the bass sounded about the same but the mids and highs were more pronounced. The EQ mode sounded distinctly better. Both modes became distorted at high volumes. As far as the 50W power output, a lot of it must be going towards the bass. Although the bass wasn't as strong, my 32-watt portable (but not ruggedized) speaker matched the W-King's volume with much less distortion. Both speakers are at a similar price point.

Sure, this mouse is made by Logitech, so it's gotta be good; well it is. It's pretty solid and I can tell it will last a long time. The mouse movement itself is accurate and it feels nice in the hand; however the size of the mouse is just too small to be considered a regular mouse (in fact it may as well be called a mobile mouse), the scroll wheel (while marketed as the most precise) just scrolls to freaking fast, and the middle-click button becomes nearly impossible to use because of that. There are no auxiliary buttons on this mouse. Just right click, left click, middle-click, scroll (and tilt-click left and right on the mouse wheel, which are also useless). The reason I say the middle-click is useless is because I'm always navigating the internet, and I'm constantly middle-clicking links to open them in new tabs. The problem is, when you try to push the middle mouse button in, the wheel scrolls up or down, resulting in a middle-click on a blank part of the page. (Which also resulted in a lot of anger and frustration with me middle-clicking all around a link up to seven times with the link only actually opening in two new tabs.) I'm sure people will dislike this review since it is hinged on a single design flaw, but the truth is if you plan on middle-clicking at any point, buy a different freaking mouse. Lastly, I'm also an artist and 3D modeler, this mouse really can't be used for programs where scrolling or middle-clicking is necessary (which is most modern programs). The scroll sensitivity is simply too high (tried changing it in Logitech's mouse settings, but it appears scroll speed is absent...or it was already at the lowest if I remember correctly) and it really cripples this mouse's functionality.

I would have been even happier if this camera had 10 Megapixels instead of 9.1 ... only so it matched others that I was comparing (I compared 12's too, pics generally were NOT as good). If it were much smaller I don't believe it would be as easy and comfortable to use. Yes!. I handled nearly a dozen of its competitors, as well. I read every review (Pro and Users) I could find anywhere (online, magazines, trade journals). Be carefull with some of them. I put a lot of "weight" in reviews by the Pros, HOWEVER I found that many of the things they said about this camera were not true. Some of their comments caused me to "pause" and almost not buy this camera. Some talked about features they wish this camera had, that others did have ... only I found that SEVERAL such features ARE present in this camera. Some features that they reviewed as a "Negative", after learning how to use them turn out to be a great "POSITIVE". The camera can adjust the ISO (as well as many other settings, in "IA" mode) to give you great shots when you can't use a flash (and you can set it to 6400 ISO for very dim non-flash shots). I was happy with my long-arrived-at choice the day I bought it. If I knew THEN what I know NOW ... I would have bought it much sooner! I enjoy it more everyday! I planned to use my "PRO Camera" (a $2500.00 Olympus system - 18 months of research) for "all the things that this camera would not be able to do" ... NOW I know that this Panasonic will do a fine job for 90 to 95% of all the camera tasks that I want to do! AND it is much much smaller and lighter! I do suggest you get a couple of 1300 Mah batteries and a couple of 8 Gig (or larger) LEXAR (Yes, the brand matters - they are much faster 20 Mb/sec) SDHC cards if you plan to do lots of serious picture taking as I do. (By the way MROCK makes a perfect case for it and a spare battery and spare memory card, I am now looking for a very small case, when I want to take just the camera in a pocket). Have FUN with it! UPDATE: I have used this camera for a very long time now! It is STILL an excellent performer! I have added larger SDHC cards to the ones I started with (that STILL WORK FINE). I will be bringing THIS CAMERA OUTFIT on our trip To "The Holy Land" from Jerusalem to Rome. During that 17 day trip I will take thousands of pictures! It will be GREAT! I hope you will enjoy this camera too! {Did my review help you decide?}

The GoScope BOOST is a solid design. The telescoping/locking mechanism is stellar; there are no screws and it feels super sturdy! The pole itself is lightweight but feels strong like bull! The aluminum-magnesium alloy feels really dependable! The grip feels like the handlebars to a bike; it's a tough rubber that gives you a great grip. If your grip fails you, there's a quality wrist strap that's included. This is a great overall product, but it's not perfect in my eyes and let me tell you why. It's great for selfie shots, but if I want to aim the GoPro in a forward direction I would have to remount the GoPro; the mount is limited to about 130 degrees with the waterproof housing. I would have liked the mount to allow for more than 180-degree-rotation like my other pole, the GoPole. I will upload pictures to show you what I'm talking about. So for this reason, I did not give the GoScope BOOST 5 stars. It was almost a deal breaker for me. Fortunately I semi-solved my problem by adding a three-way pivot arm (included with GoPro camera) so that I am able to swivel the GoPro around for forward shots on the fly. I say "semi-solved" because it doesn't give a complete 270-degree pivot but it allows about 225 degrees which is a lot better than the insignificant 130 degrees. I also like that the there are dual mounts for the GoPro; not because I would like to mount 2 GoPros at the same time, but because it stabilizes the GoPro when I set it down. Who carries around multiple GoPros anyway!? So other than that one gripe, the GoScope is a quality product. I have owned a GoPro for about 1 year. I typically use it for traveling. I have been using the GoPole for a little under a year and just recently picked up the GoScope BOOST. I just used the GoScope on a recent trip to the San Diego Safari Zoo and this was when I realized the difficulties in shooting selfies and then quickly wanting to shoot forward. I have not taken the GoScope under water so I don't know how it will do in the ocean, but the GoPole would allow water to seep in the pole. Well I hope this review helps.

This boost converter module is pretty beefy but it doesn't like batteries to be connected as an input. I have used 3 AC-DC sources to provide anywhere from 12V to 35V as an input and it worked fine. When I connected a battery to the input the unit fried itself on both the units I had. The LDO's or FET's or whaterver is heatsunk on the bottom almost immediately shorted the input to ground and killed the unit. I will try to replace it...again, and see if I can work around that issue. Edit: Turns out you can't work around the issue because the input current is limited to (or rated for) ~10A so if you want to get the full 600W from this unit you will need the 60V input, 12V won't cut it. If you use a battery, and the converter output power is set to more than 10A x input_voltage, the unit will pull more than 10A from the input and more likely than not brick your converter.

I was on the market for a simple GPS unit that would display some basic info during my MTB rides. I looked at cheaper options, including XOSS G+ and IGPSPORT iGS10, but eventually ended up buying the Garmin Edge 130 Plus for the following 3 reasons: 1. Ability to customize the display and show all and only the parameters useful to me (speed, distance, ride time, time of day, total ascent, total descent) 2. Ability to display notifications from my phone (text, whatsapp, incoming calls) 3. Ability to load a GPX track and follow it (basic navigation), useful if you're trying a new trail you have seen on Trailforks or Strava, or a friend shared with you. Overall I'm happy with the purchase, it does what I need, but I took away 2 stars for the following reasons: 1. Price. Yes it does more than the other GPS units I mentioned, but it does cost 4-5 times more. The Edge 130 is definitely overpriced at $200. 2. Complexity. Sometimes, more is not better. I have no use of all the fitness functions, like schedule, workouts, racing segments, training calendars, VO2 Max, recovery time, IQ features, hydration, heart rate zones, power zones, challenges, health stats, performance stats, courses, segments, laps, and so on... they simply add complexity in the menus of the device and - particularly - in the app. At the very least, give us the option to completely hide/disable those functions. I do acknowledge that for some people these are important features, but I think they are overkill on a small unit like this. 3. User interface / buttons. For whatever reason, they are not intuitive. It's also a consequence of having too many options, but the basic functionalities (start/pause/stop/save) should ALL require 1 push of a button, not more. Example: to start a ride you need turn on the unit, then press the start button once, confirm or select the ride type (Road/Commuting/Mountain, etc) then press again to start the clock. Another example: to save a ride, you press the start/stop button, then scroll down to Save Ride and press again. Last example: to turn it off, you need to press the power button, then again confirm power off. How about using long press a shortcut? Long press start = start a ride with the previous settings. Long press stop = save the ride. Long press power = power off. It's not that complicated, is it??? 4. No user-replaceable battery. [UPDATE 04/26/2021] I've been using the Edge 130 for a while now, and decided to add back 1 star. It works really well, and buttons are starting to make sense. Navigation is excellent, despite the small screen: I create my courses in an external GPX editor, import them into Garmin Connect and finally load them on the Edge (I do all this on a Windows PC, with the Edge connected via USB). When you're following a course, you can zoom in/out and the unit will keep that zoom level for the entire ride. This is very useful for mountain biking, as the default zoom level doesn't provide nearly enough detail when you're on a trail. [UPDATE 06/24/21] Back to 3 stars. The Courses page on the Edge 130, for some mysterious reason, cuts the course names after 16-17 characters, instead of using the full width of the (already small) screen. If you have several courses, it becomes difficult to distinguish them if the names are cut short, so you need count the characters when you name your courses, and resort to abbreviations (e.g. "Blk Mtn 2 Hdgs - S" instead of "Black Mountain to Lake Hodges - Short". End of the world? No. Annoying? A bit, yes. I reached Garmin Support and - long story short - I could not get them to move from the "it works as intended" response, which of course completely misses the fact that, the way it was intended does not really work well. I suggested to use the full width of the screen (duh) and possibly to add right-to-left scrolling when a course is highlighted, so that even longer names could be displayed in full. Nothing, it was like speaking to a wall.

Bought this to replace the dead battery in an A1708 macbook pro. While the instructions are OK, I would highly recommend viewing the various u tube videos showing how to do it. One thing I did not initially understand is why you need to remove the trackpad to do this. But I did so and the reason became apparent after I removed the center battery. There are chips on the battery side of the trackpad circuit board. If you leave the trackpad in place, it would be very easy to damage those chips when using the plastic scrapers to release the center battery. Also, on my unit there are six screws of three different lengths holding on the bottom cover. Pay careful attention to which screws come out of which holes. After installation, I charged it up and got it playing video. Ran over 5 hours and the macbook battery status changed from “needs service” to “normal”. Given that Apple wants $200 for the battery service, spending an hour to do it myself was a nice savings.

To put this in context, we purchased this camera as one of a handful of point-and-shoots; we bought a Nikon D90 shortly before having our first child, which is a stellar DSLR, to add to an old Panasonic Lumix point-and-shoot that did take pretty good pictures, despite an excessively bright flash. After a couple of years, we wanted to 'downgrade' back to to point-and-shoot cameras, given that ours is about 5 years old, and newer ones are both more high-tech and relatively inexpensive for the given level of technology. We bought 'a few' to serve a couple of more or less specific roles, all shy of the DSLR's "big heavy super-high-quality photograph field cannon" role. The purpose of this one was to be... well, the cheap one. The everyday, easy-to-use, no-brainer, compact and lightweight and easy for my wife to put in the diaper bag and take to the museum or the park with the kids. Cheap enough that if you lost it or it got scratched by car keys, no big deal, nice enough to take good basic photos but otherwise no particularly fancy features. Now, put in that context, time for the inevitable 'pros' and 'cons'. Pros: - Extremely compact, lightweight, 'sexy' design with chrome details around silver metal body - Fast start-up, about 2.5 seconds to power up - Continuous shooting can get maybe a hair more than 1 picture per second. Specs list as 0.7s intervals. - Battery life seems to be good so far, about 200 pictures and several videos over the course of 3 days with all varieties of flash and zoom and the battery still indicates fully charged - Zoom is pretty powerful for such a compact camera Cons: - Skittish. It's hard to get a clear picture from the thing even with a steady hand. Image stabilization does nothing as far as I can tell. - Because of the former, producing sharp pictures with continuous shooting is pretty much hopeless - Focus is hopeless in ISO3200. No, with any automatic or manual setting, with or without the flash, focus is hopeless. About 1 out of every 4 pictures came out well-focused. Even focused pictures seem to have blurry points in the same range as other objects that are at the same distance, even near the center of the scene. This is even for things like city scenes in full daylight. - Abandon all hope, ye who shoot photos indoors... focus is abysmal. Did I already make this point? - Because the focus is so poor, zooming in on anything, even a little, is absolutely and totally hopeless. Taking pictures of animals at the museum came out occasionally reasonably focused; zooming in as little as 2x produced worthless blurry shot after worthless blurry shot - As with pretty much every point-and-shoot, the flash creates a scene completely washed out with white light - needs to be diffused. - Very slow to become responsive after a photo; with or without a photo review, the camera takes about 5s to become responsive and available for another photo. This appears to be the case with 3mp the same as 14mp. Just very, very, very slow. - Very slow to delete a picture; deleting a picture you don't like takes 3 clicks, then about 3 seconds to complete the operation. It's a little surprising how any device (phone, camera, gps, tablet, anything) could take that long to complete a simple operation... - The shutter speed is too slow or simply wrong; if you have kids, who are naturally always in motion, they'll be a blur even if they're standing still to pose for a photo. - Slow to actually fire a shot after zooming and pushing the button - sometimes 1 to 2 second delay, which means, the subject (kids!) is often simply gone by the time it actually shoots. - Grainy. Even in broad daylight, color fields on high-res pics, like buildings and peoples' faces, is grainy and pixellated with blotchy color tones. - Video. Can't record smoothly, even at lower resolution, with a high-quality Class 6 SDHC card. Don't bother with video. To be perfectly fair and objective, I took this camera and our Samsung ST-95 outside and took two shots per camera, of each of five subjects, in the same resolution, at the same time. I chose the sharper of the two photos from each camera and renamed the file generically. I then brought up the photos on our 1080p 55" TV - the largest-format, highest-resolution screen in the house. I showed them to my wife and asked her to choose "before" and "after", letting her know that I had swapped the order of the pictures randomly (so that A wasn't always the Nikon, B wasn't always the Samsung). In 5 out of 5 cases, she picked (and I agreed) the Samsung's pictures, simply on the focus. The Nikon just can't focus correctly. For example, on the back patio, the kids' tricycle is relatively focused, but the grill right beside it - both near the center of the shot - is entirely blurred out. All of my subjects were stationary out of necessity; I could not get a single clear picture of the kids or dogs with the Nikon, so there was no relevant comparison to be made. Using "scenes" to balance the settings made absolutely no difference on focus, only color balance. Overall, this camera is a fine solution if you don't expect much and you won't do much with it. You could shoot some video or take pictures of inert objects at medium range in full daylight and maybe one out of every two or three photos will be focused enough to pass a cursory inspection (don't look too close), but beyond that I'm afraid this camera just can't perform acceptably. It'll capture images, but they won't be GOOD. Despite the aforementioned purpose for which we bought this camera, we'll probably take around one of the better / other ones instead. It's really just about as well not to take a picture of those 'precious moments', as to attempt to do so with this camera. Other folks who have claimed that they are satisfied with this camera just can't be looking very closely at their pictures; after three outings and a few hundred pictures I am just amazed at how poor the quality of the shots are, in every environment, every light, every kind of subject. It's not for lack of use or lack of knowledge/experience with digital cameras; this really just has an extremely poor-quality sensor and processor and, I would assume, sub-standard firmware. I suggest looking at other entry-level offerings such as Samsung ST-65. Or, go for a mid-range camera. You really should only consider this camera if the looks of the camera itself matter a whole lot more than the quality of the pictures it can take - and, if the quality of the pictures it takes don't matter much at all to you. If you do care about the ability to capture images, this camera will not be satisfactory. I do not recommend this camera.

BELOW IS MY ORIGINAL FOUR-STAR REVIEW, FOLLOWED BY AN EDIT EXPLAINING WHY I'VE DROPPED SEVERAL STARS AND WILL BE ASKING FOR A REFUND: All right: I work with Bluetooth headphones on to listen to music and take calls, I work out with them to listen to shows, and I fall asleep with them listening to... whatever will help me sleep that night. So I'm a power user, and have a pretty well-rounded view. Let's get the cons out of the way first (don't worry, there are plenty of pros - just "bad news first"): 1) It is a bit heavy - the larger ends (though helpful for people who fumble with buttons) can slip off if you, say, fall asleep with them. I've had other, lighter models of Bluetooth headphones, and those didn't tend to end up encircling my throat (the front of it) as I rolled over. Not a deal-breaker, and most people won't care since most people aren't attached to their headphones 24/7. 2) The mic for phone calls isn't the most sensitive: unless I'm speaking fairly loudly, the parties on the other end tend to think I'm mumbling... or they just miss my comments completely. 3) The connectivity is a LITTLE shorter than some I've used. Though unless you're going to wander 20 feet away from your music source/phone/whatever, this shouldn't be a big deal. I DO wander, but you may have guessed I'm weird by now. The pros: 1) First, the earbuds themselves are absolutely first-rate. They are extraordinarily comfortable, and practically disappear from my awareness. Working, working out, sleeping, they are literally the best-feeling buds I've used (out of MANY). 2) Good mid-range sound. If you're looking to have your skull beaten like an egg by the powerful bass of your angry music, you're out of luck - but these aren't really marketed that way, are they? These are nice, medium-range headphones that deliver crisp, clear sound without any tinny high tones - or the aforementioned skull-beating. Very nice for a wide variety of uses - talk podcasts, music, movies, etc. Phone calls also sound great from my end. 3) They DON'T yell "Battery MEDIUM!" every two hours like some models. [[VIDEOID:ad2afeb4f638b0ee0cc7cce028cef319]] I thought of getting a dash cam when I saw all of the Russian meteor videos, but wanted a camera that wouldn't attract attention to itself. Since this camera was designed for right-hand drive vehicles, the lens doesn't swivel quite as far left as I'd like it to. It goes far enough left though, in my opinion. It was packaged with an 8GB SD card, which was a nice start. It arrived set for English and included a quick start guide. The clock was not quite set correctly, despite what others have reported on their purchases, but it didn't bother me. Once you get the hang of moving through the menus on this device, it makes sense. It was a challenge to get it to sit correctly on my mirror, since my existing mirror is somewhat weak. My car mirror would sort of lock and aim onto one "sweet spot" where it would hold, so I adjusted the camera accordingly by sliding the bottom grips toward me a bit, aiming the mirror side of the camera upward. The rubber grippers hold pretty well. This solution helped me to keep the camera's mirror aimed properly rearward. It was about 90 degrees here yesterday and caused my car's mirror to sag down...this is a unique issue in my particular car. I'll have to figure a workaround to tighten the mirror's ball joint in my case... The power cable hides very well in my headliner and pillar trim. The cable is just narrow enough to fit and hide. I wanted a camera that will just run automatically, and this one does exactly that. I don't even have to think about it when I get in the car--it just starts rolling when the car turns on (my cigarette outlet switches on and off with the ignition). I picked up a 32GB SD class 10 card for it. It holds about 2 1/2 hours of video in 720 mode. I keep the included 8GB card in the glove box as a backup. I wish the camera had GoPro-like sharpness. It's hard to make out license plates on the video unless the lighting conditions are right and the license plate is within 20 feet of the front of my car. I suppose if I see reckless driving or am a victim of a hit-and-run, I'll just speak the offender's license plate number so the camera's microphone can pick it up. The audio can be enabled or disabled with this camera, but I leave the audio recording on for this reason. I always record at 720p because I heard that 1080i is only 15 frames per second. I have not tried 1080 mode yet. This camera has a parking mode (records on internal battery power for one minute if vibration is detected while the car is parked), which I haven't used very much. I don't know whether or not the lights come on when parking mode activates--I would hope that the camera stays dark if it rolls on someone messing with my car. Flashing lights on the "rear view mirror" in an empty car would be a "steal me" signal. I love the clandestine nature of this camera. It's the MAIN REASON I bought it. If I have a confrontation/collision on the road, I want no one to know I have a camera before the police show up. Also, since it's not noticeable, I'm not worried about it attracting thieves while the car is unattended. If this camera had GoPro-like video, I would have paid $250 for it, maybe more. It's not super sharp video, but I definitely think it is worth the going price. If it can clear my liability on one traffic accident, it'll more than pay for itself. Also, it's fun to load the videos into editing software and make it roll in super-fast motion! You can also stamp a number onto the video, such as your own license plate number. On my video I choose to only stamp the last three digits of my plate number (in case I get a viral video, my full license plate number isn't all over the place!). My uploaded video was shot in 720p mode. I removed the audio and showed different lighting conditions. Keep in mind that the video seen on this review will be slightly degraded from the original video quality. Amazon seems to compress these videos. The white car in the very first shot has a readable license plate, as well as the white car in the very last shot, along with the silver crossover SUV to its right. UPDATE 4/22/2014: I've owned this camera for a year now and it's still working great. It's survived the hot sun of Southern California just fine.

After spending weeks of testing this board out with a Quadro RTX6000, including purchasing a second motherboard (and one from another manufacturer as well), I've concluded that there is some extremely bad issue with running a Quadro RTX6000 GPU on it. No matter what you do, as soon as you throw a graphics workload at the card, it immediately defaults to its failsafe speed of 300MHz and refuses to budge. Running the exact same hardware anywhere else (another WRX80 board, a TRX40 board, or even an old Xeon workstation) has no problems. The worst part is ASUS' customer service. They'll only respond over email, and their automated response system loves to immediately say "let's RMA it" (despite me having two of these boards showing the exact same problem). I sent them copious amounts of information, including screenshots of the physical hardware setup as well as screenshots of the output from hardware monitors and the only thing they came back to me with after a full week was "make sure it's plugged into the first PCIe slot (pictures show it was), and make sure Above 4G Encoding is on (which is the default on the board, which I told them I was running). It seems they're just reading from a script and didn't even bother to pay any attention to my details. And this is ridiculous for something that is marketed as a workstation motherboard. To not even have validated it against workstation GPUs when that's exactly the kind of hardware you'd be using for this is ridiculous. If you want to run this with a consumer GPU, it will probably run fine. It ran my 980Ti without issue. But I don't think most people are be buying into a Threadripper Pro setup to run consumer GPUs. So two stars for it actually working, but not for working with the kinds of hardware it should be.

I loaded the internal memory and a 32Gb SD card with many folders of MP3 music in hopes of using this unit as a music streamer to replace a failed (and ancient) iPhone. So multiple taps (as if the first tap didn’t work) can trigger multiple responses that take you where you don’t want to go. So I find myself often hitting the home button and then going more slowly than I would like to work my way through the alphabetic listing of artists and albums. Because the interface is so slow I divided my artists into several top level folders separate by alpha letters; A-E, F-J, etc. This scheme eliminates a lot of finger swipes that are otherwise required to get from A to Z in a long list of artist folders. I number my tracks starting with 01 so the albums play songs in the correct order. But...and here’s a bummer...the software seems to stick on the most recent folder. When I move to a different folder (album) and start the first song it doesn’t play; instead, the first song of the prior folder plays, followed by all the songs in the prior folder. Very annoying. I haven’t found a consistent easy way to resolve this. So for now I return to the home screen and start over. It’s time consuming, but it seems to work every time. The Bluetooth connections are also flaky. The unit will connect ok but has brief (I.e. 20 ms) interruptions every five minutes or so. And, when it powers down, it won’t reconnect with a prior device unless the “forget this device” routine is performed. So I have to re-pair every time. So I am making do with the device for now. Would I buy another one? No.

I picked an HD27HDR to replace an older HD26 that I had been using. The one that I received does not have any issues with color wheel noise, but it also only has a single HDR setting unlike what Optima said they were going to do. Not sure how to get a new firmware update as it is not listed on the Optoma website. Brightness is better than the HD26, but that might have something to do with the number of hours I have on the lamp. That said, the HD27HDR is an improvement over the HD26 (which is very similar to the HD14x) in all ways. In 1080p SDR mode, the colors are deeper, the contrast is better, and I don’t get the pumping that I was seeing with the HD26. There is still a bit of banding evident, but much less than before. Also, rainbow effect is much less - I used to notice it once in a while on the HD26, but have not picked it up once on the new projector. I found the ‘gray’ screen setting useful to help with making the picture optimized for my 100” ALR screen. I have significant ambient light in my living room with off access open windows pretty much all day. Night time viewing allows the color/contrast to really shine, and I am tempted to black out everything just to get that performance all the time. I have had minimal chance to do much viewing in HDR. I have played a few games through my PS4 pro on it. Lag is unnoticeable, and HDR mode makes the colors/contrast even better in AC Odyssey. Even For Honor looks great in 4K SDR mode (doesn’t support HDR) as compared to 1080p. The projector automatically switches to HDR mode when detected. In my case, that is when a game starts up. There is about a 10 second delay as it resyncs, but other than that, it works perfectly. I did notice that I had some sync issues with a couple of my 4K certified 35’ HDMI cables, but switched to a different brand (40’) and it works just fine. The ‘bad’ cables work just fine in 1080p mode, but for some reason, won’t sync (BSOD) when switching to 4k (with or without HDR). I have visited various stores in the area, and, in my opinion, you have to triple the price before you start getting a projector with better performance. I highly recommend this projector unless you are willing to spend 3x the price.

I want to start this review by saying that I'm a relatively loyal JLab customer. I've purchased and enjoyed the J2s, J3s, and still have a pair of J5s that I use regularly. Before my first bike to work after burning these in, I was excited to have some good quality earbuds that wouldn't fall off while biking. This is where everything started to go downhill. First, the "customizable in-wire ear hooks" are really annoying to mold to your ear. When I finally had the wire around my ear, the buds didn't want to fit well into my ear. It took me an extraordinary amount of time to get the buds to fit well and stay in my ear. Even then, they still fall out during my bike ride. Second, the sound quality is not up to par with other JBuds. I had much lower and powerful bass from my J2s, 3s, and 5s than I do with these. The bass is almost non-existent. The highs seem to be ok, but still not up to previous JBuds quality. I was really disappointed with the sound quality overall. The mic works perfectly fine though; I've had plenty of conversations where people had no idea I was even on a mic. At the end of the day, I still wear these earbuds when I'm doing something active because the ear hooks do help more than they hurt. This seemed like it could be an amazing product, but JLab didn't follow through to my expectations.

I recently purchased a Kodak Playsport and saw that I could buy a remote control for it for just $10 more, so I thought, "What's there to lose?" Well, the answer to that question is: you can lose $10. This thing is a piece of crap. It reminds me of my old garage door opener where you had to push the button over and over, move it from side to side, aim it in just about every direction, shake it, and beat it, just to get it to work. Another review said that this remote works up to 30 ft (a claim that was highly influential in my decision to purchase). Yeah, right--try 6 ft. That dude probably works for Kodak. I measured it, testing its functionality at various distances. Under 6 ft, you can sort of get it to work by pushing the buttons repeatedly or holding them down for a while. Beyond 6 ft, no response at all. The worst thing about this remote is that THERE'S NO POWER BUTTON, which is the primary function I'd want in a camera remote (my fault for not paying more attention). Can't think of a single reason why anyone would ever need a remote without a power button that only works within 6 feet of the camera. If you need to toggle recording, delete files, or change the shooting mode, shouldn't you just walk back over and do it directly on the camera? After all it's only 6 feet and you just held it in your hand a moment ago to turn it on. So stay away from this guy, folks, unless you want donate your $10 to Kodak. Of course, there's a chance that this remote's performance might be better with the other camera models, but somehow, I don't think so.

I like to listen to music, but I'm not willing to spend a month's wages on an "audiophile" stereo. I needed a small form-factor amp that could drive speakers in four rooms of my house through a passive speaker selector and could nest in a 13" wide cubby in my bookcase. This is literally the only one I could find that was small and had enough power, even if I wanted to go with something in the $600 range. I wanted to hook up my wife's iPod Touch 2nd generation via her old Kensington "line-out" dock into the RCA "line-in" on this amp. I was hoping to be able to use a simple multi-disc reader (Blue Ray player) via digital coaxial cable into the amp and take advantage of the built in DAC. I contacted the seller about my speaker setup and the specs on the DAC and they replied promptly. This is NOT a well known DAC chipset, but I decided to take a chance on it. After sending back the first unit due to volume control problems (thank you Amazon Prime), I hooked everything up and...it's powerful but the DAC sounds thin and ringing in the higher registers to my ears. Abandoning my idea of a compact, bare-bones setup that would unobtrusively nest in a book case, I opted to buy a Yamaha CD S300BL CD player. It's a regular 17"+ consumer electronics format that has to sit on top of my bookcase. It has a Burr Brown DAC and allows me to connect my wife's iPod digitally to the player to take advantage of the Burr Brown DAC rather than the micro DAC on the iPod. It's not unobtrusive, but HOLY COW the Yamaha CD with this amp now sounds great and has lots of power. So, if you're looking for a powerful small form-factor amp this is for you. If you want something to stream or connect digitally and utilize the amp's built in DAC be prepared for a low-fi sound quality. It's unfortunate that Fosi Audio cut corners on the DAC chipset and filter circuitry. DAC chips, even the great ones are not that expensive. If they had put more into that, even at a higher price, the DA1210C would be an amazing amp. I mean AMAZING!!! As it is, most of it's digital capabilities add up to poor sound quality so you're paying for something you can't utilize to it's full extent. If you're used to listening to music on your computer speakers, this will be an improvement. If you've ever had a reasonably good stereo, you will only want to use the analog RCA "line-in" hook up and either buy an external DAC or a player that has a good quality internal DAC like the Yamaha S300BL. Too bad. This baby was almost perfect...

Update; I now have both antennas mounted and running. They easily make the connection over the distance I have with strong signals. However, the end speed is not what I had hoped for. The antennas are advertised to run at 30Mbps... I haven't come close to that. In fact, I have hit a peak of 20Mbps only once or twice. Typically it runs at 10-12Mbps from the gateway hub. Keep in mind that these speeds are cut in half at the remote hub. So at the remote I run at 5-6Mbps and will have slow downs to under 1Mbps. I haven't been able to identify any reasons that the antennas run at these speeds- but they are what they are. This said- The CUSTOMER SERVICE has been TOP NOTCH. I have even been in contact with the owner attempting to get the advertised speed and he has worked diligently on the problem. My end review- great company, and they are working hard to get their product up to expectations. If you need a connection at a distant location this product will serve you well- easy to set up and easy to use. If you need a high speed connection (over 10Mbps) at a distant location this product may not be up to the task. Original Review; Very easy to set up. Purchased Two to create a mesh network about 1/2 mile apart. The initial set up is very easy, just plug into the router and log into the website. They both came up within two minutes. I reset the network name and password and was good to go. My initial speed test was actually a faster connection than the traditional 2.4g router. I will update on performance once they are both mounted outside and I am able to test the range of the network.

We had high hopes for this radio. In its very own manual it states that in the daytime it can be expected to pick up a good signal within 300 miles and at night quite a lot farther. My husband had a long conversation with the seller before buying this radio to make sure it could work for us before spending a sizeable amount for a radio. It is roughly 150 miles between our home in Coquitlam, BC and Mercer Island in Seattle where KIXI AM880 radio is broadcast from. I cannot say that we had no reception, but it was poor - at 150 miles, while sitting out in the middle of our yard. Next to no reception in our house. It should have been able to give a good signal, easily, according to them. After buying it they now said that adding an antenna would probably not help; it would just amplify the hash along with the signal and you would not be any farther ahead. All in all I'm not sure who this radio would work for. Maybe if you lived on the bald prairie or on a mountaintop with absolutely nothing in between you and the radio station's signal it would be okay.

I am outputting sound from two different devices via headphone jacks (3.5mm) into an audio 'headphone mixer'. 1.) Device #1 is my monitor (which has a 3.5mm headphone jack in the back that I'm plugging into), the sound being outputted from this monitor is from my gaming console (plugged into the monitor via HDMI). 2.) Device #2 is my PC. Again, output from headphone jack. Sound being outputted is obviously my PC sound. So both devices are going into the mixer (channels 1 & 2), and then my headphones are plugged into the mixer 'headphone out' jack so that I could get both console and PC sounds simultaneously in my headphones and adjust the volumes for each independently with the mixer volume knobs. Simple enough concept. However, as soon as I connected BOTH devices into their respective inputs in the mixer, the overall sound would be overpowered by a high-pitched whine. I could have either one (PC or console) plugged into the mixer by itself without issue, but as soon as I connected the other one the whine would occur. I researched this and determined that the issue was likely a 'ground loop', since the console monitor, the console itself sending sound, the PC, and the mixer were all plugged into the same common AC power source (my home). As soon as I added one of these to either of the audio connections ("console_monitor-to-mixer audio cable" OR "PC-to-mixer audio cable"), the whine was gone. For good measure I bought a second one and put it on both audio connections. My setup now works perfectly, as desired. Note that this is NOT dangerous as it's only the 'audio cables' that the ground is being lifted from. The console_monitor, PC, and mixer devices themselves are all three still grounded via their respective AC power source. This worked perfectly for my solution, and the reason I purchased two of them (which was probably overkill) was because they are so inexpensive. I recommend this device very highly. Five stars. Of course, having said all that: every setup is different. The only way you will really figure out if it works for you is by trying it. If it doesn't do what you need, then Amazon seems to have a fairly forgiving return policy. Even without that return policy, at worst you would be out about 10 bucks. For me that was worth the risk, and I'm glad that it paid off.

It would seem that my review has turned out to be a sort of comparison of the Sennheiser HD 598s to the HD 600s. While it wasn't where I intended to go, I think the comparison is valid when deciding if the $200 premium is worth the payout (it is). I have owned/auditioned a ton of headphones over the years, and I currently have a pretty decent assortment in my stable. But these HD 600s are probably going to have all those other pairs collecting dust. About a month ago I had purchased a pair of HD 598s and they were the pair of cans that finally sold me on open phones. I really like the 598s, and they are excellent for classical, jazz, classic rock, and many other genres music. However, when it came to listening to contemporary popular music they just seemed to come up short. The HD 600s are a much better "all around" headphone, and well worth the additional $200 (in my opinion). Their superiority was evident from the moment I put them on and plugged them in. I played Chris Isaac's "Wicked Game" and I literally had a chill run up my spine. More bass than the 598s? Yes; but it's not unnatural in any way whatsoever. It just adds to the richness/quality of the overall sound. These make everything just sound more real, and they seem to do it almost effortlessly. After listening to the 600s for an extended period and then going back to the 598's, the differences become more noticeable. Again, where the 598s start to struggle, the 600s just power through. I completely understand why so many people consider these to be some of the best phones ever produced. I have also been tricked into looking around the room for that noise I just heard only to realize it was part of the recording. If you need to stick to a budget, the 598s are an excellent choice and a fantastic bargain (just watch and wait for the price to dip). However, if you can afford the premium price, the HD 600s are worth every penny. My listening setup consists of a variety of digital files played from my computer, an Onkyo C-7030 CD player, and a Nuforce Icon DAC/Headphone Amp. I should also add that I don't use any equalization with my phones. I messed around running the phones directly off the computer's headphone jack, and I have to say that I highly recommend a good DAC/Amp to get the most out of these cans, as the added power really brings them to life. And remember that to truly "Listen" to these phones you need to be in a quiet environment. A few other observations: The 600's clamp quite a bit tighter than the 598s, though they do seem to be loosening up a bit with use. I think the 598s actually sound a bit wider and a touch brighter, but my 600's only have about 15 hours on them at this writing and like the 598s, I expect them to open up after more time. I may invest in a better cable in the future, but the included cable gets the job done, and it's more flexible than the one for the 598's (which I also replaced). I had thought about comparing these to some of my other closed phones for my review, but really, I don't feel that any of them even comes close to these 600s. I've also noticed that with the 598's it is important to find that sweet spot in the volume where the sound really starts to shine, while the 600's play much better and more balanced over a wider range of volume (high and low). I am looking forward to enjoying these headphones for many years to come. If you have any comments or questions I welcome them and will try my best to answer. I did extensive research prior to this purchase, so if I can't answer a specific question I may be able to point you in the right direction. Update 1: After probably 20 more hours of listening I can clarify my comment about the 598s being a little bit brighter. On certain pieces when I hear a high-hat cymbal on the 598's, I hear it as one sound, and mostly the sound of the cymbal. On the 600's you clearly hear the stick hitting the cymbal, and the sound of the cymbal itself. So, I would say the high end of the 600s may not be perceived as being as bright as the 598's, but it is much more defined, clear, and controlled.

To be honest, these earbuds are great. The price that you pay is absolutely ridiculous especially when it comes to having ANC (active noise cancellation), Transparency mode, and the app compatibility. The design is of the earbuds are similar to the Airpods Pro by the slightest bit but I would say that the Nothing Ear 1's look slightly better with the transparent body that goes with the case as well. The unboxing experience is pretty good and better than I expected for a 100 dollar pair of earbuds. The things that come and include with the earbuds are small and large eartips and the medium eartips are preinstalled, user manuals, and the usb-a to usb-c cable. One major caviot that I AM NOT happy about at the moment is the app. I opened the earbuds, and tried connecting them with the Ear-1 IOS app, the earbuds perfectly pair to my iPhone 13 Pro Max but the app can't detect if it actually connected and for a specific amount of time, it would just say pairing failed and I would have to try again later. I reconnected them about 5-10 times before the app finally said that the pairing was succesful and the settings are pretty straight forward. You have the settings to adjust the taps on the earbuds and you can also control the ANC, TRANSPARENCY, and OFF mode on the app, and you also have a EQ which is nice but wish it could've had more settings added to change the sound of the earbuds. NOW, getting to the earbuds themselves, I had the EQ set to bass boost because thats what I prefer for these earbuds. Once I started to play music, HOLY SMOKES, I was blown away with the performance of these earbuds. The clarity of the singers voice was clear, the bass is perfect, and the highs and mids (in my opinion) were great. Don't get me wrong, there are better earbuds out there that have more adjustability to them but I believe that nothing (no pun intended) are able to compete with these whatsoever. The one thing that is pretty mixed opinion still in my head is the ANC. Once you turn them on, it blocks out most of the noise. I tested this by having my fan on full blast and it blocked out a lot of noise but you can still slightly ever hear fan spinning. Once you put them to TRANSPARENCY mode, it is also surprisingly pretty good. You can hear your surroundings pretty well but due to the eartips great noise isolation, it still kind-off blocks the noise. I haven't measured the battery life of the earbuds as much since I needed them and my days of using them were pretty busy but I would happily agree that they last all day but does needed to be charged for the night and not to mention it has wireless charging but bare in mind, it gets pretty hot and it might possibly damage the battery so I feel like charging them regularly via a plug is way better. The fit of these earbuds are comfortable, light, and have a sleek look. I've kept these on until the battery life died and my ear had no fatigue whatsoever. OVERALL, I will say that if you are in the market of buying earbuds that are not going to break the bank and want all of the great features on what 2-300 dollar earbuds sound like, these are a go. Now bear in mind that yes the sound, fit, and comfort vary on each persons experience. For me I am very satisfied with these just the app is honestly disappointing and just needs work but overall A+ for me.

I do require a larger 14mm size earbud tip which doesn't come with the product, so I replaced the stock ones with that size, and also switched to the larger ear hooks which fit under the ear cartilage with more utility than the medium. I also have the 1000xm3 which is more engaging with its noise chip turned on but this also sounds good but different. Both sound rather thin out of the box and I definitely needed the EQ in their app to boost the bass, 400hz, etc. but either unit sounds adequate once adjusted, and then its locked in and sounds better and better as I listen to them. Connection quality is good in terms of bluetooth. I use the noise reduction which takes things down to a dull roar riding in windy conditions and with cars zipping by. The 14mm tips seal out a lot of noise but the microphones bring it in and amplify it unless not in ambient mode. The music is adequately above the noise floor in any mode, but of course best in noise reduction mode. The ambient mode is great, however, in other situations where ambient noise is not too high and need of the best hearing is necessary such as during road use. I will say that these (or even the 1000xm3's for that matter) are really thin sounding out of the box and not anywhere as balanced in terms of frequency response as my baseline - which are wired earphones, Bose QC20 which I've had for 4 years now which are so good on bass, treble, etc., with overall engaging sound, and still work to this day (and Bose still sells them). I tried the Bose TWS (True Wireless) units which sounded better out of the box than the Sony's but the Bose True Wireless dropped the left earbud many times with no remedy so I had to return them - maybe Bose needs to look into creating a 2.0?

I'm an avid reader and, for a long time, I maintained that I preferred the traditional quality of books. I like the smell of books, the feeling of turning pages, writing in the margins, the dog-eared and well-loved quality of the books I've read over and over... What can I say, I'm a traditionalist. However, I decided to make the transition to an e-reader (because I've moved several times between college and law school and, as much as I love books, I hate moving them). As an added bonus, I realized I could get out-of-copyright books (which are traditionally the classics I prefer to read) for free on Kindle. Score. So I pre-ordered my Kindle, and was super excited to get it. I really enjoy having my Kindle for a number of reasons. I can take it anywhere with me and can take way more books than I expect to be able to read--and it doesn't take up all the extra room in my bag. I do read at night, and the screen looks really good. I'm not having any of the weird, distorted color problems on the screen that others have mentioned. I love the Kindle store being available (I have the 3G, no ad version), and I also really, really like being able to purchase books on my computer and have them wirelessly delivered to my Kindle. So I can shop for books on my lunch break, or whenever I think of something new I'd like to read, and it can be sent to my Kindle--whether it's sitting next to me or whether its on my bedside table at home. That's pretty sweet. All in all, I'm really glad I got the Kindle. I've never had an e-reader before, and I'm not one of those reviewers who has every single version of the Kindle ever at home to compare this one with. So, take my review for what it is--admittedly slightly uninformed. There are a few things that bug me: it's not as easy to switch a page as it is in a book. It takes a second, and there's often a weird shadow of the previous page that remains for a minute. I don't love that. I also don't love that the battery life thing seems to be a fiction. I took my Kindle with me to Jamaica within like 2 days of receiving it. I charged it completely, and then brought it with me, reading it on the plane there and intending to read it on the way back (having just received it, I was too scared to bring it to the beach with me). By the time I came home (1 week later), my Kindle was too dead to read. Eight weeks--yeah right! I charge it more often now, but it definitely doesn't last anywhere close to eight weeks. I probably charge it once a week, and read an hour or so a day when I'm in the middle of a really good book. Battery life is good, but not great. It also doesn't predict how fast I read, like advertised. As best I can tell, it comes up with a general estimate that seems to apply to almost everyone. That's not to say that I don't appreciate the estimate, but I was expecting it to speed up or slow down based on my pace, and it doesn't. That being said, the X ray feature is awesome, and helps me to remember who is who in a book with a complicated plot line and tons of characters (I just finished Les Miserables--it helped a lot!). I also really like the dictionary feature, and the ability to highlight text. I love how the Kindle opens up to the page I was previously reading--so convenient. I bought the Kindle carrying case in pink and I love that, too. It fits so snugly I can't really get it out--not that I need to. I admit--I've dropped it a few times, and the case has totally protected my Kindle. Worth the $40. I also love the cool screen savers--maybe not a major selling point, but still visually interesting (and better than the ads--totally worth $20). All in all, I think my Kindle is a really cool device. I wanted an e-reader, and that's what I got. Having something like this has made reading something that is much more a part of my every day life because (1) I don't have to carry around a bunch of heavy books (and no one knows if I'm reading something embarrassing, like 50 Shades of Grey), and (2) I can get so many books for free (or super cheap) on the Kindle store. I love that part especially because my book budget has gone down pretty dramatically, and I'm never more than a few seconds away from being lost in a great story. Would I recommend a Paperwhite over the cheaper Kindles? I'm not sure--personally, I appreciate just having the e-reader option. It may be better to purchase something cheaper (except that the lighted screen is a pretty awesome feature), but overall I'm happy with my purchase.

So what happenned with this DCS 960L. I have been laboring at this for a good 2 hours and still cannot get this connected to mydlink. The big difference with the last generation is the lost of the nic interface at the back so your very much reliant on good wireless connection, there is no cd included ( this is the usual method to connect the camera to mydlink ) and Most importantly you must have a tablet running mydlink to get it up and running. What is annoying are the devices are usually setup in a lab then deployed to a site where a local IT can get this configured. The problem is the wireless setup is locked in to a WIFI network and when brought the site cannot easily be reconfigured thru wired means. Therefore, removing the NIC interface made the entire process more difficult. The real dealbreaker is the mydlink app. I get an error BINDERR012 which further states that an error has occurred, and we were unable to add this device to your dlink account. Please contact Technical support for further assistance (ERROR CODE BINDERR012). I have tried more than 5x reset and the whole process again, tried adding the new firmware, Used desktop and ipad mydlink. Nothing works. For some reason I cannot view in IE, Firefox or Chrome the webpage that in the past generations would have been just a breeze to turn on. The only place i can see the camera working is in Safari on Ipad. On the upside I can see there is a good quality image that the camera can produce. If only I can get in mydlink and Dviewcam. Ill be updating this as I wait for DLINK's response on the matter.

I also own/have owned a clip zip, several S-Master Amp equipped Walkman's, a 5th, 5.5, and current gen iPod's, every Zune ever made, and the HiFiMan 601 to name a few. After the HM-601, with one exception I wrote off all consumer grade DAP's (Digital audio players b.k.a. mp3 players). Having a proper amp section in a player makes one heck of a difference. Purchasing this I was on the fence about buying a Colorfly C3, or a used RoCoo P or BA and in the case of the Colorfly, a C&C BH amp. My reason for player shopping is that I view my gear as a collection and I only want to own things worth owning. I plan to keep everything I purchase indefinitely. The HM-601 fully satisfies me, however it is very musical, and has a certain coloration to it's sound that is very, very lush, and analogue sounding (reminiscent of a vinyl record or the cleanest sounding cassette tape you "never" heard). I needed something that was better than consumer grade, but was still more neutral in terms of sound quality. Having owned the Fiio X3 and been dissatisfied with it's worth (not bad but not collection worthy (I would not use it once I had a better player)) I began looking and for various reasons passed on the over priced iRiver AK100 and the overly bright and thin sounding iBasso DX50 and so it left few options. I decided on the HM-700 largely because there are NO reviews on here and maybe 2 on Head-fi (you knew that was coming ;)) and it had a powerful amp section and supported FLAC. Here's what you get. A 32gb, 15 or so hour playback time, easy to use, compact and well built, drag and drop music sync'able, FLAC, APE, WAVE, WMA, MP3, etc capable, balanced headphone output equipped DAP with a set of HE-400B balanced i.e.m.'s (in ear monitor's (you may know these as earbuds or in ear phones)). Oh, and all for the price of an iPod Classic. What you should know. It is terrific. Why it is so. The fact that they actually at this price point, give you so much is simply astounding. It sounds... phenomenal and I have heard a lot of players. For one, it WILL show you a difference between lossless quality music and mp3's. Not in a brutal fashion where music that is of lower quality can't be enjoyed. But if your still rocking 160kbps mp3's, it will swiftly motivate you to step up your musical game. The combination literally was made for each other, and that being said, it is obvious. The RE400B's sound quite surprisingly, and refreshingly, good out of any "good" or "great" source you plug them into. They are neutral with the slightest hint of warmth. The player truthfully, is not as good sound quality wise taken on it's own as it is with the RE400B's. Meaning the pair together is so pronounced that pairing with other phones doesn't have the same amount of "magic". However, that being said, it is in no way a con. I know I know but stay with me for a bit. The combo is probably in honesty, better than whatever your using now unless it's AT LEAST a $600+ player with a $350 minimum i.e.m.. My reference for i.e.m.'s are my VSonic GR07 MKI's. I have things that have more technical ability, but they are the standard by which all other i.e.m.s are judged and this combo, exceeds what they, in their unbalanced form can do. What I aim to convey is that even if you take two components that are better on their own, and pit it against this player, with the bundled i.e.m.'s, you will have either a very, hard, or very expensive time besting what HiFiMan has done here. I commend them. I would give this a seal of approval as a gift, as either a set (preferably for those audio inclined), or even just the RE400's as a gift of hifi to a new comer. In summary SQ wise on 1-10, this hits hard as a combo. Can it be beat, well sure. But can it be beat for less than $600 total? Doubtful, and the point is it's not really justified to try. If you are new to this hobby, or want to give the gift of HiFi I can with all sincerity say start here. It will save you time trying and outgrowing Cowon, Sansa Clips, iPhones and iPods, etc, etc. I hope I have been helpful, to me this is collection worthy as Hifi, audiophile grade equipment. Now, off to Summit-fi :) (reference) Yes, the HM-901, HM-801, HM-802, Terra Player, AK120 etc. I'm sure are better. The purpose it to assure you that if your looking at the Fiio X3 or an amp for your iPod or cell phone etc then to my ears this combo will surpass them, handily in most situations. There are better players for unbalanced i.e.m.'s/headphones, but this isn't just good for the money. It's just good... full stop. So if you want something that is so good you will forget you bought it for your other fancy earphones/headphones, this kind Sir or Maim, is the ticket. *Edit: 2/15/2014 I have been using the player more with other i.e.m.'s instead of just the included RE400B's. I find that, it doesn't play as well with balanced armatures that are not neutral. I wouldn't recommend it for that specifically (I'm looking at you Westone 3). It is however better than I though when paired with just about any dynamic driver earphone, It is also very, very good when paired with reference quality dynamic driver i.e.m.'s such as the VSonic GR07 or the Sony MDR EX1000's or 7550's. Best Wishes

I'm giving this a 1 star because we had a surge and this product failed with a low resistance short. Every other power strip I've ever had fail has failed with an open. We lost power, and I switched to generator an hour later 2 times for about 5 seconds each. The generator bogged down each time. 10 minutes later, I found this device and it was still hot to the touch. That's not right. Now, for the photos posted in other reviews, those users overloaded this device. They think it was a crappy surge protector, but that wasn't their problem. A 15A household circuit is NOT rated for 15A continuous. Max continuous should be no more than 11.2A. If you go higher, the breaker panel will not trip, but the APC surge device will do exactly as they show in the photos. A 15A household outlet's plastic will also melt or char like that with 15A continuous. Anyway, the APC product sucks for surge protector reasons alone, not for those other user error reasons. I cut mine open and am posting a photo of the component that blew/shorted and was super hot.

I got two, to outfit a part time office I am opening in another city and will use a couple days per week. BUDGET: So the budget price was a big plus. CONTENTS FAULTY: The boxes are advertised on the box as containing "power cord + vga cord." One box came with 2 HDMI cables and zero power cables. This isn't a deal killer, you may have too many spares already or they are $7 at an office store. The other box came with one power cord, one vga cord, and one HDMI cord, more than the box listed. MOUNT: Be aware these are very simple flat monitors on a very simple budget plastic stand - no fancy height or angle features. I put them on a paper ream to be a couple inches higher. INPUTS: They do have a nice triplet set of VGA + DVI + HDMI input sockets. There is also a standard little audio patch plug, but if you drive it off HDMI the audio is built in to the HDMI cable. SPEAKER: It's quite tinny to the point of being sort of unpleasant. But there is one. CONTRAST: The contrast may not be so great - lettering on these monitors looks "gray" compared to "sharp black" on my Lenovo Laptop native monitor. It's usable but won't look good compared to a monitor that could easily be double or triple the investment. If you stop comparing monitors and just use this one your eyes adapt. RESOLUTION: On a Lenovo X1(Gen4), you have two video outputs, a standard HDMI and a MiniDisplayPort. Either offered to drive the monitor up to 1920x1080 with the Lenovo recommended you choose 1600x900. Also, FYI, if you have a laptop HDMI and/or a laptop MiniDisplayPort for low cost from Amazon you can get the cable of choice with any other output on the far end (HDMI, DisplayPort, DVI, VGA, etc.)

Working at home from time to time, this mobile laptop desk been quite handy and useful. It has locking wheels and is very adjustable for height and tilt. The only things I would change are: * The wheel locks are a bit too easy to engage. The lock tabs need to be a bit shorter, or possibly some other type of lock engagement would help. If you step too close to that part of the wheel, you'll engage the wheel lock. * The most annoying thing about this desk is that the center post does not remain a stationary pivot! So the desk has a habit of pivoting about the post while you're trying to type, or mouse on the laptop. It's a symptom of the height adjustment on the desk, which uses an inexpensive spring detent to hold the desktop at whatever height you set it. But it's the only thing keeping the 2 center posts together (one post inside the other), so they 'twist' on each other anytime you put any pressure on the desktop. The result is not a very solid feel, but a sloppy, or broken feel to the whole desk :-( . I really hate to say anything bad about this product, mostly because it does the job at a very inexpensive price. The fact is, there are several other "portable desk" products out there that (I'm sure) would perform the same task with a much more sturdy feel; but they cost quite a bit more than this desk, so I guess you have to weigh cost and function for your own use and value. This desk performs very well for everything else it's designed to do... The desk tops (separate tilting for the laptop, and one for the mouse) are very solid and have small 'shelves' on each edge to prevent anything from sliding off the desk. The colors and finish are pleasant to look at and touch, and the desk is quite compact and portable overall. I also found this product very easy to assemble out of the box. Possibly an application of duct tape will help the pivoting problem; I'll have to try it.

Very good. I have one of these on my belt all day long. This radio, unlike others I could mention, never falls off my belt. The front can be removed (and replaced) quite easily. There are 4 small screws on the back. You need a small Phillips screw driver. A #0 bit works well. There are 2 screws visible. One more is visible when you remove the battery cover. The fourth is visible when you remove the battery. You will see the board and the rubber membrane are coated with a viscous clear oil. I have no idea where it comes from. It's one of the great mysteries of the universe. Remove the rubber membrane and wash with something like dish detergent. So a new 46S30 was delivered to my house today. Out of the box I liked the look of the set. I have been loyal to Samsung LCDs (LNT-4071 and 46B650) for some 6 years now, but decided to take the plunge into a plasma. Let's just say my feelings are mixed. First of all, the TV arrived with a flaw in the screen. There are two vertical lines from top to bottom that are one pixel wide in the middle of the screen. They fluctuate in color and intensity depending on the scene being shown. So, this was not acceptable and I am sending it back. I am not keeping a screen with such a flaw but it has granted me a nice little trial period with the tv and wanted to write a review. I first used the set in the middle of the day in what I would consider a room with an average amount of light. I hooked up my PS3 and put in the Planet Earth BluRay. Initial thoughts were that colors are magnificent and motion is flawless. Previous LCDs Ive owned tend to get blocky/pixelated in the Planet Earth scenes with thousands of birds taking flight at once - that absolutely does not happen with this plasma. Now for the bad - The dark scenes are completely washed out even in a room with moderate daylight. In fact, when the screen is turned off it looks gray (light gray) - exactly the same gray as the blacks look when it is turned on in a room with daylight. My 22" JVC LCD ($200) has better blacks during the day and it isnt close. So then it got dark outside. I turned the set back on and played another BluRay. Holy Moly. The difference is like night and day (bad pun, I know). In a dark room this thing is quite amazing. Jet black blacks combined with the same great color and motion. Wow. So my conclusion is that if this TV was for a media room with no windows it would be VERY hard to beat for the price. I would definitely exchange it for another and be very happy. Unfortunately, in a room with any daylight this thing is worse than the old rear projection LCDs from the late 1990s. This doesnt suit my application (living room with floor to ceiling windows) however, so given that I am returning it for the screen defect I will be moving back to a Samsung or Sony LCD. Hope this helps anyone considering the move from LCD to Plasma.

I bought this drive as replacement for my external, back-up hard drive for my desktop system. Iomega's first solution was that the boot order in BIOS was causing the issue, and that the computer was trying to boot from the USB drive before getting to the hard drive. Funny -- that didn't happen with the previous drive. (BTW - the boot order is HDD, CD, floppy, then USB so their assertion was not correct.) The next solution was to remove the data from the drive, because a file on this drive must be causing the problem. Funny -- all the files on the drive came from its predecessor, and it didn't have that problem. Oh, and it took 5 hours to move 250 gb of data onto this drive, so I'm supposed to spend 5 hours moving the files, 3 hours erasing the data, and 5 hours to move it back after their scavenger hunt isn't successful?? Sorry, but if the data comes off this drive it is only to prepare the drive for return. I lived through the Iomega "click of death" -- I decided to give Iomega another chance, and quite evidently they did not deserve that chance. I’ve a long history with personal, portable music players. Like most, I started with an iPod and a couple years later, replaced it with another with greater storage capacity. Then I started to absolutely HATE iTunes. To me, iTunes just got in the way of everything I wanted to do. I’ve never particularly cared for Apple products (way overpriced and an arrogant company) so the iPod was the only Apple product I owned. Then I discovered Sony mp3 players that were handsome, easy to use and transferring files was drag and drop…piece of cake…and, best of all, no need for iTunes. Yay! I was no longer an iTunes Slave! I went through three or four Sonys and was quite the happy camper. About three years ago, I became interested in lossless ripping and dug out all my hundreds CDs and over a number of months re-ripped them to FLAC (lossless) format. Thought to myself, “Hmmmm…wouldn’t it be great to be able to listen to my lossless files on a personal player?” My wife, having heard my thoughts, for Christmas bought me a FIOS X-1 player that played lossless files. Loved it but quickly got tired of its bulk, relatively short battery life and cumbersome GUI (user interface). Started looking for a replacement and stumbled upon AGPtEK players on Amazon. Holy Moly!! They looked good, got great reviews and were CHEAP! So cheap that it was a no-brainer to give one a shot. I decided on the AGPtEK A20 [2017 UPGRADE] 8GB MP3 Player…and it was, like, 28 bucks with free shipping. Pulled the trigger on the Amazon Prime order and I had it in two days. Initial impression was good. Visually it looked pretty cool but it was light….VERY light. For me, that was a great feature because in a loose fitting pair of gym shorts it doesn’t flop around like a heavy cell phone. OK, about cell phones. Cell phones play music but they are not dedicated music players. To me, with a good set of earbuds, music players sound BETTER. That said, we all know that a majority of the insecure population of this country can’t go three minutes without burying their face in a phone to get the reassurance that they are not forgotten. Accordingly…most people use cell phones as music players at the gym. To me, good playback is more important than being glued to my phone. Plus, cell phones are too heavy and battery life sucks. So, back to my new AGPtEK player which I received five months ago. Oh…and please be aware that I use only one feature on this player – music playback. Never have (or will probably) used the radio, voice recorder, photos…any of that stuff. Just music. And MAN does it do that well!!! Sound is as amazing as I’ve ever experienced on a portable system. The GUI is a little bit clumsy but, come on, it was $28.00. Not only does it take a micro SD card (I use a 32GB – thousands of tracks), it also has 8GB of internal audio storage. I also like that it doesn’t have a “lock” button that you forget to use - and then when your player comes on accidentally when you drop it in the bottom of your gym bag and the battery runs out. This AGPtEK works differently and locks automatically at appropriate times. Two quick button pushes unlocks it. And another big HOLY MOLY for battery life. I’ve never tried to actually time it…but it seems to last for weeks…and then charges quickly. Best battery life of any player I’ve ever owned. THEN….at five months it died!! Dead, cold dead. Deep, dark, cold dead. I was devastated. Tried everything (yes, including the little pinhole RESET button). I think there was just a 30 day return on this player…I was screwed. But I decided to contact the seller via Amazon anyway. I did that and got an immediate reply with instructions to hook it up to USB power and hold the play button for a long time. Didn’t work. The seller at AGPtEK said “…no sweat, we will send you a replacement” which I got two days later. In the meantime, I plugged the dead player into a USB port on my PC (not the USB hub), held the PLAY button for a bit and this time it came on and started charging like nothing was wrong. Holy Moly!! I contacted them again and asked, if I paid them a little bit if I could just keep both. They said OK. Are you kidding me? Who does that? AGPtEK did!! What a great company, great product and OUTSTANDING customer service! AGPtEK makes a number of other players too. Now I’m interested in perhaps looking at one of their higher level, more expensive players. If the cheap ones are this good, then the more expensive ones must be better….maybe…have to think about this.

Do I recommend this unit: YES Does it do all that it claims: YES (as far as I can tell) Is it elegant in my living room: YES Does it produce gorgeous sound: YES The CEC system (the ability to link various components via HDMI) sucks. The Samsung plasma I have sometimes just turns off if I enable CEC. The instructions for this unit are like so many others I have owned: written to say what a given button does - but not how to use the unit effectively. So I can press a given "audio" button to select between audio modalities - but depending on the sound source, only some modalities are available, or none at all. But what does that mean? Does the system remember such choices by input? By incoming bitstream? Am I expected to choose every time I turn the unit on? When I have a particular image on the TV that is being output from the Onkyo, how do I control its format? I can't seem to (choosing the video button while in receiver mode simply says "function not available". So... how do I control how the image is being adapted to my 16:9 widescreen TV? If I'm playing a 2.5:1 movie, how do I control how its displayed on screen? If I pipe the output directly to the TV, then the Samsung has a button for messing with the aspect ratio / display modality. But how does the Onkyo do it? I suspect that the Onkyo can do it - if only they bothered to supply a genuinely useful users-manual (instead of a technical reference manual). I'm a software engineer - well educated, considered bright by most. I spend my days sleuthing out software programming puzzles, working with computers, etc., and yet I find using an AV receiver to be a major pain in the but. Lots of possible functions, but the only way to really learn is to sit there and press buttons while watching different sources, and trying to figure out what the underlying patterns are: what's available when, what buttons really do what under what circumstances, and much more importantly, how to do what I want with the unit I bought. Is it just me or is the state of home entertainment still lacking some basic user-friendliness?
