I do a little bit of everything with my home PC - browsing, streaming, gaming, programming, photo/video editing, light CAD work, spreadsheets, writing reviews on the stuff I buy. etc. I had been looking for YEARS for a 21:9 panel that had the right combination of features/price/brand but had never ran into one that I felt comfortable committing to; now that I have found the MSI MAG342CQRV, I'm glad the search took me that long. This thing is just a hair off from perfect. Colors are vivid, darks are dark enough, images don't tear or blur, the curvature is immersive from the normal 36" sitting distance from the panel, I don't find myself having to crane my neck to see what's over in this corner or that one, and frankly, it just looks GREAT sitting there on the desk. Functionally, this monitor has about 109 pixels-per-inch, which, you want 100 or better. I haven't noticed any backlight bleeding, but I usually work in a semi-well-lit area and it would take extreme bleeding for me to notice it. The buttons are in a logical position and placement under the bezel, and the menu is easy enough to navigate once you figure out how each button navigates through it. My only nitpick is that it does not have USB passthrough, which is a "nice-to-have" feature but hardly one most people will miss. As many reviews state, it *does* have a large footprint, but, it's a large monitor... I'd be more concerned if it had a SMALL footprint! As it is, the stand is simple to look at, easy to assemble, and has just the right amount of 'give' in its adjustments to where getting just the right angle doesn't require brute strength, but it also doesn't spin around on its axis if you sneeze. Some reviews point to the external power cable as a 'con' but I actually prefer it... the thinner cable is easier to route/hide than a standard C13 power cable, AND it moves the most common point of failure outside of the monitor and into a package you can replace if it ever does go bad on you. Some caveats, if you're moving from a dual-monitor setup (like I was) and consolidating to a single, large panel. Where I used to silo applications by opening them on a specific monitor, I now have to do that by dragging the app boundaries so that app occupies a given portion of the screen. It's not a big issue, but it did necessitate a workflow change that I hadn't considered prior to purchase. Also, most web pages are not built to scale to such widths, and I found myself zooming in - not because I can't see the text, but because it seems like such a waste to have a foot of white space on either side of the main page frame. All in all, I am very pleased with this monitor, it has been a huge upgrade (literally) to my twin 1080p panels, and does everything I ask of it.

This came as a gift to upgrade me from the third generation Kindle and the Kindle app on my smartphone. When given the choice between this and the Paperwhite, I chose this one due to the ability to use as a regular tablet when I'm not reading. Pros: - The picture is absolutely stunning, especially when watching tv/movies. The picture is vibrant, clear, and sharp. - It's faster than I thought it would be, including powering up and down. Much better than the third gen Kindles. - I'm able to play games like Candy Crush Saga and Wheel of Fortune without any issues. - Can access Netflix, Hulu +, and other tv apps! Cons: -The battery doesn't last as long as I had hoped when playing games but it's still better than playing them on my tiny smartphone. - The weight of the Kindle, while lighter than previous generations can feel heavy after using it for a while. This isn't a huge "con" since there are those tablet pillows I can buy to alleviate the need for me to hold it while I watch shows or read. - Every now and then, especially when the brightness is turned all the way up, the screen vibrates which can cause dizziness. It only lasts for a moment at a time but it can get annoying when it does it more than once an hour. When I have the screen dimmed it doesn't appear to have that vibration problem. Overall, this is a fabulous buy, especially for those of us who were able to get a holiday deal on it. Even full price, it's worth it. The Nook was looking good simply because it has access to Google Play and Chrome whereas the Kindle only uses their own proprietary shop (Amazon App Store). But after reading reviews from experts and consumers it seems the Kindle is still the better tablet. Besides, the way Barnes and Noble is heading, they may not be around long enough to support the new Nooks into the future. At least Amazon seems strong and doesn't appear to be going anywhere anytime soon so the Kindle will be supported for years to come. I highly recommend this for anyone older than 10 years old. Even with the parent controls on the Kindle, I would still choose Nabi and Nabi, Jr for kids under the age of 10.

To begin with the construction is cheap, and the material is flimsy. (I have a Thermaltake BlacX ST0014U dual docking station I bought for about the same money and it's made much more sturdy. After hooking it up using the supplied cables I put in a 2TB SATA drive I had been using in the Thermaltake docking station. It was formatted and had been working just fine. The computer recognized this StarTech docking station and installed the drivers for it, and showed the correct model for the SATA hard drive in the driver installation window. After the drivers were installed is showed in Devices as a USB to ATA/ATAPI Bridge. So far so good I thought, but after that it went downhill. The SATA drive did not show up at all in "Computer" (Windows 7 Ultimate). Using Paragon Hard Disk Manager 2011 the drive showed up with the wrong capacity and "Invalid". I rebooted but no still no recognition of the drive in "Computer" and the same behavior in Paragon. I took out the SATA drive and put it back in the Thermaltake docking station. The drive read properly and the data was accessible. I then attached a working 3.5" 120GB IDE drive to the StarTech via the ribbon cable and power adapter. On powering up the StarTech docking station my computer again installed drivers for it, detected it as a bridge and showed the correct hard drive model during driver installation, but again the drive would not show up in "Computer". I never got to Paragon Hard drive Manager because the system blue screened right after looking in "Computer" with a Bad_Pool_Header error. Being a glutton for punishment I re-started the system with the StarTech attached and powered on with the IDE drive. After I logged in the drive still wouldn't show up in my computer. I replaced the USB cable from the docking station to the computer with a known working cable. Upon powering up the docking staton the computer beeped as expected alerting that a USB device was connected but again no display of the drive in "Computer"; a minute later the system locked up. The mouse locked up and when I moved it, the pointer moved in jumps and very slowly, then the "busy" blue circular icon came up in place of the mouse pointer at multiple locations on the screen. I disconnected the Star Tech docking station and after about 5 minutes the system unfroze. I rebooted and everything is fine now with my system. I packed up the StarTech docking station and completed a return on it. My computer system is very stable (Intel Core i7 CPU with 12GB of memory, Windows 7 64bit Ultimate with dual monitors, a networked printer, and USB web cam. It's rarely had any problems and has worked with everything I've hooked up to it, till now. I've used different external drives in a variety of enclosures, both SATA and IDE drives, connected either through USB or eSata, and now recently the Thermaltake Dual drive Docking Station. I've connected devices through the same USB port using the same cable. This Startech is the first piece of equipment that didn't work with my system. I would say, overall, this StarTech docking station is a piece of junk and should be avoided.

I've owned my Kindle DX for three days now, and though I don't normally write reviews when there are already so many, I wanted to add my voice concerning this innovative, fun, and useful gadget. I originally bought it for two reasons: Subscribe to the newspaper without all the paper, and carry several books when traveling, without all the weight. Pluses: When reading the newspaper, I do not get ink on my hands, I do not have to deal with all the paper, and no trees are being felled for my reading pleasure. I also do not have to struggle with the large format of the paper. Though this also means I cannot see all the stories on a page at a glance, it's worth the trade-off. Magazines are often printed on glossy paper, and I find that the older I get the harder it is to read from a glossy page. The Kindle is much easier on my eyes, as long as I avoid having a direct light source directly behind me. Also related to the age of my eyes, being able to choose the font size is a great boon. I've read books recently that were hard on my eyes due to small type. With the Kindle, this is not a problem. I may just be lazy here, but the built-in dictionary and easy access to Google and Wikipedia are convenient. I don't have to get up and walk over to the dictionary or the computer to look up something I don't recognize. Instant gratification is probably a character weakness, but it's nice to be able to get books instantly (well, in about 60 seconds or so). I am developing arthritis in my thumb, and holding a book open has become painful. But the Kindle is flat and rigid, easy to hold in one hand or prop up. It doesn't flop over or flip shut like a book, or sag like a magazine or newspaper. Compared to reading on the computer, the Kindle allows me to sit comfortably in my easy chair, rather than slumped at the computer, and I find this much more relaxing. And the e-ink is easier on my eyes than the computer screen. Now the minuses. There are three I can think of: Placing the cursor on a word brings up a definition if it's in the dictionary, and a few clicks will take you to Google or Wikipedia for that word. But if you want to google a word that is not in the dictionary, you have to type it by hand on the tiny keyboard keys, which is awkward. They should have allowed the word at the cursor to be placed in the search box with just a hit on the Return key. This is not a big deal, but it would have been so easy to implement. This is a bigger issue: There is no directory structure. A device capable of holding 3,500 books needs some way for them to be organized into subdirectories or subfolders, as on all computers nowadays. There is a search function to find items, but I anticipate difficulty locating items once there are a hundred or so items on the Kindle. This also would be easy to rectify, and I regard it as a serious shortcoming that they did not address it. When you buy a book you can pass it along to someone else when you are done. To share a Kindle book with a friend you'd have to loan her your Kindle. Maybe that's the biggest drawback of all. Overall, I love this toy. It is very expensive, but if you have the money to spend, it is a great way to read newspapers, magazines, and books. I give it five stars.

Mine are working great so far, and they've solved a HUGE set of problems I was having with Yosemite. In particular, I was having major issues running large, edited .pdf's in Preview; and forget about running anything at the same time as GarageBand or Logic or ProTools. I also had persistent memory leaks and spinning beachballs. So I got the Corsair 16 gigs, quadrupled my memory, and so far, problem solved. Very easy to install (though you really need the proper magnetic screwdriver: if you "make do," you'll strip the screws). A couple of tips and tricks: First, these memory sticks are not risk-free. Mine seem to be generating a bit more heat than the factory memory-sticks. That's not great for any computer, but it's an acceptable risk for me, since I'd have to buy a new laptop if its performance didn't improve. My fan is currently running a bit louder than it used to. Second, I had to employ a weird install trick. When I put them in, my computer wouldn't turn on but kept beeping at me. The solution took some time to find and was a little bizarre: I had to loosen the four screws that hold the RAM unit in. Weird, yes? I got the tip from the Mac Forums, where some have theorized that heat, over time, warps the unit to the point that the sticks don't make proper contact. Anyway, strange as it seemed, it worked. Third: They do work. Screaming memory: my machine is almost too fast. To test the memory, I ran all my biggest memory hogs at once (Filemaker Pro, iPhoto, Mail, Preview with a huge edited .pdf, GIMP, Word, ProTools) and then opened Rome: Total War. Not only did everything run just fine and swap tasks efficiently, but I realized that my "game-rhythm" had been seriously dumbed down to accommodate the machine's slow swapping. Yowza. Multi-tasking Nirvana. Things moved much more quickly. Fourth: You're taking a risk as the mhz ratings don't match Apple's specs for all computers (mine's an Early 2011 MacBook Pro). I haven't done a battery test, but I expect that will be a trade-off. NOTE: I installed mine at the same time as a Transcend SSD: cheaper than buying a new computer, and the two together may persuade me not to abandon Apple, if they can manage Yosemite.

I received two watches, both with the exact same problem, and therefore I deduced it was an issue with the software and not a physical limitation of the watch. Essentially, if you load music onto this watch using a Mac computer and the Garmin Express software, you'd better be happy with those playlists forever, because if you try to delete them, you will never be able to recover the drive space necessary to replace them with another playlist. The only way to recover this space is to do a complete reset which wipes all of your data, including the music, which frees up disk space, but who wants to do this everytime you want to change out your playlists??? I spent over 45 min. on the phone with Garmin and the problem couldn't be deduced, so I asked for a replacement which I received. When I had the exact same issue with the second watch, I called Garmin again and told them something was wrong either with the Garmin Express software for Mac or with the firmware on their watch. They hadn't heard of this problem before and asked for screenshots of the process, which I sent to them. They are now investigating the issue, but in the meantime I decided to make my life easier and return the Garmin in favor of an Apple Watch, which I know won't give me any compatibility issues.

I bought these at the end of January 2018 and they are the revised version with the 2.5mm connectors instead of the MMCX. I've tried a number of planar headphones, Audeze LCD3, Opportunity PM-3, AudioQuest Nighthawk, HifiMan HE560 and never kept any of them. I think that I have never found a set that had the sound I liked at a price commensurate to their quality and which I would want to spend time with rather than with my Sennheiser HD800S headphones. When I came across the 1060s at under $300 I couldn't pass up the chance to try them out. For the money, they are beautifully made and presented. Out of the box they didn't sound bad, but have certainly benefited from a 60 hour burn in. Now I have to say that they are just a very musical set of phones, warm and easy to listen to. I have compared them to the HD800S running from a Schiit Jotununheim and not surprisingly they don't compare in soundstage, clarity, high end accuracy, but at the price that isn't what I am looking for. The real use for me is as a set of phones to casually listen to music from my Fiio X7 Mkii, and for this they are great. They are comfortable, a bit on the heavy side, but not to the point where I noticed it. The pads creaked a bit when first used, but have settled down and are plush and provide a good comfortable seal. I have no complaints about the cabling which is really thin, but seems solid enough and not microphonic. With the new 2.5mm at the headphone end and 3.5mm for the player connection, this is an easy cable to replace if you do have any problems. As far as the sound quality goes, they have a reasonably wide sound stage, but with not much front to back depth. Bass is slightly accentuated and top end rolls off a bit. I've seen reviews complaining about a peak at 5KHz and other problems, but I don't notice it, and for me these are NOT a pair of reference headphones, they are something to listen to music with and for me they have a pleasing musical sound, not harsh, not super sharp, but not too muddy either. A sound you can just sit back and enjoy, maybe not with a "wow" but with a long term smile. (Amazingly some people who don't notice the 5KHz problem have been asking for advice as to how to search for it so that they can be disturbed by it, weird!). They are pretty easy to drive, certainly from the X7 AM3 stock amp module. I did buy a balanced cable on Amazon and tried that output on the X7 to the M1060s. Impossible to do an A/B comparison but my impression was that the balanced gave slightly more open highs, but slightly detracted from the bass and didn't help the warmth so have sent that cable back and happily gone back to the supplied SE cable. In conclusion I am keeping the M1060s for relaxed listening. When I want to listen more seriously I'll still use my HD800Ss or my Shure SE846s for the Fiio X7 Mkii. The fact the I can listen happily to the M1060s when I am used to the sound from TOTL headphones and IEMs, speaks volumes to the quality of the M1060s and for the price a total bargain.

The fans were installed upside down (blowing into the case and towards the processor instead of away), the 4 sticks of RAM were from 3 different vendors and one stick was a different speed of RAM altogether. I purchased 2 of these machines and both were like this. In one machine, there were wires plugged into the motherboard but not connected to anything. These were not your usual unused power cables, they were to other equipment that was no longer in this case. In one machine the external venting fan was only held in by one rubber mounting screw and the fan just hung sideways in the case banging around when the computer was powered on. The other three rubber screws (used to control fan vibration) were not screws but instead were just rubber feet plugged into screw holes with no ability to ever hold an exhaust fan. The ONLY reason I even give this two stars is that it came with pre-installed Windows 10 without any bloatware, and the price was right for a couple extra desktop computers. It was just easier for me to find an extra appropriate stick of RAM, purchase new rubber screws to hold the fan,, and re-mount all the fans to vent the appropriate direction rather than return the computers.

The first part of the review is for the 8x42 binoculars which are terrific. Scroll down to read my experience with the 8x32 smaller brother. The optical performance these binoculars (8x42) provide is incredible for the price. I tried some others costing more, but so far none work as well with my eyeglasses (correcting for distance and astigmatism). Everyone's face and (if applicable) glasses are different, so your mileage my vary, but for me the optical performance of these (8x42) binoculars is wonderful. You might be tempted to point out that with the diopter adjustment one might just use the binoculars without glasses but, from my experience, that wouldn't be an optimum solution. Your glasses are probably correcting a number of your eyes' visual defects beyond just focus. When you use your glasses with the binoculars, all the defects are corrected and the resulting image is much clearer. To get this happy result, the binoculars must have sufficient eye relief and a set of adjustable eye cups. Wearing your glasses when birding also helps you find the birds in the first place. I have used these binoculars for about 12 months, including a daily average of about one hour of walking per day. I use a binocular harness to make wearing them more comfortable and I don't find them to be a burden when carried that way. I did have a problem in that several of the small internal screws that attach each eye cup have (over 8 months of careful use) backed out and fallen out, allowing both eye cups to become detached from the binoculars and allowing the screws (which are smaller than a short pencil lead) to fall out. The binoculars can't be used without the eye cups, but I found I could tape the eye cups back on with black masking tape. That worked fine in the lowered "eyeglasses" position, but since I really love the binoculars, I was disappointed in the way they looked with masking tape wrapped around both eye cups and anyway that solution wouldn't work for someone using the eye cups in the extended position. I ended up calling Celestron Customer Service and they issued a return authorization and an address in Torrance, California, where I could send the binoculars. So far so good. These Celestron's binoculars have a "Limited Lifetime Warranty" which covers "defects" but not "normal wear and tear" and to their credit they promptly sent me a new pair. They are just as optically excellent as the prior pair and I haven't had any problem with the eye cups, although I keep them taped down to reduce movement and avoid the previous problem. By the way, I noticed that a few other Amazon customers have reported eye cup screws falling out, so I think this may be more than an isolated quality issue. I bought two more pairs of Nature DX 8x42 binoculars for family members and I expect those users to be just as pleased. 8x32 Nature DX. Encouraged by the performance of the larger 8x42's, I ordered a pair of Nature DX 8x32's. After much side-by-side comparison I have concluded that the performance of my particular 8x32's is not up to the standard of the three pairs of 8x42 I have purchased and personally examined. The eye relief specs are the same, but my subjective conclusion is that I find myself pushing the 8x32's into my glasses trying to get a little more eye relief. I also notice that the dark rings that are see around the edges of the optics are fuzzy rather than sharp. I believe this is also due to slightly less eye relief. I would have expected the main advantage of the 8x42's to be optical performance in low light, but the 8x32's are noticeably less bright, even at midday. Finally, the 8x32's are just not that much smaller and lighter, so it isn't worth it to me to give up the optical performance of the 8x42's. Check out my photos for a size comparison.

Image Quality: 3.5/5 It is good enough for an ultra wide angle lens, but if you're a pixel peeper, you're eyes will hurt, especially at the edges, where sharpness is nonexistent, distortion is magnified, and chromatic aberration is frequent. Build Quality: 3.8/5 Decent build. Nothing fantastic about it, but it does feel fairly solid. It's mostly plastic, but it doesn't feel like cheap plastic. It is an external zoom, so there's a good chance it'll siphon in some dirt here or there. But it's unlikely that you'll shoot this often enough to have dirt accumulate. Features: 3.8/5 It's got a very smooth zoom and focus rotation. Feels like butter almost, so that's a plus. Has full time manual. Has an AF/MF switch, but that's pretty common these days. Autofocus is good enough (not fast, not slow, accurate enough). HSM is quiet, and I never notice any focusing sounds (doesn't mean that they don't exist - it's just not loud enough to bother me). It does lack OS (optical stabilization), but is that something a wide angle lens really needs? Also, it'd be nice if there were a zoom ring lock. I feel like a lot of people use this lens mostly for its 10mm focal length, but the zoom ring is so smooth that it slips out of place ALL THE TIME. You'll have to get used to checking the ring every time you shoot. That's about all there is to the features. Price: 4.5/5 As for what you get for what you pay, this lens is awesome. You'll find very few lenses out there cheaper than this while offering more. As for the Sigma 10-20mm f/3.5, consider if you really want to pay $150 more for a 3.5. For the most part, I use this to shoot landscapes, which usually requires a fairly narrow aperture (like f/9 or f/16). Also for the most part (99.5% of the time), I use only the 10mm focal length, where you can have the minimum aperture at f/4. So 1/3 of a stop really worth $150? (The answer is no.) Practicality: 3.8/5 I have a hard time using this lens more than 15% of the time. My other two lenses include the Sigma 17-50mm f/2.8 and the Canon 70-200mm f/4. Both lenses are noticeably sharp, even without pixel peeping. Both lenses offer me a variety of focal lengths. Still, I suppose it really depends on the photographer. If you like a wider angle, you may enjoy this lens a lot more than I do (and I still do enjoy this lens). Overall: 3.9/5 Good lens overall. It'd be nice if the lens was sharper overall. Even if corner sharpness can't be corrected, it'd be nice if the center were sharper. A lot of it really does look like rubbish at 100% crop. I'm also not a big fan of the external zoom, but for this price, I'll take it.

I am a professional Home Theater/Stereo installer. I have a great many customers who have a home theater room, but also a few rooms that they want to run sound to. Unfortunately, most modern AVR's (audio-visual-receivers/amplifiers) do not have the connections or they make the set up exceedingly difficult for non-professionals to figure out how to achieve signal distribution to other rooms/speakers. The SS4 is one of the best and most cost-effective tools to overcome these shortcomings. For instance, if you purchase an AVR with 7.1 sound, you will be able to assign the rear surround speakers of your amplifier to another task like providing sound to other rooms. However, if you simply tap into the speaker posts on your receiver, you are likely to fry your expensive receiver by not matching the impedance of the speakers which you are trying to power. Add a jumper set of wires from the receiver to this selector and you will be able to run up to 4 additional pair of speakers throughout your house without having to buy a separate amplifier. You should use the largest gauge wire for the jumpers possible - usually 12G or 14G. Then all of your runs to your other speakers should also be given the largest gauge wire possible, at least 14G. This will minimize the diminution of volume from splitting the power from your amplifier from a single set of posts to several sets of speakers. The box (SS4) will take care of protecting your amplifier. I like this piece of equipment for it's essential protection functions, ability to turn on/off speakers on a room to room basis, its' ability to provide sound to multiple rooms from an AVR that does not have that capability, and finally its' cost which is exceptional. If you have any questions feel free to contact me for more information.

This review is for the Mediasonic ProRaid HUR3-SU3S3 2 Bay 3.5" SATA Hard Drive Enclosure . I like it. I have two 3GB 7200 RPM 64 Mb cache hard drives in it. I am running it in single drive mode. I have it behind the monitor of my ground floor computer and have a USB cable that feeds my graphics computer in my basement. All I have to do is plug in which ever computer I want to back up. Even though it has eSATA and USB 3.0, you can only have one running computer attached at any time. Naturally you will have to go to disk management in Windows and initialize and format the drives. If you do this on one computer and want to backup from another, you will have to go to disk management and assign drive letters to the drives on any other computers that you may want to back up from. I just turn it off when I am not backing up. saves wear and tear on the drives. If you use it for constant automatic backups you will probably not want it near your workstation as it is loud enough to be annoying. For this price you don't get high quality noise dampening. I like it because in case of a fire all I have to do is Grab it and the cables will jerk out and my Photographs and documents are easy to save, and when I travel for extensive periods I take it with me or leave it with someone. In summary it is a cheap way to backup and keep your data safe.

I really wanted to LOVE this. We stream a lot. We are not cord cutters, but enjoy everything from movies to PBS to documentaries to old TV from the 80s on up. We also enjoy many of the premium content channels like HBO, Showtime, Starz, and Amazon to name a few. Juggling Smart TVs, XBoxes, Playstations, Tablets, iPads, iPhones, Android ... it was all just getting so frustrating this seemed like a great solution (and, for the most part, I think it is). If it was true the the Roku was supposed to do one thing and do it well, I would say this was a home run. The channels are satisfyingly varied and the content is top-notch (I can think of very little if any content we have sought that is not available on it). It is quick, it seems stable, it is intuitive, and the sound and video are great. The interface is generally elegant, intuitive, and responsive (some of the apps seem like they could use some user interface tweaks, but overall they are easy enough to work with). However, the killer features we wanted this for were providing a single, consolidated place to get all of our streaming in one place, without constant needs for system updates, reboots, re-authentication and other frustrations, and (ever more killer) the ability to plug the headphones into the remote to listen without disturbing each other. Well, both of these are fails. The sound on the TV or external speakers is very good, but the sound pumped through the remote cuts out after a brief initial period of working fine (sounds as if it is being pumped through an airplane propeller). This happens reliably on any channel source, and the only fixes are to re-pair the remote, reboot the Roku, or remove and replace the remote battteries. The second issue is that periodically, we are prompted to re-authenticate our account credentials with content providers even though nothing seems to have changed (this seems random and does not affect all providers simultaneously). A quick google search sadly reveals that this is not a new issue with the Roku 3 and has been discussed online virtually since its release. I suspect this is a Bluetooth radio or some other more proprietary similar type of RF connection, but it does not work. Making things more frustrating, the phone-based support seems to be overseas, with long hold queues. E-mail support exists but is queue-based also (ie. no single case owner to interact with). The e-mail responses are peppered with apologies, thank-yous, and terrible English (e.g., a recent e-mail stated "Please provide us the below information and we will do the needful"). Having had a case open for a while, we were asked to do some things that quite frankly did not make sense, particularly after having tried many other things, but we did them anyway (e.g., What does resetting the building's router--several floors away--have to do with the sound quality being transmitted through 10 feet of open air to the remote, in a fully unmitigated line-of-sight pathway with no other RF or Bluetooth devices within 50 feet of the unit?). They have been trying--but this is not a great way to handle support, especially because we just bought it. One final but still irritating drawback is the universal search feature ... using voice (spoken into the remote) or typing in an onscreen interface with the remote (or using a companion app on a smart device or tablet) you can enter the name of an actor, movie, TV show, or other items and get a fairly prompt list of items that match across a curated list of channels. This idea rocks! However, it is not a very refined search for us. For example, we recently searched for a title we owned via one service, but even though the title was found, it was suggested we purchase or rent it from somewhere else, rather than stating it was already in our video library. Hopefully this will improve with time. Hopefully it will get resolved ... and I still recommend it and would buy another one. The content is unparalleled and the sound/video quality is fantastic... the convenience (when we are not prompted randomly to re-input our credentials first) is unbeatable. We we may downgrade this one to a Roku 2 since the earbuds were the huge reason for the Roku 3. We have no need or desire for 4k right now.

I've only had these outdoor cameras for a few days, so I won't comment on battery life yet. But overall, I'm very happy with these cameras and most of their features. I'm nitpicking a bit here, which is why there are so many Cons. They are minor issues outweighed by the Pros. PROS: * Setup was relatively simple--once you understand it--but the instructions weren't (see below) * Infrared is awesome in the darkest environments and does a good job switching between IR and non-IR automatically * Motion detection works well, as does the 1-9 sensitivity setting, although this requires some tweaking until you find the right setting for each camera * Daytime video quality is excellent and good enough to read stationary license plates up to about 50 feet. * Audio quality is amazing! Individual birds and nearby bees can be heard easily, and normal volume conversations within about 20 feet can be understood. CONS: * The cameras seem to require an active Internet connection, not just a wifi connection (although I could be wrong). This may be because the initial setup requires you to use cloud storage. This could become a problem if your Internet connection is lost or dropped. * Initial setup requires storage in the cloud (for the free trial), even if you install a USB drive in the sync module. I have not found a way to disable the cloud storage. This cloud storage requirement may be slowing down the entire system, since it forces everything to constantly use the Internet. * Setup instructions were weird and unintuitive. The included booklet simply said to install the app. And the app is kind of confusing at first, and I ended up trying to create an account (and failing) and adding the sync module several times until I figured out what it was doing (and I'm an experienced techie). The basic problem is the app requires cameras to be installed only by following certain steps, with no other option. * Setup requires the mobile app and an active internet connection to install the cameras. * Accessing the cameras and video clips requires the mobile app. There are no desktop app or web options. * Cannot schedule individual cameras. The weekly/hourly schedule can only be set for all cameras attached to a sync module. This is unfortunate and will make the scheduling feature useless for most people. It would also be helpful to be able to set quality, motion detection sensitivity, and IR settings on a schedule. The settings I use for night time would be different than the middle of the day or when I'm not at home. * No quality setting on the audio. There are multiple settings for quality of the videos, to conserve batteries, but there's no way to turn down the audio quality, for battery conservation. The included audio quality is great, but it seems to be "too" high for the purpose of these cameras. * Only 2 AA batteries in each camera. This could become very cumbersome to replace batteries if your camera is installed in a hard-to-reach location. The cameras SHOULD have 6, 8, or 10 batteries instead, so you don't have to replace them often. I would happily pay the extra battery cost so that I wouldn't have to climb up there very often. * When a camera is "in use", its settings cannot be changed, and if you try to change the settings, you'll get an error message, causing the app's settings screen to get out of sync with the camera's actual settings, until you go back and modify the settings again. * The "Talk" feature produces garbled, broken, delayed (by 3-5 seconds) audio that is unintelligible, no matter how close the camera and sync module are to your router. I have about 115 Mbps bandwidth, and it made no difference. You will never be able to use this to have a conversation of any type, even if they could understand what you're saying. This seems like a very odd flaw since the recorded audio is so excellent. This was obviously an oversight by the engineers. * The Android app's setting to disable the vibration on notifications doesn't work. It always uses my phone's setting and ignores the app's setting. * Insects near my 4 cameras are causing 15-30 false alerts per day right now, until I can figure out a better placement or setting. Other than the wear on the batteries, this is not a huge deal, but it can be annoying. * The installation hardware is inadequate. Each camera comes with 2 large wood screws that are too big and too long for almost every installation. Much smaller wood screws and double-sided tape or Velcro would have been much more practical. I ended up not using any of the screws that came with the cameras because they were too big or impossible to use on the required surfaces. * The back panels on the cameras are VERY weird to remove for battery installation. There are no instructions that I could find on how to do this, and the included plastic tools are not intuitive. I nearly broke one of the cameras trying to get the back panel off using the included tool. There's a certain trick to hooking and unhooking the tool from the back panel that you'll have to figure out on your own. * The cameras and lenses are fully exposed to sunlight and weather, which is not ideal. The cameras should come with a small hood the lens or camera to protect it even more from weather and shade from light. * User access cannot be customized. The only way to give someone access to a camera is to give them your password to your account and entire system. It would be helpful to be able to grant someone limited or temporary access, such as a neighbor, child, relative, or visitor.

This is not an item that the average person would probably have any real use for, but for some purposes it's indispensable. In my situation I have to support touchscreen PC's that don't have a keyboard or mouse attached, and there are times when a keyboard and mouse are necessary. Rather than carrying around a full sized keyboard and a mouse, and not having a place to set either of them down while using the other (and how do you use a mouse against cinderblock walls if there's no table?), you can hold this in one hand while the other one types on the keys or uses the built-in mouse touchpad. The keys are really small, too tiny for touch-typing but then you won't want this for word processing anyhow. It's only about 8 inches wide and 6 inches front to back and maybe 5/8" thick; it has a decently long cord attached. (So many items and appliances are ruined by the mfr saving two cents and providing too-short of a cord - this one is better.) If you need to have a keyboard and mouse for a computer where there is little space, or where those things are not able to be used conveniently, this is a godsend. Possibly there could be some handicapped persons who would also benefit from a device this small that provides both the keyboard and mouse. If I have any gripes about this little mini keyboard it is that you have to make sure the num lock hasn't engaged, because if it does, some of the keys revert to typing numbers instead of regular characters as it turns some of the keys into a numeric keypad arrangement, but you get used to watching for this and avoiding it. You might also find this useful if you have a 'utility' pc tucked away as a file server, which does not usually need a keyboard and mouse left lying around. You plug this in to the USB port, Windows installs it promptly, and voila, you have a keyboard and mouse. Someone apparently thought my little mini keyboard was pretty cute and walked off with it - and I had to buy another one immediately, because for my purposes, there's nothing else like it. I showed the vendor who provides the touch screen PC's and he bought some for his employees to use, and they found out just how handy this is. It's well made, or so it seems, much like any typical computer keyboard only smaller. If you need a mouse and keyboard in a pinch, and don't have space or place to put the regular items, this is perfect.

I still love this camera, though I too had some picture quality complaints the first time I used it in bright sunshine. The reason, it seems, is that the factory setting for contrast is too hot (it was set at +3). I dialed it down to zero and the pictures are perfect. I've appended my original review. This is my 1st Pentax digicam, and I am absolutely thrilled with it thus far. The primary allure is its size: when compared to my old stand-by Canon digital Elph, this camera is less than half the bulk of the older one. The difference is immediately noticeable, as the Optio easily slips into my pants pocket without feeling too intrusive. It also looks positively 007! Secondly, it is well built. The steel case has an aircraft aluminum-type finish, which means it is easy to grip and it resists fingerprints. It is also well shaped for holding steady. Also of great value is the automatically retracting lens with automatically deployed lens cover; no more lens caps or scratched optics! The features list hits what I think is the "sweet spot" in today's digicams, namely a 3.2 megapixel resolution (allowing for nice 11" x 14" enlargements) plus a 3X true optical zoom. There are numerous other less vital features, my favorite of which is the camera's ability to remember *all* your favorite or your last settings when you power it up again. Battery life seems great, especially when the crystal clear LCD screen is off (you can still use it to review a pic you just took [for a period of time you have pre-selected from the menu] just by pressing the 'play button' on the back of the camera). My complaints are trivial: the battery charger I'm not too crazy about (long cord, not convenient for travel) and the rocker switch for accessing the menu is bedevillingly small for my big fingers. Also, as seems to be the style with all of these companies, the memory card is either too small (11 megs built-in) or not included (I bought a SD 256 card and get 356 shots at 2 megapixels of resolution). All in all though, this is the best digicam I have yet owned.

I purchased this keyboard without knowing whether it would work with my Samsung Galaxy Tab Pro 10.1. None of the reviews have discussed using it with any Android tablets, so I decided to take a chance because I liked the design and the fact that it has it's own tablet stand built-in. The keyboard is very well made. The keys are easy to type on, even though the keyboard itself is a bit small (but it's a tablet keyboard so that's not a surprise). I'm glad they included an on-off switch, but it isn't labeled so you have to remember which position is which. The popup mechanism also has a very solid sound and feel. I am happy to say that the keyboard works perfectly with my Galaxy Tab Pro. It connected without issue (although it took me a minute to realize I had to actually type in the pairing code on the keyboard). Once it was connected, it worked as expected. The lock button, home button, arrow keys all work as they should. My Tab Pro fits in the groove/stand the same way an iPad would and triggers the popup stand mechanism as well. I suspect that it would be the same with any similarly sized tablet. The keyboard is pretty much the same width as my Tab Pro. Whether in portrait or landscape, I was able to slot my tablet in. The keyboard is also very well balanced (I suspect that's why there is that extra space at the back) so that it doesn't feel like it would fall over, even in portrait. I even picked it up and gave it a decent shake and it held the tablet (I don't suggest that you do that though). Of course, you can't use the case/cover feature of the keyboard with the Galaxy Tab Pro because it doesn't have the same dimensions as the iPad or the magnetic attachment. But for what it is (a really thin and light Bluetooth keyboard), you can throw it in your bag and always have it ready. Highly recommended for adding a portable keyboard to any tablet/device.

The last review of this radio was back in 2012 so I thought I would add an updated one. First what I would recommend is make a backup copy of the GPS software. 2nd I would not try and change any backgrounds in the GPS display. Once you do this scrolling and navigating through the menu screen is fairly easy. 4th set the default volume for your start up as you desire (default is 15 my setting is 9) (Set the volume for the GPS when using it with conjunction with the radio my setting is 7.) 5th set the settings to indicate you want to hear your radio with conjunction with your GPS. 6th Also set the setting in the same manner if you plan to install a backup camera. 7th try out your dvd player and your SD card. 8th probably should be first consider having a qualified installer to put in I found a local person to install it for $40 plus parts totaling about $60. The installer took about 45 minutes for radio installation and the camera took about 2 hours and this was a separate charge. For the money the screen size is not bad for the GPS unit. You can see the screen during the day in hot bright San Antonio without any problems. I paid $140 plus tax for Magellan I purchased a year ago and did not plan to use the built in car radio GPS. Radio station is simple to operate and set your favorites in the memory. I can load a 32g SD card with mp3 music in different folders and can access them without much problems. I have created the folders labeled with rock music, modern or dance etc so I can listen to the type of music I am in the mood for. I had considered another car radio with the same features in the range of $800, I think I will wait till it drops around $200 like this one did. Now for the not so good, instructions are none existing but the website has more instructions that are not any better, the blue tooth cuts in and out when I use it not a big deal with me as I don’t really use it that much. I have not yet figured out how to download my contacts on to the radio no big deal as this is in my phone anyways. I installed a $20 dollar back up camera and the price is reflective of the performance. When you back up in the dark the screen whites out with the backup lights. During the day it works fine. Also to note I have prime membership and I received the item on a Sunday and of course had it install on a Monday now that is service. I ordered my unit from 24 hour stop don’t know if this makes a difference. For the advance user you can set the time of day going in factory settings and selecting your time zone such in my case central standard time. You can also select for the time to be set by GPS this is different from the GPS car unit clock time management. For the GPS unit you have to set the day light saving time if your region recognizes it and follows it. Otherwise the time will be off by an hour. You can also go in and select your car manufacture and it will look like a factory installed car radio. You can see some YouTube videos that explain the programming steps. The videos are not that good but are informative. Overall I gave this unit a good review as it fits my budget and needs.

This receiver looked like it was perfect for me. All I wanted was a glorified HDMI switcher and Audio Amp with Bluetooth to send audio from my smartphone. It was simple, price was right and reviewed high. It also seemed sort of future proof with HDCP 2.2 and 4k. I bought it to replace my 6+ year old pioneer receiver. I recently purchased an ASUS Chromebit to add to the Pioneer receiver but it had HDMI handshake issues so I figured a new receiver was in order and settled on this one. I unpacked it, hooked up all of my devices and sound, and went through the simple setup which auto detected my room size and speaker configurations without issue. That is where the joy ended. It started with my Roku 3 which started displaying HDCP errors and would not display a picture. Several unplugging re plugging and restarts and that seemed to iron out. The Sony bluray player worked no problem. Then on to my Chromecast which I had used without issue on my old Pioneer receiver...Nothing. No picture, No Audio. Weird I thought, so I restarted everything, Nothing. I then powered everything up in different orders..Nothing. I tried every HDMI port...Nothing. I tried HDMI pass through...Nothing. Frustrated I moved on to my Asus Chromebit (The reason i bought a new receiver). Video displayed and Audio worked. I went to change the display settings and it would not show any resolution over 1024x768. I couldn't force another resolution and I tried powering off, different HDMI ports, Powerwash etc etc etc nothing fixed it. I searched forums, looked for firmware updates, tried every setting. In the end the Chromecast never worked and the ASUS chromebit wouldn't change resolution. Bottom line is I am pretty disappointed that a modern receiver just did not play nice with these devices. It was a huge headache and letdown. That coupled with the fact that the input switching is sluggish I decided to return it and plug my old Pioneer back in (Which has no issue with the Chromecast and I have figured a solution for the Chromebit). I'm sure if all you have is a blu ray player and a TV and maybe a streamer this might work. But it was terrible with google products and did not work for me. Thankfully Amazon rocks and I returned it without issue. Good Luck!

We are converting the church sound over to in ear monitors. All the musicians I've put onto this have really liked it because they can hear themselves much better and I can do partially custom mixes for them (up to 2 people share a mix). It's working really well except for one thing. I get complaints that they can't hear themselves, which is weird to me because when I first set them up they said they didn't have any trouble with it and felt like they could really hear themselves well. Here is what I think happened. Initially they had the "me" channel all the way up, then asked for more X, Y, Z in the mix channel. Then it got to the point they couldn't hear over what was in the mix channel. So I try getting them to turn down the "mix" channel while leaving the "me" channel up all the way but it seems there is just not enough head room. If you turn the knob to half way it doesn't cut the volume enough but turn it much more and it cuts the volume too much. It needs slightly more amplification and a smoother control so that what is "half way" is closer to half the total possible volume with room to spare turning up the system. This would allow more fine differentiation between the two channels and fix the issue I keep coming back to. So far my solution has been to put more of them into the channel mix, but since I've got up to two people sharing a given mix, this has caused a few issues. I guess I need to get the second half my board in place with the digital snake, which will give me enough sends to provide a custom mix to each person. It's just frustrating to need to do that when the concept here should resolve that for me.

I needed to copy content from my cable DVR box to the Archos for viewing on business trips. The 'Travel DVR adapter' would have done the job, but for $25 more, you get the full DVR docking station. This provides a nice, stable place to leave the A605 while it's charging, you get AV output connections as well as input, AND you get the QWERTY remote control. Buy the travel DVR and you're paying nearly $60 for nothing more than a socket that does input only. I'm now $500 into this system, what with the browser, codecs and input adapters. It's kind of clunky looking - very square and a weird, slope-like design. I found the 'DVR adapter' in the original A605 box - luckily the misses hadn't thrown it away. This is a piece of silver plastic that you have to clip onto the top of the DVR station to enable your particular type of Gen5 Archos to sit on top. It's quite tricky to dock the A605 without straining the connectors - you have to insert it into a channel between 2 pieces of plastic with about a +/- 2° tolerance. if you get it right, it drops straight in. I haven't even bothered trying the DVR functionality yet, since I already have a cable DVR box. All I do is set the cable DVR playing and make the Archos do a manually started but timed finish record from its A/V inputs. Incidentally, according to Archos tech support the Travel DVR can do the timed manual recording that I wanted; it just doesn't enable the DVR scheduler. This isn't mentioned at all in the ridiculously sparse user documentation. Once the A605 is docked, it enables the 'Recorder' menu icon. The choice of encoding options is rather limited, with only AVI files with compressed WAV audio possible. I leave the aspect ratio settings on 'Auto' and it seems to figure out what size the input video signal is. Video bitrate choices are 500, 1000 or 1500kbps. Audio is either 32k or 48k. On the highest quality setting, files aren't that small - about 700MB for a 30 min TV show. I can get a whole DVD movie into that space using Handbrake. I will do some experimenting with settings and post results... I have tried using the video editing features built into the A605 firmware. This enables you to remove sections from media - e.g. commercials from a TV program. You have to manually scroll through the video file and set a start/end point for each section you want to cut out. You can only set one pair of start/end points at a time. When viewing the edited content, I notice that it always fails to cut the last 0.5s or so of video - even though I placed the marks accurately. At that point you can choose whether to save your edited file to a new file, which takes AGES since it's reading and writing several GB from/to the same HDD - lots of head movement.

This equipment breaks new ground in low dvd burner prices but it should be purchased with some knowledge of the product. The drive boasts that additional drivers are not needed, but this may not be accurate depending on your computer's operating system. The drive installed ok on my 32bit Windows 7 machine but would not install on my 64 bit computer which complained of a lack of the appropriate driver. Usually, one can find workable drivers on the manufacturer's website, but this drive lacks any brand identification. This has been a continuing problem with Windows 7--the 32 bit system installs ok but drivers are missing for the 64 bit system. A mini-cd was included which installs Nero burner code on your system and also has a driver for Windows 98 SE! Also, my AVG FREE virus software on the 64 bit machine claimed that 2 back-door Trojans were on the little cd, but a system check after the installation attempt showed no malware was installed. This is often the behavior of false alarms from the virus protection software, but it may be especially important that you have good virus software installed in order to deal with any problems. This little drive will probably work out ok for me, but I'm glad that I have a fairly solid basis of computer knowledge and experience.

I'll start off by saying all of my comments about audio are AFTER Dling the app and playing with the EQ settings but to be honest in almost all cases the default sounded the best anyway. For instance turning up the bass on the b3 EQ seemed to actually turn down the treble as if it was a tradeoff. The audio of the b3 sounds muted/dull whereas the wb2 is more bright. The only way I could recommend the b3 is if you needed the slimmer but longer profile, the longer battery life, or the party mode thing with more than 2 speakers (the wb2 supports 2) which I've read doesn't work well anyway. If you want good audio quality and to save money go for the WB2.

I've found myself quite enjoying this conference cam/speaker. Purchased through my company for home-office and group conferencing. I used to wear a headset and it's quite a relief to be able to kick back, especially on long conference calls. Microphone: For the price-point, the microphone is pretty good. Noise cancellation is quite decent and audio quality on the receiving end is pretty great as well (others on my team use this as well). Video: Video quality is quite excellent. You have the option to use the camera "plugged" directly into the unit, which is a little more sleek than having it on the stand/extender to raise it up, but the downside is that you then have the camera looking up at you... many don't find this angle flattering. Other: The remote is great, and also has good layout of buttons, and ability to pan/zoom. Cons: Really not great for "group" conferencing. The FOV (field of view) is not large enough to encompass a group unless the unit is quite far away. I've found this to be a great mate for my desk and a single person, but in terms of being a "group" conference cam, you're going to need to place it across the room.

If you intend to use it with repeaters, be warned that you can only define a single code per channel (transmit and receive will be the same). There are many repeaters out there that have separate codes for transmit and receive, and you will not be able to use this radio on those repeaters. This is a major design flaw.

More playing shows I hadn't found out what KF-type interface features are available or what they do. It isn't obvious at first glance, so poke away... THE ISSUES 1. Web browser. [DELETED: Web-based email rant. I started goofing with the email tool, found a few buttons to press that made incoming email stuff work. Still working on the outgoing stuff.] [RETAINED: I propose that the KF browser get an update with a new "knob": allow the user to create a list of sites to not be cached by the cloud. Simple for Amazon and their manufacturer to implement in software. (Now that I think about it, I'm completely unenthusiastic about Amazon imposing their servers in my email processing. They don't belong there.) It may be that the cloud chokes on [...] encryption - definitely a reason for having exceptions to the caching nonsense. Even better would be to have the cloud and the KF collaborate on the analysis, notify the user that "this happens sometimes" with web sites, and then ASK the user if an exception can be set. (It CAN'T be that hard to spot a high-frequency pattern of web updates at either end, and this is something that needs to be done only ONCE per offending web page.)] 2. Touch-screen resolution. The KF touch screen has resolution issues. I wrote two copies about complaint 1.) above that either aborted, or prematurely sent the feedback message to Amazon when I tapped the screen where I wanted to move the cursor. I have to attribute this to poor KF touch-sensor resolution. Perhaps this problem can be written off as poorly designed user interface on the feedback form, but I don't think so. [15-Dec-11] I'm getting the feeling that the touch-screen is TOO sensitive even with a screen protector: I sometimes get button hits by hovering my fingers over the screen. I've spoiled a couple Angry Birds games that way... 3. Holes in the range of applications. The app store needs more everything: I have a number of iPhone apps that have zero equivalents on the KF app store. I don't understand why there haven't been more ports - the Angry Birds folks did it, and their $0.99 price reflects the fact that their start-up costs were paid by the Apple version of the games. (I observe with some displeasure that the number of Android apps is somewhat diminished when I view them from the KF instead of my PC. Apparently there is a distinct difference between Android (phone) and Android (KF).) 4. Display settings. OK. My bad. Fonts, sizes, and screen invert appear to be on a per-app basis. I suppose this is ok, but it isn't obvious at first how to do this - you have to poke at stuff to figure it out. 5. User manual. a. The index. ADDED: What index? RETAINED: The user manual, which I have actually looked at for answers to serious questions, is deficient. The table of contents is poor - it's presently 451 pages (excuse me, "locations") long, and there is only a single page (uh, "location") of links in the index. Multiple pages of indexed entries wouldn't present unacceptable clutter. One can search for keywords, but you have to goof with the KF manual to find out which words get you to what you need - searches return a LOT of stuff.) b. Missing topics. One keyword, "credential" doesn't appear in the user manual at all. This is odd, because there are a couple "credential storage" options in the security setup. Yo! Dudes! what are these credential thingers? They have password control, and that sounds serious! c. File transfers. I started wondering how to get some of my own files onto the KF. There IS documentation for how to do this, but it isn't easy to find, so I classify it as "missing." It's almost easier to accidentally look at the "My Account" entry in the setup menu: I'm shown that I have an email account on the Amazon.com servers, and that documents sent there will be transferred to the KF. A little weird, but maybe OK. Now, it isn't clear what TYPE of documents are supported by this process. I don't know if the Amazon reader format has been published or if tools are available to produce such files (there is an inexpensive tool for the eReader.com format). PDF files are supported by a free Adobe Acrobat reader. Keeno - what else can I transfer and look at? 6. Password. One can set a lock-screen password, but you better remember it. You can turn the lock off (if you can confirm this change with your password) but you can't actually change your password. While it is entirely possible that I haven't found the password-change tool, it strikes me as terribly odd that it would be so well hidden. If I have to remember the password I set and forgot, well I guess I'm pretty well hosed there. I thought I had picked a simple password, but it took me a few panicked moments to recall what I'd typed 20 minutes earlier. [ADDED: A week later, and I still haven't figured it out, and I totally forgot what I set.] 7. Uploading & converting documents [5-Dec-2011] I found a useful technical book in pdf form for free (paid big bucks for a hard copy from a well-known e-vendor of printed material). You can convert a document from .pdf to Kindle format by emailing it to your KF account with the word "convert" in the subject line. In my case, it worked like a champ - 'cept for all them missing illustrations. (Technical books are boring, gotta have some pictures, man!) I ended up with subheadings naming the figures, and the figure captions. Not quite what I had in mind, so I'm re-sending the doc as a .pdf - the Adobe Acrobat reader app is free. While I'm on the subject, I sent the document almost three hours ago. Now, a 7.5MB doc is a pretty big file to move, but I'm right now at work, connected to a serious (OC-192) Internet node, so the doc should have arrived on my similarly-connected KF, well, almost three hours ago. Sounds like Amazon needs to provide a file-transfer tool, so I can direct-connect between my servers and my KF, or my home WiFi and the KF. 8. Media card slot (for KF v2.0) I understand the size-and-space issues, but it's tough berries if you want to directly upload jpgs from a card. Tough to install via web update, so we'll have to wait. ON THE PLUS SIDE: - the KF processor is pleasingly fast. Screen updates are quick, enabling my copy of Angry Birds to run very smoothly. This is clearly the acme of computer end-uses. - the KF screen is GREAT. It is crisp with great contrast. - KF has a nice heft to it. Lighter would be nicer, but I'll trade a few ounces for more warm-and-fuzzies about ruggedness and reliability. - setup is almost totally painless. - KF sound is really quite good, and I'm not making much concession for the small speakers. - the connection to Amazon retailing is great. (What a surprise, thought I. Maybe its too easy.) [Amazon DOES need to pull the third-party-book-vendors stick outa its collective butt. I buy technical books that are often published online by independent authors, so the KF is of zero use for some work stuff that should be simple to accommodate.] On the whole, the KF is a really good deal, despite my issues. Amazon is very very close to a 5-star product, at a VERY good price. They just have to tweak a few things.

Claims to be configurable for four scenarios. Two of which would have worked for me... but they are NOT ACTUALLY configurable as advertised. The basic restriction? There is NO WAY to turn off NAT on the router. Scenario One: Operate in Bridge Mode. But... you can not actually set the device to bridge mode. (Bridge mode is where you connect the WiFi side of the device to an existing router, and the Ethernet side to an ethernet-equipped device (or more than one if you use a switch.) In bridge mode, you "bridge" your single-ethernet (or switch-connected multiple ethernet) device(s) through the wifi to the existing router, which has the DHCP that gives out an address for each device as if they were all accessing wifi individually. But it isn't possible to do. It connects to a router via WiFi, and then fakes a new NATed network by the same name... but with different IP ranges. So you can NOT share files or do discovery among the things connected to the new and old networks. NOT "bridged" at all. In client mode, the same limitation crops up. The advertised scenario is that you can connect an ethernet only device to the wireless network. But you can NOT really. The ethernet only device can be connected to the INTERNET, but not to the wireless network. So... you want to connect your ethernet only printer? Sorry... it's behind Network Address Translation (NAT) so on a different network, and can not talk to the other computers connected to your wireless router. Shame, but the advertised function is still NOT available.

First of all, I have had NO hardware or software issues whatsoever. The 3rd Gen. Kindle has worked perfectly from day 1. I also have the Amazon lighted cover which is a great design. No, my problems with the Kindle are purely with its suitability as a reading device, and the current state of Kindle ebooks. In many cases, both suck. To summarize: 1) The Kindle is terrible for much non-fiction. - Navigation within a book slow, clunky, and can't compare at all to a physical book. At the very least I should be able to hit a single hotkey, and get the table of contents up with the section I am currently reading shown. But no, you have to pull up the menu.. arrow down to the "Go to" item.. select that.. arrow down to "table of contents" and then select that and wait for the TOC. Each step is slow and awkward. What a PITA for something that should be effortless and instantaneous. - The 6 inch screen is TINY and completely inadequate for viewing text with tables, diagrams, code, etc. The Kindle can view PDFs, but my advice is to just forget about it as they are invariably formatted for a larger page. And the current price of a Kindle DX being outrageous just for some extra screen real estate - almost at iPad territory. They must figure that the ONLY people who want to read non-fiction are business types that have business budgets for their gadgets. Wrong, Amazon. 2) Many many publishers put no effort into formatting a title for the Kindle, which greatly reduces the usefulness and ease of reading of an ebook. Amazon has NO standards for formatting of a Kindle title. You can publish ANY text dump and call it a Kindle ebook. Apple has standards for apps in the app store, so why can't Amazon have standards for Kindle ebooks? - At a minimum, every kindle ebook should have: a) An actual table of contents you can navigate from. b) Each chapter starting with a new page rather than slammed onto the end of the previous one. c) Each chapter Title set in a large title font. d) Navigation between chapters with the 4-way keys, e) Section breaks within chapters that have an actual visual break to them. Some of the worst formatting travesties are classic public domain books. They are often just OCRed scans of a book with no formatting whatsoever (a text dump of the entire book), and not even a spell check. Commercial publishers are sometimes no better - one commercial book I found actually had "Trial version e-pub conversion" notices sprinkled throughout the text! So they had just run the text through some sort of free trial version of a converter and said good enough, it is now a Kindle ebook! 3) Amazon reviews of books do NOT separate the kindle ebook from the regular paper book. This is a major annoyance because they are very different products, and a poor ebook version usually does not mean a poor print version, and a good print version does not mean a good kindle version. So the author gets penalized with bad reviews of his book just because the lazy publisher put out a sucking Kindle version, and you as a Kindle owner will happily buy a "4-star" ebook and get something much less than what you wanted. I was really excited to get my Kindle 3 last year, but that excitement has diminished considerably. If you're primarily reading fiction, you'll certainly do better. And if you do buy an ebook with poor formatting I would encourage you to complain to customer service and ask for a refund (they have a form for this - start using it). Edit: All you Vote-Downers, do you really not want Amazon to improve the Kindle experience? Or are you Amazon affiliates or something? Because I would expect the majority of actual Kindle owners would at least recognize that things like formatting standards for Kindle ebooks would be very welcome. In fact all of the problems I pointed out in the review other than screen size, are things that Amazon could immediately take action to improve. And you don't want that?

I purchased 3 of these units. One of them worked just fine, but the other two 3 of the plugs didn't work at all, The power adapter outlets didn't work. I needed these in service right away, so I took it apart, and found that there is a wire going from one side of the power strip to the other side that wasn't even connected. This could cause a potential short inside the unit as the wire is just loose inside the unit.. I just soldered the wire onto the bar, and while I was at it, but more solder on the wire going to the other bar to make sure that the connections were good. All the other connections are crimp connections, and do not require solder. It was fairly easy to dissassemble the unit, and solder the wires on. It took about 5 minutes from start to finish. Now the power adapter works great. If you need a power strip with 8 outlets, and a 25 foot cord, and are willing to open the unit and solder 1 wire, it is great. We own about 10 of these and have only had this problem with 2 of them. Hopefully it is an anomoly with just the units I received. If any of them stop working, it would be pretty easy to open it up, and solder the connectors, as the 2 solder joints don't have very much solder on them anyway. I think I'll open the others up and re-solder them for good measure, so I don't have a problem in the future.

First a disclaimer - I am a Windows/Android guy, and only use Mac equipment when absolutely necessary for my job as a software engineer. The first (and largest) problem with this mouse is that it did not work. I tried for hours trying to get it to pair with my Mac Mini (running latest build of Catalina). When I would plug it in USB, it would say that it was fully charged and paired but when I would unplug it, it would revert back to saying it wasn't connected. Bluetooth was turned on, other devices could pair to the Mac Mini with no problems. But the mouse would never pair. From a design perspective, there are two major flaws with this mouse. First, there is no LED light on the mouse telling you that the mouse is even turned on or charged. There needs to be some visual indicator on the mouse itself for letting me know it has power at least or it is tough to distinguish between a connectivity issue or a dead mouse. Second (and far more important) is that the charging port of the mouse is on the bottom of the mouse, and once connected via USB, the mouse does not work. What this means is that if this is your only mouse and you are working on something and the mouse dies, you need to stop what you are doing and wait for the mouse to charge (or have a backup handy). Every other mouse I have ever seen has the charging port at the front of the mouse so you can plug it and and continue to work on it while it is charging. If I were to use this as the mouse on my primary machine, this alone would be a deal-breaker, because in the middle of the work day, who has time to wait for a mouse to charge? Oh - and then there is the price. $80? The only reason I bought it in the first place is that I have had issues with Apple products not playing nicely together with non-Apple products, so I figured (incorrectly) this was the safest bet. I returned this mouse after a couple of days of unsuccessfully getting it to pair and instead purchased an AmazonBasics wireless mouse. It worked instantly, and only cost $15.

If you're expecting a cheap computer you'll be satisfied, but there's a few quirks you should know about. The computer has 64GB EMMC storage built in and a removable 64GB SSD, not one large 128gb drive. The OS is installed to the internal storage by default but I recommend copying it over to the SSD because its about double the speed. Before doing anything crazy like reinstalling the OS, use a program like DoubleDriver to back up the drivers that come pre-installed, as I found the touch driver provided from the Jumper website doesn't seem to work right like the one it comes with, and windows will not detect it or the hinge drivers automatically. Even though the device has USB C it doesn't seem to be fully compliant. For one the included charger is a dumb one that ONLY outputs 12v, so I wouldn't recommend risking your phone or other devices plugging into it. The good news is it DOES work with other USB C PD chargers, but instead of 12V it will want 15V. My USB PD car charger which is more than capable of 15v does not like it and won't charge the laptop unless its off for some reason. USB power banks will not charge it unless they are capable of 15V over USB C which most small ones are not. If you know what you're doing my solution to this PD charging issue was to cut the included charge cable and put a "USB-C PD Trigger Module" capable of 12V on the other end, this DIY adapter will trick PD power banks into thinking the device wants 12V and send the raw 12V into the laptop charge port like the wall charger does.

As other reviewers have said, setup is dead simple. Just plug the USB piece into the USB port and away you go. The back and forward buttons work effortlessly, and are nice and smooth to the touch. They're positioned right where my thumb is and easily reachable. Clicking and right-clicking work as you would expect, and the click sound matches that of a standard mouse. The wheel rolls smoothly with the slightest little notches as you roll so you can tell the distance. The DPI button works as advertised, increasing the mouse speed when you push it. But here's the killer feature that really made me love this little mouse: its precision! The slightest little move you make, this mouse will detect it and move the pointer accordingly. All mice are supposed to do that, and do it well, so precision is something you should expect. But my last mouse, the Tecknet cordless optical mouse - which I've owned only for a month, was precise only when moving quickly. If you ever had to make a small adjustment to reposition the pointer right next to where it was (say to get it between two characters), the Tecknet mouse would not respond. You'd have to move quickly and with a big stroke to reposition it to where you want. My wrist started to pain fighting with the Tecknet, and so I was back in the market for a mouse - this time with the wisdom to not take precision for granted. The Sharkk is exactly what I needed. The only con I give to the Sharkk is it is so short that the pad of my middle finger rests considerably past the scroll wheel instead of atop it. This means I have to bend my middle finger a lot to scroll, something I didn't have to do with the Tecknet. A few scrolls this way is not a problem. But when scrolling a lot, my finger starts to feel fatigued. So, to compensate, I've started scrolling with my index finger instead, and that solved my problem. In terms of battery, I've only owned this mouse for a couple weeks, so too early to tell. However, if the battery drain becomes a problem, I will update this review.
