=========== Update... update? - Full Refund. After an entire month of emailing back and forth with VIZIO and being ignored multiple times, I finally got them to agree to a replacement. Two weeks later they said that they could no longer offer the replacement but that they would offer a full refund instead. They sent out a box to return the system in, I packaged up everything, sent it all back, and two weeks later got a check in the mail for a full refund. The whole process required 16 emails over two months. While this hasn't exactly been a nice experience, nor has it restored my faith in their products, I can certainly say that they did eventually right this wrong and I'm content with the final outcome. Props to VIZIO for offering the refund when they most likely didn't have to. I'll leave the original review and subsequent edit below. =========== 9-month edit - IT DIED I've owned this sound bar for nine months, and it just stopped working. The power cable is still good but the sound bar won't turn on. Last night I turned the bar off and went to bed; this morning it won't turn on. I like to be pretty moderate when writing reviews but I'm extremely disappointed. When I originally purchased this product I did notice some reviewers stating that their sound bars stopped working after around a year, but I chalked it up to bad luck. Now I no longer believe it's just bad luck. I think VIZIO knew these sound bars were defective and sold them anyways. I'll leave the original review below. =========== A review for the VIZIO SB3851-D0 Sound Bar System (2016 Model) Packaging: 10/10 The box was large and irregularly shaped. It did not come in discreet packaging, so this is certainly not one you’ll want to leave on the porch for long. The protection offered was in the form of styrofoam casing. Each part was individually wrapped in easy-to-remove plastic. Unfortunately I all but completely destroyed the box trying to get it open. Likely "operator error" was to blame. Assembly: 9/10 Everything was very self-explanatory. I found myself reaching for the manual only once, when I couldn't get audio out of the soundbar via an HDMI connection. As it turns out, there is a specific method necessary to connect the soundbar to a television through HDMI. Build Quality: 8/10 The soundbar and two satellite speakers are cased in a fine black fabric. The subwoofer is cased in a hard, matte-finish plastic/ceramic. The remote has a matte black plastic front and rubberized black backing. Each component has rubber feet, and can, with the exception of the subwoofer, be wall mounted. Unfortunately, the fabric covering on the components makes them terribly difficult to clean and quite easy to damage. The soundbar rattles are a certain bass frequency. For me it's just around 88 Hz. The subwoofer itself doesn't suffer from this, so I often find myself needing to turn down the bass and turn up the subwoofer to compensate. Included in the Box: 10/10 The packaging includes the soundbar, subwoofer, two satellite speakers, remote, mounting brackets, and likely every cable you’ll need. Cables include the satellite speaker cables (~25 ft), 2x power cables (~4 ft), 1x HDMI (~5 ft), 1x Optical (~4-5 ft), 1x Coaxial, 1x Analog, 1x Aux. The only cable that it didn’t come with that you might want is an ethernet cable for the bar’s optional Casting ability. Sound Quality: 5/10 This one is unfortunately largely subjective. I’ve come from using pretty low-end desk speakers and monitor speakers so this soundbar system easily outperforms those. The bass is loud and deep, and the soundbar itself is very clear. The satellite speakers leave much to be desired, however. They sound tinny and distant, even when working in harmony with the sub. The reason I took so many points off in this category, and the reason the review lost a star: sound level fluctuation. Something that bothers me terribly is fluctuations in sound level, especially when sitting so close to the speakers. The soundbar is doing some sort of audio processing other than the bare minimum. At certain parts of songs or videos the audio will fade out slightly, just to come back to full volume a second or two later. It’s not random: it always happens at the exact same moment. I figure that it's likely the soundbar is attempting to do some sort of audio leveling, but it’s failing miserably. Furthermore, vocals seem to be partially drowned out by instruments in many songs. As an important note, I have all sound effects disabled on both my PC and the soundbar itself, namely TruSound and TruVolume. This fluctuation happens while using bluetooth, HDMI, and optical. I’ve contacted support, and they were unable to assist. You also might be sorely disappointed when listening to music on this. "Busy" songs - those with lots of instruments or synthesizers in the background - sound suboptimal. Vocals are terribly drown-out: some songs sound alright, whilst others I can just barely make out the words. Switching the EQ mode from "movie" to "music" makes the sound very flat and dull, basically disabling the bass. I exclusively leave the soundbar on "movie." As already stated in the build quality section, the soundbar rattles at around 88 Hz. Unfortunately, this is around the range that a lot of movies use for low-frequency background noise, so it's a problem more often than I'd like to see. This really reflects on the build quality, and is certainly not something I want to see for a soundbar of this price. Ease of Use: 6/10 The buttons on the top of the soundbar work fine and are self-explanatory, but the soundbar itself has no display, save for a small array of lights on the far left side. These lights give you feedback on audio levels and modes whilst using the remote or built-in buttons. They are not, however, very intuitive. The remote is even more frustrating, however. It has a small, hard to see, non-lit screen built in that tells you the current menu item you’re editing, whether it be volume level, balance, bass, ect. The remote works via IR, and therefore needs to be in direct line-of-sight of the bar to work. I believe there may be multiple IR receivers in the front of the soundbar, as the remote works even in extreme close proximity with the bar. The remote’s menu navigation is difficult and frustrating to use, as you have to scroll through a large amount of seemingly randomly organized options to get to the one that you want to change. Another star was lost on the remote alone. Price: 8/10 The price is pretty great for what’s included. A 5.1 surround sound system for 250 USD is pretty great. One more step up and you’ll easily pay 600 USD or more. This system is going to work great for the majority of people looking for some good sound without breaking the bank. Other Quirks: When changing the input mode to bluetooth, the sound bar makes an awfully loud “paring” sound (subwoofer included in the unnecessarily loud clamor), and a similar noise is made when a device is paired and unpaired. I’ve actually woken family members up accidentally when trying to play some quiet music over bluetooth. The sound bar has "Eco power" mode (which should be called "Auto Off" mode but that's just me) that automatically turns off the sound bar if sound input is lost for a certain amount of time (I think it's probably somewhere around 10-15 minutes). It's an awesome feature with a catch. While I love the fact that the device turns off automatically, it's doesn't turn back on automatically which would have been really convenient. Edit after a month of use: wow this thing gets really dirty! It's a dust magnet, every spec of dust is extremely visible against the black fabric, and it's very difficult to clean (imagine using a dust cloth to dust off your blankets). I think they should have gone with a matte plastic or acrylic top for the sound bar itself. I’ve included a plethora of photos that will hopefully give you a better idea of what the system looks like. I find that the majority of the time the photos included by the seller are pretty terrible.

Build: Solid metal, and well finished plastic. The knob is aluminum and the action is smooth. The plugs are gold plated and seem sturdy; there is a satisfying click when inserting the 3.5mm cable which does require a fair bit of force. The rubber feet are also of good quality. Sound: Unfortunately, the actual headphone amplification circuit seems to have been an afterthought. The VU meters are certainly cool and a conversation starter, but the amplifier clips on the input side. That means if you overdrive the amp (and it doesn't take much, my phone was able to do it), it will clip no matter the volume. This means nasty distortion, and a lot of it. The remedy is to lower the volume/voltage on the input side. The sound after compensating for the clipping seems good enough, but it is a bit weak, weaker even than the Little Bear portable tube amp. At $70 I can hardly complain.

I was a little skeptical, but after reading some online magazine and user reviews, I decided to give this remote a try. Like others have said, it takes time to get the remote set up. I spent the better part of an afternoon setting everything up and testing and changing the settings numerous times. But once it's done, it's a great remote. I would have to say the included instructions did not provide me with too much useful information. Out of the box, you'll need to install the lithium-ion battery in the remote and then charge using the included charger. I took others' advice and just installed the latest Harmony software from the Logitech site. Upon opening the software (which connects to the internet), you'll have to initially set up a username and password. The remote and wireless rf extender use the same included usb cable to connect to your pc. After signing in and connecting the remote, an online firmware update was found which prompted a download and update of the firmware (same when connecting the wireless rf extender). When setting up the remote, you are prompted to enter the brand and model number of your components (one by one). If the brand and model is in the online database, the commands will be stored in the remote. I've added 8 components for control so far (Sony Widescreen RPTV; Denon A/V receiver; Denon DVD; Pioneer DVD; Sony DVD Recorder; Scientific Atlanta HD Cable Box; DirecTV HD Receiver; and Sony VHS). I'm currently not using the wireless rf extender (I guess I could have purchased the Harmony 880 instead???). The Sony vhs and dvd recorder were the only components not fully recognized initially. The software prompted me to use the original remotes to send some commands to the Harmony before they were fully added as components. There's also an option if you don't have the original remotes as well as being able to manually specify a remote action. After adding your components, you'll need to define `activities' such as "watch a dvd" or "listen to a cd," etc. Once you're done adding components and setting the activities and saving them, you'll then need to transfer/update these settings to the remote using the connected usb cable by pressing the `update remote' button on the home page of the remote software. There is much flexibility in setting what components turn on and also in choosing a setting for the component. For example, when choosing what I defined as my "watch denon dvd" activity, the tv, dvd and a/v receiver turn on; the tv changes to input 7 (dvi) and the receiver changes to its dvd input. This all happens with a press of one button as these were the actions that I defined for this activity in the software setup. If I subsequently press the activity button for "play vcr", the remote turns both the receiver and dvd player off, turns the vcr on and sets the tv input to channel 3. You define and name your activity. Once the activities are set up, the remote is relatively simple to use. In other words, your spouse/family members/friends can actually turn on and use your tv without you having to explain multiple remote controls. There is also the option of controlling a specific component by pressing the `device' button on the remote. Depending on the component and how the commands were stored in the remote, you can use either or both of the commands displayed in the lcd portion of the remote or the command buttons on the lower part of the remote. There is also a global `off' button that can be used to turn all components off. The remote also seems to be motion activated, e.g., the backlight turns on when you move the remote. Very handy in the dark.

Summary: missing features, underclocked CPU, run on outdated firmware (highly unlikely it will receive any more firmware since this do not receive firmware directly from Asus). First of all, this is not a 130 dollars router that repackaged as a 53 dollars router. This router is known to be underclocked to 800 Mhz instead of 1 Ghz. That 20% performance. If you read the RT68 reviews and thinking this is the same. They are not. I purchased this router just right around KRACK exploit publicly announced. Bad timing on my part. FYI, potential buyers: this router DOES NOT run the latest Asus firmware. The firmware is ancient in firmware releasing time. This means that this router is easily more vulnerable than the regular RT68U. Of course, some will say that you can install stock firmware back to this router and restore it to 1 Ghz. It is NOT that easy. It is very difficult to do so because the router that shipped to me has the latest firmware from T mobile installed and let me assure you that you can not push 3 buttons, plug in the power cord, turn on the power button, run the firmware restore, click a few thing. ALL by yourself in a small window of time that the router allowed you to do so. Also if you are using a recent laptop, it is likely that you are using a USB to Ethernet adapter (add on to the chance of affecting the connection to the router during the restoring process). You are trying to save money, so there is not need to buy additional adapters to test out the methods to get this router back to stock firmware. In addition, I browsed through the menus on the router and I immediately saw a few features that missing from a full-fledged RT68 (I am currently using one). Notable is the Repeater mode. In the end, if you are looking for a good router like the RT68, spend a little more and buy it instead of this. Or buy a newer mid range model. This and RT68 ARE NOT the same. Whoever told you so is a liar...unless that person is willing to restore the stock firmware, clocked it back to 1Ghz for you (free of charge for everything of course) to prove me wrong. :)

PROS ===== - Screen. Tablets are all about a screen. Period. And Everybody knows Samsung has the best screen in the world. LG also has good ones, btw. - An OK price point with a bundled deal. Probably will go even lower on Black Friday. - Performance. Very fast. It's such a joy when browsing the web etc. - Clean design and no company logo or any markings, at least on the front. They took about 10 years to finally realize that removing the Samsung logo is the way to go. - High quality speakers for a tablet. - Lightweight. CONS ====== - Wifi antenna position problem in horizontal mode. It's a well-known hardware design defect that's documented in the news articles and reviews. Look it up. No software fix possible. When I tested to see if it's actually true, the download speed dropped to almost 0.5 Mbps from 30 Mbps. Maybe not a big deal to some of you but you have to be mindful of it EVERYTIME you hold the tablet in horizontal mode. But how long mindful? Be mindful every single day for years until the device dies. That's another thing you'll need to keep it on your chest as a psychological burden. Returned back to Amazon. Of course, you can choose not to return it. And Samsung will think like, "OK, we made a critical mistake but it still sells fine". Teach them a lesson by returning your defective product if you're concerned, so they can take the high return rate as a wake up call. Otherwise, they will keep pushing out defective products. - "You phone has restarted". That's the message you see when you restart the *tablet*. Samsung probably missed it when they ported their Android software from their Galaxy phone to the tablet. It's a minor issue but you can see that Samsung is not run by a person like Steve Jobs and they don't pay attention to minor details like this. And it makes me wonder, "If they missed this, what else did they miss under the hood?" Something unthinkable for a big global corporation like them. - Performance. Slow when gaming as shown in other reviews probably due to their lower end graphics chip and the mid upper range CPU. I'm not a gamer therefore it wouldn't bother me though. Also, it's kind of expected for this price. - Camera bump. Who uses a high res camera on a tablet? It causes a camera bump. It's a problem if you're anti-camera bump. Again, they took about 10 years to finally realize that removing the Samsung logo from the front is the way to go. I'll give them another 10 years to finally remove the camera bump. - Documentation. Looks like it was written by some Korean engineer, which is fine. But don't they have it proofread before publishing it? Again, something unthinkable for a big global corporation like them. They should have a documentation department with native speakers for the language. SUGGESTIONS TO MANUFACTURER ============================== - Use pure stock Android or Android One and stop wasting time and energy customizing it and publishing your half-baked software. Bixby sucks, for example. How many web articles do you see about tutorials on how to remove the Bixby button? People don't want it. Focus on what you do best -- hardware. Shift your energy and capital away from software. - Test well. Both software and hardware. The wifi antenna problem would have been easily caught by some basic testing. But it looks like the test engineers missed it. But how? They don't give their 100% when they are not treated well. - Lower camera specs so you can get rid of the camera bump, which will lower the price even more. Again, who uses a camera on a tablet? Of course you sometimes need it for a video chat but you don't typically need a high resolution one. Actually, a lower res camera is even better because you don't want to drop too many real-time UDP audio/video packets due to the bandwidth consumption by high resolution camera.

I've only had my Kindle for about 3 weeks, seems like 3 months and thats a good thing. Love the concept and I'm glad I invested the money. However, I do wish I had waited for the next generation because I am sure there will be welcoming improvements. I enjoy the ease of reading. Purchasing books is a pleasure, it's quick and it's easy. I can carry it anywhere and read anytime, having so many books available at one time is incredible and I doubt I will ever go back to paper books. There are a couple of things I don't care for. The most important, the sensitivity of the page navigation buttons. There is little to nowhere to hold it without pressing one of them once or twice and then trying to figure out where you were. I wanted to buy one for my father who was very interested in it, but he lost the interest because, he kept pressing buttons he didn't mean to press or pressing the wrong buttons. Turning it on and off is a bit of a challenge, especially if it's in the case that comes with it. I love the case and it is actually the only thing that makes holding onto it without pressing the infamous buttons happen a little less often. It's difficult enough getting it to stay in place and then you remember the buttons to turn it on and to turn the wireless on are located on the back so then you have to start all over trying to get it to stay in the holder but now the page navigation buttons are active and you you will most definetly press buttons you didn't mean to press, etc... It sometimes is like a comedy of errors. Patience is a virtue when dealing with some little but huge issues. I would imagine that like everything else one will get use to all the little things that need tweaking. The page numbering system is not like reading a paper book, it is based on location numbers which don't seem to follow any rhyme or reason and hard to find where you were if you hit one of those sensitive navigation page buttons. Stay as far a way from the back button while reading as you can it takes you back to the beginning and I haven't figured out wether or not there is a way to get back to where you were, so I have to press the next page buttons many, many, many times to find where I was. I'm thinking that the next generation should have smaller and less page navigation buttons this will make it hopefully easier to hold. The on and off buttons should be on the front so that once you get it to stay in the case it can stay there. These little changes would make it top notch in the user friendly category. It would also be nice to have a light built in that illuminates the pages at night so the need for a lamp wouldn't be necessary. What I don't understand is how the people involved in approving the design didn't notice the page navigation issues. I realized it within a few minutes of using it and so have many others. I'm hoping that when the next generation comes out existing Kindle users get a huge break in price since we are the pioneer users of the first.

At first I had difficulty getting my Mac to recognize the video input and thought it might be a driver problem (the included DVD doesn't have any Mac drivers and the only ones on the internet for this product line don't work for current versions of OSX), but I eventually figured out the problem was the small USB extension cable included with the dongle. The Acer Chromebook and Chromebooks/Chrome OS in general takes the outdated concept of having a full-featured dedicated operating system like Windows or OSX on your local computer and replaces that functionality utilizing their massive server farms. What did it for me when when I lost an online auction due to a Windows security update that started as I was trying to get my bid in. This should not happen. You just want your browser to work without disruptions at the most critical times. Thankfully, Google and provided us with a modern desktop OS that does everything I need it to do. You get functioning USB ports that recognize wired or wireless mice (i'm using a Logitech wireless mouse), or flash drives or external hard drives. You get a built-in file manager that recognizes Chrome supported file types. This means that you also have a built-in media player with a picture viewer for jpegs, audio player support for mp3's and video player support with WebM. I am using a 16gb SD card for additional storage or file transfers and a WD 1tb passport portable hard drive as my main storage for content. All of my photos already work with the media player and the same goes for all of my music. For video, you would think that H264 would work, but the Chromebook while recognizing the file type, does not actually play the mp4 file. However, WebM (Google's codec), works flawlessly. In fact, I compared all of my H264 videos with all of my WebM videos and the WebM videos played back flawlessly on both the Chromebook and Windows 7 PC, but the H264 videos had very minor playback issues like ever-slight shading or discoloration and syncing of audio or an occasional stutter. But these issues are very slight and don't really affect the enjoyment of the content. Even so, the quality of WebM is unsurpassed, so I have have been converting all of my video content from WMV, H264, and DVD to WebM. I am using software from Bigasoft to perform the conversions and I highly recommend this software. It works really really well. For MS Office functionality, I am using a combination of a Chrome app called Live Documents and Microsoft Live which allow you to edit Word, Power Point and Excel documents. Of course Google Docs is another option. I also use a Chrome calculator app for quick calculations and Scratchpad app for quick notes. Netflix: With full streaming support coming to Chromebooks after only three and a half weeks after launch, this was a priority for both Google and Netflix. Initially, you saw a popup stating that streaming would be coming in a few months and they were working with Google to support it. Nice job. The update also saw a 50% increase in performance with faster page loads and rendering in the browser. Hulu: The full free browser version of Hulu was available from day one. I don't know why I was surprised at this (Google TV?) This is why the Acer kills the Samsung. With the HDMI port, you can stream free Hulu content to your TV. Obviously, all of the Google services work great like Gmail, Google Music, calendar and contacts. Google Talk for video chat. I use other Chrome apps like Tweetdeck, Kindle, Google Books, Graphicly and Marvel for digital comics, Amazon Cloud Player, You Tube and of course Angry Birds from the Chrome Web store. Basically, with the ability to have local storage for off-line access using the SD and USB ports, a built-in media player and file manager to access my content and HDMI for playback on a TV, full support for document editing, the ability to access my digital content like books, movies and music, a complete browsing experience with ALL content the Web has to offer with continuous seamless and transparent security and performance updates and improvements, super-fast boot-up time in seconds, excellent battery life and extremely light and portable, and I don't miss my PC one iota. The only things I use my PC for that I can't do on the Chromebook are: PC gaming from Steam, file conversions (music and video), and uploading content to the cloud like music and video to Amazon and Google's servers. It's important to note that I am always connected to the Internet via WiFi networks or my own personal MiFi hotspot. Big kudos to Sundar Pichai and the entire Chrome OS team. This is not a half-baked product. This is a complete solution and works really really well. I am very excited about this platform and would recommend Chrome OS and Chromebooks in general to any PC user who primarily uses their computer to access the Web and has consistent reliable access to it, both in fixed space and from a mobile perspective and has a portable hard drive for off-line access and storage.

The hardware is fantastic, but the monitor software (the embedded UI) is barely usable. It doesn’t always respond when you touch a button. It takes a second or two to wake up if you just closed the menu. The UI will enter different states based on what’s going on. If you wake the monitor by touching a button on the display, you get one set of buttons. If you click a button on the puck, another set of buttons. Sometimes you only get monitor input options. Sometimes you get presets plus the “go to the regular menu” button. It’s rather confusing. The KVM concept is nice in theory, but it’s really clunky in practice. Buttons on the display and on the included hoTkey puck (i see what you did there Benq) are customisable, but only for single functions. Want to switch USB source _and_ monitor input source? It’s going to take a few clicks to switch the USB source and then a few clicks to swap the input. All in all, a great display, but I wish the embedded software was better.

Purchased this product to mount my new Panasonic 65" plasma TV - model # TCP65GT50. Wanted a fully articulating mount so I could move it easily to adjust viewing angle as well as access connections on back of the TV, and also wanted a slim profile so it would sit as close to the wall as possible when fully retracted. This mount does all of these things well. I was originally looking at the VLF311 which appeared very similar to the VLF410 except the VLF311 only accomodates TVs up to 65" and costs less, so I emailed Sanus asking about the difference and one of the reps immediately replied and asked that I call him so he could explain. He told me that the VLF410 is the 'second generation' of the VLF311 and offers improved balancing of large TVs. This made sense because I did recall seeing a few customer reviews of the VLF311 saying that their TVs wouldn't hang perfectly level. Of course, this begs the question of why they are still selling the VLF311 when they have admitted it needed to be updated. Anyway, I needed to mount my TV centered between two windows, but the two 16" studs I had to use were exactly four inches off center of where the mount neeeded to be hung. Since the VLF411 has multiple pre-drilled slots which are designed to accomodate studs between 14" and 22" apart, I was able to use two "unmatching" slots to compensate for three of those four inches but this still left me with the mount being one inch off-center between my two windows. To get that last inch, I hung the TV on the mount and then simply slid the TV one inch to the left so it was hanging one inch off-center of the mount, but perfectly centered between my two windows. Problem solved? No, the 86 lb. TV would ever-so-slightly tilt to the left since it was hanging off-center. So much for 2nd generation improvement of the mount! It still has very little tolerance for TVs not hanging perfectly centered. Undeterred, and deciding that the TV was hanging about 6" lower than where I really wanted it, I started over and installed the mount 6" higher and INTENTIONALLY a bit off-level to the right, so when I reinstalled the TV one inch to the left of center on the mount, it hung perfectly. Bottom line -- the multiple pre-drilled mounting slots give you some flexibility to accomodate 'off-center' studs, but if you need more than 3 or 4 inches of wiggle room then be prepared to take more creative action.

Fantastic case. I am very over RGB software (it's all bloatware that fights with other RGB software. So when we were doing our biannual in-house computer hand-me-downs (there are 4 of us, parents included, with gaming PCs in home, and this process often involves a case and/or cooler change) and my daughter wanted RGB, I looked for a solution that would allow for lights with no light software. This case was it. It comes with three RGB fans in the front and a couple of buttons on the top of the case that let you change the light pattern and color. There are plenty of good-looking options here, and this is 100% built into the case and requires no software. HOWEVER, you can still connect these three RGB fans to a mobo header and control with software (ASUS Armoury Crate is the recommended app, yuck), and if you do this you lose the built-in case control - so you can have it either way but not both. There's also an RGB strip that faces outward along the bottom of the glass. Overall I am thrilled with this case because my kid is thrilled, and it is recommended. I do have some gripes and some instances where I would absolutely not recommend it. Pros: - Fantastic looking, built-in RGB looks great and has lots of options without invasive RGB software but you can still software control the RGB if you want - It's much thinner than most ATX midtowers (still just as tall). It has just barely enough room to fit a big air cooler (I installed a ThermalRight Peerless Assassin which is one of the tallest at 157mm and it just barely fits; max clearance is 160mm). Note that I doubt you'd be able to fit a 4080 or 4090 in here with the power cable and close the glass. FTW3 3070 Ti fit fine though. - Material quality and construction is high - Airflow is stellar Cons: - It absolutely needs some more holes along the top of the mobo. You really can't feed cables through here except at the corners. - While the bottom of the mobo is better (more holes) there still aren't as many holes as most other cases. - There are no holes in the middle of the PSU shroud for GPU power cables, there's only a hole at the front near the fans so GPU cables need to go all the way to the front by the bottom fan then come back (are we noticing a theme here with the not enough holes?) - You should NOT BUY THIS CASE if you're doing any 3.5" drives. The caddy for these occupies nearly the entire bottom of the case cross-ways (it blocks the space under the PSU shroud) so unless you remove the HDD caddy it'd be an absolute nightmare to route cables across the whole bottom of the case - like the GPU power cables). I honestly can't believe this aspect of the design; the HDD caddy should sit long-ways not cross-ways. If you remove the HDD caddy you're all good. There are two 2.5" HDD mount points on the back of the mobo area and this was enough for our build (One NVME on mobo, two 2.5" SSD on the back of the mobo). And the last (but not at all least) con - the primary picture on Amazon shows the empty case with the three RGB fans and an exhaust fan on the back of the case. YOU DO NOT GET THIS EXHAUST FAN. It's just the three RGB fans. Other pictures show this (not the primary one though). Got a three pack of Antec 120 white fans and used one for rear exhaust and two for top exhaust and it's fine now, but I don't like the misleading advertising. All told, as I said, my daughter is thrilled and so am I. So some important caveats but if you go in understanding those you'll be pleasantly surprised.

For me, WD has been reliable but the most expensive, and Seagate has been cheaper but unreliable. So when faced with the two traditional options, I went for option three -- Toshiba. I bought a 4TB 128MB Toshiba drive about two years ago and it's been a champ for me -- great performance, great reliability, excellent value -- which is why I came back for the 8TB 256MB version for an additional storage drive. I am happy with a CrystalDiskMark6 score of 204/193 on the 8TB drives, and even the older 4TB is delivering 150/143 after two years of daily access (it's my games drive). But I will join the choir in noting that the 8TB drive is quite audible when seeking/defragmenting, at least compared to non-Toshiba drives. Whatever other companies are doing to quiet their drives, Toshiba is not; you will hear that distinctive rumble during operation. But you have to know there's going to be a trade-off at such a lower price point. Where this drive does not skimp is performance; that's what I wanted, along with saving a few bucks. The noisy performance is an acceptable compromise, you can get a quality drive for a good price,.

My suggestion is drop sending the bag and reduce the tripod price accordingly. All in all both are very good values for the money but the shortcomings in design on the 25 make it my last choice to field carry, especially in cold weather.

At $300, the most expensive around the neck bluetooth headset, there's an expectation of near perfection which this product doesn't have. The good: - Sound quality is great. Great as in lots of base which is what Bose EQ is known for...while still doing well at the the mid and high tones. - When noise cancellation is turned up, it also is doing noise cancellation on the mic for the person you're talking to...and doing it pretty well. - Once Bose went to the in-ear with extra noise baffle, it does a good job at reducing noise in addition to the extra tech that also does noise reduction. The Bad: - The around the neck is almost equally proportioned in it's design. It's counting on it's rubberized material to be sticky enough not to twist around (which it's constantly doing). Any around the neck needs to have a shape that allows gravity to help keep heavier weighted areas in the lowest position (eg LG Tone Ultra). See pic on how it's constantly spinning. - The earphones can't be attached to the neckband, which means they're constantly dangling/catching on things. Magnetic clipping to the ends would alleviate this problem, but would already increase the size of these large ear accessories. - No fast forward/reverse buttons - The primary microphone is in the right earbud, which means if you are wanting to just one-ear it, you have to do the right ear or risk having the mic constantly having scratching noise from it rubbing against shirt/chest. Long term concerns: - Since the earphones are always dangling, I'd expect with long term use I'm going to loose more than one ear mold getting caught and popping off. - Having owned 3 other Bose over-ear Quietcomfort headsets (which all have had earpad and headpad deterioration of materials after 2 years), I know they have their industrial design honed for 2-3 year material breakdown. I'm concerned that the rubber used will start becoming sticky and intolerable after 1-2 years of use (like my Bose SoundSports have become). - I have right ear hearing damage from using a Bose Bluetooth headset Series 2 for podcast/music listening at too high a volume (trying to use it in too noisy environments), so I am very careful now with volume and single ear use. When doing voice audio content (podcasts/audio books etc) I specifically always use both ears to make sure I don't turn the volume too loud and cause hearing damage. A good note is I've been able to keep the volume at a lower level than my other headsets, so I don't think I have to worry too much. Noise Cancellation Notes: I came with the expectation of similar noise cancellation as my QuietComfort headsets. You could turn it off (and hear whatever ambient noise comes thru), or you could turn it on (it does it's best to eliminate all background noise period). That is not how the noise cancellation works with these (and ultimately why the battery life of the QC30 is as short as it is). When the headset it powered on, the headphones are constantly outputting sound. Using the Bose app, what you're adjusting with more/less noise cancellation is the amount of sound that is either relayed from the mic thru the headphones, or how much external noise is cancelled by the headphones. Why I say this, is because if you turn off all noise cancellation thru the app, you can hear everything around you like you didn't have any earphones in. However if you power down the headphones, you get the natural noise reduction of having an in-ear headphone occluding external noise. I think this is a conscious engineering choice, and serves two purposes: 1) It makes the "noise cancelling" feature seem more impressive as you adjust it's level up and down 2) Technically I think they designed the headset to be worn 100% of the time, and adjusting the noise cancellation level using the two dedicated buttons when the situation around you is you're talking with someone, or when you want to block out as much as possible all external noise. I think this decision is flawed for several reasons: 1) It's quicker/easier to just pull the earphones out rather than spend the 4-6 seconds constantly adjusting the noise cancellation amount up/down based on the situation 2) Designing earphones for 8-12hr regular usage is fundamentally flawed. If you were trying to leave noise cancellation up, you are going to be affecting your hearing long-term. You also get what I'd call "ear fatigue" because having the noise cancellation enabled for 2-3hrs, then taking them off you can feel a difference, and your ears adjust/recover from the noise cancellation experience. 8+hrs of constant earphone use is not productive and ultimately fatiguing: Why I love the around the neck design is precisely that I CAN remove the earphones when not in active use quickly and easily, and put them back in when you need them. The engineering choices of this headset work against this use case. At $150, I might consider putting up with it's flaws for the sound quality or without knowing ultimately because of materials/use I'm probably only going to get 2, maybe 3 years use out of them...but ended up sending them back in the end. The search continues for the best around the neck bluetooth headset.

So I ended up installing this antenna on my roof about 20 feet high according to the directions. I then connected the antenna to a HD Homerun tuner so that I could stream the TV channels to all my TV's without having to run cables all over the place. At first I could only about get 20 channels and most had pixalation issues. I live in Southern California about 25 miles from the the TV towers so I knew I should be getting channels with better signals. So I thought that the antenna was not pointing in the right direction. After several attempts at re-pointing and rescanning on the HD Homer tuner, I could not improve the signal quality for most channels. So I thought either the antenna was bad (afterall it feels cheap) or it did not like the connection to the HD Homerun tuner. After more troubleshooting, I figure out that the power suppply that came with antenna was the problem. Instead of "amplifying" the signals it was interfering with them, causing the pixalation and low signal strenght issues. I got rid of the power suppy, (don't care about the remote control rotation capabiltiy) I now just have the antenna connected straight to the HD Homerun tuner and get every channel as clear as cable or satellite TV. Maybe when you are closer to the TV towers, the amplication feature is not needed and in my case made the signal worse.

this is a very long but preliminary review, k. the monitor came in december '20 and i've been entranced ever since. so by the time of this writing, i've only spent 12 - 16 hours on this thing and will share some initial thoughts. a gamer i'm not but when i do play, i like to enjoy a better experience. the biggest knock i've seen against this display is price but it's $600 now - not cheap but not $700 either. have a gtx 1650 pushing vids and i've played the relatively slow warframe for a several minutes and it's all good. i say "good" because the raptor 27 replaces my 6 yo 4k 28" from acer. the diff was not very dramatic but the graphics and experiences are definitely improved. so no regrets there at all. let me add that for me, 1440 provides a better visual experience on win 10 than 2160 (4k). i'll mention my asus vg27aq experience later. in real life, i primarily stream and surf - the normal boring stuff. for me, here's where the raptor shines. i did a minor adjustment of the color settings per rtings.com, and again, could not discern much of a difference except for brightness over its default gaming profile. colors are natural and even in a bright room, had to turn down the luminance to 50 - 60%. the colors are stunning but as with any edge lit ips monitor, a blank black screen will show some bleed through. so if you're the type that enjoys blank screens, expect some disappointment. in the wild, the blacks are certainly dark enough and i have no complaints. btw, our tv's are 55" oleds, k. so i know a highly contrasted dark or black color when i see one. the dot-com reviewers are reporting technical results based on their metrics; what i'm sharing is a very subjective experience, so you may hate it. also, for those that likely have much more experience than me, i've just returned an asus vg27aq i bought after a previous week of pain with it. rtings.com rates it as the best gamer for 2020. again, subjectively, i prefer this raptor 27, and by far, even if the vg27aq had no issues (read on). i use 2 inputs on a display - displayport and hdmi. our security nvr uses hdmi and is always hot. what i really like with the raptor 27 is that u can disable its auto-scan feature, so when the 'puter is shutdown, the raptor "sleeps." this is very unlike the asus vg27aq which also has auto-scan but it can't be disabled; so in my situation, it remains on since it will hunt for the next hot port when the computer is off - hate that! the raptor's rgb lights in its base can be managed - off, on and a host of in between stuff. i find this lighting beneficial when working at my desk at night. these rgb lights are great! just enough to provide some downward illumination without having to turn on some other light source. i can see (not read) my papers and additional plug & play stuff that i may use. i hope razer considers additional lighting at the rear of the panel for a more soothing environ. yeah, imagine that, a gaming monitor that is so much better for normal stuff simply due to a well thought out design. let's hope other manufacturers are reading. lastly, u may see some negative comments about the raptor's cable management methodology and their difficulties. perhaps there was an engineering change since its original release or i'm just too old, but for their utility, it's a superb idea and quite ez to navigate! just eliminating the cord clutter behind the display was big plus and now we have an very stylish and modern look on the desk as well. i will add, that i lucked out in as much as the cable length was just enough to reach my tower-on-floor layout. but if u need more length, you'll need male-female extensions as the cables supplied are for direct connection from monitor to 'puter. the power cord has a brick much like the older thinkpad laptops. the cable is long enough but some may require an extension cord. wrapping up, while it's certainly a nice-to-have, i really could care less about its gaming prowess. we now have a fashion statement for a monitor that complements the lighted keyboard on the hooker desk it sits upon. if u believe this is just for kids, i'm here to say that u can have it both ways! the younguns can play when they come to visit and once they leave, gramps can kick back and be very cool takin' care of business - be it gaming or writing a powerpoint presentation. Weeks after Purchase: returned this device due to a problem with the rgb underlights on the base! it appears that one or more leds had some flicker which occurs when in the "static" setting. amazon customer service was superb. she actually listened and made some very thoughtful suggestions. my replacement is scheduled to arrive in a couple days. Now and after my 3rd panel, and discussion with Rapter support, they finally fixed the problem with a firmware update. 22 Month - UPDATE: with my new the RTX 3070, it's like night and day when compared to GTX 1650. i tried windows hd and am sticking with it. Many gamers will talk about the need for higher refresh rates for most of us, we barely process 60 hz. still, i can understand the smoothness at 120hz, beyond that, it seems like emotion. i love this ips monitor. let's just hope it lasts longer than other products from razer.

My husband needed a Bluetooth headset because our Ragdoll, Little Man, has a cord fetish - especially for skinny cords like the ones on most headphones and mics. He (my husband, not the cat) is not a huge fan of tiny earbuds or huge, over the head "cans." I convinced him to try this headset and he loves them. He listens to hours of streamed Amazon Prime movies and TV shows (or music on Spotify) at the PC while playing World of Warcraft, and also finds these terrific for Ventrilo. (Note: If you have issues with the microphone sound quality in Ventrilo, simply adjust the quality level higher in that program.) Seeing hubby so happy with his Kinivos, I decided to buy myself a pair but had issues with them. They worked briefly, but then didn't seem to want to pair with my PC (or my Mac, or any other BT device in the house). I procrastinated for months before contacting BlueRigger for warranty support, and was thrilled to receive a courteous and prompt response with troubleshooting tips. When I responded that the headset still didn't work, BlueRigger immediately issued a replacement headset via Amazon. Not used headphones, not JUST the headphones, a whole new, BRAND NEW shrink-wrapped retail unit - that works as wonderfully as my husband's pair, I am happy to report. I would not hesitate to buy from BlueRigger in the future. Products slip through QC sometimes, or can even receive damage during shipping that is invisible to the eye. What is important is the warranty support (in this case, from BlueRigger). I didn't wait days for a response, they didn't make me jump through unreasonable hoops to prove the item was defective - I didn't even have to box up and pay to ship back the old headset. Impressive. I would not hesitate to recommend this headset. Sound-wise I am no audiophile, but I personally think it's quite good for BT headphones in that price range, and my husband has also been satisfied (he's the picky one in the family). Sound quality, however, is such a hugely personal thing that you'd really need to hear them to make your own conclusions. I will say that they are better overall than many of the more expensive BT headsets - if you don't believe me, start checking reviews. I actually prefer them over my pricier LG HB-700s, which are very nice, but better suited for when I want to isolate myself from all outside noise. With the Kinivo, I can choose to also hear game sounds in WoW through my Harmon Kardon Soundsticks (the original USB Mac ones; connected to my PC and still amazing) while listening to Ventrilo or music through the headphones. Or I can, you know, actually manage to hold a conversation with my husband as we share our home office, sitting at our respective PCs and listening to our respective music playlists (we have common musical interests, but there are some glaring disparities!). Also, while we admittedly don't blast the headphones as we'd like to retain some hearing in our elder years, there is no bleedthrough - I can't hear what he's listening to even when I'm not wearing any headphones. I hope our experiences will help you decide whether these headphones are a viable option for you!

I have used the "old" Kindle for several years. The Oasis has many improvements, trade-offs, and annoyances. Overall, most of the new configuration is a good step up from the original, but I would like more user-flexibility. IMPROVEMENTS and benefits: The screen size is the same as the old one, but the overall size and weight is a fraction of earlier models. I can carry the Oasis in a trouser pocket. The illuminated screen is excellent, the extra battery is pure genius, the size is a delight, and the self contained cover with magnetic interactives is great. The touch screen is a paradox - Some of the touch screen implementations are among the best features and some are among the worst (see below). Reading in any light is a pleasure. Access to the full purchased library and multi-instrument sharing is a terrific addition. Access to Wi-Fi is very convenient. Overall response time is excellent. You can display PAGE NUMBERS, finally. One of the nicest features is the ability to bookmark a page with a touch and return to that page immediately. NEEDS WORK: Navigation is about as intuitive as a slide trombone. Touching the screen usually does something, but it is neither intuitive nor consistent. Navigation is mostly "Try it and see what happens." The owners manual is poorly written and barely outlines the operation. Even after reading several times, many ops are "cut and try." The inconsistency of the touch screen really hinders learning the device. BAD STUFF: The incessant ads for magazines etc. are infuriating. They rarely appear in the text you are reading, but sometimes show up if you hit some magic spot on the screen. They are always on the "Sleep" screen. Needs an "ads off" switch. I have found no way to drop the Wi-Fi and switch to 3G. I cannot mark the books on the list. On the old Kindle when I added a title to a collection, it no longer appeared on the "Home" screen. Thus I knew that I could have the collections sort the "read" items, and they did not appear on the open list. I have found no good way to mark books as "read," but I'm working on it. The "Owners Manual" (on screen) is pitiful and needs to be updated to a comprehensive reference. The touch screen is inconsistent as to pressure to perform a function, and it is too easy to "fat-finger" and hit the wrong spot. Sometimes you can pound on it and produce nothing, and other times the slightest touch anywhere will produce multiple effects. Finally, the price is too high for many. Overall, I like it a lot, but I'm hoping for some upgrades soon.

I purchased the 500GB SSD version of this computer because I wanted something reasonably affordable, with Windows 7 pre-installed, and with a solid state hard drive - and I wanted it fast. So far, I'm very happy with the purchase. It could have been a little better, but for the price it's a very respectable deal. I like that the tower is pretty small, it still includes a DVD burner (so many don't these days), and it comes with Windows 7. I'm not a fan of Windows 8/8.1 and I don't want to deal with Windows 10 and all its creepy privacy issues. I like 7. I do wish it had come with a proper backup of Windows 7 instead of a Windows 8 restore disk, though. You can make your own restore disks, but it's just annoying to have to do so. With an SSD, the computer boots extremely fast. I would have liked to have the option to purchase a 1TB SSD, but I can always upgrade or add a drive later. The graphics card (well, the lack thereof) is probably the biggest issue that needs to be fixed right away. You're dealing with the built-in graphics here, which means you'll need to buy a better graphics card if you want to support multiple monitors.The ports available by default are a DisplayPort and a VGA, and I ended up finding a small, low-profile PCI Express card for the x16 slot that was able to fit and give me an HDMI slot. I suppose I could have opted for a DisplayPort to HDMI dongle, too. Be warned, the case is narrow (slots about 3 inches wide) and the motherboard is a bit smooshed, so you will need a small video card if you go that route. If you want wifi instead of wired access to the internet, you'll also need to purchase that separately. Again, the narrow case will be a consideration if you use a card-based solution. There are USB options that work reasonably well, too. In terms of bloatware, they have installed a bit of extra junk, but it's not as bad as if you bought something at Best Buy. I didn't have to spend hours removing all the "bonuses". The computer also comes with a free keyboard and mouse, but I wish it didn't. They're total garbage, and I feel bad always tossing the free extras in the garbage. Nobody ever wants them. In all, I would definitely recommend this computer for most people. If you need some really intense processing power for gaming, video editing, etc., you'll need to do a lot to make this suitable, but it's more than sufficient for most people who would need it for business or home use.

I have been very pleased with this purchase. It certainly is the best camcorder I have ever owned to date, although I would probably have purchased the CX12 if I were to purchase again (see comments below for reason). I purchased this SR11 because I wanted an HD video recorder for my daughter's wedding. My previous recorder was a Sony DCR-HC26 which used MiniDV tapes. The camcorder overall has a very nice weight and feel. It does not feel like some plastic toy that might break easily. One has a sense of quality and durability while holding it. One friend who held it exclaimed, "Wow. This is a very nice camcorder." I am very pleased with the quality of the videos. The colors are much deeper and truer than my last two Sony camcorders. I usually record in HD at 7MP, two steps down from the highest setting. Even video that I burn directly onto standard DVD, which is being downgraded through standard RCA cables, looks much better on my 1080P 52" Samsung TV than any of my other camcorders. That alone makes me happy with my purchase, since I don't yet have the ability to burn to Blu-Ray, and most of my friends probably couldn't play them even if I could. So while I record in HD, most of what I share with others will probably still be on standard DVD for now. The low light quality and focusing ability seems to work very well. People often complain about increased graininess in images recorded under low light, but I realize how problematic this can be for camcorders. In my opinion, the SR11 does it very well. It also has an infrared lamp, but no colors with that method, so I use it only when there is virtually no light at all. The face recognition is very interesting. It creates little boxes around faces when it recognizes them, giving the user security that the camera is focusing and adjusting exposure on the right subject. I like that, and it seems to work remarkable well. There is a nice dial on the front which has a button that can be pressed to switch to manual focus instantly. Turn the dial to focus, and it even displays a decimal number to show how far away the focus is set. I like this easy to access manual focus for situations where my subjects are always the same distance away. My previous camcorder forced me to navigate menus to switch to manual focus. However, the automatic focus does seem to work better than my previous camcorder, so I might not be using this feature as much as I have in the past with my previous camcorder. There is an easy to reach backlight adjustment button on the front of the camcorder, which makes it very easy to adjust exposure when there is a bright window behind your subject. An icon appears to remind you that backlight adjustment is on. Press the button again to toggle it off. The pictures it takes are very good at 10 MP. There is a very bright flash on the camcorder that really lights up the area for pictures, even far across a room. The only downside is that everyone in every shot will have red eyes, but the provided software makes it very easy to automatically adjust settings with a single click, then take out red eye by clicking red eye and then clicking on the red eyes to turn the pupils dark. I read that this camcorder takes pictures even while recording video, but I have found pictures taken this way are not as sharp as pausing the video and then taking a picture. I think pictures taken while recording are actually capturing a frame from the recording video. Cons 1. No DV (Firewire / 1394) connection to my DVD recorder or computer 2. Harddrive not good for bumps or shakes I am accustomed to using my DV cable to connect my camcorder directly to my DVD recorder and computer. The DV cable lets me control the camera from my video editing software. This camcorder does not have a DV connection. I was surprised by this elimination and will have to learn how to deal with that as time goes on. The camera does have an HDMI output which I have used to view video directly on my HD TV. It also has USB and a nice docking station for the camcorder. I have not yet started using the camera with my video editing software via USB, so I can't comment on that yet. The camcorder does come with a remote control, which is nice, especially considering the elimination of the DV connection. The remote control can navigate menus, play video, show pictures, record, control lens zoom, etc. This is my first hard drive video camcorder. I have found that bumps and shakes can dramatically affect the images recorded on hard drives. The nice thing about the hard drive is the huge amount of recording media available. However, I really like the option to record to memory card, and if I had to make the purchase again, I think I would opt for the Sony HDR-CX12. This is basically the same camcorder but with only the memory card, not the hard drive. The CX12 is smaller because of this, which makes it more attractive for me. Initially I went with the SR11 because it would be less expensive than buying memory cards, but I find that I have been buying memory cards anyway. I like how I can just take out the memory card and directly plug it into my Playstation 3 and view both video and pictures right away. While the SR11 also records to memory cards, the CX12 is smaller and uses less power. Also, I figure the hard drive is going to give out someday, while the memory card will probably continue to work for many years longer. Overall, the SR11 is a very excellent camcorder. It is clearly the best camcorder that I have owned to date, but if you like this camcorder, give a hard look at the Sony HDR-CX12 before purchasing. It is too bad that the SR11 and CX12 does not use SD media, because the cost of memory cards for SD is so much lower than Sony's Memory Stick Pro Duo media.

Hello world! I must say that i was very excited when I heard about this router. I researched it against the Asus Black Diamond but, ultimately, made the jump for the Netgear WNDR4500. When I received the router, packaging was great and the box was unharmed. Once opened, directions were sparse, but I've hooked up a few routers and it was "color" coordinated, so easy enough. I walked through the quick start guide and hooked up my tower in the 1st floor office(or that room in the basement as my wife refers to it :)). Gigabit service was quickly achieved after running through the web interface and upgrading the firmware. Then, I quickly ran around the house and proceeded to setup the wireless for my Linux laptop, Nook Color, PS3, and finally my wife's XP based Dell laptop. Everything seemed to be fine at first. I walked all over with the Nook and my laptop and got full strength signal everywhere in my house (didn't check the attic, but...). I was pretty excited the first few days. I played games on the PS3 wireless while my wife worked on her laptop with Lotus and networking remotely. This was FAST...I can't stress that enough. I tried pushing the envelope and decided to torrent a few Linux distros that didn't have enough seeders while updating my Linux Mint LXDE 11. All while continuing Call of Duty on the PS3 and my wife working on her laptop. Then....it happened. My modem must have reset without the router knowing it. Browsing was not possible, but torrents continued. All my devices showed great signal strength, but no browsing. After a few more minutes, torrenting and ftp stopped working. I reset the router and the modem and then refreshed my connections. All was good again. This went on for a week, resetting once a day, restoring connections. I stopped torrenting thinking that would help, but it didn't matter. In fact, I didn't even need to have anything on. My wife called me at 8 am at work and I had to walk her through the reset because it just wouldn't stay connected. Then it got worse. I didn't need to ftp, torrent, browse, or anything, the just router wouldn't connect to the internet despite the radios transmitting at great strength. I called support at Netgear. This was a calamity. They read from a script, insulted my intelligence, and then were quite condescending upon reconnection. I'm sure it was the language barrier ;/ After an hour and ten minutes of "coaching", I was told to return the router. I exchanged the router with another of the same model through Amazon(thank you!) Unfortunately, I hooked it up yesterday and still having the same problem. WW-DRT doesn't support it yet, but I shouldn't need to go there. This is supposed to be top of the line but it just turned out to be a good wired gigabit router, hence the 2 stars. I didn't even get into the Readyshare feature which only worked with certain devices, but no matter, this router isn't ready for primetime. If anyone from Netgear is reading this, get your act together! And, No, I don't want to speak with the horrible customer service reps again...I felt like I worked for them most of the time we were on the phone....

I have had this unit for 3 months and enjoy it greatly. It is hooked up to a 65" TV and, despite the fact that the sound bar is narrower than the TV, the sound spread is very good. Pros - Very good frequency response and sound quality. - Bluetooth connection works well. - Surprisingly good bass given that there is no external subwoofer (an external sub would of course give extra punch to movie soundtracks with explosions and collisions and starships). - It is simple to add an external powered sub-woofer if you decide you want stronger bass. - The "Clear Voice" function helps dialogue stand out over background noise. - The Bluetooth function works well. Cons - This is definitely not surround sound because sound bars simply cannot be expected to provide "real" surround sound. However, this unit has a good sound stage that is definitely more 3-D than plain stereo. - The indicator lights are very tiny and on top of the unit, and therefore are hard to see while sitting down. - There is no indicator for bass or treble level, so arriving at satisfactory levels of bass and treble involves trial and error adjustment. - The unit is fairly expensive compared to the many similar units at a lower price range (but compares favorably to units that cost much more). I was planning to buy an external subwoofer to enhance the bass but so far I haven't felt the need to do so; however, anyone who wants bass that will crack windows or shake pictures off the wall will want an external sub. As for sound quality, when I used the Bluetooth to play some classical music for my musician wife she was amazed, perhaps the first time in a period of decades that she ever expressed excitement about a piece of sound equipment (guys, you know what I mean). Bottom line: I would buy it again and if the sound bar for my other TV ever conks out I will replace it with one of these.

Overall, I'm happy with the P2450H. Pro 1: 3 inputs - DVI, VGA, HDMI. HDMI added about $50 to the cost of this monitor but it definitely came in handy when I was able to hookup the HDMI output from a cheapo graphics card on a new computer. So I was running three computers using one monitor - really great. When I got rid of the old computer, I kept the new one on HDMI - picture looks fantastic. Pro 2. After a few days, I found I did not need the so called fast response time or maximum brightness. I have set it using the supplied software to "Internet" and find the monitor is sufficiently bright in my room. Sometimes, I bump it up to a custom user configuration when watching video. BTW, this monitor can be dazzling bright if you so need and can be adjusted via software depending on the time of day and room light levels. Pro 3. People complain about the touch buttons but once you understand them they work fine. Touch once to activate (labels light up so you can see where the touch buttons are) before using. After the initial settings, you rarely need to touch them except to switch inputs - you can control the monitor from software, i.e. Magictune. Con 1: Magictune x64 software for Windows 7 64-bit is rather flaky and will sometimes disable itself requiring me to kill it and restart. I often get 3 icons in the system tray in addition to a LCD gamma icon. Update: one suggested solution is to use the 32 bit version of Magictune instead of the 64 bit version - so far so good. Con 2: Magictune does not save more than one user configuration. Big win if Samsung would add this. Con 3: Slightly wobbly stand, not bad but not great like a Dell stand. Con 4: No height adjustment or swivel on the stand. Con 5: Limited viewing angle. I understand that this monitor has pretty good viewing angles given the technology used (TN). Becoming acclimated to the many options (color, warmth, brightness, contrast, response time) and finding the right combination of those options takes time. I have to say I wasn't a happy camper for a few days. A week later, I am satisfied with what seems to be a decent monitor for a working guy that does not do games or professional graphic work.

It's hilarious how they advertise that you don't need to wet the contacts before putting on the monitor. The hilarious part of that is that wetting the contacts would be far less frustrating than dealing with this device as it comes. This device has two major problems, which I'm calling dropdowns and dropouts. Drop downs means that it randomly miscalculates the heart rate, and places it at a significantly lower BPM than it should be. Dropouts means that it completely disconnects at random times. The drop-downs tend to happen when the device is on your arm, and your arm is below your heart in some sort of compression exercise. The dropouts happen during other types of compression, mostly twists in yoga. Another issue is the syncing. The device regularly will go into a state where it flashes blue and red, won't sync with anything, and won't even turn off at all. In this situation, the only two options are to let the battery drain, or plug it into the charger. I've never let the battery drain, and don't even know how long the battery would last, because this situation happened so frequently that I have no choice but to just go ahead and charge it to get it out of the situation. I've tried this HRM in all of the six different available configurations, and multiple times each. I've tightened the band, I've loosened the band. I've tried on a full charge, I've tried on a low charge. This thing is the single most annoying piece of tech I have ever had to displeasure of using. I mustered up the strength to give it three stars, because it does technically track heart rate and sync with devices most of the time. It just doesn't do it consistently enough to deserve anything more. If I had read this review before buying, I would not have bought.

The CC pot firstly has a massive dead zone at the minimum range, secondly, the output current is dependent on the input voltage. The higher the input voltage the higher the output current will be allowed to rise. So you cannot protect your electronics reliably if your input voltage is all over the place. Which is the case of a battery supply as the input would definitely become problematic. I couldn't get the current to go below 4A on the output and the current just rise more and more as the input voltage goes up. The input current also increases so I have no idea where the CC came from because neither side is constant anything. Edit: The CC function is greatly dependant on the differences between the input voltage and the output voltage. And I have found that if you create too much load on the output and the output potential is too low it will collapse and pump through more of the input voltage. (kinda think of it in terms of how the resonance of the circuit works) if you collapse the resonance you just start pushing through power directly from the input. Maybe if this was a buckboost converter with cc you could mitigate this problem. But from all 4 units this is how it behaved. So I don't think they are defective you just have to be weary about how boost converters work and their pitfalls. The behavior is the same on my other smaller booster too. But not my buck converter, with buck converters the CC function is rock solid. So I'm going to give this a 3 star because through learning more I figured out its less of a problem with this specific design and more of a compromise with any boost converter this simple.

Model: Wifi with No Ads Background: I had a Kindle Touch for 2 weeks this summer, but returned it to wait for this model. Screen Light - Only in Emergencies The screen light level can be changed between 0 and 25. At zero, the screen looks just as flat, matte, and lovely as the Kindle Touch, and is a pleasure to read on. I actually thought the light was off at zero, but when I turned off my lamp, the Kindle was glowing faintly. I loved the flat text of the Kindle Touch, and I'm glad the Kindle Paperwhite, on zero, is just as pleasurable a reading experience. The text looked great during outdoor reading as well. I feel like the screen might produce more glare in direct sunlight than the Touch, but I don't have a Touch on-hand for a side-by-side comparison The device light setting out-of-the-box was 22. My eyes hurt by the time I completed the set-up. Level 22 is very bright and is not unlike looking at a computer screen, my mobile phone, or a tablet. The technology may be different (front-lit vs. back-lit), but the end result seems to be the same. I immediately turned the light down after the set-up was complete, and opened a book. I found my eyes hurt at level 10 as well. The light shining was out from the device. I have heard the light described as if a lamp were shining on the Kindle as opposed to light coming from the screen, and I disagree completely. At very low Kindle light levels, the brightness goes away. This is the only Kindle light level I find tolerable, and it is basically the same as reading on the Kindle Touch. Next, I tried reading in a relatively dark room. I tried to adjust the light to a comfortable level. I found reading at low settings, such as 5, to be very difficult. The screen background and the text background were both darker; the contrast was lost. At higher settings, the contrast is good, but the screen is so bright, it's just like looking into my bright computer screen at night. I'm disappointed by the light, but I feel like my expectations were set unachievably high by Amazon. I will use the Kindle to read with the light on level zero. I will only use the light for very short periods of time, such as if I'm finishing a chapter outdoors at dusk. For bedtime reading, I'll be turning on a lamp, not the Kindle light. Translation: Bing Translator Integration Lacking This generation of Kindle uses Bing for foreign language translation. I thought if I pressed a word in a foreign language novel that the translation would appear, just like the dictionary definition would in an English book. This is not the case. The pop-up says the word is not defined (because it's looking in the English dictionary), but I can select "More." Then I can select "Translate," and then Bing appears and will translate the word (if I'm connected to the internet). This is far too many clicks for how often I need words translated. Plus, if I'm not connected to the internet (such as during a plane flight), Bing will not be available. So, I downloaded a French-English Kindle translation dictionary ($6 on Amazon), and now the word is translated when I press it. This works just like it did on the old model (Kindle Touch). If I want to translate phrases or passages, I can highlight them and go through the steps for Bing translation. I do this far more seldom, so I don't mind the extra clicks, and I appreciate this feature. I might be more upset that the Bing translator wasn't more integrated if I didn't already own the French-English dictionary from use on previous devices. Cover: Auto-sleep and Auto-wake Feature is Fab The best part of the case is how the screen turns on and off when opening and closing the case. The on/off button on the Kindle is a little awkward, so the convenience of having it auto-wake when the case is opened and auto-sleep when the case is closed is one of the best features of this Kindle. The Kindle resumes on whatever screen I was on when I closed the case, not a home screen or an ad. (I have the no-ad version of the Kindle, so I don't know if the ad version works differently). I love this cover. When the Kindle is inserted, it feels completely integrated, like it's a single product. The case has a nice texture, and is easy to carry around. I don't have to worry about smudging the screen or dropping the Kindle because I'm hanging on to it by the edges. It also works well for me when I'm reading lying down on my side, as the screen is propped up by the case. The case clasp is magnetic, so it doesn't flop open no matter what position it's in. The top case flap can also fold behind the Kindle for easy one-handed holding. I thought I would only use the case for travel, but I believe I'll be using it full-time. Time Remaining: Susceptible to Inaccuracies The time remaining in a chapter is calculated by your reading speed. It's nice to have some indication of how many pages are left in a chapter since checking by flipping pages forward on a Kindle is far harder than with a book. However, for me, the time remaining is just a broad estimate, as sometimes I drift off while reading, or just set the Kindle down for a minute. Plus, my reading speed will be much slower when I'm reading foreign language books, which means estimates will be wrong when I'm reading both English books and French books because it's averaging the two. The time remaining is definitely better than nothing, and I'm happy to have the feature, but Amazon, how about showing the number of pages remaining in the chapter instead? (Yes, I understand this varies with font and type, but that can be accounted for in the calculation). No Ads Version: Eliminates Swipe but not Recommended Books I paid to not have ads. I do not have to swipe the screen after turning the unit on. I do, however, still have the book recommendations in Cover View, and there is no setting to turn this off. I resent this because I paid to not have ads. I resent having to swipe the page to see the rest of my books. Having the Book Recommendations take up half of the Cover View screen negates the usefulness of this new feature. I am using the List View instead. I am actually interested in seeing book recommendations, but not at the cost of the functionality of the Cover View. I don't need to see them every time I'm looking at my books. Amazon, how about moving the Recommended Books to the end of the Cover View list or being able to toggle it on and off? Home Button: Need Virtual Equivalent Clicking the top of the screen and then the Home icon every time I want to switch books doesn't sound that cumbersome, but it becomes tedious. It would be nice if I could swipe the screen or click a certain region (such as top-left) and go directly to the Home screen. Power Adapter: Standard Micro USB Connection I don't mind that the unit comes with a USB charger and not a wall charger. It's a standard micro-USB connection, same as my Android phone and Bluetooth handset. So, I'll just plug the Kindle in as needed to one of the many chargers I have sitting around my house. To me, the inclusion of USB charger is a bonus.
