UPDATE: I managed to kill this hub less than a month in :( My 'USB-C to dual-bay 2.5" enclosure', when not using its AC adapter, draws more power than is normally provided by a USB port (both C and A). When I plugged this into the back USB-C port of the hub, it seemed to have overloaded the entire hub. As a result: 1. the hub no longer works with its 65W power adapter 2. it power cycles when it's connected to the host 3. the power cycling happens too fast and too frequently, preventing me from going into Windows' Device Manager and hardware-disabling the malfunctioning ports With the exception of the front USB-C port, the back USB-C ports can output up to 7.5W. High-power devices cannot be plugged into the back USB ports. Original review below: I had an Anker 10-port USB3 hub for the past 12-13 years (!), and I've been having connection issues due to its age. Basically the hub would lose its connection for several seconds every time it happens. 3-4 of the hub's ports were busted. In short, I needed a new USB-C data hub that *doesn't* have anything else besides USB-A and USB-C ports. Why no display? I can simply swap one of the USB-C modules for a DisplayPort or HDMI module… on the Framework. What's connected to the hub: - mechanical keyboard - wired mouse - USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter - USB-C to dual-bay 2.5" enclosure - USB-C thumb drive or microSD card reader - laptop cooling pad The bad: - no Power Delivery support for its host connection - only 5Gbps support, not 10Gbps, let alone Thunderbolt 3/4 or 20Gbps via USB4 (1 star minus) - no video support on any USB-C downstream port - fairly high price vs. features The good: - 65W dedicated power supply for the hub itself, and is actually more compact than I expected - 3 USB-C and 4 USB-A ports, of which one C port can output up to 15W and one A port at 7.5W - host connection cable is *removable* and included - thin profile - no connection issues that seem to be fairly common with many USB-C hubs/docks powered via USB-PD

I bought these for my elderly father who has tone deafness and the habit to turn the sound up until everyone’s ears bleed. These felt like a good fix. I considered wireless speakers that sit behind him or attach to the wall but I thought that might just create an odd effect soundwise. These seemed perfect. The pros I’ve seen: pretty simple setup. The sound is controlled completely separately from the television and act in addition to the television so he can turn his sound up and leave the television at a reasonable level for us. The most amazing thing is that the way they angle, I can barely tell if these are on at all half the time, and sometimes find myself checking just to make sure, but they have made him MUCH happier about hearing what he’s watching! The cons: you must turn the tv to a basic sound setting instead of the surround sound or whatever, otherwise these only give static. While we figured it out rather quickly, and it only needed to be changed once, I bet we’ll forget the next time we replace the TV and it might lead to some confusion. As a result however, the TV sound which was wonderful, is now a little blah because of the setting change. I probably would have given 5 stars if not for that. Next, the speakers have a single button to change the sound which is just a “left side=volume down” “right side=volume up”, its rather simple, but my father is elderly and has motor control issues, so he struggles to find and feel the button and he still has a tendency to either hold it and turn it all the way up or all the way down, so I usually have to set it for him. He will often remove it from the back of the chair trying to figure it out and either disconnect the cords (which are plugged in thank God so nothing breaks), or can’t get them back on and he winds up putting them around his next like he thinks they are headphones. Unfortunately, the speakers are then pointed away from his head and not only do I worry he’ll hurt the speakers or choke himself, but they don’t help and he HATES asking for assistance, so this has been common. There is a mute button that is very close to the volume button and on the inside. Sometimes while playing around with them, he hits that by mistake. Over all, I’m very happy I got these. I don’t like the way I had to send a special message in regards to the color I wanted “or else it won’t be shipped”, as every other product I’ve bought has some kind of drop down button to choose that. I would like it better if there were perhaps a way of KNOWING it had been muted such as a light, because it’s sometimes difficult to know if he hit that or simply turned it down all the way. I also would like to see the volume button either larger or a different color and maybe both volume and mute placed on the outside of the speaker than the inside and the front respectively, as I think it would be less apt to be accidentally hit, or a napping head to press. I do like these however. They are a bit pricey, but overall they are a good solution to our specific problem, and not being an AV enthusiast, I was baffled at how best to resolve it.

I have been looking for a photo bag that includes room for a hydration system for a while and am happy to say that this is pretty close to what I was looking for. I will get the major criticisms out first. The biggest issue I have is that there is no ability to strap my travel tripod to the bag in a convenient way. The trekking pole loops aren't sturdy enough to support the weight (nor do I expect them to be) and the bottle sleeve is too tight to get more than one leg of my smallest travel tripod in. I have resorted to storing it inside the pack itself down the right side between the camera pouch and the outer bag. It can be a tight fit but it works. The second complaint is minor by comparison; the description says the bag will hold a 2 liter hydration bladder. I have a High Sierra 2L pouch and it doesn't actually fit with 2 liters of water in it. Even dumping some of the water the bladder has to be crammed into the hydration pocket and compressed vertically to fit. Those two criticisms aside, this is a great bag. It holds my entire walkabout micro 4/3 kit of 4 prime lenses and a zoom, camera body, 2 spare batteries, and a couple of filters. Even when carrying a larger zoom like the Panasonic 100-300 there is room for everything in it. Now, I normally carry an Olympus EM-5 II, so it is a very compact and space conscious kit. For those that carry something heftier like a Panasonic GH5, your lens space is going to be smaller. The non-camera storage is perfect for day hiking. I've taken it out for small 3 mile walks and 14 mile hikes in the mountains and the water was a godsend and there was plenty of room for snacks. I have even been caught out in the mountains when a thunderstorm rolled in with crazy rain. I can say the rain cover was well tested and kept everything dry, and I was doubly glad that the bag was big enough for my rain jacket. The storm killed most of my photography ambitions that day but was a wonderful field test of the pack and its ability to protect my gear.

Does everything it's advertised for very well. I personally used STP CAT6A with STP RJ45 end terminations to connect the units, as it was moving through crawlspace and other imperfect zones and wanted to avoid any crosstalk, since the data throughput of 4K needs to be ideal. My run was around 40 feet in total. The screw-on type power supply connector is real nice touch and I wish more AV manufacturers would do this as a lot of these devices get buried inside A/V cabinets or racks and it's real easy over time to accidentally pull the power lead out and cause problems. However these units get VERY HOT. Hot enough to almost think you're going to burn yourself. I'm seriously considering affixing a large heatsink to each unit's case. The bi-directional IR feature is a bit obscure, but it's as simple as one might think: You can pass a signal from A to B, and/or from B to A. I was hoping it might be a shared pool signal, i.e. I could do A->B, B->A, A->A, B->B, so I could use the IR signal locally as well as remotely. This is not the case, but it was never specifically advertised as doing so, so no penalty to the rating. I got around it using other equipment to split the signals. UPDATE 7/26/18: I ordered the aforementioned heatsinks (I used [[ASIN:B071K8MW4S SODIAL(R) 1 pcs Aluminum Radiator Heat Sink Heatsink 60mm x 60mm x 10mm Black]] and these fit PERFECT. Adhered them to the case with [[ASIN:B078JKRS8H Beevivo 25m x 20mmx0.25 Double Side Thermal Tape Apply for Heatsink LED Lights IC Chip Computer CPU GPU Modules]] ) and the heat soaked RIGHT up into the sink, the units are significantly cooler now. I would highly advise you either mount the unit to a thick metal (perforated?) sheet with the included brackets or use a heatsink setup like I did. Those heatsinks fit perfectly in the dead-center of the top of the case between the vent holes and the two printed gray lines. If you're mounting the unit on a wall, make sure to orient the heatsink so that air can pass through the fins vertically. Honestly, I have no idea why Monoprice didn't think to do this themselves, it probably extends the lifespan of these systems many times over!

I matched this JVC head unit with the Beat Sonic MVA-12L adaptor harness [[ASIN:B008H7H2DQ Beat-Sonic MVA-12L]] to replace the Mark Levinson unit in my wife's 2004 SC430. While the JVC unit is very nice and has good features for the money, we were very disappointed to find that after installation (2 days work in an un-airconditioned garage in July!) the screen is impossible to use in daylight conditions, even when the convertible top is up. This is due to severe glare reflected from the seats. At night or when driving in dark cloudy conditions, the screen is fine. I have ordered a screen visor to try to install to reduce the glare, but this will not do anything about the seat reflections. Also, though not directly the fault of JVC, I found there the double DIN JVC unit would not clear the vehicle trim by about 1/4 inch when the face plate opens to expose the DVD slot. So Double DIN is a standard measurement, but apparently JVC didn't take into consideration that the moving face plate would exceed those dimensions when in motion. This required me to modify the Lexus console trim components, because they all snap together when inserted in position with no room for slack. Essentially, I had to take the heated seats control module and cut the plastic to refit it against the console glove box closure and refashion a way to keep that module in place, since the plastic clips would no longer retain it. So, my advice is to use another style head unit in the Lexus SC430 to avoid all this hassle. And if your vehicle has white/high reflective surfaces, you had better check for screen glare before investing in expensive head units. This is likely to be true for any make/model where seats are close to the same dash level as the touch screen.

*Edit to A Once Short Novel. After purchasing an antenna, to verify Over The Air broadcast TV signals were available, we bought a 1 TB Recast device. The first 5 months or so, it worked as advertised. Even the Fire TV App. (required) even made connecting the Recast fairly easy. Despite the Recast not having any written instructions, aside from connecting it to the Antenna: Fire TV Stick; and household power, the set-up was easy. The Fire TV App. is REQUIRED for set-up of the Recast. The App. is also supposed to aid in controlling your Fire TV devices. The Alexa voice recognition, works well enough in setting-up future recordings of individual programs or series. The Fire TV App, couldn't seem to stay connected to my Fire TV Sticks. It simply lost connection, with no warning. It could be reconnected, but it often only reconnected for just a few moments, before again disconnecting. The issues we began having with the Recast started a few months back. At first small barely noticeable issues, such as showing the Bell Symbol, that is visible next to the Settings option on the main page, Going to the notice, showed that the Recast device has lost its connection. And initially, didn't seem to make any difference, as both Live TV viewing & our Recorded programs were still accessible & still being recorded. But eventually, when trying to view Live TV, we began having major issues. All, not just some, of the Over The Air broadcast channels, started having Pixel Issues; Buffering Lag: Freezing: & view/voice synchronization issues. These issues weren't with just the channels having weaker signals, but all channels. I first thought it may be a problem with the antenna, since we could still view our recorded DVR Recast programs. But, the antenna worked fine, when not connected to the Recast. Next, we tried performing a restart of the Recast, using our Fire TV Stick. (Settings:/Live TV:/Live TV Sources:/Fire TV Recast:/Restart). But, this only resulted in loosing all contact with the Recast, and an alert, triangle with a (!) In the center, showing just right of where it says Network. Here is where we received an alert notice, to use the Fire TV App, in order to try and re-establish contact with our Recast device. After several failed attempts to reconnect with the App, I reached out to Amazon for some service assistance. In my request I chose the, (be contacted by phone option). And to Amazons credit, I got a call within minutes. After explaining my problem in detail, the tech then walked me through some of the same things I had already tried, on TWO of our different Fire TV Stick devices. This included allowing the tech to remotely access our equipment. After several failed tries of reconnecting with two of our Fire TV Sticks, the tech had me confirm that we were using the same network on both the recast and the Fire TV Sticks. I was able to confirm this using an App. I had previously loaded, from our (ISP) Internet Service Provider (AT&T U-verse). And after confirming we were using the same Network on all of our equipment, the tech suggested that although our (ISP) Network was the same, there are both 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz band options, within the same Network. I later found out is basically like having TWO DIFFERENT NETWORKS, and that wasn't just possibly why the connection couldn't be made, it was the exact reason The Recast & Fire TV Stick couldn't stay connected. The selection of which band, 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz, to use, isn't an option, using the default settings on the combination Arris BGW210-700 Modem/Router, that AT&T U-verse provides. You can convince/get them to separate the two bands, and split the signal, if you are lucky enough to connect with someone on the phone that actually knows what they are doing. BUT, doing this can weaken the signal strength, along with other possible problems. *Note: The Recast Ad, HERE, where the Recast is sold, only states that Recast devices must be used on the same WiFi Network as your Fire devices, with no mention of WiFi Networks that provide 2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz band options being any problem. A well informed AT&T U-verse tech, that came out, informed me that even though the 2.4 GHz & 5.0 GHz bands are on the same Network, they essentially like have two separate networks. So, before buying one, make sure you have the ability to connect to the 2.4 GHz or 5.0 GHz bands, with ALL of your Amazon devices. Not doing so, will result in the above problems we experienced. Final thoughts: If you have a few broadcast programs that you want to record, or, not every TV you have is close to a window, so it can use it's own dedicated antenna, A Recast may be an option to consider. I'd first suggest buying a single antenna, flat and amplified, are available here for under $30.00 U.S., to see what broadcast channels are available. Or, see if any of the Apps. Available on Prime TV offer free delayed rebroadcasts, of your favorite network affiliated programs. Also, make sure your (ISP) Internet Service Provider, offers equipment with the ability to select which of the two bands 2.4 GHz or 5.0 GHz, you can connect with. AT&T U-verse uses a combination Modem/Router, that makes this more difficult to accomplish. It is possible, but much more difficult. Using a separate router, that allows you to designate, which device connects to which band, within your network, works much better. I discovered that someone at Amazon does look over these reviews, and sometimes even on the same day that they are made. One such individual, reached out to me and offered to provide a replacement Recast device. And one of their technical support people, even gave me a follow-up call the next day, to confirm my problem was solved.

We bought 2 of these for our small business, and they arrived quickly, very clean and looking like new. user setup with Windows 10 pro was straightforward, and performance was zippy like an i7-4590 should be. Our various software installed nicely, with no noticeable lags in performance for anything. These come with absolutely NO extra garbage installed...."free" antiviruses and other junk that usually just take up space and annoy you with solicitation to buy or upgrade. Of course Windows 10 does have its own annoyances with silly games they automatically put in, but they're easy to get rid of. These are probably 1/3 or less the cost of new units, and I consider them a good bargain (I generally build my own from components, but no way can I match the cost with comparable hardware and Windows 10 Pro). Now the "other" side...after all, nothing is perfect. If you have no technical knowledge and expect an out-of-the-box unit with everything you need and all set up for your personal needs, you may be better off sticking with new units and their long warranties and "tech" support. Both of these units needed the CMOS batteries replaced...when they were unplugged and rebooted, you'd get a time and date warning and default reset. Replaced them and all was fine. One of the units, after a day of installing and setting up software, suddenly would not boot, and it turned out the SSD had failed...very unusual, but no question the drive was corrupted. The rebuilder responded quickly and sent a replacement (however, they shipped it UPS ground cross-country which took a week, so in the meantime I just bought a replacement rather than wait). With a flash drive loaded with the latest Windows 10, it installed without a problem, and it has worked flawlessly since. One thing to note is that these have NO factory recovery partition like you'd normally get with an HP, Dell, etc., but in a way that's fine as long as you know how to install a fresh copy of Windows from a flash drive. Normally I would install drivers from HP's website after installing Windows, but the machine is working so well, with no issues whatsoever, that I think the Windows 10-installed drivers are fine. With these tower cases, there is room to install more drives. These HP's come with vertical laptop-like DVD drives, but you can install a DVD-rw or Blu-ray drive in the other slot. The front panel trim piece pops out to allow room for a full sized drive, but the trim panels are somewhat difficult to find (it doesn't look bad without the needed trim panel, but you can find them at online auction sites inexpensively). The graphics chip in this i7-4590 should easily handle up to a 4k display, so unless you're a gamer, an add-on video card is probably unnecessary. Overall, I would buy these again, as they're about 1/3 the price of a business machine would have been new. They should be good for many years of use, and I've had good luck with the other refurb HP's I've bought. Performance is smooth and speedy, and they are spotlessly clean like new.

As I'm writing this, I'm desperately trying to salvage files from a defective unit. After using this unit with Raid 0 configuration for 5 months with GUID partition table and HFS+ with journaling, I started to run into HFS+ journal corruption. Considering this a fluke and perhaps the fault of the OS, I corrected the issue using Apple's hfsutils to restart the partition's journal. Within a month of this incident the drive became ripe with IOerrors at the physical layer. Some days the drive would be stuck on the G-Technology Red Blink of Death with a light and repetitive "click" sound, and this could only be resolved by holding the drive to a specific angle until the red blink and click went away and the drives re-initialized. These units, while fast and effective at first, tire quickly. In the G-RAID Mini series, the drives do not power down when you shut your computer down (even with a full ACPI halt). If using the USB option, the drives will only spin down once the AC/DC transformer is disconnected. When connected via a powered IEEE 1394b connection, as long as your PC or Macintosh's power supply is powering peripherals, the drives are still working. When your data is being trusted to Hitachi "Deathstar" drives that can be on for days-on-end, it's no wonder this series encounters problems. Do not rely on this drive and definitely do not rely on G-Technology's warranty; it covers a storage device and not your data. G-Technology does not repair drives nor does it attempt any data restoration service in the case of failure. If you get the Red Blink of Death, they will simply send you a new drive if you're lucky enough to be within warranty.

WARNING: If you set this up and it only hears "CO" from your smoke detector, RETURN IT IMMEDIATELY! If you are going to need replacing the detectors to make this work, you might as well get one(s) with z-wave that don't need a listener to hook into Ring alarm. Full story below: If you buy this, and during the setup it detects your smoke alarm sound as "CO", and doesn't detect "smoke/fire", your detector is likely incompatible with this listener. I had mine set up for over a year, the listener was in state "actively listening", with no indication of a compatibility issues. When we had an actual fire started in the kitchen (grease fire on stove), the smoke alarm went off for over 15 minutes because the whole house filled with smoke. This listener detected NOTHING during the fire despite all the noise from my smoke alarm and the listener being no more than 2 inches from the alarm. After spending hours on the phone with Ring support, I'm told it's because my detector is incompatible with the listener. The only evidence of incompatibility is that the listener only detected "CO" alarm and not smoke/fire. Since I'm finding this out over a year from installation, I'm unable to return this product. I don't even know what detector to replace mine with that will actually work with this listener. As an added bonus, during troubleshooting I managed to trigger it while not in testing mode and ended up having a firetruck show up at the house days after the fire. Ring: HOW MANY HOMES / LIVES HAVE TO BE LOST BEFORE YOU CHANGE YOUR PRODUCT? Users should get a warning (preferably one that's very obvious and hard to ignore), if their detector is incompatible. Technical detail: My alarm emits a continuous rapid beeping (I'd even wager this is the most common type in homes). This listener is looking for T3 pattern for smoke (three long beeps followed by a pause, repeated), or T4 pattern (four short beeps, pause, repeated) for CO. I talked to two Ring support techs and neither one knew the detail on T3/T4 temporal patterns. The listener gets "confused" by the continuous beeping and reports T4/CO was heard during setup and won't (didn't) trigger during actual alarm event. This listener product should be updated to detect continuous beeping and either be able to alarm on it or report the incompatibility. Techs should have been trained on the T3/T4 pattern details, and know what to listen for on customer calls.

As an engineer, the first thing to do is open it up and take a look. What I found was a decently built product with large cells. A rather complex circuit board to control the charging. You can leave the charger and your device connected for a backup power configuration. The magic behind the device is that the DC power plug module outputs 12.6 volts which is just high enough to charge the batteries without providing excess voltage to your devices. The charged unit itself output 12.48 volts with no load. This product will not likely work well with any other power plug module.One drawback is that it is too easy for the switch to be accidentally pressed off. Since it extends beyond the case, any pressure, such as a bump against a surface will turn it off (or on). They should design in a ridge around the switch to help prevent turn-off (or have it recessed). The plastic case is good, but not waterproof in any way. What I found counter intuitive is that the red LED on the case never turns green. It makes the unit seem like it never gets fully charged. The LED on the power module does change color however. Instructions are typical ambiguous Chinese to English translations.

I upgraded from the 1st generation Fire Stick and the performance is like night and day. If you’re wondering if you should upgrade or not, here are a few main reasons why you should: 1. If you notice any lag on the home screen or in any apps 2. If you encounter network issues (slow speeds or weak/dropped signals) 3. If you experience overheating (can cause lag or shut off Fire Stick) 4. If you use the voice remote feature through the app (although you can purchase the voice remote separately) I experienced the first three issues above on a regular basis and the new Fire Stick has yet to show any of them (even after using Kodi or other intensive apps such as TiVo DVR streaming). I actually had the 1st generation Stick that came with the voice remote and rarely use it. The main thing I use it for is to search for an app to download since it is much faster than typing it in. Depending on what you use on your Stick, the voice remote can actually be pretty powerful. Upgrades: Faster processor - Has a quad-core porecessor now Faster WiFi - Uses the latest AC standard. This is really only helpful if you have an AC router and fast enough internet speeds to utilize the speed increase Bluetooth - Uses the 4.1 standard now instead of 3.0 Support for High Efficiency Video Codec (HEVC) (for higher resolution at lower bandwidth) Included in the box: - Fire Stick - Voice Control Remote - Wall Outlet and USB Cable - 2 Amazon Basics AAA Batteries (for remote) - HDMI Extender Overall I was very glad that I upgraded from the older generation. If you aren't experiencing issues with your first gen stick then there isn't any need to upgrade. However, if you want a Fire Stick that is faster then definitely upgrade. The new Stick is slightly bigger but not so much that it would cause any inconvenience. I love the Fire Stick and think it's much better than Chromecast or Apple TV. The newer processor also also for better game play if you use the Stick for that. Something to note: My first generation stick with voice remote came with a female to female HDMI adapter instead of an HDMI extender. I like the adapter much more than the extender because it lets me use my HDMI cable to connect the Fire Stick instead of having it plugged in directly to the TV. In my opinion, the HDMI extender doesn't provide enough length if you experience network issues. It's really only good for someone who had a crowded HDMI location on their TV and can't plug the stick in due to its size. The new Fire Stick doesn't come with the adapter so you will need to buy one separately if you want one.

I built this for a general use PC for my mother-in-law. As such, I am very happy with this unit (as is my mother-n-law, which is where it really counts). A caveat that is a Windows problem (other reviews indicate the same does not apply to various varieties of Linus), Windows 7 won't install to any USB drive (as the main drive that the "Windows" folder would reside on). I was then forced to buy an mSATA drive. I was able to install Windows 7 from a USB stick, so you don't need to buy an external USB DVD drive. The 3 USB ports is a bit limiting, I'd suggest getting a powered USB hub to supplement. I was able to use a "Mickey Mouse" wall-to-charger plug from a dead laptop charger for the included power brick, which does not come with the wall plug, only the unit-to-powerbrick section of the power cable. The unit delightfully mounts to the back of an old (5 years) VGA flat-screen monitor. Some Dell flat-screens use the VESA mount holes for the primary stand, so this won't mount to those (also some of these mounts are recessed which may not work with the mounting plate). It will mount to one that comes with a stand that mounts to the bottom, with VESA mount holes in the center of the back of of the monitor unused. Even my ultra-cheap off-brand 23-inch HDTV in the spare bedroom would allow this to mount to it as well (most HDTVs should have "bottom" stands that don't use the VESA mount holes, so using this as an HTPC should be sweet for keeping your cables minimalized). IMPORTANT: Make sure to download drivers to a USB drive ahead of time, Windows 7 wouldn't work out of the box without the Ethernet driver from Intel's site, so you will not likely be able to access Intel's site to download them directly to this unit. This will save you a headache.

There are already lots of reviews on Amazon about this and I concur that this is a great tripod. I use a Sony SLT-A55 + Tamron 18-270 mm lens. The camera+lens combination weighs less than 2.5 lbs and for this combo, this tripod is sheer overkill. I am 5' 10"; with all legs fully extended, and center column extended about 1/2 way, I can comfortably stand and view through the viewfinder. WIN! Allright, I'll dive straight into the CONS 1) The ball head cannot be removed...at least not without tools that I can see. I was thinking of getting a monopod for hikes, screwing the ball head (which by the way is incredibly sturdy) on the monopod...but looks, like that will not be possible. UPDATE: I was wrong! The ballhead can be unscrewed to reveal a larger screw than most ball heads mount on. Its very tight! You'll first need to lock the screws so the ball head does not rotate at all and give it a firm twist. This is a sturdy tripod and did not buckle under such a heavy twist. Impressive. But the point is that the ball head can be unscrewed afterall. Sorry about the misinformation. 2) Now, coming to the "case" of the case...its very nice...strap is very nice and the tripod fits perfectly...a little too perfectly. Its not easy to put the tripod back in and close the zipper. You have to fit the head in the right angle or else the zipper won't close. All this quality, they couldn't afford to leave a 1/4" clearance? 3) The locking plate mechanism. As others have said, its not the usual locking plate combo seen on many tripods. The plate mounted on the camera slides in easily and a pin is released which makes sure the camera does not fall off. However, in this position, the camera is not tightly mounted and to do that, you'll need to tighten the screw on the side. This combo prevents the camera from being "quickly" mounted and dismounted as in other systems. A slight inconvenience. HOwever, this combo is also super sturdy and will probably hold heavier combinations better than the regular locking mechanisms. 4) Some parts are not precise. For example, the retractable rubber feet. one of them is a couple of millimeters longer than the other two. So, in fully unscrewed position, the tripod is not completely level as clearly indicated by the bubble level. I'm not bothered much because my camera has a inbuilt level indicator. But others might be. You could always sand off one or more. That's about it. I am very pleased with the purchase. I had to leave my camera mounted and leave the room. I was very confident to do so. Thanks for reading.

I live in illinois, about 30 miles from the broadcast towers in St. Louis which are about 232 degrees southwest of my position. This antenna is able to pick up all local HD channels really well. I have tried other types of antenna, but at the given range in this area this is the only indoor antenna that will work. I was on the fringe between buying this, the amplified model or the HDTVi, the un-amplified model. I'm glad I got this one, however, because the little bit of signal boost provided by the amp makes all the difference in receiving channels 2-1 and 30-1 without drops. The log periodic design of this antenna is very sensitive to direction. You must point it directly to the area where your signals are broadcast from for it to pull them in. If your city has towers spread all over that are more than 18 degrees or so apart then this is not the antenna for you. The advertised range is 45 miles, but I'm sure that's really pushing it and is most likely based on a direct line of sight transmission. I would guess that the 30 miles I am getting is basically the upper limit in range for an indoor antenna like this one. Plus, it looks really cool. Update: After using this antenna for a week or so, I have been able to tune a broadcast that is 61.2 miles away (according to antennaweb) with about 60% signal strength. This is really amazing for an indoor antenna, and it definitely reaffirms my recommendation.

I was shopping within this price point so I can't be two disappointed about several issues. First, the sound is really fantastic, if you have really good speakers and I do. With a 15" sub-woofer it shakes the house. The the auto sound setup for the room is perfect. I set it up, let it configure and wow, very nice sound profile with a lot of depth. Basically, I'm very happy with the sound aspects of the receiver. There are a few drawback I think are significant. First, the on screen display for the receiver will not output through the HDMI cable to your HD TV. You have to make a separate S-Video or component connection to see them. This is kind of annoying and confusing as it's only in the fine print in the manual. There's no excuse for Pioneer to not support the on screen functions via the HDMI connection to the TV. What where they thinking? The second issue is that the receiver is fairly complex so if reading the manual is not your game to figure this thing out, then you'll be totally lost. For example, my son pressed the DVD button to switch from the DVR to the DVD, but accident hit another button. The sound went off and it took me 30 minutes to figure out how to get the sound back. I am pretty good with technical hardware since that's what I do for a living. So get it setup and don't touch the controls, except for maybe switching sound modes. The Big drawback is that despite the fact that multiple sites and forums name this receiver as a unit that support digital audio through the HDMI ports, it doesn't support it. If you want to hear digital audio from your digital source, you must make a second digital connection via a optical or coax cable to hear your 7.1 surround sound. The HDMI is pass-through only. Interestingly enough, your HD TV can play audio through the HDMI cable, but the receiver will not. If you can get past these three issues, you'll enjoy the powerful sound coming out of this receiver. I hope this helps everyone. Good Luck.

When I came to enter my review, I saw reviews from 2018 complaining about the software. I guess things have changed . I just transferred 8.2 GB from a Surface Pro 3 to a Surface Pro 7 in 7 minutes. The cable has an activation code for the software, which I downloaded from Barvura to each computer. The code activated the software (NOT just a 30-day free trial) on each machine and both machines recognized the cable. The software asks what kind of task you want to complete (moving data from one computer to another and syncing data between two computers are two tasks I remember seeing). When I selected transfer data, it immediately gave me a window asking if that computer was old or new computer. Then it presented a window showing the folders it would transfer. I glanced at the list and then started the transfer. Seven minutes later it was done. I can go back and try again, this time selecting any folders the program didn't automatically choose, but I doubt there will be much to do there. The only possible issue is the program stops when it finds a conflict (and it WILL, see below) and awaits your decision. If you walk away, the transfer sits awaiting your return. No big deal, unless you are moving 1TB of data and want to be productive somewhere else in the meantime. The conflict it found was it's own install program on the two Surfaces, noting a conflict between slightly different install times. When I clicked ignore, it raced on ahead. No hesitation to recommend this product. The easiest data transfer I've ever done between two computers. BY FAR.

I will first start off by saying, this is my first powered gimbal experience. I am a professional still photographer getting more into the world of motion photography (Cinema). I have the pro SLR's that shoot video, but for intuitiveness I purchased a GoPro Hero 7 Black. Really easy to use, great quality camera for $350. I know the GPH Blk 7 has HyperSmooth - which is great! But to keep my shots level with the horizon, I was looking for something that would help with that aspect. Enter the Hohem iSteady Pro 2 action camera stabilizer. Out of the box it is rather intuitive. There were actual instructions (quick start guide) in the package. An aside, the packaging was rather impressive for a $100 Amazon purchase. Very nice case and all of the equipment needed to go. The instructions walk you through step by step how to get going. First step is charging the battery - which you should give it a few hours to complete. Mine came with 4 bars of power on it, but it still took a couple hours to peak it out. Once I had it charged, I was off to the races! Learning the 4 modes for a gimbal beginner is interesting - but it is nice that this gimbal is organized by these 4 separate modes of operation. I found use for the first 3, but the fourth is more for artistic movements... Maybe? The panning of the gimbal with the thumb operated joystick is rather fluid. With the app, you can adjust how fluid it pans, and really customize the heck out of this item. I really like the timelapse movement feature in the app. This allows you to have the gimbal automatically pan a shot over a specified timeframe. Cannot wait to play with that feature more. Calibrating it is pretty easy with the app. It runs you through gymnastics of calibrating it on a table. Quick tip - you can fine tune this in the app - i.e. roll, pitch, or yaw. The app is recommended highly because it allows you to do so much. This is a great gimbal for someone wanting to create video with an action camera on a low budget. I imagine you can use this with one of the $50 action cameras as well as a $400 GoPro model. As a matter of fact, it might even be the way to go with a lower cost action camera that does not have HyperSmooth. Basically you are building a DJI OSMO equal for around $150. Another positive to mention is the ability to charge your camera through the gimbal. It does add weight to the rig, so you may have to make some small in-app tweaks to roll and tilt, but otherwise it is great! The negatives... Every product has them... The first negative is how this gimbal is positioned realtive to my on-button of my GoPro 7. The way the camera sits on the Gimbal puts the power button against one of the pivot points. That makes powering my GoPro more difficult. I have to use my GoPro app or I have to power down the Gimbal, then remove it from the mount to power down. That is a great segway into the next negative... The mount... It is somewhat awkward to push your camera in and out of a friction mounting system. It does hold onto the camera really well - but it is just so awkward mounting and dismounting my camera. I wish there was a 'quick release' or something available for attaching various camera models - even as an accessory. The only other thing I have to mention is that the gimbal has the ability to control the stop and start of certain cameras. it is a bluetooth item and I was hoping it would connect to my GoPro to act as a stop/start remote - but I cannot figure out how this would work. I will do some googling to see if someone has figured this out yet through the bluetooth of the camera and the gimbal. Not a deal killer, but it would be a nice add-on is WiFi to setup as a WiFi remote for the GoPro. All in all, this is a pretty nice accessory for my GoPro for a very approachable price point. I hope to get some use out of this item moving forward and maybe upgrade to a Gimbal for my pro DSLR cameras once I get the hang of this action gimbal! I would definitely recommend this - especially to those just starting out!

[[VIDEOID:a80617b2cc6163bf4bf9fbf1b3dafc59]] As you can see it works! First the setup was easy, 10 min from box to working. Sorry I can't say more about the battery life, but I don't use it except to get videos like this. The mounting is also as easy as they claim. It truly is purely magnetic, WITHOUT needing a steel mount behind it to mount. They do provide a separate mounting bracket though with its own steel backing to mount it on a nonmagnetic surface. This is not why I bought this device though, there are better ones if you want to spend the time drilling holes to mount an outdoor cam. But for the convenience of this, it can't be matched. See the picture of how I have it now. It's not screwed or glued in any way to that (steel) lawn chair. Just put the mounting base (which is a powerful magnet) near anything steel or iron and pop! Right in place and quite secure. You'll actually want to be careful putting it in place it's such a strong magnet you might pinch a finger as it binds to a steel structure. It's been mounted like this for over a week now to get the closer shots that I wanted as in the video. In that time, there's been below freezing temperatures at night, and wind gusts over 20 MPH, and a few hard rainstorms (yes, it's totally weatherproof too!). So that's real too. The little red light on it lights up when it's recording (it picked me up getting close to take that picture). That's how you know it's on. To be clear, it does NOT record all the time, in a loop in other words. It's motion based. I guess there may be a way to set it up as some kind of streaming cam, but I haven't looked into that. It rotates very easily in the base, but never loses grip so you can point it at virtually any angle, and it will still be secure. By default, the night vision comes on automatically, and full color automatically, depending on the light levels, but I think you can change it (in the app) so that the night vision is always on, or always off. I'm not sure though, as I checked now and it's not clear what the different modes there do. Anyway, it's good enough for me. A few points of clarity for those wondering some other things I was wondering: YES, it has 16 GB of storage space ON the DEVICE. For me it wasn't clear from the advertisement if the storage was somehow cloud based (I didn't understand how they were using the words "local" and "hub", they weren't used correctly in my opinion). You can download them from the device onto your phone via the app (and a wireless connection between the two obviously). Then you can upload it from your phone to a cloud service of your choice and from there download onto any device with access to the same cloud service. Easy peasy. The charge port is also a USB-C connection, so I imagine it would be possible to connect a USB-C cord to the device directly and download them directly to a computer, but I don't know for certain as I haven't tried that. It's easy enough to get the videos as I wrote. You don't have to download them to your phone to view the videos you can stream them from the device to select the ones you want. DEFINTELY recommend. I gave 4 stars for the picture quality because it's not true "2K" quality in my opinion but it's pretty high definition I'd say. You can judge for yourself from the video.

After dropping my car keys at the marina, I located the keys using my GoPro camera. BUT I wanted a real-time view to make the recovery. I also have an interest in underwater photography and thought this would be a great excuse to purchase an underwater drone. The GOOD Things: • The video is good for a 1K resolution (focus range is limited). • The 50 ft tether w/buoy meets my needs. • The small size makes for easy transit for most any situation. The BAD things: • This particular Chasing Dory had marginal WiFi connections from the first use in water. The buoy was less than 3 feet from me. • Today, the Dory stopped communicating via WiFi. The WiFi connection is what caused me to decide to return the Dory. DESIGN COMMENTS: • The tethering with a buoy is good for typical consumer uses. • A physical controller would be better than the virtual one used in the Chasing App. • I lost several short recordings when the WiFi disconnected. I was able to recover some, but not most. When WiFi is lost, the recording stops but the app record button appears "active". Having a removable SD Card would be better. • The WiFi password is "12345678" AND there is no way to change it. • The virtual controls are supposed to be programable. There are no instructions how to change other than from "Japanese" to "USA". Strange way to describe it since Chasing is a Chinese company. By trial and error in clear water, I could see which virtual control did what. • The charger power supply cable has no locking ring. Since it is the same type plug as the tether, it should be easy to include one. Without the locking ring, the charger connection to the Dory can easily work free. OPERATIONAL COMMENTS: • In clear water, the propellers cause little disturbance unless the Dory is "on the bottom". • In turbid water the propellers stir up lots of loose sediment. This is not a complaint, rather a situational constraint. I overcame it by attaching an adhesive GoPro base to the top of the Dory. Adapting a 12 ft painters extension pole to the GoPro base, I was able to keep the Dory propellers OFF but record with the camera and light ON. Sadly, this is where the Chasing Dory's WiFi totally stopped. The battery was at 100% this morning. It was used for about 15 minutes this afternoon. I do believe that this particular Dory has some electrical faults and potential sealing issues. Hence, I am returning this Dory. I will be searching for a more robust solution for my underwater photography.

Not one, not two, not three, but FOUR SFP+ cages, in a switch that's Layer 2 managed with a separate management port and 8 gigabit ports for under $200? This replaced my Ubiquiti US-XG-6PoE 6-port (4x ethernet, 2x SFP+) switch which cost 3x as much. While this QNAP is the only network gear in my house or rack that's not Ubiquiti, so it's a separately managed device, the price was VERY compelling for the amount of SFP+ ports it has. I have my Mac Mini with 10Gbit ethernet wired up to a 10GTek RJ45 transceiver in one of the ports, my Synology DS1821+ with Intel X520-DA2 10Gbit NIC I got off eBay connected to the second port with a SFP+ DAC cable, and my FreeNAS server with X520-DA2 connected via fiber (although honestly wish I used DAC since it's way more forgiving in a home lab setup that I'm constantly moving stuff around in - but DAC cables aren't expensive so I can always get one when I inevitably break my fiber - again). Setup was a breeze and in iperf3 I get a sustained ~8gbit between machines. The actual speeds I see are much less if the data's not on the fast cache drive(s), as I'm limited by the speed of spinny hard disks, but I can run multiple transfers over the 10Gbit links without worry about saturating the line at all. The power adapter is an interesting design, but it works really well and lets me rotate it (since it's a barrel plug connector in the end) out of the way so I have options on where/how to place the switch. The addition of the 8 gigabit ethernet ports is also huge, giving me more expansion capability in my home lab that I don't need to buy yet more big expensive switches for. I considered getting the model with some combo RJ45/SFP+ ports but honestly that's pointless when I can just buy a RJ45 SFP+ transceiver for 30-40 bucks if I need that connectivity, allowing me to connect mostly everything via DAC or Fiber due to how versatile SFP+ is. I will say though, the RJ45 transceiver does get fairly hot compared to fiber as it uses a TON more energy to transmit over copper, but it's nothing I'm concerned about. I'm thoroughly surprised at how much function you get in this device which costs under $200. It might not be part of the Unifi ecosystem, but that's ok since it's still web manageable. Incredible value for the money so far. 2021-07-03 Update: I take it back, I take it all back. The firmware is buggy, no matter what configuration I have the switch can't connect to the internet to check NTP or firmware updates. I manually updated to the latest firmware and the switch's management interface shows "QSW-error" and still can't connect to the internet. If I plug my main computer in to either the gigabit or 10g port (with an RJ45 transceiver), it can establish a connection to other devices and servers on my network but after the first few packets the connection just...hangs. I tried with both jumbo frames and normal 1500 MTU. And this is with bone stock switch configuration. Plug the computer into any other switch and it works fine (a 100% Unifi network). It should've been indicative of things to come when I went into the switch config and looked at the ports page, and there was a 'legend' for ports that were active, 10g, link up/down, etc, but none of the ports had any of the indicators from the legend on it. The entire management interface feels half-finished in some areas. I ended up returning this as even up until a month or so ago there are forum posts with my same experience and "Hopefully the next firmware fixes it". At first I was very happy to have a unit to listen to music while doing my workout/ rehab in the pool. I thought that the negative reviews were from people who did not use the correctly--until the problems started w/ me. The same problems that you read elsewhere, are endemic to the unit's design and implementation--probably more the implementation. That is the quality of the unit is more worth $20, not $40. The ear buds constantly come off in the ear, just what one desires while in the middle of a workout. Also, there is no way to easily pull the bud from your ear. The wires connecting the ear buds to the headband are VERY thin, with no reinforcement at the connecting points, so failure is imminent at some point due to this low quality of design! At the $20 price point you might expect this lack of quality, but at $40, this is not acceptable. The exec(s) who made this decision never wore the unit to test or are just greedy jerks intent on ripping off the consumer (something new, right?!) Now on the MP3 unit itself. Early on I thought that the problems I was having were due to the earbuds not fitting correctly and intermittently cutting out--one side, then the other, or the level of sound would decrease out of the blue. Come to find that the cause is a cheaply made housing (female contact) for the Mp3 player. The hole itself which the USB male end fits into, does not securely hole the metal contacts in place, even w/ the tension created by the opposite end clicking into the headband, as a matter of fact, I have found that the unit works better without the MP3 being clicked in to the headband--again failure of design quality implementation. So it is a matter of time before the unit falls out of the headband because it does not function correctly--a situation worth $20, not $40. Next item, battery life. I think that the batteries must be the old (cheap) NiCad batteries, because they certainly seem to have a memory whose time diminishes. The batteries, even new did not match the time quoted in the item specs. The time which the battery works decreases over time, so again, the battery is destined to become useless--do I have to say it again? $20 product not $40! So, why were none of these problems found at the product testing stage and corrected? Either they didn't give a crap, or production is flawed and inconsistent, and they didn't give a crap. As these are designed for sports activity--working out--sweating/swimming--there is no more an aggravating problem than to have to disrupt the rhythm of the workout to have to screw around with the MP3 player. I was going to give this MP# 2 stars because the sound is decent, especially in the water, which brings out the low end--that is when it is working correctly. Also, the sound would block other noises in the pool, such as screaming children. This is a positive point for the unit, for over the several hours of working out, having good sound help to focus on the workout, and not let external elements be a distraction. Some people have commented about the inability of the unit to organize the songs (never put books on, would not be able to concentrate on info). One reason I bought this unit was the versatility of the formats that the MP3 would play--that is a positive--when it works correctly. I actually enjoyed the eclectic aspect of the replay being alphabetical. So, all the music I loaded was played back to me as a good radio station would play a wide array of songs--remember when FM was not crap! So I enjoyed that aspect as a bass player. I could repeat a song if so desired, but it really took some getting used to the controls. I thought that they could be a bit more user friendly. While trying to repeat a song or adjust sound level, many times I hit the on/off button, because they are so close, that wasn't the end of the world though, compared to the other inconsistencies of the unit. So, why 1 star, not two or more? As I stated above, for the $40 price point, the quality should plain and simply be better. I was just wearing them, and got PO'd because the sound kept cutting in and out while walking/hiking (because pools are still closed due to Covid19) then the battery just quit, couldn't even get through 2 sessions. As I stated earlier, this is more the norm, rather that the exception of the MP3's performance--hence 1 star. So, its your money, you make the decision--this was my experience with the Tayogo 8GB unit. Would I buy it again-- What do you think?
