I love the unit and what it does. I use it, with a VGA flat screen, to create a large remote display for a digital still camera used for taking close up shots. I don't care about the image color rendition or quality as much as I care about being able to easily see the composition of the shot. Rather than repeat the other pros and cons comments, which I agree with, I'll tell you why I dinged it one star; the instructions. Okay, I'm one of those geeks who actually *reads* instructions. The instructions included with this unit are written in English translated by an obvious "B Team" Chinese translator. The opening line: "Use Display Device instead of monitor, consumedly save the cost of monitoring." It doesn't get much better. If you are technically saavvy you can pretty much stumble through the functions of the six push-buttons located on the back side of the converter ...this seller doesn't show those buttons but they're there ...to properly configure the converter based on the type of video input you feed it; to match the resolution of your monitor; to tweak the color (brightness, chroma, color, hue) and to use the Picture in Picture function. I was able to set up the converter because I was able to get the gist of the pigeon-English instructions and the technical aspects it was attempting to address. If you are not a "techie" then you're potentially gonna have some issues. I suspect those who haven't been able to get the converter to work more than likely have selected (or have failed to select) a resolution supported by their monitor. The goal in selecting a monitor resolution is to use one that's either an exact match (aka "native resolution") or is as close as possible (and supportable by your monitor). If you choose or fail to select a supportable monitor resolution you won't get an image and you may get a message on your monitor: "resolution not supported" ...or something like it. The button cryptically labelled "P.P." scrolls through the available resolutions this converter will generate. There are two buttons on this converter critical to getting an image; they are labelled "AV/SV/VGA" and "P.P." Connect your monitor and connect the source video signal then power up everything. "AV/SV/VGA" selects which of the video signals is input to the converter. "AV" is really the composite video input (the yellow RCA jack); SV is S-Video and VGA is, well, VGA. Each push of any of the buttons on the converter scrolls through that button's menu of selections. Make sure you select the appropriate input ...it should appear on the monitor screen (in the upper right corner) as you push the "AV/SV/VGA" button. Use the "P.P." button to select a screen resolution. If you know the maximum resolution of your monitor find the match or the closest supportable resolution. Again, as you scroll through the menu the resolutions will display on the monitor in the upper right corner OR you'll get a message saying the resolution isn't supported. Paying attention to these two function buttons will go a long way in the success of getting this thing to work for you. Because trying to wade through the "painful" pigeon-English is anything but fun ...or all that positively informative.

This review is going to be a bit lengthy lol. First of all be prepared to receive absolutely NO instructions with this ring light whatsoever. I'm a wig maker so I purchased the ring light to take better pictures of my mannequins wearing my wigs. I've attached 4 pics with this review, 2 pics taken with natural sunlight, and 2 taken with this ring light so you can decide for yourself which looks best. For me there wasn't a ton of difference. Natural sunlight looks just as beautiful as the ring light to be honest. The ring light did create more definition in the HAIR itself, but because of the ring light's brightness I lost definition in the mannequin. This kind of evened things out for me in terms of deciding which lighting, natural or ring light, is best for MY particular needs. I did go ahead and give this ring light 5 stars. Why? Certainly not because of the great instruction manual that came with it (scathing sarcasm). Because of the PRICE. Name brand ring lights of this size are literally hundreds of dollars, and I got this one for just a little over $120 on sale. This price, along with the fact that it was well packaged, with all of the necessary pieces/parts and performed well once I fired it up and started taking pics with it earns it 5 stars. But was it this incredible, MAGICAL halo of light that transformed my pics into something out of this world?? Nope. Not at all. For my specific purposes this light is only slightly better than natural sunlight. As you'll see in my pics. In all fairness though, I have to mention that I haven't taken any VIDEO using this ring light, which is typically what these lights are used for. Folks who make videos LOVE and swear by these things, so this may be absolutely fantastic for creating beautiful videos. But again for my purposes of photographing my mannequins/wigs, the difference in using the ring light versus not didn't blow me away. I do eventually plan to make videos using this light so I will come back and edit this feedback at some point once I see how it works for that application. In the final analysis, because of the awesome price of this ring light for what you get, I can definitely recommend it. But had this ring light been $200-$300 dollars or anywhere NEAR, it'd be going back.

I bought this weather radio to replace my older WR-100 model. I thought the extra features would come in handy, including the radio. Tonight we had very severe weather in our area and I came to be very disappointed with how this model works. First, you cannot just push the large weather button to stop the alarm and hear the message (like you can on the WR-100). Instead you have to press the small alarm on/off button and then the weather button. The loss of the few seconds means you miss the type of alert and basically start getting the counties impacted. You then have to wait for the message to repeat, wasting precious time if it is a tornado warning (which we found out was being issued). To add insult to injury, when you press the weather button the backlit display goes off so you cannot see the type of alert being issued (on the WR-100 the display remained on for awhile as the weather radio was playing--quite a bit longer than this unit does). The only other option is to have the backlit display on all of the time. The extra information this radio can display cannot be viewed in a dark situation unless you turn the unit on, and then only for a few seconds. The display can only be viewed clearly from about a 30 degree angle--if you view it from slightly above the unit the display begins to fade out and becomes unreadable. Again, precious time is lost trying to get the info you need quickly from the radio. We did appreciate the AM/FM option when our cable TV went out--we could hear the local news that way in addition to the weather radio itself. All in all I found this unit promising but not user friendly in the midst of severe weather. I am a NWS trained weather spotter and was looking forward to the extra features on this radio. However, given our experience with this model during severe weather I would not recommend this radio because of the issues noted above. Instead I would recommend the WR-100 model from the same company, which is easier and quicker to use (and less expensive).

Low levels of ambient noise trigger recording and cause hour-long audio files of nothing. No way to adjust this. It's not even apparent where the microphone is. So I will express opinions on legality. Some states are "two party" states and others are "one party," meaning only one person needs to consent to recording. In no case is it legal to record conversations without consent to which you, the recorder, are not a party. There are two consequences to recording illegally. One is that the recording might not be admissible in court. (It would certainly be listened to by police if it involved criminal activity.) The other is that anyone whose privacy was infringed can sue you for invasion of privacy. It is a rare case where damages would be awarded and no lawyer will take the case for that reason, so lawsuits are rare. Most private investigators are willing to risk a lawsuit to get the information. And most people whose privacy is infringed have done something bad. Google "Anthony Pellicano" to read about a PI who crossed the line. However, recording a public conversation is different than wiretapping, because no one expects their telephone calls to be intercepted. I am not a lawyer in your state and this is not legal advice. Be aware that you can be sued for violating the laws of whatever state you live in. This warning is contained in the instruction manual, as it should be. Consider removing the label that says "voice recorder," because you can't tell what this is by looking at it. And set it to not flash its lights while recording.

First let us establish what this device is not: It is NOT by any stretch of anyone's definition a surge suppressor. There is also no GF (ground fault) detection. Any device that requires a safety ground (i.e. a 110V AC lamp with a metal body) should NOT be connected to this strip. It is a power strip with a switch and four USB ports. That switch may be a resettable circuit breaker (impossible to determine from an external examination). That is ALL it is.There is an LED to indicate when power is switched on. There is also a capacitor and I believe two resistors used to power that LED. The safety grounds of the three 110V outlets are connected each other and nothing else. This by itself is a dangerous design decision. If one device with a safety ground and conducting chassy shorts out then the conducting chassy of any other device connected to this power strip will also be electrified. While some people extoll the advantages of the non-polarized plug they should be aware that only totally insulated/isolated circuits should be connected to this power strip. FYI: that includes most desktop/tower computers. Devices that utilize power bricks or wall warts should be safe. The reason I purchased this strip is that it works for my intended use which is to provided power for lights and display for a photographic copy stand. The lights and camera are USB powered. The Display uses a 12 Volt wall wart. I also know and have marked the side of the plug that should be oriented to the 'hot' side of the receptacle.

It fits the MacBook Pro M1 Max but is not 100% flash—there is about a 1mm extrusion. This doesn't bother me as I won't snag on the edge. However, you can feel the edge of the adaptor if you run your fingers along the edge of the laptop. The build quality is good—plastic for the most part with an aluminum finish on the outside. Removal of the SD card is easy using your nails, and the same can be said for the adaptor itself... although it is a little tighter. This is a USHII-rated adaptor so the advertised max speed is 312MB/s. The card reader in my M1 Max is rated the same. I have yet to use a card that meets the max-rated speed. The read/write speeds are way below advertised speeds. I use this with a SanDisk Ultra 400GB microSD XC 1 card. This class 10 card is supposed to run at 120MB/S max, but never does. In its provided SD adaptor—37MB/s Write, 81 MB/s Read. In the BaseQI adaptor—35 MB/s Write, 89 MB/s Read. The BaseQI is slightly slower but negligible. I won't really know if the BaseQI lives up to its speed classification until I find a microSD card that meets the same rating. Essentially, this is a functional solution to adding and keeping a microSD card in your MBP, especially if you move your laptop around much. It keeps the card safe and it won't catch or snag as you move about. However, if you need high speeds for your microSD card, keep looking elsewhere. Jet Drive is an option but the price is much higher, and you don't have the option to change SD cards as needed. I use this for storage of my music files and it works okay. I will keep using this until another option becomes available (other than Jet Drive). I don't regret this purchase as this is my only option and it works, but consider your need for speed before buying.

I admit I've had this hub for only a few hours, but I'll be back to update / correct if anything "funny" turns up. It "just works" right out of the box, which is a LOT more than I can say for some (ahem) other vendors' products. The combination of on-board USB 3.0 and 2.0 is brilliant. This is actually called the MondoHub, made by Manhattan Products (per the product insert in the box). My system: *** - MacBook Air (2012 model) w/max memory, two USB 3.0 ports and one Thunderbolt port - 10 USB 2.0 devices connected to this hub: four kinds of printers, USB audio, external keyboard with mouse plugged into the keyboard, DVD-RW drive, Epson scanner, 1 Jawbone bluetooth headset in its charging connector, and an occasionally connected iPhone - 3 USB 3.0 devices (2 external hard drives, 1 USB 128gb thumb drive) *** I have tested all of these devices attached together to the MondoHub and they are all working perfectly. In particular, the external drives (2 TB each) are doing the critical backups (both Time Machine and other) on the system, and are "talking" to one another and the laptop very reliably. (You can count, so you can tell I have a lot of USB ports still available.) Is it enough to have four USB 3.0 ports? In my case, absolutely. Think about it: what do you need the higher speeds of USB 3.0 for? For data drives, of course. You don't need it for printers, keyboards, audio, and other such basic devices. So why pay for all-3.0 when you don't need it? Plus, by far the vast majority of device types are still USB 2.0 anyway: it's everywhere, universally supported, and very stable. For many years the odds are that most brand-new devices you buy will still be USB 2.0. Now you've got one hub to rule them all. (Sorry, couldn't help myself.) I'm enthusiastic partly because, for many years, I've had to gang together several 2.0 hubs, but with wildly varying results. When I was running Windows, it was pretty ridiculous -- devices dropping off and coming back on for no apparent reason, taking forever to connect, etc. After I switched to a Mac a couple of years ago, things got instantly better. But things were still messy, and I still didn't have USB 3.0. I just did my own personal benchmark, and can affirm that I am definitely getting the same speeds from the MondoHub's USB 3.0 ports as if the same drives were connected directly to my on-board ports on the MacBook Air: 6 mins. 33 seconds to transfer a 9.86 gb file (an iPhoto library) from the MacBook to the external drive. And this was even while the system was doing a large Time Machine backup to the 128gb thumb drive also attached to the MondoHub. I haven't decided if the on/off buttons for each port are a big help or not. (I imagine they would be if, for some reason, you wanted to reboot a USB connection.) And the USB cable from the hub is hard-wired, so you can't just jack in your own (longer) cable. (Now that I think about it, this is a big plus because it means that The Worst cannot happen: the main cable to your hub accidentally slipping out, and trashing all the live connections to all your external drives all at the same time. THAT thought makes me shudder.) OK, so the built-in cable is fine for my needs: about 3 feet long. So far, all I really need to know: it works. (And I was highly skeptical it would.) The only thing that at first concerned me was, on first boot-up after connecting it, my MacBook took a couple of minutes to finally boot. This has NOT happened on subsequent boots, which are very fast, presumably because the first boot involved drivers being configured for the first time. CONCLUSION: THIS IS INDEED THE HUB YOU'VE BEEN LOOKING FOR. I sure as heck have -- for years. It's great to get an item exactly "as described". Thanks to Manhattan Products for FINALLY solving a longstanding personal computing problem that no one else has noticed yet. I will update as new information arises. ________________ UPDATE - OCT. 27, 2012: Seems to work great under Windows as well. I boot my MacBook Air to Windows occasionally to work with my one essential work application that is Windows-only. I realized I hadn't tested that. As usual with booting to Windows, I found it best to first unplug the hub from the laptop, then do the boot-up. (As with all other hubs I have used in this scenario, if I boot with any hub plugged in, Windows takes FOREVER to boot up. Plugging in after the boot clears that up.) But, once booted and plugged in, all devices I tested work fine: trusty black-and-white laser printer, external sound card, keyboard and mouse combination. But, most importantly, ALL of my USB 3.0 external drives were there (as well as one USB 2.0 drive that I keep formatted for NTFS). I certainly don't use all of my USB 2.0 devices under Windows (as I only occasionally need Windows), but the tested ones work great. So, I continue to say about this hub: Go for it! ________________ UPDATE - MAY 28, 2013: Not much new to report except that all is still well and working as described above. As the manufacturer notes clearly in the product documentation, this hub (like all others I've seen) does not output sufficient voltage to charge an iPad. With an iPad, you are always best off using a dedicated iPad charger, or your on-board USB port. Still a great hub and very glad I found it. ________________ UPDATE - Sept. 11, 2013 - USE THE GREAT MAGNET MOUNTS This hub comes with magnets embedded in the feet on the bottom. Update 8/7/22 - I am looking to purchase a new case for my iPad Air, this one has had it. I had bought this case because of the features and the very pretty designs that were available but about 3 months after I got it, the faux leather started peeling. I put up with it for a while, and then finally needed to use clear packing tape to reinforce the spine where it was too bad to ignore. It’s worked well for what I needed for that past 21 months - most importantly it has protected my iPad and my Apple Pencil (which fits into its own slot and never gets lost). Yesterday I noticed that there was a crack in the case where it is cut out around the camera, so it is no longer protecting the way it needs to. I have put up with the ugliness of the rips and tears all this time because I did not want to spend more money just because of aesthetics, but now it’s time for a new one. I have been a loyal fan of Fintie for 7 years, but it’s time to try something new. I’m going to trade in their pretty designs for a case that will hopefully protect just as well, but won’t peel apart soon after buying. Original Review (5 Stars) - I ordered the Shades of Blue case for my new iPad Air 4 10.9"/2020 (that is the Only iPad that this case will fit), as I already had the Fintie Z-Blossoms case on my old iPad that I still use from time to time. They are both beautiful patterns. I wouldn’t even take my new iPad out of the box until the case arrived, as I felt that it is too delicate when unprotected. At first, I was a bit disappointed that the new case design didn’t fold into a slot on the back to put into a standing position like the last incarnation, but the new design works quite well with 3 different standing options plus the ability to lay completely flat - it just takes up a bit more table space. I believe that it is probably more sturdy this way, and that the material will not give out at the bending point, like the last design eventually did after about 3 &1/2 years. I love how the Apple Pencil snaps securely into its own protective slot, and can't pop out accidentally. This case is so thoughtfully designed...all the cut outs are perfectly lined up, and the snap-in hard-back is very convenient. I likely will not use the elastic closure except when traveling, as the last design didn’t even have one and it worked well without it - also, I've had them stretch out from continual usage (on a different company's product) in the past.

I bought this as a precaution for my home office area where I have my home networking devices and laptop set up. Surge protectors are tricky to review because you never really know if it really works until you have a power surge BUT I can provide you a few things to keep in mind: PROS- 1. Protection: rated at about 1500 Joules. For those of you who aren't particularly computer saavy (I admit I had to do some research on this) the higher it is rated, the more it can take before it fails to protect. For 15 bucks, 1500 joules of protection is a steal. Will it protect your belongings from a lightning strike on your ungrounded home? Probably not. Will it protect and prolong your devices from spikes and surges? Absolutely. 2. Features & Functions: 8ft chord makes it adaptable and easy to locate an outlet for it. Ground indicator light makes me feel safe and secure ( I live in an older home while going to school and wiring is suspect). Protection light and auditory warning system nice touches to tell you if the unit needs replacing. Color coded outlets and included tags make it easy to identify wires. Coaxial a nice feature usually reserved for more expensive protectors and I haven't noticed any Internet speed decreases from using it. 3. Price: Mentioned before, but if you can get this unit for 15 bucks as I have, look no further. 4. Extra goodies: Includes a Monster coaxial cable (if you are one of those people that HAS to have top of the line cables). CONS- Look: Purple and multicolored. This is purely a matter of opinion, but I prefer my other APC protector's matte black finish. That being said, it is a surge protector, not a fashion statement. 1. Warranty: Do NOT be fooled by thinking just by purchasing you suddenly do not need homeowner's insurance. Monster is a business and as such WILL try to find a way to screw you if they can. Nothing against Monster, but a business is a business. They will not honor their warranty claims without making you jump through some hoops first. Read some other reviews on here for horror stories. That being said, this is the truth with most companies in this business. Conclusion: Monster hasn't developed a sterling rep for nothing. This is an awesome protector at a great price. In my opinion, they are second only to APC's protectors. But when you factor in the price compared to the protection, you really can't go wrong with this protector. I know I haven't.

Out of the many small LCD screens for the Raspberry Pi, I think this is the best I have found. It came with no dead pixels, and I was able to get it running on Raspbian Jessie without using any proprietary image. Below I will attempt to give all or most of the instructions on how to get it running but please keep in mind I am NOT a Linux expert so I will not be able to provide support in the event this doesn’t work for you. It should still get you really close as mine works. There are many contradicting instructions on the web due to many different ways of doing things and many changes to Linux/Raspbian. What I write below may not be the best way but... it worked for me after many days of research and work. My instructions on getting the LCD to work assume you have downloaded and installed the latest Jessie distribution from RaspberryPi's website. You will need to SSH into the RPI board to follow my instructions. Update firmware: sudo rpi-update Update distribution: sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get upgrade Github user "Swkim01" has kindly provided overlay files to make it easier to enable the LCD on the standard Jessie distribution. The files needed to get it working are on github. Main Github page: [...] Clone the repository in your home folder (the default location) by running: git clone[...] According to your LCD's type (the posting is for the 3.5 version), copy the overlay file waveshare32b-overlay.dtb or waveshare35a-overlay.dtb to /boot/overlays as root (read UPDATE at the bottom) by running: sudo cp waveshare-dtoverlays/waveshare35a-overlay.dtb /boot/overlays/ Delete cloned git folder to clean up as it is no longer needed: sudo rm –r waveshare-dtoverlays/ Use raspi-config to enable SPI (read UPDATE at the bottom) and Device Tree: sudo raspi-config Select Advanced Options, then SPI and Device Tree enabling both. Pick yes if it asks to load SPI kernel automatically. Reboot to activate new settings. Specify the appropriate overlay file in your /boot/config.txt and while you are at it check whether SPI is now active: To edit: sudo nano /boot/config.txt Check if this appears (at least one instance without the # in front of it!): dtparam=spi=on Add this at the bottom: dtoverlay=waveshare35a Note: SPI can also be enabled simply by removing the # (comment symbol) before dtparam=spi=on while you are editing the config.txt file. You can configure some parameters of the lcd module by adding options to the dtoverlay line like this: dtoverlay=waveshare35a:rotate=270 Find more in the .dts source file: [...] 89 __overrides__ { 90 speed = <&waveshare35a>,"spi-max-frequency:0"; 91 rotate = <&waveshare35a>,"rotate:0"; 92 fps = <&waveshare35a>,"fps:0"; 93 debug = <&waveshare35a>,"debug:0"; 94 }; -- In order to see console output during boot, add the following kernel argument to /boot/cmdline.txt To edit: sudo nano /boot/cmdline.txt fbcon=map:10 To make console font a usable size on the small screen add kernel argument to file /boot/cmdline.txt fbcon=font:ProFont6x11 With this alternative font you get a smaller font... fbcon=font:VGA8x8 Make sure not to add any carriage returns to this file, all instructions have to be one single line. -- Now you must move console to be shown on the SPI LCD using the following command: con2fbmap 1 1 To reverse the command above you can type the following (do not do it unless you do not want console to appear on the LCD): con2fbmap 1 0 At this point if you reboot you should see the booting process on your LCD screen. I was left with a single underscore on my LCD until I used raspi-config to configure my system to automatically log me in as pi user. After doing so I have the command line on screen. -- Additional info that may help: It is possible to move the graphical environment to fb1 as well by editing /usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d/99-fbturbo.conf and simply changing the fb0 entry to fb1. sudo nano /usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d/99-fbturbo.conf By changing this setting my RPI started booting in graphical mode so I had to configure it to boot to text console via preference settings. Do not change the setting above if you do not care to display the graphical interface on the LCD. -- SPI controller driver with DMA support The spi-bcm2835 driver has now gotten DMA support, so we don't need the out-of-tree spi-bcm2708 anymore. This means that you will no longer need a custom FBTFT kernel. To maximize throughput, make sure txbuflen is 16k or 32k (default is usually 4k). This is needed because of the dma mapping/engine overhead per transfer that spi-bcm2835 has. /etc/modules: Device Tree: txbuflen = <32768>; fbtft_device txbuflen=32768 To check run: dmesg | grep graphics This may only be required if you use the graphical interface as when you run the dmesg command it references ‘fb1’. In my case I am running my RPI in text mode (‘fb0’) so I do not think making the changes above have actually done anything. -- Touchscreen: The latest kernel does not use the ads7846_device module any more but uses device tree configuration instead, therefore ads7846 settings are in config.txt instead. I mention this due to conflicting (likely old) information you may find online. Add the following to /boot/config.txt in order to enable the touch screen functionality (if it is not working or working right – check first by booting to the GUI): add line: dtoverlay=ads7846,speed=500000,penirq=17,swapxy=1 The swapxy option may vary for you. In my case I needed the LCD to be in landscape mode but upside-down. -- Settings below may be needed if you want to customize the touchscreen for use in the GUI. The site I got the info below from was: [...] xinput_calibrator may automate the calibration. /usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d/99-calibration.conf: Section "InputClass" Identifier "calibration" MatchProduct "ADS7846 Touchscreen" Option "Calibration" "3900 240 240 3900" EndSection Table below might help for the above setting... not sure as this may be old info: Our screen is now always in landscape mode, we might want to turn it around to portrait mode. And once again our friends on GitHub already realized that by modifying the -1,0x36,0x28 sequence in init we can turn the screen around, more specifically we need to edit the 0x28 byte. Problem with editing this is that it will also change the screen resolution and the touch screen x and y axes configuration. Through several experiments I have collected the correct parameter combinations below: init width height swapxy calibration 0x28 480 320 1 "3900 240 240 3900" 0x48 320 480 0 "3900 240 3900 240" 0x88 320 480 0 "240 3900 240 3900" 0xE8 480 320 1 "240 3900 3900 240" To use them you need to modify the byte in init, change width and height arguments accordingly, change swap_xy argument for the touch screen, and finally edit touch screen calibration in /usr/share/X11/xorg.conf.d/99-calibration.conf. We decide to try the second to last line, which is in fact the native mode of our touch screen input, since its calibration has no x or y axis swapped. Discussions on GitHub suggest that some other people with the same device have small variations in the touch screen calibration. After reboot our device screen has turned 90 degrees and still looks nice. ****************************************************************************************************** UPDATE - APRIL 2016 - If you update your RPI's firmware or installing a newer Jessie image you may end up with kernel 4.4 or above. In that case your LCD screen may go all white as if it were not initialized. To fix it, you need to rename the overlay file from: waveshare32b-overlay.dtb >>> waveshare32b.dtbo or waveshare35a-overlay.dtb >>> waveshare35a.dtbo ...and make sure it is in the /boot/overlays/ folder. To rename the file I actually just made a copy changing its name using this command: sudo cp waveshare35a-overlay.dtb waveshare35a.dtbo Modify the command above to match the file name you need, and run it within the /boot/overlays/ folder as there is no path. Also, it seems like this overlay file gets rid of the need to turn SPI on so you can ignore the bit above about turning SPI on. If you do, it still works fine but it isn't needed.

I am an experienced still photographer, beginning to shoot movies. I already had a Nikon D5100 and love it. I needed a second camera for moviemaking and decided to try the EOS Rebel T3i, so I bought one and have been using it for a couple of months alongside the Nikon. It's okay for full-motion HD video, with somewhat more control over exposure than the Nikon. For still photography, it sucks. One of the motivations for a DSLR instead of a pocket digital camera is the expectation that the DSLR will take the picture when you press the button. The Canon T3i doesn't. The Nikon always does. This difference is infuriating. Any decent photographer knows when to take the picture. If the camera waits a couple of milliseconds--or full seconds, in the case of the Canon T3i--you can't capture the moment. It's also cheaply made, compared with the Nikon--all kinds of minor shortcuts to reduce the cost. I'm not sorry I bought it, but I am more than a little disappointed and will use the Nikon as my primary camera, with the Canon as a backup for movies, and leave it in the camera bag when I am shooting stills.

Setup was SUPER easy. Senors work fine, not perfect. Customer service has been great. However, the system and the siren pad need work. The siren pad is the worst part of this system. First, it's not very loud. If the TV is on upstairs, you can barely hear the siren downstairs. If it's off and your upstairs, it is still quieter then the vaccum cleaner. When standing next to the siren, again it's not very loud. It should be loud to the point you can't be next to it and you should be able to hear it upstairs with no problems. When the system senses something, it takes 2-3 mins before the siren goes off. This is an issue in that it talks telling you to disarm the system which would just lead a thief directly to it. Then all you have to do is unplug it and it is completely down. Yes, it will still send you an alert to your phone but big deal, by the time you do something about it, the thief is gone while drawing NO ATTENTION to your house. The purpose of an alarm should be to deter a thief IMMEDIATELY upon entering you home. That doesn't happen with this system. The simple fix for this would be to have a rechargeable battery in the base just strong enough to sound the siren for 5 mins once it gets unplugged. Also, like most wifi based systems, when your power is out or your wifi is down, this system will do you no good. Again, it will still send alerts to your phone but nothing AT your house to deter any thieves. The batteries in the sensors are pretty weak. They've only lasted a couple months before having to replace them. Hopefully the new batteries will last longer. The discount they claim they will help you with DOES NOT fully offset the price of the monitoring service; especially since the cost of the monitoring service KEEPS GOING UP. With the monitoring service, I'm not always available to speak on a phone. So if you can't/don't answer, their service will send the police. I've already had a few false alarms happen and that would cause the police to come out unnecessarily. After a couple of those, the police/city will charge you. So in regards to my title, if you have this system WITH A SEPARATE battery powered camera system, I think you would be very well setup. If the alarms go off, you could simply check the cameras to determine the real need of getting the police out. The best reason to have a separate camera system is that if the thieves disable the Kangaroo system, you've still got camera backup. Most thieves are under the impression there would only be one system and once they defeat it, they would go in with a false sense that they are good to go. ****UPDATE**** Over the course of 5 days since my review, the whole system has failed. The siren pad is changing modes on its own. Two more of the Entry and Motion sensors have stopped working and won't reset. I sent customer service an email and they clearly are too lazy to look up my account to see what I bought and what is going wrong. They can't even read the entire email!!!! Total garbage. Wish I could get my money back but of course the system failed after the return window closed.

The main problem with the D905 is that it is not certified by Google via their SafetyNet attestation. Without that you really can not play any legitimate streaming video. Roku and Vudu give: Ineligible Device Connected Playing content is not supported on rooted devices SafetyNet became foolproof in 2020 and most Andriod TV manufacturers have not gotten their devices certified. The exception seems to the early major Andriod TV manufacturers of Nvidia, AirTV, Xiaomi, and Sony. D905 is an excellent device and very good value and I hope they will make the effort to get their device certified in the future. It did not come with batteries for the remotes, but I have lots of rechargable AAA batteries so that was no problem. As to Android TV versus Roku, Roku has much simplified interface which works OK with a remote, but it is very restrictive. Android TV has a lot more flexability, but it is very hard to run via a remote (practically impossible). With Android TV you can do everything you could do with a Chromebook (totally awesome), but you need a keyboard and mouse. Fortunately Android TV boxes almost always come with USB connections (one USB 1.0 and one USB 2.0 with the D905). I would recommend you get a standard PC USB keyboard with dual USB output ports (to connect the mouse and maybe a webcam). You could also get a simple USB hub if a PC USB keyboard with dual USB ports is a problem. The AV connector is very important as with a $2 cable you can get a cable to convert you AV port to RCA Video output (red, white, and yellow) for older TVs which don't support HDMI. One of the big advantages of an Andriod TV Box is that they usually come with an ethernet connector, often 100 mbps for budget boxes and 1,000 mbps for high end boxes. However, for just streaming video, 100 mbps is fine. The advantage of this connector is that if your WiFi is congested with lots of devices using the WiFi, a streaming video or two can sink the service for all users and devices. Using a cable to connect your streaming devices frees up WiFi for phones and such. The D905 as shipped is not configured to do any streaming video out of the box. To access most of the free streaming services (with and without ads) you need to add apps, but the apps you really need aren't in the Google Play Store. Doh! However, if you go into Chrome on the D905 you can google search for TroyPoint Downloader. Normally that gives you a link to webpages which tell you how to get the apps you need. They have lots of ads and are hard to follow though, but you can skip much of the confusion by going to the domainname/dl (for the downloader you want) and then when you are running the downloader you can go to the domainname/tpapp and get the rapid app installer. The Rapid App Installer is most helpful and get you several useful Android TV apps such as the Cinemax app which is not generally available through other channels. I am sorry that I can't give you better descriptions of how to get the apps, but Amazon policy does not permit external links and there are no internal links which solve these problems.

I waited to write this review until I had the YI camera for a while so I could give a reliable review. I fell in love with the camera right away and the setup was a breeze. The picture quality is superb and it does not miss a beat. The pan/tilt feature is amazing. I only need one camera to see my entire living room. The close zoom is not crystal clear, but that is not of importance to me. I just want to be able to see my living room while I am not home, check on my dog, and to capture activity of my front and back door. The camera proved it's worth within a few days of setting it up. My home alarm went off whIle I was away and I was able to pull my camera up instantly to make sure everything was okay at my house before cancelling the police dispatch. The camera saved me a warning notice and gave me peace of mind. I have also been able to check in on my children with the help of the two way communicator. With all of that said, I still had a nagging desire to purchase a more expensive and well-known brand, the Arlo. Since they are so popular and the reviews are good, I felt that the Arlo would be even better than my YI. However, my experience with the Arlo was quite the contrary. I was less than satisfied from the moment I opened the Arlo box. The batteries turned me off right away and the setup was a little more difficult. The arlo cameras do not have as good of a viewing range, the pan is not as encompassing, it does not have tilt, and the zoom was a joke. The picture quality is not as clear and the view is like looking through a fish bowl. Not to mention the batteries started draining immediately. Just to give the more well-known, expensive brand a chance, I put one Arlo beside my YI to do a comparison for a day. The YI won hands down. I could not see or do half as much as I can with my YI. The arlo even went offline over night. Needless to say the Arlos went back to the store and now I am going to just buy another YI or two to put in other areas of my home...maybe to catch the outside view or a different inside angle. The only cons to the YI camera would be that they are not weatherproof, even though I have read plenty of positive reviews of them being used outside. Another con might be that the YI does not connect with Amazon Echo. Despite these two minor things, I am thoroughly satisfied with my YI camera. Make sure to purchase the YI camera with the SD card slot and to purchase an SD card. Everything is saved to the SD card and can be viewed on your phone or tablet and saved or edited from there to a permanent storage device. I have not tried to hang my YI yet but it does come with the hardware to do it. Hanging it would definitely make it harder for a would-be-theif to take off with the camera. It has a power plug that can be easily hidden with a little ingenuity so that should not be a deterrence from your purchase of this product. I definitely recommend purchasing this camera. It is much cheaper than a few other brands and does a much better job.

I bought this to mount a Vizio 22 inch flat screen in my kitchen. Because the location was a wall with a 180 degree view, I wanted a mount with the smallest profile possible and this mount only puts the TV about half an inch off the wall. It is not adjustable as far as tilting goes, and that was also fine for the application. The mount is very solid construction and a straight forward installation. There is more hardware than you will need. One bracket screws to the back of the TV, and the second bracket screws into the wall. You then just slide the TV into the bracket. There was only one tricky part for my particular installation. Because the mount is so low profile, when you connect your coax cable, ac adaptor, etc., to the back of the set, you cannot slide it into position - the cables protrude further out the back than the half inch space provides. We solved this problem by cutting a 6 inch x 1 inch channel into the wall so the problem cable had enough space slide the wall as the TV was mounted. Another option would have been to install a recess box into the wall. The one I saw at Home Depot cost more than three times what I paid for this mount (my option of cutting into the wall was free).

I bought this Fire TV Stick for my 85 year old grandmother who has trouble navigating through technology. I knew that this device would be helpful because instead of navigating through the apps (which is a foreign concept to her) she is able to ask Alexa directly to play her shows. Pros: - Easy to set up. I set this up in my Grandmother's rehabilitation center while she was recovering from a broken hip. I plugged into her TV and paired with the Rehab Center's free Wifi. No problem! -Grandma is easily able to ask Alexa to play 'This is Us' - her favorite show! It was difficult for her to understand at first that she would need to navigate to Hulu and then open 'This is Us.' The major benefit of having Alexa is that she can easily ask for a specific show (ie: "Alexa, play the most recent episode of 'Modern Family'" or "Play 'Queer Eye'") without having to know which app to go to. -She also asks Alexa what the weather is or to play some Frank Sinatra or Michael Buble. Cons: - Grandma had trouble understanding the button meanings, but I explained them to her and she jotted them down for reference. I believe she is grasping it now. The limited amount of buttons is actually ideal and less confusing. - She did have a bit of difficulty toggling between live TV and the Firestick (HDMI1 vs. TV) but practicing or writing down for reference is helpful. Overall, very happy with this product for my Grandmother. Apps, Streaming services, etc, are difficult for her to understand. However, this userinterface was fairly simple and only took a day or so for her to grasp. Plus I love that she likes to ask "Alexis" instead of "Alexa." Pretty cute.

This review is based on the new Shield TV (2019) product (the one that's tube shaped), NOT its slightly more expensive cousin. Just to give some background, this is the first "high end" streaming device I've purchased. I've always been in the $30-50 range with Roku and Fire devices. So maybe someone with experience using an Apple TV or other top tier product would have a different point of view. But if you're coming from those lower tier devices, this is a HUGE upgrade. I suspect it might be an upgrade even if you're coming from a more expensive device. Reasons I love this unit: *SNAPPY performance. I'm used to there being a certain amount of lag inherent in streaming with apps like YouTube TV or even Pluto TV. You know, that sometimes long delay between hitting play and the video starting, or the similar delay when moving from the "Live TV" portion of the app to the recordings... etc etc. With the Shield, there's almost no lag, ever. Everything just works how you want, quickly. *Fantastic Remote! I'm used to the remote being a compromise on streaming devices, something that you have to 'live with'.... but not here. This one is ergonomically designed, back-lit (automatically lights when you pick it up), and it controls your TV and soundbar. This is one area I'm confident to say that this device beats even the Apple TV. I do not think there's any streaming device out there right now at any price point with a remote that compares with this one. *Gaming features. I've barely tapped into this, and I may update this review after further testing. But you can pair your Xbox One OR Playstation 4 controller (or a host of other controllers), and take advantage of games using Nvidia's streaming platform. This includes both free games included with their 'GeForce Now' service, or you can even stream games from your PC. Cool addition that isn't rivaled anywhere else as far as I can tell. *Android TV interface. I unexpectedly love Android TV. It is smooth, easy to navigate, and has everything you need. I haven't found any major apps I need that are unavailable. I really haven't found anything I don't like about the interface at all. It is superior to Roku and Fire TV, in my personal opinion. *Built in Chromecast. This is extremely handy, and so far works very well. We had previously owned an old first gen Chromecast, and the one included in this device works miles better. *Google Assistant. We are an Alexa household, and I believe that some form of Alexa support is built into this device... but we're perfectly content using the Google Assistant built in. If I hit the voice control button and tell it to go to AMC, it automagically knows that I mean the AMC channel on YouTube TV, and we're off. If there's something more ambiguous that might be on multiple platforms, you can specify. Example: "Play Walking Dead on Netflix".... Boom, it starts playing. Excellent. I can't speak on the 4k up scaling, as we are still using an HD set that isn't 4k capable (gasp!). But I think we might be ordering a 4k set soon enough, and will update as needed. This device has exceeded my expectations by a mile, and this will absolutely be my streaming platform of choice going forward until further notice.

Executive summary: good cam; small with clear images; neat windshield install solution; top-drawer customer service; ok 3rd party free Android app. A keeper. If you want a 23-minute in-depth review, and I mean in depth, search on YouTube for Jabber Tech, "RedTiger WiFi GPS Dash Camera..." This video has long sequences of drive video -- day, dusk, night. Jabber's drive videos match my experience around clarity, automatic light compensation, and audio. Mounting RedTiger supplies 2 pieces of what they call electrostatic film that goes between your windshield and the 3M super-sticky adhesive on the GPS module. (You just slide the camera off the GPS module during installation.) The film has moderate but very effective adhesive on the windshield side. Repositioning the camera without the film would result in destruction of the 3M sticky. Repositioning with the film involved simply peeling the film off the windshield and re-sticking. I'm now on my 3rd reposition. Position 1 gave me a viewpoint that contained a whole lot of the rear view mirror mount on the left of the image. This cam is REALLY wide angle. Moved it an inch or so to the right, thanks to the film, and no more mirror mount close-ups. Then I discovered that the dotted top-of-windshield shading on my 2003 Toyota Avalon's windshield seriously blocked acquisition of GPS satellites. My theory is that the dots are metallic frit burned onto the glass rather than plain old silkscreen ink, and the metal content is absorbing/blocking the GPS signals. Position 3 now puts the GPS module on clear glass about 1/32" inch below the dotted shading. GPS signal acquisition is now as fast as it's going to be (takes some time) and once locked in, it stays locked in for the duration of the trip. My experience is that, after car start, it's about 3 minutes of driving or about 2 miles before the GPS location and ground speed kicks in. Controls WIth a camera this small, there's no real estate for tons of buttons. This means that every button has multiple functions that depend on what you're doing at the moment. The manual, which is very good, is about as clear as you can get around this, but you should expect a bit of a learning curve. The only way out is through -- spending time working out how to alter settings, take a snapshot, manually turn off the camera, find the configuration of the many options, and so on. Alternatively you can just go with the factory defaults: video begins recording when power reaches the camera, drive segment files are 1 minute long (there is no lag between each successive MP4 1-min. file), resolution is 3840 x 2160 pixels at 30 frames per second. Customer service: Via email. It is top-drawer support whose access point in the US is in Colorado. I found RedTiger's service VERY responsive and got replies in 12 hours. In my case, the manual was a tad ambiguous around repositioning, whether you pulled the GPS sticky off the film or the film off the windshield (it's the latter). Rose immediately sent me new 3M stickies and electrostatic films free, so I'll be able to reposition this cam till the cows come home. SD Card The manual recommends at least a Samsung 64 GB micro SD Class 10 U3 card. I'm finding that a (cheaper) Best Buy Samsung 128 GB Class 10 U1 card is working just fine. The manual cautions you not to turn to eBay or Amazon for the micro SD to avoid getting stuck with poor-performing fakes. The Android App To connect, I found I had to get away from any WiFi that I already had saved. In may case, this was a distant corner on an out-of-the-way strip mall parking lot. It's cool to see what the camera's seeing and to do rudimentary file diving. But transmission is too slow for downloading files from the F7N to the Android. For that, you're going to want to pop the micro SD card out and use a card reader, either OTC for the phone or USB for computers. Don't drop the card in your car because there are dozens of nooks and crannies for it to hide itself. It never falls in plain sight. As me how I know.... Summary I think it's a really good camera at what has become a low-middle range of price. I spent a long time watching those YouTube car crash / idiot driver videos, looking at the time stamps at the bottom of the images, figuring out which brands had the best images. Then, because I'm cheap, I cross-ruffed against price -- the high-end cams are about as good as this RedTiger F7N... for 2.5-3x the RedTiger price.

I have old Nikkor 35mm f2.0 and f2.8 lenses. On my D7000 this Rokinon is much better in all areas of the image, especially the corners. There is very little chromatic aberration. If there is some barrel distortion present it is not enough to be noticeable in interior architecture shots. The focus is perhaps a little heavy, but very smooth and it stays where you put it without creeping even when the camera is pointed down.. Be aware that this is a very large lens, extending about 4 inches beyond the mounting ring and about 3.2 inches in diameter. The fancy hood takes it out about another 2 inches and brings the diameter to 4 inches at the end. That's easily twice the size of my old 35mm Nikkors. It's pretty heavy weighing much more than most small zooms. You'll need to carve out some serious space for this lens in your bag. I bought this lens primarily for carefully shot landscapes using a tripod. The manual focus is perfect for that application. The amount of rotation required to go from infinity to 3 feet is a relatively large 7/8 inch which gives me plenty of precision for shooting focus-stacked images. Cinematographers would like that large focus throw too. The manual focus would also appeal to studio and product photographers. But if you're a rapid-fire, handheld type of guy, you may be happier with an autofocus lens. Have been playing with this beauty all day, and have to say I am well pleased with what I'm seeing on the screen and on a few large test prints. I would say that for areas that are in sharp focus, this lens is "pixel-sharp" on my 16mp sensor from around f2.8 to just past f8, and just about that good at f2.0 and 1.4. I own several lenses hand-picked for quality, and this is one of the sharpest and most aberration-free lenses I own. Not only is it a really good deal for the money, it's a flat-out great piece of optics!

Of the many joys of Rogue ownership, I used to not include backing up. I purchased a Peak PKC0RB Wireless Back-up Camera ($87.80 from Amazon.com). This allows a view, on the 3½" color screen, low and straight behind the vehicle. Included on the screen are guide lines which serve to allow lining up with lines in the parking lots. Now I enjoy backing into most parking spots and into my garage. The package comprises 3 cables and 3 units, a screen/receiver, a transmitter, and the camera. Installation of the screen/receiver was a no brainer. To mount the camera, it is necessary to open the little panel in the center of inside of the lift gate. Then you have to remove the backup lamp assembly (See owner manual for changing a backup lamp bulb.). I chose to solder the wires from the device to those from the right side backup lamp. Stripping the rather fine wires requires care. To mount the camera, I drilled out the plastic nuts that held the license plate screws and used the machine screws provided with the package. I fed the wire from the camera through one of the plate mounting holes (along with the screw) and backed things up with rubber grommets. A 10 mm wrench is needed to hold the nuts from turning while tightening the machine screws that hold the camera and license plate. I used a plastic wire tie to secure the transmitter to a heavy cable inside the lift gate panel. See photos. The device works as advertised, but it has a couple of quirks. One is that it's blue LED blinks on and off continuously, mildly annoying at night. The other is that sometimes the screen comes alive while you're just driving along. I suspect the receiver picks up WiFi signals from computer networks. By and large, the backup camera is a good addition to my Rogue.

Updated in April 2015 I have had this tripod for more than three years now and I have used and abused it. It is still going strong. As mentioned at the bottom I most frequently use it with a different ball head but I still lug the original one in the bag's pocket as it sometimes comes in handy. I found it best to clean the sand and mud after a day out so that the fine sand does not impede the retraction of the legs or grit their articulation. I also use that tripod in the studio for its height and sturdiness especially with heavy camera/lens combo. Finally I procured the inexpensive Ravelli tripod dolly and have been using them together. I was a little concerned about the stability as with the legs fully extended the dolly is small enough that the legs won't be at their first locking angle - I was afraid the center column would tilt sideways but no, even with a 7lbs load the result was stable and felt solid. The weight of the tripod becomes an asset as it dampens the vibrations coming from the wheels. I usually go around with lighter tripods but when I want stability and solidity this is the one I grab. I stand by my earlier reviews below. At below $70 I am considering buying a second one just in case. What follows is the original review: ______________________________________ I bought this tripod three weeks ago and it was already a great bargain at the price, which went down $20 since then. It has already been through the jungle and sand (I live in Costa Rica). At something like 15 pounds it is heavy but to me this is a feature: it is very stable and doesn't vibrate in the wind. I don't count it as a pro for obviously weight has its downside. Pros: - Excellent, sturdy construction - All joints friction are adjustable; the Allen wrenches are provided - The three legs are adjustable independently, not only in length (duh!) but also with three different angles (see the photo I uploaded) - The center column has a standard camera screw at the bottom, allowing to position the camera (or the ball head) below for close-to-the-ground shoots (see photo). - The ball head can be locked in place using three screws under the column top plate - more on these later on (see photo). - The ball head itself is probably worth close to the price of the whole thing. Once adjusted it is very solid, even tilted 90 degrees with a heavy camera / battery pack / lens combination (see photo). Cons / caveats: - Be sure to have the Allen wrenches in the bag: with heavy usage some of the frictions may have to be adjusted. I use the ball head with a pretty heavy camera combination and I find myself adjusting the friction to my liking about once every few shooting days. There is a pocket on the side of the tripod bag, whre I typically store the head and other equipment - I have to pay attention not to drop them. Not a big deal - If you don't use the three screws to lock the ball head on the center column, they tend to get loose and might fall due to vibrations in your trunk. If you don't want to use them ever this is not a problem, and they don't budge if you lock the head with them (see photo). Not a big deal. - The removable plates that attach to the camera (there are two identical ones) are pretty big, which make them not too comfortable when holding the camera by the battery grip to shoot portrait (see photo). Not a big deal. - The plates slide in easily and lock in place without problem (even in the mud of Tortuguero) but the clearance makes it not very sturdy unless you tighten lightly the side thumb screw (see photo) once the plate is in place - it quickly becomes a habit and the third time you do it you won't even notice you did it. - The plates feature a spring loaded round pin to align the camera, for those models which have the corresponding smooth hole next to the standard 1/4" screw mount. The spring is a simple blade that pushes the pin against the camera through a plate hole - if your camera does not have the corresponding smooth hole, the spring stays pushed back. It weakens and can move aside, letting the pin go. I didn't loose any yet but I am confident I will. And so what? Honestly this is not a problem for me. - The size of the plate is such that when I mount it to the lens (not the camera) the plate has to be mounted backwards not to interfere with the battery grip. This means that the pistol grip of the ball head is front to back. Not a problem for me: I hardly notice. Conclusion: At less that $100 this is an absolute must if you need a solid, sturdy tripod. This is one of my best buys ever. Oh, and yes the "free" tripod that comes with it is flaky, especially when the third segment of the legs is extended. Don't dump it, though, as it can be used for a point and shoot, an external flash (a light one!) or to hold a reflector. Anyway for the price of the main tripod they could as well have left this thingy out. ___________________________ Addition February 2013 I bought another of the [[ASIN:B001BPE3KQ DMKFoto Heavy Duty Ball Head with Quick Release Plate]], the same I already used on my heavy-duty monopod, and now have it almost permanently on this tripod. Still my best tripod so far.

The DS212j is *amazing*. I've never actually found a NAS I liked before... normally they are cheaply build, work off of FAT32 formatted drives, or are super slow. Yes, some may say the case is a little cheap plastic feeling... however the thing runs silently, has amazing software, and the internal components look to be a pretty high quality. I've been using it for a day now, and am already completely in love. The thing pumps out NFS shares like no-ones business. The torrent search and download ability is top notch. Setup was easy, and they even include Linux setup software on the disc they ship you! Pros: * Quiet * Very Linux / Open Source friendly * Acts as more of a server than a NAS file share * Top notch applications * Amazing web gui * Easy setup * Fast boot * Feature packed. IPv6, DDNS, uPnP, dlna, firwall, IP auto block, web server (apache 2.2 as of DSM 4.0), auto sleep and wakeup, FTP/AFS/NFS/Samba/Dav, syslog server, LDAP server, SNMP, terminal... and tons more! Cons: * Doesn't feature hot-swap drives. (they are in the DS212j's order DS212 brother) * Erases everything on your installed disks at first run. (make backups!, or use new drives) I would highly recommend putting at least two 2TB drives in this bad boy... I put two 1TB drives and am a little afraid i'll run out of space and have to migrate all my data onto it all over again in ~1year+

When using them like this however you must be very careful because the sound isolation is so great that even persons shouting will have a very difficult time getting your attention. They are cheap and durable; unlike ear buds they stay in your ears when you are working or playing.

Wished I had my hands on the specs before buying because the user's manual states 60Hz-18kHz frequency response so forget low end bass as well as trusting YouTube sound samples that post frequency response graphs and record with binaural mics. The W-King does have smooth rounded and punchy bass with non-EDM drum tim-tom hits retaining good bell tone which means they carefully designed the roll off bass octaves below 60Hz to not sound boxy and thonky like the old boomboxes in the '80's. The W-King maintains a well balanced sound with most music styles but it does not have as big a sound as the YouTube samples suggest. EQ effect has two settings, one enhances vocals and higher frequencies to come across louder with more clarity, the other setting is more compressed and a bit muffled. I didn't hear an increase in louder, deeper bass between the two EQ settings but that could be due to the songs I was playing. But it does explain why most of the YouTube sound test videos samples electronic digital music with its clean digital waveforms and balanced sound. Even though they're not portable my Boston Acoustic small satellite mains with small boxy subwoofer I bought at Salvation Army for $6 back in 2004 has much more fuller and lower end bass for its similar small size but with murky highs. I get better clarity with the Boston Acoustics on my Spectrum digital cable box analog output where the highs sound normal. The advantages of DSP streaming I guess, but every cable channel has somewhat different sound dynamics, some better, some worse so its the signal, not the speakers at fault which also applies to the W-King. Give it a clean balanced signal and it will deliver it. The W-King's 12in. long enclosure box has main drivers about 7 inches apart that pretty much cancels out any stereo effect when listening for L/R cross channel reflection and wide pan stereo presence where it just ends up sounding like a very loud mono speaker. I test panned left to right channels using my MacMini's Sound Pref settings to confirm it's a stereo signal but I had to have my ears inches from the mains to be sure. Just to be clear this stereo sounding mono applies to all boombox speakers in this class. Directional frequencies in mains have to be spread out at least 3 ft apart to hear the stereo effect from a reasonable distance. You certainly don't want to listen to these W-Kings at loud volumes standing 3 feet away. It's downright uncomfortable. At least at loud volumes they deliver a clean signal. I didn't hear any scratchy noise in the highs as it is with most boomboxes cranked up loud at my local park. The W-King is a VERY GOOD AND LOUD outdoor MONO sounding speaker with very little distortion but lacks low end bass. It's also built of solid construction. The "big-ness" of the sound is just not what I expected going by YouTube sound tests. I'm going to keep the W-King for reference purposes as someone who is fascinated with audio reproduction technology improvements in the past decades.

I may end up returning the camera, as I love my old nikkors... they worked perfectly using the previous focus assist on NEX 6/7. I post this review here for two reasons: 1) None of the "preview" reviews of the camera mentioned it, because they are mostly run by people who know nothing about photography. Shame on them. 2) Sony shouldn't market the camera as a replacement for the NEX 6/7 and then remove via software the one feature that was most useful about those cameras for manual focus glass. ------- I really hate it when features are removed from a camera that were there in the manufacturers previous "version". There is no way for me as a consumer to know not to buy this camera because said feature had been removed. This is a software modification that wasn't in the specs. Caveat Emptor. I will update this review if there is something I missed because I have only had the camera a few hours. I will also update if I hear about a firmware update that restores the functionality of NEX 6/7. Until then, I consider this camera broken for manual focus glass, and a major step backward from NEX 6/7 in that regard.

Needed a DVD drive to burn an ISO to install/repair the OS of an ultralight laptop. Initially was not recognized by my desktop (Win 10 Pro). Great little product that my wife and I use to watch Netflix after the kids go to bed. Only one issue: it comes with a terminal for a ground lead, and you actually do need to use it - if you don't, you'll get static, sometimes quite bad Now, the device description does say that it comes with a ground screw, but If you're anything like me, you might have assumed you didn't need to use it. In fact, it turns out that making sure audio equipment has a shared ground is really important I guess? Anyway, it's not as bad with my wife's laptop, but with mine it leads to really annoying noise on the line if I don't ground it. And the problem is, my laptop, like most out there I'm guessing, does not come with a ground screw terminal, nor does the aux cord I use come with a separate ground lead. I'd say this is a very good product, but be aware that to really use it properly you will need a grounding solution.

First impressions were great. Well packaged. Concise and clear instructions. The aluminum body looks classy and the power and speaker connections felt solid and well put together. I noted that even though the packaging looked brand new my aluminum case had marks & scratches on. No matter I thought. I could see no evidence of use on the plastic end caps. I had it hooked up in 2.1 configuration in no time. One pair of channels were connected to some 6x9 speakers and the other pair were bridged to a sub woofer. My first impressions on power up were good. The logo glows pleasingly and there was plenty of adjustment on the amp itself. Levels, crossover, little bit of EQ, options for full, low pass & high pass. It was all looking so good. I lived with it for about 5 days. I spent hours trying to get it adjusted right. No matter what I tried I couldn't quite get it to sound right. It sounded kind of muddy and not really present. It sounded lacklustre and cheap. Very hard to explain. It was very subtle. During this time I figured out that you could drive channels 1 & 2 hard. Or drive channels 3 & 4 hard. But as soon as the sub (which was bridged on outputs 3 & 4) did any work then outputs 1 & 2 distorted quite badly and lost some volume. I checked the power voltage when the distortion thing was happening and it was good. Same as when idle. So in the end I took it out and connected my 6x9's back to my head unit and I couldn't believe how clear and punchy it sounded with no amp at all! Even without the sub. My conclusion could be that this is a crappy amp. What else would you expect from $100.... but I am the only one here who hasn't given it 5 stars. I must have got a bad one? Who knows, but I returned for a refund.

Are you looking for a dashcam that has great 4K recording but has features that don't work and overheats after about 30 minutes of use? Then this dashcam is perfect for you. Dashcam was received with latest firmware, reflashing it made no difference, nor did resetting to defaults nor trying iOS or Android. Parking mode using Viofo HK3 just records all the time, even when it's set to only record incidents. Camera overheats in parking mode and then doesn't turn on with ignition. Worked correctly once or twice with a cool night but then stopped when the temperature got warmer. Gave up on WiFi and parking mode and just used it with the cigarette lighter USB adapter to find that it overheats with about 30 minutes of use using that too. Taking the memory card out when the camera locks up at this point almost results in burnt finger tips the memory card is so hot. For the 30 minutes the camera works the recording image quality is fantastic at 4K front and 1080P rear. I have had a number of other dash cams in my vehicle and never had one that overheats. Don't be tempted to get this on sale like I did. Get a different 4K dashcam from another brand like Thinkware or BlackVue. Wish I could return this useless product but it's passed the return window now. I would give negative stars if that was possible.

Vislla stuck by their product. I own a pair of the older version and had charging issues with them when I first bought them. I contacted Vislla customer service and explained the situation to them which prompted them to send me another pair. That to me spoke volumes in today's retail market. I enjoy the new design along with the updated charging. The sound is okay. Good customer service experience is why I bought the new design. Update: After using for a few weeks I've had the chance to really put these to use. A couple of dislikes, the Bluetooth range is very minimal, connection cuts out under 20ft. (unsatisfactory). At times I like the volume loud when I'm at the gym to drown out what they're playing, and I found myself having to turn the volume up to almost full blast. Although the sound quality is clear, this is somewhat of a pet peave of mine. The older versions had far better connectivity and volume control. On the plus side Vislla did fix the charging issue and this model is certainly an upgrade from the old. I've only charged the base (with earphones included) one time since I've had them and they're still holding a charge. I'd say I've gotten 12-15 charges off the base since first charging them. The older version charging ports were reset into the unit, and now they redesigned them to be protruding out for a much better contact for charging. Because of the lack of connectivity and volume issues I deducted one star. Overall a decent Bluetooth headset but next time will try another brand. Second update (April 27th 2022: 4 months in and the right side will not charge making it useless. This is a similar problem this company had with the old design, although better overall design still the same issue. Who wants to keep paying $25 every three to four months for a new pair of earbuds? Not this guy! Spend a little extra on a good pair to save yourself the hassle. I have to deduct another star because of this. I don't write many reviews so take my word for it, this is clearly not a fluke but a manufacturing defect.

This may be a fine computer, but just so you know HP is CRIMINALLY NEGLIGENT IMHO in not writing documentation for this variant. Specifically when I received mine 5/18/2021 I could find NOT A SHRED of documentation on how the OSD button was supposed to work. The one-sheet Setup Instructions that came with the AiO identified this button existed but nothing about how it worked. I bought this model because it has an HDMI INPUT and it fits well in place of the 27 inch monitor I was using. I needed it to display the output of a KVM switch so I could operate some other PCs. When you go to the HP page for this variant and click MANUALS it shows you options including Users Guide PDF. Clicking that takes you to a page titled Generic cDT User Guide – c06366166.pdf! Not a word in that document about the OSD button on this variant. And I spent 45 minutes on text chat with Deepak (that was his name) confirming he could also find NO DOCUMENTATION on OSD button (he told me there would be an Input Select button but that was some other model not 27-d0072). If you too need to know this: Display can select between (Internal)PC and the HDMI IN. OSD button is 4 directions plus center push. Facing the PC, reach behind to the OSD button and press TWICE TOWARDS THE RIGHT. My screen goes blank for 5 seconds or so, then toggles to the other Display choice (PC to HDMI, or HDMI to PC). Be sure to connect the other device to the HDMI IN only. Good luck!

The price of this case is MUCH lower than the Apple version, and is the main reason I bought it. I was a bit leery of what I would get for such a low price, but I am very pleased with the quality of the product. I purchased this case for an iPad Air 2, and have been using it for about two days. The iPad fits securely in the case, and is held in by friction with the sides and corners of the case. It seems like the fit could become loose over time if the iPad is repeatedly placed in, and removed from the case. I intend to leave it in the case, so I don't see this as an issue. The case is very similar to the Apple smart cover and case. The iPad powers up when the case is opened, and shuts off when it is closed. The cover portion has three fold points (the Apple version has four), which allows it to be used as a stand (3 different ways) for the iPad, or it can lie flat against the back of the iPad. With the four fold points, the Apple case can be used to create a hand hold for their case. The three fold points on this case's cover prevent this case from doing that. Adding the case to the super slim iPad Air 2 obviously adds some bulk to to it. The additional protection for the iPad that this case provides makes up for the slight increase in size. The thickness of this case is a bit thinner than the Apple version. The surface of the case is more like silicone then plastic, but it does not have a sticky feel to it. I do not consider the case slippery. The opening for the power, ear phone, audio controls, speakers, and camera/mic are ample and allow easy access to the controls.

I bought this drive during last year's Cyber Monday sale in hopes that I'd be able to back up some of my larger files. I'm a patient person, so I didn't really mind the long write time; I was copying over 100+ gigabytes of various file formats, so I anticipated that aspect of using this. I, upon receiving the drive, took an entire day off to monitor and complete the file transfer. First thing I noticed was that getting it on a keychain with my other drives was an absolute pain. The strange design of the hole (as in, the part that swept up) made sliding it on only possible if I flipped it a certain way. It certainly didn't play well with the other drives on the ring, fitting strangely alongside them whilst making the entire keyring now awkward in how it sat on my desk. Next thing was the write time, of course. It took over six hours; by the end of the whole ordeal, it took eight. Why, you may ask? Because about halfway through the transfer, I noticed that the files it was copying over ceased to be openable, and after further investigation, I realized they had been corrupted. Individually copying each file again to replace the corrupted versions worked for a while, though if I tried to copy over more than twenty files (mind you, when I tried this, I was working with images) or so at a time, it would corrupt it again. It had worked fine before the halfway point, which made it extremely tedious to manually have to go through the drive and see what had and hadn't copied over correctly. After several hours of this, I decided to return the faulty drive and get an external hard drive instead (which copied over all of those files in a single hour). Do not buy this drive. It will corrupt your files, time, money, and your faith in thumbdrives as a whole.
