This is an upgrade from my D5000. I'm very happy with it so far. I love the red color, which looks more true red than the image that appears on my screen. The color aides in being able to tell my camera bodies apart at a glance as well, which is actually why I chose the red. It's both smaller and lighter than my D5000, which is very nice as every ounce counts when you're predominantly an outdoor and nature photographer like I am. The grip is deeper and more comfortable. Changing lenses feels much smoother on this model. The LCD screen is noticeably larger, easier to see, and display of higher quality visually. The touch screen works well and makes quick operation easier. The touch screen has some fun and interesting capabilities too, namely touch focus and shutter release when in live view. However, I found that while the first couple of times taking photos using the screen as a shutter release is fun, it quickly becomes a nuisance when every accidental touch of the screen becomes a photo you didn't mean to take. So, I disabled that feature early on. But, I did keep the touch screen's spot focus feature on. Though I'm predominantly a viewfinder shooter, being able to focus right where I want just by touching the screen when I am using live view is great. You can also get pinpoint focus accuracy by zooming in while in live view. I'll still rely on my viewfinder and spot focusing manually for the majority of my shooting though just because that's what I'm more comfortable with. But I suspect that LCD spot focusing capability will be a well used feature among many. My favorite upgrade is the expanded ISO. It goes to 25,600 whereas my old camera only went to 3,200. This gives me MUCH more capability and flexibility in lower lighting. I ran some high ISO tests the first day I got it and was happy to see that I can easily go to several thousand ISO and still have an acceptable image, especially after applying a noise reduction filter in post processing. The built in flash is not quite as powerful as my old one, but still enough to do the trick when you're not using a speed light, but need something more than the available light. I'm pleased with the results of my flash and exposure compensation tests. They've moved some buttons around, but, I'm finding operation pretty much the same as the D5000, or at least an intuitive jump from the older model. There's been nothing that I haven't been able to quickly and easily discern after using the D5000 for years. I think anyone familiar with any of Nikon's models in this series will find switching to this one an easy transition. One negative I noticed in my initial tests is that settings change and a noticeable reduction in image quality is visible if using the continuous shooting mode compared to single shot mode in low light, high ISO tests. Focus seemed far more challenging for hand held shots in continuous shooting mode even though the camera automatically increased the shutter speed while shooting in aperture priority mode. I suspect this is due to mirror movement, but am disappointed since continuous is my preferred mode. I'll be running more tests in better lighting outside once we're out of this cold snap and will try to remember to update this review with my results. Nonetheless, this is my only disappointment thus far. I'm very pleased with everything else. In summary, I'd highly recommend this camera body to anyone on somewhat of a budget who wants a good quality DSLR that accommodates everyone from the point and shoot hobby photographer to the fully manual serious photographer. Due to its size and weight, it's particularly great for anyone who does a lot of outdoor work and/or has to lug their gear around a lot. It's the kind of good quality you'd expect from Nikon.

Nice machine. Third machine bought in a short period of time. Other two were Dell Precision 5510 and Asus ZenBook Pro. Both were Core i7 machines, had 4K displays and cost much more than this one did. 4K turned out to be unusable because so many applications scale so poorly. I ended up reducing the display resolution to full HD or a bit higher. Ended up sending both laptops back. This machine is full HD, and had the processor minimum that I was looking for (at least a Core i5). Among the documentation that came with the machine was a one-leaf sheet that explained that the machine had an additional M.2 slot inside for an SSD. There were no instructions on opening the machine or installation of the SSD. 10 screws on the bottom. I'm game! I ordered a Samsung 500 SSD with the correct physical dimensions and 32GB of RAM. Removing the 10 Philips head screws from the bottom panel was easy. Unfortunately, the bottom was still firmly attached. As firmly as before the screws were removed. I had not a clue on how to open the machine up. I looked. I pried with my fingers. I dropped it off the dining room table (not really!). Finally, I sought help on YouTube. Not finding anything on this exact model, I did find a video where a similar machine was opened. The video author used a credit card, inserted around the seam between top and bottom halves and slid around freeing the tabs inside. I think this is what a spudger would be used for, but a credit card did the trick. Five minutes later the halves were apart, nothing was broken or damaged and there wasn't even a fingerprint on the thing. Finding the memory slots for the SO-DIMMs took a moment. There's a shield covering them. Five screws or so, and that came off. The hard drive was obvious. That would stay in until I transferred all the partitions to the M.2 SSD. Then it would come out and find a useful life as an external drive, wherever needed. Removing the hard drive also decreased the weight of the machine by a couple of ounces. Now... where to put the M.2 card. About the size of a stick of chewing gum, there was only one place it seemed to fit. Unfortunately, I didn't see a socket for it to plug into. I was stymied for some time until I found the screw provided to hold the SSD down and verified, with a small flashlight, that the surface mounted "chip" I thought was just that turned out to be a socket for the card edge of the SSD. Installation of that then took a minute, and I closed up the case. Seagate software mirrored the 1TB hard drive to the 1/2 TB SDD and I then removed the former. The machine booted up into Windows 10 the first time and all was fine. I was able to upgrade Windows 10 Home to Pro at no cost by updating 10 to the latest, applying Microsoft's generic key for Windows 10 (Google for it), letting Windows upgrade itself with the generic key, then activating Windows 10 Pro with a Windows 7 Pro product key. That took about an hour, including the Googling. There are two small issues with the machine. I called Samsung support, but they were not helpful (they did offer to have me send the machine in for service, something I don't feel was necessary). Issue one: Sometimes after the lid has been closed and is reopened and the machine wakes up, the mouse pointer is gone and the keyboard is turned off. No combination of putting the machine into and taking it out of tablet mode helps. Folding back and unfolding the keyboard doesn't help either. I have turned off the option to ask before entering tablet mode and set it to never enter tablet mode. We'll see if that helps. [Update: After a week, so far, so good.] Issue two: The keyboard backlight state (on or off) is controlled by the ambient light censor (a tiny hole in the case just above the F2 key). You can set the duration of the backlight and the intensity, but if the room is bright, the light will go off anyway. One of the reasons I returned the Dell was that the backlight shut off in 10 seconds. No matter what. A software upgrade was able to increase that duration to five minutes on the Dell. The Asus ZenBook Pro backlight turned off after one minute. I think backlights that turn off on their own are maddening. No MacBook Pro does this! I am hoping that some software update on the Samsung will keep the backlight lit no mater how long the keyboard remains untouched and no matter how bright the room is. Despite these two issues, I am very happy with the machine. It's on my desk at the office and let's me take care of non-work-related tasks while at work. It's small enough to fit on a shared desk with three other monitors, two phones and some other stuff. With the SSD, the machine is fast. All in all, it's a modern machine, with a very nice display, some features I don't need (tablet!), ample storage (500GB), and generous RAM (32GB). With the enhancements, the machine still came in at under a grand.

I would consider myself just a notch above a rank novice astronomer, but I do own 2 other telescopes, and this is by far the worst of the 3. I am giving it 2 stars, only because I feel 1 star is unfair due to the price you pay. It is a very inexpensive telescope. I, however, also own an equally inexpensive telescope that blows this one out of the water. The mount: This is called a German Equatorial Mount - and this one is light, flimsy and shakes the view uncontrollably if the slightest breeze blows. I am talking about a breeze so slight that your hair would barely move. That smallest of breezes will shake the view so violently that it will be virtually impossible to actually see what you are trying to view. The slow motion controls, which are designed to allow you to track the motion of objects in the sky, also make the mount shake uncontrollably. Oh yes, the screws that are supposed to hold the telescope steady once you have located the object you wish to view? Yeah, they don't do that. You can still move the scope around, even after tightening them completely down. The finder scope. This is a cheap, all plastic, almost completely useless piece of equipment. It shows everything to you upside down and backwards. Try spotting something in that and let the frustration begin. I immediately swapped it out with a 9 x 50 RACI (right angle, correct image) finder I had lying around. I simply could not take the frustration. The eyepieces and 3x Barlow lens. The 20mm and 4mm eyepieces are probably fine for inexpensive eyepieces. Much like any beginner telescope in this price range. No complaints with them. The 3x Barlow? No way, no how. This is as big a piece of cheap junk as the finder scope. Maybe bigger. It is ALL plastic, weighs about an ounce, and if you try to view anything through the included eyepieces magnified by this 3x barlow, you will be going backwards in image quality. The included EQ-1 motor may be a fine piece of equipment, but mine arrived in non-working condition, so I do not know. I honestly don't know that it would be able to help all that much with tracking anything, because the mount would still be shaking like mad. Forget about astrophotography unless you make some major modifications to the entire setup. The focuser is a very standard, inexpensive rack and pinion unit with no fine controls. Nothing spectacular, but it would do the job just fine IF THE MOUNT DIDN'T SHAKE UNCONTROLLABLY WHEN YOU FOCUS (are you beginning to see a pattern to this?). It is virtually impossible to get anything in focus, because it is shaking so bad that you can't actually see it. The telescope itself. The optics on this scope may be fine. Heck, for the price they may be spectacular, but I wouldn't know. The only thing I could actually see were the leave on the tree across from my house. I used that as a target to align my finder scope with the telescope this afternoon. Of course, that was indoors - with no breeze - and the legs on the tripod in the shortest position available which makes it far steadier. For the same money as this telescope, I also bought (last year) an Orion SkyScanner 100. It is a very simple reflector telescope on a small, tabletop Dobsonian mount. You can, if you happen to have one, attach it to a photo tripod so that you do not need to set it on a table. Far superior views, far less shaky, same basic focuser (but you can actually see to focus) and extremely easy to set up and use. My third scope, in case you were wondering, is a 6 inch, computerized, push-to Dobsonian scope. It does cost 4x what this scope did, but is immeasurably better. You do the math. ;-) For the record, tonight I was checking out Jupiter and M42, the Orion Nebula. Both amazing sites in any decent telescope. Not all that impressive in this one. You know, when I could even see them through the shaking eyepiece.....

Beautifully packaged. Beautifully designed. Beautiful Sound, but there are some negative issues. After two days: These are just "falling short" for me, I just ordered Sennheiser HD1 In-Ear Wireless Headphones to compare. After 1-day: The sound is noticeably beautiful and smooth, very pleasant, and not thankfully not scratchy sounding like the much of the cheap stuff. I think that most people will absolutely love the magically smooth sound. The audio-processing electronics are noticeably much-better than the cheap-stuff. But, there are some sound tonal inaccuracies that I think are because of "driver" (speaker) inaccuracies. I was hoping for audiophile-quality natural / flat-sounding drivers (speakers), but there is a bit of tonal inaccuracy that changes the sound of some non-electronic musical instruments in songs that I am familiar with. I would probably not notice except that I've gotten familiar with the sound of some music on high quality sound systems. This may be because of the limitations of Bluetooth technology, but I think the issue is with the speakers. I think I'll try Sennheiser Bluetooth to compare. Female vocals, and deep Country Music male vocals are absolutely beautiful and warm. Thin sounding male voices sound even more thin. Bass is nice and smooth, but in music with heavy-bass, vocals seem pushed into the background. Natural percussion instruments like a non-electronic snare drums, cymbals, and "fingers snapping" sound like they are electronic, thin, and un-natural. Acoustic guitar in some of the songs I've tried also sounds thin. The ones I received have an issue with occasional clicking sound that sounds like "cutting out", that sounds like loss of Bluetooth signal, even when my andoid phone is only 24 inches away. Though the design is beautiful in appearance, the piece that fits behind the neck falls down. The wires to the speakers are a bit too long, such that they can rub on my face a bit. Using these under a collared shirt would look great, and would also help control the long wire issue. If the battery is dead, they will not work while a charger is connected. I think most people will absolutely love the warm sound and beautiful design. I may be asking for more performance than this technology, in this price range can provide. I don't think this design will stay in place well with heavy physical movement.

Works but too many catches. So I assume people who are reading this review have a basic understanding how Garmin devices work. The Tempe from a hardware standpoint is great. Small foot print, easy to attach etc... Software is where things take a dramatic U turn. If your buying this your probably assuming this works as any sensor does once paired, provide a stream of continuous data of the metric you are trying to capture. The Temp does not do this. Data updates cycle once per minute. Doesn't seem like a big deal until you understand these bullet points. - Tempe doesn't remember last reading & data sync time up to 1 minute. - this is not a activity enabled sensor. That means you can't record temperature data from the Tempe! - if your using a Fenix like me you understand that once you started a gps activity you're looked into those screen sets. Customization give you two tempture options, min and max of the last 24hour period. So the watches internal temperature sensor is useless during a activity as well. This review just confirms what others have previously wrote. Tempe will be considered a failure to most people buying it.

The good: Its hardware based encoding design means that the conversion from analog video to mpeg2 is done inside a chip on the device, not by your computer's cpu. It also menas that while digitizing video it doesn't hog your PC's cpu nor does the resulting file need any post processing. The bad: the bundled Ulead editor is a big pain in the back end. If you just want to do quick edits and cut scenes out pretend that the included Ulead software is missing and install VideoReDo instead. ([...]) Install was flawless for me on WinXP home. The bundled video capture application on my CD was Capwiz version 3.1 dated February 2004. If you check the Adstech.com web site you can find Capwiz 3.5, which adds "on the fly" capture and burning to optical media, but I suggest everyone buying this device to stay with Capwiz 3.1. ADSTech technical support warned me in no uncertain terms back in Nov 5, 2004 that there were still "stability issues". "Note that many customers have reported stability problems with this version so if you have any problems with it we strongly recommend getting rid of it and going back to version 3.1". Version 3.1 of Capwiz, still offered on the site and I guess for a reason, seems to have everything a user might need, without "feature bloat" or "instability" warnings. Speaking of which, a new beta version of Capwiz 3.6 has been released in mid-December, adding yet more features to the mix like "direct capture into DivX" (mpeg4), but that sends cpu requirements through the roof and defeats the whole idea of a hardware based mpeg encoder because it's you cpu which has to then convert the mpeg2 video sent by the device to mpeg4, thus requiring a 2.4 Ghz. P4. In short: I've found the bundled VideoStudio 7 editing software to be a poor choice. The bundled Capwiz 3.1 is ok and you should use that to save digitized video to your hard drive. Then I suggest you check our VideoRedo for editing. I give this unit 4 stars. It delivers what it promises... decent quality hardware MPEG2 encoding for common people (people doing professional video work will surely need a higher-bitrate capture board). And it comes at a price that anyone can afford.

I am a long time trackball user, preferring finger operated trackballs to the thumb design. I have currently been using a Kensington Expert Trackball for about 8 years and it is a fantastic mouse. I have heard nothing but raving reviews from the owners of CST trackballs so I wanted to give it a shot. I have owned and tried just about every style of mouse/trackball current stock is the Kensington Expert trackball, Elecom EXG trackball (thumb), Logitech 502, WoW Joypen, Evolute Vertical Mouse, and the Adesso Vertical mouse. So back to the CST, which I will have to compare it to my Kensington Expert for this review. The trackball feels very solid and well built, the ball is just slightly bigger than the Expert but in normal use it is not noticeable. The ball rests on three rollers, as opposed to the bearings in the Expert. Granted my Expert is very well broken in, but the CST just fells a bit harder to move about. Had I no reference point I think this would be a non issue, and I expect the action to get smoother with use. The scroll knob is buttery smooth, its just not in a good position for me to easily reach without moving my hand from the buttons. In contrast the scroll ring on the Expert is no where as nice, though after removing the magnet, it is much much smoother, but most importantly it is right at my finger tips. The glowing ball is a nice touch, though if your looking to do the pool ball swap, the glow is useless. I did notice that the ball has one or two inconsistent areas on it, they are very small and hardly noticeable. Now for my biggest issue I have with the mouse the button clicking. When I use my Expert I keep almost all my hand off the mouse, it is the most comfortable position for me, and the placement of the buttons and their action on the Expert make click with my Thumb (left click) and Pinky (right click) very easy. On the CST the buttons hinge in the palm area. The switch is located on either side centered with the ball. While you are able to click on either the top or the bottom of the very large buttons, it is noticeably harder to quickly click/double click the bottom as compared to the top. If there was a way to swap the buttons so they pivoted from the top, it would be perfect, but there isn't. I am planning on keeping the mouse and rigging up the extra buttons and assigning them to left and right click then moving the current buttons to back and some other command. In summary, the CST Trackball is very nice excellent device. Personally for me it is going to take some getting used to before I feel comfortable enough to use it for anything other than standard web browsing / general computer use. I will keep my Kensington for gaming.

I don't normally leave reviews for products, but after trying out a few pairs, I felt compelled to write one for anyone trying to decide which pair they should get. I've tried a bunch of over-ear headphones with wireless capability, and the top three contenders are the Sennheiser Momentum 2.0 Wireless, Sony H.ear on wireless NC, and the V-Moda Crossfade Wireless. They are all in a similar price range, so here are my opinions regarding the build quality, design, sound, comfort and functionality. Build/Design/Comfort: The V-Moda's win in this category, feeling the most sturdy, They feel like you could drop them off of your roof and they'll still be intact. It comes with braided cords and a great case. Unfortunately, they do not fold up which can make portability a bit more difficult, but they more than make up for that fact with their durability. Plus out of the three, they are the best looking when you put them on. Their design is stylish and sleek without looking gigantic or weird. I was able to wear them for hours at a time without any complaints. For added comfort, you can get the XL pads which improve them comfort even further. The Sennheiser's are a close second. They are the lightest and definitely most comfortable, but the design is industrial looking, which may not be for everyone. I found them quite ugly to be honest. If you have a small head, the ends will stick out past the ear pads, making it just look weird. The cords attached to the headphones through the headband are also very noticeable and curl up, which makes their design look kind of messy. They do fold up though. Build quality is average. I tried the Sony's but found myself not being able to tolerate them for more than an hour, leaving my head and ears sore. They come in a chic array of bright colors and are definitely the most streamlined looking, with no loose cords visible. They also have the best controls, separate ones for volume and track control on the right side. The other two have only volume and a multi function button to rewind/skip tracks (double click to advance, triple click to advance). However, they feel somewhat cheap like they may break. And I did not like the bulky drive units, they stick out way too much to the side and look extremely weird. For a headphone that is as much as a fashion statement as it is for Hi-fi music, I found this a major drawback. V-Moda: 4.5/5 Sennheiser: 4.25/5 Sony: 4/5 Sound: I'm gonna keep this short because I am no audiophile and I think you probably won't go wrong with any of the three choices above. I use them for daily listening when traveling to and from work since I take public transportation V-moda: Has the loudest bass, but other sounds are still noticeable and appreciable. It doesn't drown out the rest of the song, but if you don't like bass then these are not the headphones for you. Does not offer any active noise cancellation (ANC), but has passive noise isolation that drowned out most ambient sounds, but still allows you to hear something loud/close by. Sennheiser: I thought these had the best sound (but not by much over the V-moda). Bass is there but not as loud as the V-moda, and the mids and highs are bright and clear. They give your music that special quality that really makes you want to listen to everything over again. Has ANC but isn't the best for that. You could also hear yourself walking which I did not like. Sony: These had the worst sound out of the three for me, but that doesn't mean they are bad. Bass was tight, treble was controlled but the mids seemed muffled to me. There were parts in songs that seemed muted compared to the other two. ANC was slightly better than the Sennheisers. Their price is high and I don't think it's worth $350 for the sound that you get. For all three wired was better than wireless, offering a fuller sound. I think this would be true of all headphones. You could listen to all of them in either mode if you prefer. I wouldn't get any of them for the noise cancellation because it's honestly not that great (I felt like I was able to hear the same amount of ambient sounds on all three). If that is your prime factor in deciding which pair you should get, then I recommend the Bose QC 35, which has amazing ANC but average sound. Sennheiser: 5/5 V-Moda: 4.75/5 Sony: 4.5/5 In the end, I chose the V-Moda because I liked the design much more than the other two. They just look sleek and fashionable, are not gigantic looking and sound is great. If you don't like loud bass then I would recommend the Sennheisers. If you are solely concerned with the look and colors, then try the Sony's. Plus they are cheaper (because there is no ANC). Minor gripes with the V-Moda that I can easily look past but may be annoying: In line control on wire does not offer volume controls When wired, if you have the headphones extended the wire may brush against you clothes causing a bit of a weird sound Do not fold up.

I bought this kit to replace my LifeShield system. When I ordered I got enough kit to replace sensor for sensor. All of the kit arrived and I started the process of setting it up. The base connected to my network without a hitch but I wasn't unable to get ANY of the other devices to connect to the base. I had keypads, contact sensors, motion sensors, water and fire sensors and NONE of them would connect. So I reached out to support via email. In hind sight I should have just called but I was hoping for a short, quick answer that would solve all of my problems. That didn't happen and I got pretty frustrated. After several hours over several days of finding other reports online and trying what they had tried I was ready to throw in the towel. Then Danielle contacted me. She put me in touch with Nick in tech support and he tried for over an hour with me to get something, anything to connect. He had me disconnect other stuff in my house that could be causing interference with no luck. Finally I gave up out of frustration. I really wanted this kit to work because I already have Ring cameras and wanted an all-in-one solution. I waited a couple of days for Danielle to get back to me. In the mean time I spent time here and there trying to see if I could get something to connect, but with no success. Until today. Today I literally shut off the power to every single thing in my house except for my internet connection gear and I started over. Base station came right up. Plugged in the keypad and it looked like it was going to fail like it always has, until it CONNECTED! Contact sensor? CONNECTED! Motion? Water? Fire? Other keypads? All CONNECTED! My existing alarm is from LifeShield. Turns out I had two repeaters I did not remember installing that were causing interference and preventing the sensors from communicating with the base. Once those were off I had no issues connecting up the rest of the kit. I still have not installed this as my active alarm but I will get that done soon. Bottom line is that my initial review and bad experience with this alarm were all caused by other kit in my house. The support I got from Ring, even when I wasn't kind, was great. For that they get 5 stars and I will come back and update this review once I have some experience with the system.

I retired an old netgear wnr3500L and replaced it with this router R6700 V3 as my main router. I have another netgear router set as a wired AP (6300 V2). First of all if you want to use Cisco anyconnect VPN over wifi, its not going to happen. There are many bad reviews regarding that issue alone. I've googled to the ends of the internet and have not found a solution. I've tried changing much of the settings including: MTU ,port forwarding, DMZ, QOS and more without luck. If anyone does figure out a solution please post a reply. The other issue I had was wifi handoff between the 6700 and my AP(6300). In particular my fire stick would constantly drop internet connection briefly ever 5-20 mins (also saw this on cell phones, certain rooms were worse than others). None of these issues happened with the old router and same AP. This is the first router I've owned in 20 years that hasn't been able to handle a very simple and standard home router setup. Unfortunately I threw out the packaging, wrongly assuming that I could fix the issues, otherwise I would be returning it. As a workaround, I swapped my routers yesterday and am using the 6300 as my main router and downgraded my new 6700 to be used as my access point at the other end of my house. I was able run anyconnect VPN for 8 hours without any dropouts(per log file) and the rest of my devices have had a solid connection as well. I had been a fan of netgear products, but their latest firmware releases seem to be problematic on several router models they sell. I will most likely choose a different manufacturer in the future.

Wonderful TV. The presence of this TV is really awesome in the living room. I actually love the speakers on this TV. I think they give the TV a bigger presence in the room, and just look great. The whole front of the TV is just pure black, so you don't really see where the screen ends and the frame begins, so the whole big frame looks like the TV. Really beautiful. Also, the little bit of wedge shape on the sides of the TV looks great. The sides are very mirror-like shiny graphite and look really nice. The picture quality of the screen is just mind blowing. The characters come to life and you see details that you have never noticed before. Just every small detail in the scenes becomes much more vivid and noticeable because you are able to see big and clear. I was a bit hesitant about getting such a big TV, but after having this, I think it enhances the viewing so much, that I think it is worth the splurge. It gives you that cinematic experience. Ultra HD content looks amazing on this, but even HD content looks pretty decent. I have found the Apps on the TV very useable and responsive. I use Amazon prime video and netflix and youtube, and all work flawlessly. Youtube actually has a nice feature, you can just click on the mike button on one of the remotes and it does a voice search. That makes searching so much painless and spontaneous. I also have the apple TV connected to it, and you can easily do airplay from your mac and the whole TV becomes your computer screen. Makes for fun browsing on your TV with your laptop just being used for keyboard and trackpad. With such a big screen, you actually see stuff like text better on the TV than on your tiny laptop. A little bit about my settings: I tried watching with picture mode set to standard which has brightness set to 30 by default. However, most of my viewing is in a well-lit room, specially during the day when I have windows right behind my back in front of the TV. I set the brightness to maximum and that just elevates the daytime watching experience so much more. Brightness of this TV is just backlight, so making it more doesn't change colours or anything, it's just how bright you want the screen (compare it to the screen brightness on your mac, for example). Also, the colours are set to neutral by default. i changed them to expert1, which I think make them much more natural. Neutral was a bit too blue in my opinion, but with colours set to expert1, that just makes the colours so natural. Also, I set the contrast to max (default setting on standard), and black enhance and adv. contrast enhance to medium (again, both are default to this on standard mode). I set auto dimming to high and extended dynamic range to high. With these settings for daytime watching, you just have to look at the picture to believe the quality. Everything comes alive. In Summary, this is a great TV that just gives you the best viewing experience available as of 2016. I doubt there is anything on the market today that will give you a better viewing experience by any meaningful margin. The TV just looks wonderful and it is an absolute attention grabber for any one who visits you. Update Settings (April 2016): After owning and playing with settings for a few weeks, this is my latest. I set black enhance and advance contrast enhance to off. I keep auto dimming to high. These radios do everything the manufacturer says they will. I have used quite a few different types of FRS/GMRS radios, and find that the performance of these is comparable to most. Of course, different brands and models or FRS radios are all over the place in terms of performance, so it's difficult to make a direct comparison. I have had better "sounding" radios, particularly Motorolas with their compander circuits (when you use them with other Motorolas). However, considering the processing that's going on to accomplish the channel hopping, I think these sound just fine. The audio sounds "processed", but there are no artifacts from the hops, and I am impressed by that. You'd think you'd hear clicking or something, but they have it figured out to where you don't. Besides, the TOTAL PRIVACY that these radios offer makes any slight compromise on the audio quality WELL worth it. Regarding the privacy, anyone who's used FRS/GMRS radios knows what kind of knuckleheads/children you'll encounter. It is SO nice to have a totally quiet channel until someone you know transmits, and also to know that no one is eavesdropping. I would think the latter would be particularly important if you have kids using them, or if you are using them for a business and need confidentiality and/or uninterrupted comms. And with FRS, if you were using CTCSS ("privacy codes"), you didn't know for sure if you were transmitting over someone else unless you monitored the channel first. XRS eliminates that problem too. Like FRS, the range of these radios is HIGHLY dependent on obstructions. Maybe even slightly more so with these due to the much higher frequency. I found that sometimes they didn't connect when I thought they would, and sometimes they'd connect when I didn't think they would. Pretty much par for the course. I still think they'd work fine for most typical applications that you'd use FRS for. The text messaging is kind of a novelty, as far as I'm concerned. There is no handshaking or acknowledgment, so if the message doesn't get through, you have no way of knowing from the transmitting end. Also, I have found that the signal quality has to be pretty good for the message to go through, so the range for text messaging is SIGNIFICANTLY shorter than for voice. This is not a dealbreaker for me. I'm not sure that it would cause me to buy the lesser model (TSX100) without the text messaging, because for just a few dollars more for the TSX300, you get quite a few more features (like 10-digit channel codes) The 10-digit channel code thing is kinda neat; if you have a large group of people, you can all just enter your phone number with area code, and you friends or co-workers don't have to memorize any new numbers. Also, the "call waiting" thing is quite cool. You can have a bunch of people talking on a shared group channel, and an individual can contact another individual on their private channel, and the radio will let you know there's a call coming in. The VALUE is incredible. Two radios of this caliber, with NiMH batteries, a drop-in charger, and two headsets for under $70, I feel like I got a really good deal. So far, I have found the battery life with the included NiMH packs to be quite good. Haven't really used them for a long time continuously yet though. I like that the drop-in charger runs on 12 vdc. A simple cigarette lighter adapter would allow you to charge these from your car during a road trip. Only one glitch so far, I have had a couple of instances where a call came in from a radio I knew was on my group channel, yet on the receiving radio the display said "Private Message Waiting" and asked for confirmation. Not sure what I might have done to cause that (if anything), but the radios recovered quickly. This also happened at extreme range, so maybe it was a temporary loss of sync or something. Again, not even close to being a dealbreaker, these radios are VERY cool. Kudos to the engineers at Tri-Square, I think they really did their homework!

If you see this TV at a great price, yes buy it, but read this review plus the negative reviews FIRST so you understand the quirks especially if you are coming from a Roku TV. This TV has to please several people with different wants and tastes. If you love quality sound for music, purchase a separate speaker system and use the optical for connection. If you are the only person using the TV or you are buying for public viewing for a lot of people, it’s okay. My situation is that it’s for a family of highly opinionated of adults. This TV’s life with us started out with “return it.” We’ve had the TV for a view months so I decided to write a detailed review to help the next buyer make a confident purchase. Had I understood these things I probably would have purchased a Roku TV because the family understands the Roku quirks whereas with this Google TV, the family has to learn the details of a Google ecosystem. There is a learning curve. Listen, if you want brighter colors or darker colors, take the time to make the adjustments using the supplied remote. If you want better sounding music, order a sound bar. If you want to learn more, keep reading. Like: - larger screen - like it a LOT. - some movies are 4K and can see the hairs on the actors scalp. - no streaming device needed to connect to streaming services - need TV remote and separate remote for cable tv - almost all-in-one - connected 15 minutes - just plug into electricity and connected to internet well. ————- Dislike: - Legs screw in at an angle making it time consuming work. Solution: Be calm and work as a team. There is no easy workaround. - Sound has zero base and treble is blunted and dull. Cellphone speaker is better than this TV. If you’ve listened to good music then hear it on Spotify or YouTube then you’ll know how terrible the TV sounds. Solution: bought a sound bar with woofer. - Google app slows down and stops working when a lot of Amazon Prime streaming is used in a day. TV has to be turned off several times to reboot. - one family member doesn’t like the 4K because “it feels like I’m behind the camera rather than in the audience.” On the other hand, our elder with poor near vision becomes totally immersed in shows like Air Disasters. We are long time Roku users and prefer the Roku interface experience. So we don’t know if it’s the 4K that we don’t like or we are watching non 4K or if it’s the TV itself, but some shows feel artificial - just strange. HD movies look great like at the movies. Our space is small so the 55 inch is an amazing size to see small details. When watching Scenic Relaxation on YouTube in 4K, the details were surprisingly immersive visually but missing the sound because the newly ordered sound bar has not yet arrived. The feeling is as if I am right there flying on the drone. When flying through the clouds, the clouds come right at me. That’s my point - the 4K feels like I’m behind the camera instead of sitting in the audience. Some people like the behind the camera feeling but I do not. I prefer the distance myself from the camera. Maybe 4K takes some adjustment. The new generation won’t know any other viewing experience. - Google knows too much. Zero privacy. Must admit that Roku has a simpler easier to use design. - Google AI makes makes irrelevant suggestions if someone else uses my profile to watch their shows. When I start at the Home page of the TV, I’m immediately presented with YouTube suggestions. For some people, that’s great news but for me it’s awkward especially if someone else uses my profile. Google judges by the profile. On a Roku TV every user starts out equal until they open an app. The Google Home Screen looks cluttered. If you have never used a Roku TV, then you won’t know the difference. One adult family member stated that if she had known the Home Screen would be dramatically different than Roku, and the TV was her purchase, she would have returned the TV. Wow. I was surprised. I would not return the TV for that reason, but some would. - Must purchase Amazon movies on my phone first before can watch on TV. This is the most awkward and annoying feature. Should you buy this TV? The answer depends on what features are important to you like what’s your budget? Consider paying for an extended warranty (we did not) and purchasing a sound bar with woofer. If sound becomes an issue due to hearing loss, we will purchase a portable speaker system for the hard of hearing to use with this TV also found on Amazon. The reality is that the adult kids all have their own TV systems that are quite fancy and high tech, so this low tech TV was a bit of a shock to them, but highly advanced for the parents. If this TV is a gift for someone, let the receiver decide if they like it and stop complaining. Purchase the warranty and send a gift receipt. Mom says if the recipient is happy, then you be happy too. We hope this review will help you as you decide which TV to purchase. For people who are easy to please, this TV is a good purchase. Mom says new tech always starts out very expensive. By the time people pay off the debt, the tech is old and something new appears and the cycle starts again. Mom says stay within your budget and invest in relationships with family not tech unless buying stock :-) If you can’t please everyone in the family with a purchase, oh well. Life will go on. There’s always something better over the horizon. Learn to stay within your budget and make things work. Mom says read the reviews including negative reviews. Negative reviews help you understand what you are buying when things go wrong so there are no surprises. Some negative reviews also provide solutions. Doesn’t mean don’t buy. Means buy with knowledge and confidence. Mom says a lot of stuff :-) Cheers y’all.

This mouse is extremely comfortable, the external materials are wonderful, excellent weight, long battery life, and good functionality. The options of using bluetooth or the Logitech receiver is awesome. There's one serious problem: THE SCROLL WHEEL HAS SERIOUS ISSUES. I've already had this replaced once, and after I return this second one I won't be purchasing another. The "ratchet" mode of the scroll wheel starts out very clicky and definite as it should, then slowly degrades over a period of 1-2 weeks (with my moderate usage) until it's pretty much indistinguishable from the freespin mode, which is also accompanied by heavy drifting. Why does this one problem give this product a one star review? Because for one, this severely inhibits the usefulness of this mouse, as scrolling is obviously a critical action most users will be using every few seconds during normal usage. The other is that Logitech refuses to acknowledge this problem despite heaps of reviews here and complaints on their forums asking for a solution. I seriously wonder if a lot of the single-sentence reviews on this Amazon page were paid for by Logitech to boost their sales. Making the situation even more frustrating is all the video reviewers/unboxers judging the product positively based only on their first impressions of it. If they actually used the product for more than a few hours, the scrolling problem would become much more apparent and maybe Logitech would stop ignoring it and actually pay attention to their users. As someone who relies on using the computer for their livelihood, the concept of the MX master is my dream, and I'd be willing to pay even twice as much as it costs now to just have it last a long time and be reliable. Sadly, it seems Logitech has gone the cheap route and are likely making a huge profit off this thing considering its MSRP of $99 and its actual street price of around $70 and marketing it as a serious professional mouse.

You almost have to cover your ears when you turn it up to 100%. I played with the Sony CT-100 and Sony CT-500 (might have missed a letter) and both of those sounded very weak compared to the Yamaha. The Polk bar I played with is okay, but expensive. My living room is 3-sided, and about 15 x 23. Once I started using the sound bar for more than a week, the results were night and day between my standard Samsung LN46A650 built-in speakers. The design of the sound bar is nice and simple. It has a glossy finish which sort of matches my TV. Also, the remote interacts with the sound bar and not the sub woofer unit. Some people like to try and hide the sub woofer, which you can't do with the Sony CT-100. The bad: If you want this sound bar thinking that it is going to create a "virtual surround" experience, then you'll be disappointed. I knew ahead of time that it wasn't going to be that amazing as far as virtual surround goes. Yamaha has fancier products that cost 2x-4x, which bounce sound off walls to create a more accurate virtual surround sound. The main sound bar came with a few mounting accessories, but not the screws that you'd need to hold it up against the wall. It should have been cheap enough for Yamaha to include. Summary: A sound bar that is able to produce far better sound than your TV and remain low-key in your home. It is easy to connect to and ultimately met my requirements: something affordable, simple, and able to really fill the room with theater-like volume.

I'm really happy with this little guy. It makes a nice second (or third) monitor without taking up space and being very easy to install. It was especially cool to have this as a second display on my laptop The beauty here is that you don't need to fiddle with extra video cards. You just plug it in via USB and you're set. I'm running Windows Vista on my desktop and laptop, and it installed without a hitch... although it was not immediate. Windows Vista found the driver online (automatically) so it took about 10 minutes before I was able to use it (yeesh). Still, not having to install anything from the disc was great, and the install process is painless. The device looks great on a desk. The stand is very stylish. The display is super sharp. 800x480 on something this small is quite a treat. I had to increase the font size of my IM client to be able to read it, but that was fine by me. It's a 7" diagonal, which is about 6" x 3½". With the base, it stands about 8½" tall and is about 4" deep. You can also remove the base, and mount it to just about any compatible frame or hold it in your palm I suppose. Video and graphics are very sharp, although I can't recommend this for high-quality video as the refresh rate (over USB) is just too slow. If you're watching YouTube it will be fine. Whoever designed the packaging definitely deserves a raise, while the person who wrote the included manual needs to be fired. The manual is ugly and full of translation errors, but really you won't need it. The built-in webcam works as well as any other webcam. I haven't tried the mic or headphone jack yet. Note that this model does not have built-in speakers. The device driver lets you easily rotate the display (and physically, you just turn it, the stand supports it just fine). The driver also lets you set the display to "Mirror" mode which mirrors your existing monitor (and changes its resolution to 800x480). There are three drawbacks: The device requires TWO USB ports to function. It's awesome that this doesn't need AC power, but be ready to give up two USB ports. If you want to use the microphone or headphone jack, you'll need to plug in two more cables -- one for the mic and another for headphones. The data is NOT carried over USB as I would have imagined. I think this is pretty lousy but perhaps there's a good reason. The driver installed two extra processes that must run for the display to work, called DisplayLinkManager.exe and DisplayLinkUI.exe. Together, these take 24 MB of RAM. In my book, that's acceptable. Whatever that software is doing should be off-loaded onto the hardware.

TL; DR: Pros: -Good color accuracy -Good peak brightness -Genuine 4K 60Hz IPS panel performance -Can be connected and powered with only 1 cable -Glossy screen -Built-in speakers Cons: -Unclear generic branding -Requires some manual tuning to get the best out of it (settings see below) -The cables that come free within the box are quite flimsy and not high quality (but works) -Cannot remember screen brightness after powered off -Bought 2 from different vendors, one of which got artifacting lines within the 1st day of use. Had to return. -HDR support is a mess I have the 4K version of the display. First, this is not "Corkea" brand stuff. It has a blue startup logo screen of "Magedok", whose official website is so incomplete that you cannot find any sensible information on it. In fact, it even doesn't have my particular model listed. What's even weirder is in NVIDIA control panel the display is identified as "Stargate Technology/AT&T HCDZ". In fact, I got 2 same model displays from different vendors and both devices shows up having serial number "demoset-1". Also the AIDA64 software recognizes neither panel model nor panel manufacturer. So yes this is a pretty "Generic plug-and-play display" as Windows Device Manager says. It possibly uses some generic driver PCB and OEM laptop display panels. Not that this display is trash though: It is indeed a 4K display with an IPS panel judging from its color and viewing angle. The color accuracy is surprisingly good after some manual tuning. In fact, its color accuracy is comparable to that of my XPS15 laptop! Touch input also works, no drivers needed. Peak brightness is also pretty high, no problem using it under sunlight. Though some people might not like the glossy screen on the 4K model - I personally prefer glossy screen over the matte screen on the 1080P model. Additionally, it is possible to drive this display with 1 USB Type C cable. I'm using a NVIDIA 20 series card and the Type C connector has no problem powering up and providing signal to this monitor. Even more surprisingly, this display is G-Sync compatible! This display also have a lot of small issues when I first got it. One of the 2 I bought works fine. However another one failed on the day arrived and had a lot of random green horizontal lines over it - even at boot screen. Also, this display does not remember its brightness settings after powered off - you have to manually dial back to the brightness you need after each powering on, which is quite annoying. The cables come in the box does work, however the connectors are not very robust and I highly recommend to get another USB Type C cable that supports display signal to get it work. Sometimes the display doesn't turn on even after plugging in and you need to re-plug the display multiple times to actually firmly connect the cables. Also sometimes it is a graphics card drivers issue. The HDR support is unusable and I don't recommend turning on either in Windows or in the display OSD menu, but frankly few monitors on the market has true HDR support (most HDR displays are not really capable of HDR - such as display HDR 400 standard is pointless and not much better than any generic display). So, after a lot of trial and error, here's what I think the best settings for this display: Color Temp: USER and R, G, B all to 50 Brightness: DCR On (this overrides brightness settings and defaults to max brightness on my end) Misc: OD On, Low blue light 0 Windows HDR support: off NVIDIA control panel: Video Color settings - Color- brightness - 60%

After quite a bit of research on various types of netbooks, I went with the Toshiba NB305. After 2 weeks of use I'm very happy with it. The most striking feature of the netbook is the chiclet keyboard. It's fantastic, and much more comfortable than keyboards I've tried on other netbooks. The touch pad is also excellent. It is quite large for a netbook and has some nice multi-touch features. This netbook is extremely lightweight and the battery life is as advertised. For normal usage such as web surfing, listening to music, and word processing, I get 8-10 hours of battery life. Toshiba software makes it easy to alter the power settings, depending on whether you want max battery life or increased processor performance. The design of this laptop is very appealing. I bought the white version and it looks very nice, mildly contrasting against the matte silver keyboard and stainless strip covering the hinge. Also I very much appreciate that all the surfaces on this laptop are matte, rather than glossy. It keeps it looking nice and clean as opposed to smudgy from fingerprints. My one gripe about this computer is that it comes with Windows 7 "Starter." What a crappy operating system. Among (many) other limitations, it restricts the number of applications you can run concurrently and simple features such as changing the background art are unavailable in the starter version. So basically you need to upgrade as soon as you get this computer. That makes the cost of this laptop $500, including the cost of upgrading to usable version of Windows 7. Personally, I would have preferred a full version of Windows XP as in the Toshiba NB205. Operating system aside, this is an excellent netbook and I would strongly recommend it over the Asus Eee PC 1005HA or Acer 532H netbooks.

I doubt that I will ever find anything actually useful to do with these, but they have been quite interesting to play around with. I've gotten some striking, and unexpected results. This product Ion Audio Cassette Adapter is what I've been looking for. I do not have a CD player or a radio with an Aux in port. So in order to play my tunes I was either needing to use an FM transmitter or a cassette adapter. The FM transmitter option didn't pan out for me as the radio frequencies in this area are very crowded and the few stations the transmitter is capable of using are already used. In fact there are not any stations that are free. Lets add to that, the quality of the signal was not that great with white noise or the music cutting in and out. So the next option was a cassette adapter. I tried a few of the inexpensive options and no luck. either poor materials were used or the head did not align up properly. You also had the unsightly cord hanging out of your cars dash. So I find this product and give it a try. At first the adapter would only work on the flip side and the Auto reverse wheel (in the picture attached) was the culprit. After opening the adapter up and removing it (being careful to ensure the other gears were still properly aligned) and putting the whole thing back together it works like a charm. Pros - Great sound - No cords other than when you have to charge - Includes a mic for hands free use (I have not used or tested) - Works with any cassette player - Auto shut off (can be bypassed if desired) Cons - You cannot use and charge at the same time - 2 hour battery is good for daily driving but poor for long trips - Some players will try to auto fast forward when there is no music playing (which stops the cassette from playing and activating the auto off feature) - Some modification is required for proper use in some players with auto reverse.

First, some info. The peddles are "wired" to produce A, B & C as though typed from a keyboard. I have no idea if the included software actually allows you to do anything useful in terms of re-mapping the pedals to other keystrokes or not, as I never installed it. I already had a copy of Controller Mate (I'm on a Mac) in use, so I simply added this device to it, which worked great. Unfortunately, my problems started almost immediately. Almost immediately after beginning to use the product, the centre peddle began to "stick", locking in the triggered position, even though the physical peddle itself would return to the resting (up) position just fine. I took the peddle apart (carefully), I was pleased to discover that rather then cheap mechanical switches, they had built the system using an LED and a solid state light sensor. A plastic tab on the foot peddle breaks the light beam to trigger the "switch". A large spring ensures a solid return. While the system is almost entirely plastic, and there is no feedback in the peddle of triggering the "switch" with no moving parts, or contacts to wear out, this seemed a surprisingly solid design for a cheap product. Unfortunately, my delight was short lived. A little diagnostics showed that one side of this duo was not working, as triggering the switch would leave it locked in the "on" position until a small flashlight was shone on the receiving side, at which point it would promptly shut off. As this was still cheap, even for a double peddle, I continued to use it. The very next time I attempted to use the unit, another peddle developed the exact same behaviour. I wrote the company for return authorization, and they promptly refunded my money without any hassle. So, the company did right by me, but the product was significantly less reliable then the design would otherwise indicate. I suppose that this is probably just a case of bad components, and I give it 2 stars based on the design (which should be good), but I can't rate it higher in good conscious since it didn't really work. Another unit, from a different batch of components might be just fine, but I haven't bothered to take a chance on ordering another.

I wake up multiple times in the night. I have also found that meditation helps get me to sleep. If my wife is snoring when I wake up, it can be tough to get back to sleep. So part of the reason I wanted this is to help with this issue. I also have had a difficult time getting to sleep anywhere but my home. I used to be able to sleep anywhere. Not any more. So when I travel and backpack it’s always a struggle to get a good nights sleep. I was really hoping that the hoomband would be the solution. From a physical standpoint, the hoomband seems pretty decent. Lightweight and made of comfortable materials, it seems to have a decent build quality. However, it’s just too dam small. I know I have a big head. I bought the M/L and it still squeezes my head. It’s starting to stretch out after a week, but it’s still too tight. I think they should have three sizes, not two. A true large would be a better idea. I also have a gripe about the speaker placement. I can’t get the speaker to cover my ears properly. The interior band hold the speakers and the Bluetooth module doesn’t get big enough. Yes I have a large head. I shouldn’t have to contemplate cutting the interior band and sewing and extra piece of fabric to make it fit properly. If I want to place the speakers properly over my ears, the headband covers my eyes. I don’t need a sleep mask/headphone combo. I just need sleep headphones. For me, the biggest selling point of the hoomband is it’s app. It makes a lot of promises about content, being able to repeat tracks, set timers, etc. The only thing that is worthwhile is the content. I do like it. The rest of the app is a hot mess. Want to put an ambiance on repeat? Doesn’t work. Even if you download the content. Wanna add stuff to a queue? Nothing to indicate that the icon you touch adds things to the queue. It just changes color. No pop up or modal to say “added to queue”. The only icon that works is the play/pause button. The only reason that works is because you can hear the track starting. Help documentation is either non-existent or doesn’t provide any real help. The interface has no text, tool tips, modals or anything that describes what the function is. Just a bunch of icons that change color when you touch them and no confirmation dialog. I could deal with the lack of functional indicators if the ones they had ACTUALLY WORKED. My biggest gripe is that the repeat function has NEVER worked in an entire week of trying. Here is what happens. I set a repeat timer for six hours. I usually wake up and hit the head at least once in six hours. I can then skip forward to the next track, which also goes for six hours. What actually happens is the track stops after it finishes and the app is frozen for the rest of the time. So now I have to fiddle around with the app and my phone trying to get it working again. Nothing like trying to figure out why your SLEEP AID isn’t working while you are trying to sleep. If the app quality is like this, I am beginning to wonder if the hardware is going to last. My suggestion is that the company cut the price in half and publish a Spotify playlist with their content. At least I know that the Spotify repeat function works.

This is like the holy grail of travel backpacks! I travel a lot, and always take only a carry on if I can. I have tried now probably 5+ different travel backpacks and I am officially in love with this one! There is always some major issue to make me try another bag, but this one is comfortable to wear, has a large main compartment, fits more than you'd expect and opens up fully like a suitcase. I was thinking about getting an Osprey far point 40L for a while, but didn't want to make the leap and spend that much, because I spent a ton not too long ago on a cotopaxi bag and didn't love it. So this was a similar alternative and I think its actually better than the osprey just from checking it out in stores and people's reviews on it! Reasons why: it still has the 40L main compartment that opens the same way, BUT the laptop pocket is located near your back rather than in the front of the bag (better for weight distribution and you don't have to worry about you laptop flapping over when you open the bag), and the mesh water bottle holder can actually hold a water bottle, and after taking this out on travel, I did not have to worry about it falling out of there, and finally I just like the look of this bag better. It looks very clean and professional, which is perfect when I have to travel for work and want to look like less of a backpacker. And for the price it is well worth it, bc trust me, I have spent a LOT on travel bags in my search for the perfect one. The only downside I can see, is if you absolutely must have a bag with a hip strap, bc it doesn't have one. I have had bags with and without the hip band, and while it does add to carrying comfort if you will be wearing it a long time, I felt like this bag was incredibly comfortable to wear on my back for quite a bit of time even with no hip strap. Oh! and as a bonus, its got a hidden pocket on the back, perfect for your passport and boarding pass and two tiny little pockets on the shoulder straps where you can hide some cash for if you need to pay for a taxi or something right out of the airport. It appears to be constructed very well, I can't speak as to long term durability, since I've only had it a few weeks, but it seems like its well built, not like a cheaply made bag from China. I would recommend this bag to anyone who is looking for a travel backpack!

UPDATE: I recently wrote a 1 Star review where I noted that after several frustrating hours of trying to install this Startech Print Server (SPS), I finally gave up. However, while waiting for a return authorization, I started researching comparable units from other companies and quickly discovered that they are apparently all hard to install and many have other issues that make them less desirable than the Startech. So, I decided to try the install again, and this time I finally succeeded. The hardest part of my install was getting the SPS to connect wirelessly to my router. I will cut to the chase and tell you that the easy way to do this is to push the WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) button on your router, then push the small black WPS button on the front of the SPS, wait a few minutes while the lights blink and “VOILA!!!” your SPS will be wirelessly connected to your network router. This simple procedure, which isn’t mentioned anywhere in the Startech instruction manual or on their support website, could have saved me hours of frustration trying to make this connection with both the supplied software and the instructions on the Startech support website. I discovered it purely by accident. Hopefully, your router has a WPS button (most modern routers do) and this will work for you. If not, please know that the installation manual and software provided with the SPS unit are beyond useless. I wouldn’t even bother installing the software, it is a waste of time and disk space. In fact, by searching the Startech support website, I learned that some of the information in the paper manual, such as the reset procedure, is WRONG. If you don’t have a WPS button on your router, my best advice is to go to the Startech website, click on the “support” tab and go to the support page for model PM1115UW. Scroll down to the FAQ section and follow the instructions for your computer operating system. Good luck! You can confirm that the SPS is wirelessly connected to your router by “pinging” the SPS from your computer. To “ping” the SPS, press the “Windows key + R”. this will bring up a black and white command box. Type cmd and press Enter. Then type ping followed by one space and the IP address listed on the bottom of your SPS. For example, type ping 198.162.0.10. If the ping is successful, you should get a response from the same IP number that you entered. If you get a response from any other IP you are NOT communicating with the SPS. In my case, I initially could successfully ping the SPS if it was hard wired to my computer with an Ethernet cable, but not wirelessly. However, after the WPS procedure, I could successfully ping the SPS wirelessly. Once the SPS is wirelessly connected to your router (ping is successful), the final step is to install the printer on your computer. This process is also a bit involved. There are instructions on the Startech support website, but they are not easy to find, so I will repeat them for you here. 1. Press the “Windows” key and select “Settings” (the gear-like icon on the lower left of your screen). 2. Click “Devices>Printers and Scanners>Add a Printer”. 3. Windows will now search for available printers but won’t find your SPS. 4. Click “The printer I want isn’t listed” after it appears. 5. Select “Add a local printer or network printer with manual settings” > Next. 6. Select “Create a new port” and change the “Type of port” to a “Standard TCP/IP Port” > Next. 7. In the “Hostname or IP address” box, type in the IP address of the SPS (it is on the bottom of the unit, the default IP is 198.162.0.10) > Next. 8. Click “Custom>Settings>LPR”. Under “LPR Settings” enter a “Queue Name”. This is whatever name you want to identify the printer connected to your SPS, and it can be any set of letters and/or numbers. It is the name that will later appear in your list of available printers. Click “OK” > Next. 9. Select the best available driver for the printer connected to your SPS. You may need to click the Windows refresh to get a more complete list of printers (it takes several minutes to do the refresh). If you can’t find your exact printer, choose the closest available match. 10. Keep clicking Next until you are asked to send a test page to the printer to confirm that the printer was successfully added. Hopefully, that page will print, and from then on, your printer will show up on your computer in the list of available printers. You will probably need to repeat this “add a printer” process once on each computer that you want to access the SPS. I truly hope that this help others avoid the issues I had installing the Startech Print server. You might also be able to get help from the tech support people at Startech, but they were closed while I was going through all of this, so I can’t speak to how helpful they might be. I have now raised my rating to 2 Stars because, once installed, the SPS is working fine. However, the install was far more painful than it needed to be. Original Review I seldom write reviews, but I need to add to the warnings of others about this product. I should have heeded the warnings already posted by others. The installation of this print server is an absolute nightmare. I am not a tech genius, but I have successfully built my own computers and troubleshot computers for years, and I can normally solve a computer problem without too much hassle. But, after wasting several hours trying to get this unit to connect to my laptop or to my network it completely stopped showing up at all, and I just gave up and will hopefully send it back. Looking more closely at other reviews, including one by an experience network tech warning about a very difficult install, I should have heeded those warnings. The manual and installer software are totally useless and the unit seems to be incompatible with many modern routers, apparently including my century link router. I would strongly encourage you to look elsewhere for a better solution. I am awaiting a response from the seller about returning this useless POS.

So, this is a very nice hard shell for the 2018 and 2019 models of the MacBook Air. I ordered the "Clear Frost" or whatever they are calling it and its a very pleasant color that is translucent enough to let the Macbook's design features, logos and color be shown off. I've previously had the "crystal clear" hard shell. I think this matte frosted on is a better choice because it seems less fragile and more pliable. The crystal one, seemingly by the nature of the material seems to need to be that more rigid stuff so it can have its gloss and mine lasted less than 2 weeks before developing stress cracks in the corners and then having the mounting tabs start to splinter off. I'm not as thrilled with Ibenzer themselves. This was bought directly from the manufacturer. Firstly, they played the old shipping game. They clearly couldn't deliver the product within the timeframe promised, even with Amazon's current extended delivery windows (why exactly am I still being charged for Prime?). So to prevent cancellation, they created a shipping label on Saturday, and didn't actually deliver the product to UPS until Thursday. its a common tactic in e-commerce, one I personally detest, and it makes me question the business ethics of the vendor. Speaking more to that. This cover is described in the listing as being compatible with the 2020 MacBook Air. But in reality it isn't. It's a misleading statement and practically all the vendors on Amazon are doing the same thing. This was made for the 2018-19 MacBook Air. The 2020 model, while apparently identical to those, in fact isn't. Having received the scissor keyboard upgrade it is about 0.5mm thicker on the bottom. The top shell fits perfectly. On the bottom, that tiny difference keeps the bottom shell from being able to snap on successfully on both sides. Again, business ethics. The case does stay on, with a friction fit, and it does function as protection, so I"m going to keep it until an actual 2020 version is produced. Right now, nobody seems to have a 2020 version of a hard shell. Even InCase, Apple's in-house case company seems to have been caught flatfooted. Either everyone expected the 2020 model to be exactly identical or the Coronavirus caused manufacturing snags, I don't know, but I'm too fastidious about new tech to not have a perfect fit. it just bothers me. First maker to have an actual case for this model will get my business.

This product was a total disappointment. I live in the North East and have a hard time waking up in the winter time when it's really dark out, so I was looking forward to simulating a small sunrise in my bedroom to help my body wake up naturally. There are a few things wrong with the design of this clock: 1) After 30 mins of the light getting progressively lighter so that you can wake up, the clock starts beeping in a very obnoxious tone. It's very similar to the noise that a regular red LED clock from the dollar store makes. Basically, if you don't manage to wake up in 30 minutes you get the "rude awakening" experience. 2) The clock is very lightweight, so if you push any button (like trying to turn the obnoxious alarm off) you push it off the nightstand. It's basically a two-handed operation, so you better be very coordinated early in the morning if you are trying to push any buttons. 3) All the buttons on the front are the same size. You have to remember where they are oriented in space on the front of the clock to determine which one to push. However, at this point the clock is probably already on the floor because you have frantically been trying to turn off the obnoxious alarm noise... This seems like extra work when I'm sleepy. Some pros: 1) I think the concept overall is great, and I wish they had executed it better. Maybe I shouldn't have skimped and gotten the $120 version. 2) The brightness of the red LED time can be dimmed so that the numbers are not too bright at night (I really like that feature, but during the day they are barely visible and the clock becomes useless) Overall, this product did not work out for me. Mainly I found that when I'm sleepy, my body turns away from the light to catch some more Zzzs and then I get the obnoxious alarm to start blaring. When I did use the clock, it would usually end up on the floor because of the silly button design. Instead, I've been using the Sleepcycle app on my iPhone, which wakes you up when you are in your lightest sleep phase. It was free and has a selection of really nice wake up alarm sounds. I wish I could get my money back for the clock :(

Got the Deco X95 (AX7800) to replace an Amplifi Alien mesh setup that had started frequently rebooting. So far, Im really happy. Im not a home networking expert, but Im also not a novice - somewhere inbetween. Ive set up many of these in the past (from Orbi to Eero and Amplifi), and use some of the customization features. Setup was simple. Took me less than 5 minutes to have the entire mesh network set up. Every device connected (except one, Sonos), and I have about 60 devices in the house including all the IoT stuff. The app was easy to use and pointed me in the right direction, step by step. After a full week, I have had zero devices drop or have connection issue in a 4k sqft house. Stability is probably the #1 requirement for me, both my wife and I work from home. As mentioned, Sonos didnt work within the 1st hour I had set up the Deco. Sonos is notoriously bad with mesh networks, which is unfortunate because I love their products otherwise. I fiddled with some security settings (set it to WPA2/WPA3), rebooted my sonos devices...and decided to work on it the next day. Im not sure if it was the security setting or the reboot - but miraculously the next day all of my sonos devices appeared on the network map and were working (I have 8 of them). So, I know it can be frustrating, but I at least wanted to share one experience of sonos working with Deco, since I saw a few comments about it in other reviews. Edit 2/15/23: Just wanted to share that this has been 100% rock solid and stable for a month now. Very happy with performance, range, stability. Even though the unit is not as fancy as my Amplifi Alien, it was an upgrade in performance and range which matters more than the cool on screen display the Alien had.

I had a strange issue with my Xfinity service where I use TIVO and cable card. On certain HD channels I would see pixelation and channel degradation to the point where it was un-watchable. I thought it was my TIVO Bolt or even the cable card which Xfinity provides but since the signal problem only affected specific channels I determined this had to be the incoming signal. So, as a last resort before calling Xfinity (ugh) I decided to try this amplifier and install where it comes into my house. I also bought new 6 foot coax cables and some 75ohm terminators to cap off any unused ports around the house as well as on this amplifier. If you don't cap the empty ports off they can act as an antenna and could result in more noise on the channels or even a visit from Comcast due to excessive broadcasts into the air. FCC requires Comcast and others to prevent this as it could interfere with other users systems. I figured for a few bucks I would just purchase a pack of 5 terminators and cap off the unused ports and avoid any issues plus do the job correctly. They simply screw on to the coax port....nothing complicated. I removed my existing splitter and installed this amplifier (which is also a splitter), a couple of terminators for unused ports and connected the incoming Comcast cable and the power adapter. This amplifier DOES REQUIRE an OUTLET nearby as it is powered to help deal with less than ideal incoming signals from Comcast (or whatever service you have). I've seen a lot of posts about this issue from many people using various services so this is NOT just a comcast issue. Keep in mind, this will boost the INCOMING SIGNAL to compensate for signal loss but it CANNOT FIX AN ALREADY BAD INCOMING SIGNAL. It will simply boost whatever is coming into your house. If the signal is low or poor for other reasons like bad cabling from their incoming box to your house then this likely won't do much other than boost a bad signal. For our issue, it was specific HD channels during evening hours when usage was likely higher on Comcast's systems and there was no indication the signal coming into our house was bad across the board. Only for a handful of channels. I don't know if Comcast can do anything about specific channel's signals or not but I didn't want to deal with them if I could avoid it as involving them is always a headache and they rarely make anything better and often create other problems in my experience. They always want to blame our cabling or router or whatever and I can do the same things their technicians would do in order to troubleshoot issues. In this case, I seem to have found the solution thanks to other postings so I wanted to detail my issue too. Ideally, it would be nice if customers could call Comcast and get them to fix it but in many posts I've seen their solution is to do exactly the same thing...install this amplifier, terminators, etc. to resolve the issues for customers. Clearly, they want to avoid having to run NEW OUTSIDE CABLING and digging up a yard and so on and I am sure most customers don't want that either unless the cabling is found to be truly bad, broken, cut, etc. Then it is worth it but for this random pixelation issue on only certain HD channels at certain times of the day this seems to resolve it. So far we have not seen any additional pixelation issues on the problem channels and our HD channels are as clear as ever. Again, buy this amplifier, a 5 or 10 pack of 75 ohms terminators to cap any unused ports in your house (i.e. where cable ports are in your rooms) as well as on the amplifier itself and make sure you have an outlet nearby to power the amplifier. The best location is where it comes into the house. Good luck!
